а.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic а, from Proto-Slavic *a ('and, whereas, but'), traced to a Proto-Indo-European pronominal ablative particle *h₁ōd ('from that, on the other hand'; compare Lithuanian õ 'and, whereas' and Sanskrit āt 'then, and').

history.meaning: from that, on the other hand

а.notes: Unlike и (which simply adds items together) and но (which states a direct contradiction), а contrasts two parallel facts or shifts the topic ('and as for...', 'whereas').

абонемент.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French abonnement ('subscription, season ticket'), derived from abonner ('to subscribe, fix a limit or fee', from Old French bone 'boundary marker, limit').

абонент.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from German Abonnent ('subscriber, pass holder'), remodeled with the Latinate agent ending -ent from French abonné (past participle of abonner 'to subscribe').

абрикос.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century from Dutch abrikoos (plural abrikozen) or German Aprikose, via French abricot and Spanish albaricoque from Arabic الْبَرْقُوق (al-barqūq, 'plums, apricots'), itself via Byzantine Greek πραικόκιον from Latin (persica) praecocia ('early-ripening [peaches]').

абсолютно.etymology: Adverb formed from абсолютный ('absolute, complete'), borrowed via German absolut or French absolu from Latin absolūtus ('freed, unrestricted, complete, unconditional'), the past participle of absolvere ('to loosen from, set free, complete').

абсолютный.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century via German absolut and French absolu from Latin absolūtus ('loosened from restriction, complete, unconditional, absolute'), past participle of absolvere ('to set free, complete', from ab- 'from' + solvere 'to loosen').

абстрактный.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German abstrakt or Polish abstrakcyjny from Late Latin abstractus ('drawn away, detached from concrete reality'), the past participle of abstrahere ('to drag away, detach'). The Latin verb combines ab- ('away from') with trahere ('to draw, pull', from PIE *tragh-), adapted with the productive Russian adjectival suffix -ный. It is a direct cognate of English abstract and tractor.

history.meaning: to draw away → detached from concrete matter

аванс.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century from French avance ('advance payment; lead, step forward'), deverbal noun from avancer ('to move forward, advance'), from Vulgar Latin *abantiāre (from Late Latin abante 'in front, before', whence French avant).

history.meaning: in front → to advance → advance payment
advance payment (on wages or a contract)

авантюра.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Aventure / French aventure (and Polish awantura) from French aventure ('adventure, risky enterprise'), from Vulgar Latin *adventūra ('that which is about to happen', from Latin advenīre 'to arrive, happen').

history.meaning: thing about to happen, chance event

авария.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (originally in maritime law as 'damage to a ship or cargo at sea') via Italian avaria, French avarie, or German Havarie, all from Arabic 'awāriyya ('damaged merchandise'), from 'awār ('defect, damage'). In 20th-century Russian the word broadened to any utility breakdown, pipe burst, or road accident.

автобус.etymology: Borrowed in the early twentieth century via French autobus / German Autobus, a blend of авто- ('automobile', from Ancient Greek αὐτός 'self') + -бус (clipped from омнибус, from Latin omnibus 'for all', dative plural of omnis).

автограф.etymology: Borrowed via French autographe / German Autograph and Late Latin autographum from Ancient Greek αὐτόγραφον (autógraphon 'written with one's own hand, original manuscript'), from αὐτός ('self') + γράφω ('to write').

автомобиль.etymology: Borrowed at the end of the 19th century from French automobile ('self-propelled vehicle'), a hybrid classical compound coined in France from Ancient Greek αὐτός (autós, 'self') + Latin mōbilis ('movable', from movēre 'to move').

автор.etymology: Borrowed via Polish autor and Byzantine/Medieval Latin pronunciation (where Latin au before a consonant was read av- under Greek influence) from Latin auctor ('originator, creator, author'), an agent noun from augeō ('to increase, originate, promote').

авторитет.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from German Autorität ('authority, prestige, influential expert'), from Latin auctoritas ('authority, prestige, influence', derived from auctor 'originator, promoter').

авторский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ский from автор ('author, creator'), borrowed via Polish autor from Latin auctor ('originator, promoter, author', from augere 'to increase, originate').

ага.etymology: Conversational interjection shared across East and West Slavic (Ukrainian ага [aha], Polish aha, Czech aha) and German aha, expressing recognition ('aha! so that's it!') or casual affirmative agreement ('uh-huh, yeah'). In southern Russian and Ukrainian-influenced speech the middle г was traditionally pronounced as a voiced pharyngeal/glottal fricative [ɦ].

агар-агар.etymology: Borrowed via European scientific vocabulary from Malay agar-agar ('red algae Gelidium/Gracilaria and the gelatinous substance extracted from it').

агент.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Agent and Polish agent (or French agent) from Renaissance Italian agente and Medieval Latin agēns (genitive agentis, 'one who acts, representative'), present participle of Latin agere ('to drive, do, act').

агентство.etymology: Formed in Russian from агент ('agent, representative', borrowed via German Agent / French agent from Latin agens, present participle of agere 'to act, do, drive') + the institutional noun suffix -ство.

агрессивный.etymology: Borrowed from French agressif / German aggressiv + Russian suffix -ный, derived from Medieval Latin aggressivus, from Latin aggredi (past participle aggressus 'to approach, attack, assail', from ad- + gradi 'to step, walk').

ад.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic адъ ('hell, underworld'), borrowed from Ancient Greek ᾍδης / Ἅιδης (Háidēs 'Hades, god of the underworld; the netherworld').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: ад

адвокат.etymology: Borrowed under Peter the Great (early 18th century) via German Advokat and Polish adwokat from Latin advocātus ('one called to aid a party in court, legal witness or counsel'), past participle of advocāre ('to summon, call to one's aid', from ad- 'to' + vocāre 'to call', from vōx 'voice').

history.meaning: to call to one's aid → legal counsel

адвокатский.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ский from адвокат ('lawyer, defense attorney'), borrowed under Peter the Great via German Advokat and Polish adwokat from Latin advocātus ('one summoned to give legal counsel', from advocāre 'to call to one's aid').

адекватный.etymology: Borrowed via German adäquat or French adéquat from Latin adaequatus ('made equal to, matched, commensurate'), past participle of adaequare (from ad- 'to' + aequus 'equal').

администратор.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Administrator (or French administrateur) from Latin administrātor ('manager, steward, director'), derived from administrāre ('to manage, attend to, serve'), built on ad- + ministrāre ('to serve, attend', from minister).
администратор.notes: In Russian hotels, restaurants, and salons, **администратор** is the standard word for the front-desk receptionist or floor manager.

администрация.etymology: Borrowed via Polish administracja or German Administration from Latin administratio ('management, direction, government'), derived from administrare ('to manage, assist, direct', from ad- + ministrare 'to serve').

адреналин.etymology: Borrowed from international scientific Latin adrenalinum / English adrenaline (coined in 1901 by Jokichi Takamine for the hormone isolated from the adrenal glands), formed from Latin ad ('near, at') + renes ('kidneys', i.e. suprarenal/adrenal gland) + chemical suffix -in.

адрес.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French adresse ('direction of a letter, street address', originally 'straightening, directing toward') or German Adresse, from Old French adrecier ('to direct straight toward'), from Vulgar Latin *addīrectiāre (built on Latin dīrēctus 'straight, direct').

history.meaning: direction on a letter, street address

аж.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic аже ('even, up to, so that'), formed from the conjunction/particle а + the emphatic enclitic particle же (Proto-Slavic *a + *že).

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: аж

азартный.etymology: Derived from азарт ('gambling fervor, excitement, passion'), borrowed in the eighteenth century from French hasard ('dice game, game of chance, risk'), ultimately via Spanish azar from Arabic الزَّهْر (az-zahr 'playing die').

азот.etymology: Borrowed from French azote (coined in 1787 by Antoine Lavoisier and colleagues because pure nitrogen gas cannot sustain living creatures), from Ancient Greek ἄζωτος (ázōtos 'lifeless'), formed from privative ἀ- ('without') + ζωή ('life').

history.meaning: without life, unable to sustain life

ай.etymology: Primary expressive interjection of sudden pain, fright, or surprise, inherited from Proto-Slavic *aj (and paralleled across Indo-European and other languages, compare German ei, French aïe, Sanskrit ē).

айфон.etymology: Borrowed in 2007 from English iPhone, the smartphone brand introduced by Apple Inc., coined from the prefix i- (originally standing for 'internet, individual, instruct, inform, inspire' in the 1998 iMac) + phone (short for telephone, from Ancient Greek φωνή 'voice, sound').

академия.etymology: Borrowed via Polish akademia and Latin Academia from Ancient Greek Ἀκαδήμεια (Akadḗmeia, the olive grove near Athens sacred to the hero Akademos where Plato taught philosophy).

аквапарк.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from international/English aquapark, combining Latin aqua ('water') + park ('recreational park').

акварель.etymology: Borrowed from French aquarelle, from Italian acquerella ('watercolour'), a diminutive built on acqua 'water', from Latin aqua.
акварель.notes: In Russian акварель names both the paint medium (писать акварелью 'to paint in watercolour') and a finished watercolour picture.

акварельный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from акварель ('watercolour'), borrowed via French aquarelle from Italian acquerella (diminutive built on Latin aqua 'water').

аквариум.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century via English/German Aquarium from Latin aquarium ('watering place, water tank'), neuter substantive of aquarius ('relating to water', from aqua 'water').

акклиматизация.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French acclimatation / German Akklimatisation ('adaptation to a new climate or environment'), formed from the Latin prefix ad- ('to') + French climat ('climate', from Ancient Greek κλίμα klíma 'inclination of the earth toward the sun, latitude, climate') + -isation / -ация.

аккорд.etymology: Borrowed from French accord (and Italian accordo), from Vulgar Latin *accordare 'to bring into harmony, tune together', built on Latin ad- 'to' + cor 'heart'.

аккуратненько.etymology: Affectionate diminutive adverb formed with the suffix -енько from аккуратно ('neatly, carefully'), derived from аккуратный (borrowed in the Petrine era via German akkurat from Latin accuratus 'prepared with care', from ad- + curare 'to take care').

аккуратно.etymology: Adverb of аккуратный ('neat, tidy, careful, punctual'), borrowed in the Petrine era via German akkurat (or Polish akuratny) from Latin accūrātus ('done with care, exact, careful'), past participle of accūrāre ('to take care of, attend to carefully': ad- + cūra 'care').
аккуратно.notes: Unlike English *accurate* ('correct'), Russian **аккуратный / аккуратно** emphasizes neatness, tidiness, and gentle care (*неси аккуратно* 'carry it carefully').

аккуратный.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via German akkurat (or Polish akuratny) from Latin accūrātus ('done with care, exact, careful'), the past participle of accūrāre ('to take care of', from ad- + cūra 'care') + Russian adjectival suffix -ный.

акт.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Akt / Polish akt from Latin actus ('action, deed, stage act') and actum ('official document, record'), derived from agere ('to do, act, perform').

активированный.etymology: Past passive participle and adjective of активировать ('to activate'), borrowed via German aktivieren from French activer, built on Latin āctīvus ('active', from agere 'to act, do'). Most familiar in Russian in the pharmacy term активированный уголь ('activated charcoal').

активистка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the feminine person suffix -ка from активист ('activist'), derived in the early 20th century from актив / активный ('the active core of an organization / active'), from Latin āctīvus ('active').

активно.etymology: Adverb formed from активный ('active'), borrowed via German aktiv / French actif from Latin activus ('active, practical', from agere 'to act, do').

актриса.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French actrice ('actress'), feminine of acteur ('actor'), from Latin āctrīx / āctor ('doer, stage performer', from agere 'to act, perform').

актёр.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French acteur ('stage actor'), from Latin āctor ('doer, orator, dramatic performer'), agent noun from agere ('to drive, do, act on stage').

акула.etymology: Borrowed via northern Russian Pomor fishermen on the White and Barents Seas from Sami akkula / akkli, itself borrowed from Old Norse hákarl ('Greenland shark', a compound of hár 'shark, dogfish' + karl 'man, fellow').

акустика.etymology: Borrowed as a scientific and musical term via French acoustique or German Akustik from Ancient Greek ἀκουστικός ('relating to hearing'), derived from ἀκούω ('to hear').

акцент.etymology: Borrowed via German Akzent or Polish akcent from Latin accentus ('stress, tone, intonation'), a morphological calque of Ancient Greek προσῳδία formed from ad- ('to') + cantus ('song, chant', from canere 'to sing').

акция.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (originally in the financial sense 'joint-stock share' via Dutch actie / German Aktie, and later in the general sense 'public campaign, action') from Latin actio ('action, legal claim, right to a share of dividends', from agere 'to act, do').

алгебра.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Algebra and Polish algebra from Medieval Latin algebra, from Arabic al-jabr (الجبر, 'restoration, reunion of broken parts; completion of equations'), taken from the title of the 9th-century treatise *Kitāb al-mukhtaṣar fī ḥisāb al-jabr wa-l-muqābala* by the mathematician al-Khwārizmī.

алиби.etymology: Borrowed via French/German legal usage from the Latin adverb alibi ('elsewhere, at another place'), old locative form of alius ('other').

history.meaning: alibi (proof of being elsewhere during a crime)

алкаш.etymology: Colloquial and derogatory Russian noun formed by truncating алкоголик ('alcoholic') to its initial stem алк- and adding the expressive colloquial person suffix -аш.

алкоголик.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via German Alkoholiker and French alcoolique from алкоголь ('alcohol'), which entered European languages via Medieval Latin alcohol from Arabic al-kuḥl (الكحل, 'kohl, finely powdered antimony; later any distilled essence or spirit').

алкоголь.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Alkohol or French alcool from Medieval Latin alcohol, originally borrowed from Arabic الْكُحْل (al-kuḥl, 'finely powdered antimony/kohl eye cosmetic obtained by sublimation'). Renaissance alchemists (notably Paracelsus) extended alcohol from 'any fine sublimated powder' to 'distilled spirit of wine' (alcohol vini).

history.meaning: sublimated essence → distilled spirit of wine

аллергия.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from German Allergie, coined in 1906 by the Viennese pediatrician Clemens von Pirquet from Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, 'other, different') + ἔργον (érgon, 'work, reaction'), literally 'altered reactivity' of the immune system.

алло.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th century via French allô from English hallo / hello, the telephone greeting popularized by Thomas Edison in 1877 (originally an attention-calling shout of huntsmen and ferrymen).

алмаз.etymology: Attested in Old East Slavic since the fifteenth century (in Afanasy Nikitin's journey); borrowed via Turkic almaz / almas and Arabic أَلْمَاس (ʾalmās) from Ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adámas 'unconquerable, hardest steel, diamond', from privative ἀ- + δαμάω 'to tame, subdue' — the same Greek source as European diamond).

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: алмаз

аль.etymology: In culinary phrases such as аль денте ('al dente'), borrowed from the Italian contracted preposition al ('to the', from Latin ad illum); as a colloquial Russian conjunction ('or'), shortened from али (< а + ли).

амбициозный.etymology: Borrowed via French ambitieux / German ambitiös from Latin ambitiosus ('eager for public office or favor, ambitious'), derived from ambitio ('going around to canvass for votes, ambition', from ambire 'to go around').

амбиция.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish ambicja from Latin ambitiō ('going around to canvass for votes; striving for honour or favour, ambition'), derived from ambīre ('to go around', from ambi- 'around' + īre 'to go').

history.meaning: canvassing for office; desire for honour, ambition

американец.etymology: Formed in Russian from Америка ('America', named in 1507 after the Italian navigator Amerigo Vespucci) + the ethnonym suffix -анец.

американо.etymology: Borrowed in the late twentieth century from Italian (caffè) americano ('American-style coffee', espresso diluted with hot water to approximate American drip coffee).

амнезия.etymology: Borrowed from New Latin amnesia, from Ancient Greek ἀμνησία (amnēsía 'forgetfulness, oblivion'), formed from privative ἀ- ('without, not') + μνῆσις ('remembrance, memory', related to μιμνήσκω 'to remember').

аморальный.etymology: Formed with the Greek privative prefix а- ('without, non-') + моральный ('moral', from Latin moralis 'pertaining to morals or customs', from mos, moris 'custom, character').

ампула.etymology: Borrowed from Latin ampulla ('small two-handled globular flask or vial for oil or medicine'), a diminutive of amphora ('two-handled jar', from Ancient Greek ἀμφορεύς).

анализ.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French analyse and German Analyse from Medieval Latin analysis, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλυσις (análysis, 'an unloosing, resolving a whole into its parts'), from ἀναλύω (analýō, 'to unloose, undo'). In everyday Russian, анализ (plural анализы) is also the standard word for a medical laboratory test (blood test, etc.).

ананас.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via German Ananas / French ananas and Portuguese ananás from Old Tupi naná ('pineapple', literally 'excellent/fragrant fruit').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: ананас

ангел.etymology: Borrowed into Old East Slavic ангелъ via Old Church Slavonic ангелъ from Byzantine and Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos, 'messenger, envoy; messenger of God, angel', translating Biblical Hebrew mal'ākh 'messenger').

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

английский.etymology: Relational adjective formed from Англия ('England', from Medieval Latin Anglia, the land of the Germanic Angles / Anglii) + the adjectival suffix -ский.

аневризма.etymology: Borrowed in medical terminology via New Latin aneurysma from Ancient Greek ἀνεύρυσμα (aneúrysma, 'a widening, dilation of an artery'), from ἀνευρύνω (aneurýnō, 'to widen, dilate', from ἀνά 'up, throughout' + εὐρύς 'wide').

анекдот.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from French anecdote ('unpublished historical detail; short witty story'), from Ancient Greek ἀνέκδοτα (anékdota 'things unpublished', title of Procopius's Secret History, from privative ἀν- + ἔκδοτος 'given out, published').

history.meaning: curious historical incident, short witty tale

анкета.etymology: Borrowed in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century from French enquête ('inquiry, investigation, survey'), from Old French enqueste, from Vulgar Latin *inquaesita (from Latin inquirere 'to inquire into, investigate').

анклав.etymology: Borrowed from French enclave ('territory completely surrounded by another state'), derived from enclaver ('to enclose, lock in'), from Vulgar Latin *inclavare (from in- + clavis 'key').

history.meaning: to lock in with a key

анна.etymology: Borrowed via Byzantine Greek Ἄννα (Ánna) from Biblical Hebrew חַנָּה (Ḥannā), meaning 'grace, favour' (from the Semitic root ḥ-n-n 'to show favour, be gracious').

аннулировать.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German annullieren (and Polish anulować) from Late Latin annullāre ('to bring to nothing, annul'), built from Latin ad- ('to') + nullus ('none, nothing').

анонсировать.etymology: Borrowed via German annoncieren from French annoncer ('to announce, advertise beforehand'), from Latin annūntiāre ('to bring news, announce', from ad- 'to' + nūntius 'messenger').

антибиотик.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-twentieth century from English antibiotic (coined in its modern medical sense in 1941 by Selman Waksman from French antibiotique), formed from Ancient Greek ἀντί ('against') + βιωτικός ('pertaining to life', from βίος 'life').

антиквариат.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from German Antiquariat ('antiquarian bookshop or trade in antiques'), derived from Latin antiquarius ('relating to antiquity, student/dealer of ancient things', from antiquus 'ancient, old').

антрекот.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French entrecôte ('cut of beef taken from between the ribs'), compounded from entre ('between', Latin inter) + côte ('rib', Latin costa).

history.meaning: meat cut from between the ribs

аншлаг.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from theatrical German Anschlag ('placard or notice posted at the box office announcing that all tickets are sold out'), derived from anschlagen ('to nail up, post a notice').

апартаменты.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via French appartement / German Appartement from Italian appartamento ('suite of rooms set apart'), derived from appartare ('to separate, set apart', from a parte 'aside, apart').

апельсин.etymology: Borrowed from Dutch appelsien, itself modelled on French pomme de Sine, literally 'apple from China', reflecting the sweet orange's trade route from East Asia to northern Europe.
апельсин.notes: Compare персик ('peach', originally 'Persian fruit') for another Russian fruit name preserving an old geographic origin.

апельсиновый.etymology: Formed in Russian with the relational suffix -овый from апельсин ('sweet orange'), which was borrowed in the Petrine era from Dutch appelsien (literally 'Chinese apple', calqued from French pomme de Sine, because sweet oranges were brought to Europe from China by Portuguese and Dutch traders).

history.meaning: orange (made of or flavoured with oranges)

аперитив.etymology: Borrowed from French apéritif ('alcoholic drink served before a meal to stimulate the appetite'), from Medieval Latin aperitīvus ('opening'), derived from Latin aperīre ('to open').

аплодировать.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German applaudieren and French applaudir from Latin applaudere ('to clap the hands in approval', from ad- 'to, at' + plaudere 'to clap, strike').

аплодисменты.etymology: Plural-only noun borrowed in the 18th–19th century from French applaudissements (plural of applaudissement, 'clapping, applause'), derived from applaudir ('to applaud', from Latin applaudere).

аппарат.etymology: Borrowed via German Apparat from Latin apparatus ('preparation, equipment, instruments, gear'), derived from apparare ('to prepare, make ready', from ad- + parare).

аппаратура.etymology: Formed from аппарат ('apparatus, device', from German Apparat < Latin apparatus 'equipment, preparation', from apparare 'to prepare, equip') + the collective Latinate suffix -ура (compare German Apparatur).

аппендицит.etymology: Borrowed at the end of the 19th century from international medical New Latin appendicītis (coined in 1886 by American physician Reginald H. Fitz), from Latin appendix (stem appendic-, 'vermiform appendix, appendage', from appendere 'to hang upon') + the Greek-derived medical suffix -ītis ('inflammation', Russian -ит).

аппетит.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via French appétit or German Appetit from Latin appetītus ('longing, desire, appetite for food'), derived from appetere ('to strive after, desire eagerly', from ad- + petere 'to seek, aim at').
аппетит.notes: Used in the standard mealtime wish **Приятного аппетита!** ('Bon appétit! / Enjoy your meal!').

аппетитно.etymology: Adverb formed from аппетитный ('appetizing'), derived from аппетит ('appetite'), borrowed via German Appetit or French appétit from Latin appetītus ('longing, desire, appetite', from appetere 'to strive after').

аппетитный.etymology: Formed in Russian with the adjective suffix -ный from аппетит ('appetite', borrowed in the early 18th century via German Appetit and French appétit from Latin appetītus 'desire, longing for food', from appetere 'to strive after, desire').

аптека.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th–17th centuries via Polish apteka (and Middle High German apotēke) from Medieval Latin apothēca ('storehouse, wine cellar, apothecary's shop') and Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη ('storehouse, repository', from ἀποτίθημι 'to put away for storage' — the same Greek word that separately gave French boutique).

аптекарь.etymology: Entered Russian in the 16th–17th centuries via Polish aptekarz and Middle High German apotheker from Medieval Latin apothecarius ('storekeeper, apothecary'). That noun derives from Ancient Greek apotheke ('storehouse, repository'), built from apo- ('away') and tithenai ('to put, place', from PIE *dheh1- 'to put, do'). It shares its Greek source directly with English apothecary and boutique.

cognates.meaning: small shop (from the same Greek word)

аптечка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from аптека ('pharmacy, apothecary shop', borrowed via Polish apteka and Medieval Latin apotheca from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη 'storehouse, repository').

арбуз.etymology: Borrowed via Kipchak/Tatar qarpyz / xarbuza from Persian خربزه (xarboza / xarbūza 'melon, watermelon'), literally 'donkey-cucumber' (from xar 'donkey', used as an augmentative prefix for large size, + būza 'cucumber, gourd').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: арбуз

арена.etymology: Borrowed from Latin harena / arena ('sand; sand-strewn central floor of a Roman amphitheater where gladiators fought').

аренда.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century via Polish arenda ('lease of land or property') from Medieval Latin arrenda / arrendāre ('to rent out, lease at a fixed return', compare Spanish arrendar and French arrenter), built on Latin ad- + reddita / *rendita ('return, revenue, rent', from reddere 'to give back, yield').

арест.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via German Arrest and Polish areszt from Medieval Latin arrestum ('seizure, detention by order of a court'), from Vulgar Latin *arrestāre ('to cause to stop, detain', from ad- 'to' + restāre 'to remain, stand back', whence also French arrêt).

арестовать.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via Polish aresztować and German arretieren / arrestieren from Medieval Latin arrestāre ('to stop, detain by legal authority'), formed in Russian with the verbal suffix -овать on арест ('arrest').

арестовывать.etymology: Imperfective of арестовать ('to arrest'), borrowed in the Petrine era via German arretieren and Polish aresztować from Medieval Latin arrestāre ('to cause to stop, detain in custody', from ad- 'to' + restāre 'to stay back, remain').

арка.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via Italian arca / arco, German Arke, or Polish arka from Latin arcus ('bow, vault, arch'). In Russian city architecture (especially in St Petersburg), арка often refers to the vaulted carriageway passage leading from the street into an inner courtyard (двор).

армейский.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian from армия ('army', borrowed in the Petrine era via German Armee / Polish armia from French armée, from Latin armata 'armed force') + suffix -ский.

армия.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Armee and Polish armia from French armée ('armed force, army'), substantivized feminine past participle of armer ('to arm'), from Medieval Latin armāta ('armed force', from Latin arma 'weapons, arms').

аромат.etymology: Borrowed (first via Old Church Slavonic ароматъ in liturgical use, and later reinforced by French aromate and German Aromat) from Latin arōma (stem arōmat-), from Ancient Greek ἄρωμα, ἀρώματος (árōma, 'sweet herb, spice, fragrant smell').

арочный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from арка ('arch', inserting a fleeting о and palatalizing к → ч before -н-), borrowed via Polish arka / German Arche or Italian arca from Latin arcus ('bow, arch').

morphemes.meaning: arch (арка, with fleeting о and к → ч)

арт-директор.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English art director ('head of artistic design or creative events', from art + director).

артист.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th centuries from French artiste ('artist, stage performer'), from Medieval Latin artista ('master of the liberal arts, craftsman'), derived from Latin ars, artis ('art, skill').

артистка.etymology: Feminine personal noun formed with the suffix -ка from артист ('performer, actor, artist', borrowed in the nineteenth century from French artiste, from Medieval Latin artista, derived from Latin ars, artis 'art, skill').

архив.etymology: Borrowed under Peter the Great (early 18th century, originally feminine архива) via German Archiv and French archives from Late Latin archīum / archīvum ('public records office'), from Ancient Greek ἀρχεῖον (arkheîon, 'town hall, magistrate's residence where public records were kept'), derived from ἀρχή (arkhḗ, 'beginning, rule, magistracy').

архивный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from архив ('archive'), borrowed via German Archiv / French archives from Late Latin archivum and Ancient Greek ἀρχεῖον (arkheîon, 'town hall, repository of public records', from ἀρχή 'magistracy, beginning').

архитектор.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Architekt / Polish architekt (reshaped in Russian with the agent ending -ор after Latin architectus / -tor nouns) from Latin architectus and Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων ('master builder, chief craftsman'), a compound of ἀρχι- ('chief, master') + τέκτων ('carpenter, builder').

аспирин.etymology: Borrowed from German Aspirin (coined in 1899 as a trademark by Bayer AG for acetylsalicylic acid), formed from a- (for Acetyl 'acetyl') + -spir- (from Spirsäure 'salicylic acid', named after the meadowsweet plant Spiraea ulmaria) + chemical suffix -in.

асфальт.etymology: Borrowed via German Asphalt / French asphalte and Late Latin asphaltum from Ancient Greek ἄσφαλτος (ásphaltos 'bitumen, mineral pitch used to bind masonry').

атмосфера.etymology: Borrowed via German Atmosphäre or French atmosphère from New Latin atmosphaera, coined in the 17th century from Ancient Greek ἀτμός (atmós, 'vapor, steam') + σφαῖρα (sphaîra, 'sphere, globe').

history.meaning: sphere of vapor surrounding a planet

аттестация.etymology: Borrowed via Polish atestacja or French attestation from Late Latin attestatio ('testimony, certification'), derived from Latin attestari ('to bear witness to, attest', from ad- + testari 'to witness', from testis 'witness').

аудитория.etymology: Borrowed via Polish audytorium and German Auditorium from Latin auditorium ('lecture room, place for hearing, assembled listeners'). The Latin noun is formed from audire ('to hear, listen', from PIE *h2ew-is-dh- 'to perceive sharply with the ears') plus the instrumental/locative suffix -torium. It is a direct cognate of English auditorium, audience, and audio.

history.meaning: to hear → lecture hall, assembly of listeners

аукцион.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Auktion / Dutch auctie from Latin auctio ('increase, public sale by increasing bids'), derived from augere ('to increase, augment').

афера.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French affaire ('business matter, transaction, affair', univerbated from Old French à faire 'to be done'). In Russian the word specialized pejoratively to mean 'a speculative, fraudulent business venture, swindle, scam'.
афера.notes: Spelled and pronounced in standard Russian with е (афéра), not ё.

аферист.etymology: Derived in Russian from афера ('shady deal, swindle', borrowed from French affaire 'business, affair, scheme', from à faire 'to do') + the personal agent suffix -ист.

аферистка.etymology: Feminine form of аферист ('swindler, con artist', from афера 'scam' < French affaire) formed with the feminine suffix -ка.

афишировать.etymology: Derived from афиша ('playbill, poster', borrowed from French affiche, from afficher 'to post up, display publicly') + the verbal suffix -ировать.

ах.etymology: Expressive interjection inherited across Slavic and reinforced in 18th-century literary usage by German ach!, voicing a sudden intake or release of breath at surprise, admiration, delight, or regret.

history.meaning: exclamation of surprise, delight, or dismay: 'ah!, oh!'

аэродром.etymology: Borrowed in the early twentieth century from French aérodrome (coined in the 1890s), compounded from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr 'air') + δρόμος (drómos 'racecourse, running track').

аэропорт.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century from French aéroport (and English airport), combining classical aero- (from Ancient Greek ἀήρ aḗr 'air') + port (from Latin portus 'harbour, port').
аэропорт.notes: Takes the locative ending -у after в/на: в аэропорту ('at the airport').

баба.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic баба ('grandmother, old woman, midwife'), from Proto-Slavic *baba, an ancient nursery reduplication (*ba-ba) found across all Slavic languages.

бабка.etymology: Formed with the suffix -ка from баба ('grandmother, old woman', inherited from Old East Slavic баба, Proto-Slavic *baba). In the plural slang sense бабки ('money, cash'), it arose either from knucklebones (бабки) used as stakes in traditional games or from 18th–19th-century Imperial banknotes bearing the portrait of Empress Catherine II ('Grandma').

history.meaning: grandma, old woman; (pl. бабки) money, cash

бабник.etymology: Colloquial Russian noun formed from баба ('woman, peasant woman', Proto-Slavic *baba) + the personal suffix -ник, designating a man fond of chasing women.

бабочка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -очка from баба / бабка ('grandmother, ancestral spirit'); in Slavic folk belief, moths and butterflies were viewed as the embodied souls of female ancestors (hence also meaning 'bow tie' and in slang 'ночная бабочка' = night butterfly).

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: бабочка

бабуля.etymology: Affectionate hypocoristic form of баба / бабушка ('grandmother, old woman', from Proto-Slavic *baba, nursery Lallwort) formed with the affectionate suffix -уля.

бабушка.etymology: Formed in East Slavic as the affectionate diminutive in -ушка of баба ('grandmother, married peasant woman, old woman'), from Proto-Slavic *baba ('grandmother, old woman'), a nursery kinship word built on infant syllable reduplication (*ba-ba).
бабушка.notes: Stress always stays on the first syllable: **бабушка**.

багажник.etymology: Formed in Russian with the container/compartment suffix -ник from багаж ('luggage, baggage'), borrowed in the 18th–19th century from French bagage ('luggage', from Old French bague 'bundle, pack').

багет.etymology: Borrowed from French baguette ('long thin loaf of bread; carved picture-frame molding; wand'), from Italian bacchetta ('little rod, wand'), diminutive of bacchio < Latin baculum ('staff, stick').

history.meaning: wand, frame molding, long French loaf

багор.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic багъръ ('boat hook, gaff, pike pole'), from Proto-Slavic *bagъrъ, related by Vasmer to Old High German bāgan ('to contend, fight') or Germanic terms for a curved hook or grapnel.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: багор

база.etymology: Borrowed via French base and German Basis from Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis, 'stepping, pedestal, foundation, base'), derived from βαίνω (baínō, 'to step, walk'). In modern usage база also serves as a colloquial shortening of база данных ('database').

базилик.etymology: Borrowed via French basilic / German Basilikum and Latin basilicum from Ancient Greek βασιλικόν (basilikón, literally 'royal [herb]'), neuter of βασιλικός ('royal, kingly'), from βασιλεύς (basileús, 'king').

бай.etymology: In colloquial exclamations of surprise (ой бай!), borrowed from Turkic bay ('rich man, lord, master'; compare Kazakh and Tatar бай), where Ой, бай! is a ubiquitous Central Asian and Volga exclamation ('Oh my!'). Also coincides with the native lullaby refrain баю-бай (from баять 'to speak, chant', Proto-Slavic *bajati) and casual English bye.

байк.etymology: Borrowed in the late twentieth century from English bike (colloquial shortening of bicycle or motorbike).

байкер.etymology: Borrowed in the late twentieth century from American English biker ('motorcyclist, member of a motorcycle club'), derived from bike + agent suffix -er.

бак.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine maritime era from Dutch bak ('wooden bowl, trough, cistern, forecastle of a ship') and French bac ('vat, trough, ferry').

балаган.etymology: Borrowed via Turkic balaqan / balaxana from Persian بالاخانه (bālā-xāna 'upper room, balcony, wooden pavilion'), which in Russian came to denote a temporary wooden fairground booth for theatrical farces, and figuratively 'rowdy farce, circus'.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: балаган

баланс.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from French balance ('pair of scales, equilibrium, accounting balance sheet'), from Vulgar Latin *bilancia, from Late Latin bilanx ('having two scale-pans', from bis 'twice' + lanx 'plate, scale-pan').

балбес.etymology: Colloquial word attested since the 18th–19th centuries; most commonly traced by Vasmer and other linguists to Turkic bilmez ('ignoramus, one who knows nothing', negative participle of bil- 'to know'; compare Kazakh/Tatar bilmes), or connected with dialectal балбешка ('wooden block').

history.meaning: one who does not know, ignoramus

балда.etymology: Attested in Russian first in the sense 'heavy wooden mallet, knobbed club, sledgehammer' (likely borrowed from Turkic balda / balta 'axe, heavy club, pommel') and transferred metaphorically to a 'thick-headed person, blockhead, dummy'.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: балда

балерина.etymology: Borrowed from Italian ballerina ('female ballet dancer'), feminine of ballerino ('dancer'), derived from ballare ('to dance', from Late Latin ballare).

балет.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from French ballet, from Italian balletto ('theatrical dance'), diminutive of ballo ('dance', from ballare 'to dance', Late Latin ballare < Ancient Greek βαλλίζω 'to dance, jump about').

балка.etymology: Borrowed via Polish belka / balka from Middle High German balke (modern German Balken, 'wooden beam, rafter, joist'), continuing Proto-Germanic *balkô (cognate with English balk and balcony).

балкон.etymology: Borrowed via French balcon from Italian balcone 'balcony, gallery', built on a Germanic word for a wooden beam or scaffold (*balko, akin to English balk and Russian балка 'beam').

балл.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from French balle ('small ball, ballot ball'), used in voting and academic grading where white or black balls were dropped into an urn to score candidates; hence 'grade mark, score point, wind/earthquake force level'.

history.meaning: point, mark, score (in grading or competitions)

баловать.etymology: Inherited East Slavic verb (compare Ukrainian балувати 'to spoil, pamper'). Vasmer notes that its ultimate origin is uncertain: scholars have connected it either with Old Church Slavonic балии ('healer, charmer', from *bajati 'to speak, charm') or with an expressive Proto-Slavic stem *bal- denoting carefree play and chatter.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: баловать

баловаться.etymology: Reflexive of баловать ('to spoil, indulge, frolic'), inherited from East Slavic (compare Old Church Slavonic балии 'healer, enchanter', баяти 'to speak, charm, tell tales'), originally 'to chatter idly, indulge, play around'.

history.meaning: to mess around, play about; to treat oneself to

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: баловать

бальзамический.etymology: Derived from бальзам ('balsam, aromatic resin or balm', via German Balsam and Latin balsamum from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον, of Semitic origin) + the adjectival suffix -ический (in culinary usage translating Italian aceto balsamico 'balsamic vinegar').

бамбук.etymology: Borrowed via German Bambus and French bambou (or Dutch bamboes) from 16th-century Portuguese bambu / mambu, which Portuguese traders in India adopted from Malay mambu or Kannada bambu.

бампер.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English bumper ('impact-absorbing bar at the front or rear of an automobile'), derived from the verb bump.

банан.etymology: Borrowed via French banane (or German Banane) from Portuguese banana, itself borrowed in the 16th century from a West African language (most likely Wolof banaana).

бандерлог.etymology: Borrowed from Rudyard Kipling's *The Jungle Book* (1894), where Bandar-log is the name of the chattering, lawless monkey tribe, compounded from Hindi बंदर (bandar, 'monkey') + लोग (log, 'people, folk'). Popularized in Russian through translations and the classic Soviet animated *Mowgli* films.

бандит.etymology: Borrowed via German Bandit or French bandit from Italian bandito ('outlaw, proscribed brigand'), substantivized past participle of bandire ('to banish, outlaw, proclaim under a ban', of Germanic *bannjan origin).

бандитский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ский from бандит ('bandit, gangster'), borrowed via German Bandit / French bandit from Italian bandito ('proclaimed outlaw, brigand', past participle of bandire 'to banish, outlaw').

банк.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via German Bank (or French banque) from Italian banca / banco ('moneychanger's bench or counter table'), itself an early borrowing from Lombardic/Germanic *banki ('bench'). When a medieval Italian banker failed, his bench was broken (banca rotta, whence банкрот 'bankrupt').

history.meaning: moneychanger's table or bench → financial bank
bank (financial institution; pot in card games)

rootFamily.gloss: banquet (from the same Italian root banco 'bench')

банка.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century via Polish banka / bańka ('globular vessel, jar, cupping glass') from Medieval Latin bancia / *banca or related Romance/Germanic vessel terms. In Russian it became the standard word for a glass jar (*стеклянная банка*) or metal tin/can (*жестяная банка*).
банка.notes: Genitive plural inserts a fleeting -о-: *пять банок* ('five jars/cans').

банкет.etymology: Borrowed in the late 17th or early 18th century via German Bankett (and Polish bankiet) from French banquet ('feast, ceremonial dinner'), itself borrowed from Italian banchetto, a diminutive of banco ('bench, table'), originally referring to a light meal or snack eaten on a bench before coming to mean a grand formal dinner.

rootFamily.gloss: bank (from the same Italian root banco 'bench')

банкетный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from банкет ('banquet, formal feast'), borrowed in the Petrine era via German Bankett / French banquet from Italian banchetto (diminutive of banco 'bench, table').

банкир.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via German Bankier / French banquier from Italian banchiere ('money-changer, banker'), derived from banca ('money-changer's bench or counter', of Germanic origin).

банкомат.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from German Bankomat / Italian and Swiss French bancomat, a European blend of банк / Bank ('bank') + автомат / Automat ('automatic machine, vending machine').

банкрот.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Bankrott / Dutch bankroet from Italian banca rotta ('broken bench', referring to the custom of breaking an insolvent money-changer's counter).

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: банкрот

банкротство.etymology: Formed in Russian from банкрот ('bankrupt', from Italian banca rotta 'broken bench') + the abstract condition suffix -ство.

баня.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic баня ('steam bath, bathhouse'), from Proto-Slavic *baňa, an early borrowing from Vulgar Latin *bānea (Classical Latin balnea, plural of balneum 'bath'), itself from Ancient Greek βαλανεῖον (balaneîon, 'bathhouse').

бар.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from English bar ('counter across which drinks are served; pub, drinking establishment'), which comes from Old French barre ('barrier, rod, counter separating the server from patrons').

барабан.etymology: Attested in Russian since the sixteenth–seventeenth centuries; borrowed from Turkic (compare Kazan Tatar دارابان daraban 'drum'), itself from Persian دربان / تبره or an onomatopoeic Turkic-Persian military term for a kettle-drum.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: барабан

баран.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic баранъ ('ram, wether'), from Proto-Slavic *baranъ / *beranъ, an ancient pastoral term with parallels in Balkan, Iranian, and Mediterranean sheep-herding vocabulary (compare Greek βάριον 'sheep').

бараний.etymology: Possessive and relational adjective formed with the animal suffix -ий from баран ('ram, sheep', attested in Old East Slavic баранъ / боранъ, Proto-Slavic *baranъ).

morphemes.meaning: possessive/animal adjective suffix (fem. баранья, neut. баранье)

барахлить.etymology: Twentieth-century colloquial denominal verb derived from барахло ('junk, worn-out stuff') + verbal suffix -ить, originally in aviation and automotive slang meaning 'to sputter, malfunction like a piece of junk'.

барахло.etymology: Originally a northern and Siberian dialectal collective noun for 'old clothes, household chattels, junk'; connected by Vasmer and Trubachev either with Old East Slavic борошень ('travelers' baggage, household goods', Proto-Slavic *boršьno) with expressive -х- suffixation, or with Mongolian бараа ('goods, wares').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: барахло

барашек.etymology: Diminutive of баран ('ram, sheep', Old East Slavic баранъ, Proto-Slavic *baranъ), formed with the diminutive suffix -ек on an altered stem бараш- (by analogy with diminutives in -шек such as кармашек).

барбарис.etymology: Borrowed via German Berberitze / Polish berberys from Medieval Latin berberis / barbaris ('barberry shrub and berry').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: барбарис

бардак.etymology: Originally borrowed via Ottoman Turkish bardak ('drinking glass, jug') or adapted in the 19th century as a phonetic alteration of French bordel ('brothel', blended with Turkish bardak or Tatar bardaq); subsequently generalized in colloquial Russian to mean 'utter mess, chaos'.

баржа.etymology: Borrowed via French barge or English barge from Medieval Latin barga / barca ('flat-bottomed freight boat, bark').

барин.etymology: Contracted in allegro address in Russian from боярин ('boyar, nobleman, feudal lord, master'), attested in Old East Slavic бояринъ / боляринъ (from Danube Bulgarian боляринъ 'magnate, grandee').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: барин

баркас.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from Dutch barkas ('large ship's boat, longboat, launch'), from Spanish barcaza (augmentative of barca 'boat', from Late Latin barca).

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: баркас

бармен.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English barman ('bartender'), a compound of bar ('tavern counter') and man.

барный.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ный from бар ('bar, pub; drinks counter', borrowed from English bar).

history.meaning: bar → of a bar (e.g. барная стойка 'bar counter')

барон.etymology: Borrowed via German Baron / French baron ('baron, feudal lord'), from Medieval Latin baro (from Frankish *baro 'freeman, warrior, king's vassal').

барракуда.etymology: Borrowed via English and Spanish barracuda ('large predatory tropical sea fish of the genus Sphyraena'), of Caribbean indigenous origin.

бархатный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from бархат ('velvet'), borrowed in late medieval Russian via Middle High German barchāt ('fustian, rich pile fabric'), ultimately from Arabic barrakān ('coarse camlet or heavy woven cloth').

барьер.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French barrière ('gate, turnpike, obstacle, hurdle'), derived from Old French barre ('bar, beam across an entrance', from Vulgar Latin *barra).

бас.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th–18th centuries from Italian basso ('low, bass voice or part'), which comes from Late Latin bassus ('thick, low, short in stature'). In musical terminology, Italian basso designated the lowest foundational voice or left-hand accompaniment of a score, spreading into all European languages. It is the exact counterpart of English bass.

rootFamily.gloss: to speak in a deep bass voice

басовый.etymology: Formed inside Russian from the musical noun бас ('bass voice or register', borrowed from Italian basso 'low', Late Latin bassus) with the relational adjectival suffix -овый. It designates instruments, strings, clefs, or notes belonging to the lowest musical range. It parallels English bass in compounds such as bass string and bass clef.

бассейн.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from French bassin ('basin, ornamental water pool, river basin'), from Old French bacin, from Vulgar Latin *baccinum ('water vessel, bowl').

батарейка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from батарея ('artillery battery; array of linked Leyden jars or galvanic cells'), borrowed from French batterie (from battre 'to beat, strike'; applied by Benjamin Franklin in 1748 to a linked bank of electrical condensers).

батарея.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from French batterie ('artillery battery', originally 'a beating, bombardment', from battre 'to beat'). Because a cast-iron central-heating radiator is assembled from a row ('battery') of identical ribbed sections, Russian extended батарея (отопления) to mean a household heating radiator, as well as an electric battery.

history.meaning: artillery battery; row of linked units
artillery battery; electric battery; heating radiator

батарея.notes: In everyday Russian home life, **батарея** most often means a hot-water wall radiator (*тёплая батарея*).

батюшки.etymology: Exclamatory plural of батюшка ('dear father; village priest'), an affectionate derivative of батя ('father, dad', from Proto-Slavic *batja). Originally a shortened pious or startled invocation (such as Батюшки-святы! 'Holy fathers!'), now an everyday exclamation of surprise ('Goodness gracious!, Oh my!').

history.meaning: dear father → goodness gracious!, oh my!

батя.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *baťa ('father, elder brother, kinsman'), which Vasmer explains as an ancient familial hypocoristic shortened from *bratrъ (Russian брат, 'brother') and transferred affectionately to one's father.

history.meaning: dad, the old man (folksy); respected commander/boss

бахилы.etymology: Originally a Russian dialectal and northern word for high soft leather or wading boots worn by hunters and fishermen (possibly connected with башмак or Finno-Ugric/Latin baxeae); in modern Russian specialized for disposable medical or museum overshoes.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: бахила

башня.etymology: Developed from Old East Slavic башта, borrowed via Polish baszta or Czech bašta from Italian bastia 'fortified tower, bastion'. In Russian the ending was reshaped with the native place suffix -ня (as in пашня, таможня).

cognates.meaning: fortified projection (from the same Italian family)

башня.notes: Notice the fleeting vowel in the genitive plural: одна башня -> много башен.

бдительность.etymology: Formed from бдительный ('vigilant, watchful', derived from Old Church Slavonic бьдѣти / Russian бдеть 'to stay awake, keep watch', from Proto-Slavic *bъděti < PIE *bʰewdʰ- 'to be awake, aware') + the abstract noun suffix -ость.

бегать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бѣгати, from Proto-Slavic *bēgati ('to run around, flee repeatedly'), the multidirectional and iterative counterpart of *běžati (Russian бежать 'to run'), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰegʷ- ('to flee, run'; cognate with Lithuanian bėgti 'to run' and Ancient Greek φέβομαι).

history.meaning: to run (habitually, around, or back and forth)

бегом.etymology: Fossilized instrumental singular of бег ('run, running', from Proto-Slavic *běgъ, verbal noun of *běžati / *běgati): literally 'by a run', hence 'at a run, on the double, running'.

бегство.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic бѣгьство ('flight, escape'), formed from бѣгъ ('running, flight', from Proto-Slavic *běgъ) + the abstract noun suffix -ьство.

беда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бѣда ('misfortune, calamity, need, compulsion'), from Proto-Slavic *běda (originally 'compulsion, distress', related to *běditi 'to compel, force', preserved in победить 'to conquer, overcome'), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ- ('to compel, urge, persuade'; cognate with Latin fīdō, Ancient Greek πείθω, and Gothic baidjan 'to compel').
беда.notes: The conversational reassurance **Не беда!** means 'No big deal! / Never mind!'.

бедлам.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from English bedlam ('uproar, chaos, madhouse'), which is the Middle English colloquial contraction of Bethlehem — referring to the Hospital of St Mary of Bethlehem in London, used as an asylum for the mentally ill from around 1400.

history.meaning: London asylum → madhouse, scene of chaos

бедненький.etymology: Affectionate and compassionate diminutive adjective formed from бедный ('poor, unfortunate', from беда 'misfortune, distress', Proto-Slavic *bědьnъ) + the diminutive suffix -енький.

бедный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бѣдьныи ('afflicted, unfortunate, poor'), from Proto-Slavic *bědьnъ, formed from *běda ('calamity, distress, need'; Russian беда 'trouble, misfortune', from PIE *bʰeydʰ- 'to force, press, compel') + the adjectival suffix *-ьnъ. Originally 'struck by misfortune or hardship', it came to mean both 'poor (lacking money)' and 'unfortunate, poor thing'.

бедняга.etymology: Expressive common-gender personal noun formed in Russian from бедный ('poor, unfortunate', from Proto-Slavic *bědьnъ) + the colloquial suffix -яга.

бежать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бѣжати ('to run, flee'), from Proto-Slavic *běžati (stem *běg-), continuing Proto-Indo-European *bʰegʷ- ('to flee, run'), directly cognate with Lithuanian bėgti ('to run') and Ancient Greek φεύγω ('to flee', whence English fugitive).
бежать.notes: Alternates between **г** and **ж** in the present tense: **я бегу, они бегут**, but **ты бежишь, он бежит, мы бежим, вы бежите**.

без.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic безъ ('without'), from Proto-Slavic *bez, closely cognate with Lithuanian bè ('without'), Latvian bez, and Sanskrit bahíṣ ('outside').
без.notes: Always takes the genitive case: чай без сахара ('tea without sugar'), без десяти восемь ('ten to eight').

безвкусно.etymology: Adverb formed from безвкусный ('tasteless, bland, lacking good taste'), derived from the prepositional phrase без вкуса ('without taste', combining без 'without' + вкус 'taste', probably a partial semantic calque of French sans goût).

бездельник.etymology: Formed with the agent suffix -ник from безделье ('idleness, lack of occupation') or бездельный ('idle'), derived from без ('without') + дело ('work, business, deed', from Proto-Slavic *dělo).

бездельничать.etymology: Denominal verb formed from бездельник ('idler, loafer', derived from без дела 'without work/business', from без 'without' + дело 'work, deed') + the verbal suffix -ничать.

бездомный.etymology: Formed from the privative prefix без- ('without, -less') + дом ('house, home', inherited from Old East Slavic домъ, Proto-Slavic *domъ, PIE *dómh₂os, cognate with Latin domus) + the adjective suffix -ный. Used both as an adjective ('homeless, stray') and as a substantivized noun ('homeless person').

безжалостно.etymology: Adverb formed from безжалостный ('pitiless, merciless, ruthless'), derived from без жалости ('without pity', from без 'without' + жалость 'pity, compassion', built on жаль).

беззащитный.etymology: Formed in Russian from the privative prefix без- ('without, -less') + защита ('defense, protection', from защитить 'to defend, shield', built on щит 'shield', Proto-Slavic *ščitъ) + the adjective suffix -ный.

безлактозный.etymology: Modern compound adjective formed from the privative prefix без- ('without, -free') + лактоза ('lactose, milk sugar', coined in French by J.-B. Dumas in 1843 from Latin lac, lactis 'milk' + chemical suffix -ose) + adjectival suffix -ный.

безнравственно.etymology: Adverb formed from безнравственный ('immoral'), derived from без- ('without') + нравственный ('moral', from нрав 'character, custom, temper', Old Church Slavonic нравъ, Proto-Slavic *norvъ).

безобидно.etymology: Adverb formed from безобидный ('harmless, inoffensive'), derived from без обиды ('without offense/harm', from без + обида 'offense, injury, wrong').

безобидный.etymology: Formed from the prepositional phrase без обиды ('without offense or injury'), combining без ('without') + обида ('offense, wrong, harm', from Proto-Slavic *obida) + the adjectival suffix -ный.

безобразие.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic безобразиѥ ('formlessness, ugliness, unseemliness'), formed from без- ('without') + образъ ('form, image, seemly appearance', Proto-Slavic *obrazъ), originally calquing Ancient Greek ἀμορφία / ἀσχημοσύνη.

безопасно.etymology: Adverb and predicative form of безопасный ('safe, secure'), formed from без- ('without') + опасный ('dangerous', from older опасъ 'caution, peril, fear', related to опасаться 'to beware'): literally 'without danger'.

history.meaning: free of danger, safe → safely; it is safe

безопасность.etymology: Formed from безопасный ('safe, free from danger') + the abstract feminine noun suffix -ость: 'safety, security'.

безопасный.etymology: Formed in Russian from the prepositional phrase без опаса ('without fear or danger', or by prefixing без- 'without' to опасный 'dangerous'), built on the Slavic root *pas- ('to watch over, guard, beware'; compare опасаться 'to beware, fear' and пасти 'to tend, herd'): literally 'free from anything one must beware of'.

history.meaning: without danger or cause for caution

безответственный.etymology: Formed in Russian from the privative prefix без- ('without, ir-') + ответственный ('responsible'), which derives from ответственность ('responsibility') and ответ ('answer, account', from ответить 'to answer', Proto-Slavic *otъvětъ).

безработица.etymology: Formed in nineteenth-century Russian from безработный ('unemployed, workless', from без работы 'without work') + the abstract/state noun suffix -ица.

безработный.etymology: Formed from the privative prefix без- ('without') + работа ('work, job', from Proto-Slavic *orbota) + the adjective suffix -ный.

безразличный.etymology: Formed from the privative prefix без- ('without') + различие ('difference, distinction', from различный 'different', Old Church Slavonic различьнъ, built on лик / лицо 'face, form') + -ный, literally 'making no distinction, indifferent'.

безумец.etymology: Formed from безумный ('mindless, mad, foolish', from Old Church Slavonic безумьнъ, from без ума 'without mind/reason') + the personal agent suffix -ец.

безумие.etymology: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic and Old East Slavic безумиѥ ('lack of reason, folly, madness'), formed from без ('without') + умъ ('mind, reason, intellect', Proto-Slavic *umъ), calquing Ancient Greek ἄνοια / ἀφροσύνη.

безумно.etymology: Adverb formed from безумный ('mad, crazy, mindless'), inherited from Old East Slavic безумьныи / Old Church Slavonic безумьнъ, from без ('without') + ум ('mind, reason', Proto-Slavic *umъ).

безумный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic безумьныи ('lacking reason, foolish, mad'), formed from без ('without') + ум ('mind, reason', Proto-Slavic *umъ).

безупречно.etymology: Adverb of безупречный ('impeccable, irreproachable, spotless'), formed from the phrase без упрёка ('without reproach or flaw'), where упрёк ('reproach, blame') comes from упрекать / упрекнуть (built on Old Church Slavonic прѣкъ 'transverse, contrary, objection'; compare вопреки 'contrary to').

безупречный.etymology: Formed from the privative prefix без- ('without') + упрёк ('reproach, blame', deverbal noun from упрекать) + the adjective suffix -ный (with к > ч palatalization), calquing French sans reproche / irréprochable ('beyond reproach').

безусловно.etymology: Adverb and parenthetical discourse marker from безусловный ('unconditional, absolute'), formed from без условий ('without conditions', calquing German unbedingt).

бейджик.etymology: Diminutive formed in late twentieth-century Russian with the suffix -ик from бейдж ('name badge, ID tag'), borrowed from English badge.

бейсбол.etymology: Borrowed in the twentieth century from American English baseball, compounded from base ('station on the playing field') + ball.

бекон.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth or early twentieth century from English bacon ('cured back and side meat of a pig'), from Old French bacon, of West Germanic origin (*bakō 'back, ham, flitch of pork').

белка.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бѣлъка (originally 'white squirrel pelt used as a fur unit of currency', shortened from бѣла вѣверица 'white squirrel', replacing the ancient Slavic word вѣверица), derived from белый ('white', Proto-Slavic *bělъ).

белладонна.etymology: Borrowed via scientific Latin Atropa belladonna from Italian bella donna (literally 'fair lady', referring to the Renaissance Italian practice of women using the plant's juice as eye drops to dilate their pupils for cosmetic beauty).

белок.etymology: Formed from белый ('white', Proto-Slavic *bělъ) + the noun suffix -ок, originally designating the white of an egg or the sclera of the eye, and in nineteenth-century chemistry adopted as a calque of German Eiweiß / Latin albumen for 'protein'.

белоснежный.etymology: Compound adjective formed in Russian from белый ('white', Proto-Slavic *bělъ) + linking vowel -о- + снежный ('snowy', from снег 'snow', Proto-Slavic *sněgъ): 'white as snow, snow-white'.

белый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бѣлъ / бѣлыи ('white, bright, shining'), from Proto-Slavic *bělъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *bʰēlos ('shining, white', from *bʰel- 'to shine, flash'; compare Lithuanian bãltas 'white', Sanskrit bhāla 'brightness', and English bald, originally 'white-patched').

бельгийский.etymology: Relational adjective formed from Бельгия ('Belgium', from Latin Belgica / Gallia Belgica, named after the Celtic-Germanic tribe of the Belgae) + the adjectival suffix -ский.

бельё.etymology: Collective noun formed in Russian with the suffix -ьё (< Proto-Slavic *-ьje) from белый ('white', inherited from Old East Slavic бѣлыи, Proto-Slavic *bělъ, from PIE *bʰel- 'white, shining'): originally 'bleached white linen fabric', and hence 'bedding, household linen, laundry, and underwear' (paralleling French linge from lin 'flax/linen').

history.meaning: white → bleached white linen, laundry, underwear

бельё.notes: Singular-only collective noun: нижнее бельё ('underwear'), постельное бельё ('bed linen'), стирать бельё ('to do the laundry').

бензин.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from German Benzin (coined in 1833 by the chemist Eilhard Mitscherlich for benzene, derived from Benzoeharz 'benzoin resin', ultimately from Arabic لُبَان جَاوِيّ lubān jāwī 'frankincense of Java/Sumatra', later applied in German and Russian to petroleum motor fuel).

берег.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic берегъ ('riverbank, shore, steep slope', showing East Slavic pleophony -ере- corresponding to Old Church Slavonic брѣгъ), from Proto-Slavic *bergъ ('bank, slope, hill'), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰérǵʰos ('height, hill'; cognate with German Berg 'mountain').
берег.notes: Takes the stressed locative ending -у after на/в: на берегу ('on the shore/bank'), and stressed -а in the nominative plural: берега.

бережно.etymology: Adverb formed from бережный ('careful, cautious, thrifty'), derived from беречь ('to guard, take care of, preserve', inherited from Old East Slavic беречи, from Proto-Slavic *berťi, cognate with German bergen).

беременная.etymology: Feminine form of беременный ('pregnant', originally 'burdened, carrying a load'), inherited with East Slavic pleophony -ере- from Proto-Slavic *bermenьnъ, derived from *bermę (Old Church Slavonic брѣмѧ / Russian бремя 'burden, load', from PIE *bʰer- 'to carry, bear').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: беременная

беременность.etymology: Formed from беременная / беременный ('pregnant', from Proto-Slavic *bermenьnъ, derived from *bermę 'burden, load') + the abstract noun suffix -ость.

беременный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic беремяньныи ('pregnant', literally 'carrying a burden'), displaying East Slavic pleophony -ере- (compare Old Church Slavonic брѣменьнъ), derived from беремя ('load, burden, armful', standard Russian бремя 'burden'), from Proto-Slavic *bermę ('load, that which is borne'), from the PIE root *bʰer- ('to carry, bear'; cognate with English bear and birth).

history.meaning: burden, load → carrying a child, pregnant

rootFamily.gloss: to take (from the same PIE root *bʰer-)

беречь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic беречи (present берегу; showing East Slavic pleophony -ере-; compare Old Church Slavonic брѣщи), from Proto-Slavic *bergti ('to guard, care for, preserve'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *bʰergʰ- ('to keep safe, protect, hide'; cognate with German bergen 'to rescue, shelter').

history.meaning: to guard, treasure, take care of

беречься.etymology: Reflexive form of беречь ('to guard, keep safe, spare') with the reflexive enclitic -ся ('oneself'). The base verb descends from Old East Slavic беречи and Proto-Slavic *bergti ('to guard, watch over, care for'), from PIE *bhergh- ('to hide, protect, keep safe'). Through that Indo-European root it is cognate with German bergen ('to rescue, shelter') and English bury and borrow.

history.meaning: to watch out, take care of oneself

берлога.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic берлогъ / берлога ('wild animal's lair, bear's winter den'), from Proto-Slavic *bьrlogъ / *bьrloga, derived from *bьrl- ('bedding of twigs, mud, litter', cf. Bulgarian бърлок) + suffix *-ogъ; later associated by folk etymology with Germanic Bär ('bear') + логово ('lair').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: берлога

берёзовый.etymology: Relational adjective derived from берёза ('birch tree') + suffix -овый. Russian берёза descends via Old East Slavic береза from Proto-Slavic *berza ('birch'), which goes back to PIE *bherHgo- ('birch', literally 'the bright, white-barked tree', from *bherHg- 'to shine, white'). It is directly cognate with English birch, German Birke, and Sanskrit bhurja.

беседа.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic бесѣда ('seat outside, bench, gathering, conversation'), from Proto-Slavic *besěda, traditionally analyzed as *bez- ('outside') + *sěda ('sitting', from *sěděti 'to sit'), i.e. 'sitting together outdoors talking'.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: беседа

бесить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бѣсити ('to drive mad, possess with a demon'), denominal causative verb from бѣсъ (Russian бес 'demon, evil spirit', Proto-Slavic *běsъ < PIE *bʰóydʰos 'causing terror').

беситься.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бѣситися ('to be possessed by a demon, rage, go mad'), reflexive of бесить (from бес 'demon, evil spirit').

history.meaning: to rage, be furious; to romp wildly

бесконечно.etymology: Adverb formed from бесконечный ('endless, infinite'), built from бес- (voiceless variant of без- 'without' before к-) + конец ('end', Old East Slavic коньць, Proto-Slavic *konьcь) + the adjective suffix -ный.

бесконечный.etymology: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic бесконьчьнъ ('endless, infinite'), formed from the prepositional phrase без конца ('without end', from без 'without' + конец 'end', Proto-Slavic *konьcь) + adjectival suffix -ный.

бесплатно.etymology: Adverb of бесплатный ('free of charge', spelled безплатный before the 1918 orthography reform), formed from без платы ('without payment') + -ный/-но, where плата ('pay, fee') comes from платить ('to pay', Proto-Slavic *platiti).

бесплатный.etymology: Formed in Russian from the prepositional phrase без платы ('without payment'), combining prefix бес- (voiceless variant of без- 'without' before п) + плата ('pay, fee', from Proto-Slavic *plata) + adjectival suffix -ный.

беспокоить.etymology: Formed in Russian from без покоя / беспокойный ('without peace/rest'), combining prefix бес- ('without', variant of без- before п) + покой ('peace, rest, quiet', from Proto-Slavic *pokojь) + verbal suffix -ить: literally 'to deprive someone of peace and quiet, disturb, bother'.

history.meaning: to deprive of rest → to bother, disturb, worry

беспокоиться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed with -ся from беспокоить ('to disturb, trouble, deprive of rest'), built from бес- (variant of без- 'without') + покой ('rest, peace, calm', inherited from Old East Slavic покои, Proto-Slavic *pokojь).

history.meaning: without rest → to disturb → to worry, be anxious

беспокойство.etymology: Formed in Russian from беспокойный ('restless, anxious, troublesome', from без покоя 'without peace/rest', built on покой 'rest, peace', Proto-Slavic *pokojь) + the abstract noun suffix -ство.

бесполезно.etymology: Adverb and predicative form of бесполезный ('useless'), built from бес- (variant of без- 'without') + польза ('use, benefit, advantage', borrowed via Old Church Slavonic польза alongside native Old East Slavic польга 'ease, relief, benefit', from the root of лёгкий 'light, easy') + -ный.

беспорядок.etymology: Formed in Russian with the privative prefix без- / бес- ('without, lack of') and порядок ('order, sequence, tidy arrangement', derived from по- + ряд 'row, line, order', Proto-Slavic *rędъ).

history.meaning: lack of order, disorder, mess; (pl.) riots/disturbances

беспредел.etymology: Originated in twentieth-century Russian prison and criminal argot as a back-formation from без предела ('without limit/bounds', combining без 'without' + предел 'limit, boundary', from Old Church Slavonic прѣдѣлъ), denoting utter lawlessness or violation of unwritten rules.

бессердечный.etymology: Formed from the prepositional phrase без сердца ('without a heart', from без + сердце 'heart', Proto-Slavic *sьrdьce) + the adjectival suffix -ный.

бессильный.etymology: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic and Old East Slavic бессильнъ ('without strength, powerless'), formed from без силы ('without strength', from без + сила 'strength, power', Proto-Slavic *sila) + suffix -ный.

бессмысленный.etymology: Formed from без смысла ('without sense or meaning', combining без 'without' + смысл 'sense, meaning, reason') + the adjectival suffix -енный.

бессовестный.etymology: Formed from бес- (voiceless variant of без- 'without') + совесть ('conscience', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвѣсть, a calque of Ancient Greek συνείδησις 'shared knowledge, conscience', from съ- + вѣдѣти 'to know') + the adjective suffix -ный.
бессовестный.notes: The middle -т- is silent in everyday pronunciation: [бессовесный].

бессрочный.etymology: Formed in Russian from без срока ('without a fixed term or deadline', combining без 'without' + срок 'appointed time, term', Old East Slavic сърокъ) + the adjectival suffix -ный.

бесцеремонный.etymology: Formed from без церемоний ('without ceremony', calquing French sans cérémonie; церемония from Latin caerimonia 'sacred rite, ceremony, formality') + the adjectival suffix -ный.

бесчувственный.etymology: Formed from без чувств / без чувства ('without feeling or consciousness', from без + чувство 'feeling, sense') + the adjectival suffix -енный.

бетон.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French béton (and German Beton, 'concrete'), from Old French betun ('mortar, cement, rubble'), from Latin bitūmen ('mineral pitch, asphalt, binding mortar').

бечёвка.etymology: Formed with -ёвка from бечева ('towline, strong hauling rope used to pull river barges upstream'), which Vasmer traces as an early borrowing via Turkic from Persian پیچ (pēč 'twist, coil, cord').

бешамель.etymology: Borrowed from French (sauce) béchamel ('white roux-and-milk sauce'), named in seventeenth-century France in honor of Marquis Louis de Béchameil de Nointel (1630–1703), chief steward to King Louis XIV.

history.meaning: white sauce named after Louis de Béchameil

бешенство.etymology: Formed from бешеный ('mad, rabid, furious', from бесить 'to madden', derived from бес 'demon') + the abstract condition suffix -ство.

бешеный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бѣшеныи, originally the past passive participle of бѣсити / бесить ('to possess with a demon, drive mad', from бес 'demon', Proto-Slavic *běsъ).

библиотека.etymology: Borrowed (first via Church Slavonic вивлиофика and then re-borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish biblioteka / German Bibliothek / Latin bibliothēca) from Ancient Greek βιβλιοθήκη ('book-repository, bookcase, library'), a compound of βιβλίον ('book, papyrus scroll') + θήκη ('case, chest, repository' — the same second element as in аптека).

биде.etymology: Borrowed from French bidet ('low washbasin which one straddles', originally 'small riding pony' in Old French, from bider 'to trot', because using the basin required straddling it like a pony).

бизнес.etymology: Borrowed from English business ('commercial activity, trade, occupation'), derived from busy (Old English bisig 'careful, anxious, occupied') + -ness.

бизнесмен.etymology: Borrowed in the twentieth century from English businessman, compounded from business (from busy + -ness) + man.

билет.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century from French billet ('short note, written pass, ticket'), a diminutive of Old French bille ('written document, sealed note', which also gave English bill), from Medieval Latin bulla ('round seal, sealed papal document').

history.meaning: ticket (for transport, theatre, cinema, or an exam card)

биржа.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Dutch beurs or German Börse ('merchants' exchange'), named after the Van der Beurze family Square in 14th-century Bruges, ultimately from Medieval Latin bursa ('leather purse', from Greek βύρσα 'hide, wineskin').

бирка.etymology: Recorded in Russian first in the sense 'notched wooden tally stick used by tax collectors or herdsmen, trade tag'; Vasmer notes competing proposals, most often linking it either to an early Scandinavian borrowing (compare Old Swedish birk 'market jurisdiction/tally rule') or to regional Turkic/Tatar birkä ('tally mark').

history.meaning: luggage tag, price or garment label

бита.etymology: Derived from бить ('to beat, strike, hit', from Proto-Slavic *biti, originally the feminine past passive participle бита) for a heavy throwing piece in lapta/gorodki, and later applied to a baseball bat.

биткоин.etymology: Borrowed in the early 21st century from English bitcoin, coined in 2008 in the cryptocurrency white paper by Satoshi Nakamoto from bit ('binary digit') + coin.

бить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бити, from Proto-Slavic *biti ('to strike, beat'), continuing the Proto-Indo-European root *bʰeyh₂- ('to strike, hew'), cognate with Old Irish benaid ('strikes, cuts'), Old High German bīhal ('axe'), and Latin perfines.

history.meaning: to strike, beat, chime (of a clock)

бить.notes: Conjugates with a soft-sign stem in the present tense: *я бью, ты бьёшь, часы бьют двенадцать* ('the clock strikes twelve').

rootFamily.gloss: to knock out; to blow (a fuse)

биться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic битися, formed from бить ('to strike, beat, smash') + the reflexive/middle suffix -ся: means both 'to beat, throb' (of the heart), 'to struggle/fight', and — of fragile glass or porcelain — 'to break, shatter easily'.

history.meaning: to beat (of a heart); to break/shatter (of dishes)

биться.notes: *Осторожно, стекло бьётся!* ('Careful, fragile glass / glass breaks!').

благо.etymology: Borrowed in this non-pleophonic -ла- form from Old Church Slavonic благо ('good, blessing, welfare'; native East Slavic had болого), substantivized neuter of благъ ('good, blessed', Proto-Slavic *bolgъ).

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: благо

благодарить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благодарити ('to give thanks'), a morphological calque of Ancient Greek εὐχαριστέω (eukharistéō), combining благо- ('good, well', translating Greek εὐ-) + дарити ('to give, bestow', from даръ 'gift').

благодарность.etymology: Formed with the abstract noun suffix -ость from благодарный ('grateful, thankful'), built on Old Church Slavonic благодарити ('to thank, give thanks'), a loan-translation (calque) of Ancient Greek εὐχαριστέω (eukharistéō): благо- ('good', translating Greek εὖ-) + дарить / дар ('to give / gift', translating χάρις 'grace, favour, gift').
