благодарный.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ный from благодарить ('to thank', Old Church Slavonic calque of Greek εὐχάριστος 'grateful, thankful').

благодаря.etymology: Preposition ('thanks to, owing to') grammaticalized from the present adverbial participle (деепричастие) благодаря ('thanking') of благодарить ('to thank'; compare French grâce à and English thanks to).

благополучие.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic благополучиѥ ('good fortune, well-being'), a compound calque of Ancient Greek εὐτυχία / εὐκληρία, combining благо- ('good, well', Proto-Slavic *bolgъ) + получие ('lot, destiny, attainment', related to получить 'to receive, obtain' and случай 'chance').

благоразумие.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic благоразумиѥ ('good sense, prudence, wisdom'), a compound calque of Ancient Greek εὐφροσύνη / φρόνησις combining благо- ('good, well') + разумъ ('reason, mind, understanding').

благоразумный.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic благоразумьнъ ('prudent, sensible, wise'), compounded from благо- ('good, well') + разумный ('reasonable, intelligent', from разум 'reason, mind').

благородно.etymology: Adverb formed from благородный ('noble, highborn, generous'), an Old Church Slavonic compound calque of Ancient Greek εὐγενής ('well-born, noble').

благородный.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic благородьнъ ('well-born, of noble birth'), a morphological calque of Ancient Greek εὐγενής (eugenḗs): formed from благо- ('good, well', translating εὐ-) + родъ ('birth, kin, lineage', translating γένος) + -ный.

благословить.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic благословити ('to bless, praise, speak well of'), a morphological calque of Ancient Greek εὐλογέω (eulogéō): formed from благо- ('well, good') + словити ('to speak', from слово 'word').

благословлять.etymology: Imperfective of благословить ('to bless'), from Old Church Slavonic благословляти, calquing Ancient Greek εὐλογέω ('to speak well of, bless', from благо 'good' + слово 'word').

благотворительность.etymology: Formed from благотворительный ('charitable, beneficent', from Old Church Slavonic благотворити 'to do good', calquing Greek εὐεργετέω) + the abstract noun suffix -ость.

благотворительный.etymology: Derived from Church Slavonic благотворитель / благотворити ('to do good, perform beneficence', a compound calque of Ancient Greek εὐεργέτης / εὐεργετέω from благо- 'good' + творить 'to do, make') + suffix -ный.

блат.etymology: Entered general colloquial Russian in the early 20th century from thieves' cant (блатная музыка, where блат meant 'criminal underworld, insider protection, illicit pull'), borrowed via Polish żargon / Yiddish בלאַט (blat, 'sheet of paper, note; in cant: one in the know, insider') from German Blatt ('leaf, sheet of paper, written pass').

history.meaning: sheet of paper, pass → insider, illicit connection

бледный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic блѣдыи / блѣдьныи ('pale, wan, pallid'), from Proto-Slavic *blědъ ('pale'), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleyd- ('pale, dim'; cognate with Old English blāt 'pale, livid' and Lithuanian blaivas).

блекло.etymology: Adverb from блёклый / блеклый ('faded, pale, withered, dull'), originally an l-participle adjective from блёкнуть ('to fade, wither', from Proto-Slavic *blьknǫti, zero-grade related to *blěskъ 'shine' and *blědъ 'pale').

блендер.etymology: Borrowed in the late twentieth century from English blender ('electric kitchen appliance for mixing or puréeing food'), agent/instrument noun from blend ('to mix together').

блеск.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic блѣскъ ('shine, glitter, flash'), from Proto-Slavic *blěskъ (< PIE *bʰloysk-os, related to блестеть 'to shine' and бледный 'pale').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: блеск

блестеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic блестѣти / блистати ('to shine, flash, gleam'), from Proto-Slavic *blьstěti ('to shine, glitter'), built on the Balto-Slavic and Indo-European root *bʰl̥g- / *bʰleyǵ- ('to shine, flash, gleam'; compare Lithuanian blizgėti 'to glitter', блеск 'shine, lustre', and English בליץ / bleak / blank).

блестяще.etymology: Adverb formed from the adjective/participle блестящий ('shining, brilliant'), the present active participle of блестеть ('to shine, glitter'). The verb goes back to Proto-Slavic *blьstěti ('to flash, gleam'), from PIE *bhles- ('to shine, gleam'). Both the literal sense 'sparklingly' and the figurative sense 'brilliantly, splendidly' mirror English brilliantly.

блестящий.etymology: Adjectivalized present active participle in -ящий of блестеть / блестить ('to shine, sparkle, gleam', Proto-Slavic *blьstěti). Just like French brillant and English brilliant, it means both literally 'shiny, glossy, glittering' and figuratively 'brilliant, outstanding'.

history.meaning: to shine → shining, shiny; brilliant, superb

блефовать.etymology: Formed in Russian with the verbal suffix -овать from блеф ('bluff'), borrowed in the late 19th or early 20th century from English bluff ('deception in poker or politics', likely from Dutch blaffen / verbluffen 'to boast, baffle').

history.meaning: to feign confidence with a weak hand

ближайший.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic ближаишии, superlative/comparative degree formed with suffix *-jьš- from близъ / близкий ('near, close', Proto-Slavic *blizъ).

ближний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ближьнии (and reinforced by Old Church Slavonic ближьнии 'neighbour, fellow human'), formed from близ / близко ('near', Proto-Slavic *blizъ) + the soft relational suffix -ний (with з → ж).

history.stage: Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic

близкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic близькыи (extended with the adjectival suffix -к- from older близъ 'near'), from Proto-Slavic *blizъ / *blizъkъ ('near, close').

близко.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic близько, neuter short form and adverb of близкий ('near, close'), formed with the suffix *-ъkъ from Old East Slavic близъ ('near', Proto-Slavic *blizъ). Its comparative ближе ('closer, nearer') shows regular palatalization of *z + *j → ж.

блин.etymology: Altered in Old East Slavic блинъ from earlier млинъ (with dissimilation of м-н > б-н; compare Ukrainian млинець), from Proto-Slavic *mlinъ ('pancake, flat cake made of ground flour'), derived from the root of молоть ('to grind grain in a mill', Proto-Slavic *melti, PIE *melh₂-). In modern colloquial Russian, блин! is also widely used as a minced oath ('damn! shoot!') substituting for a taboo profanity sharing the initial бл-.

history.meaning: to grind → batter cake made of ground meal

блинчик.etymology: Diminutive in -чик of блин ('pancake, blini'), altered in Old East Slavic from млинъ ('pancake', literally 'something ground/milled from flour'), from Proto-Slavic *mlinъ (from *melti 'to grind', Russian молоть).

блокнот.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th century from French bloc-notes ('tear-off notepad, notebook'), a compound of bloc ('block, pad of paper sheets glued along one edge') + notes ('notes').

блюдо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic блюдо ('large platter, dish, course of food'), from Proto-Slavic *bľudo, an early borrowing from Proto-Germanic *biudaz / Gothic biups ('table, Wooden serving platter, dish', derived from *beudaną 'to offer, present at table', cognate with Old English bēod 'table, bowl' and English bid).

history.meaning: dish (both a serving platter and a prepared food course)

блюдце.etymology: Formed with the neuter diminutive suffix -це (Proto-Slavic *-ьce) from блюдо ('large serving dish, platter'), so a блюдце is literally 'a tiny dish' placed under a teacup or saucer. Блюдо comes from Proto-Slavic *bľudo ('platter'), an early borrowing from Gothic biups ('table, platter', Proto-Germanic *beudaz).
блюдце.notes: Genitive plural inserts a fleeting -е-: *пять блюдец* ('five saucers').

бог.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic богъ ('God'), from Proto-Slavic *bogъ (originally 'fortune, share, wealth' — still seen in богатый 'rich' and убогий 'poor' — and 'giver of good fortune, god'). Widely linked by Vasmer to Indo-Iranian *bhaga- (Sanskrit bhága 'dispenser, lord, fortune', Old Persian baga 'god') from PIE *bʰag- ('to apportion, share out').

history.meaning: good fortune; dispenser of fortune, god

бог.notes: Traditionally pronounced *бох* in the nominative singular (reflecting older spirant pronunciation of *г* in church vocabulary).

богато.etymology: Adverb formed from богатый ('rich, wealthy, abundant'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *bogatъ (derived from *bogъ in its original Indo-Iranian-related sense 'fortune, share, wealth', cognate with Sanskrit bhága 'prosperity, share').

богатство.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic богатьство ('wealth, riches'), formed from богатый ('rich', Proto-Slavic *bogatъ, from *bogъ 'fortune, share') + the abstract suffix -ьство.

богатый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic богатыи (and Old Church Slavonic богатъ), from Proto-Slavic *bogatъ ('rich, wealthy, endowed by fortune'), formed with the suffix *-atъ from the archaic noun sense of *bogъ ('share, portion, wealth, good fortune', cognate with Sanskrit bhága- 'fortune, wealth, dispenser/lord' and Avestan baγa-; the same word that gave Бог 'God', originally 'giver of good fortune/shares').

богатырь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic богатырь (attested in thirteenth-century chronicles initially for Mongol-Tatar commanders and then Russian epic heroes); borrowed from Old Turkic bagatur / Mongolian баатар ('valiant warrior, hero').

history.meaning: bogatyr (epic hero), man of great strength

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: богатырь

богач.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic богачь, formed from богатый ('rich, wealthy', Proto-Slavic *bogatъ) + the personal suffix -ач.

бодрить.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bъdriti ('to make alert, rouse, invigorate'), causative verb from *bъdrъ (Russian бодрый 'vigorous, alert, wide-awake', related to бдеть 'to stay awake', PIE *bʰewdʰ-).

бодрость.etymology: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic and Old East Slavic бъдрость ('wakefulness, vigilance, vigor'), formed from бодрый ('alert, brisk, vigorous', Proto-Slavic *bъdrъ) + the abstract noun suffix -ость.

бодрый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бъдрыи ('vigilant, awake, brisk, lively'), from Proto-Slavic *bъdrъ, formed with the adjective suffix *-rъ from the root of *bъděti ('to be awake, keep watch', Russian бдеть, будить), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰrós (cognate with Lithuanian budrus 'vigilant, alert').

бодрящий.etymology: Present active participle of бодрить ('to invigorate, brace, cheer up'), derived from бодрый ('vigorous, alert, brisk', from Old East Slavic бъдрыи and Proto-Slavic *bъdrъ, built on the same Indo-European root *bʰewdʰ- 'to be awake, alert' as будить 'to wake').

боевик.etymology: Formed in Russian at the turn of the twentieth century from боевой ('combat, militant, dynamic; box-office hit', derived from бой 'battle, fight', Proto-Slavic *bojь) + the noun suffix -ик; originally 'armed militant' and then 'box-office hit / action film'.

боевой.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian from бой ('battle, fight, combat', deverbal o-grade noun from бить 'to beat, strike', Proto-Slavic *bojь) + the adjectival suffix -евой.

боец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic боиць / боець ('warrior, fighter'), formed with the agent suffix -ец from бой ('battle, combat, beating', from Proto-Slavic *bojь, o-grade noun of *biti 'to strike, beat').

божественно.etymology: Adverb formed from божественный ('divine, godlike'), borrowed via Old Church Slavonic божьствьнъ ('divine'), derived from божество ('deity, divinity') and бог ('God', Old East Slavic богъ, Proto-Slavic *bogъ).

божественный.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic божьствьнъ ('divine, godly'), derived from божьство (божество 'deity, divinity', from богъ 'God', Proto-Slavic *bogъ) + the adjectival suffix -енный.

боинг.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from the American aerospace manufacturer name Boeing (founded in Seattle in 1916 by aviation pioneer William E. Boeing, 1881–1956, from the German surname Böing).

history.meaning: aircraft built by the Boeing Company

бой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бои ('beating, battle, combat'), o-grade action noun from бить ('to beat, strike'), from Proto-Slavic *bojь (from *biti 'to strike').

бок.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бокъ, from Proto-Slavic *bokъ ('side, flank').

rootFamily.gloss: on the side, from the side

бок.notes: Takes the stressed locative ending -у after на/в: лежать на боку ('to lie on one's side'), and stressed -а in the nominative plural: бока.

бокал.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French bocal or Italian boccale ('jug, goblet, drinking glass') from Late Latin baucālis, itself from Ancient Greek βαύκαλις (baúkalis, 'vessel for cooling wine or water').

бокс.etymology: Borrowed at the turn of the 20th century from English box / boxing ('the sport of fighting with fists', from Middle English box 'a blow, cuff'). (A homonymous technical borrowing бокс 'isolation cubicle, garage bay, box' comes from English box 'container, compartment'.)

боксировать.etymology: Formed in Russian from бокс ('boxing', borrowed in the nineteenth century from English box / boxing 'to strike with the fists') + the verbal suffix -ировать.

болгарский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ский from болгарин / Болгария ('Bulgarian / Bulgaria', Old East Slavic българинъ / болгаринъ). In Russian culinary usage, болгарский перец ('Bulgarian pepper') is the universal everyday term for sweet bell pepper, which spread into Russia via Bulgarian market gardeners in the 17th–19th centuries.

rootFamily.gloss: Bulgarian woman; (colloq.) angle grinder (first imported from Bulgaria in the 1970s)

более.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic болѣе (compare native Russian больше), the comparative adverb of велий / большой ('big, great, much'), from Proto-Slavic *boľe, continuing a Proto-Indo-European comparative stem *bél-yos- ('stronger, greater'; compare Sanskrit báliyas- 'stronger' and बल bála 'strength').

history.meaning: more (in compound comparatives and phrases like более или менее)

более.notes: Used to form analytical comparatives (*более тихий* 'quieter') and in fixed expressions like **тем более** ('all the more so') and **более или менее** ('more or less').

болезненный.etymology: Formed from болезнь ('illness, sickness, pain', from Old Church Slavonic болѣзнь, derived from болѣти 'to ache, be ill', Proto-Slavic *bolěznь) + the adjectival suffix -енный.

болезнь.etymology: Borrowed with Old Church Slavonic suffix -знь from болѣзнь ('pain, suffering, illness'), derived from болѣти ('to ache, be ill', from Proto-Slavic *bolěti, from *bolь 'pain').

болеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic болѣти ('to hurt, ache, be ill'), from Proto-Slavic *bolěti, built on *bolь ('pain, ache, illness'; Russian боль), which Vasmer connects with Old High German balo ('evil, sickness, ruin') and English bale / baleful.

history.meaning: pain, ache → to ache, be sick
to ache, hurt; to be ill; to root for a team

болеть.notes: In the meaning 'to ache, hurt' (3rd person *болит / болят*): *У меня болит голова* ('My head hurts'). In the meaning 'to be ill' it conjugates in the 1st conjugation (*я болею, ты болеешь*).

болоньезе.etymology: Borrowed in the late twentieth century from Italian (ragù) bolognese ('Bolognese meat sauce'), relational adjective from the city of Bologna in northern Italy (from Latin Bononia).

history.meaning: meat sauce in the style of Bologna

болт.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from Low German or Dutch bout / German Bolzen / English bolt ('crossbow quarrel; metal fastening pin or bolt'), from Proto-Germanic *bultaz.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: болт

болтать.etymology: Inherited East Slavic expressive/onomatopoeic verb (compare Ukrainian бовтати 'to stir, splash, chatter'), originally meaning 'to shake, stir, slosh liquid back and forth' (as in болтать ногами 'to dangle/swing one's legs' or болтунья 'scrambled eggs'). By metaphor ('wagging one's tongue'), болтать языком became the standard colloquial verb for 'to chatter, chat, blab'.

history.meaning: to stir, splash, swing back and forth
to swing, stir; to chat, chatter idly

болтливый.etymology: Formed in Russian from болтать ('to chatter, prattle, stir/shake liquid about', of expressive origin) + the adjectival suffix -ливый.

боль.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic боль ('pain, sickness, grief'), from Proto-Slavic *bolь ('pain, ache', related to *bolěti 'to hurt, ache').

больница.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic больница ('infirmary, hospital, house for the sick', attested in monastery rules from the 11th century), formed from больной ('sick, ill', from боль 'pain, illness') + the place/institution suffix -ница.

больничный.etymology: Substantivized relational adjective from больница ('hospital', derived from больной 'sick person', from боль 'pain') + suffix -ный; as a noun, clipped from больничный лист ('official medical sick-leave certificate').

больно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate formed from the neuter short form of больной ('painful, sore, sick'), derived from боль ('pain, ache'), from Proto-Slavic *bolь ('pain, sickness').

больной.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic больныи ('sick, painful'), from Proto-Slavic *bolьnъ, formed from *bolь ('pain, sickness'; Russian боль) + the adjectival suffix *-ьnъ.

history.meaning: sick, ill; sore; patient (as a noun)

больной.notes: Notice the stress contrast in the short predicate forms: **он болен, она больна, они больны** ('he/she/they are ill').

больше.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic больше ('more, bigger'), the neuter comparative degree of большой / великий, from Proto-Slavic *bolje / *boljьše ('more, larger').

больший.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic большии ('greater, larger'), comparative adjective from Proto-Slavic *boljьjь ('larger, better, stronger', cognate with Sanskrit báliyas- 'stronger', from PIE *bel- 'strong').

большой.etymology: Developed in East Slavic from Old East Slavic большии, which was originally the comparative degree ('bigger, greater') of велии / великыи ('big, great'), from Proto-Slavic *boljьjь ('larger, stronger'; compare Sanskrit bála 'strength, power'). In Russian большой shifted from 'bigger' to the ordinary positive adjective 'big, large'.

бомж.etymology: Late Soviet bureaucratic acronym БОМЖ — Без Определённого Места Жительства ('[person] without a fixed place of residence', used in police protocols from the 1970s), lexicalized in Russian as a common noun for a homeless person.

history.meaning: without a fixed place of residence

бонжорно.etymology: Borrowed as a jocular or situational greeting from Italian buongiorno ('good day, hello'), a univerbation of buon ('good', from Latin bonus) + giorno ('day', from Late Latin diurnum).

бонус.etymology: Borrowed from English bonus ('extra dividend, reward, or perk'), which originated in 18th-century London financial slang as a playful transfer of Latin bonus ('good [man]') to mean 'a good thing, extra premium'.

бордо.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French bordeaux ('red wine from Bordeaux; dark purplish-red wine color'), from the southwestern French port city of Bordeaux (Latin Burdigala).

борец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic борьць ('fighter, wrestler, champion'), formed from бороть / бороться ('to fight, wrestle', Proto-Slavic *borti) + the agent suffix -ец (Proto-Slavic *borьcь).

борисовна.etymology: Russian feminine patronymic formed from the given name Борис (Old East Slavic Борисъ, attested since the 11th century from Bulgar Turkic Bogoris or as a short form of Борислав 'famous in battle') + possessive suffix -ов- + feminine patronymic suffix -на ('daughter of Boris').

бормотать.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bъrmotati ('to mutter, mumble, rumble'), an onomatopoeic verb formed with the expressive suffix -отать (compare грохотать, шептать) on the sound-imitative root *bъr- / *bur- (compare бурчать 'to grumble' and Latin murmurāre).

борода.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic борода ('beard, chin', with East Slavic pleophony -оро-; compare Church Slavonic брада), from Proto-Slavic *borda, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰéh₂ ('beard'; cognate with Latin barba, Lithuanian barzda, and English beard).

бороться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic боротисѧ ('to wrestle, fight, struggle'), East Slavic pleophonic form of Proto-Slavic *borti sę ('to fight, contend'; compare Old Church Slavonic братисѩ).

боррелиоз.etymology: International medical term (New Latin borreliosis) formed from the bacterial genus name Borrelia (named in 1907 after the French bacteriologist Amédée Borrel, 1867–1936, who studied spirochetes) + the Greek-derived medical condition suffix -оз (-osis).

борт.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from Dutch boord or German Bord ('side or gunwale of a ship, deck'), from Proto-Germanic *burdą ('board, plank; ship's side').

history.meaning: side of a ship/vehicle; board; lapel

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: борт

борщ.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic борщ (Ukrainian борщ), from Proto-Slavic *bъrščь, which originally denoted common hogweed (Heracleum sphondylium, modern Russian борщевик), named after its jagged, bristly leaves (from PIE *bʰr̥stis 'bristle, sharp point', cognate with English bristle and German Borste). Medieval Slavs brewed a sour soup from fermented hogweed shoots before beetroot became the signature base of modern borscht.

history.meaning: hogweed soup → beetroot and cabbage soup, borscht

rootFamily.gloss: to go too far, overdo it (literally 'to put too much into the borscht')

борьба.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic борьба ('wrestling, struggle, fight'), formed from бороть / бороться ('to wrestle, fight', Proto-Slavic *borti) + the archaic action-noun suffix -ьба (Proto-Slavic *borьba).

босс.etymology: Borrowed via American English boss ('employer, chief, political or criminal leader'), from Dutch baas ('master, household head, foreman').

ботанический.etymology: Derived from ботаника ('botany, plant science', via German Botanik / French botanique from Ancient Greek βοτανική 'study of plants', from βοτάνη 'pasture, herb, plant') + the adjectival suffix -еский.

ботинок.etymology: Formed in 19th-century Russian with the native singulative suffix -ок from French bottine ('ankle boot, half-boot'), itself a diminutive of botte ('boot').

боцман.etymology: Borrowed under Peter the Great from Dutch bootsman (or Low German bōtsman, 'boatswain'), a compound of boot ('boat') + man ('man').

боязно.etymology: Impersonal predicate and adverb formed from боязный ('fearful, scary'), derived from боязнь ('fear, dread', from бояться 'to fear, be afraid', Proto-Slavic *bojati sę).

history.meaning: it is scary, one feels afraid

бояться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic боятися ('to fear, be afraid'), from Proto-Slavic *bojati sę, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰóyH-e- (cognate with Lithuanian bijotis 'to fear' and Sanskrit bháyate).

бравада.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French bravade ('boastful display of courage, swagger'), from Italian bravata / Spanish bravada (derived from bravo 'bold, fierce, brave').

браво.etymology: Borrowed via French bravo from Italian bravo! ('well done!, bold!, brave!'), originally an adjective meaning 'bold, wild, untamed' (likely from Vulgar Latin *brabus, from Latin barbarus or pravus).

брак.etymology: In the sense 'marriage, wedlock', adopted from Old Church Slavonic бракъ ('wedding, marriage'), formed from *bьrati / брать ('to take [a bride]', Proto-Slavic *borkъ) + suffix *-kъ. (Homonymous брак 'defective goods' is a seventeenth-century borrowing via Polish brak from Middle Low German brak 'flaw, breach', from breken 'to break'.)

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: брак

бракованный.etymology: Past passive participle of браковать ('to reject as defective, cull'), derived from брак ('flaw, defective merchandise'), borrowed in the seventeenth century via Polish brak / German Brack from Middle Low German brak ('breach, defect, substandard goods', from breken 'to break').

браковаться.etymology: Passive/reflexive form of браковать ('to sort out and reject defective goods', from брак 'defect' < Middle Low German brak 'flaw, break') + -ся.

бракосочетание.etymology: Adopted from Church Slavonic бракосъчетаниѥ ('joining in marriage, wedding ceremony'), a compound calque of Ancient Greek γαμοσυναφία combining бракъ ('marriage') + linking -о- + сочетание ('joining together, union').

браслет.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French bracelet ('wristband, bracelet'), diminutive of Old French bracel, from Latin brāchiāle ('armlet, bracelet'), derived from brāchium ('arm', from Ancient Greek βραχίων).

брат.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic братъ (older братръ), from Proto-Slavic *bratrъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr ('brother') — one of the most stable kinship words across Indo-European languages, cognate with English brother, Latin frāter, and Sanskrit bhrātṛ.
брат.notes: Notice the irregular collective-origin plural: **братья**, genitive **братьев**.

братан.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic братанъ (originally 'cousin, brother's son, elder brother' in Old East Slavic and dialects), formed from брат ('brother', Proto-Slavic *bratъ) + the kinship/augmentative suffix -ан; in modern colloquial Russian used for 'bro, pal'.

братец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic братьць, affectionate diminutive formed from брат ('brother', Proto-Slavic *bratъ < PIE *bʰréh₂tēr) + the suffix -ец.

братишка.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed with the suffix -ишка from брат ('brother'), inherited from Old East Slavic братъ, from Proto-Slavic *bratrъ / *bratъ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr.

братский.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic братьскыи, relational adjective formed from брат ('brother', Proto-Slavic *bratъ) + the suffix -ский.

брать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic брати (present беру, береши; Old Church Slavonic бьрати), from Proto-Slavic *bьrati ('to gather, take'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- ('to carry, bear, take'), directly cognate with English bear, Latin ferō, Ancient Greek φέρω, and Sanskrit bhárati.
брать.notes: Forms a classic suppletive aspect pair with perfective **взять** ('to take').

браться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic братися, reflexive of брать ('to take', Proto-Slavic *bьrati < PIE *bʰer- 'to bear, take') + -ся, meaning 'to take hold of, undertake, come from'.

history.meaning: to take hold of, get down to; to come from

браузер.etymology: Borrowed in the 1990s from English browser (short for web browser), agent noun from browse ('to look through casually, leaf through a book, graze').

бревно.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic брьвьно ('log, beam, timber'), derived from Proto-Slavic *brъvьno, from *brъvь ('plank, footbridge, beam, brow'; cognate with бровь 'eyebrow').

бред.etymology: Deverbal noun from брести (бреду, 'to wander aimlessly, wade') and бредить ('to rave, talk in one's sleep or fever', literally 'to wander in mind'), from Proto-Slavic *bresti (*bredǫ).

history.meaning: to wade, wander; to wander in mind

бременский.etymology: Relational adjective formed from the German city name Бремен (Bremen, famous in Russian culture through the Brothers Grimm tale and 1969 animated musical Бременские музыканты 'The Bremen Town Musicians') + suffix -ский.

бригада.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century (originally in the military sense 'brigade') via German Brigade from French brigade, from Italian brigata ('company, troop, crew'), derived from briga ('strife, bustle'). In the 20th century, Russian extended бригада to mean a coordinated work crew, medical team, or film crew.

бриллиант.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via German Brillant from French brillant ('shining, sparkling; cut diamond'), present participle of briller ('to shine, sparkle', from Italian brillare).

бритва.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бритва ('razor'), formed with instrument suffix -тва from брить ('to shave, cut'), from Proto-Slavic *britva (from *briti 'to shave, cut with a sharp edge').

брить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic брити (1sg. брѣю / брею), from Proto-Slavic *briti ('to shave, cut with a razor'), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreyH- ('to cut, shear'; cognate with Sanskrit bhrīṇāti 'to cut, injure').

бриться.etymology: Reflexive of брить ('to shave', inherited from Proto-Slavic *briti 'to cut with a sharp edge, shave', from PIE *bʰreyH- 'to cut sharply', cognate with Sanskrit bhrīṇāti) + -ся.

бродить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бродити ('to wade through water, wander about; to ferment'), from Proto-Slavic *broditi (iterative to *bresti 'to wade, plod', also the source of брод 'ford').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: бродить

бродяга.etymology: Formed in Russian with the expressive common-gender person suffix -яга (compare трудяга, бедняга) from бродить ('to wander, roam, tramp about', inherited from Old East Slavic бродити, Proto-Slavic *broditi, related to брод 'ford').

бронежилет.etymology: Compound coined in 20th-century Russian from броня ('armour', Old East Slavic броня 'coat of mail, breastplate', from Proto-Slavic *bronja) + linking vowel -е- + жилет ('vest, waistcoat', borrowed from French gilet).

history.meaning: armour + vest → bulletproof vest, body armor

бронзовый.etymology: Relational and colour adjective formed with the suffix -овый from бронза ('bronze'), borrowed in the eighteenth century via French bronze / German Bronze from Italian bronzo ('bell metal, bronze', of contested Persian or Late Latin origin).

бронирование.etymology: Verbal noun in -ние formed from бронировать ('to reserve, book'), built in 20th-century Russian on броня / бронь ('official reservation, protected quota', originally 'armour, protective breastplate').

бронированный.etymology: Past passive participle of бронировать ('to armor-plate'), derived from броня ('armor, mail', Old East Slavic броня, borrowed in Proto-Slavic *bronja from Gothic brunjo 'breastplate, coat of mail').

бронировать.etymology: Formed in 20th-century Russian with the verbal suffix -ировать from броня / бронь ('official protection, reserved quota, booking', which developed metaphorically from Old East Slavic броня 'armour, breastplate': securing a ticket or hotel room as if behind protective armour).

history.meaning: to secure a quota → to book, reserve

бронировать.notes: With stress on **-и-** (**бронировать**), it means 'to book, reserve' (a hotel room or ticket); with stress on **-а-** (**бронировать**), it means 'to armour-plate'.

бронхит.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from international medical New Latin bronchītis, formed from Ancient Greek βρόγχος (brónkhos, 'windpipe; pl. βρόγχια bronchial tubes') + the medical suffix -ītis ('inflammation', Russian -ит).

бронь.etymology: Formed in 20th-century Russian as a back-formation or clipped variant of броня ('official exemption, reserved quota, reservation'), which developed metaphorically from Old East Slavic броня ('coat of mail, armour', an early Slavic borrowing via Proto-Germanic *brunjǭ 'breastplate') — originally an 'armour-plated' ticket or official protection from requisitioning, then any hotel or ticket reservation.

бросать.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic бросати (originally 'to scrape, strip off, fling away'; compare Church Slavonic бръснути 'to shave, scrape' and Proto-Slavic *brъsati). In Russian its sense generalized from 'stripping or flinging off' to the everyday verb 'to throw, cast; to abandon'.

бросаться.etymology: Reflexive of бросать ('to throw, hurl, cast', in Proto-Slavic *brosati originally 'to scrape, strip off, scatter quickly') + -ся, meaning 'to throw oneself, rush, leap'.

бросить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бросити, from Proto-Slavic *brositi ('to scrape off, strip, fling, throw'). Originally referring to stripping flax or scraping off bark/buds, in Russian it became the general perfective verb for 'to throw, fling' and figuratively 'to abandon, quit, leave someone'.

history.meaning: to throw; to quit; to leave/dump (someone)

брошка.etymology: Colloquial diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from брошь ('brooch', borrowed from French broche).

брошь.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French broche ('ornamental pin, brooch; spit, needle'), from Vulgar Latin *brocca ('pointed tool, spike'), from Latin broccus ('projecting, buck-toothed', of Gaulish origin).

брусок.etymology: Diminutive in -ок of брус ('squared timber beam, bar'), inherited from Old East Slavic брусъ and Proto-Slavic *brusъ ('squared beam; whetstone, block').

history.meaning: beam → small block, bar (of wood or stone), whetstone

брызгать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic брызгати, from Proto-Slavic *bryzgati ('to splash, spurt, sprinkle'), of expressive/onomatopoeic origin.

брысь.etymology: Expressive interjection used to shoo away a cat, connected by Vasmer with брызгать ('to splash, spurt, scatter') or an imitative sibilant call.

history.meaning: exclamation to chase away a cat

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: брысь

брюки.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from Dutch broek or Low German brōk ('sailor's breeches, trousers'), from Proto-Germanic *brōks ('breeches, trousers', cognate with English breeches).

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: брюки

бублик.etymology: Borrowed into Russian from Ukrainian бублик ('ring-shaped boiled and baked bread roll'), diminutive of бубль ('bubble, swelling, round bump', from Proto-Slavic *bǫbьlь 'bubble, swelling, bud').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: бублик

буддийский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ский from буддизм / Будда ('Buddha'), borrowed from Sanskrit बुद्ध (Buddha, literally 'the Awakened One, the Enlightened One', past participle of budh- 'to awake, perceive, understand', cognate with Russian будить 'to wake up').

буддист.etymology: Formed from Будда ('the Buddha', from Sanskrit बुद्ध Buddha 'the Awakened/Enlightened One', past participle of budh- 'to awake, understand') + the personal suffix -ист.

будильник.etymology: Formed in Russian (partially calquing German Wecker or French réveil) from будильный ('waking'), built on будить ('to wake someone up', from Old East Slavic будити, Proto-Slavic *buditi, the o-grade causative of *bъděti 'to be awake, keep watch', from PIE *bʰewdʰ- 'to be awake, aware') + the instrument suffix -ник.

будить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic будити ('to wake up, rouse'), from Proto-Slavic *buditi (causative of *bъděti 'to be awake, keep watch'), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰowdʰéyeti ('to make awake, make aware').

будни.etymology: Plural noun arising by contraction of older Russian будние дни ('ordinary waking/working days', as opposed to church feast days), from the adjective будний (Old East Slavic будьнии дьнь), built on Proto-Slavic *budьnъ ('waking, alert, ordinary'), from the root *bud- / *bъd- of будить ('to wake') and бдеть ('to stay awake').

будто.etymology: Univerbation in Middle Russian of будь то ('be it that, suppose that'), combining будь (the second-person singular imperative of быть 'to be') with the neuter demonstrative pronoun то ('that').

будущее.etymology: Substantivized neuter of будущий ('future, coming'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бѫдѫщии (future active participle of быти 'to be', built on the future stem бѫд- / буду, Proto-Slavic *bǫdǫtjb), calquing Greek τὸ μέλλον and Latin futurum.

history.meaning: that which will be, the future

будущий.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic бѫдѫщии ('that which will be, future'), the active participle formed from the future stem бѫд- / буд- ('will be', 1st sg. буду) of быти / быть ('to be', Proto-Slavic *bǫdǫ from PIE *bʰuH- with nasal infix).

history.meaning: future, next (and neuter noun будущее 'the future')

буйабес.etymology: Borrowed in culinary usage from French bouillabaisse ('Provençal fish stew'), which comes from Provençal Occitan bolhabaissa, a vivid compound of two verb forms: bolhir ('to boil') + abaissar ('to lower [the heat]' — i.e., 'when it comes to a boil, lower the heat').

буйный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic буиныи ('fierce, bold, turbulent, luxuriant'), derived from Old East Slavic буи ('bold, fierce, wild, foolish', from Proto-Slavic *bujь 'vigorous, overgrown, wild', from PIE *bʰewH- 'to grow, swell, thrive').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: буйный

буква.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic букы (genitive букъве, plural букъви; Old Church Slavonic боукы, 'letter of the alphabet; beech tree'), from Proto-Slavic *buky, an early Slavic borrowing from Proto-Germanic *bōkō ('beech tree; carved beechwood rune-tablet, book', ancestor of English book and beech and German Buch / Buche). The modern nominative singular буква was rebuilt from the oblique stem букв-.

буквально.etymology: Adverb formed from буквальный ('literal, word-for-word'), calquing Latin litterālis / French littéral, built on буква ('letter of the alphabet', from Proto-Slavic *buky).

букет.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French bouquet ('nosegay, bunch of flowers; aroma of wine'), originally a Norman-Picard dialectal diminutive of Old French bosc / bois ('wood, grove, little clump of trees').

history.meaning: little wood, clump of foliage → bunch of flowers; wine aroma

букинист.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French bouquiniste 'dealer in second-hand and antiquarian books', from bouquin 'old book', itself taken from Middle Dutch boeckin ('little book').
букинист.notes: Букинистический магазин is the standard Russian name for a second-hand or antiquarian bookshop.

букинистический.etymology: Adjective formed with -ический from букинист ('dealer in second-hand and antiquarian books'), borrowed from French bouquiniste, from bouquin ('old book'), which French borrowed from Middle Dutch boeckijn ('little book', diminutive of boec 'book').

cognates.meaning: book (same Germanic root as Dutch boec)

буклет.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English booklet ('small thin book or folded printed brochure'), formed from book + the diminutive suffix -let.

букмекер.etymology: Borrowed in the late nineteenth century from English bookmaker ('person who takes and records bets in a betting book at races'), compounded from book + maker.

history.meaning: betting agent who keeps a book of odds

булочка.etymology: Formed in Russian as the affectionate diminutive (with suffix -очка) of булка ('white wheat roll or loaf'), borrowed via Polish bułka from Middle High German bulle or Latin bulla ('round swelling, bubble, round loaf').

булыжник.etymology: Formed with the suffix -ник from dialectal булыга ('rounded boulder, heavy lump of fieldstone, club'), an East Slavic word compared by Vasmer with Lithuanian bulis ('buttock, rounded mass') and Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- ('to swell, rounded object').

бульон.etymology: Borrowed from French bouillon 'broth', from bouillir 'to boil', which goes back to Latin bullire 'to bubble, boil' from bulla 'bubble'.
бульон.notes: Note how Russian spells the palatal French -ill- with льйо -> льо: бульон.

бумага.etymology: Recorded in Old Russian from the 14th century, first meaning 'cotton wool' (still seen in хлопчатобумажный 'cotton') and then 'rag paper'. Vasmer considers borrowing from Italian bambagia ('cotton', from Medieval Greek βάμβαξ, ultimately Persian pambak) the likeliest route.

бумажка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from бумага ('paper; official document'), attested in Old East Slavic since the 14th century (originally 'cotton wool, cotton rag paper', borrowed via Italian bambagia from Medieval Greek βαμβάκιον and Persian پمبه panba 'cotton').

бумажник.etymology: Formed in Russian from бумага ('paper; paper banknote') + the noun suffix -ник: originally a pocket case for carrying folded paper notes and documents, hence 'wallet'.

history.meaning: pocket wallet for notes and papers

morphemes.meaning: paper (from бумага with г -> ж alternation)

бумажный.etymology: Formed in Russian from бумага ('paper', historically 'cotton, rag paper' in 14th-century Old Russian, borrowed from Italian bambagia 'cotton') + the adjectival suffix -ный (with regular palatal alternation г → ж).

бункер.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from German Bunker ('reinforced underground shelter; coal storage compartment on a steamship'), which German had borrowed in the 19th century from English bunker (originally Scots bunker 'bench, chest, coal bin').

бунтарь.etymology: Formed in Russian from бунт ('mutiny, rebellion, riot', borrowed via Polish bunt from Middle High German bunt 'league, alliance, confederacy against authority', related to binden 'to bind') + the personal agent suffix -арь.

бургер.etymology: Borrowed in the late twentieth century from English burger, clipped from hamburger ('ground beef patty in a round bun', originally named after the German port city of Hamburg).

бурный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бурьныи, formed with the adjective suffix -ный from буря ('storm, tempest', inherited from Old East Slavic буря, Proto-Slavic *buŕa).

бурый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic буръ ('dark brown, greyish-brown'), cited by Vasmer either as an early borrowing from Turkic bur ('fox-colored, reddish-brown') or via Persia from Proto-Indo-European *bher- ('dark, brown').

буря.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic буря ('storm, tempest'), from Proto-Slavic *burja, from Proto-Indo-European *bheur- ('to boil, seethe, rage').

бутафорский.etymology: Derived in Russian with the adjective suffix -ский from бутафория / бутафор ('stage prop maker'), borrowed from Italian buttafuori ('stage manager, prop handler', literally 'throw outside', from buttare 'to throw' + fuori 'outside').

бутерброд.etymology: Borrowed from German Butterbrot, 'bread and butter', a compound of Butter 'butter' and Brot 'bread'. In Russian the word widened to any open sandwich, so a бутерброд can carry cheese or sausage and no butter at all.
бутерброд.notes: A sandwich made of two slices is often called сэндвич; бутерброд is usually open.

бутик.etymology: Colloquial Russian clipping of бутерброд ('open sandwich') suffixed with the diminutive -ик, shaped playfully as a homonym of бутик ('boutique'); бутерброд itself was borrowed from German Butterbrot ('buttered bread').

бутылка.etymology: Formed in Early Modern Russian (attested from 1695 in the Petrine era) with the native suffix -ка from бутыль ('large glass bottle, carboy'), borrowed via Polish butelka / butla from French bouteille ('bottle'), which goes back to Late Latin buticula ('small wine-skin or flask').

бутылочка.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed with the suffix -очка from бутылка ('bottle'), which entered Russian in the Petrine era (1694) via Polish butelka / Ukrainian бутель from French bouteille ('bottle'), ultimately from Late Latin butticula ('small cask or flask').

буфетчик.etymology: Formed in Russian from буфет ('sideboard, refreshment counter, buffet') + the agent suffix -чик; буфет was borrowed in the 18th century from French buffet.

буханка.etymology: Formed with -ка from dialectal бухон 'round loaf', borrowed via Polish bochen 'loaf of bread' and Old High German fohhenza, ultimately going back to Latin focacium 'hearth-baked bread' (from focus 'hearth', the same Latin source as Italian focaccia).

бухать.etymology: Colloquial Russian verb ('to drink alcohol heavily, booze'), derived from onomatopoeic бухнуть / бухать ('to thump, bang, splash, pour or dump liquid heavily into a glass').

буше.etymology: Borrowed from French bouchée ('mouthful; small filled pastry or sponge cake'), a derivative of bouche ('mouth'), from Latin bucca ('cheek, mouth').

бы.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бы ('would'), originally the 2nd and 3rd person singular aorist of быти ('to be', from Proto-Slavic *byti, Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH-), which grammaticalized into the conditional/subjunctive particle.

бывать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic бывати ('to happen, occur, visit frequently'), from Proto-Slavic *byvati, iterative/frequentative of *byti ('to be').

history.meaning: to happen, occur; to be (from time to time)

бывшая.etymology: Substantivized feminine form of бывший ('former, past'), historically the past active participle of быть ('to be'), from Proto-Slavic *byti, from Proto-Indo-European *bheuH- ('to become, be').

бывший.etymology: Lexicalized past active participle of быть ('to be', Old East Slavic быти, Proto-Slavic *byti, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- 'to become, grow, be'). From its literal participial sense 'having been', it became the standard adjective for 'former, ex-'.

быстрее.etymology: Comparative degree formed with the productive comparative suffix -ее from быстрый ('fast, quick, swift', from Old East Slavic быстръ, Proto-Slavic *bystrъ).

быстренько.etymology: Colloquial adverb formed from быстренький, the affectionate diminutive (with suffix -еньк-) of быстрый ('fast, quick'), from Proto-Slavic *bystrъ ('swift, clear, sharp').

быстро.etymology: Adverb formed from the short neuter of быстрый ('fast, swift, rapid'), inherited from Old East Slavic быстръ ('swift-flowing, keen, quick'), from Proto-Slavic *bystrъ.

быстрый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic быстръ / быстрыи ('swift-flowing, rapid, keen'), from Proto-Slavic *bystrъ (originally applied to rushing mountain streams, with an epenthetic -t- inserted in the cluster -sr- from an older root *bys-rъ 'gushing, rushing'; compare Old Norse bysia 'to gush forth').

быть.etymology: Быть is an inherited Slavic verb. Vasmer compares Lithuanian būti and older Indo-European words for being, becoming and coming into existence. That older family helps explain why the history of this everyday verb reaches beyond the modern English gloss to be.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: быть

бюджет.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via French budget and English budget ('chancellor's leather bag containing financial statements; financial plan'), from Middle French bougette ('small leather pouch'), diminutive of bouge (from Latin bulga 'leather bag', of Gaulish origin).

бюджетный.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ный from бюджет ('budget'), borrowed in the 19th century via French budget from English budget (originally 'the leather pouch or bag in which the Chancellor of the Exchequer carried his financial statement to Parliament', from Old French bougette 'little leather bag').

history.meaning: leather pouch → state financial plan, budget

бюллетень.etymology: Borrowed from French bulletin ('official report, ballot slip'), from Italian bullettino ('official note, pass'), diminutive of bulletta / bulla, from Medieval Latin bulla ('sealed document, papal bull'). In Soviet and modern Russian also used for a medical sick-leave certificate.

бюро.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th centuries from French bureau ('writing desk; office, agency'), originally Old French burel ('coarse woollen baize cloth used to cover writing tables', then the writing table itself, and finally the office room where clerks worked). Indeclinable in Russian (e.g. бюро находок 'lost-and-found office').

в.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic въ, from Proto-Slavic *vъ(n) ('in, into'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *h₁en ('in') with a prosthetic labial glide *v- added before the reduced vowel. Its original final nasal *-n survives in combinations with third-person pronouns (в нём, в него) and in older compounds such as внутрь.
в.notes: Takes the prepositional case for static location (в комнате) and the accusative case for motion into a place (в комнату); becomes во before certain consonant clusters (во дворе).

в-третьих.etymology: Parenthetical adverbial formed from the preposition в ('in') + the locative plural of третий ('third'), from Proto-Slavic *tretьjь ('third'), from Proto-Indo-European *tritjos.

вагон.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via French wagon or German Waggon from English waggon / wagon ('wheeled cart, railway car'), itself from Dutch wagen, from Proto-Germanic *wagnaz ('wagon').

важный.etymology: Borrowed via Ukrainian важливий / важний and Polish ważny ('weighty, important'), derived from waga ('scales, weight'), itself borrowed from Middle High German wāge ('balance, weight').

ваза.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French vase or German Vase from Italian vaso, from Latin vasum / vas ('vessel, dish, utensil').

вакансия.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish wakans / wakancja from Medieval Latin vacantia ('an unoccupied post or church benefice'), derived from Latin vacāns, present participle of vacāre ('to be empty, unoccupied, free').

вакцина.etymology: Borrowed via French vaccine or scientific New Latin vaccina from Latin vaccinus ('relating to cows', from vacca 'cow'), coined by Edward Jenner in 1798 for cowpox inoculation against smallpox.

валенок.etymology: Singular back-formation with -ок from plural валенки ('felted wool boots'), derived from the passive participle валеный of валять ('to full, felt wool, roll'), from Proto-Slavic *valjati.

валет.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French valet ('page, squire, knave in playing cards'), from Old French vaslet / varlet ('young nobleman, squire'), from Medieval Latin vassellittus, diminutive of vassallus ('vassal').

валик.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ик from вал ('cylindrical roller, shaft, axle'), which was borrowed via Polish wał from Middle High German wal / walle ('cylinder, roller', related to German Walze 'roller').

history.meaning: shaft, roller → paint roller, cylindrical bolster cushion

валить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic валити ('to roll, topple, heap up; to surge in a crowd'), from Proto-Slavic *valiti (causative/iterative of *velti 'to roll', cognate with волна 'wave'). From the intransitive sense 'to surge or pour out in a mass' (народ валит) developed the colloquial imperative and slang sense 'to clear out, get lost' (Вали отсюда!).

history.meaning: to knock down; to blame (валить на кого-то); (slang) to get lost, leave

rootFamily.gloss: to knock down; (slang) to take off, leave

валиться.etymology: Reflexive and intransitive counterpart of валить ('to topple, throw down, roll'), inherited from Old East Slavic валитисѧ, from Proto-Slavic *valiti sę ('to topple, tumble down').

history.meaning: to tumble down, collapse, fall apart

вальс.etymology: Borrowed from French valse, which in turn comes from German Walzer, a noun from walzen 'to turn, to roll'. The dance is named for its turning steps.

валять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic валяти ('to roll, tumble'), from Proto-Slavic *valjati, an iterative-causative verb related to *valiti ('to roll, throw down'), from Proto-Indo-European *welH- ('to turn, roll').

history.meaning: to roll, felt; to play the fool (валять дурака)

валяться.etymology: Reflexive and middle-voice form of валять ('to roll, toss about') with the suffix -ся, from Proto-Slavic *valjati sę ('to roll oneself, lie scattered around').

вампир.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via Western European languages (German Vampir, French vampire) from Serbian вампир, descending from Proto-Slavic *ǫpyrь ('vampire, revenant', compare native Russian упырь).

ванильный.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ный from ваниль ('vanilla'), borrowed via French vanille and German Vanille from Spanish vainilla ('vanilla pod', literally 'little sheath'), diminutive of vaina from Latin vagina ('sheath, pod').

ванна.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from German Wanne ('bath, tub'), from Old High German wanna ('winnowing basket; oval bathing tub'), itself an early borrowing from Latin vannus ('winnowing fan or basket').

history.meaning: bathtub; bath (принять ванну 'to take a bath')

ванна.notes: Distinguish ванна (the bathtub itself, or a bath: принять ванну) from ванная (substantivized adjective for the bathroom: в ванной).

ванная.etymology: Substantivized feminine adjective from ванная комната ('bath room'), derived from ванна ('bathtub'), which was borrowed in the 18th century from German Wanne ('tub, bath', originally 'winnowing basket', from Latin vannus).
ванная.notes: Declines like a feminine adjective (**в ванной**, **из ванной**); the bathtub itself is the noun **ванна**.

варвар.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic варъваръ from Byzantine Greek βάρβαρος (várvaros, earlier bárbaros, 'foreigner, non-Greek'), an onomatopoeic reduplication imitating unintelligible foreign speech ('bar-bar').

варварство.etymology: Formed with the abstract noun suffix -ство from варвар ('barbarian'), ultimately from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος ('non-Greek, foreigner').

варенье.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic варение ('boiling, cooked dish, fruit preserves'), a verbal noun from варить ('to boil, cook', from Proto-Slavic *variti, causative of *vьrěti 'to bubble, boil', from PIE *wer- 'to burn, be hot'). In Russian cuisine варенье specifically names whole-berry or fruit preserves boiled in sugar syrup.

history.meaning: to boil, cook → boiled dish, preserves

вариант.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via German Variante or French variante from Latin variāns (genitive variantis, 'varying, differing'), present participle of variāre ('to vary, change, diversify'), from varius ('varied, diverse').

варить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic варити ('to boil, cook, brew'), from Proto-Slavic *variti, causative of *vьrěti ('to boil, bubble, seethe'), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- ('to burn, heat').

вариться.etymology: Reflexive and middle/intransitive form of варить ('to boil, cook', from Proto-Slavic *variti) formed with the enclitic -ся.

варёный.etymology: Adjectival passive participle of варить ('to boil, cook'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *variti ('to boil, cook'), causative of *vьrěti ('to boil, bubble'), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- ('to burn, heat').

вафельный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from вафля ('waffle, wafer').

вафля.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from German Waffel ('waffle, wafer'), from Middle Low German wāfel ('honeycomb-patterned cake'), related to Proto-Germanic *wabila- / *webaną ('to weave', after the grid pattern of the waffle iron).

ваш.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вашь (f. ваша, n. ваше), from Proto-Slavic *vašь ('your, yours [plural]'), formed from the second-person plural oblique pronoun stem *va- / *vo- (seen in вас, вам; compare Latin vōs 'you') + possessive suffix *-sjь.

вбегать.etymology: Imperfective of вбежать ('to run in'), formed from в- ('in, into') + бегать ('to run', inherited from Old East Slavic бѣгати, Proto-Slavic *běgati).

вбежать.etymology: Formed from the directional prefix в- ('in, into') + бежать ('to run', inherited from Old East Slavic бѣжати, from Proto-Slavic *běžati).

вбить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from в- ('into') + бить ('to beat, strike'), from Proto-Slavic *vъbiti ('to drive in, hammer in'), from *biti ('to strike').

history.meaning: to hammer in; to enter into a bill

вверх.etymology: Univerbation of the Old East Slavic directional phrase въ вьрхъ ('into the top, upward'), combining the preposition в ('into') with the accusative singular of верх ('top, upper part', from Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ).

вверху.etymology: Adverb formed in East Slavic by fusing the preposition в ('in, at') with верху (locative singular in -у of верх 'top, upper part', from Old East Slavic вьрхъ and Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ).

ввести.etymology: Borrowed or shaped via Old Church Slavonic въвести (and inherited Old East Slavic въвести), from в- ('in, into') + вести ('to lead'), from Proto-Slavic *vesti ('to lead').

ввинтить.etymology: Formed with the prefix в- ('in, into') + винтить ('to screw'), a denominative verb from винт ('screw, spiral thread'), which entered Russian via Polish gwint from Early New High German Gewinde ('spiral thread, winding, screw', from winden 'to wind, twist').

history.meaning: screw → to screw in, bolt in

вводить.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of ввести, formed from в- ('in, into') + водить ('to lead', iterative of вести), from Proto-Slavic *vъvoditi ('to lead in, bring in').

вводиться.etymology: Passive and reflexive derivative of вводить ('to introduce, bring in') formed with the postfix -ся, from в- + водить + -ся.

ввязаться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed from в- ('into') + вязать ('to tie, bind, knit', inherited from Old East Slavic вѧзати, Proto-Slavic *vęzati) + -ся: literally 'to tie or knot oneself into something', hence 'to get entangled or mixed up in a fight, argument, or risky venture'.

history.meaning: to get mixed up in, get embroiled in

вдвое.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в двое ('into two, twofold'), combining the preposition в with двое ('two, a pair', collective numeral from Proto-Slavic *dъvoje, built on два 'two').

history.meaning: in two, twice as much, twofold

вдвойне.etymology: Adverb formed from the preposition в ('in') + the old locative singular of двойной / двойня ('double, twofold'), derived from двое / два ('two', Proto-Slavic *dъva).

вдвоём.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в двоем ('in a group of two'), from в ('in') + locative singular of the collective numeral двое ('two', from Proto-Slavic *dъvoje).

history.meaning: the two of us/them, two together

вдоль.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в доль ('in length, lengthwise'), from в ('in') + доль ('length, valley', related to дол and длинный, from Proto-Slavic *dolъ / *dьlgъ).

вдох.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from вдохнуть ('to breathe in, inhale'), built from prefix в- ('in') + дохнуть / дышать ('to breathe', from Proto-Slavic *dъxnǫti, with strong yer ъ vocalized to о in вдох; from the same root as дух 'breath, spirit' and воздух 'air').

вдохнуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective formed from the prefix в- ('in') + дохнуть ('to breathe', from Proto-Slavic *dъxnǫti, related to дух 'breath, spirit' and дышать 'to breathe').

вдруг.etymology: Formed from the preposition в ('in, at') + друг ('other, one another', from Proto-Slavic *drugъ), originally meaning 'all at once, together with one another' before shifting to 'suddenly'.

вдыхать.etymology: Imperfective verb paired with вдохнуть ('to inhale, breathe in'), formed with prefix в- ('in') + дыхать ('to breathe', iterative stem of дышать / дохнуть, from Proto-Slavic *dyxati, related by lengthened ablaut to дух 'breath, spirit').

вегетарианец.etymology: Formed in Russian with the person suffix -ец from English vegetarian (and German Vegetarianer / French végétarien), coined in England in the 1840s from vegetable (from Late Latin vegetābilis 'growing, flourishing, plant', from Latin vegetāre 'to enliven') + -arian.

вегетарианка.etymology: Feminine noun in -ка from вегетарианец ('vegetarian'), borrowed in the late 19th century from English vegetarian (coined in Britain c. 1839–1847 from vegetable + -arian, ultimately from Late Latin vegetābilis 'animating, growing').

вегетарианский.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ский from вегетарианец ('vegetarian'), borrowed in the late 19th century from English vegetarian (coined in the 1840s from vegetable + -arian, ultimately from Late Latin vegetabilis 'animating, growing').

ведомо.etymology: Surviving mainly in the phrase без ведома ('without someone's knowledge'), originally the neuter singular present passive participle вѣдомо ('known') of вѣдати ('to know'), from Proto-Slavic *věděti ('to know'), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- ('to see, know').

ведомость.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣдомость ('knowledge, report, inventory'), formed with the abstract suffix -ость from вѣдомыи ('known', old present passive participle of вѣдати 'to know', Proto-Slavic *vědati, from PIE *weyd- 'to see, know'). Under Peter the Great, Ведомости also became the title of Russia's first printed newspaper (1702).

history.meaning: official list, register, payroll or grade sheet

ведро.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣдро ('bucket, pail, liquid measure'), from Proto-Slavic *vědro, derived with the instrument suffix *-ro from Proto-Indo-European *wed- ('water'; cognate with вода 'water').

ведущий.etymology: Substantivized and adjectival present active participle of вести ('to lead, conduct'), from Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic ведущии, from Proto-Slavic *vedǫtji ('leading').

ведь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣдь, originally a shortened form of the ancient perfect/present verb вѣдѣ ('I know') or imperative вѣждь ('know!'), from Old East Slavic вѣдѣти ('to know', Proto-Slavic *věděti). It grammaticalized into a conversational discourse particle meaning 'after all, as you know, you see'.

вежливо.etymology: Adverb formed from вежливый ('polite, courteous'), derived from Old East Slavic вѣжа ('knower, person well-versed in customs and etiquette', from вѣдати 'to know', Proto-Slavic *vědati; compare the negative counterpart невежа 'boor, rude person').

вежливость.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from вежливый ('polite, courteous'), which derives from Old Russian вѣжа ('one who knows customs and manners'), from вѣдати ('to know', Proto-Slavic *věděti).

вежливый.etymology: Developed from Old Russian вѣжливыи ('knowing how to behave, courteous, well-mannered'), derived from older вѣжа ('one who knows customs, an expert', the positive counterpart of modern невежа 'boor, ignorant person'), built on the Old East Slavic verb вѣдати ('to know', from Proto-Slavic *věděti, PIE *weyd- 'to see, know'; cognate with English wit and wise).

history.meaning: to know → one who knows proper custom

везде.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьсьде ('everywhere', Old Church Slavonic вьсьде), from Proto-Slavic *vьsьde, compounded from the stem of весь ('all, every', Proto-Slavic *vьsь) + the locative adverbial suffix *-de (seen in где 'where' and здесь 'here'), with regular voicing сд > зд after loss of the weak yer.

morphemes.meaning: all, every (from вьсь, with с → з before д)

везти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic везти (1sg. везу), from Proto-Slavic *vezti ('to convey in a vehicle'), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- ('to go, transport in a vehicle'; cognate with English wagon, way, weigh, and Latin vehere). The impersonal idiom кому-либо везёт ('someone is lucky') arose from the image of one's cart or sledge pulling smoothly.

history.meaning: to transport by cart, boat, or sledge
to transport, drive; (impers.) везёт 'to be lucky'

везунчик.etymology: Colloquial noun formed in Russian with the affectionate person suffix -чик from везун ('lucky person'), derived from the impersonal verb везти (кому-либо везёт 'someone has good luck').

history.meaning: to have luck → lucky person, lucky dog

век.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣкъ ('lifespan, age, century, eternity', originally 'vital force, vigor'), from Proto-Slavic *věkъ, from Proto-Indo-European *weyk- ('vital force, energy'; cognate with Lithuanian viekas 'strength, life').

велеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic велѣти ('to command, wish'), from Proto-Slavic *velěti ('to wish, command'), from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- ('to choose, wish'; cognate with Latin velle and English will).

великий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic великыи (and Old Church Slavonic великъ, extended with -ик- from older вель / велии 'great'), from Proto-Slavic *velikъ ('great, large').
великий.notes: In modern Russian, the long form **великий** means 'great, eminent' (Пётр Великий), whereas the short form **велик / велика / велики** means 'too big (in clothing/shoe size)' (*костюм мне велик*).

великоватый.etymology: Formed with the attenuative suffix -оват- ('somewhat, slightly too') from великий ('big, great; too large in short forms велик'), from Proto-Slavic *velikъ ('big, great').

великодушно.etymology: Adverb derived from великодушный ('magnanimous, generous'), an Old Church Slavonic calque (великодушьнъ) of Greek μεγαλόψυχος (megalópsychos, 'great-souled'), from великий ('great') + душа ('soul').

великолепие.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic великолѣпиѥ ('magnificence, splendor'), a calque of Greek μεγαλοπρέπεια (megaloprépeia, 'befitting a great person, magnificence'), from великий ('great') + лѣпыи ('fitting, beautiful').

великолепно.etymology: Adverb formed from великолепный ('magnificent, splendid'), derived from Old Church Slavonic великолѣпие, a calque on Ancient Greek μεγαλοπρέπεια (megaloprépeia, 'magnificence'), from великий ('great') + лѣпый ('fitting, beautiful, comely', Proto-Slavic *lěpъ).

великолепный.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic великолѣпьнъ ('magnificently fitting, majestic, splendid'), a calque of Ancient Greek μεγαλοπρεπής (megaloprepḗs, 'befitting a great person, magnificent'), compounded from великъ ('great') + лѣпъ ('fitting, comely, beautiful', from Proto-Slavic *lěpъ, preserved in нелепый 'absurd, unfitting' and Ukrainian ліпий / гарний).

величество.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic величьство ('greatness, majesty'), formed from великий ('great', Proto-Slavic *velikъ) + abstract suffix -ьство, later used as a translation of Latin maiestas ('Majesty') in royal titles.

велосипед.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French vélocipède ('early bicycle', coined in 1818 in France), a classical compound of Latin vēlōx (stem vēlōci-, 'swift, rapid') + pēs (stem ped-, 'foot') — literally 'swift-foot'. While French later replaced vélocipède with bicyclette / vélo, Russian kept велосипед as the standard word for a bicycle.

венец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣньць and reinforced by Old Church Slavonic вѣньць ('wreath, crown'), diminutive of Proto-Slavic *věnъ ('braided wreath, garland'), from *viti ('to twist, weave', PIE *weh₁y-).

веник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣникъ ('bundle of leafy twigs, besom broom'), from Proto-Slavic *věnikъ, derived from *věnъ ('bundle, wreath'), from *viti ('to plait, bind').

венок.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣнъкъ ('garland, wreath'), a diminutive with suffix -ок of Proto-Slavic *věnъ ('braided wreath'), from the root of *viti ('to weave, plait').

вентиль.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th centuries from German Ventil ('valve, tap, shut-off cock'), from Medieval Latin ventīle ('sluice gate, air-vent'), derived from Latin ventus ('wind, air').

вентилятор.etymology: Borrowed via German Ventilator from Latin ventilator 'winnower, airer', an agent noun from ventilare 'to fan, wave in the air', itself built on ventus 'wind'.

вентиляция.etymology: Borrowed via German Ventilation or French ventilation from Latin ventilatio ('an airing, winnowing'), from ventilare ('to fan, air, winnow'), derived from ventus ('wind').

венчик.etymology: Diminutive of венец ('crown, rim') or веник ('twig broom, whisk') formed with the suffix -чик, used in culinary Russian for a wire whisk (originally a bundle of peeled twigs used for whipping).

вера.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣра ('faith, trust, oath'), from Proto-Slavic *věra ('faith, belief'), from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁ro- ('true, trustworthy'; cognate with Latin verus 'true' and German wahr).

веранда.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via English veranda and French véranda from Hindi varanda / Bengali baranda, itself borrowed from Portuguese varanda ('railing, balcony, terrace').

вердикт.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via French verdict and English verdict from Anglo-Norman verdit ('true declaration of a jury'), from Medieval Latin vērē dictum ('truly said, true finding', from Latin vērus 'true' + dictum 'said, statement').

верить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣрити ('to believe, trust'), a denominative verb formed from вѣра ('faith, belief, trust'), from Proto-Slavic *věra (related to Latin vērus 'true' and German wahr 'true', from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁ro-).

вериться.etymology: Impersonal reflexive verb formed with -ся from верить ('to believe'), from Old East Slavic вѣрити ('to believe, trust'), derived from вѣра ('faith, belief', Proto-Slavic *věra).

верно.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣрьно ('faithfully, truly'), adverb of вѣрьныи (modern верный 'faithful, true, correct'), derived from вера ('faith, trust, truth', from Proto-Slavic *věra).

верность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from верный ('faithful, loyal, true'), from Old East Slavic вѣрьныи, derived from вѣра ('faith, trust', Proto-Slavic *věra).

вернуть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьрнути ('to turn back, give back, return'), formed with the semelfactive/perfective suffix -нуть (with simplification of *rtn > рн) from the Proto-Slavic root *vьrtěti ('to turn', modern Russian вертеть, from PIE *wert- 'to turn'; cognate with Latin vertō).

вернуться.etymology: Reflexive form of вернуть ('to turn back, return', with simplification of -тн- > -н- from вертнуть, semelfactive of вертеть 'to turn, spin', from Proto-Slavic *vьrtěti) + -ся.

верный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣрьныи (and Old Church Slavonic вѣрьнъ 'faithful, true, trustworthy'), formed with the suffix -ный from вѣра ('faith, trust, truth'), from Proto-Slavic *věra (cognate with Latin vērus 'true' and German wahr 'true').

вероятно.etymology: Adverb and parenthetical word formed from вероятный ('probable, likely'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вѣроѩтьнъ ('credible, worthy of belief'), a compound calque of Ancient Greek πιθανός / Latin vērīsimilis combining вѣра ('faith, belief', Proto-Slavic *věra) + ѩти ('to take, accept', Proto-Slavic *jęti — literally 'acceptable on faith, believable').

версия.etymology: Borrowed via French version and German Version from Medieval Latin versiō ('a turning, translation, rendering, interpretation'), derived from Latin vertere ('to turn').

верующий.etymology: Present active participle (and substantivized noun meaning 'a religious believer') of веровать ('to believe, have religious faith'), inherited via Old Church Slavonic вѣровати and Old East Slavic вѣровати from вера ('faith, belief', Proto-Slavic *věra, cognate with Latin vērus 'true').

верх.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьрхъ ('top, summit, upper part'), from Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ, from Proto-Indo-European *wers- ('top, peak, high point'; cognate with Lithuanian viršus 'top' and Latin verruca).

верхний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьрхьнии ('upper, top'), derived from верх ('top, summit, upper part', from Old East Slavic вьрхъ, Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ, cognate with Lithuanian viršùs 'top, peak') + the spatial adjectival suffix -ний.

верхушка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the suffix -ушка from верх ('top, upper part, summit'), inherited from Old East Slavic вьрхъ and Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ.

history.meaning: top → very top, tip, crown (of a tree or pastry)

вершина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьршина ('top, summit'), formed with the singulative/locative suffix -ина from вьрхъ (modern верх, 'top, upper part'), from Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ ('peak, top').

вершить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьршити ('to top off a stack, bring to completion, decide'), denominative verb from вьрхъ (верх, 'top, summit', Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ).

верёвка.etymology: Diminutive-type derivative of dialectal and Old East Slavic вервь ('cord, measuring rope'), from Proto-Slavic *vьrvь ('rope, cord'), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- ('to turn, twist, bind').

вес.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣсъ ('weight, balance scale'), from Proto-Slavic *věsъ ('weight, hanging'), avrddhi-grade noun from the root of *visěti ('to hang') and *věsiti ('to hang, weigh').

веселиться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic веселитисѧ ('to rejoice, make merry'), reflexive of веселить ('to gladden, cheer'), derived from весёлый ('merry, cheerful, joyful', Proto-Slavic *veselъ).

весело.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicative form of весёлый ('merry, cheerful, joyful'), inherited from Old East Slavic весело, from Proto-Slavic *veselo ('merrily, joyfully').

веселье.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic веселие ('joy, merriment, feast'), abstract noun derived from весёлый ('merry, joyful, glad', from Proto-Slavic *veselъ).

весенний.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ний from весна ('spring', inserting a fleeting е in the stem весн-), inherited from Old East Slavic весна and Proto-Slavic *vesna ('spring', from Proto-Indo-European *wésr̥, cognate with Latin vēr and Lithuanian vasara 'summer').

весна.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic весна ('spring'), from Proto-Slavic *vesna, from Proto-Indo-European *wésr̥ (genitive *wesnós, 'spring'; cognate with Lithuanian vasara 'summer', Latin ver, and Sanskrit vasantá).

вести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вести (1sg. веду, 'to lead, conduct'), from Proto-Slavic *vesti, from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰ- ('to lead, conduct'; cognate with Lithuanian vesti).

весть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣсть ('news, Tidings, report'), from Proto-Slavic *věstь ('knowledge, message'), formed from *věd-ti (the root of *věděti 'to know', PIE *weyd-).

весь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьсь (f. вься, n. вьсе, pl. вьси), from Proto-Slavic *vьxъ / *vьśь ('all, the whole'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *wih₁so- ('all, whole'; cognate with Lithuanian vìsas 'all' and Sanskrit víśva 'every, all').

весьма.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вьсьма ('completely, altogether, very'), an archaic instrumental form built on вьсь (весь, 'all, whole', Proto-Slavic *vьxъ / *vьsь).

весёлый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic веселыи (and Old Church Slavonic веселъ 'merry, joyful, glad'), from Proto-Slavic *veselъ ('joyful, merry'), with close Baltic cognates (Latvian vesels 'healthy, whole, hale'). The semantic shift between 'healthy, hale, vigorous' (Baltic) and 'merry, cheerful' (Slavic) is an ancient Balto-Slavic development.

ветер.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣтръ ('wind'), from Proto-Slavic *větrъ, derived with the instrument/agent suffix *-trъ from *věti ('to blow', Russian веять), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁ntos ('wind'; cognate with Latin ventus and English wind).

ветеран.etymology: Borrowed via French vétéran or German Veteran from Latin veteranus ('old, experienced soldier'), derived from vetus, genitive veteris ('old, aged'; cognate with Russian ветхий 'ancient, decrepit').

ветеринар.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via French vétérinaire and German Veterinär from Latin veterīnārius ('relating to draught cattle and beasts of burden; cattle physician'), derived from veterīnae ('beasts of burden').

ветерок.etymology: Affectionate diminutive of ветер ('wind') formed with the masculine diminutive suffix -ок (with fleeting vowel е). Russian ветер descends from Old East Slavic вѣтръ and Proto-Slavic *větrъ ('wind, air'), built with the instrumental suffix *-trъ on the PIE verb root *h2weh1- ('to blow'). It is directly cognate with English wind, weather, and Latin ventus.

ветка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from earlier ветвь ('branch, bough, twig'), inherited from Old East Slavic вѣтвь, from Proto-Slavic *větvь (related to вить 'to twine, plait').

веточка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -очка from ветка ('branch'), itself from Proto-Slavic *větvь ('branch, twig').

ветреный.etymology: Formed with the adjective suffix -еный from ветер ('wind', inherited from Old East Slavic вѣтръ, from Proto-Slavic *větrъ, from PIE *h₂wéh₁tros 'wind', cognate with English wind and weather). From 'swept by the wind' came the figurative sense 'flighty, fickle, changeable like the wind'.
ветреный.notes: Spelled with a single -н- (ветреный день 'windy day', ветреный человек 'fickle person'), except when prefixed (безветренный 'windless').

ветчина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ветъшина ('cured or aged meat, ham', attested in the 16th-century Domostroi), formed with the meat-designation suffix -ина (as in свинина, говядина, баранина) from ветхий ('old, aged', Old East Slavic ветъхъ, Proto-Slavic *vetъxъ 'old', cognate with Latin vetus 'old'), with dissimilation of -тш- > -тч-. Originally ветчина meant 'aged/cured salted pork' as opposed to fresh pork (свежина).

вечер.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вечеръ, from Proto-Slavic *večerъ, closely cognate with Lithuanian vãkaras and Latvian vakars ('evening'), and compared by Vasmer with Latin vesper and Ancient Greek ἕσπερος.

вечеринка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the compound suffix -инка (diminutive of dialectal/archaic вечерина 'evening gathering') from вечер ('evening', Old East Slavic вечеръ, Proto-Slavic *večerъ).

вечерний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вечернии ('of the evening'), formed from вечер ('evening', from Proto-Slavic *večerъ) + the temporal adjectival suffix -ний.

вечером.etymology: Lexicalized instrumental singular of вечер ('evening'), used adverbially to express time when ('in the evening'). Inherited from Old East Slavic вечеръ, from Proto-Slavic *večerъ (compare Lithuanian vãkaras 'evening').

вечно.etymology: Adverb formed from вечный ('eternal, perpetual'), derived from век ('age, century, lifetime', from Proto-Slavic *věkъ).

вечность.etymology: Derived with the abstract noun suffix -ость from вечный ('eternal'), from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic вѣчьныи, derived from вѣкъ (век, 'age, lifetime, eternity', Proto-Slavic *věkъ).

вечный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣчьныи / Old Church Slavonic вѣчьнъ ('eternal, everlasting'), formed with the suffix -ный from век ('age, lifetime, eternity', from Proto-Slavic *věkъ).

вешалка.etymology: Formed with the instrument/place suffix -лка from вешать ('to hang up'), iterative of весить ('to hang'), from Proto-Slavic *věšati ('to hang repeatedly').

вешать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣшати ('to hang, suspend'), from Proto-Slavic *věšati, causative/iterative related to висеть ('to hang', *visěti).

вешаться.etymology: Reflexive form of вешать ('to hang') with the suffix -ся, from Proto-Slavic *věšati sę ('to hang oneself, cling to someone').

history.meaning: to hang oneself; to throw oneself at someone
