вещдок.etymology: 20th-century Russian legal and police syllabic abbreviation of вещественное доказательство ('material/physical evidence'), combining вещественный ('material, physical', from вещь 'thing') and доказательство ('proof, evidence').

вещество.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вещьство ('nature, essence, substance'), formed from вещь ('thing, matter', Proto-Slavic *vektь) + abstract suffix -ьство, used as a calque of Greek οὐσία and Latin substantia.

вещичка.etymology: Affectionate diminutive of вещь ('thing, item') formed via вещица + suffix -ка; вещь comes from Old Church Slavonic вещь ('thing, matter'), from Proto-Slavic *vektь.

вещь.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вещь ('thing, matter, word', with South Slavic щ < *ktj), from Proto-Slavic *vekťь, related to *věkťati (Russian вещать 'to speak solemnly, proclaim'), originally 'something spoken of, matter, affair'.

взаимно.etymology: Adverb derived from взаимный ('mutual, reciprocal'), built on the older phrase въ заимъ ('on loan, in exchange'), from заимъ / заём ('loan, taking in turn', from за- + ять / иметь 'to take').

взаимность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from взаимный ('mutual, reciprocal'), from the historical phrase въ заимъ ('in exchange, reciprocally').

взаимовыгодный.etymology: Compound adjective formed from взаимно / взаимо- ('mutually') + выгодный ('profitable, advantageous', from выгода 'benefit, profit').

взаймы.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в займы (accusative plural of заём, Old East Slavic заимъ 'loan'), formed from за- + *jęti ('to take', Proto-Slavic *zaiti / *zajьmъ).

взбесить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вз- ('up, into an intense state') + бесить ('to madden, enrage'), which derives from бес ('demon, evil spirit', Proto-Slavic *běsъ).

history.meaning: to infuriate, drive into a rage

взбивать.etymology: Imperfective of взбить ('to beat up, fluff up, whisk'), formed from the upward/intensive prefix вз- + бить ('to beat, strike', from Proto-Slavic *biti).

взбить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вз- ('upward') + бить ('to beat, strike', Proto-Slavic *biti), literally 'to beat up into a froth or fluff'.

history.meaning: to whip, beat (eggs, cream), fluff up

взбодрить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вз- ('up') + бодрить ('to invigorate, cheer up'), from бодрый ('brisk, cheerful, alert', Proto-Slavic *bъdrъ 'watchful, awake').

взбодриться.etymology: Reflexive form of взбодрить ('to perk up, invigorate') with the suffix -ся, built on вз- + бодрить (from бодрый 'vigorous, alert', Proto-Slavic *bъdrъ).

взвешивать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ива- from взвесить ('to weigh'), from вз- ('up, lifting on scales') + весить ('to weigh, hang', from вес 'weight', Proto-Slavic *věsъ).

взвод.etymology: Deverbal noun from взводить / взвести ('to lead up, raise, cock a gun hammer', from prefix вз- 'up' + водить / вести 'to lead'); hence both 'cocking mechanism (на взводе = cocked, on edge)' and 'platoon (a detachment led up into line)'.

history.meaning: to lead up; to cock a trigger
platoon; notch of a gunlock (на взводе 'on edge')

взгляд.etymology: Deverbal noun from взглянуть / взглядывать ('to look up, cast a glance'), formed from the prefix вз- ('up') + гляд (from глядеть 'to look', Proto-Slavic *ględěti).

взглянуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective verb in -нуть formed from взглядывать ('to cast a glance upward or at something'), built on prefix вз- ('up, suddenly') + глядеть ('to look, gaze', from Proto-Slavic *ględati).

history.meaning: to cast a glance, take a quick look

вздохнуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective verb formed from prefix вз- ('up') + root дох- ('breathe') + single-action suffix -ну-ть. The root alternates with дых- / дух- and descends from Proto-Slavic *dъxnǫti ('to draw a breath') and *duxъ ('breath, spirit'), from PIE *dhew-s- ('to breathe, blow'). In Russian it means to draw a deep breath or let out a single audible sigh.

history.meaning: to draw up a breath, sigh

вздумать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вз- ('up, suddenly') + думать ('to think', inherited from Old East Slavic думати, Proto-Slavic *dumati): 'to suddenly take it into one's head to do something'. Especially common in negative warnings: Не вздумай! ('Don't you dare! / Don't even think about it!').

history.meaning: to suddenly think up, take it into one's head

взлетать.etymology: Imperfective of взлететь ('to fly up, take off'), formed from вз- ('up, upward') + летать ('to fly', inherited from Old East Slavic лѣтати, Proto-Slavic *lětati).

history.meaning: to take off (of an aircraft or bird), soar upward

взлететь.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вз- ('upward') + лететь ('to fly', Proto-Slavic *letěti), literally 'to fly up, take off'.

взлом.etymology: Deverbal action noun from взломать ('to break open'), formed from вз- ('up, open') + лом ('breaking', from ломать 'to break', Proto-Slavic *lomiti).

взломать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вз- ('up, open by force') + ломать ('to break', Proto-Slavic *lamati / *lomiti), meaning to prize open a lock or door, and in modern usage to crack or hack a system.

взорваться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed from взо- (prevocalic/cluster variant of вз- 'up, violently outward') + рвать ('to tear, rend, burst', inherited from Old East Slavic ръвати, Proto-Slavic *rъvati) + -ся: literally 'to tear itself upward and apart, explode'.

history.meaning: to blow up, explode, burst (with anger)

взрослеть.etymology: Inchoative verb formed with the suffix -еть ('to become') from взрослый ('grown-up, adult'), historically a past participle derived from взрасти / взрости ('to grow up', from вз- + расти).

взрослый.etymology: Formed from the past active participle or verbal adjective of взрасти / взросло ('to grow up'), built from the upward prefix вз- ('up') + рос- (the past-tense stem of расти 'to grow', from Proto-Slavic *orsti) + -лый. Functions both as an adjective ('adult, grown-up') and as a substantivized noun ('an adult').

взрыв.etymology: Deverbal noun from взорвать / взрывать ('to blow up, tear up from underneath'), formed from вз- ('upward') + рыть ('to dig, tear', or рвать 'to tear', conflated in East Slavic *vъzryvati).

взятка.etymology: Formed in Russian from взять ('to take', from Old East Slavic възяти, a compound of въз- + яти 'to take') with the noun suffix -ка. Originally meaning simply 'that which is taken, a levy, exaction, or trick in cards', it specialized in administrative and everyday usage to mean an illicit payment or 'bribe'.

взяточник.etymology: Formed in Russian with the agent suffix -ник from взятка ('bribe', with stem alternation к > ч before -ник), itself derived from взять ('to take', Old East Slavic възяти).

взять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic възяти (future возьму, past взял; Old Church Slavonic възѧти), from Proto-Slavic *vъzęti ('to take up, pick up'), formed from prefix *vъz- ('up') + *jęti ('to take, grasp', from PIE *h₁em- 'to take'; compare занять 'to occupy' and принять 'to accept'). Serves as the suppletive perfective partner of брать.
взять.notes: Future tense vocalizes the historical yer vowel of the prefix *въз-*: **я возьму, ты возьмёшь, они возьмут**.

взяться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of взять ('to take'), inherited from Old East Slavic възяти, from Proto-Slavic *vъz-jęti ('to take up'), meaning 'to take hold of, undertake' or 'to appear, come from'.

history.meaning: to appear, come from; to undertake

вид.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic видъ and Old Church Slavonic видъ ('sight, look, appearance, form, species'), from Proto-Slavic *vidъ, built on the Indo-European visual root *weyd- ('to see, know', cognate with видеть 'to see' and Latin vidēre).

видать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic видати, iterative/frequentative of видеть ('to see', from Proto-Slavic *vidati / *viděti).

видео.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English video, which was coined in television technology in the 1930s (as a counterpart to audio) from Latin videō ('I see'), first-person singular present of vidēre ('to see', cognate with Russian видеть).

history.meaning: I see → television/visual signal and recording

видеозапись.etymology: 20th-century compound of видео- (from English video, from Latin video 'I see') + запись ('recording, entry', deverbal noun from записать 'to write down, record').

видеокарта.etymology: Coined in late 20th-century computing terminology as a compound calque of English video card, combining видео- (from Latin videō 'I see') + карта ('printed circuit expansion card', from карта 'card').

видеонаблюдение.etymology: Modern compound combining видео- ('video', from Latin video 'I see') + наблюдение ('observation, surveillance', from наблюдать 'to watch, observe').

видеорегистратор.etymology: Modern compound of видео- ('video', from Latin video) + регистратор ('recorder, registrar', from Medieval Latin registrator, from regerere 'to record').

видеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic видѣти ('to see'), from Proto-Slavic *viděti, from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- ('to see, know'; cognate with Latin videre and Ancient Greek εἶδον).

видеться.etymology: Reciprocal verb formed with -ся from видеть ('to see'), inherited from Old East Slavic видѣти, from Proto-Slavic *viděti ('to see'), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- ('to see, know'; cognate with Latin vidēre and English wit).

history.meaning: to see each other, meet up

rootFamily.gloss: to see each other, meet up (pf) (Увидимся! 'See you!')

видимо.etymology: Adverb and parenthetical word formed from видимый ('visible'), present passive participle of видеть ('to see', from Proto-Slavic *viděti).

видимость.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from видимый ('visible', originally the present passive participle of видеть 'to see', Proto-Slavic *viděti).

видно.etymology: Short neuter form and predicative adverb of видный ('visible, prominent'), derived from вид ('sight, view, appearance') and видеть ('to see', from Proto-Slavic *viděti).

history.meaning: it is visible, one can see; apparently

видный.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ный from вид ('view, appearance, sight'), from Proto-Slavic *vidъ ('sight, look'), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- ('to see').

визит.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish wizyta and German Visite from French visite ('social or official call, visit'), deverbal noun from visiter ('to go to see, visit'), from Latin vīsitāre (frequentative of vidēre 'to see').

history.meaning: to see → to go to see, visit

визитка.etymology: Colloquial univerbation with suffix -ка of визитная карточка ('visiting card, business card'), from визит ('visit'), borrowed from French visite (from visiter, Latin visitare 'to go to see').

викин.etymology: Possessive adjective formed with the suffix -ин from Вика, the standard Russian hypocoristic short form of the female given name Виктория (from Latin Victoria, 'victory').

вилка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of вилы ('pitchfork'), inherited from Old East Slavic вила / вилы ('forked branch, pitchfork') and Proto-Slavic *vila ('fork', originally something twisted or branching in two, related to вить 'to twist, wind'). When the table fork entered Russian dining, the diminutive вилка became its everyday name.

вилла.etymology: Borrowed via Italian villa (or German Villa) from Latin vīlla ('country house, estate, farmstead'), related to vīcus ('village, group of houses').

вина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вина ('cause, reason, fault, blame, fine'), from Proto-Slavic *vina ('cause, fault, guilt'; cognate with Lithuanian vaina 'fault, blame').

винить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic винити ('to accuse, blame'), from Proto-Slavic *viniti, a denominative verb built on *vina (Russian вина, 'fault, guilt, blame').

винный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic виньныи ('relating to wine'), formed with the adjective suffix -ный from вино ('wine'), borrowed in Proto-Slavic (*vino) from Gothic or Latin vinum.

вино.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вино (and Old Church Slavonic вино), borrowed in the Proto-Slavic period (*vino) via Gothic wein or directly from Latin vīnum ('wine'), an ancient Mediterranean wanderword shared with Ancient Greek οἶνος (oînos).

виноватый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic виноватыи ('guilty, at fault, to blame'), formed with the suffix -оватый from вина ('fault, guilt, blame, cause', from Proto-Slavic *vina, cognate with Lithuanian vainà 'fault, blame').

виновный.etymology: Derived via виновный / виноватый from вина ('fault, guilt, cause'), inherited from Old East Slavic вина ('cause, blame, guilt'), from Proto-Slavic *vina.

виноградник.etymology: Formed with the place suffix -ник from виноград ('grapes, grapevines'), from Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic виноградъ ('vineyard, grapevine'), a Gothic borrowing (*weinagards 'wine-garden').

винотека.etymology: Borrowed from Italian vinoteca or formed internationally from вино ('wine', Latin vinum) + -тека ('collection, repository', from Ancient Greek θήκη thḗkē 'case, repository').

history.meaning: wine collection, wine cellar or boutique

винт.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century via Polish gwint ('screw thread, screw') from Early Modern High German Gewinde ('spiral thread, winding, screw'), a collective noun from winden ('to wind, twist', cognate with English wind).

винтик.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ик from винт ('screw, spiral thread'), borrowed via Polish gwint ('screw thread') from Middle High German gewinde / German Gewinde ('winding, screw thread', from winden 'to wind, twist').

вирус.etymology: Borrowed via Western European scientific usage from Latin virus ('slimy liquid, poison, venom'), from Proto-Indo-European *weys- ('poison, slime').

висеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic висѣти (present вишу, висит), from Proto-Slavic *visěti ('to hang, be suspended'), an intransitive stative verb in *-ěti related to transitive вешать ('to hang something up').

виски.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from English whisky / whiskey, itself an anglicization of Scottish Gaelic uisge-beatha and Irish uisce beatha ('water of life', a calque of Medieval Latin aqua vītae; compare the parallel formation of Russian водка from вода 'water').

вишня.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вишня, from Proto-Slavic *višňa ('sour cherry, Morello cherry'). Vasmer connects the Slavic word with Old High German wīhsela (German Weichsel 'mahaleb/sour cherry'), Ancient Greek ἰξός (ixós), and Latin viscum ('mistletoe, sticky birdlime', referring to the sticky gum exuded by cherry bark).
вишня.notes: In Russian, вишня refers specifically to the tart sour cherry, whereas sweet dark cherries are called черешня.

вишнёвый.etymology: Relational and colour adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ёвый from вишня ('sour cherry', inherited from Old East Slavic вишня, Proto-Slavic *višňa).

вкладывать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ыва- from вкласть / вкладывать ('to put in, lay in, invest'), from в- ('in, into') + класть ('to lay, put', Proto-Slavic *klasti).

включать.etymology: Imperfective partner of включить ('to include, insert into a circuit, turn on'), formed from prefix в- ('in, into') + ключ ('key, clasp, switch', from Proto-Slavic *kľučь). Originally 'to lock or clasp into a whole ('include')', and from the era of electrical engineering 'to close a switch into the circuit, turn on (a light or appliance)'.

history.meaning: to include; to switch on, turn on (imperfective)

включить.etymology: Formed from prefix в- ('in, into') + ключить (built on ключ 'key, bolt, switch', from Proto-Slavic *kľučь). First meant 'to enclose, include in a list or bill', and in the late 19th–20th centuries acquired the technical and everyday sense 'to engage a valve or electrical switch, turn on'.

history.meaning: to include; to turn on (light, water, heating)

включиться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed with -ся from включить ('to switch on, include, engage'), built from в- ('in, into') + ключить / ключ ('key, bolt, switch', Proto-Slavic *kľučь).

history.meaning: to switch on, come on; to join actively in an activity

вколоть.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from в- ('into') + колоть ('to prick, pierce, stab'), from Proto-Slavic *kolti ('to stab, cleave'), from Proto-Indo-European *kelH- ('to strike, prick').

history.meaning: to stick in, inject (with a needle)

вкус.etymology: Deverbal noun from вкусить ('to taste, try, partake of', from Old Church Slavonic въкусити), formed from въ- ('in') + кусити ('to taste, try, bite', a early Slavic borrowing from Gothic kausjan 'to taste, test').

вкусненький.etymology: Affectionate diminutive adjective formed with the suffix -еньк- from вкусный ('tasty, delicious'), derived from вкус ('taste'), from Old Church Slavonic въкусъ ('tasting, trial', ultimately a Gothic borrowing from kausjan 'to taste, test').

вкусно.etymology: Adverb and predicative short neuter form of вкусный ('tasty, delicious'), formed with the suffix -ный from вкус ('taste, flavor').

вкусный.etymology: Formed with the adjectival suffix -ный from вкус ('taste, flavour'), a deverbal noun from вкусить ('to taste, sample, take a bite of'), built on prefix в- + кусить / кусать ('to bite, taste', from Proto-Slavic *kǫsiti, which itself was an early borrowing from Proto-Germanic *kausjaną 'to taste, test, choose', cognate with Gothic kausjan and English choose).

вкуснятина.etymology: Colloquial expressive noun formed with the suffix -ятина from вкусный ('tasty, delicious'), itself from вкус ('taste', Old Church Slavonic въкусъ 'tasting, trial').

владелец.etymology: Formed with the agent suffix -ец from archaic владелый / владеть ('to own, possess, rule', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic владѣти, corresponding to native East Slavic володеть, from Proto-Slavic *volděti).

владелица.etymology: Feminine agent noun formed with the suffix -ица from владелец ('owner, proprietor'), derived from владеть ('to rule, possess'), a Church Slavonicism from *volděti.

владеть.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic владѣти ('to rule, govern, possess'; compare native East Slavic володѣти), from Proto-Slavic *volděti ('to rule'), cognate with Gothic waldan and English wield.

власть.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic власть ('rule, dominion, authority, power'), corresponding to native East Slavic волость ('district, territory under a ruler', with pleophony -оло-), from Proto-Slavic *volstь, formed with the suffix *-tь from *volsti (1st sg. *voldǫ, 'to rule, govern', whence владеть; cognate with Gothic waldan and English wield).

влево.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в лево ('to the left'), from в ('into, to') + short neuter accusative of левый ('left', from Proto-Slavic *lěvъ).

влезать.etymology: Imperfective of влезть ('to climb into, fit into; to meddle'), formed from в- ('in, into') + лезть / лезать ('to climb, crawl', inherited from Old East Slavic лѣзти, Proto-Slavic *lězti).

history.meaning: to climb in, fit into; (colloq.) to butt in, interfere

влезть.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from в- ('in, into') + лезть ('to climb, crawl'), from Proto-Slavic *lězti ('to crawl, climb').

history.meaning: to climb in, fit into, intrude

вливаться.etymology: Reflexive and middle-voice form of вливать ('to pour in'), formed from в- ('in, into') + ливать (iterative of лить 'to pour', Proto-Slavic *liti) + -ся.

history.meaning: to flow into, blend into a group

влиться.etymology: Reflexive of влить ('to pour in', from prefix в- 'in, into' + лить 'to pour', Proto-Slavic *liti) + -ся, literally 'to flow into, merge into a stream', figuratively 'to blend in smoothly with a group'.

history.meaning: to flow into; to blend in, join smoothly

влияние.etymology: Verbal noun from влиять ('to influence', in Old Church Slavonic вълияти 'to pour into', from въ- 'into' + лияти / лить 'to pour'). In the late 18th century Nikolai Karamzin and his contemporaries gave влияние the figurative sense 'influence' as a semantic calque of French influence and Medieval Latin influentia (from in- 'into' + fluere 'to flow').

history.meaning: a flowing in → moral or personal influence

влиятельный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -тельный from влиять ('to influence') and влияние ('influence', a semantic calque of French influence).

влиять.etymology: Back-formed in the 19th century from влияние ('influence'), which was coined by N. M. Karamzin from Old Church Slavonic въли˫аниѥ ('pouring in') as a calque of French influence / Medieval Latin influentia (from in- 'into' + fluere 'to flow').

вложенный.etymology: Past passive participle of вложить ('to put in, enclose, invest'), formed from в- ('in, into') + ложить ('to lay, place', Proto-Slavic *ložiti).

вложить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic въложити ('to put in, insert'), formed with prefix в- ('in, into') from ложить ('to lay, put', from Proto-Slavic *ložiti).

history.meaning: to invest; to put in, enclose

влюбиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed with the prefix в- ('into') + любить ('to love', from Proto-Slavic *ľubiti) + -ся. Literally, 'to enter into a state of love, fall in love' (constructed with в + accusative: влюбиться в кого-то).

влюблённый.etymology: Past passive participle of влюбить ('to inspire love in', usually reflexive влюбиться 'to fall in love'), formed from the prefix в- ('into') + любить ('to love', from Proto-Slavic *ľubiti).

вляпаться.etymology: Colloquial prefixed reflexive verb from в- ('into') + ляпать ('to slap, splash, blunder', an expressive/onomatopoeic Slavic verb *lępati) + -ся, literally 'to step or splash right into mud'.

history.meaning: to step into a mess, land in trouble

вместе.etymology: Univerbation of the Old East Slavic prepositional phrase въ мѣстѣ ('in [one] place'), combining the preposition въ ('in') with мѣстѣ, the locative singular of мѣсто ('place, spot', modern Russian место): literally 'in the same place', hence 'together'.

вместо.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в место ('in place of'), from в ('in, into') + место ('place, spot', inherited from Old East Slavic мѣсто, from Proto-Slavic *město).

вмешать.etymology: Formed with the prefix в- ('in, into') + мешать ('to mix, stir, blend', inherited from Old East Slavic мѣшати and Proto-Slavic *měšati, from Proto-Indo-European *meyḱ- 'to mix', cognate with Latin miscēre and English mix).

history.meaning: to fold in, mix into a batter or dough

вмешаться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed from в- ('into') + мешать ('to mix, stir, mingle', inherited from Old East Slavic мѣшати, Proto-Slavic *měšati) + -ся: literally 'to mix oneself into a matter', hence 'to intervene, interfere, step in'.

history.meaning: to mix oneself in, intervene, interfere (pf)

вмешивать.etymology: Imperfective verb derived with prefix в- ('into') and iterative suffix -ива- from мешать / месить ('to mix, knead'). The root goes back to Proto-Slavic *měšati / *měsiti ('to mix, stir, knead'), from PIE *meyk- / *meyg- ('to mix'). It is a direct Indo-European cognate of English mix, Latin miscere, and Ancient Greek mignymi.

вмешиваться.etymology: Imperfective partner of вмешаться ('to intervene, interfere, meddle'), formed with the imperfective suffix -ива- from в- ('into') + мешать ('to mix, stir', Proto-Slavic *měšati) + -ся.

вначале.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в начале ('in the beginning'), from в ('in') + locative singular of начало ('beginning', from начать 'to begin', Proto-Slavic *načęlo).

внедриться.etymology: Reflexive form of внедрить ('to implant, introduce, instil'), derived from Old Church Slavonic вънѣдрити ('to place into the bosom/depths'), from въ ('in') + нѣдра ('bosom, depths, interior', Proto-Slavic *nědro).

внезапно.etymology: Adverb formed from внезапный ('sudden, unexpected'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вънезаапѫ / вънезапьнъ ('suddenly / sudden'), built from въ ('in') + не ('not') + *zaapъ ('expectation, suspicion', connected by Vasmer with Old Russian запы 'expectations' and dialectal запать 'to expect, catch').

внеплановый.etymology: 20th-century compound adjective formed from the preposition вне ('outside of', Proto-Slavic *vъně) + плановый ('planned, scheduled', from план 'plan', borrowed via German Plan / French plan from Latin planum).

внести.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb inherited from Old East Slavic вънести, formed from в- ('in, into') + нести ('to carry', from Proto-Slavic *nesti, PIE *h₁neḱ-). Alongside literal 'to carry inside', it is standard in official and financial Russian for 'to pay in (a deposit or installment), enter (in a document), submit (a proposal)'.

history.meaning: to carry in; to pay in, enter, submit

rootFamily.gloss: to carry in; to pay in (impf)

внешне.etymology: Adverb formed from внешний ('external, outer, outward'), borrowed via Old Church Slavonic вънѣштьнь ('outer, external'), derived from вънѣ (Russian вне, 'outside', from Proto-Slavic *vъně, related to вон 'out').

history.meaning: external, outward → externally, outwardly, in appearance

внешний.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic вънѣшьнии ('outer, external'), formed from the adverb/preposition вънѣ (modern вне 'outside, without', from Proto-Slavic *vъně, related to вон 'out').

внештатный.etymology: Compound administrative adjective formed from вне ('outside of') + штатный ('on the permanent staff/roster'), from штат ('staff establishment, state'), borrowed via German Staat / Dutch staat from Latin status.

вниз.etymology: Formed by univerbation of the prepositional phrase в низ ('into the bottom, downward'), combining the directional preposition в ('into') with the accusative of низ ('bottom, lower part', from Proto-Slavic *nizъ).
вниз.notes: Indicates motion downward (*идти вниз* 'go downstairs'); static location below is **внизу**.

внизу.etymology: Formed by univerbation of the prepositional phrase в низу ('at the bottom, in the lower part'), combining the preposition в ('in') with the locative singular (-у) of низ ('bottom, lower part', from Proto-Slavic *nizъ).

внимание.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вънимание ('heeding, listening closely, attention'), the verbal noun of вънимати / внимать ('to take in with the mind or ears, heed'), formed from вън- ('into', with epenthetic -н-) and имати ('to take', iterative of яти, Proto-Slavic *jьmati).

внимательно.etymology: Adverbial form in -о of внимательный ('attentive, observant'), derived from внимать ('to heed, listen closely, take in'), built on prefix в- ('in') + -нимать (from Proto-Slavic *jьmati / *jęti 'to take').

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

внимательность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from внимательный ('attentive, observant'), derived from внимать ('to pay heed, take in', from Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic вънимати).

внимательный.etymology: Formed in Russian with the adjective suffix -тельный from внимать ('to heed, listen closely, pay attention to'), inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic вънимати ('to take in with the mind or ears'), built from вън- ('in') + *-jьmati ('to take, grasp', PIE *h₁em-).

history.stage: Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic
history.meaning: to take in, attend to, heed

вновь.etymology: Univerbation of the Old Russian prepositional phrase въ новь ('into the new, anew'), from въ ('in, into') + новь ('new state, virgin soil', feminine i-stem noun from новый 'new', Proto-Slavic *novь).

внук.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вънукъ ('grandson, descendant'), from Proto-Slavic *vъnukъ (with prosthetic v- before *onukъ), related to Old High German eninchil (German Enkel 'grandson') and Latin anus.

внутренний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вънутрьнии / Old Church Slavonic вънѫтрьнь, formed with the adjective suffix -ний from внутрь ('inside, within', from Proto-Slavic *vъnǫtrь, from *vъn- 'in' + *ǫtrь 'interior, entrails', cognate with Latin inter and Ancient Greek ἔντερα).

внутри.etymology: Univerbation of Old East Slavic вънутри ('on the inside'), combining the preposition въ ('in') + нутри (locative singular of нутро 'interior, insides', from Proto-Slavic *jьnǫtrь / *vъnǫtrь, continuing PIE *h₁en-tero- 'inner', cognate with Latin inter and interior).

внутрь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вънутрь ('into the interior, inward'), combining the directional preposition въ ('into') with the accusative of *nǫtrь ('interior, inside', from Proto-Slavic *vъnǫtrь, PIE *h₁en-tero- 'inner').
внутрь.notes: Indicates inward motion (*проходите внутрь* 'come on inside'), whereas **внутри** indicates static location (*внутри тепло* 'it is warm inside').

внучек.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed with the suffix -ек (with regular palatalization к → ч) from внук ('grandson'), inherited from Old East Slavic вънукъ, from Proto-Slavic *vъnukъ ('grandson', cognate with Lithuanian anū̃kas and German Enkel).

внучок.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed with the suffix -ок from внук ('grandson'), inherited from Old East Slavic вънукъ ('grandson, descendant'), from Proto-Slavic *vъnukъ (with prosthetic v- before PIE *h₂enōpōts / *nepot-).

внушить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вънушити ('to give ear to; to instil into someone's ears/mind'), formed from вън- ('into') + ухо / уши ('ear / ears', Proto-Slavic *uxo).

history.meaning: to put into the ears, inspire

внятно.etymology: Adverb derived from внятный ('distinct, intelligible, audible'), originally derived from Old Russian въняти ('to attend to, hear, grasp', from вън- + яти 'to take', Proto-Slavic *vъnęti).

во-вторых.etymology: Introductory adverbial formed from preposition во ('in [the rank of]', supplying ellipsis of словах/пунктах 'points') + вторых (locative plural of второй 'second', from Proto-Slavic *vъtorъ).

во-первых.etymology: Introductory adverbial formed from preposition во ('in') + первых (locative plural of первый 'first', inherited from Proto-Slavic *pьrvъ 'first').

вовремя.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase во время ('in time, at the right time'), from во ('in') + время ('time', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врѣмя, from Proto-Slavic *vermę).

history.meaning: on time, at the right moment

вовсе.etymology: Univerbated adverbial phrase formed from the preposition во ('in, into') and все / всё ('all, everything', from Proto-Slavic *vьxъ / *vьśь). Originally meaning 'in all respects, completely, altogether', in modern Russian it is most often used as an intensifier with negation: **вовсе не** / **вовсе нет** ('not at all, by no means').

вода.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вода, from Proto-Slavic *voda, continuing the ancient Proto-Indo-European root *wódr̥ ('water'), cognate with English water, German Wasser, Ancient Greek ὕδωρ, and Lithuanian vanduo.

водитель.etymology: Formed with the agent suffix -тель from водить ('to lead, guide, drive', inherited from Old East Slavic водити, from Proto-Slavic *voditi, iterative of *vesti 'to lead').

водить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic водити ('to lead, guide'), from Proto-Slavic *voditi, the iterative-causative counterpart of *vesti ('to lead'), from Proto-Indo-European *wedh- ('to lead').

history.meaning: to lead; to drive a vehicle

водичка.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed via водица + -ка from вода ('water'), inherited from Old East Slavic вода, from Proto-Slavic *voda, from Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥ ('water').

водка.etymology: Formed as a diminutive of вода ('water', Old East Slavic вода, Proto-Slavic *voda) with the suffix -ка. First documented in Russian and Polish sources in the 15th–16th centuries for medicinal herbal tinctures and distilled spirits, paralleling Latin aqua vītae ('water of life') and Gaelic uisge beatha ('whisky').

history.meaning: little water → medicinal tincture, distilled grain spirit

водопад.etymology: Compound noun formed from вода ('water') + connecting vowel -о- + пад- (stem of падать / пасть 'to fall'), calquing German Wasserfall ('waterfall').

водостойкий.etymology: Compound adjective built inside Russian from вода ('water', Proto-Slavic *voda, PIE *wed-) + linking vowel -о- + стойкий ('steadfast, resistant, durable', from стоять 'to stand', Proto-Slavic *stojati, PIE *stah2-). Literally 'standing firm against water', it mirrors German wasserfest and English water-resistant / waterproof.

водяной.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic водѧныи, formed with the relational adjective suffix -яной from вода ('water', from Proto-Slavic *voda, from Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥ 'water', cognate with English water). As a substantivized masculine noun, водяной also denotes the bearded water-spirit of Slavic folklore.

воевать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic воевати, from Proto-Slavic *vojevati ('to wage war, campaign'), a denominative verb from *vojь ('warrior; pl. вои army, host', related to война 'war' and воин 'warrior').

history.meaning: to fight in a war, wage war

военный.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ный from война ('war', Old East Slavic воина), from Proto-Slavic *vojьna ('war, military campaign'), related to *vojь ('warrior').

возбуждающий.etymology: Adjectival present active participle of возбуждать ('to excite, stimulate, arouse'), an Old Church Slavonicism (възбуждати) from въз- ('up') + будити ('to wake, rouse', Proto-Slavic *buditi).

возбуждение.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възбуждениѥ ('awakening, stirring up, arousal'), verbal noun of възбудити / възбуждати (from въз- 'up' + будити 'to awaken').

history.meaning: excitement, arousal; initiation (of a legal case)

возбуждённый.etymology: Past passive participle of возбудить ('to excite, rouse, initiate'), from Old Church Slavonic възбудити ('to awaken, rouse'), from въз- + будити ('to wake', Proto-Slavic *buditi).

возводить.etymology: Imperfective of возвести ('to raise, erect, trace back'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възводити, formed from въз- ('up') + водити ('to lead, bring', from Proto-Slavic *voditi).

возврат.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from возвратить ('to return, give back'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възвратити (showing the South Slavic non-pleophonic root -врат- corresponding to native Russian ворот- 'turn'), from *vъz- ('back') + *vortiti ('to turn').

возвращать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възвращати ('to turn back, return, restore', corresponding to native East Slavic ворочать), formed from въз- ('back') + вращати ('to turn', from Proto-Slavic *vorťati).

возвращаться.etymology: Borrowed or reshaped with Church Slavonic vocalism (-вращ- rather than native East Slavic -вороч-) from възвращатися ('to turn back, return'), built on въз- ('back, up') + вращати ('to turn', from Proto-Slavic *vortiti).

возвращение.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възвращениѥ ('turning back, return'), verbal noun from възвратити / возвратить ('to return, bring back', with Church Slavonic alternation *tj > щ), built on *vъz- ('back') + *vortiti ('to turn').

возглавить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed with Church Slavonic воз- ('up, onto') + глава ('head, chief', Old Church Slavonic глава, Proto-Slavic *golva), meaning 'to place oneself at the head of, to lead'.

history.meaning: to head, take the lead of

возглавлять.etymology: Imperfective of возглавить ('to place oneself at the head of, lead'), a Church Slavonicism formed from воз- + глава ('head, chief', corresponding to East Slavic голова, Proto-Slavic *golva).

воздаяние.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възда˫аниѥ ('recompense, retribution, reward'), verbal noun of възда˫ати ('to give back, render'), from въз- ('back, in return') + да˫ати ('to give', Proto-Slavic *dajati).

воздух.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въздухъ ('breath, rising vapour, air'), formed from the prefix въз- ('up', Russian воз-) + духъ ('breath, spirit', from Proto-Slavic *duxъ, related to дышать 'to breathe' and дуть 'to blow').

воздушный.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ный from воздух ('air'), from Old Church Slavonic въздухъ ('air, breath, mist rising upward'), from въз- ('up') + духъ ('breath, spirit', Proto-Slavic *duxъ).

возить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic возити ('to convey, transport, haul by vehicle'), from Proto-Slavic *voziti (iterative/causative of *vezti 'to convey, carry by vehicle', Russian везти), from Proto-Indo-European *woǵʰéyeti.

возиться.etymology: Reflexive form of возить ('to transport, carry by vehicle; to move about', iterative of везти, Proto-Slavic *voziti) + -ся, developing the colloquial sense 'to bustle about, potter, fuss over'.

history.meaning: to fuss with, potter about, horse around

возле.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic възлѣ ('beside, alongside'), univerbated from the preposition въз ('up along, by') + the locative/dative form лѣ (from the archaic Proto-Slavic root *lě- / *lěv- or *lьg-; Vasmer favors a formation parallel to подлѣ 'beside', remodelled on въз-).

возместить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възмѣстити ('to put in place of, repay, compensate'), from въз- ('in return') + мѣсто ('place', Proto-Slavic *město).

возможно.etymology: Adverb and predicative formed from возможный ('possible'), derived from Old Russian / Church Slavonic възмочь ('to be able, manage'), from въз- + мочь ('to be able, have power', Proto-Slavic *mogti).

возможность.etymology: Abstract noun in -ость formed from возможный ('possible, feasible'), derived from возмочь ('to be able, manage'), from воз- + мочь ('to be able, have power', Proto-Slavic *mogti).

возможный.etymology: Derived with the suffix -ный from возмочь ('to be able, manage to', from воз- + мочь 'to be able', Proto-Slavic *moťi).

возмутительно.etymology: Adverb and predicative derived from возмутительный ('outrageous, indignant'), from возмутить ('to stir up, agitate, shock'), from Church Slavonic възмутити (въз- 'up' + мутити 'to muddy, stir up, trouble', Proto-Slavic *mǫtiti).

возмутительный.etymology: Formed in Russian with the adjective suffix -тельный from возмутить ('to stir up, agitate, outrage'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възмѫтити ('to stir up sediment, trouble water or the mind', from *vъz- 'up' + *mǫtiti 'to muddy, stir up', Russian мутить).

возмущение.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic възмѫщениѥ ('stirring up, commotion, agitation'), verbal noun from възмѫтити / возмутить ('to stir up, trouble, outrage', from *vъz- 'up' + *mǫtiti 'to muddy, agitate', with Church Slavonic *tj > щ).

вознаграждаться.etymology: Passive and reflexive form of вознаграждать ('to reward, recompense'), formed from воз- ('in return') + награждать ('to reward', from награда 'reward').

возникнуть.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възникнути ('to spring up, rise up, emerge'), formed from въз- ('upward') + никнути ('to sprout, bend or rise', Proto-Slavic *niknǫti).

возобновить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from Church Slavonic воз- ('again, anew') + обновить ('to renew, restore', from об- + новый 'new', Proto-Slavic *novъ).

возражать.etymology: Imperfective of возразить ('to object, retort, reply against'), borrowed via Old Church Slavonic възразити ('to strike back, counter, repel'), built from *vъz- ('back, against') + *raziti ('to strike', related to раз 'stroke, blow' and поразить 'to strike').

history.meaning: to object, mind (Вы не возражаете? 'Do you mind?')

возражение.etymology: Verbal noun from возразить ('to object, reply against'), formed from Church Slavonic въз- ('back, against') + разити ('to strike', Proto-Slavic *raziti).

возразить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възразити ('to strike back, counter, reply'), formed from въз- ('back, against') + разити ('to strike, hit', Proto-Slavic *raziti), shifting from physical counter-striking to verbal objection.

возраст.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic възрастъ ('growth, stature, maturity, age'), deverbal noun from възрасти ('to grow up', corresponding to native Russian вырасти, from *vъz- 'up' + *orsti 'to grow', Russian расти, with South Slavic ра- < *or-).

возродиться.etymology: Reflexive form of возродить ('to regenerate, revive'), from Old Church Slavonic възродити ('to beget anew, regenerate'), from въз- ('anew, up') + родити ('to give birth', Proto-Slavic *roditi).

возрождаться.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of возродиться, formed from Old Church Slavonic възраждати сѧ / Russian возрождать ('to revive, regenerate', from воз- + рождать) + -ся.

воин.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic воинъ and Old Church Slavonic воинъ ('warrior, soldier'), formed with the singulative suffix -инъ from вои ('warriors, army'), from Proto-Slavic *vojь ('warrior', PIE *weyh₁- 'to pursue').

воинский.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic воиньскыи, formed with the relational adjective suffix -ский from воин ('warrior, soldier'), which is built with the singulative suffix -ин on Old East Slavic вои ('warriors, host', Proto-Slavic *vojь).

войлок.etymology: Borrowed from a Turkic language (compare Tatar ojlyk, Kazakh ojlyq, Chagatai ojluk 'felt covering, saddlecloth'), derived from Turkic *oj- / *ojla- ('to cover, wrap').

война.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic воина ('war, military campaign'), from Proto-Slavic *vojьna, derived from *vojь ('warrior; army, host', preserved in воин 'warrior' and войско 'army'), from Proto-Indo-European *weyh₁- ('to pursue, hunt, strive after'; compare Lithuanian výti 'to chase' and Latin vis 'force').

войско.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic воиско, from Proto-Slavic *vojьsko ('army, armed host'), a collective neuter noun derived from *vojь ('warrior', related to война 'war' and воин 'warrior').

войти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic въити ('to go in, enter'), formed from the prefix во- / въ- ('in, into') + идти ('to go, walk', from Proto-Slavic *jьti).

вокзал.etymology: Borrowed in 1837 from English Vauxhall (Vauxhall Gardens, a famous London pleasure garden with a concert pavilion, itself named after the Anglo-Norman lord Falkes de Breauté's hall, Falkes' Hall). When Russia's first railway opened from St Petersburg to Pavlovsk in 1837, the grand musical pavilion at the Pavlovsk terminus was named Вокзал, and the word soon generalized to any major railway station.

history.meaning: London pleasure garden and concert hall

вокзальный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from вокзал ('railway station terminal'), which entered Russian in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries from English Vauxhall (Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens in London), first meaning a concert pavilion at the Pavlovsk terminus of Russia's first railway (1837) and then any major railway station.

history.meaning: railway station → station (adjective: вокзальные часы 'station clock')

вокруг.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase во круг ('in a circle'), from во ('in, into') + круг ('circle, ring', inherited from Old East Slavic кругъ, from Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ).

волк.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вълкъ, from Proto-Slavic *vьlkъ ('wolf'), from Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos ('wolf'; directly cognate with English wolf, German Wolf, Lithuanian vil̃kas, Latin lupus, and Sanskrit vṛka).

волнение.etymology: Verbal noun in -ние formed from волновать / волноваться ('to stir up waves; to agitate, worry'), derived from волна ('wave', from Proto-Slavic *vълna). Preserves both the literal sense 'rough water, choppiness of the sea' and the emotional sense 'nervousness, excitement, agitation'.

history.meaning: surging of waves → agitation, nervousness, excitement

волновать.etymology: Derived with the verbal suffix -овать from волна ('wave, billow', inherited from Old East Slavic вълна, from Proto-Slavic *vьlna, from PIE *welH- 'to roll, surge'), developing metaphorically from 'to stir up waves' to 'to agitate, worry, move emotionally'.

волноваться.etymology: Reflexive form of волновать ('to agitate, stir up waves'), derived from волна ('wave', from Old East Slavic вълна, Proto-Slavic *vълna, from PIE *welH- 'to roll, surge'; cognate with German Welle 'wave'). Literally 'to surge with waves', hence figuratively 'to feel anxious, worry, be nervous'.

history.meaning: wave → to be agitated, worry, be nervous

волос.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic волосъ (showing East Slavic pleophony -оло-; compare Old Church Slavonic власъ and Polish włos), from Proto-Slavic *volsъ ('hair'), with close Indo-Iranian cognates (Avestan varəsa- 'hair of the head', Persian gurs).
волос.notes: Singular **волос** refers to a single strand of hair; hair on the head collectively is plural **волосы** (genitive plural **волос**).

волшебник.etymology: Formed with the agent suffix -ник from волшебный ('magical, enchanting'), derived from Old East Slavic вълшьба / Old Church Slavonic влъшьба ('sorcery, magic, divination') and вълхвъ / волхв ('pagan magus, sorcerer, seer', from Proto-Slavic *vъlxvъ).

волшебно.etymology: Adverb derived from the adjective волшебный ('magical, enchanting') with adverbial suffix -о. The adjective comes from Old Church Slavonic and Old East Slavic влъшьба ('magic, sorcery') and вълхвъ ('magician, sage, seer', Proto-Slavic *vъlxvъ), a word connected with ritual poetic speech and incantation. In everyday Russian волшебно means both 'by magic' and 'enchantingly, wonderfully'.

волшебный.etymology: Derived from archaic волшба ('sorcery, magic, divination', from Old Church Slavonic влъшьба), related to волхв ('pagan priest, magus, sorcerer', from Proto-Slavic *vъlxvъ).

волшебство.etymology: Derived with the abstract suffix -ство from волшебный ('magical') and Old Russian вълшьба ('sorcery, divination'), derived from вълхвъ (волхв, 'pagan magus, sorcerer', Proto-Slavic *vъlxvъ).

воля.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic воля ('will, wish; freedom'), from Proto-Slavic *voľa ('will, desire'), from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- ('to wish, choose'; cognate with Latin velle, German wollen, English will).

вон.etymology: Two homonymous words merged in form: (1) pointing particle 'over there!' from prosthetic в- + demonstrative pronoun он ('that one', Proto-Slavic *onъ); (2) directional adverb 'out, away!' from Old East Slavic вънъ ('outside', Proto-Slavic *vъnъ).

вонь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic воня ('smell, scent, fragrance'), from Proto-Slavic *voňa ('odour, scent, breath', from the PIE root *h₂enh₁- 'to breathe', cognate with Sanskrit ániti 'breathes' and Latin animus). Whereas Old Church Slavonic воня, Czech vůně, and Polish woń mean a pleasant 'fragrance, aroma' (preserved in Russian благовоние 'sweet incense'), in everyday Russian вонь underwent pejoration to mean 'stench, foul smell'.

history.stage: Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic

rootFamily.gloss: sense of smell (preserving the neutral meaning)

вонять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic воняти ('to smell, emit an odor', originally either pleasant or unpleasant, as in Church Slavonic благовоние 'fragrance'), denominative from воня (вонь, 'smell, stench'), from Proto-Slavic *vonja (related to *vějati 'to blow').

вообще.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в обще ('in general, in common'), combining the preposition в/во ('in') with the short neuter accusative/locative of общий ('common, general', borrowed in its Church Slavonic form общии with щ < *tj, from Proto-Slavic *obьťь 'around, shared in common').

history.meaning: in general, on the whole; (with не) at all

вообще-то.etymology: Formed from вообще ('in general', from во + общее 'the common/general whole', from общий 'common, general', Old Church Slavonic обьщь) + the conversational hedging particle -то.

history.meaning: actually, as a matter of fact

вопрос.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic въпросъ ('question, inquiry'), a deverbal noun from въпросити ('to ask, inquire'), built on prefix въ- + просити ('to ask, request', from Proto-Slavic *prositi).

вопросик.etymology: Colloquial diminutive formed with the suffix -ик from вопрос ('question'), which was borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въпросъ ('question, inquiry', from въпросити 'to ask', Proto-Slavic *vъprositi).

вор.etymology: Attested in Russian from the late 16th century (originally meaning 'state criminal, traitor, rebel, impostor' — as in Тушинский вор for False Dmitry II — before narrowing in the 18th century to 'thief', displacing older тать). Usually connected by Vasmer to the same root as врать ('to lie, babble, deceive', with o-grade ablaut вор- < *vorъ 'deceiver, crook'), though Finno-Ugric connections have also been proposed.

ворваться.etymology: Prefixed reflexive verb formed from во- ('in, into') + рваться ('to tear, rush, burst', from рвать 'to tear', Proto-Slavic *rъvati) + -ся.

воркута.etymology: Toponym Воркута, an Arctic coal-mining city in the Komi Republic founded around a major Stalin-era Gulag camp complex in the 1930s; named after the Vorkuta River, from Nenets варка яха (varka yakha, 'river abundant in bears', from vark 'bear').

history.meaning: Vorkuta (Arctic city and former Gulag site)

воробей.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic воробии and Proto-Slavic *vorbьjь 'sparrow', widely traced by Vasmer and Slavic etymologists to an expressive sound-imitating root echoing the bird's quick chirping.
воробей.notes: Declines with soft -ь- throughout the oblique stem: воробей -> воробья, воробьи, воробьёв.

воровать.etymology: Denominative verb formed with the suffix -овать from вор ('thief, criminal', attested from the 16th century). While Old East Slavic stole was красти (modern красть / украсть), воровать became the everyday colloquial and general imperfective verb for 'to steal, pilfer, embezzle'.

history.meaning: rogue, rebel, thief → to commit crimes, steal

воровка.etymology: Feminine noun formed with the suffix -ка from вор ('thief', in 16th–17th century Muscovite Russian 'rebel, state criminal, fraudster', derived via воровать from врать 'to lie, deceive' or an expressive root).

воровство.etymology: Formed with the abstract activity suffix -ство from вор ('thief'; in 16th–17th-century Muscovite Russian, 'state criminal, rebel, impostor, traitor', connected by Vasmer with врать 'to lie, deceive').

history.meaning: rebel, criminal, thief → crime, treason; theft

воронка.etymology: Diminutive in form from older Russian ворона / воронок ('funnel; bunghole in a cask'). Vasmer notes two proposed origins within Russian: either from вороной ('black, raven-coloured', referring to the dark hole of a cask or whirlpool) or from воротить / вертеть ('to turn, swirl', referring to a swirling vortex or funnel).

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: воронка

ворота.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ворота (neuter plural, showing East Slavic pleophony -оро-; compare Old Church Slavonic врата), from Proto-Slavic *vorta ('gate, double doors'), derived from the root *vьrtěti / *vorotiti ('to turn, swing shut', from PIE *wert- 'to turn').
ворота.notes: Plural-only (*pluralia tantum*) in Russian: **ворота открыты**, genitive **у ворот**.

ворочаться.etymology: Reflexive form of ворочать ('to turn, roll heavy things'), an East Slavic iterative-intensive verb from воротить ('to turn', Proto-Slavic *vortiti, from *vьrtěti 'to turn').

ворсинка.etymology: Singulative diminutive formed with the suffix -инка ('a single tiny particle or strand of') from ворс ('nap, pile of fabric, fuzz'), recorded in Russian since the sixteenth century (compared by Vasmer with Iranian/Avestan varəsa- 'hair, filament' and Old East Slavic вълсъ / волосъ).

history.meaning: nap, pile → a single fibre, speck of lint

ворчать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic върчати ('to grumble, mutter, growl'), from Proto-Slavic *vъrčati, an onomatopoeic verb imitating low rumbling or growling sounds.

ворюга.etymology: Augmentative/pejorative derivative formed with the expressive suffix -юга from вор ('thief', in 16th–17th century Muscovite Russian 'rebel, traitor, criminal', from Proto-Slavic *vorъ, related to врать 'to lie, talk nonsense').

восемнадцать.etymology: Contracted from the Old East Slavic numeral phrase осьмь на десяте ('eight upon ten'), from Proto-Slavic *osmь na desęte (with prothetic initial в- before о- as in восемь 'eight').

восемь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic осьмь (with prosthetic East Slavic в- added before the rounded initial vowel o-), from Proto-Slavic *osmь ('eight', originally a feminine noun built with *-mь by analogy with *sedmь 'seven'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw ('eight', cognate with English eight and Latin octō).

восемьдесят.etymology: Univerbation of the Old East Slavic numeral phrase осьмь десятъ ('eight of tens'), where осьмь (> восемь 'eight') governed десятъ, the old consonant-stem genitive plural of десять ('ten').

morphemes.meaning: of tens (archaic genitive plural of десять)

восемьсот.etymology: Univerbation of the Old East Slavic numeral phrase осьмь сътъ ('eight of hundreds'), where осьмь (> восемь 'eight') governed сътъ (> сот), the genitive plural of съто ('hundred', modern Russian сто).

воск.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *voskъ 'wax', from a Balto-Slavic and Indo-European word for beeswax shared directly with Lithuanian vaskas and English wax.

воскресенье.etymology: Adapted from Old Church Slavonic въскрьсение ('resurrection', calquing Koine Greek ἀνάστασις 'resurrection [of Christ]'), which replaced older East Slavic недѣля as the name for Sunday ('the day of the Resurrection').

воскресный.etymology: Relational adjective formed from воскресенье ('Sunday', originally 'Resurrection' in Old Church Slavonic въскрьсениѥ), built on въскрьснути ('to rise again').

воспитание.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въспитаниѥ ('nourishing, rearing, upbringing'), verbal noun from въспитати / воспитать ('to rear, bring up', from *vъz- 'up' + *pitati 'to feed, nourish', Russian питать).

воспитанный.etymology: Adjectival past passive participle of воспитать ('to bring up, educate'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въспитати ('to nourish, rear, bring up'), from въс- ('up') + питати ('to feed, nourish', Proto-Slavic *pitati).

воспитатель.etymology: Agent noun formed with the suffix -тель from воспитать ('to raise, bring up, educate'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въспитати ('to nourish, rear up', from *vъz- 'up' + *pitati 'to feed, nourish').

воспитательница.etymology: Feminine counterpart of воспитатель ('educator, tutor, mentor'), formed with -ница from воспитать ('to bring up, rear, educate').

воспитать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въспитати ('to nourish, rear up, bring up a child'), formed from *vъz- ('up') + питати (Russian питать, 'to feed, nourish', Proto-Slavic *pitati, from PIE *peyt- 'food, nourishment', cognate with пища 'food'): literally 'to nurture/feed up to maturity' (just like Latin ēducāre and alumnus from alere 'to nourish').

воспитывать.etymology: Imperfective of воспитать ('to bring up, raise, educate'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въспитати ('to nourish, rear, bring up'), formed from въс- ('up') + питати ('to feed, nourish', from Proto-Slavic *pitati).

воспользоваться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed with the Church Slavonic prefix вос- (*vъz-) + пользоваться ('to use, make use of, benefit from'), derived from польза ('use, benefit, advantage', Old Church Slavonic польза).

history.meaning: to make use of, take advantage of (perfective)

воспользоваться.notes: Takes the instrumental case for the thing or opportunity used: воспользоваться случаем ('to take advantage of the opportunity').

воспоминание.etymology: Verbal noun from воспоминать ('to recall, remember'), formed from Church Slavonic въс- ('up') + поминать ('to remember, mention', from помнить 'to remember', Proto-Slavic *pomьněti).

воспринимать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of воспринять ('to perceive, receive, take in'), formed from Church Slavonic вос- ('up') + принимать ('to take, accept', from при- + имать, Proto-Slavic *jьmati).

воспринять.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въсприѩти ('to receive, take up, accept'), formed from въс- ('up') + приѩти (принять, 'to take, accept', from при- + *jęti 'to take').

восприятие.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въспри˫атиѥ ('receiving, acceptance'), verbal noun of въсприѩти (воспринять), used in modern Russian philosophy and psychology as a calque of Latin perceptio ('perception').

воссоединение.etymology: Verbal noun of воссоединить ('to reunite'), formed with Church Slavonic вос- ('again, back together') + соединение ('union, joining', from со- + единый 'one, united').

воссоздать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from Church Slavonic вос- ('anew, again') + создать ('to create, build', from Old Church Slavonic съзьдати 'to build, fashion').

восстановить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from Church Slavonic вос- ('up, back again') + становить ('to set up, place', from стан 'standing, camp', Proto-Slavic *stanoviti).

восстановление.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ение (and labial epenthesis в → вл) from восстановить ('to restore, rebuild, re-establish'), built with the Church Slavonic prefix вос- (*vъz- 'up again, re-') + становить ('to set upright, place', from стать 'to stand', Proto-Slavic *stati).

восток.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic въстокъ ('sunrise, rising, east'), a loan-translation of Ancient Greek anatole ('rising of the sun; the east'), built on въз- ('up') + -токъ ('flowing, rising, course').
восток.notes: Used in the singular: на восток ('to the east'), на востоке ('in the east'), с востока ('from the east').

восторг.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въсторгъ ('ecstasy, rapture, being snatched up in spirit'), a deverbal noun from въсторгнѫти / восторгнуть ('to tear/snatch upward'), built from въз- ('up') + торг- ('to tear, pull, jerk', as in расторгнуть 'to tear up a contract' and тормошить). Originally a mystical religious term translating Greek ἔκστασις ('ecstasy, transport of the soul'), it became the everyday word for 'delight, enthusiasm, rapture'.

восхитительный.etymology: Formed with suffix -тельный from восхитить ('to carry away in rapture, delight'), a Church Slavonic loanword (въсхитити, literally 'to snatch upward, carry aloft in ecstasy', built from въс- 'up' + хитити 'to snatch, seize', related to хватать).

history.meaning: to snatch upward, transport with rapture

восхищать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въсхищати ('to snatch up, carry away, enrapture'), from въс- ('up') + хищати ('to seize, snatch', iterative of хитити, Proto-Slavic *xytiti); the modern sense 'to delight' reflects 'to carry away in rapture'.

history.meaning: to snatch up, transport with rapture

восхищаться.etymology: Reflexive form of восхищать ('to carry away, delight') with the suffix -ся, evolving from 'to be carried away in ecstasy' to 'to admire, marvel at'.

history.meaning: to be caught up in rapture

восхищение.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въсхищениѥ ('rapture, being caught up'), verbal noun of въсхитити / въсхищати ('to snatch up, enrapture').

восход.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въсходъ ('ascent, rising of the sun'), from въс- ('up') + ходъ ('going, motion', Proto-Slavic *xodъ).

восьмилучевой.etymology: Compound adjective formed from восьми- (genitive/combining stem of восемь 'eight', Proto-Slavic *osmь, PIE *oḱtoh3) + лучевой ('rayed', from луч 'ray, beam of light', Proto-Slavic *lučь, PIE *lewk- 'light, bright'). Literally 'having eight rays', it is the standard Russian term for an eight-pointed star or compass rose.

восьмой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic осьмыи (with initial prosthetic в- added before rounded о-, just as in восемь), from Proto-Slavic *osmъ ('eighth'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *oḱt-mós ('eighth'; compare Lithuanian ãšmas).

вот.etymology: Formed in East Slavic by combining the deictic interjection во ('look, there!', from Proto-Slavic *vo) with a reduced enclitic form of the demonstrative pronoun тот ('that'). Used to point directly to something visible or just handed over ('here is').

вот-вот.etymology: Reduplicated expressive adverb formed by doubling the demonstrative particle вот ('here is, look!'), expressing that an action is on the verge of happening ('any second now, just about to').

history.meaning: right now, any moment now, just about to

воткнуть.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from во- ('in, into') + ткнуть ('to poke, thrust, jab', semelfactive with -нуть of Old Russian тъкати 'to thrust, weave', Proto-Slavic *tъknǫti).

вощёный.etymology: Adjectival passive participle of вощить ('to rub or coat with beeswax'), derived from воск ('wax') with the consonant alternation ск → щ before suffix -ён-ый. Russian воск descends from Old East Slavic воскъ and Proto-Slavic *voskъ ('beeswax'), from PIE *wosko- ('wax'), making it an exact cognate of English wax and German Wachs.

впадать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of впасть ('to fall into, flow into'), formed from в- ('into') + падать ('to fall', Proto-Slavic *padati).

history.meaning: to fall into (a state); to flow into (of a river)

впервые.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в первые ('for the first time'), from в ('in, for') + accusative plural of первый ('first', Proto-Slavic *pьrvъ).

впереди.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в переди ('in the front'), from в ('in') + locative singular of перёд ('front part', inherited from Old East Slavic передъ, with East Slavic pleophony -ере-, from Proto-Slavic *perdъ).

вперёд.etymology: Univerbation of the Old East Slavic directional phrase въ передъ ('into the front, forward'), combining the preposition въ ('into') with передъ ('front part', showing East Slavic pleophony -ере- from Proto-Slavic *perdъ, built on the same Indo-European root *per- as первый 'first').

впечатление.etymology: Coined by N. M. Karamzin at the turn of the 19th century from Old Church Slavonic въпечатьлѣниѥ ('imprinting with a seal', from печать 'seal, stamp') as a semantic calque of French impression and German Eindruck.

вписываться.etymology: Reflexive form of вписывать ('to write in, inscribe, fit into a space'), formed from в- ('into') + писывать / писать ('to write, paint', Proto-Slavic *pьsati) + -ся.

впиться.etymology: Prefixed reflexive perfective verb formed from в- ('into') + пить ('to drink', Proto-Slavic *piti) + -ся; literally 'to drink oneself into', originally of leeches or ticks sinking their mouthparts into skin, then generally 'to sink teeth/claws/eyes into'.

history.meaning: to sink teeth/claws into, dig into, fix one's gaze on

вполне.etymology: Univerbation of the Old East Slavic prepositional phrase въ пълнѣ ('in full'), combining the preposition въ ('in') with пълнѣ, the old short locative singular of полный ('full', from Proto-Slavic *pъlnъ).

вправду.etymology: Colloquial univerbation of the prepositional phrase в правду ('in truth'), from в ('in') + accusative singular of правда ('truth', Old East Slavic правьда, from правый 'right, true').

вправе.etymology: Predicative adverbial formed by univerbation of в праве ('within one's right'), from в ('in') + locative singular of право ('right, law', Proto-Slavic *pravo).

вправо.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в право ('to the right'), from в ('into, toward') + neuter short form of правый ('right-hand, straight', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

впрочем.etymology: Fused discourse conjunction from the prepositional phrase в прочем ('in the rest, as for the rest'), combining в ('in') + прочем (prepositional singular neuter of прочий 'other, remaining', from Old Church Slavonic прочии / Proto-Slavic *pročь 'away, further on').

history.meaning: in other respects, for the rest

впустить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from в- ('in, inside') + пустить ('to let go, allow', Proto-Slavic *pustiti).

впутывать.etymology: Imperfective of впутать ('to entangle in, drag into'), formed from в- ('into') + путать ('to tangle, fetter, confuse'), which is derived from путо / путы ('hobbles, fetters tied around a horse's legs', inherited from Old East Slavic путо, Proto-Slavic *pǫto).

history.meaning: to entangle in, drag into (an affair)

rootFamily.gloss: to confuse, mix up; to tangle

враг.etymology: Borrowed in its South Slavic / Old Church Slavonic form врагъ ('enemy, foe; the Devil'), alongside native East Slavic ворогъ (with pleophony -оро-), from Proto-Slavic *vorgъ ('enemy, outcast, persecutor'; compare Lithuanian var̃gas 'misery, distress' and Gothic wrikan 'to persecute', English wreak/wretch).

враньё.etymology: Colloquial collective and action noun formed with the suffix -ьё from врать ('to lie, tell falsehoods'; in Old East Slavic врати 'to babble, chatter'), from Proto-Slavic *vьrati ('to speak, babble', PIE *werh₁-).

врасплох.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в расплох, where older Russian расплох ('sudden alarm, confusion, unpreparedness'; compare переполох 'commotion, alarm' and оплошность 'oversight') comes from the Proto-Slavic root *plox- ('startled, frightened, bad', seen in плохой and полошить 'to startle').

history.meaning: in a state of sudden alarm or unpreparedness
off guard, unawares, by surprise (застать врасплох)

вратарь.etymology: Introduced into Russian sports vocabulary around 1910 (as a native replacement for the English loan голкипер) by reviving the Old Church Slavonic noun вратарь ('gatekeeper, monastery doorkeeper'), formed from врата (the Church Slavonic non-pleophonic counterpart of native Russian ворота 'gate; sports goal', Proto-Slavic *vorta) + the agent suffix -арь.

morphemes.meaning: gate, goal (Church Slavonic counterpart of ворота)

врать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьрати ('to babble, talk nonsense, lie'), from Proto-Slavic *vьrati ('to speak, chatter'). In older Russian up to the 18th century, врать often meant simply 'to chatter idly, babble'; Vasmer connects the root with Old Prussian īrist ('to say') and Ancient Greek εἴρω (eírō, 'to speak') and ῥήτωρ (rhḗtōr, 'orator', from PIE *werh₁- 'to speak', cognate with English word and Latin verbum), and compares врач ('physician', originally 'incantation speaker, healer').

history.meaning: to talk nonsense → to tell lies

врач.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic врачь ('physician, healer'), from Proto-Slavic *vračь, formed with the agent suffix *-čь from *vьrati ('to speak, recite charms', modern Russian врать). Originally врач denoted a traditional folk healer or medicine man who cured sickness by reciting incantations; in standard Russian врать shifted to 'to tell lies', while врач became the formal word for a medical doctor.

history.meaning: to speak charms → incantation healer, physician

вредитель.etymology: Agent noun formed with the suffix -тель from вредить ('to harm, damage'), derived from вред ('harm, injury', an Old Church Slavonic borrowing врѣдъ, corresponding to Proto-Slavic *verdъ).

вредно.etymology: Adverb and predicative form of вредный ('harmful, unhealthy; spiteful'), derived from вред ('harm, damage'), which was borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врѣдъ ('injury, wound, harm', corresponding to native East Slavic веред 'boil, sore, ulcer', from Proto-Slavic *verdъ).

history.meaning: harmful → harmfully; it is bad for you

вредный.etymology: Formed with the adjective suffix -ный from вред ('harm, damage, injury'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врѣдъ (corresponding to East Slavic веред 'boil, sore, injury', from Proto-Slavic *verdъ).

врезаться.etymology: Reflexive form of врезать / врезаться ('to cut into, crash into'), formed from the prefix в- ('into') + резать ('to cut', from Proto-Slavic *rězati) + -ся.

history.meaning: to cut into; to crash into, slam into

временно.etymology: Adverb formed from временный ('temporary, provisional'), derived from время (stem времен-, 'time', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врѣмя, from Proto-Slavic *vermę).

временный.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ный from время (stem времен-, 'time'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врѣмѧ ('time', Proto-Slavic *vermę, from *vьrtmen- 'turning, rotation').

время.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врѣмя ('time, season', replacing native East Slavic веремя), from Proto-Slavic *vermę, from *vertmen- (derived from *vьrtěti 'to turn, revolve', originally 'turning, cycle of time').

вроде.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в роде ('in the kind or manner of'), formed from the preposition в ('in') and the locative singular of род ('kind, sort, kin', from Proto-Slavic *rodъ).

history.meaning: in the sort or manner of

врун.etymology: Colloquial agent noun formed with the suffix -ун from врать ('to lie, fib', Old East Slavic вьрати 'to chatter, lie', Proto-Slavic *vьrati).

врунишка.etymology: Affectionate or mildly deprecatory diminutive formed with the suffix -ишка from врун ('liar'), itself an agent noun built on врать ('to lie, tell fibs', from Old East Slavic вьрати, Proto-Slavic *vьrati).

history.meaning: to lie → liar → little liar, fibber

вручную.etymology: Adverb formed by univerbation of the prepositional phrase в ручную ('by hand, manually'), from в ('in') + feminine accusative singular of ручной ('hand, manual', from рука 'hand', Proto-Slavic *rǫka).

вряд.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в ряд ('in a row, in line', from ряд 'row, order', Proto-Slavic *rędъ), used with the interrogative particle ли (вряд ли 'hardly, unlikely', originally questioning whether something fits into order).

все.etymology: Plural form ('all, everyone') of the pronoun весь ('all, whole'), inherited from Old East Slavic вьсь (plural вьси), from Proto-Slavic *vьxъ / *vьśь ('all, whole'), cognate with Lithuanian visas ('all') and Sanskrit viśva- ('all, every').

всегда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьсегда ('always'), from Proto-Slavic *vьsegda, formed from the pronominal stem *vьse- ('all', modern Russian весь / всё) + the temporal adverbial suffix *-gda (compare когда 'when' and никогда 'never').

всего.etymology: Adverbialized genitive singular masculine/neuter form of весь ('all, whole', inherited from Old East Slavic вьсь, from Proto-Slavic *vьsь).

всезнайка.etymology: Colloquial common-gender compound noun formed from всё ('everything', from весь 'all', Proto-Slavic *vьsь) + знай- (stem of знать 'to know', Proto-Slavic *znati) + agentive suffix -ка.

вселенная.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вьселѥнаꙗ ('the inhabited world, universe'), a substantivized feminine passive participle calquing Ancient Greek οἰκουμένη (γῆ) ('the inhabited [earth]'), derived from вьселити ('to settle, populate', built on вьсь 'all; village').

всерьёз.etymology: Adverb formed from в ('in') + серьёз (back-formed noun from серьёзный 'serious', borrowed in the 18th century from French sérieux, from Medieval Latin seriosus, Latin serius 'earnest, grave').

вскрываться.etymology: Reflexive and passive form of вскрывать ('to open up, unseal, dissect, reveal cards'), formed from вз-/вс- ('up, open') + крывать (iterative of крыть 'to cover', Proto-Slavic *kryti) + -ся.

history.meaning: to come to light; to show one's cards

вслепую.etymology: Adverb formed by univerbation of в слепую ('in a blind manner'), from в ('in') + feminine accusative singular of слепой ('blind', Proto-Slavic *slěpъ).

вслух.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в слух ('into hearing'), from в ('into') + слух ('hearing, rumor', inherited from Old East Slavic слухъ, from Proto-Slavic *sluxъ).

всплыть.etymology: Formed from the upward prefix вс- / вз- ('up') + плыть ('to swim, float', inherited from Old East Slavic плыти, from Proto-Slavic *plyti, from PIE *plew- 'to flow, float').

history.meaning: to float up, surface, come to light

вспоминать.etymology: Imperfective of вспомнить ('to recall, remember'), formed from the prefix вс- ('up') + поминать ('to remember, mention', iterative of помянуть, from Proto-Slavic *pominati).

вспомнить.etymology: Formed from the prefix вс- / вз- ('up, forth') + помнить ('to remember', inherited from Old East Slavic помьнити, from Proto-Slavic *pomьniti, from the root *mьněti 'to think, keep in mind').

вспыхивать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of вспыхнуть ('to flare up, flash, blaze up'), formed from вс- ('up') + пыхать ('to blaze, puff, breathe hot air'), from an expressive Proto-Slavic root *pyxati ('to puff, blaze').

вставать.etymology: Imperfective of встать ('to stand up, get up'), inherited from Old East Slavic въставати, formed from въ- ('up') + ставати (iterative of стати 'to stand', from Proto-Slavic *stavati).

вставить.etymology: Formed with the prefix в- ('in, into') + ставить ('to set, place, stand', from Old East Slavic ставити and Proto-Slavic *staviti, causative of *stati 'to stand').

history.meaning: to insert, set in, mount in a frame

вставлять.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of вставить ('to insert, set in, put in'), formed from в- ('in, into') + ставлять / ставить ('to place, stand, set', Proto-Slavic *staviti).

встать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic въстати ('to rise, stand up'), from Proto-Slavic *vъstati, formed from *vъz- / *vъ- ('up') + *stati ('to stand, become').

встревать.etymology: Colloquial imperfective counterpart of встрять ('to get stuck in, butt in, meddle'), formed from в- ('into') + стрять / застрять ('to stick, jam', related to Proto-Slavic *strěti / *stьrčati).

встретить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic въстрѣтити ('to meet, encounter'), formed from въ- + срѣтити / стрѣтити (with epenthetic -т- in the cluster -ср-), from Proto-Slavic *sъrětiti ('to meet, find').

встретиться.etymology: Reciprocal/reflexive form of встретить ('to meet', from Old East Slavic въстрѣтити, Proto-Slavic *sъrětiti) + -ся.

встреча.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from встретить / встречать ('to meet, encounter'), inherited (with prefix в- added in Russian) from Old East Slavic сърѣча / сърѣтити ('to meet'), from Proto-Slavic *sъrětiti ('to come upon, find, meet').

встречать.etymology: Imperfective partner of встретить ('to meet, greet'), developed (with prefix в- added in East Slavic) from Old East Slavic сърѣчати / сърѣтити ('to meet, come upon'), from Proto-Slavic *sъrětiti ('to encounter, find').

встречаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive/reciprocal verb formed from встречать ('to meet'), derived from встретить ('to meet'), which goes back to Old East Slavic въстрѣтити (with epenthetic -т- inserted in the cluster -ср-), from Proto-Slavic *vъz- + *sъrětiti ('to encounter, come upon').

history.meaning: to meet, go out to greet
to meet each other; to date, go out

встречный.etymology: Formed in Russian from встреча ('meeting, encounter') + the relational adjective suffix -ный; встреча goes back to Old East Slavic въстрѣча, built on the verb сърѣсти / встретить ('to meet, encounter', Proto-Slavic *sъrěsti).
встречный.notes: In the idiom первый встречный ('the first person one happens to meet on the street'), встречный functions as a noun meaning a random passerby.

вступать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed from prefix в- ('in, into') + ступать ('to step, tread', Proto-Slavic *stǫpati, related to *stǫpiti 'to step' and стопа 'footstep'). Literally 'to step into', it is used across Russian both for entering an organization or conversation and, in music, for a soloist or duet partner entering on cue.

history.meaning: to enter, come in on cue

вступить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from в- ('in, into') + ступить ('to step, tread', Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti).

вступиться.etymology: Reflexive derivative of вступить ('to step in') with the suffix -ся, developing the idiomatic meaning 'to step in on someone's behalf, to stand up for'.

history.meaning: to stand up for, intercede for

всякий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьсякыи ('every, any, of all kinds'), from Proto-Slavic *vьjakъ, formed from *vьsь ('all', Russian весь) + the pronominal qualifier suffix *-jakъ ('of what kind').

всё-таки.etymology: Compound concessive particle formed in Russian from всё ('all, still, nonetheless', neuter singular of весь 'all') and the emphatic particle таки ('after all, even so', derived from так 'thus, so', Proto-Slavic *tako).

history.meaning: all the same, after all, nevertheless

вторник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic въторникъ ('Tuesday', Old Church Slavonic въторьникъ), formed with the noun suffix -ник from второй ('second', from Proto-Slavic *vъtorъ): literally 'the second day of the week' counting from Monday (понедельник).

morphemes.meaning: noun suffix naming a day or agent

второй.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic въторыи (Old Church Slavonic въторыи, 'second, the other of two'), from Proto-Slavic *vъtorъ, related to Sanskrit ántara ('other, second') and Lithuanian añtras ('second, other').

втроём.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase в троем ('in a group of three'), from в ('in') + locative singular of the collective numeral трое ('three', from Proto-Slavic *troje).

history.meaning: the three of us/them, three together

втягивать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of втянуть ('to pull in, draw in, involve'), formed from в- ('in, into') + тягивать / тянуть ('to pull, draw', Proto-Slavic *tęgnǫti).

history.meaning: to pull in, drag into, involve

втянутый.etymology: Past passive participle of втянуть ('to pull in, draw in, involve'), formed from в- ('in, into') + тянуть ('to pull, stretch', Proto-Slavic *tęgnǫti).

вуаля.etymology: Borrowed from French voilà ('there it is, behold!'), itself a contraction of the imperative phrase vois là ('see there!', from voir 'to see' + là 'there').

вход.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic въходъ ('entrance, entry'), deverbal noun from входить ('to enter, go in'), from в- ('in') + ход ('motion, walk', from Proto-Slavic *xodъ).

входить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic въходити ('to go in, enter'), imperfective counterpart of войти, formed from prefix в- ('in, into') + ходить ('to walk, go', from Proto-Slavic *xoditi).

history.meaning: to go in, enter, fit inside, be included

входной.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ной from вход ('entrance', from в- + ход).

вчера.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic въчера ('yesterday', Old Church Slavonic вчера), from Proto-Slavic *vъčera, historically an old petrified genitive-ablative or instrumental case form of *večerъ ('evening', modern Russian вечер): 'from last evening', hence 'yesterday'.

вчерашний.etymology: Temporal adjective formed with the suffix -шний (used to form adjectives from time/place adverbs, as in сегодняшний, домашний, здешний) from вчера ('yesterday'), which goes back to Old East Slavic вьчера, originally the genitive singular of вечеръ ('evening', Proto-Slavic *večerъ).

въехать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from въ- ('into') + ехать ('to ride, drive, travel by vehicle', Old East Slavic ѣхати, Proto-Slavic *ěxati, PIE *yeh₂-).

history.meaning: to drive in, move into; (slang) to get it

вы.etymology: Вы is an inherited Slavic second-person plural pronoun, already present in Old Russian and Old Church Slavonic.
