Vasmer relates it to forms such as Latin vos and discusses how older pronoun forms were remodelled within the Slavic case system. Addressing one person politely is a use of the plural pronoun, not its original basic meaning.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: вы

выбегать.etymology: Formed in Russian from the prefix вы- ('out') + бегать ('to run', inherited from Proto-Slavic *běgati).

выбежать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out') + бежать ('to run', Old East Slavic бѣжати, Proto-Slavic *běžati).

выбирать.etymology: Imperfective of выбрать ('to choose, select, take out'), formed from the prefix вы- ('out') + -бирать (iterative stem of брать 'to take', from Proto-Slavic *bьrati).

выбираться.etymology: Reflexive and passive form of выбирать ('to choose, elect; to get out', from вы- + -бирать, iterative of брать 'to take') + -ся.

history.meaning: to get out, make one's way out; to run for office

выбить.etymology: Formed from the prefix вы- ('out') + бить ('to beat, strike, hit', inherited from Old East Slavic бити, from Proto-Slavic *biti).

history.meaning: to knock out; to blow (a fuse)

выбиться.etymology: Prefixed reflexive perfective verb formed from вы- ('out') + бить ('to beat, strike', Proto-Slavic *biti) + -ся, meaning literally 'to beat one's way out', hence to exhaust one's strength (выбиться из сил) or rise in status (выбиться в люди).

history.meaning: to break out, work one's way up, become exhausted

выбор.etymology: Deverbal noun from выбрать ('to choose, pick out'), built on the prefix вы- ('out') + the o-grade root -бор (from брать 'to take', Proto-Slavic *borъ / *bьrati).

выборы.etymology: Plural of выбор ('choice, selection'), formed as a deverbal noun from выбирать / выбрать ('to choose, elect'), built from the prefix вы- ('out') and брать ('to take', from Proto-Slavic *bьrati). In the plural, выборы specialized in the political sense of 'elections'.

выбрасывать.etymology: Imperfective of выбросить ('to throw out, discard'), formed with prefix вы- ('out') from брасывать / бросать ('to throw'), from Proto-Slavic *brosati.

выбрать.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vybьrati, formed from the prefix вы- ('out') + брать ('to take', from Proto-Slavic *bьrati), literally 'to take out [of a group], select'.

выбраться.etymology: Reflexive derivative of выбрать ('to take out, pick out', from вы- 'out' + брать 'to take', Proto-Slavic *bьrati) + -ся: literally 'to pull or work oneself out of an enclosed or difficult place'.

history.meaning: to get out, extricate oneself; to manage to get away

выброс.etymology: Deverbal noun from выбросить ('to throw out, eject, emit'), formed from вы- ('out') + бросить ('to throw', Proto-Slavic *brositi).

выбросить.etymology: Formed from the directional prefix вы- ('out') + бросить ('to throw, cast', from Proto-Slavic *brositi).

выбыть.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out, away') + быть ('to be', Proto-Slavic *byti), literally 'to cease to be inside a group or competition, to drop out'.

history.meaning: to drop out, leave, be eliminated

вывеска.etymology: Built natively from the verb вывесить 'to hang out' (вы- 'out' + весить 'to hang') + -ка: literally 'something hung outside' over a shop door to show its name or trade.

вывести.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out') + вести ('to lead', Proto-Slavic *vesti), meaning to lead out, deduce, remove a stain, or (from вывести из себя) drive someone mad.

history.meaning: to lead out, remove; to exasperate

вывихнуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective verb formed with -нуть from вывих ('dislocation, sprain'), from вы- ('out of place') + Old East Slavic вихати ('to shake, twist, bend', Proto-Slavic *vixati).

вывод.etymology: Deverbal noun from выводить / вывести ('to lead out, deduce', from вы- 'out' + водить / вести 'to lead', Proto-Slavic *voditi); the logical sense 'conclusion, inference' developed from 'drawing out' a consequence (compare Latin deductio and conclusio).

history.meaning: to lead out, deduce -> withdrawal; logical conclusion

вывод.notes: Сделать вывод means 'to draw a conclusion'.

выглядеть.etymology: Formed from вы- ('out') + глядеть ('to look', from Proto-Slavic *ględěti), modeled as a semantic calque of German aussehen ('to look, appear', literally 'to look out').

выглядывать.etymology: Imperfective of выглянуть ('to look out, peek out'), formed from the prefix вы- ('out') + глядеть / -глядывать ('to look', from Proto-Slavic *ględěti).

выгнать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix вы- ('out') and гнать ('to drive, chase'), inherited from Old East Slavic гънати, from Proto-Slavic *gъnati ('to drive cattle, chase', from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen- 'to strike, drive').

history.meaning: to drive out, kick out, expel

выгода.etymology: Formed with prefix вы- and the Slavic root *god- ('suitability, favourable time', as in годный 'fit, suitable' and угодить 'to please'), likely reinforced by Polish wygoda ('convenience, comfort').

выгодно.etymology: Adverb and predicative derived from выгодный ('profitable, advantageous'), from выгода ('benefit, advantage, profit').

выгодный.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ный from выгода ('benefit, advantage'), formed from вы- + год- (the root of годиться 'to suit, be fit' and угодить 'to please', Proto-Slavic *godъ 'fitting time/thing').

выгонять.etymology: Imperfective of выгнать ('to drive out, expel'), formed from the prefix вы- ('out') + гонять ('to drive, chase', iterative of гнать, from Proto-Slavic *goniti / *gъnati).

history.meaning: to drive out, kick out, fire

выгореть.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix вы- ('out, completely') and гореть ('to burn'), inherited from Old East Slavic горѣти and Proto-Slavic *gorěti. In colloquial Russian (especially in the negative: дело не выгорело 'the deal didn't pan out'), the figurative sense 'to succeed, come off' arose from metallurgy, brick-firing, or tar-distilling, where a batch had to burn through properly to yield a good result.

history.meaning: to burn out/down; (colloq.) to pan out, succeed

выгуливать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed from вы- ('out') + гуливать / гулять ('to walk, stroll'), taking pets or children out for fresh air and exercise.

history.meaning: to walk (a dog), take out for a walk

выдавать.etymology: Imperfective of выдать, formed from the prefix вы- ('out') + давать ('to give', inherited from Proto-Slavic *davati, iterative of *dati 'to give').

history.meaning: to hand out, issue; to give away, betray

выдать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic выдати ('to hand over, give out, betray'), formed from the prefix вы- ('out') + дать ('to give', from Proto-Slavic *dati).

history.meaning: to issue, give out, hand out; to betray

выдаться.etymology: Reflexive form of выдать ('to give out, yield', from вы- + дать 'to give', Proto-Slavic *dati) + -ся, developing the sense 'to jut out' and 'to turn out, happen to be (of a day or occasion)'.

history.meaning: to turn out, happen to be

выдающийся.etymology: Lexicalized present active participle of выдаваться ('to jut out, stand out', from выдавать + -ся): literally 'jutting forward beyond the line, standing out from the rest'.

history.meaning: to project, jut out, stand out

выдвигать.etymology: Imperfective of выдвинуть ('to move out, pull out, put forward, nominate'), formed from the prefix вы- ('out, forward') + двигать ('to move, shift', from Proto-Slavic *dvigati).

history.meaning: to pull out; to put forward, nominate

выдвинуть.etymology: Formed in Russian from the prefix вы- ('out, forward') + двинуть ('to move, shift once', from Proto-Slavic *dvignǫti).

history.meaning: to pull out (a drawer); to put forward, nominate

выделение.etymology: Verbal noun in -ение formed from выделить ('to single out, allocate, secrete'), built from вы- ('out') + делить ('to divide, share', from Proto-Slavic *děliti).

history.meaning: to single out, allocate -> allocation, secretion

выделить.etymology: Formed from the prefix вы- ('out') + делить ('to divide, apportion, share', inherited from Old East Slavic дѣлити, from Proto-Slavic *děliti), literally 'to apportion out from a whole'.

history.meaning: to allocate, earmark; to single out

выдержать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out, through to the end') + держать ('to hold, keep', Old East Slavic дьржати, Proto-Slavic *dьržati).

выдержка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from выдержать ('to hold out, endure, age to maturity'), built from prefix вы- ('out, through to completion') + держать ('to hold, keep', Proto-Slavic *dьržati). Because выдержать means both 'to hold one's nerve under pressure' and 'to keep wine, cheese, or a recipe maturing over time', выдержка means both 'composure, self-control' and 'vintage, aging'.

history.meaning: to hold out / age → composure; vintage

выдернуть.etymology: Prefixed semelfactive perfective verb formed from вы- ('out') + дёрнуть ('to pull, tug, yank', from дёргать, Proto-Slavic *dьrgnǫti).

history.meaning: to pull out, yank out; to call away

выдох.etymology: Deverbal noun back-formed from выдохнуть ('to exhale, breathe out'), formed from the prefix вы- ('out') + дохнуть (from the root of дух 'breath' and дышать 'to breathe', Proto-Slavic *dъx-).

выдумать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out, thoroughly') + думать ('to think', Proto-Slavic *dumati), meaning 'to think up, invent, fabricate'.

выдумывать.etymology: Imperfective of выдумать ('to think up, invent'), formed from вы- ('out') + думать ('to think', from дума 'thought, counsel', an early Germanic loan into Proto-Slavic *duma) + the imperfectivizing suffix -ывать.

выезд.etymology: Deverbal noun from выехать / выезжать ('to drive out, depart'), formed from вы- ('out') + езд ('riding, driving', Proto-Slavic *ězdъ).

выезжать.etymology: Imperfective of выехать ('to drive out, depart'), formed from вы- ('out') + -езжать (the regular imperfective/iterative stem corresponding to ехать 'to ride, drive', from Proto-Slavic *ěxati / *ězditi).

history.meaning: to drive out, depart, move out

выехать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out') + ехать ('to go by vehicle, ride', Proto-Slavic *ěxati).

history.meaning: to drive out, depart, set off

выживание.etymology: Verbal noun in -ние formed from выживать ('to survive', imperfective of выжить, built from вы- 'through, out' + жить 'to live', Proto-Slavic *žiti).

выжить.etymology: Formed from the prefix вы- ('out, through to the end') + жить ('to live', inherited from Proto-Slavic *žiti and Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃w-): literally 'to live through a danger or ordeal and remain alive'.

вызвать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix вы- ('out') and звать ('to call', Old East Slavic зъвати, Proto-Slavic *zъvati). Literally 'to call out', whence 'to summon (a doctor, taxi, or witness), challenge, or cause'.

history.meaning: to call out, summon; to cause

выздоравливать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of выздороветь ('to recover health'), formed with suffix -ива- and root vowel lengthening (-оравл-) from вы- + здоровый ('healthy', Proto-Slavic *sъdorvъ).

выздороветь.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out, completely') + здороветь ('to grow healthy'), from здоровый ('healthy', Old East Slavic съдоровъ, Proto-Slavic *sъdorvъ).

выздоровление.etymology: Verbal action noun formed with -ение from выздороветь ('to recover from illness'), built on вы- + здоровый ('healthy', Proto-Slavic *sъdorvъ).

вызов.etymology: Deverbal noun from вызывать / вызвать ('to call out, summon, challenge'), built from вы- ('out') + the root of звать ('to call', Old East Slavic зъвати, Proto-Slavic *zъvati) with regular vocalization of the strong yer (ъ -> о in зов).

history.meaning: to call out, summon -> call, summons, challenge

вызов.notes: Covers both an emergency or service call (вызов врача, вызов такси) and a challenge (бросить вызов 'to throw down a challenge').

вызывать.etymology: Imperfective of вызвать ('to call out, summon, cause, provoke'), formed from the prefix вы- ('out') + звать / -зывать ('to call', from Proto-Slavic *zъvati).

выигранный.etymology: Past passive participle of выиграть ('to win'), formed from вы- ('out, by playing') + играть ('to play', Proto-Slavic *jьgrati).

выиграть.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix вы- ('out, winning through action') and играть ('to play', from Old East Slavic играти, Proto-Slavic *jьgrati). Literally, 'to obtain or come out ahead by playing'.

history.meaning: to win (a game, prize, or election)

выигрывать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of выиграть ('to win'), formed with the iterative suffix -ыва- from вы- ('out') + играть ('to play', Proto-Slavic *jьgrati).

выигрыш.etymology: Formed in Russian with the noun suffix -ыш from выиграть ('to win [a game or lottery]'), itself from вы- ('out') + играть ('to play', from игра 'game', Proto-Slavic *jьgra).

выйти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic выити ('to go out, exit'), formed from the prefix вы- ('out') + идти ('to go, walk', from Proto-Slavic *jьti).

выкидывать.etymology: Imperfective of выкинуть ('to throw out, discard'), formed from вы- ('out') + кидать ('to throw, cast', Proto-Slavic *kydati) + the imperfectivizing suffix -ывать.

history.meaning: to throw out, discard; to pull a stunt

выкинуть.etymology: Formed from the directional prefix вы- ('out') + кинуть ('to throw, cast', semelfactive of кидать, from Proto-Slavic *kynǫti).

выкладывать.etymology: Imperfective corresponding to выложить ('to lay out'), formed from вы- ('out') + -кладывать (iterative of класть 'to lay, put', from Proto-Slavic *klasti); colloquially used for laying all facts out on the table ('spilling the truth') or posting content online.

history.meaning: to lay out, unpack; to spill (everything one knows)

выключатель.etymology: Formed with the instrument/agent suffix -тель from выключать ('to switch off, turn off, exclude'), derived from вы- ('out') + включать / ключ ('key, switch', from Proto-Slavic *kľučь).

выключать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of выключить ('to switch off, turn off, exclude'), formed from вы- ('out') + ключать / ключить (derived from ключ 'key, bolt', Proto-Slavic *ključь).

выключить.etymology: Coined in late 19th- / early 20th-century technical Russian as a semantic calque of German ausschalten ('to switch off, disconnect a circuit'), formed from вы- ('out') + ключить (built on ключ 'key, switch', from Proto-Slavic *kľučь 'hook, key, bolt'), as the antonym of включить ('to include; to switch on').

выключиться.etymology: Reflexive and middle-voice form of выключить ('to switch off, turn off') with the suffix -ся, meaning to power down or (colloquially) pass out/lose consciousness.

history.meaning: to turn off by itself; to black out

выкрасть.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out') + красть ('to steal', Old East Slavic красти, Proto-Slavic *krasti).

выкуп.etymology: Deverbal noun from выкупить ('to ransom, redeem, buy back'), formed from вы- ('out') + куп- (stem of купить 'to buy', Proto-Slavic *kupiti, an early Germanic borrowing from *kaupōną).

выкупать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of выкупить ('to buy out, redeem, ransom'), formed from вы- ('out') + купать / купить ('to buy', Proto-Slavic *kupiti).

выкупить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic выкупити ('to redeem, ransom, buy out'), formed from вы- ('out') + купити ('to buy', Proto-Slavic *kupiti).

history.meaning: to buy out, buy back, ransom

вылезать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of вылезти ('to climb out, crawl out'), formed from вы- ('out') + лезать (iterative stem of лезть 'to climb, crawl', Proto-Slavic *lězti).

вылезти.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vylězti, formed from the prefix вы- ('out') + лезть ('to climb, crawl', from Proto-Slavic *lězti).

вылетать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of вылететь ('to fly out, depart by air'), formed from вы- ('out') + летать ('to fly', iterative of лететь, Proto-Slavic *lětati).

вылететь.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out') + лететь ('to fly', Proto-Slavic *letěti); colloquially also 'to be expelled or fired'.

history.meaning: to fly out, take off; to get kicked out

выливать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of вылить ('to pour out'), formed from вы- ('out') + ливать (iterative of лить 'to pour', Proto-Slavic *liti).

вылить.etymology: Formed with prefix вы- ('out') from лить ('to pour'), inherited from Old East Slavic лити, from Proto-Slavic *liti ('to pour').

вылиться.etymology: Reflexive-intransitive verb formed from вылить ('to pour out', from вы- 'out' + лить 'to pour', Proto-Slavic *liti) + -ся; figuratively 'to spill over into, result in'.

history.meaning: to pour out -> to spill out, turn into (a consequence)

выложить.etymology: Formed with the prefix вы- ('out') + -ложить ('to lay, put', from Proto-Slavic *ložiti, causative of *legti 'to lie'): 'to lay out, unpack, pave or line a surface'.

выломать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out') + ломать ('to break', Proto-Slavic *lamati / *lomiti), meaning 'to break out or down by force'.

выманить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out') + манить ('to beckon, lure, entice', Proto-Slavic *maniti).

вымачивать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of вымочить ('to soak thoroughly, steep'), formed from вы- ('thoroughly, out') + мачивать / мочить ('to wet, soak', causative of мокнуть, Proto-Slavic *močiti).

вымолить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out, obtaining by effort') + молить ('to pray, beg, implore', Proto-Slavic *moliti).

history.meaning: to obtain by begging or praying

вымыть.etymology: Formed with the completive prefix вы- ('thoroughly, clean') + мыть ('to wash'), inherited from Old East Slavic мыти and Proto-Slavic *myti.

вынести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вынести ('to carry out'), formed from the prefix вы- ('out') + нести ('to carry', from Proto-Slavic *nesti).

history.meaning: to carry out, endure; to hand down a ruling

вынимать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of вынуть ('to take out'), historically reshaped from вы- ('out') + -нимать (from Old East Slavic выимати, with epenthetic н- after prepositions, Proto-Slavic *jьmati 'to take').

выносить.etymology: Imperfective of вынести, formed from вы- ('out') + носить ('to carry', iterative of нести, from Proto-Slavic *nositi); the sense 'to bear, tolerate, endure' developed from bearing a load all the way through.

history.meaning: to carry out; to bear, endure

вынужден.etymology: Short masculine past passive participle of вынудить ('to force, compel, extort'), showing Church Slavonic жд (< *dj, compare East Slavic нудить / нужда 'need, compulsion', from Proto-Slavic *nuditi / *nuda).

вынужденный.etymology: Adjectival past passive participle of вынудить ('to force, compel', with Church Slavonic жд from *dj), formed from вы- + нудить ('to compel', from нужда / нужа 'need, compulsion', Proto-Slavic *nuditi).

выпадать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of выпасть ('to fall out; to occur, fall to one's lot'), formed from вы- ('out') + падать ('to fall', Proto-Slavic *padati).

history.meaning: to fall out; to come along (of a chance)

выпарить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out, away') + парить ('to steam, stew', denominative from пар 'steam, vapor', Proto-Slavic *pariti).

выпасть.etymology: Formed with prefix вы- ('out') from пасть (паду, 'to fall'), inherited from Old East Slavic пасти, from Proto-Slavic *pasti ('to fall').

history.meaning: to fall out; to fall (of snow/luck)

выпекать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the prefix вы- ('out, thoroughly') + пекать (iterative of печь 'to bake', from Proto-Slavic *pekti).

history.meaning: to bake thoroughly, bake (bread or pastry)

выпечка.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -ка from выпечь / выпекать ('to bake'), built on prefix вы- + печь ('to bake', from Proto-Slavic *pekti). Denotes both the process of baking and baked pastries or bread.

history.meaning: to bake → baking; baked goods, pastries

выпивать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of выпить ('to drink up, have a drink'), formed from вы- ('out, up') + пивать (iterative of пить 'to drink', Proto-Slavic *piti); used intransitively for drinking alcohol.

history.meaning: to drink up; to drink alcohol socially

выпивка.etymology: Colloquial deverbal noun formed with the suffix -ка from выпивать ('to drink alcohol'), referring both to alcoholic drinks and to a drinking session.

выпирать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of выпереть ('to push out, bulge out, jut out'), formed from вы- ('out') + пирать (iterative of переть 'to press, push', Proto-Slavic *pьrati / *perti).

выписать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic выписати ('to copy out, write out'), formed from the prefix вы- ('out') + писать ('to write', from Proto-Slavic *pisati).

history.meaning: to write out, issue, prescribe; to discharge from hospital

выписка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with the suffix -ка from выписать / выписывать ('to write out, extract; to discharge from a hospital').

выписывать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of выписать ('to write out, subscribe to, discharge from hospital'), formed from вы- ('out') + писывать (iterative of писать 'to write', Proto-Slavic *pьsati).

history.meaning: to write out, prescribe, discharge from hospital

выпить.etymology: Formed by prefixing вы- ('out, completely') to пить ('to drink', from Old East Slavic пити, Proto-Slavic *piti, from PIE *peh₃(y)- 'to drink'; cognate with Latin bibō, Ancient Greek πίνω, and Sanskrit píbati).

history.meaning: to drink up, have a drink (perfective)

выплата.etymology: Deverbal noun from выплатить / выплачивать ('to pay out, pay off'), formed from вы- ('out') + плата ('payment', from платить 'to pay', Proto-Slavic *platiti).

выполнить.etymology: Formed with prefix вы- ('out, completely') from полнить ('to fill'), derived from полный ('full'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *pьlnъ ('full'), literally 'to fill out to completion, fulfill'.

выполнять.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of выполнить ('to fulfill, carry out, perform'), formed from the prefix вы- ('out, completely') and полнить ('to fill', from полный 'full', Old East Slavic пълныи, Proto-Slavic *pъlnъ, cognate with English full). Literally, 'to fill out to completion, fulfill' (compare English fulfill from full).

выпотрошить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with вы- ('out') + потрошить ('to gut, disembowel'), a denominative verb from потроха ('entrails, giblets, offal', inherited from East Slavic *потрохъ).

history.meaning: to gut, clean out (fish or poultry); colloquially to empty out (pockets or a bag)

выпросить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out, obtaining by effort') + просить ('to ask, beg', Proto-Slavic *prositi).

выпрыгнуть.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out') + прыгнуть ('to jump, leap', semelfactive of прыгать, from an expressive East Slavic root прыг-).

выпуск.etymology: Deverbal noun from выпустить / выпускать ('to let out, release, publish, graduate'), formed from вы- ('out') + пуск ('letting go', from пустить, Proto-Slavic *pustiti).

выпускать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of выпустить ('to let out, release, issue, produce'), formed from вы- ('out') + пускать ('to let go', Proto-Slavic *puskati).

выпустить.etymology: Formed with prefix вы- ('out') from пустить ('to let go, release'), inherited from Old East Slavic пустити, from Proto-Slavic *pustiti.

history.meaning: to release, to let out; to publish/produce

выражать.etymology: Imperfective of выразить ('to express, convey'), built with вы- ('out') on the Church Slavonic / Slavic root *raz- ('strike, cut, stamp an image', as in образ 'image, form' and разить 'to strike'), likely shaped in literary Russian as a calque of Polish wyrażać and Latin exprimere / French exprimer.

morphemes.meaning: stamp, form, express (from *raz- with з -> ж)

выражение.etymology: Verbal noun from выразить ('to express'), formed in the 18th century as a semantic calque of French expression (from Latin expressio), built on вы- ('out') + разить ('to strike, cut, stamp an image').

выразить.etymology: Formed from вы- ('out') + разить ('to strike, carve, imprint', from Old Russian разъ 'stroke, cut, image', Proto-Slavic *raziti), reshaped semantically in the 18th century as a calque of French exprimer / German ausdrücken ('to express').

выразиться.etymology: Reflexive form of выразить ('to express') with the suffix -ся, calquing French s'exprimer ('to express oneself, phrase a thought').

history.meaning: to express oneself, put into words

вырастать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of вырасти ('to grow up, sprout'), formed from вы- ('out, up') + растать / расти ('to grow', Proto-Slavic *orsti).

вырасти.etymology: Formed from the perfective prefix вы- ('out, up') + расти ('to grow', inherited from Old East Slavic рости, influenced by Church Slavonic расти, from Proto-Slavic *orsti).

вырастить.etymology: Formed by prefixing вы- ('up, to full growth') to растить ('to grow, raise, cultivate', with Church Slavonic ра- instead of East Slavic ро- as in рост), causative of расти ('to grow', from Proto-Slavic *orsti).

вырвать.etymology: Formed from the prefix вы- ('out') + рвать ('to tear, pluck', from Old East Slavic ръвати, Proto-Slavic *rъvati).

вырезать.etymology: Formed with the prefix вы- ('out') + резать ('to cut, carve, slice'), inherited from Old East Slavic рѣзати and Proto-Slavic *rězati ('to cut, incise').

history.meaning: to carve out, cut out, engrave

вырезка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with the suffix -ка from вырезать ('to cut out'), from вы- ('out') + резать ('to cut, slice', Proto-Slavic *rězati); in butchery and cooking, the prime tenderloin cut out from along the spine.

вырубить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out, down') + рубить ('to chop, hew, fell', Proto-Slavic *rǫbiti); colloquially used for cutting off power or knocking someone unconscious.

history.meaning: to chop down; (colloq.) to switch off, knock out

выручать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of выручить ('to rescue, help out; to gain revenue'), derived from вы- ('out') + рука ('hand', via порука 'bail, surety', literally 'to take out on bail or into one's hands').

history.meaning: to help out, come to the rescue

выручить.etymology: Formed from вы- ('out') + -ручить (derived from рука 'hand', Proto-Slavic *rǫka; compare поручиться 'to vouch for, stand surety'): originally an old legal and commercial term meaning 'to release a debtor or prisoner by standing surety (giving one's hand), or to recover money from a sale', whence 'to rescue, bail out, help in a pinch'.

history.meaning: to redeem from pledge or custody by standing surety
to help out, rescue, bail out; to make (money from a sale)

выручка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with -ка from выручить / выручать ('to rescue; to take in money from a sale'), signifying both 'aid, rescue' and 'commercial takings, revenue'.

history.meaning: to help out; to net from sales

высадить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out') + садить ('to seat, plant, set', causative of сесть, Proto-Slavic *saditi), meaning to set passengers down or transplant plants.

history.meaning: to drop off (passengers), disembark; to plant out

выселять.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of выселить ('to evict, move out of a dwelling'), formed from вы- ('out') + селить ('to settle', from село 'settlement, village', Proto-Slavic *seliti).

выселяться.etymology: Reflexive form of выселять ('to evict, move out') with the suffix -ся, meaning to vacate a room or check out of a hotel or apartment.

history.meaning: to move out, check out, vacate

выскочить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out') + скочить ('to leap, bound, jump', Old East Slavic скочити, Proto-Slavic *skočiti).

history.meaning: to jump out, pop out, rush out

выслать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out, away') + слать ('to send', Old East Slavic сълати, Proto-Slavic *sъlati).

history.meaning: to send out, dispatch; to exile, deport

выследить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out, thoroughly') + следить ('to track, follow footprints', from след 'footprint, track', Proto-Slavic *slědъ).

выслушать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the exhaustive prefix вы- ('out, to the end') and слушать ('to listen', from Proto-Slavic *slušati). Means 'to listen to someone all the way through, hear someone out'.

history.meaning: to hear out, listen to the end

высокий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic высокыи ('high, tall'), from Proto-Slavic *vysokъ, formed with the suffix *-okъ from the root *vys- (compare высь 'height'), from Proto-Indo-European *oups- ('high, up'; cognate with Ancient Greek ὕψος).

высоко.etymology: Adverbial and predicate form in -о of высокий ('high, tall'), inherited from Old East Slavic высоко and Proto-Slavic *vysoko (built on the Indo-European root *оups- / *ūps- 'up, high').

высота.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic высота ('height, elevation'), formed with the abstract suffix -ота from высокъ (высокий, 'high, tall', Proto-Slavic *vysota).

высохнуть.etymology: Formed from the perfective prefix вы- ('out, completely') + сохнуть ('to dry, wither', inherited from Proto-Slavic *sъxnǫti, related to сухой 'dry').

выспаться.etymology: Formed in Russian with the completive/saturative circumfix вы-...-ся added to спать ('to sleep', from Old East Slavic съпати, Proto-Slavic *sъpati): literally 'to sleep oneself out thoroughly, get one's fill of sleep'.

history.meaning: to get enough sleep, sleep one's fill

выспрашивать.etymology: Imperfective of выспросить, formed from вы- ('out', extracting information) + спрашивать ('to ask, inquire', iterative of спросить / просить, from Proto-Slavic *prositi).

history.meaning: to question thoroughly, worm information out of

выставить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic выставити, formed from the prefix вы- ('out, forth') + ставить ('to put, place, stand', causative of стать, from Proto-Slavic *staviti).

history.meaning: to put up, set out, exhibit

выставка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with the suffix -ка from выставить ('to set out, put on display, exhibit'), built from вы- ('out') + ставить ('to put, place upright', Proto-Slavic *staviti). Like Latin expositiō / English exhibition, it literally means 'a setting out on public view'.

history.meaning: setting out on display → exhibition, show, expo

выстрел.etymology: Deverbal noun from выстрелить ('to shoot, fire a shot'), formed from вы- ('out') + стрелить / стрелять ('to shoot', originally 'to shoot an arrow', from стрела 'arrow', Proto-Slavic *strěla).

выстрелить.etymology: Perfective verb formed from вы- ('out') + стрелить / стрелять ('to shoot', originally 'to shoot an arrow', derived from стрела 'arrow', Proto-Slavic *strěla).

выстроиться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of выстроить ('to build up; to array in a line or formation'), formed from prefix вы- + строить ('to arrange in order, build', from Old East Slavic строити and Proto-Slavic *strojiti, from *strojь 'order, formation, row').

history.meaning: row, order → to arrange in formation
to draw up in a line → to line up

выступать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of выступить ('to step forward, step out; to perform or speak in public'), formed from the prefix вы- ('out, forth') and ступать ('to step, tread', from Proto-Slavic *stǫpati). Literally, 'to step out in front of an audience or assembly'.

history.meaning: to step forward → to speak in public, perform on stage

rootFamily.gloss: to step on; to come (of time)

выступить.etymology: Formed from вы- ('out, forward') + ступить ('to step, tread', from Old East Slavic ступити, Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti): literally 'to step forward out of the line', whence 'to come forward to speak or perform in public'.

history.meaning: to step forward; to perform or speak publicly

выступление.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ение from выступить ('to step forward, come out, perform, speak publicly'), from вы- ('out, forth') + ступить ('to step', from Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti).

высший.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вꙑшьшии ('higher, highest, supreme'), the synthetic comparative/superlative degree of высокий ('high, tall', Proto-Slavic *vysokъ, comparative *vyšьjь).

высылать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of выслать ('to send out; to exile, deport'), formed from вы- ('out') + сылать (iterative stem of слать 'to send', Proto-Slavic *sylati).

history.meaning: to send out, dispatch; to deport

вытаскивать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of вытащить ('to pull out, drag out'), formed from вы- ('out') + таскивать / таскать ('to drag, pull', iterative of тащить).

вытащить.etymology: Formed from the directional prefix вы- ('out') + тащить ('to drag, pull, haul', from Old East Slavic тащити).

вытереть.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix вы- ('out, clean, dry') and тереть ('to rub, wipe', 1st sg. тру), inherited from Old East Slavic терти and Proto-Slavic *terti ('to rub, grate, wipe', from PIE *terh₁- 'to rub, turn', cognate with Latin terō 'to rub, wear away' and Greek τείρω).

вытирать.etymology: Imperfective of вытереть ('to wipe dry, rub out'), formed from the prefix вы- ('out, clean') + -тирать (iterative of тереть 'to rub, wipe', from Proto-Slavic *terti).

вытянутый.etymology: Adjectival past passive participle of вытянуть ('to stretch out, pull out'), formed from вы- ('out') + тянуть ('to pull, stretch', Proto-Slavic *tęgnǫti).

вытянуть.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out') + тянуть ('to pull, draw, stretch', Old East Slavic тянути, Proto-Slavic *tęgnǫti).

history.meaning: to pull out, stretch out; to endure

выучить.etymology: Formed from the completive prefix вы- ('thoroughly, to the end') + учить ('to teach, learn', inherited from Proto-Slavic *učiti).

выход.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from выходить ('to go out, exit'), from prefix вы- ('out') + ход ('going, motion', from ходить 'to walk, go', Proto-Slavic *xodъ).

выходить.etymology: Imperfective partner of выйти ('to go out'), formed from the prefix вы- ('out') + ходить ('to walk, go', from Proto-Slavic *xoditi). When speaking of windows or doors (окна выходят во двор), it means 'to look out onto, face onto'.

history.meaning: to go out, exit; (of windows) to face onto

выходка.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -ка from выходить ('to step out, come forward', from вы- + ходить); originally a theatrical or fencing 'stepping out', hence an unexpected or outrageous stunt, prank, or antic.

выходной.etymology: Adjective formed from выход ('exit, going out; day off from duty'), derived from выходить / выйти ('to go out, step out'). Substantivized from выходной день ('day when workers or servants are free to go out from work'), выходной (plural выходные 'weekend') became the standard noun for a day off.

history.meaning: going out → day off work; (pl.) weekend

выходные.etymology: Substantivized plural of выходной (день) ('day off work, rest day'), derived from выход ('exit, leaving work, stepping out', built on выходить / выйти 'to go out'). Originally 'a day when workers are free to go out', the plural выходные became the standard Russian word for the weekend.

выцветший.etymology: Past active participle in -ший of выцвести ('to fade, lose colour'), formed from prefix вы- ('out, away') + цвести ('to bloom, glow with colour', from Proto-Slavic *kvisti, related to цвет 'colour, blossom').

history.meaning: to lose colour, bleach out → faded

вычесть.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out, away') + честь ('to count, reckon, read', Old East Slavic чисти / чьту, Proto-Slavic *čisti 'to count, read, honor').

вычитать.etymology: Formed from вы- ('out') + читать ('to read; to count, reckon', from Proto-Slavic *čitati): as perfective вычитать it means 'to glean or discover by reading', while as imperfective вычитать (paired with вычесть) it preserves the older sense of *čitati 'to count, reckon' and means 'to subtract, deduct'.

history.meaning: to find by reading (wyčitat'); to subtract (vyčitát')

вышвырнуть.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out') + швырнуть ('to hurl, fling, chuck', semelfactive of expressive Russian швырять 'to hurl, toss').

выше.etymology: Comparative degree of высокий ('high, tall') and высоко ('high'), inherited from Old East Slavic выше, from Proto-Slavic *vyše (from *vys- + comparative suffix *-jьše).

выщипать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from вы- ('out') + щипать ('to pinch, pluck', Old East Slavic щипати, Proto-Slavic *ščipati).

выяснить.etymology: Formed with prefix вы- ('out') and verbal suffix -ить from ясный ('clear, bright'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *jasnъ ('clear, bright, distinct'), literally 'to make clear, bring to light'.

history.meaning: to find out, clarify, sort out

выяснять.etymology: Imperfective of выяснить ('to clarify, make clear, find out'), formed from the prefix вы- ('out') + ясный ('clear, bright', from Proto-Slavic *jasnъ).

history.meaning: to find out, clarify, sort out

вязальный.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -льный from вязать ('to knit, bind, tie', Proto-Slavic *vęzati), designating tools or yarn used for knitting.

вязаный.etymology: Adjectival passive participle of вязать ('to knit, tie'), from Old East Slavic вязати ('to tie, bind'), from Proto-Slavic *vęzati.

вязать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic вязати ('to tie, bind'), from Proto-Slavic *vęzati ('to bind, tie, plait'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enĝh- ('to narrow, tie tightly').

вялый.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic вялыи ('wilted, faded, sluggish'), historically an l-participle of вянуть ('to wither, wilt, fade'), from Proto-Slavic *vęnǫti ('to wither, droop').

гад.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гадъ ('reptile, creeping creature, vermin'), from Proto-Slavic *gadъ ('reptile, loathsome creature'), related to *gaditi ('to soil, disgust') and used figuratively for a vile person or scoundrel.

гадость.etymology: Abstract and concrete noun formed with the suffix -ость from гадкий ('nasty, repulsive, vile') and гад ('reptile, creeping creature, vermin'), inherited from Old East Slavic гадъ and Proto-Slavic *gadъ ('reptile, snake, loathsome creature', originally an old taboo-avoidance word connected with disgust, cognate with Lithuanian gėda 'shame, disgrace' and Old High German quāt 'filth, dung, evil').

history.meaning: nastiness, filth, vile thing or act

газ.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th centuries via French gaz or Dutch gas, a scientific neologism coined around 1648 by the Flemish chemist Jan Baptist van Helmont, who modelled Dutch gas on Ancient Greek χάος (kháos, 'chaos, primordial air, empty space', with Dutch spirant g- matching Greek χ-).

history.stage: Dutch (coined by J. B. van Helmont, 1648)

газ.notes: In cafés and shops, **вода с газом** is sparkling water and **вода без газа** is still water.

газета.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French gazette from Italian gazzetta, originally a Venetian small coin (named after Venetian gazeta 'magpie') that was the price of a early Venetian news sheet.

history.meaning: small Venetian coin; news sheet costing one gazzetta

газовый.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -овый from газ ('gas'), borrowed via French gaz and German Gas, coined by the Flemish chemist Jan Baptist van Helmont in the 17th century after Dutch geest ('spirit') and Greek χάος (kháos, 'chaos, primordial atmosphere').

галактика.etymology: Borrowed via Late Latin galaxias / modern scientific usage from Ancient Greek γαλαξίας (galaxías, short for γαλαξίας κύκλος 'milky circle', the Milky Way), derived from γάλα, stem γαλακτ- (gála, galakt-, 'milk').

галлюцинация.etymology: Borrowed via French hallucination or German Halluzination from Late Latin hallucinatio ('a wandering of the mind, delusion'), from Latin alucinari / hallucinari ('to wander in mind, dream, talk idly').

галстук.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) from German Halstuch (or Dutch halsdoek), a compound of Hals ('neck') + Tuch ('cloth, kerchief'): literally 'neck-cloth'. Initial German H- was regularly rendered as г- in 18th-century Russian loans.

гамма.etymology: Borrowed in the musical sense ('scale, range of notes or colors') from French gamme, from Medieval Latin gamma (used by Guido d'Arezzo for the lowest note of the medieval hexachordal scale), from Ancient Greek γάμμα (gámma, third letter of the Greek alphabet).

гараж.etymology: Borrowed in the early twentieth century from French garage ('shelter for vehicles, docking place'), derived from garer ('to dock a boat, shelter, park'), itself of Frankish origin (*waron 'to guard, watch over').

history.meaning: to shelter, dock -> vehicle shed, garage

гарантировать.etymology: Borrowed via German garantieren from French garantir ('to warrant, guarantee'), derived from garant ('guarantor, warrant'), of Frankish origin (*warand).

гардероб.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French garde-robe ('wardrobe, cloakroom'), a compound of garder ('to keep, guard', of Frankish origin) + robe ('dress, garment').

гарем.etymology: Borrowed via French harem or German Harem from Ottoman Turkish harem, from Arabic ḥarīm / ḥaram ('forbidden or sacred place; women's quarters of a household', from the root ḥ-r-m 'to forbid, make inviolable').

гармонировать.etymology: Borrowed via German harmonieren or formed in Russian with -ировать from гармония ('harmony'), from Latin harmonia, from Ancient Greek ἁρμονία (harmonía, 'joint, agreement, concord of sounds').

гармонично.etymology: Adverb derived from гармоничный ('harmonious'), formed with the adjective suffix -ный from гармония ('harmony', from Ancient Greek ἁρμονία).

гарнир.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth–nineteenth centuries from French garnir ('to garnish, trim, furnish a dish'), from Old French garnir ('to equip, fortify'), of Frankish origin (*warnjan).

history.meaning: to garnish, accompany a main dish

гарнир.notes: In Russian menus and home cooking, гарнир primarily means the substantial side dish (potatoes, rice, buckwheat, pasta, or vegetables) served alongside meat or fish.

гасить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гасити ('to extinguish, put out'), from Proto-Slavic *gasiti (causative of *gasnǫti 'to go out, be extinguished'), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷes- ('to extinguish'; cognate with Lithuanian gesyti).

гастарбайтер.etymology: Borrowed in the late twentieth century from German Gastarbeiter (literally 'guest worker'), a compound of Gast ('guest', an Indo-European cognate of Russian гость) + Arbeiter ('worker', from Arbeit 'work').

гастроли.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century (originally via singular гастроль) from German Gastrolle ('guest role performed by a visiting actor'), a compound of Gast ('guest') + Rolle ('theatrical role', from French rôle).

гастроном.etymology: Borrowed from French gastronome ('gourmet, connoisseur of fine food', from Ancient Greek γαστήρ 'stomach' + νόμος 'law, rule'); in twentieth-century Russian (after famous food emporia and Soviet state food halls titled Гастроном) it shifted to mean a grocery and delicatessen store.

гвоздик.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ик from гвоздь ('nail, peg'), inherited from Old East Slavic гвоздь, from Proto-Slavic *gvozdь (originally ' sharp woody peg, thicket, nail').

где.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic къде ('where', Old Church Slavonic къде; loss of the weak yer ь caused voicing of кд > гд), from Proto-Slavic *kъde, formed from the interrogative stem *kъ- ('what, which', from PIE *kʷú-) + the locative particle *-de (compare здесь 'here' and везде 'everywhere').

где-нибудь.etymology: Indefinite adverb formed from где ('where', Old East Slavic къде, Proto-Slavic *kъde) + the indefinite particle -нибудь (from ни будь 'be it whatever', imperative of быть 'to be').

где-то.etymology: Indefinite adverb formed by attaching the indefinite enclitic particle -то ('some-', historically the neuter demonstrative pronoun то 'that') to где ('where', from Old East Slavic къдѣ and Proto-Slavic *kъdě).

гельминтоз.etymology: Medical term formed in New Latin as helminthosis, from Ancient Greek ἕλμινς, stem ἑλμινθ- (hélmins, helminth-, 'parasitic worm') + the pathological condition suffix -оз (-osis).

гематома.etymology: Borrowed from medical New Latin haematoma, coined from Ancient Greek αἷμα, stem αἱματ- (haîma, haimat-, 'blood') + the tumor/swelling suffix -ωμα (-ōma).

ген.etymology: Borrowed from German Gen, coined in 1909 by Danish geneticist Wilhelm Johannsen from Ancient Greek γένος (génos, 'race, birth, offspring') and the Greek-derived suffix -γενής ('born of, producing').

генерал.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-17th century via German General and Polish generał from French général (shortened from capitaine général, 'captain in overall command'), from Latin generālis ('general, pertaining to the whole class or army'), from genus ('kind, race, class').

history.meaning: general, overall → commander of the whole force

генерал-майор.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from German Generalmajor (compare French major-général), combining Latin generalis ('general, overall') and maior ('greater, senior', comparative of magnus).

генеральный.etymology: Borrowed via Polish generalny and German генераль- from Latin generalis ('relating to all, general, chief'), from genus, stem gener- ('kind, race, class').

генератор.etymology: Borrowed via German Generator or French générateur from Latin generator ('begetter, producer'), agent noun from generare ('to beget, produce, generate').

гениально.etymology: Adverb and predicative short neuter form of гениальный ('brilliant, of genius'), derived from гений ('genius', from Latin genius).

гениальный.etymology: Borrowed from German genial or French génial ('marked by genius, brilliant'), from Latin genialis ('relating to a tutelary spirit, festive, creative'), derived from genius ('tutelary spirit, innate talent, genius').

гений.etymology: Borrowed via German Genius / French génie from Latin genius ('tutelary deity or attendant spirit of a person or place, innate talent, inspiration'), from gignere (root *gen-, 'to beget, produce').

history.meaning: inborn tutelary spirit, innate gift, genius

геолокация.etymology: Late 20th-century borrowing from English geolocation, combining geo- (from Ancient Greek γῆ gê 'earth') + location (from Latin locatio 'placement', from locus 'place').

герб.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th–17th centuries via Polish herb ('coat of arms') and Old Czech erb from Middle High German erbe ('inheritance, patrimonial estate, ancestral crest'). The Germanic word descends from Proto-Germanic *arbiją ('inheritance, heritage'), because a coat of arms was the hereditary symbol passed down through a family line.

герметик.etymology: Formed in twentieth-century technical Russian with suffix -ик from герметический / герметичный ('hermetic, airtight'), borrowed via French hermétique and Medieval Latin hermeticus from Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary patron of alchemy credited with inventing an airtight glass seal.

герой.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (replacing earlier Ирой, which followed Byzantine Greek pronunciation) via French héros / German Heros and Latin hērōs from Ancient Greek ἥρως (hḗrōs, 'demigod, defender, hero').

гибнуть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гыбнути ('to perish, be lost'), from Proto-Slavic *gybnǫti ('to bend, sink, perish'), nasal-infix inchoative from *gybati ('to bend').

гигиена.etymology: Borrowed via French hygiène and German Hygiene from Ancient Greek ὑγιεινή (hugieinḗ, short for ὑγιεινὴ τέχνη 'art of health'), from ὑγιής (hugiḗs, 'healthy, sound').

гид.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French guide ('tour guide; guidebook'), from Italian guida ('leader, guide'), derived from a Frankish / Germanic verb *wītan ('to show the way, look after', from the same Indo-European root *weyd- 'to see, know' as Russian видеть).

гимнастика.etymology: Borrowed via German Gymnastik or French gymnastique from Latin gymnastica, from Ancient Greek γυμναστική (gumnastikḗ, 'athletic training'), from γυμνάζω ('to train naked, exercise', from γυμνός gumnós 'naked').

гипноз.etymology: Borrowed via French hypnose and German Hypnose from New Latin hypnosis, coined by the Scottish surgeon James Braid in the 1840s from Ancient Greek ὕπνος (húpnos, 'sleep') + -osis.

гипнотизировать.etymology: Borrowed from German hypnotisieren / French hypnotiser ('to hypnotize'), formed from the stem of Ancient Greek ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós, 'putting to sleep', from ὕπνος 'sleep') + verbal suffix -ировать.

history.meaning: to put into a hypnotic state

гипнотизёр.etymology: Borrowed from French hypnotiseur ('hypnotist'), agent noun from hypnotiser ('to hypnotize', ultimately from Ancient Greek ὕπνος 'sleep').

гипотеза.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via German Hypothese or French hypothèse from Late Latin hypothesis and Ancient Greek ὑπόθεσις (hupóthesis, 'foundation, supposition'), from ὑπό ('under') + θέσις ('placing, proposition').

гипс.etymology: Borrowed via German Gips from Latin gypsum ('plaster, gypsum'), from Ancient Greek γύψος (gúpsos, 'chalk, gypsum, plaster'), itself a Semitic loanword (compare Arabic jibs, Akkadian gaṣṣu).

гирлянда.etymology: Borrowed from French guirlande ('garland, wreath'), from Italian ghirlanda, ultimately connected with words for twisting or braiding foliage and wire.

history.meaning: floral garland; string of festive lights

гитара.etymology: Borrowed via French guitare from Spanish guitarra, from Andalusi Arabic qīṯāra, from Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára, 'cithara, lyre-like stringed instrument').

гитарист.etymology: Borrowed from French guitariste or formed in Russian from гитара ('guitar') + the musician/agent suffix -ист.

глава.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic глава ('head; chief; chapter heading'), the South Slavic non-pleophonic doublet of native Russian голова ('head', from Proto-Slavic *golva). Used in Russian for the 'head' of an organization or a 'chapter' of a book (calquing Greek κεφάλαιον and Latin capitulum 'little head, chapter').

главврач.etymology: Soviet-era syllabic compound (сложносокращённое слово) contracted from главный врач ('chief physician'), combining главный ('chief, head', from Church Slavonic глава 'head') and врач ('doctor, physician', from Proto-Slavic *vračь).

history.meaning: head doctor, chief medical officer of a hospital

главный.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic главьнъ ('chief, principal, head'), formed with the suffix -ный from глава ('head, chief, chapter', corresponding to East Slavic голова, from Proto-Slavic *golva).

глаголить.etymology: Archaic or ironic verb from Old Church Slavonic глаголати ('to speak, say, utter'), denominative from глаголъ ('word, speech'), from Proto-Slavic *golgolъ (reduplicated *gal- / *gol- 'to call, speak', cf. голос).

history.meaning: to speak, utter (ironic or elevated, e.g. устами младенца глаголет истина)

гладиатор.etymology: Borrowed via German Gladiator or French gladiateur from Latin gladiator ('swordsman, arena fighter'), derived from gladius ('sword').

гладить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гладити ('to make smooth, stroke'), from Proto-Slavic *gladiti, denominative verb from *gladъ / *gladъkъ (гладкий, 'smooth, even').

history.meaning: to stroke, pet; to iron clothes

гладкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гладъкыи ('smooth, even'), from Proto-Slavic *gladъkъ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰlādʰ- ('smooth, shining'; cognate with Latin glaber 'smooth, hairless' and English glad).

глаз.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic глазъ (originally 'smooth round pebble, glass bead, marble', attested in this sense before replacing око as the everyday word for 'eye' in the 16th–17th centuries), from Proto-Slavic *glazъ.

глазеть.etymology: Colloquial denominative verb formed in Russian with suffix -еть from глаз ('eye', recorded in Old East Slavic глазъ first as 'smooth pebble, polished glass bead, eyeball', before replacing око as the everyday word for 'eye'): literally 'to make big eyes at, stare, gawk'.

глазунья.etymology: Formed in Russian from глаз ('eye') + the expressive feminine noun suffix -унья (originally in the phrase яичница-глазунья): fried sunny-side-up eggs whose unbroken round yolks look like staring eyes.

глазурь.etymology: Borrowed from German Glasur 'glaze (on pottery or pastry)', formed on Glas 'glass' because a glaze dries to a smooth, glass-like shine.
глазурь.notes: Covers both ceramic glaze and sweet culinary icing (лимонная глазурь, шоколадная глазурь).

глеб.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic Глѣбъ, borrowed in the Varangian period from Old Norse Guðleifr ('heir/descendant of the gods', from guð 'god' + leifr 'heir, descendant').

глина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic глина ('clay'), from Proto-Slavic *glina, formed with the suffix *-na from Proto-Indo-European *gley- ('to smear, stick, clay'; cognate with Ancient Greek γλοιός and English clay).

глинтвейн.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century from German Glühwein ('mulled wine', literally 'glowing/heated wine', reshaped in Russian with epenthetic -нт- afterolder German glühender Wein 'glowing wine').

глист.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic глистъ / глиста ('earthworm, intestinal worm'), from Proto-Slavic *glista ('worm'), connected with the root *glina / *glьjь ('clay, slime, slippery matter').

глоток.etymology: Derived with the suffix -ок from глотать ('to swallow, gulp'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *glъtati / *glъtъ ('gullet, swallow').

глубже.etymology: Comparative degree of глубокий ('deep') and глубоко ('deeply'), inherited from Old East Slavic глубже, from Proto-Slavic *glǫbje (built on the root *glǫb- + comparative suffix *-je).

глубокий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic глубокъ / глубокыи ('deep'), from Proto-Slavic *glǫbokъ, formed with the dimensional suffix *-okъ (compare широкий 'wide' and высокий 'high') from the root *glǫb- ('depth, hollow', preserved in глубь 'depth').

глубоко.etymology: Adverb formed from глубокий ('deep'), inherited from Old East Slavic глубокыи, from Proto-Slavic *glǫbokъ ('deep, hollow').

глупец.etymology: Formed with the personal noun suffix -ец from глупый ('foolish, stupid'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *glupъ ('foolish, dull').

глупо.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate formed from the neuter short form of глупый ('stupid, foolish'), from Proto-Slavic *glupъ ('foolish, dull, deafened').

глупость.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from глупый ('stupid, foolish', from Proto-Slavic *glupъ). Denotes both the quality of foolishness and a specific foolish act or remark ('nonsense, silly thing').

глупый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic глупыи ('foolish, silly, dull-witted'), from Proto-Slavic *glupъ ('foolish, stupified'), often connected by Vasmer with the same expressive root family as глухой ('deaf, dull, muted').

глухой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic глухыи ('deaf, muted, overgrown'), from Proto-Slavic *gluxъ ('deaf, silent, blocked'), related to *glъxnǫti ('to grow deaf or overgrown').

глядеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic глядѣти ('to look, gaze'), from Proto-Slavic *ględěti, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰlendʰ- ('to shine, look'; cognate with Middle High German glinzen and English glint, glance).

глянуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective formed with the suffix -нуть (with simplification of -дн- > -н-) from глядеть ('to look, gaze', from Proto-Slavic *ględěti).

history.meaning: to take a quick look, glance

гнать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гънати (1sg. жену, 'to drive, chase, pursue'), from Proto-Slavic *gъnati (present *ženǫ), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen- ('to strike, drive'; cognate with Lithuanian ginti 'to drive cattle' and Sanskrit hánti).

гнев.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гнѣвъ ('anger, wrath'), from Proto-Slavic *gněvъ, often connected with *gniti ('to rot, smolder, fester') or Proto-Indo-European *gʰney- ('to burn, glow with anger').

гнездо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гнѣздо ('nest, brood'), from Proto-Slavic *gnězdo, from Proto-Indo-European *nisdós ('nest', literally 'place to sit down', from *ni- 'down' + *sed- 'to sit'; cognate with English nest and Latin nidus).

гнида.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гнида ('nit, louse egg'), from Proto-Slavic *gnida ('nit'), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱníd-eh₂ (cognate with Ancient Greek κονίς and Old English hnitu 'nit'); used colloquially as a contemptuous insult.

гнилой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гнилыи ('rotten, putrid'), past participial adjective in -лой from гнить ('to rot, decay'), from Proto-Slavic *gnilъ (from *gniti 'to rot').

гном.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century via German Gnom / French gnome from New Latin gnomus ('subterranean earth-spirit, dwarf guarding underground treasures'), coined in the 16th century by the Swiss alchemist Paracelsus (probably from Ancient Greek γνώμη gnṓmē 'intelligence, thought' or γνοφός 'darkness', or modeled on genomos 'earth-dweller').

говорить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic говорити, from Proto-Slavic *govoriti, originally an expressive verb meaning 'to murmur, hubbub, talk noisily' (still heard in говор, 'local speech, murmur of voices'). Over centuries it replaced older рещи and молвить as the neutral verb 'to speak'.

говядина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic говядина ('beef, cattle meat'), formed with the meat suffix -ина from the archaic noun говядо (Proto-Slavic *govędo 'head of cattle, ox', from Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws 'cow, ox', cognate with English cow and Sanskrit gó).
говядина.notes: Although the base noun *говядо ('ox, cattle') disappeared from everyday Russian, its derivatives говядина and говяжий remain the standard words for beef.

говяжий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic говяжии and Proto-Slavic *govęďь ('bovine, relating to cattle'), the possessive adjective formed from *govędo ('head of cattle, ox').

год.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic годъ ('suitable time, appointed season, year'), from Proto-Slavic *godъ ('fitting time, festive season'; compare Polish gody 'Christmastide, wedding feast'), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰodʰ- ('to fit together, join'; cognate with English good and gather). In Russian год displaced older лето (now 'summer', preserved in сколько вам лет?) in the singular and nominative plural.
год.notes: After 1–4 use forms of **год** (один год, два года), while from 5 upwards the genitive plural switches to **лет** (пять лет).

годик.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed with the suffix -ик from год ('year'), from Old East Slavic годъ ('time, appointed season, year'), from Proto-Slavic *godъ ('fitting time, year').

history.meaning: little year (used of a young child's age)

годиться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic годитися ('to be fitting, suit, come in handy'), built on the original sense of Proto-Slavic *godъ ('that which fits, suitable time', from PIE *gʰodʰ- 'to fit together', the same root that gave Russian год 'year', погода 'weather', and English good).

history.meaning: to be suitable, do, serve the purpose

годность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from годный ('fit, suitable, valid'), derived from год / годиться ('to be fit, suit', Proto-Slavic *godьnъ 'pleasing, suitable').

годовщина.etymology: Formed in Russian with the suffix -щина from годовой ('annual, yearly'), built on год ('year', from Old East Slavic годъ 'time, fitting season, year' and Proto-Slavic *godъ).

гол.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th or early 20th century with football terminology from English goal ('boundary post, target, point scored in a ball game'). (Distinct from native short adjective гол 'naked, bare' < *golъ.)

history.meaning: target posts, point scored in sport

голкипер.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century from English goalkeeper, a compound of goal ('target, net') + keeper ('guardian', from keep).

голова.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic голова ('head', showing East Slavic pleophony -оло-; compare Old Church Slavonic глава 'head; book chapter'), from Proto-Slavic *golva, closely cognate with Lithuanian galvà ('head').

головокружение.etymology: Compound noun formed from голова ('head', Proto-Slavic *golva) + connecting vowel -о- + кружение ('spinning, whirling', from кружить 'to spin, circle'), calquing German Schwindel / French vertige.

голод.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic голодъ ('hunger, famine'), from Proto-Slavic *goldъ ('hunger, craving'), from Proto-Indo-European *gheldh- ('to crave, desire').

голодать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic голодати ('to suffer hunger, fast'), denominative verb from голодъ (голод, 'hunger', Proto-Slavic *goldъ).

голодный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic голодьныи ('hungry'), derived from голод ('hunger, famine', showing East Slavic pleophony -оло- from Proto-Slavic *goldъ; compare Old Church Slavonic гладъ and Sanskrit gárdha 'greed, eager desire').

голос.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic голосъ ('voice, call', showing East Slavic pleophony -оло-; compare Old Church Slavonic гласъ), from Proto-Slavic *golsъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *gʰolH-so- ('call, sound', cognate with English call and Old Norse kalla).

голосование.etymology: Verbal noun of голосовать ('to vote'), derived from голос ('voice, vote', Proto-Slavic *golsъ), calquing French voter / German stimmen (where voix and Stimme mean both 'voice' and 'vote').

голосовать.etymology: Formed in Russian from голос ('voice; vote', from Proto-Slavic *golsъ with East Slavic pleophony -оло-) + the verbal suffix -овать, following the European semantic pattern in which 'voice' also means 'vote' (compare French voix and German Stimme).

голосовой.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -овой from голос ('voice'), inherited from Old East Slavic голосъ (with East Slavic pleophony -оло-), from Proto-Slavic *golsъ.

голосок.etymology: Diminutive formed in Russian from голос ('voice', from Proto-Slavic *golsъ) + the masculine diminutive suffix -ок.

голубка.etymology: Feminine diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from голубь ('pigeon, dove', Proto-Slavic *golǫbь), also used traditionally as an affectionate term of address ('my dove, darling').

голубой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic голубыи (originally 'dove-colored, ash-gray with a bluish sheen'), derived from голубь ('pigeon, dove', from Proto-Slavic *golǫbь).

голубок.etymology: Masculine diminutive formed with the suffix -ок from голубь ('pigeon, dove', Proto-Slavic *golǫbь), used both literally ('little dove') and affectionately ('lovebird, dear').

голубь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic голубь ('dove, pigeon'), from Proto-Slavic *golǫbь, formed with the bird/animal color suffix *-ǫbь (compare Latin columba 'dove, pigeon').

голый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic голъ and Proto-Slavic *golъ ('naked, bare'), cognate with Old High German kalo (modern German kahl 'bald, bare') and English callow.

гольф.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th–20th century from English golf, from Scots golf / gowf (attested from the 15th century, likely related to Dutch kolf 'club, bat').

гонорар.etymology: Borrowed via German Honorar from Latin honorarium (short for honorarium donum 'gift of honor, professional fee'), from honos / honor ('honor, esteem').

гонять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гоняти ('to chase, drive repeatedly'), from Proto-Slavic *gonjati, the multidirectional iterative of *gъnati (гнать, 'to drive, chase', PIE *gʷhen-).

history.meaning: to chase; to drive or ride fast

гоняться.etymology: Reflexive form of гонять ('to chase, drive about') with the suffix -ся, meaning 'to chase after, pursue eagerly'.

гора.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гора ('mountain, hill, high bank'), from Proto-Slavic *gora, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH- ('mountain, wooded height'; cognate with Sanskrit girí- and Lithuanian giria 'forest').

гораздо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гораздъ / гораздо ('skilful, clever, very much'; in Old Russian гораздъ meant 'capable, adept at something'). Vasmer traces Proto-Slavic *gorazdъ either to an early borrowing from Gothic *ga-razds ('eloquent, well-spoken', from razda 'speech, voice') or to an inherited Slavic formation. In modern literary Russian гораздо specialized as the intensifier before comparatives ('much / far more': гораздо лучше 'much better').
гораздо.notes: Used specifically to intensify comparatives: **гораздо теплее** ('much warmer'), **гораздо быстрее** ('far faster').

гордиться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гърдитися ('to be proud, boast'), formed with -ся from гордый ('proud, haughty', from Proto-Slavic *gъrdъ).

гордо.etymology: Adverb derived from гордый ('proud'), from Old East Slavic гърдыи ('proud, haughty'), from Proto-Slavic *gъrdъ.

гордость.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гърдость and Proto-Slavic *gъrdostь ('pride, haughtiness'), formed with the abstract noun suffix -ость from гордый ('proud', Proto-Slavic *gъrdъ).

гордый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гърдыи ('proud, haughty, grand'), from Proto-Slavic *gъrdъ ('proud, dignified, terrible'), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷr̥dʰo-.

горе.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic горе ('grief, woe, misfortune'), from Proto-Slavic *gorje ('grief, burning sorrow'), derived from the root of *gorěti ('to burn', PIE *gʷʰer- 'to be hot, burn').

горелка.etymology: Instrument noun formed with the suffix -лка from гореть ('to burn', inherited from Old East Slavic горѣти, from Proto-Slavic *gorěti).

гореть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic горѣти ('to burn, blaze'), from Proto-Slavic *gorěti, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- ('to be hot, burn'; cognate with жар 'heat', греть 'to warm', Ancient Greek θερμός, and Sanskrit gharmá).

горец.etymology: Formed with the inhabitant suffix -ец from гора ('mountain', Old East Slavic гора, Proto-Slavic *gora), especially referring to the peoples of the Caucasus mountains.

горечь.etymology: Abstract feminine i-stem noun formed from горький ('bitter', Old East Slavic горькыи, Proto-Slavic *gorьkъ, literally 'burning, stinging to the taste', from *gorěti 'to burn').

горло.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гърло and Proto-Slavic *gъrdlo ('throat, gullet', with regular East Slavic simplification of *dl -> л; compare Polish gardło), built with the instrument/place suffix *-dlo on the Indo-European root *gʷerh₃- ('to swallow, devour').

горлышко.etymology: Formed in Russian with the diminutive suffix -ышко from горло ('throat, gullet', from Old East Slavic гърло, Proto-Slavic *gъrdlo, from PIE *gʷr̥h₃-dʰlom 'swallower, throat'; cognate with Lithuanian gurklỹs 'crop, throat' and Latin gula). Applied both affectionately to a person's throat and metaphorically to the narrow neck or pouring spout of a bottle, jug, or kettle.

history.meaning: little throat; bottle neck, pouring spout

гормон.etymology: Borrowed via English hormone and German Hormon, coined in 1905 by the English physiologist Ernest Starling from Ancient Greek ὁρμῶν (hormôn, 'setting in motion, urging on'), present participle of ὁρμάω (hormáō, 'to impel, excite').

горничная.etymology: Substantivized feminine adjective from горничный ('pertaining to the upper/clean rooms'), derived from горница ('clean upstairs room in a traditional house', from горний 'upper, high', derived from гора 'mountain, height').

город.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic городъ ('fenced enclosure, fortified settlement, town', with regular East Slavic pleophony -оро-; compare Church Slavonic градъ), from Proto-Slavic *gordъ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰórdʰos ('enclosure'; cognate with English yard and garden).

городской.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ской from город ('city, town', from Proto-Slavic *gordъ).

гороскоп.etymology: Borrowed via French horoscope or German Horoskop from Latin horoscopus, from Ancient Greek ὡροσκόπος (hōroskópos, 'nativity, observer of the hour of birth'), from ὥρα (hṓra, 'hour, time') + σκοπέω (skopéō, 'to look at, examine').

горчить.etymology: Denominative verb in -ить formed from горький ('bitter', from Proto-Slavic *gorьkъ, with regular к -> ч palatalization).

горшок.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гърньшькъ / горшок, diminutive of гърнъ ('potter's kiln, clay pot', from Proto-Slavic *gъrnъ 'furnace, kiln, fired clay vessel', from PIE *gʷʰer- 'to heat, burn').

горький.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic горькыи and Proto-Slavic *gorьkъ ('bitter, pungent, burning to the taste'), derived from the verb *gorěti (Russian гореть 'to burn'): literally 'burning, stinging the tongue'.

горько.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic горько ('bitterly'), adverb and short neuter of горький ('bitter, burning', from Proto-Slavic *gorьkъ, derived from *gorěti 'to burn', i.e. 'burning/pungent to the taste').

горючий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic горючии (historically the East Slavic present active participle of горѣти 'to burn', Proto-Slavic *gorěti), lexicalized as an adjective meaning 'flammable, combustible' (and in folklore горючие слёзы 'burning/bitter tears').

горяченький.etymology: Affectionate diminutive adjective formed with the suffix -еньк- from горячий ('hot', historically the old present participle of гореть 'to burn', Proto-Slavic *gorętjь).

горячий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic горячии ('burning, hot'), historically an old present active participle of гореть (Old East Slavic горѣти, Proto-Slavic *gorěti 'to burn', from PIE *gʷʰer- 'to be hot'; compare жар 'heat', греть 'to warm', and Ancient Greek θερμός 'hot, warm').

горячо.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate continuing the short neuter singular of горячий ('hot'), which originated as the Old East Slavic present active participle (горячии) of гореть ('to burn', Proto-Slavic *gorěti).

гособеспечение.etymology: 20th-century Soviet administrative compound of гос- (clipping of государственный 'state', from государство 'state') + обеспечение ('provision, maintenance, support', from обеспечить 'to secure, provide for').

госпитализация.etymology: Borrowed from French hospitalisation or formed in Russian from госпиталь ('hospital', borrowed in the Petrine era via German Hospital / Dutch hospitaal from Medieval Latin hospitale 'guest house, hospital', from Latin hospes 'guest, host').

господи.etymology: Preserved Old Church Slavonic and Old East Slavic vocative singular (господи! 'O Lord!') of господь ('the Lord, master'), from Proto-Slavic *gospodь ('master, lord of the house, host'). Like боже ('O God!') and отче ('O Father!'), господи survives in modern Russian as one of the few fossilized vocative forms, used as an everyday exclamation.

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

господин.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic господинъ ('master, lord'), singulative formed with -ин from господь ('lord, master of the house'), from Proto-Slavic *gospodь, an ancient compound corresponding to Latin hospes (< *hosti-potis 'master of guests, host').

гостевой.etymology: Formed in Russian with the relational suffix -евой from гость ('guest', from Old East Slavic гость, Proto-Slavic *gostь, continuing PIE *gʰóstis 'stranger, guest'; cognate with English guest and German Gast).

history.meaning: guest (e.g. гостевой дом 'guesthouse', гостевая комната 'guest room')

гостеприимный.etymology: Compound adjective borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гостьприимьнъ ('hospitable'), a calque of Greek φιλόξενος, formed from гость ('guest', Proto-Slavic *gostь) + приимати / принимать ('to receive, welcome').

гостеприимство.etymology: A compound modelled on Church Slavonic word-building: гость 'guest' + linking vowel -е- + приим- 'receive, welcome' (related to принимать 'to receive') + abstract noun suffix -ство — literally 'guest-receiving'.

гостиная.etymology: Substantivized feminine form of гостиный ('for guests', as in гостиная комната 'guest room, drawing room'), derived from гость ('guest', Old East Slavic гость, Proto-Slavic *gostь, cognate with Latin hostis and English guest).

гостиница.etymology: Derived in Russian with the place suffix -ица from гостиный ('relating to guests or visiting merchants', from гость 'guest; foreign merchant', Proto-Slavic *gostь): originally an inn or hostelry where visiting merchants stayed.

гостиничный.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ный from гостиница ('hotel, inn'), which was formed with -ица from гостиный ('pertaining to guests or merchants', from гость 'guest, visiting merchant', Proto-Slavic *gostь).

гость.etymology: An inherited Slavic word. In Old Russian, гость could mean a guest, a foreigner or a visiting merchant. Vasmer compares German Gast and Latin hostis, whose senses include foreigner and enemy. These related words show how an outsider could be viewed differently in different languages.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: гость

гостья.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гостья ('female guest'), formed with the feminine suffix -ья (Proto-Slavic *-ьja) from гость ('guest', from Proto-Slavic *gostь, PIE *gʰóstis).

государственный.etymology: Adjective formed from государство ('state, realm, dominion'), derived from государь (older господарь, 'lord, sovereign, master'), from Proto-Slavic *gospodarь (from *gospodь 'lord, master').

государство.etymology: Inherited from Middle Russian государство ('sovereignty, realm, state', attested from the 15th century), formed with the suffix -ство from государь ('sovereign, lord, monarch'), which contracted in East Slavic from earlier господарь ('lord, master'), derived from господь ('lord, master', Proto-Slavic *gospodь).

государь.etymology: Phonetic reduction in late medieval/Muscovite Russian (due to high-frequency rapid address) of господарь ('lord, master, sovereign'), derived from господь ('lord', Proto-Slavic *gospodь).

готовить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic готовити ('to make ready, prepare'), a denominative verb from готовый ('ready', from Proto-Slavic *gotovъ). In everyday Russian, in addition to 'to prepare', готовить is the standard verb for cooking a meal.

готовиться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive verb formed by adding -ся to готовить ('to prepare; to cook'), derived from готовый ('ready', Old East Slavic готовыи, Proto-Slavic *gotovъ).

готовка.etymology: Colloquial deverbal action noun formed with the suffix -ка from готовить ('to prepare; to cook food'), derived from готовый ('ready, prepared', Proto-Slavic *gotovъ).

готовность.etymology: Abstract noun formed in Russian from готовый ('ready, prepared; cooked', from Proto-Slavic *gotovъ) + the suffix -ность (-н- + -ость).
готовность.notes: In kitchen usage, довести до готовности means 'to cook until done'.

готовый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic готовъ / готовыи ('ready, prepared'), from Proto-Slavic *gotovъ, shared across all Slavic languages (compare Polish gotowy and Old Church Slavonic готовъ; Vasmer also compares Albanian gat 'ready').

грабить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic грабити ('to seize, plunder, rob'), from Proto-Slavic *grabiti ('to snatch, rake, seize'), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebh₂- ('to seize, grab'; cognate with English grab).

грабли.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic грабли (pluralia tantum, 'rake'), from Proto-Slavic *grabľě ('rake'), an instrument noun derived from *grabiti ('to seize, gather, rake').

градус.etymology: Borrowed as a scholarly term from Latin gradus 'step, rung, degree (on a scale or circle)', from gradi 'to step, walk'.
градус.notes: Covers both compass/geometry angles (на девяносто градусов) and temperature (двадцать градусов тепла).

гражданин.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гражданинъ ('townsman, citizen', with South Slavic гражд- < *gordj-; compare native East Slavic горожанин 'townsman'), derived from градъ ('walled town, city', Proto-Slavic *gordъ).

гражданка.etymology: Formed with the feminine suffix -ка from гражданин ('citizen'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гражданинъ ('townsman, citizen', showing South Slavic -ра- in градъ 'city, town', corresponding to East Slavic город).

гражданский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with -ский from гражданин ('citizen', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гражданинъ 'inhabitant of a city, citizen', built on градъ 'city').

гражданство.etymology: Derived with the suffix -ство from гражданин ('citizen'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic гражданинъ ('townsman, citizen', with South Slavic жд from *dj, corresponding to East Slavic горожанин, from градъ / город 'town, city').

грамм.etymology: Borrowed from French gramme (introduced in the metric system of 1795), from Late Latin gramma ('a small weight, one twenty-fourth of an ounce'), from Ancient Greek γράμμα ('written letter; small weight').

граната.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Granate or Italian granata ('pomegranate; explosive shell'), from Medieval Latin pōmum grānātum ('many-seeded apple, pomegranate'): early round iron hand-shells packed with powder or pellets were named after the seed-filled pomegranate fruit.

граница.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic граница (attested from 1375), from Proto-Slavic *granica, built on грань 'edge, boundary marker, facet' + -ица.
граница.notes: Idioms: за границу 'abroad (motion)', за границей 'abroad (location)', из-за границы 'from abroad'. Interestingly, German Grenze was borrowed from Slavic *granica.

гратен.etymology: Culinary borrowing from French gratin ('dish baked with a browned crust of cheese or breadcrumbs; originally the browned scrapings from the pan'), from gratter ('to scrape, grate', of Frankish origin *krattōn).

history.meaning: crust browned in baking; gratin dish

граф.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish graf from German Graf ('count, earl'), from Old High German grāfo ('royal official, count').

график.etymology: Borrowed via German Graphik and French graphique from Ancient Greek γραφικός (graphikós, 'relating to writing or drawing', from γράφω 'to write, draw'); the Russian sense 'work schedule, timetable' arose from plotted railway and industrial time-charts (график движения).

граци.etymology: Colloquial borrowing from Italian grazie ('thank you, thanks'), plural of grazia ('grace, favour'), from Latin grātia.

гребешок.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ок from гребень ('comb, crest, ridge', Proto-Slavic *grebenь, from *grebti 'to comb, scrape, row'); in culinary usage, морской гребешок ('sea scallop', calquing the ribbed comb-like shell).

грек.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic грькъ ('a Greek'), from Proto-Slavic *grьkъ, borrowed from Latin Graecus ('Greek'), from Ancient Greek Γραικός (Graikós).

грести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic грети / гребсти ('to row, rake, dig'), from Proto-Slavic *grebti ('to scrape, dig, rake, row'), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebh₂- ('to dig, scratch').

history.meaning: to row (with oars); to rake in
