греть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic грѣти ('to warm, heat'), from Proto-Slavic *grěti ('to warm'), from the same Proto-Indo-European root *gʷʰer- ('warm, hot') as гореть ('to burn') and жар ('heat').

греться.etymology: Reflexive form of греть ('to warm, heat', inherited from Old East Slavic грѣти, from Proto-Slavic *grěti, from PIE *gʷʰer- 'warm, hot') + -ся.

грех.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic грѣхъ ('error, fault, sin') and Old Church Slavonic грѣхъ, from Proto-Slavic *grěxъ ('crookedness, error, transgression'), related to *grěti or Baltic words for 'crooked, twisted' (Latvian greizs).

гречка.etymology: Colloquial univerbation with suffix -ка of гречневая крупа / гречиха ('buckwheat', literally 'Greek grain'), from Old East Slavic грьчьска жита, because buckwheat was cultivated and traded in Kievan Rus' via Byzantine Greeks and Greek monks.

грешный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic грѣшьныи ('sinful, erring'), formed with the adjective suffix -ный from грѣхъ (грех, 'sin, fault', Proto-Slavic *grěxъ).

гриб.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic грибъ, from Proto-Slavic *gribъ ('mushroom, fungus', especially boletus). Vasmer connects *gribъ with the Slavic verb грести / гребу ('to scrape, dig, rake up the earth', Proto-Slavic *grebti), referring to how mushrooms push up through the forest soil and leaf litter (or are dug out of moss).

гриль.etymology: Borrowed from French gril and English grill ('cooking grate, gridiron'), going back through Old French graïl to Late Latin crāticulum ('fine wickerwork, small grate', diminutive of crātis 'hurdle, grate').

грипп.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French grippe ('influenza'), either from French gripper ('to seize, grip suddenly', of Frankish origin) or, conversely, borrowed into French and German from Russian хрип ('hoarseness, wheezing').

гроб.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гробъ (originally 'dug grave, burial pit, tomb', later 'coffin'), from Proto-Slavic *grobъ, o-grade noun from *grebti (Russian грести 'to dig, scrape, bury'; cognate with German Grab and English grave).

гроза.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гроза ('terror, threat, awe; thunderstorm'), from Proto-Slavic *groza ('horror, menace, storm').

грозить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic грозити and Proto-Slavic *groziti ('to threaten, inspire dread'), a denominative verb from гроза (*groza 'terror, menace; thunderstorm').

грозиться.etymology: Reflexive/middle derivative formed from грозить ('to threaten', from гроза 'threat, thunderstorm') + -ся, used in colloquial speech for making threats or vowing to do something.

history.meaning: to threaten -> to make threats, vow

грозный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic грозьныи and Proto-Slavic *grozьnъ ('inspiring awe or dread, formidable, stern'), formed from гроза ('dread, menace, thunderstorm') + -ный.
грозный.notes: In historical Russian, Иван Грозный meant 'Ivan the Formidable / Awe-Inspiring' before English settled on the translation 'Ivan the Terrible'.

громкий.etymology: Formed with the adjectival suffix -кий from гром ('thunder, loud rumbling noise', from Old East Slavic громъ, Proto-Slavic *gromъ, an o-grade noun from *grьměti 'to thunder, resound', from PIE *gʰrem- 'to rumble, roar'; cognate with Ancient Greek χρόμος 'crashing sound' and German grimm). Literally 'thunderous, loud'.

громко.etymology: Adverb formed from the short neuter of громкий ('loud'), derived from гром ('thunder'), inherited from Old East Slavic громъ and Proto-Slavic *gromъ ('thunder, loud rumbling').

громче.etymology: Comparative degree of громкий ('loud'), derived from гром ('thunder, loud noise'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *gromъ ('thunder').

грубить.etymology: Denominative verb in -ить formed from грубый ('coarse, rough, rude', inherited from Proto-Slavic *grǫbъ).

history.meaning: rude, coarse -> to speak or act rudely

грубиян.etymology: Borrowed in the seventeenth–eighteenth centuries via Polish grubian / grubianin from German Grobian ('boor, lout', a sixteenth-century humanist mock-Latin coinage from German grob 'coarse, rude'), reshaping its initial vowel in Slavic by association with the native adjective грубый ('rude').

грубо.etymology: Adverb formed from грубый ('coarse, rough, rude'), inherited from Old East Slavic грубыи ('coarse, unrefined, ignorant'), from Proto-Slavic *grǫbъ ('coarse, thick, rough', compare Polish gruby 'thick, fat, coarse' and Lithuanian grumbùs 'rough, uneven, calloused').

грубый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic грубыи ('coarse, rough, unrefined, ignorant'), from Proto-Slavic *grǫbъ / *grubъ ('coarse, thick, rude').

грудка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from грудь ('chest, breast', Proto-Slavic *grǫdь), used in culinary Russian specifically for poultry breast (куриная грудка, утиная грудка).

грудь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic грудь ('chest, breast, bosom'), from Proto-Slavic *grǫdь ('rise, mound, breast', related to *grǫda 'clod, heap, mound').

груз.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic грузъ ('weight, sinker, cargo'), back-formed from грузити ('to sink, submerge, load down carefully into a boat'), from Proto-Slavic *grǫziti (causative of *gręznǫti 'to sink, bog down').

грузить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic грузити ('to sink, immerse; to load a vessel until it settles in the water'), from Proto-Slavic *grǫziti, causative of *gręznǫti ('to sink into mud or water').

history.meaning: to load (cargo); (slang) to burden with talk

грузовик.etymology: Formed in Russian with the noun suffix -ик from грузовой (автомобиль) ('freight vehicle, truck'), derived from груз ('load, cargo, weight', related to грузнуть 'to sink under weight', from Proto-Slavic *grǫzъ).

грузовой.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -овой from груз ('cargo, freight, load'), from Proto-Slavic *grǫziti ('to load, weigh down').

грузчик.etymology: Formed in Russian with the agent suffix -чик from грузить ('to load freight'), built on груз ('load, cargo, weight'), from Old East Slavic грузъ / грязнути ('to sink under weight', from Proto-Slavic *grǫzъ).

группа.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (originally in painting/sculpture for a clustered arrangement of figures) via German Gruppe and French groupe from Italian gruppo ('knot, cluster, group'), of Germanic origin (*kruppaz 'round mass, lump').

группировка.etymology: Deverbal and collective noun formed with -овка from группировать ('to group'), from группа ('group'), borrowed via German Gruppe and French groupe from Italian gruppo ('cluster, knot, group').

грустить.etymology: Denominative verb formed from грусть ('sadness, melancholy, wistful longing'), from Proto-Slavic *grustь (historically from *gruz-tь, related to грызть 'to gnaw' and Lithuanian graudùs 'heart-rending, sorrowful': grief conceived as 'gnawing at the heart').

грустно.etymology: Adverb and predicative short neuter of грустный ('sad, melancholy'), derived from грусть ('sadness, sorrow'), inherited from Old East Slavic грусть (from Proto-Slavic *grustь, originally 'gnawing grief or heartburn', related to грызть 'to gnaw').

грустный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from грусть ('sadness, melancholy'), inherited from Old East Slavic грусть (and Old Church Slavonic гроусть 'grief, sorrow'), from Proto-Slavic *grustь, originally derived from *gruda / *gruzti ('to gnaw, crush, weigh heavily upon the heart', related to грызть 'to gnaw' and Lithuanian graudùs 'heartbreaking, sad, brittle').
грустный.notes: The **т** in the cluster **-стн-** is silent in pronunciation: **[грусный]**.

грусть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic грусть ('sorrow, grief, heartache'), from Proto-Slavic *grustь, related to *grustiti / *gryzti ('to gnaw, torment inwardly').

груша.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic груша ('pear, pear tree'), from Proto-Slavic *gruša / *kruša ('pear'), an ancient European Wanderwort shared with Lithuanian kriaušė and Albanian dardhë.

грызун.etymology: Formed with the agent suffix -ун from грызть ('to gnaw, nibble'), from Old East Slavic грызти, from Proto-Slavic *gryzti ('to gnaw, bite'), calquing scientific Latin Rodentia / French rongeur.

грязно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate continuing the short neuter singular of грязный ('dirty, muddy'), derived from грязь ('mud, dirt', Proto-Slavic *gręzь).

грязный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from грязь ('mud, dirt, mire'), inherited from Old East Slavic грязь, from Proto-Slavic *gręzь ('mud, mire, bog'), derived from the nasal-vowel verb *gręznǫti ('to sink into mud or mire', Russian погрязнуть, cognate with Lithuanian grim̃zti 'to sink into water or mud').

history.meaning: to sink in mire → mud, mire

грязь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic грязь and Proto-Slavic *gręzь ('mud, mire, bog'), related to the nasal-infix verb *gręznǫti (Russian погрязнуть 'to sink into mud or mire').

губа.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic губа ('lip; mushroom, sponge'), from Proto-Slavic *gǫba ('spongy growth, swelling, lip').

губернатор.etymology: Borrowed under Peter the Great (early 18th century, when Russia was divided into губернии in 1708) via Polish gubernator from Latin gubernātor ('helmsman, pilot of a ship; ruler, governor'), from gubernāre ('to steer a ship, govern'), itself an ancient borrowing from Greek κυβερνάω (kybernáō, 'to steer').

history.meaning: to steer a ship → helmsman, governor

губить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic губити ('to destroy, ruin'), from Proto-Slavic *gubiti ('to ruin, destroy'), the o-grade causative counterpart of *gybnǫti (гибнуть, 'to perish').

губка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from губа (in its older Slavic sense 'tree fungus, polypore, sponge', from Proto-Slavic *gǫba 'fungus, spongy growth, lip').

гудеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гудѣти ('to play a stringed or wind instrument, drone, hum'), from Proto-Slavic *gǫděti ('to make a resonant droning sound').

гулкий.etymology: Formed with the adjectival suffix -кий from гул ('deep rumble, hollow echo, boom'), an East Slavic onomatopoeic noun imitating a low, resonant booming sound.

гульнуть.etymology: Colloquial semelfactive perfective verb formed with the suffix -нуть from гулять ('to stroll; to carouse, party, make merry').

history.meaning: to go on a spree, party hard

гулять.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic гуляти ('to stroll, be at leisure, make merry'). Vasmer notes that its deeper etymology is debated, comparing either expressive Slavic stems meaning 'to shout, make merry' (гул) or dialectal words for an open pasture or clearing.

history.meaning: to be at leisure, stroll, feast

гурман.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French gourmand ('fond of good food, epicure; glutton'), which merged semantically in Russian with gourmet ('connoisseur of fine food and wine').

гусиный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гусиныи ('relating to geese'), formed with the possessive/animal adjective suffix -иный from гусь ('goose', Proto-Slavic *gǫsь, PIE *ǵʰh₂éns).

густо.etymology: Adverb derived from густой ('thick, dense'), from Old East Slavic густыи ('thick, dense'), from Proto-Slavic *gǫstъ; often used in the colloquial litotes не густо ('not much, sparse').

густой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic густыи ('thick, dense'), from Proto-Slavic *gǫstъ ('dense, thick').

гусь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic гусь, from Proto-Slavic *gǫsь ('goose'), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰh₂éns ('goose'; compare German Gans, English goose, Latin ānser, and Ancient Greek χήν).

да.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic да ('may, let it be; and; yes'), from Proto-Slavic *da, originally an optative and affirmative particle ('so be it!, thus') from a Proto-Indo-European demonstrative stem *do- / *dō-.

history.meaning: so be it, let, and, yes

давай.etymology: Hortative particle grammaticalized from the second-person singular imperative of давать ('to give, let', from Proto-Slavic *davati): literally 'give! let (us)! go on!'.
давай.notes: Followed by a first-person plural future verb or an infinitive to mean 'let's...' (давай пойдём 'let's go'), and used alone at parting in colloquial speech for 'take care / see you'.

давать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic давати (present даю, даеши), from Proto-Slavic *davati, the iterative and imperfective partner formed with suffix *-vati from *dati ('to give', modern Russian дать, from PIE *deh₃-).

даваться.etymology: Reflexive and passive form of давать ('to give', iterative of дать, Proto-Slavic *davati) + -ся, developing the idiomatic sense 'to yield to effort, come easily (in learning or work)'.

history.meaning: to be given; to come easily

давить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic давити ('to press, choke, strangle'), from Proto-Slavic *daviti ('to press, squeeze, throttle'), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰew- ('to press, choke').

давление.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ение from давить ('to press, squeeze, crush', inherited from Old East Slavic давити, from Proto-Slavic *daviti).

давний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic давьнии ('ancient, of long ago'), from Proto-Slavic *davьnъ, derived from *davě / *davьno ('long ago'; cognate with Ancient Greek δήν / *dwoā- 'for a long time').

давно.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic давьно ('long ago'), adverb from давьныи (modern давний 'ancient, long-standing'), from Proto-Slavic *davьnъ, from Proto-Indo-European *dū- / *dewə- ('distant in time or space').

history.meaning: long ago; for a long time

давность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from давний ('old, long-standing, of long ago'), built on давно ('long ago', from Proto-Slavic *davьno).

history.meaning: long-standing → remoteness in time, age, antiquity

даже.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic даже ('even, up to'), formed by fusing the affirmative/optative particle да ('so, let it be, and') with the emphatic particle же ('indeed').

дайвинг.etymology: Late 20th-century borrowing from English diving ('underwater swimming with breathing equipment, scuba diving'), verbal noun of dive (from Old English dūfan / dȳfan).

далее.etymology: Borrowed or shaped via Old Church Slavonic далѣѥ ('further, farther on'), comparative of далекъ / даль ('far, distance', Proto-Slavic *daľe).

далеко.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic далеко, neuter short form of далёкий ('far, distant'), formed with suffix -ек- from даль ('distance'), from Proto-Slavic *daleko.

дальневосточный.etymology: Compound geographical adjective formed from Дальний Восток ('the Far East'), combining дальний ('distant, far', Proto-Slavic *daľьnь) + восточный ('eastern', from восток 'east, sunrise').

дальний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дальнии and Proto-Slavic *dalьnьjь ('distant, far-off'), derived from даль (*dalь 'distance', built on the same root as далёкий 'far').

дальше.etymology: Comparative degree formed from далёкий ('far, distant') and далеко ('far'), built on the root даль ('distance', from Proto-Slavic *dalь) + comparative suffix -ше.

далёкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic далекыи ('distant, far-off'), from Proto-Slavic *dalekъ, an extended adjective built on *dalь ('distance', related to *dьlь 'length').

дама.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via French dame (and German Dame / Polish dama) from Latin domina ('mistress of a household, lady'), feminine of dominus ('master, lord', from domus 'house'). Denotes both a lady and the queen in playing cards or chess.

дамочка.etymology: Colloquial and often ironic diminutive formed with the suffix -очка from дама ('lady'), borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish dama and German Dame from French dame (from Latin domina 'mistress, lady').

данные.etymology: Substantivized plural passive participle of дать ('to give', Proto-Slavic *dati): literally 'things given', formed in nineteenth-century Russian as a semantic calque of French données and Latin data.

данный.etymology: Adjectival past passive participle of дать ('to give', Old East Slavic даныи, Proto-Slavic *danъ), used as a determiner ('this, given, in question') calquing Latin datus and French donné.

дар.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic даръ and reinforced by Old Church Slavonic даръ ('gift, offering, talent'), from Proto-Slavic *darъ ('gift'), formed from the root *da- ('to give', PIE *deh₃-ro-, cognate with Greek δῶρον).

дарить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дарити ('to bestow, present with a gift'), derived from дар ('gift'), from Proto-Slavic *dariti (from *darъ 'gift', formed with suffix *-rъ from *dati 'to give').

даром.etymology: Adverbialized instrumental singular of дар ('gift'), literally 'as a gift, free of charge', and by extension 'for nothing, in vain'.

дата.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via Polish data or German Datum / French date from Medieval Latin data ('given [at such a place and day]', the opening word of the chronological formula data Romae... at the end of Latin letters and charters), feminine/neuter plural past participle of dare ('to give').

history.meaning: given (at a specified place and time)

датчик.etymology: 20th-century Soviet technical term formed from the stem дат- (from дать / подать 'to give, transmit a signal') + instrument suffix -чик, designating a device that transmits measurement signals ('sensor, transmitter').

дать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дати ('to give'), from Proto-Slavic *dati (reduplicated stem *dad-), continuing Proto-Indo-European *deh₃- ('to give'), cognate with Latin dō / dare (whence English donate and data), Ancient Greek δίδωμι, Lithuanian dúoti, and Sanskrit dádāti.

дача.etymology: Inherited from Old Russian дача ('something given; a land grant bestowed by the tsar on a noble'), formed with suffix -ча from дать ('to give', Proto-Slavic *dača); shifted from 'royal suburban land grant' to 'country house, summer cottage'.

два.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дъва (masculine; feminine/neuter дъвѣ > две), from Proto-Slavic *dъva, continuing the Proto-Indo-European dual numeral *dwóh₁ ('two'), cognate with English two, Latin duo, Ancient Greek δύο, and Sanskrit dvā.
два.notes: Keeps its historical gender distinction in the nominative/accusative: **два** стола / окна (masculine and neuter), **две** комнаты (feminine).

двадцатка.etymology: Colloquial univerbation formed with the noun suffix -ка from двадцать ('twenty', Old East Slavic дъва десяте 'two tens'), denoting a twenty-ruble note, twenty thousand, or a group of twenty.

history.meaning: a twenty (banknote, bus route, or sum)

двадцатый.etymology: Ordinal numeral derived from двадцать ('twenty'), which contracted from the Old East Slavic phrase дъва десяте ('two tens').

двадцать.etymology: Contracted from the Old East Slavic numeral phrase дъва десяти ('two tens', with десяти in the nominative/accusative dual of десять 'ten'). In rapid speech the unstressed second word reduced from десяти to -дцать.

дважды.etymology: Borrowed in its Church Slavonic form дважды ('twice', with Church Slavonic жд < *dj; compare native Old East Slavic двашьды / дважды), formed from два ('two') + the multiplicative adverbial suffix -жды (Proto-Slavic *-šьdy, originally built on the root *šьd- 'going, step': 'in two goings').

двенадцатый.etymology: Ordinal numeral derived from двенадцать ('twelve'), contracted from Old East Slavic дъвѣ на десяте ('two upon ten', from Proto-Slavic *dъvě na desęte).

двенадцать.etymology: Contracted from the Old East Slavic phrase дъвѣ на десяте ('two upon ten'), from Proto-Slavic *dъva / *dъvě na desęte.

дверца.etymology: Diminutive of дверь ('door') formed with the feminine diminutive suffix -ца. Russian дверь descends from Old East Slavic двьрь and Proto-Slavic *dvьrь ('door'), from PIE *dhwer- ('door, doorway, courtyard gate'). While дверь refers to full-sized room or building doors, дверца specifically denotes smaller hinged doors on vehicles, ovens, cupboards, and carriages. It is a direct cognate of English door.

дверь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic двьрь (frequently plural двьри for double gates), from Proto-Slavic *dvьrь, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwōr ('door, gate'), cognate with English door, German Tür, Latin foris, and Sanskrit dvār.

двести.etymology: Univerbation of the Old East Slavic phrase дъвѣ сътѣ ('two hundreds'), where both words stand in the old nominative/accusative dual: feminine/neuter dual дъвѣ ('two') + neuter dual сътѣ (dual of съто 'hundred', modern Russian сто).

двигать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic двигати ('to move, lift, stir'), iterative of двигнути, from Proto-Slavic *dvigati ('to raise, move, shift').

двигаться.etymology: Reflexive and intransitive form of двигать ('to move, shift', from Proto-Slavic *dvigati) formed with the enclitic -ся.

движение.etymology: Borrowed/adapted from Old Church Slavonic движениѥ ('movement, motion'), the verbal noun of движити / двигать ('to move', from Proto-Slavic *dvigati).

history.meaning: movement, motion; road traffic; social movement

двое.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic двоѥ, collective numeral ('two together, a pair'), from Proto-Slavic *dъvoje, built on *dъva ('two', modern два, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁).

двойка.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -ка from двое ('two, a pair', collective numeral from два 'two', Proto-Slavic *dъvoje), denoting the digit 2, a pair, or a failing school grade (2 out of 5).

двойной.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ной from двое ('two [collective]', inherited from Old East Slavic дъвое, from Proto-Slavic *dъvoje).

двор.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дворъ ('courtyard, household, princely court'), from Proto-Slavic *dvorъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *dʰwor-o- ('enclosed space outside the door'), an o-grade noun from the same root as дверь ('door'; compare Latin forum 'outdoor marketplace, court').

дворец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дворьць, originally a diminutive in -ец of двор (дворъ 'court, yard, princely household', from Proto-Slavic *dvorъ), which specialized in Muscovite administrative usage to mean the sovereign's court and palace.

дворик.etymology: Formed in Russian as the diminutive of двор ('courtyard, yard', from Proto-Slavic *dvorъ) with the masculine diminutive suffix -ик.

дворник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic двьрьникъ / дворьникъ (originally 'house steward, innkeeper, keeper of a princely court'), formed with the agent suffix -ник from двор ('courtyard, homestead, court', from Proto-Slavic *dvorъ).

history.meaning: yardkeeper, street sweeper, janitor; windshield wiper

дворянский.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ский from дворянин ('nobleman'), originally a member of the prince's court (двор, Old East Slavic дворъ 'courtyard, princely court', Proto-Slavic *dvorъ).

двоюродный.etymology: Compound kinship adjective from Old East Slavic двоюродьныи ('related in the second degree, first cousin'), formed from двою (archaic genitive-locative dual of два 'two') + родъ ('kin, birth, generation').

дебаты.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via French débats (plural of débat 'discussion, parliamentary debate') or English debates, from Old French debatre ('to fight out, argue, discuss', from de- + batre 'to beat', from Latin battere / battuere).

девать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дѣвати and Proto-Slavic *děvati ('to put, place, do with'), the imperfective of деть (*děti 'to put, do', from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- 'to put, do', cognate with English do and deed).

девичник.etymology: Inherited from traditional Russian wedding custom: formed with -ник from девица / девий ('maiden, bride-to-be', from дева 'maiden', Proto-Slavic *děva), originally the ritual farewell gathering of the bride's female friends on the eve of her wedding.

history.meaning: bridal eve gathering; modern bachelorette party

девочка.etymology: Double diminutive formed from девка ('girl, maid') + suffix -очка, ultimately from дева ('maiden, virgin'), inherited from Old East Slavic дѣва and Proto-Slavic *děva. In modern standard Russian, девочка is the neutral everyday word for a female child ('little girl'), while девка became rustic or pejorative.

девушка.etymology: Formed with the diminutive/expressive suffix -ушка from дева ('maiden, virgin, girl'), inherited from Old East Slavic дѣва, from Proto-Slavic *děva.

девчонка.etymology: Colloquial and affectionate diminutive formed in Russian from девка / девочка (ultimately from дева 'maiden, girl', Proto-Slavic *děva) with the expressive suffix -онка.

девяносто.etymology: Distinctively East Slavic numeral (attested in Old East Slavic from the fourteenth century as девяносто, replacing older девять десятъ 'nine tens'), clearly built from the roots of девять ('nine') and сто ('hundred'); the exact origin of the medial -но- element remains debated (Vasmer discusses hypotheses linking it to an older *devęn-osъto 'nine-ten of a hundred').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: девяносто

девяностый.etymology: Ordinal numeral formed in Russian from девяносто ('ninety'); in the plural (девяностые) it also refers to the decade of the 1990s.

девятнадцатый.etymology: Ordinal numeral derived from девятнадцать ('nineteen'), which contracted from Old East Slavic девять на десяте ('nine upon ten').

девятнадцать.etymology: Contracted from the Old East Slavic phrase девять на десяте ('nine upon ten'), from Proto-Slavic *devętь na desęte.

девятый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic девятыи ('ninth'), from Proto-Slavic *devętъ, ordinal of *devętь ('nine', Russian девять), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥tos.

девять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic девять (Old Church Slavonic девѧть), from Proto-Slavic *devętь ('nine'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥ ('nine'; cognate with English nine and Latin novem), with initial *n- assimilated to *d- under the influence of the following numeral *desętь ('ten').

девятьсот.etymology: Compound cardinal numeral formed by univerbation of девять ('nine', Proto-Slavic *devętь) + сот (genitive plural of сто 'hundred', Proto-Slavic *sъto).

дегустатор.etymology: Borrowed via French dégustateur from Latin degustator ('one who tastes'), agent noun from degustare ('to taste, sample food or wine', from de- + gustare 'to taste').

дегустация.etymology: Borrowed via French dégustation or Polish degustacja from Latin dēgustātiō ('a tasting, sampling'), derived from dēgustāre ('to taste, sample', from dē- + gustāre 'to taste').

дед.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дѣдъ, from Proto-Slavic *dědъ ('grandfather, ancestor, old man'), originating as an expressive reduplicated nursery word (*dē-d-) with close Baltic relatives (Lithuanian dė̃dė 'uncle, old man') and Greek τήθη ('grandmother').

дедовский.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ский from дед (possessive дедов, 'grandfather's, ancestral'), inherited from Old East Slavic дѣдъ ('grandfather, ancestor', Proto-Slavic *dědъ).

дедовщина.etymology: Late 20th-century Soviet military colloquialism formed with the suffix -щина from деды ('grandfathers', army slang for senior conscripts in their final six months of service), denoting informal seniority rule and hazing of new recruits.

дедушка.etymology: Affectionate derivative formed with the suffix -ушка from дед ('grandfather, old man'), inherited from Old East Slavic дѣдъ, from Proto-Slavic *dědъ (a reduplicated nursery word *dē-dē).

дедушкин.etymology: Possessive adjective formed with the suffix -ин from дедушка ('grandfather').

дежурить.etymology: Formed in Russian from the adjective/noun дежурный ('on duty'), which was borrowed in the eighteenth century from the French military and court phrase (officier) de jour ('[officer] of the day', from de 'of' + jour 'day').

history.meaning: of the day (appointed for the day's duty)
on duty -> to be on duty, keep watch

дежурный.etymology: Substantivized and adjectival form coined in the 18th century with suffix -ный from the French phrase de jour ('of the day, on duty for the day', as in officier de jour).

history.meaning: on duty; person on duty, attendant

дежурство.etymology: Formed with the abstract noun suffix -ство from дежурить ('to be on duty') / дежурный ('on duty'), borrowed in the eighteenth century from the French military and court phrase (être) de jour ('to be on duty for the day', from de 'of' + jour 'day').

действие.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дѣиствиѥ ('action, operation, effect'), derived from дѣяти ('to do, act', Proto-Slavic *dějati, PIE *dʰeh₁- 'to put, do').

действительно.etymology: Adverb derived from действительный ('real, actual, valid'), formed from действие ('action, effect, reality'), an Old Church Slavonic derivative of дѣяти ('to do, act', from Proto-Slavic *dějati, cognate with English do).

действовать.etymology: Denominative verb formed with the suffix -овать from действие / действо ('action, deed, operation'), borrowed via Old Church Slavonic дѣиство from Proto-Slavic *dějьstvo, built on *dějati ('to do, act', cognate with дело 'deed, business').

действующий.etymology: Present active participle of действовать ('to act, operate, function'), derived from действие ('action', Old Church Slavonic дѣиствиѥ).

декрет.etymology: Borrowed via Polish dekret or German Dekret from Latin decretum ('decree, decision', from decernere 'to decide'); the everyday Russian sense 'maternity leave' arose as short for декретный отпуск, instituted by a 1917 Soviet decree (Декрет) on maternity insurance.

делать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дѣлати ('to work, make, do'), from Proto-Slavic *dělati, a denominative verb derived from *dělo ('deed, work, thing made', modern Russian дело), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- ('to put, set, do, make', cognate with English do and deed).

делегация.etymology: Borrowed via Polish delegacja or German Delegation / French délégation from Latin delegatio ('assignment, deputation'), from delegare ('to send as a representative, delegate').

деликатес.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via German Delikatesse from French délicatesse ('delicacy, fine food, refinement'), derived from délicat, from Latin delicatus ('alluring, dainty, luxurious').

деликатный.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via Polish delikatny and French délicat / German delikat from Latin delicatus ('alluring, dainty, tender, fastidious').

делить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дѣлити ('to divide, share, apportion'), from Proto-Slavic *děliti, denominative from *dělъ ('part, share'; cognate with Gothic dails and English deal).

делиться.etymology: Reflexive and reciprocal form of делить ('to divide, share', inherited from Old East Slavic дѣлити, from Proto-Slavic *děliti, derived from *dělъ 'part, share') + -ся.

дело.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дѣло ('deed, work, business, matter, cause'), from Proto-Slavic *dělo, formed with the neuter noun suffix *-lo from the Proto-Indo-European root *dʰeh₁- ('to do, make, place', cognate with English do and deed).
дело.notes: Plural **дела**, as in the everyday greeting **Как дела?** ('How are things?').

деловой.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -овой from дело ('deed, work, business, affair'), inherited from Old East Slavic дѣло, from Proto-Slavic *dělo ('deed, work', built on *děti 'to do, place' with the instrument/result suffix *-lo).

дельный.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ный from дело ('deed, business, work, matter'), inherited from Old East Slavic дѣло ('work, deed, affair', Proto-Slavic *dělo, from *děti 'to do, place').

демократия.etymology: Borrowed via Polish demokracja and Western European languages from Medieval Latin democratia, from Ancient Greek δημοκρατία (dēmokratía, 'rule by the people'), from δῆμος (dêmos, 'common people') + κράτος (krátos, 'power, rule').

history.meaning: popular government, rule of the people

демонстративно.etymology: Adverb in -о formed from демонстративный ('demonstrative, ostentatious'), borrowed via French démonstratif or German demonstrativ from Late Latin dēmonstrātīvus (from dēmonstrāre 'to point out, show openly').

демонстрация.etymology: Borrowed via Polish demonstracja or German Demonstration from Latin demonstratio ('pointing out, proof, display'), from demonstrare ('to point out, show clearly', from de- + monstrare).

денежки.etymology: Affectionate plural diminutive formed with the suffix -к- (with regular г -> ж palatalization) from деньги ('money'), plural of деньга ('coin', borrowed in the fourteenth century from Turkic tängä 'silver coin').

morphemes.meaning: money (from деньги with fleeting е and г -> ж)

денежный.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ный from деньга / деньги ('money'), borrowed in Old Russian (деньга 'silver coin') from Turkic (Chagatai/Tatar täŋkä 'silver coin').

денте.etymology: Borrowed as part of the Italian culinary phrase al dente ('to the tooth', i.e. pasta or vegetables cooked so as to remain firm when bitten), from Italian dente ('tooth'), from Latin dens, stem dent- ('tooth').

history.meaning: to the tooth, firm to the bite

день.etymology: An inherited Slavic word for day, recorded in Old Russian and Old Church Slavonic. Vasmer compares Baltic and other Indo-European relatives. The reduced vowel in the older form helps explain the alternation between день and forms such as дня.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: день

день.notes:
- The vowel is dropped in most forms: день, but дня, дню.
- *День рождения* = birthday; *добрый день* = good afternoon.

деньги.etymology: Plural of historical деньга (attested in 14th-century Old Russian), borrowed from Turkic (compare Tatar täŋkä and Kazakh теңге), originally denoting a stamped silver coin. As small copper деньга coins lost value, the plural деньги became the general word for money.
деньги.notes: Plural-only in modern Russian: **деньги лежат**, genitive **денег**.

денёк.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ёк from день ('day', inherited from Old East Slavic дьнь, Proto-Slavic *dьnь).

history.meaning: day -> nice little day; busy day (ironic)

денёк-другой.etymology: Colloquial idiomatic compound combining денёк (affectionate diminutive of день 'day', Proto-Slavic *dьnь, with suffix -ёк) + другой ('another, a second', Proto-Slavic *drugъ).

депозит.etymology: Borrowed via German Deposit and French dépôt from Latin dēpositum ('something laid down for safekeeping, deposit'), neuter past participle of dēpōnere ('to lay down, entrust').

депортировать.etymology: Borrowed via German deportieren or French déporter from Latin dēportāre ('to carry away, banish to an island or province'), from dē- ('away') + portāre ('to carry').

депрессия.etymology: Borrowed via German Depression or French dépression from Late Latin depressio ('a pressing down, sinking'), derived from Latin deprimere ('to press down', from de- + premere).

history.meaning: lowering of spirits or economy, depression

депутат.etymology: Borrowed via Polish deputat and German Deputat from Late Latin deputatus ('appointed representative, deputy'), past participle of deputare ('to allot, assign, destine').

дерби.etymology: Borrowed from English derby ('major horse race; match between local rival sports teams'), named after the 12th Earl of Derby, who inaugurated The Derby horse race at Epsom Downs in 1780.

history.meaning: Epsom horse race; local sports rivalry match
derby (sports rivalry match or horse race)

деревенский.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ский from деревня ('village, countryside').

деревня.etymology: Inherited from Old Russian деревня (originally 'plot of arable land cleared of trees, homestead with ploughed land', later 'hamlet, village'), derived from дерево ('tree', or *dьrvati 'to tear up, clear timber from land', compare Lithuanian dirva 'arable field').

дерево.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дерево (with East Slavic pleophony -ере-; compare Old Church Slavonic дрѣво), from Proto-Slavic *dervo, from Proto-Indo-European *dóru / *dréwo- ('tree, oak, wood'), cognate with English tree.

деревушка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ушка from деревня ('village'), denoting a small or humble country hamlet.

деревянный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic деревяныи ('made of wood'), formed from дерево ('tree, wood', from Proto-Slavic *dervo) + the material suffix -ян(н)ый. Together with стеклянный ('glass') and оловянный ('tin'), it is one of the three classic Russian -янный adjectives that double the н in spelling.
деревянный.notes: One of the famous schoolroom trio of -янный exceptions with double **нн**: **стеклянный, оловянный, деревянный**.

держать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дьржати (present дьржу, дьржиши), from Proto-Slavic *dьržati ('to hold fast, keep, possess, rule'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *dʰerǵʰ- ('to hold firmly, grasp'; cognate with Sanskrit dṛṃhati 'makes firm, fastens').

держаться.etymology: Reflexive form of держать ('to hold, keep', inherited from Old East Slavic дьржати, from Proto-Slavic *dьržati) + -ся.

history.meaning: to hold on, stay in place

дерзкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дързъкыи / Old Church Slavonic дрьзъкъ (Proto-Slavic *dьrzъkъ 'bold, daring, audacious'), from the Indo-European root *dʰers- ('to dare, be bold', cognate with English dare and Ancient Greek θρασύς 'bold').

десант.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from French descente ('descent; landing of troops from ships, later from aircraft'), feminine participial noun from descendre ('to descend, dismount', from Latin dēscendere).

history.meaning: military landing force; airborne troops, paratroopers

десантник.etymology: Formed in twentieth-century Russian from десант ('military landing force, airborne troops') + the personal agent suffix -ник.

десерт.etymology: Borrowed from French dessert 'sweet course at the end of a meal', from desservir 'to clear the table' (des- 'un-' + servir 'to serve'), since dessert was brought out once the main dishes had been cleared.

десертный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from десерт ('dessert'), borrowed from French dessert (from desservir 'to clear the table').

десяток.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic десятъкъ ('set of ten'), formed with the suffix -ок from десять ('ten', Proto-Slavic *desętь, PIE *déḱm̥t).

десятый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic десятыи ('tenth'), from Proto-Slavic *desętъ, ordinal of *desętь ('ten', Russian десять), from Proto-Indo-European *deḱm̥tós.

десять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic десять (Old Church Slavonic десѧть), from Proto-Slavic *desętь ('ten'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥t ('ten'), cognate with English ten, Latin decem, Ancient Greek δέκα, and Sanskrit dáśa.

деталь.etymology: Borrowed from French détail ('small particular, item, piece cut off'), derived from détailler ('to cut into pieces, retail'), from dé- + tailler ('to cut').

детектив.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th–20th century from English detective (short for detective policeman, from detect, Latin detectus 'uncovered, exposed', from de- 'un-' + tegere 'to cover'); used in Russian for both the investigator and the detective fiction genre.

детектор.etymology: Borrowed via English detector or German Detektor from Late Latin detector ('discoverer, revealer'), derived from Latin detegere ('to uncover, expose, detect').

дети.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дѣти ('children', originally a collective feminine i-stem noun дѣть before becoming the plural of дитя 'child', and in modern Russian the suppletive plural of ребёнок), from Proto-Slavic *děti, continuing the Proto-Indo-European root *dʰeh₁(y)- ('to suckle, nurse'; cognate with дева 'maiden', Latin fīlius 'son', and Ancient Greek θῆλυς).
дети.notes: Functions in modern Russian as the standard plural of **ребёнок** ('child').

детишки.etymology: Affectionate plural diminutive formed in Russian from дети ('children', inherited from Proto-Slavic *děti) + the expressive diminutive suffix -ишк-и.

детка.etymology: Colloquial singular diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from дети ('children', plural of дитя, Proto-Slavic *dětę).

детская.etymology: Substantivized feminine form of детский ('children's', short for детская комната 'children's room, nursery'), derived from дети ('children', Proto-Slavic *děti).

детский.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дѣтьскыи, formed with the adjective suffix -ский from дети ('children', plural of дитя, from Proto-Slavic *dětę / *děti).

детство.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дѣтьство ('childhood'), formed with the abstract suffix -ство from дети ('children', from Proto-Slavic *děti).

деть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дѣти ('to put, place, do'), from Proto-Slavic *děti ('to put, lay, do'), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- ('to put, place, do'; cognate with English do and Greek τίθημι).

деться.etymology: Reflexive-intransitive verb formed from деть ('to put, place, do with', from Old East Slavic дѣти, Proto-Slavic *děti) + -ся: literally 'to put oneself somewhere, end up, vanish from sight'.

history.meaning: to put -> to go to, disappear, get to

деться.notes: Common in questions and idioms like Куда он делся? ('Where did he disappear to?') and Никуда не денешься ('There is no getting around it').

децибел.etymology: Borrowed from English decibel, coined in the 1920s from deci- ('one tenth', from Latin decimus) + bel (a unit of relative power named in honor of telephone pioneer Alexander Graham Bell).

history.meaning: one tenth of a bel, unit of sound intensity

дешевле.etymology: Comparative degree of дешёвый ('cheap', Old East Slavic дешевыи) and дёшево ('cheaply'), formed with the comparative suffix -е and regular labial palatalization (в -> вл).

дешёвый.etymology: Attested in Old Russian дешевыи from the 15th century. Its deeper origin is uncertain: Vasmer reviews and cautions against several competing proposals, including a derivation from десить ('to find, obtain', Old Church Slavonic десити) or a borrowing from an Eastern trade term.

джедай.etymology: Borrowed from English Jedi, coined by filmmaker George Lucas for Star Wars (1977), inspired by Japanese 時代劇 (jidaigeki, 'period drama' about samurai).

history.meaning: member of the fictional Star Wars order

джентльмен.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from English gentleman ('man of good breeding and chivalrous conduct'), a Middle English partial calque of Old French gentilz hom (from Latin gentilis 'of noble family' + English man).

джинсы.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-20th century from English jeans ('twilled cotton trousers'), from jean fustian ('heavy twilled cotton cloth from Genoa'), via Middle French Jannes from Italian Genova ('Genoa').

джип.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-20th century (initially via World War II Lend-Lease vehicles) from American English jeep, likely from the initials GP (U.S. Army designation General Purpose vehicle) and reinforced by the cartoon character Eugene the Jeep (1936).

дзынь.etymology: Onomatopoeic Russian interjection imitating the sharp, high-pitched ringing of metal or glass when struck ('ting!, clink!, clang!').

дзынь-дзынь.etymology: Reduplicated Russian onomatopoeic interjection (from дзынь) imitating the bright metallic double ring of a shop-door bell, bicycle bell, or telephone.

диагноз.etymology: Borrowed via German Diagnose from New Latin diagnosis, from Ancient Greek διάγνωσις (diágnōsis, 'discernment, medical examination'), from διαγιγνώσκω ('to distinguish, discern', from διά 'apart, through' + γιγνώσκω 'to know').

диагностика.etymology: Borrowed via German Diagnostik and scholarly New Latin from Ancient Greek διαγνωστικός (diagnōstikós, 'able to distinguish or discern'), from διαγιγνώσκω ('to discern thoroughly, tell apart').

диван.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French divan and Turkish divan from Persian دیوان (dīvān, 'bundle of written sheets, register, council of state, council chamber lined with cushioned benches along the walls'). From the long cushioned seating in an Ottoman council hall, the word came to mean a 'sofa, couch' across Europe and Russia.

history.meaning: state council hall → cushioned bench along its walls

диванчик.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed with the suffix -чик from диван ('sofa, couch'), which was borrowed via French divan and Turkish divan from Persian dēvān ('council chamber lined with cushions, cushioned bench').

диверсификация.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English diversification / French diversification, from Medieval Latin diversificatio ('variation'), from Latin diversus ('turned different ways, diverse') + facere ('to make').

диета.etymology: Borrowed via Polish dieta or German Diät from Medieval Latin diaeta and Ancient Greek δίαιτα (díaita, 'way of life, daily regimen, prescribed medical diet').

дизайн.etymology: Borrowed in the second half of the twentieth century from English design, which goes back via French dessein and Italian disegno to Latin dēsignāre ('to mark out, devise, plan').

дизайнер.etymology: Borrowed in the second half of the 20th century from English designer, agent noun from design (from French désigner / Italian disegnare, from Latin designare 'to mark out, devise').

дикий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дикыи ('wild, untamed, wasteland'), from Proto-Slavic *dikъ (alongside *divьjь 'wild'; cognate with Lithuanian dykas 'empty, idle, wild').

диктовать.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish dyktować or German diktieren from Latin dictāre ('to say repeatedly, dictate for writing, prescribe'), frequentative of dīcere ('to say, speak').

history.meaning: to dictate, read out; to impose terms

диктофон.etymology: Borrowed from English Dictaphone (originally a trademark registered in 1907 by the Columbia Graphophone Company), coined from Latin dictare ('to dictate') + Greek φωνή (phōnḗ, 'voice, sound').

дикция.etymology: Borrowed via Polish dykcja or French diction from Latin dictiō ('saying, utterance, manner of speaking'), derived from dīcere ('to speak, say').

cognates.meaning: manner of enunciation or word choice

динамика.etymology: Borrowed via French dynamique and German Dynamik from New Latin dynamica (coined by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in 1692), from Ancient Greek δυναμικός (dunamikós, 'powerful, forceful'), from δύναμις (dúnamis, 'power, force').

динамить.etymology: 20th-century colloquial verb formed from динамо ('dynamo, generator; also the Soviet sports society Dynamo'), from the slang phrase крутить динамо ('to spin a dynamo', i.e. to string someone along, stand someone up, or dodge a promise).

history.meaning: to stand up, blow off, string along

диплом.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French diplôme from Latin diploma ('official state letter of recommendation'), from Ancient Greek δίπλωμα (díplōma, 'folded document, charter'), from διπλόω ('to fold double').

дипломат.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French diplomate ('diplomat'), back-formed during the French Revolution from diplomatique ('pertaining to official documents and treaties'), from Ancient Greek δίπλωμα (díplōma, 'folded state document or credential').

history.meaning: folded paper, official letter of credence

директор.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Direktor (or Polish dyrektor) from Late Latin dīrēctor ('guide, leader, manager'), an agent noun from Latin dīrigere ('to set straight, direct, guide').

дирижировать.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via German dirigieren from French diriger ('to direct, conduct an orchestra') and Latin dirigere ('to direct, guide, align').

диск.etymology: Borrowed via German Diskus / French disque from Latin discus ('quoit, platter, disc'), from Ancient Greek δίσκος (dískos, 'throwing quoit, flat round plate').

дискотека.etymology: Borrowed in the second half of the 20th century from French discothèque ('record library; nightclub where recorded music is played for dancing'), coined from disque ('record, disc') + -thèque (Greek θήκη 'repository').

диссертация.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via Polish dysertacja or German Dissertation from Latin dissertatio ('discourse, disquisition, scholarly discussion'), derived from dissertare ('to examine and argue at length').

дистанция.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish dystancja and German Distanz from Latin distantia ('distance, remoteness'), from distare ('to stand apart').

дисциплина.etymology: Borrowed via Polish dyscyplina and German Disziplin from Latin disciplīna ('instruction, teaching, branch of learning; orderly conduct, military or monastic order'), derived from discipulus ('pupil, learner'), from discere ('to learn').

history.meaning: to learn → pupil → instruction, orderly training

дичь.etymology: Collective feminine i-stem noun formed in Russian from дикий ('wild, untamed', Proto-Slavic *dikъ), originally denoting 'wild birds and animals hunted for food (game)' or 'wilderness', and colloquially 'wild nonsense, absurdity'.

длина.etymology: Derived with the abstract noun suffix -ина from *dьlь ('length', with loss of the reduced vowel ь; compare длинный and долгий, from Proto-Slavic *dьlgъ 'long').

длинный.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ный from длина ('length') / Old East Slavic дьлина, ultimately from the Proto-Slavic root *dьl- / *dьlgъ ('long').

для.etymology: Shortened in East Slavic from Old East Slavic дѣля ('for the sake of, on account of', originally placed after its noun), from Proto-Slavic *dělja, an old grammaticalized case or derivative of *dělo ('deed, work, matter', modern Russian дело).
для.notes: Always followed by the genitive case: для вас ('for you'), для гостей ('for the guests').

дневной.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дьньвьныи / дьньныи, derived from день (genitive дня, 'day', from Proto-Slavic *dьnь, an old consonant-stem with oblique stem *dьn-ev-).

дно.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дъно ('bottom, ground'), from Proto-Slavic *dъno (from earlier *dъbno), cognate with Lithuanian dugnas ('bottom') and, more distantly, English deep.

history.meaning: bottom (of a vessel, box, or body of water)

дно.notes: Irregular plural **донья** (genitive plural **доньев**), though in everyday speech *дно* is used almost exclusively in the singular.

до.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic до ('up to, until, before'), from Proto-Slavic *do, continuing a Proto-Indo-European directive particle *do ('to, toward'), directly cognate with English to and German zu.
до.notes: Always governs the genitive case: до завтра ('until tomorrow'), до вечера ('until evening').

добавить.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix до- ('up to a measure, additionally') and the archaic causative stem бавить ('to cause to be, increase, prolong', preserved in прибавить, убавить, избавить, and разбавить), which goes back to Proto-Slavic *baviti, the old o-grade causative of *byti ('to be', Russian быть).

history.meaning: to be → to cause to be, make more

morphemes.meaning: cause to be / increase (historical causative of быть)

добавка.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -ка from добавить ('to add'), built on prefix до- ('up to full measure, in addition') + бавить ('to add, increase, cause to be', old causative of быть 'to be', from Proto-Slavic *baviti).

history.meaning: to add → addition, supplement; second helping of food

добавлять.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of добавить ('to add, supplement'), formed with the labial epenthetic -л- and imperfective suffix -я- from до- + бавить (historical causative of быть 'to be', Proto-Slavic *baviti 'to cause to be, increase').

добиваться.etymology: Imperfective of добиться ('to achieve by persistent effort, obtain'), formed from до- ('all the way to, until reaching') + бивать / бить ('to beat, strike', Proto-Slavic *biti) + -ся: literally 'to strike or fight one's way through to a goal'.

history.meaning: to strive for, seek persistently, court

добиваться.notes: Takes the genitive case for the goal sought: добиваться правды ('to strive for the truth'), добиваться успеха ('to achieve success').

добираться.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of добраться ('to reach, get to with effort'), formed from до- ('up to, as far as') + бирать (iterative of брать 'to take', Proto-Slavic *bьrati) + -ся.

history.meaning: to get to, make one's way to

добиться.etymology: Prefixed reflexive perfective verb formed from до- ('all the way to a goal') + бить ('to beat, strike, strive', Proto-Slavic *biti) + -ся, literally 'to strike one's way through to an objective'.

добраться.etymology: Prefixed reflexive perfective verb formed from до- ('as far as, up to') + брать ('to take', Proto-Slavic *bьrati) + -ся, meaning 'to make one's way to a destination'.

добреть.etymology: Inchoative verb formed with the suffix -еть ('to become...') from добрый ('kind, good', inherited from Old East Slavic добрыи, from Proto-Slavic *dobrъ).

добро.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic добро ('goodness, virtue; property, goods'), substantivized neuter singular of the adjective добрый ('good, kind, fitting', from Proto-Slavic *dobrъ). Also preserved in the traditional welcome formula Добро пожаловать! ('Welcome!', literally 'you are welcome in a good/kindly hour').

доброжелательный.etymology: Compound adjective derived from Old Church Slavonic доброжелатель ('well-wisher', calquing Greek εὔνους / εὐνοϊκός), combining добро ('good', Proto-Slavic *dobro) + желать ('to wish', Proto-Slavic *želati).

доброта.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic доброта and Proto-Slavic *dobrota ('goodness, kindness, virtue'), formed from добрый (*dobrъ 'good, kind') + the abstract noun suffix -ота.

добрый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic добръ / добрыи ('good, noble, fitting'), from Proto-Slavic *dobrъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *dʰabʰ-ro- ('fitting, well-made, skilful'; cognate with English dapper, German tapfer 'brave', and Latin faber 'craftsman'). Its older general meaning 'good' is preserved in greetings like добрый день ('good afternoon') and доброе утро ('good morning').

добывать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of добыть ('to obtain, procure, extract'), formed from до- ('up to') + бывать (iterative of быть 'to be', Proto-Slavic *byvati).

history.meaning: to obtain, procure; to mine, extract

добыть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic добыти and Proto-Slavic *dobyti ('to reach, acquire, procure'), formed from the prefix до- ('up to, reaching') + быть (*byti 'to be').

довезти.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from до- ('as far as, up to') + везти ('to convey by vehicle', Proto-Slavic *vezti, PIE *weǵʰ-).

history.meaning: to drive someone to, give a lift to

доверие.etymology: Formed with the abstract noun suffix -ие from доверить ('to entrust, confide'), derived from до- + верить / вера ('faith, trust', from Proto-Slavic *věra).

доверить.etymology: Formed from the prefix до- ('fully, to someone') + верить ('to believe, trust', derived from вера 'faith, trust', Proto-Slavic *věra).

довериться.etymology: Reflexive form of доверить ('to entrust, confide'), formed from до- ('completely') + верить ('to believe, trust', from вера 'faith, trust', Proto-Slavic *věra) + -ся.

history.meaning: to trust in, put oneself in someone's hands

доверять.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of доверить ('to entrust, confide, trust'), formed from the prefix до- and верить ('to believe, trust', from вера 'faith, trust', Proto-Slavic *věra).

довести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic довести and Proto-Slavic *dovesti ('to lead up to'), formed from до- ('up to, as far as') + вести ('to lead, conduct', Proto-Slavic *vesti).

history.meaning: to lead/bring to a destination; to drive someone to (tears, despair)

доводить.etymology: Imperfective of довести, formed from до- ('up to, to a point') + водить ('to lead', iterative of вести, from Proto-Slavic *voditi).

history.meaning: to bring to, reduce/drive to a state

довольно.etymology: Adverb and predicate formed from довольный ('satisfied, content; sufficient'), derived from Old East Slavic доволъ ('sufficiency, abundance'), built from до ('up to') + воля ('will, wish', Proto-Slavic *voľa), literally 'up to one's wish or heart's content'. Functions as a degree adverb ('quite, rather, fairly'), an exclamation ('enough!'), and a predicate ('pleased').

history.meaning: up to one's wish → sufficiency → sufficient, content

довольный.etymology: Derived from доволь / довольно ('enough, sufficiency'), formed from до ('up to') + воля ('will, wish', from Proto-Slavic *voľa), literally 'having up to one's wish, satisfied'.

догадаться.etymology: Perfective reflexive formed with prefix до- ('reaching a conclusion') and -ся from гадать ('to guess, divine, ponder'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *gadati ('to suppose, divine, speak').

догадываться.etymology: Imperfective of догадаться ('to guess, figure out'), formed from до- ('reaching the answer') + гадать ('to guess, conjecture, divine', from Proto-Slavic *gadati) + -ывать + -ся.

догнать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic догънати ('to overtake, catch up with'), formed from the prefix до- ('up to') + гнать ('to chase, drive', from Proto-Slavic *gъnati).

договариваться.etymology: Imperfective of договориться ('to reach an agreement, negotiate'), formed from до- + говаривать (iterative of говорить 'to speak', from Proto-Slavic *govoriti) + -ся.

history.meaning: to agree, make a deal, negotiate

договор.etymology: Deverbal noun from договориться ('to talk through to an agreement'), formed from the prefix до- ('up to a conclusion') + говор ('speech, talk', from Proto-Slavic *govorъ).

договорить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from до- ('to the end, to completion') + говорить ('to speak, say', Proto-Slavic *govoriti).

history.meaning: to finish speaking, finish what one was saying

договориться.etymology: Formed from the prefix до- ('to completion') + говорить ('to speak, talk', from Proto-Slavic *govoriti) + the reciprocal/reflexive enclitic -ся ('to talk with one another until reaching agreement').

history.meaning: to agree, come to an agreement

договорной.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ной from договор ('agreement, contract, treaty'), which comes from договориться ('to come to an agreement by talking', from до- + говорить); in sports, договорной матч denotes a pre-arranged or fixed match.

догонять.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the prefix до- ('up to, reaching') + гонять ('to chase, drive', iterative of гнать, from Proto-Slavic *goniti / *gъnati).

доделать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from до- ('to completion') + делать ('to do, make', Old East Slavic дѣлати, Proto-Slavic *dělati).

додуматься.etymology: Prefixed reflexive perfective verb formed from до- ('up to a conclusion') + думать ('to think', Proto-Slavic *dumati) + -ся, meaning 'to hit upon an idea by thinking, to think of'.

history.meaning: to think of, come up with, figure out

доедать.etymology: Imperfective of доесть ('to finish eating'), formed from completive до- ('to the end, finishing off') + едать / есть ('to eat', from Proto-Slavic *ěsti).

history.meaning: to finish eating, eat up the rest of

доесть.etymology: Formed by prefixing до- ('up to the end, finish') to есть ('to eat', from Old East Slavic ѣсти, Proto-Slavic *ěsti, continuing Proto-Indo-European *h₁édti 'eats'; cognate with English eat and Latin edō).

доехать.etymology: Formed from the prefix до- ('up to, reaching a destination') + ехать ('to go by vehicle, ride', from Old East Slavic ѣхати, Proto-Slavic *ěxati).

дожать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from до- ('all the way, to the end') + жать ('to press, squeeze', Old East Slavic жати / жьму, Proto-Slavic *žęti).

history.meaning: to squeeze to the end, press home, wear down

дождаться.etymology: Prefixed reflexive perfective verb formed from до- ('until the awaited outcome') + ждать ('to wait', Old East Slavic жьдати, Proto-Slavic *žьdati) + -ся.

history.meaning: to wait until something happens, live to see

дождливый.etymology: Formed with the adjective suffix -ливый ('prone to, abounding in') from дождь ('rain', inherited from Old East Slavic дъжчь / Old Church Slavonic дъждь, from Proto-Slavic *dъždžь).

дождь.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dъždžь (Old East Slavic дъжчь; modern spelling дождь follows Church Slavonic tradition). Vasmer favours reconstructing an older Indo-European compound *dus-dyu- ('bad/cloudy sky', built on the sky root *dyew-), though the pre-Slavic etymology retains some debate.

дожидаться.etymology: Imperfective of дождаться ('to wait until someone/something arrives'), formed from до- ('until the point of') + -жидать (the old iterative stem of ждать 'to wait', from Proto-Slavic *žьdati) + -ся.

дожить.etymology: Formed from the prefix до- ('up to, until') + жить ('to live', inherited from Proto-Slavic *žiti): literally 'to live up to a certain time, age, or state'.

history.meaning: to live to see, reach an age

дожить.notes: Often used in the ironic exclamation Дожили! ('Look what we have lived to see! / What has the world come to!').

доза.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century via German Dosis and French dose from Late Latin dosis, from Ancient Greek δόσις (dósis, 'a giving, a measured portion of medicine'), from δίδωμι (dídōmi, 'to give').

дозвониться.etymology: Prefixed reflexive perfective verb formed from до- ('through to the recipient') + звонить ('to ring', from звон 'ringing sound', Proto-Slavic *zvoniti) + -ся.

доиграть.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from до- ('to the end') + играть ('to play', Old East Slavic играти, Proto-Slavic *jьgrati).

history.meaning: to finish playing (a game or piece)

дойти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic доити ('to reach, walk as far as'), formed from the prefix до- ('up to, as far as') + идти ('to go, walk', from Proto-Slavic *jьti).

history.meaning: to reach, walk as far as

доказательство.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -ство from доказать ('to prove, demonstrate'), from до- + казать ('to show, point out, say', Proto-Slavic *kazati).

доказать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix до- ('up to the end, thoroughly') and казать ('to show, point out, state', from Proto-Slavic *kazati). Literally, 'to show all the way through, demonstrate conclusively, prove'.

доказывать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of доказать ('to prove, demonstrate'), formed with the iterative suffix -ыва- from до- + казать ('to show, declare', Proto-Slavic *kazati).

докатиться.etymology: Formed from до- ('up to, all the way to') + катиться ('to roll', from катить + -ся, Proto-Slavic *kotiti); in everyday speech it figuratively means 'to slide downhill morally or socially, sink to a low point'.

history.meaning: to roll as far as; (colloquial) to sink to a low state

докладная.etymology: Substantivized feminine form of докладной (short for докладная записка 'memorandum, written report'), derived from доклад ('report, presentation'), from докладывать ('to report, lay before a superior').

докладывать.etymology: Imperfective corresponding to доложить, formed from до- ('up to; in addition') + -кладывать (iterative of класть 'to lay, put', Proto-Slavic *klasti); the administrative and military sense 'to report, brief a superior' developed from 'laying a document or case before an authority'.

history.meaning: to add more; to report, brief

доклеить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from до- ('to completion') + клеить ('to glue, paste', denominative from клей 'glue', Proto-Slavic *kľьjь).

докрасить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from до- ('to completion') + красить ('to paint, dye, color', originally 'to adorn, make beautiful', from краса 'beauty, color', Proto-Slavic *krasiti).

доктор.etymology: Borrowed via Polish doktor or German Doktor from Latin doctor ('teacher, instructor; holder of the highest university degree'), agent noun from docēre ('to teach'). As with English doctor, the academic title of a Doctor of Medicine became the everyday word for a physician.

документ.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Dokument or Polish dokument from Latin documentum ('lesson, proof, official record'), derived from docere ('to teach, show').

долг.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дългъ (and Old Church Slavonic длъгъ 'debt, duty'), from Proto-Slavic *dъlgъ ('debt, obligation'). Vasmer compares Gothic dulgs ('debt'), noting an early shared Germanic-Slavic legal/economic term.

долгий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дългыи and Proto-Slavic *dъlgъ ('long'), from Proto-Indo-European *dl̥h₁gʰós ('long', cognate with Sanskrit dīrghá, Latin longus, and English long).

долго.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дълго ('for a long time'), adverb and short neuter of долгий ('long', from Proto-Slavic *dьlgъ, from Proto-Indo-European *dl̥h₁gʰós).

долгожданный.etymology: Compound adjective formed from долго ('for a long time', from долгий 'long', Proto-Slavic *dьlgъ) + жданный ('awaited', past passive participle of ждать 'to wait', Proto-Slavic *žьdati).

долететь.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from до- ('as far as, up to') + лететь ('to fly', Proto-Slavic *letěti).

history.meaning: to fly as far as, arrive by air

должен.etymology: Short masculine predicate form of должный ('obliged, owing, due'), inherited from Old East Slavic дължьнъ ('in debt, obliged'), derived from долг ('debt, duty', from Proto-Slavic *dъlgъ).

morphemes.meaning: short masculine adjectival suffix (with fleeting е)

должник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дължьникъ, formed from должный ('owing, indebted', from долг 'debt, obligation', Proto-Slavic *dъlgъ) + the personal agent suffix -ник.

должность.etymology: Formed in Russian with the abstract noun suffix -ость from должный ('due, obligatory', from долг 'duty, obligation', Proto-Slavic *dъlgъ): originally 'one's official duty or obligation', whence 'an official post, office, or job title'.

history.meaning: obligatory, due -> official duty -> post, position

должный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дължьныи ('owing, obliged, due'), derived from долг ('debt, duty', Old East Slavic дългъ, from Proto-Slavic *dъlgъ; compare Gothic dulgs 'debt'). Used primarily in its short forms должен, должна, должно, должны ('must, supposed to, owes').
должный.notes: Most often used as the modal predicate **должен / должна / должны** + infinitive ('must, supposed to') or with a dative person ('owes': *Я вам должен сто рублей*).

должок.etymology: Colloquial diminutive formed with the suffix -ок from долг ('debt'), inherited from Old East Slavic дългъ ('debt, obligation', Proto-Slavic *dъlgъ; compare Gothic dulgs 'debt').

доллар.etymology: Borrowed from English dollar, which came via Low German daler from German Taler (short for Joachimstaler, a large silver coin minted from 1519 at Sankt Joachimsthal — 'Saint Joachim's Valley', now Jáchymov in Bohemia).

доложить.etymology: Formed from до- ('up to; in addition') + ложить ('to lay, place', Proto-Slavic *ložiti); in Muscovite and Imperial chancery usage, 'laying a paper or matter before a superior' came to mean 'to report, announce officially'.

history.meaning: to add more; to report, announce

доля.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic доля ('share, portion, lot, fate'), from Proto-Slavic *doľa ('share, allotted portion'), derived from the same root as *děliti (делить, 'to divide, share').

дом.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic домъ, from Proto-Slavic *domъ, from Proto-Indo-European *dómh₂os ('house, household'), directly cognate with Latin domus (whence English domestic), Ancient Greek δόμος, and Sanskrit dáma.

дома.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дома ('at home'), an ancient petrified locative/genitive form of домъ ('house, home', from Proto-Slavic *doma < *domъ, Proto-Indo-European *dómh₂os).

домашний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic домашнии ('of the house, domestic'), formed from the archaic adverb дома ('at home') / *domašь (from домъ / дом 'house, home', Proto-Slavic *domъ, PIE *dómh₂os, cognate with Latin domus) + the soft relational adjectival suffix -ний.

доминировать.etymology: Borrowed via German dominieren or French dominer from Latin dominari ('to be lord and master, rule, dominate'), from dominus ('master, lord of the house', from domus 'house').

домогаться.etymology: Prefixed reflexive verb formed from до- ('up to a goal') + могать (iterative of мочь 'to be able, exert power', Proto-Slavic *mogti) + -ся, evolving from 'to strive hard to obtain' to 'to solicit, harass sexually'.

history.meaning: to strive for; to make unwanted advances, harass

домой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic домови ('homeward, to home'), the ancient dative singular of the u-stem noun домъ ('house, home', from Proto-Slavic *domovi, with loss of intervocalic -в- > домои > домой).

домработница.etymology: 20th-century Soviet syllabic compound contraction of домашняя работница ('domestic worker, housekeeper'), combining домашняя ('home, domestic', from дом 'house') + работница ('female worker', from работа 'work').

домчать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from до- ('all the way to') + мчать ('to rush, speed along', Old East Slavic мъчати, Proto-Slavic *mъčati 'to push, speed').

history.meaning: to rush someone to a destination

донести.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from до- ('as far as, up to') + нести ('to carry', Proto-Slavic *nesti); the sense 'to inform on, denounce' comes from 'to carry a report to the authorities'.

history.meaning: to carry all the way; to report, inform on

доносить.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of донести ('to carry to; to report, inform on'), formed from до- ('up to') + носить ('to carry', multidirectional of нести, Proto-Slavic *nositi).

history.meaning: to inform on, snitch; to carry to

допивать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of допить ('to finish drinking'), formed from до- ('to the end, to the bottom') + пивать (iterative of пить 'to drink', Proto-Slavic *piti).

дописать.etymology: Formed from the completive prefix до- ('to the end, up to a point') + писать ('to write', inherited from Old East Slavic писати, from Proto-Slavic *pisati).

допить.etymology: Formed from the completive prefix до- ('to the end, to the bottom of the glass') + пить ('to drink', inherited from Proto-Slavic *piti).

доплатить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from до- ('additionally, making up the remainder') + платить ('to pay', Proto-Slavic *platiti).

history.meaning: to pay extra, pay the difference

доплачивать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of доплатить ('to pay extra'), formed with the iterative suffix -ива- from до- + платить ('to pay', Proto-Slavic *platiti).

доползти.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from до- ('as far as') + ползти ('to crawl, creep', Old East Slavic пълзти, Proto-Slavic *pьlzti).

дополнительный.etymology: Formed in Russian with the suffix -ный from дополнить ('to supplement, fill to completion'), itself built from до- ('up to the brim') + полнить (from полный 'full', Proto-Slavic *pъlnъ).

допрашивать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of допросить ('to interrogate, question formally'), formed with the iterative suffix -ива- from до- + просить ('to ask', Proto-Slavic *prositi).

допрос.etymology: Deverbal noun from допросить ('to question thoroughly, interrogate'), formed from до- ('thoroughly, to the bottom') + просить ('to ask', Proto-Slavic *prositi).

допросить.etymology: Formed from the completive/investigative prefix до- ('thoroughly, to a result') + просить ('to ask', from Proto-Slavic *prositi), specializing in judicial Russian to mean 'to interrogate, question formally'.

допрыгаться.etymology: Colloquial verb formed with the circumfix до-...-ся (expressing 'doing an action to excess until it brings about an unpleasant consequence') on прыгать ('to jump, hop around'): literally 'to caper about until one lands in trouble'.

history.meaning: to jump around -> to push one's luck too far, land in trouble

morphemes.meaning: to the point of (a bad consequence)

допрыгаться.notes: Compare similar colloquial warnings in до-...-ся such as доиграться ('to play around until disaster strikes') and договориться ('to talk oneself into trouble').

допускать.etymology: Imperfective of допустить, formed from до- ('up to, near') + пускать ('to let go, allow', from Proto-Slavic *puščati): originally 'to let someone approach or enter', whence 'to allow, tolerate, admit as possible'.

допустить.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix до- ('up to') and пустить ('to let go, allow', from Proto-Slavic *pustiti). Literally 'to let someone come up to a place, grant access', whence 'to allow, permit, admit (a possibility), or commit (an error: допустить ошибку)'.

history.meaning: to allow, admit; to suppose (допустим 'let's suppose')

дорабатывать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of доработать ('to finish working on, refine, rework'), formed from до- ('to completion') + рабатывать / работать ('to work', from работа, Proto-Slavic *orbota).

доработать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from до- ('to completion') + работать ('to work', from работа 'work', Proto-Slavic *orbota).

history.meaning: to refine, improve, finish working on

дорада.etymology: Borrowed in culinary usage from Spanish dorada / Portuguese dourada (and French dorade), from Late Latin deaurāta ('gilded', from Latin aurum 'gold'), named after the characteristic golden band between the eyes of the gilt-head sea bream (Sparus aurata).

дорадо.etymology: Culinary borrowing from Spanish dorado ('gilt-head bream / mahi-mahi', literally 'gilded, golden'), past participle of dorar ('to gild'), from Late Latin deaurare (from Latin aurum 'gold').

дорасти.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from до- ('up to') + расти ('to grow', Old East Slavic рости, Proto-Slavic *orsti).

history.meaning: to grow up to, become mature enough for

дорога.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дорога ('road, way', with East Slavic pleophony -оро-), from Proto-Slavic *dorga (originally 'cleared strip, furrow, or ravine pulled through forest', related to дёргать 'to pull, tear up').

дорого.etymology: Adverb and predicate formed from the neuter short form of дорогой ('dear, precious, expensive'), inherited from Old East Slavic дорогыи (showing East Slavic pleophony -оро-; compare Old Church Slavonic драгъ and Polish drogi), from Proto-Slavic *dorgъ ('dear, precious, high-priced').

дороговато.etymology: Colloquial adverb and predicative formed with the attenuative suffix -оват- ('a bit too, somewhat') from дорогой / дорого ('expensive, dear', Proto-Slavic *dorgъ).

дорогой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дорогъ / дорогыи ('dear, precious, costly', showing East Slavic pleophony -оро-; compare Old Church Slavonic драгъ), from Proto-Slavic *dorgъ ('precious, dear'). Means both 'expensive' in price and 'dear, beloved' in affection and greetings.

дорожить.etymology: Denominative verb formed from дорогой ('dear, precious, costly', Old East Slavic дорогыи, Proto-Slavic *dorgъ), meaning 'to hold dear, value highly, treasure'.

дорожка.etymology: Diminutive formed in Russian from дорога ('road, way', from Old East Slavic дорога, Proto-Slavic *dorga with East Slavic pleophony) + the diminutive suffix -ка (with regular г -> ж palatalization).

history.meaning: road -> path, walkway, runner rug, lane

дорожный.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian from дорога ('road, journey', Proto-Slavic *dorga) + the suffix -ный (with regular г -> ж palatalization).

досада.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic досада and Proto-Slavic *dosada ('vexation, chagrin, annoyance'), deverbal from досадить (*dosaditi 'to gall, vex, offend', literally 'to thrust or plant all the way in', from до- + садить 'to set, plant').

history.meaning: to thrust in, gall -> vexation, annoyance

доска.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дъска ('board, plank, table'), from Proto-Slavic *dъska, an early borrowing via Proto-Germanic *diskaz ('dish, table, board') from Latin discus and Ancient Greek δίσκος (dískos, 'disc, platter').

дослушать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from до- ('to the end') + слушать ('to listen', Proto-Slavic *slušati, related to *sluxъ 'hearing').

history.meaning: to listen to the end, hear out

дослушивать.etymology: Imperfective of дослушать ('to listen to the end'), formed from completive до- ('to the end') + слушать ('to listen', from Proto-Slavic *slušati) + the imperfectivizing suffix -ивать.

history.meaning: to listen to the end, hear out

доставать.etymology: Imperfective of достать ('to reach; to get, take out; to pester'), inherited from Old East Slavic доставати, formed from до- ('up to') + ставать ('to stand, reach', Proto-Slavic *stavati): originally 'to stand or stretch far enough to touch something', then 'to fetch/take out from a shelf or pocket', and in modern slang 'to get to someone, pester beyond patience'.

history.meaning: to reach; to take out, get; (colloq.) to pester, annoy

rootFamily.gloss: to reach, get, take out; to annoy (pf)

доставить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic доставити ('to bring to a place, supply'), formed from до- ('up to a destination') + ставить ('to put, place, set', from Proto-Slavic *staviti).

history.meaning: to deliver; to cause or afford (pleasure, trouble)

доставка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Russian with the suffix -ка from доставить / доставлять ('to deliver', from до- 'to a destination' + ставить 'to place').

достаточно.etymology: Adverbial and predicate form in -о of достаточный ('sufficient, adequate'), derived from достаток ('sufficiency, abundance') and достать ('to reach, suffice, obtain', built on до- 'up to' + стать 'to stand, suffice').

достать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic достати ('to reach, suffice, obtain'), formed from the prefix до- ('up to, as far as') + стать ('to stand, reach', from Proto-Slavic *dostati).

history.meaning: to reach; to get, take out

достаться.etymology: Reflexive-intransitive derivative of достать ('to reach, obtain', from до- + стать 'to stand, become', Proto-Slavic *stati) + -ся: 'to fall to someone's lot or share' (and impersonally with a dative pronoun, ему досталось, 'he caught it / got a scolding or beating').

history.meaning: to reach, get -> to fall to one's share; to catch it

достигнуть.etymology: Borrowed or shaped via Old Church Slavonic достигнути ('to overtake, reach, attain'), formed from до- ('up to') + стигнути ('to stride, reach', Proto-Slavic *stignǫti, PIE *steygʰ- 'to stride, climb').

достоинство.etymology: Derived with the abstract noun suffix -ство from достойный ('worthy, deserving', from Old Church Slavonic достоинъ, derived from достоитъ 'it is fitting, it costs/merits', from до- + стоять 'to stand, be worth').

достойно.etymology: Adverb derived from достойный ('worthy, deserving, dignified'), from Old Church Slavonic достоинъ ('worthy, fitting'), derived from досто˫ати ('to be fitting, be worth', from до- + стоять 'to stand').
