достойный.etymology: Inherited via Old Church Slavonic достоинъ and Old East Slavic достоиныи ('worthy, fitting, deserving'), formed from достояти ('to stand up to the mark, be fitting or worth', built on до- 'up to' + стоять 'to stand', from Proto-Slavic *stojati).

достояние.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic досто˫аниѥ ('inheritance, property, that which belongs by right'), verbal noun from досто˫ати ('to belong by right, be fitting', from до- + стоять 'to stand').

доступно.etymology: Adverb derived from доступный ('accessible, affordable, easy to understand'), from доступ ('access'), formed from до- ('up to') + ступить ('to step, tread', Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti).

доступный.etymology: Adjective formed with suffix -ный from доступ ('access, approach'), deverbal noun from доступить ('to step up to, reach'), from до- ('up to') + ступить ('to step', Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti).

досчитать.etymology: Formed from the completive prefix до- ('up to a number, to the end') + считать ('to count', from Proto-Slavic *sъčitati).

history.meaning: to count up to, finish counting

дотащить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from до- ('all the way to') + тащить ('to drag, pull, haul').

history.meaning: to drag or carry all the way to

дотла.etymology: Univerbation of the Old Russian prepositional phrase до тъла ('down to the ground/floor'), where тъло is the genitive of тло ('ground, bottom, floor, base', Proto-Slavic *tьlo, cognate with Latin tellus 'earth' and Old High German dili 'board, floor').

history.meaning: to the ground, completely (especially of burning)

дотянуть.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from до- ('as far as, until') + тянуть ('to pull, stretch, last', Proto-Slavic *tęgnǫti).

history.meaning: to stretch to; to hold out until

доучить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the completive prefix до- ('up to the end, to completion') + учить ('to learn, teach'). The base verb descends from Proto-Slavic *učiti ('to teach, accustom'), causative of the PIE root *h1ewk- ('to become accustomed, learn by practice'). Adding до- highlights finishing the remaining unlearned portion of a piece or lesson.

history.meaning: to finish learning to the end

morphemes.meaning: up to the end, to completion

дофаршировать.etymology: Prefixed perfective culinary verb formed from до- ('to completion') + фаршировать ('to stuff with forcemeat'), derived from фарш ('stuffing, forcemeat, ground meat', borrowed via German Farce from French farce, from Latin farcire 'to stuff').

доход.etymology: Inherited from Old Russian доходъ ('arrival; revenue, income'), formed from доходить / дойти ('to come in, reach', from до- + ход 'going', Proto-Slavic *xodъ), denoting money that comes in.

доходить.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of дойти ('to reach on foot, arrive; to ripen/finish cooking; colloquially, to sink in mentally'), formed from до- ('up to') + ходить ('to walk, go', Proto-Slavic *xoditi).

history.meaning: to reach; to finish cooking; to dawn on someone

доча.etymology: Colloquial affectionate hypocoristic truncation of дочь / дочка ('daughter'), inherited from Old East Slavic дъчи (stem дъчер-), from Proto-Slavic *dъkti, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰugh₂tḗr ('daughter').

доченька.etymology: Affectionate diminutive in -енька of дочь (genitive дочери, colloquial дочка, 'daughter'), inherited from Old East Slavic дъчи (stem дъчерь-), from Proto-Slavic *dъkti (from PIE *dʰugh₂tḗr 'daughter').

дочитать.etymology: Formed with the completive prefix до- ('up to the end, to completion') + читать ('to read', from Old East Slavic читати and Proto-Slavic *čitati).

history.meaning: to finish reading, read up to a point

дочка.etymology: Affectionate diminutive of дочь ('daughter'), inherited from Old East Slavic дочка (from дъчи, genitive дъчере) with the diminutive suffix -ка.

дочь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дъчи (accusative дъчерь, which reshaped the modern nominative дочь, while the archaic consonant stem -ер- is preserved in the oblique cases дочери, дочерью, дочерей), from Proto-Slavic *dъkti (genitive *dъktere), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰugh₂tḗr ('daughter'; compare Lithuanian duktė̃, Ancient Greek θυγάτηρ, Sanskrit duhitṛ, German Tochter, and English daughter).

дощечка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ечка (from earlier доска / дощечка with ск > щ palatalization before front vowel) from доска ('board, plank', from Proto-Slavic *dъska).

драгоценный.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic драгоцѣньнъ ('of great price, precious'; compare East Slavic дорогой), a compound of драгии ('dear, costly', Proto-Slavic *dorgъ) + цѣна (цена, 'price, value', Proto-Slavic *cěna) + -ьнъ.

драка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with the suffix -ка from драться ('to fight, scuffle'), reflexive of драть ('to tear, flay, thrash', Old East Slavic дьрати, Proto-Slavic *dьrati, PIE *der- 'to split, tear').

дракон.etymology: Borrowed via Middle Greek δράκων or Western European languages (French dragon, German Drache) from Latin draco / Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn, 'serpent, dragon', literally 'the sharp-sighted one', from δέρκομαι 'to see clearly').

драма.etymology: Borrowed via German Drama / French drame and Late Latin drama from Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma 'deed, action, stage play'), derived from δράω (dráō 'to do, act, perform').

драматический.etymology: Borrowed via German dramatisch or French dramatique (with suffix -ический) from Late Latin dramaticus, from Ancient Greek δραματικός (dramatikós, 'pertaining to theatrical plays'), from δρᾶμα (drâma, 'deed, action, play').

драться.etymology: Reciprocal form of драть ('to tear, flay, flog, beat', inherited from Old East Slavic дьрати, from Proto-Slavic *dьrati, from PIE *der- 'to split, tear, flay') + -ся, literally 'to tear at / beat one another'.

history.meaning: to tear at one another, fight

древний.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic дрѣвьнь ('of old, ancient'), derived from дрѣвлѥ ('formerly, in olden times'), from Proto-Slavic *dervьnъ ('primeval, ancient', which Vasmer connects with *dervo 'tree, old-growth wood', Russian дерево).

дрель.etymology: Borrowed from German Drellbohrer / Drillbohrer or Dutch drilboor ('boring tool, drill'), from drillen ('to turn in a circle, bore a hole', from Proto-Germanic *þriljaną).

дрова.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дръва ('firewood', plural of дръво 'tree, wood'), from Proto-Slavic *dьrva (nominative plural of *dьrvo / *dervo 'tree, wood', Russian дерево), from Proto-Indo-European *dóru / genitive *dréws ('tree, wood, oak'; cognate with English tree, Welsh derwen 'oak', and Ancient Greek δόρυ 'wood, spear' / δρῦς 'oak'). In Russian, singular дерево means 'living tree / wood as material', while the old zero-grade plural дрова specialized to mean 'split firewood'.

дрожать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дрожати ('to tremble, shiver'), from Proto-Slavic *drъžati (related to дрожь 'tremor, shiver' and дрыгать 'to twitch, jerk').

друг.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic другъ ('companion, comrade, friend; another'), from Proto-Slavic *drugъ (originally 'comrade-in-arms, fellow member of a retinue or household', as in дружина), continuing Balto-Slavic *draugas (cognate with Lithuanian draũgas 'friend, companion' and Proto-Germanic *driuganą 'to serve in a host').
друг.notes: Plural is **друзья** (genitive **друзей**); the reciprocal phrase **друг друга** means 'each other'.

другой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic другыи ('the other, second, another'), the long pronominal/adjectival form of другъ ('companion, fellow, the other of a pair', from Proto-Slavic *drugъ). From 'companion, match' developed the sense 'the other one, another'.

дружба.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дружьба and Proto-Slavic *družьba ('comradeship, friendship'), formed from друг (*drugъ 'friend, companion', with г -> ж) + the abstract noun suffix -ба.

дружбан.etymology: Colloquial expressive noun formed with the slang augmentative/familiar suffix -бан from дружба ('friendship') / друг ('friend', Proto-Slavic *drugъ).

дружеский.etymology: Derived from друг ('friend', stem дружеск- with palatalization before -ск-) + adjective suffix -ский, from Old East Slavic дружьскыи ('friendly, comradely', Proto-Slavic *družьskъ).

дружить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дружити and Proto-Slavic *družiti ('to be companions, associate with'), a denominative verb in -ить formed from друг (*drugъ 'friend, comrade').

дружище.etymology: Affectionate colloquial form of address derived from друг ('friend', Proto-Slavic *drugъ, with г -> ж) + the augmentative/expressive suffix -ище (historically retaining an old vocative-like ending -е).

дружно.etymology: Adverb in -о formed from дружный ('united, harmonious, friendly'), derived from друг ('friend, companion', Proto-Slavic *drugъ).

history.meaning: harmonious, united -> in unison, amicably, all together

дружный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дружьныи ('friendly, united, harmonious'), formed with the suffix -ный from друг ('friend, companion', from Proto-Slavic *drugъ).

дружок.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ок (with г > ж palatalization) from друг ('friend', from Proto-Slavic *drugъ).

дрянь.etymology: Collective feminine i-stem noun derived from дрянной ('rotten, trashy'), related to Old Russian дрянь ('rotted wood, sweepings, refuse') and the verb драть ('to tear, shred', Proto-Slavic *dьrati) or *dręnь ('flaccid, rotted').

history.meaning: rubbish, junk; (of a person) rotter, scum

дуб.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дубъ (Old Church Slavonic дѫбъ, 'oak tree; deciduous tree'), from Proto-Slavic *dǫbъ. Vasmer connects it with an Indo-European root *dʰewb- ('hollow, deep' — old oaks being characteristically hollow-trunked) or *dʰemh₂- ('dark-coloured heartwood').

дубинка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of дубина ('heavy wooden cudgel, club'), which is derived from дуб ('oak', Proto-Slavic *dǫbъ): originally a stout oaken staff, now used for a police baton or truncheon.

history.meaning: oak -> heavy oaken club -> baton, truncheon

дубликат.etymology: Borrowed via German Duplikat from Medieval Latin duplicātum ('something doubled, second copy'), neuter past participle of Latin duplicāre ('to double', from duplex 'twofold').

history.meaning: duplicate, replacement copy (of a key or document)

дубль.etymology: Borrowed from French double ('double, duplicate; second take or understudy'), from Latin duplus ('twofold, double'). In cinema and television, a single filmed 'take' of a scene.

дублёнка.etymology: Univerbation with the noun suffix -ка of дублёная шуба ('tanned sheepskin coat'), from дублёный ('tanned'), passive participle of дубить ('to tan hides in an infusion of oak bark'), derived from дуб ('oak', Proto-Slavic *dǫbъ).

history.meaning: to tan with oak bark -> tanned -> shearling sheepskin coat

дублёнка.notes: Unlike an older fur coat covered with cloth on the outside, a дублёнка is worn with the tanned suede leather facing out and the sheared fleece on the inside.

дубовый.etymology: Relational/material adjective formed with the suffix -овый from дуб ('oak tree, oak wood'), inherited from Old East Slavic дубъ and Proto-Slavic *dǫbъ ('oak, tree').

дуга.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дуга ('arc, bow, rainbow') and Proto-Slavic *dǫga ('curve, bow, wooden arch, stave'), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *danga. In traditional Russian life дуга also denoted the painted wooden shaft-bow arching over a horse's neck on a troika, and its root forms the second half of радуга ('rainbow', literally 'merry/bright arc').

дудка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from дуда ('reed pipe, folk wind instrument'), from Proto-Slavic *duda, an onomatopoeic reduplication imitating the sound of blowing a pipe.

думать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic думати ('to take counsel, deliberate, think'), derived from дума ('council, thought, deliberation', from Proto-Slavic *duma, an early Slavic borrowing from Proto-Germanic *dōmaz 'judgment, council, opinion', the ancestor of English doom and deem).

дура.etymology: Feminine counterpart of дурак ('fool'), from older Russian adjective дурый ('foolish, mad, wild'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *durъ ('stupefied, wild, frantic'; cognate with Lithuanian padūrmai 'vehemently, madly').

дурак.etymology: Attested in Russian since the 14th–15th centuries (initially often as a protective non-calendar secular name Дурак given to ward off evil spirits, before becoming the common word for 'fool'). Formed with the suffix -ак from the Slavic adjective дурый ('foolish, wild, crazed', compare dialectal дурь 'folly', Ukrainian дурний 'stupid', and Lithuanian padùrmai 'wildly, impetuously').

дурацкий.etymology: Adjective formed from дурак ('fool, idiot') + the adjectival suffix -ский (where к + -ский regularly fuses into -цкий). Literally, 'befitting a fool, foolish, stupid, ridiculous'.

дурачиться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed with -ся from дурачить ('to make a fool of'), derived from дурак ('fool', from older Russian дурый 'foolish, mad').

дурдом.etymology: Colloquial syllabic compound contraction of дурной дом ('madhouse, psychiatric hospital', literally 'foolish/mad house'), combining дурной ('mad, foolish, bad') + дом ('house', Proto-Slavic *domъ).

дурной.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -ной from older Russian дурый ('foolish, crazed, bad', compare dialectal дурь 'folly, madness'), from Proto-Slavic *durъ ('stupefied, wild, foolish', cognate with Lithuanianpadūrmai 'furiously').

дуть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дути (1sg. дую / дъму, 'to blow'), from Proto-Slavic *dǫti ('to blow, inflate'), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰemH- ('to blow').

дуться.etymology: Reflexive form of дуть ('to blow, puff up', Old East Slavic дути, Proto-Slavic *dǫti, PIE *dʰemH-) + -ся, literally 'to puff oneself up, swell one's cheeks or lips', hence 'to pout, sulk'.

дух.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic духъ / Old Church Slavonic духъ ('breath, wind, spirit, soul'), from Proto-Slavic *duxъ, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰówh₂os ('breath, vapor, smoke'; cognate with Lithuanian dausos 'air' and Russian дым 'smoke', душа 'soul').

духи.etymology: Plural-only noun specialized in eighteenth-century Russian (influenced by French esprits and senteurs) from the plural of дух ('breath, scent, odour, spirit', inherited from Old East Slavic духъ, Proto-Slavic *duxъ).
духи.notes: Stress distinguishes духи ('perfume', always plural) from духи ('spirits, ghosts', plural of дух).

духовка.etymology: Coined in Russian as a compact everyday noun from духовой ('heated by hot enclosed air', in духовая печь 'hot-air baking oven') + -ка, ultimately from дух 'breath, air, heat'.
духовка.notes: In modern Russian kitchens духовка means the enclosed baking oven of a cooker, whereas печь often suggests a traditional masonry stove or bakery oven.

духовный.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic духовьнъ ('spiritual, ecclesiastical', calquing Greek πνευματικός), formed from духъ (дух, 'spirit, breath', Proto-Slavic *duxъ).

душ.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century (via German Dusche or directly from French douche 'shower, jet of water') from Italian doccia ('water pipe, gutter, shower'), derived from Vulgar Latin *ductia ('conduit'), from Latin dūcere ('to lead, channel').

душа.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic душа (and Old Church Slavonic доуша), from Proto-Slavic *duša ('breath, vital spirit, soul'), formed from *duxъ ('breath, spirit, air', Russian дух) with the suffix *-ja (where *xj palatalized to *š). Cognate with Lithuanian daũsos ('air') and Gothic dius ('breathing creature, wild animal', English deer), from PIE *dʰewh₂- ('to breathe, smoke, blow').

душевая.etymology: Substantivized feminine form of душевой (short for душевая комната / кабина 'shower room'), derived from душ ('shower'), borrowed via French douche from Italian doccia ('water pipe, gutter, shower', from Late Latin ductia, from Latin ducere 'to lead, conduct').

душегуб.etymology: Compound noun inherited from Old Russian душегубьць / душегубъ ('destroyer of a soul, murderer'), formed from душа ('soul, life', Proto-Slavic *duša) + connecting vowel -е- + губить ('to destroy, ruin', Proto-Slavic *gubiti).

душить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic душити and Proto-Slavic *dušiti ('to choke, strangle, suffocate'), causative verb built on the root of дух / душа (*duxъ 'breath', *duša 'breath, soul'): literally 'to cut off someone's breath'.

history.meaning: breath -> to deprive of breath, choke

дуэль.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via French duel and German Duell from Medieval Latin duellum ('combat between two persons'), an archaic Old Latin form of bellum ('war', reinterpreted by folk association with duo 'two').

дуэт.etymology: Borrowed via German Duett from Italian duetto ('musical composition for two performers'), derived from due ('two', from Latin duo).

дым.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дымъ (and Old Church Slavonic дꙑмъ), from Proto-Slavic *dymъ ('smoke'), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós ('smoke, vapor, breath'; exact cognate with Lithuanian dūmai, Sanskrit dhūmá-, Latin fūmus, and Ancient Greek θυμός 'breath, spirit').

дыра.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дыра / дира ('hole, tear, gap'), from Proto-Slavic *dira / *dyra, zero-grade / lengthened-grade nominal derivative of *dьrati (Russian драть 'to tear, rend').

дырка.etymology: Diminutive-type derivative with suffix -ка from дыра ('hole, gap'), from Old Russian дыра / дира ('tear, rent, hole'), related by ablaut to драть (Old East Slavic дьрати 'to tear, rend', Proto-Slavic *dira / *dyra).

дырочка.etymology: Double diminutive formed with the suffix -очка from дырка / дыра ('hole', from Proto-Slavic *dyra).

дыхание.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic дыханиѥ ('breath, breathing, spirit'), verbal noun from дыхати ('to breathe'), iterative of дъхнути (Proto-Slavic *dyxati, from the root of *duxъ 'breath').

дышать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дышати ('to breathe'), from Proto-Slavic *dyšati (iterative/durative of *dъxnǫti 'to take a breath'), from the root of *duxъ ('breath, spirit').

дьяволица.etymology: Feminine noun formed with the suffix -ица from дьявол ('devil'), borrowed via Old Church Slavonic ди˫аволъ from Byzantine Greek διάβολος (diábolos, 'slanderer, accuser, devil', from διαβάλλω 'to throw across, slander').

дюжина.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine maritime era from Dutch dozijn or French douzaine / Italian dozzina ('group of twelve, dozen'), from Latin duodecim ('twelve', from duo 'two' + decem 'ten').

дядька.etymology: Colloquial/expressive form in -ка of дядя ('uncle'), inherited from Old East Slavic дядя, from Proto-Slavic *dědja (a nursery reduplication/derivative of *dědъ 'grandfather, elder kinsman').

дядя.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дядя ('uncle; prince's tutor'), from Proto-Slavic *dędja, a reduplicated nursery formation related to дед ('grandfather', *dědъ).

дятел.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic дятълъ ('woodpecker'), from Proto-Slavic *dętьlъ ('woodpecker'), generally derived with the bird/agent suffix *-tьlъ from *dęti / *dьlbiti ('to peck, hollow out'). Colloquially used for a stubborn blockhead or informer.

дёргать.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic дьргати ('to pull, pluck, tug'), from Proto-Slavic *dьrgati, an iterative-intensive verb from the root *dьrg- ('to pluck, twitch'; cognate with Old English tergan 'to tug, tease').

history.meaning: to pull, tug, jerk; to pester

дёргаться.etymology: Reflexive form of дёргать ('to pull, jerk') with the suffix -ся, meaning 'to twitch, flinch' and colloquially 'to fidget, get worked up or nervous'.

history.meaning: to twitch; to fret, get nervous

дёрнуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective counterpart of дёргать ('to pull, tug'), formed with the single-action suffix -нуть from Proto-Slavic *dьrgnǫti ('to give a tug or jerk').

history.meaning: to pull, yank; (colloq.) to have a quick drink

дёшево.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate continuing the short neuter singular of дешёвый ('cheap', Old East Slavic дешевыи); further origin outside East and West Slavic is uncertain (Vasmer discusses a possible connection with Old Church Slavonic десити 'to find, obtain').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: дешёвый

евро.etymology: Borrowed from the international currency name euro (adopted by the European Council in Madrid in 1995), clipped from Европа / Europe (ultimately from Ancient Greek Εὐρώπη Eurṓpē).

европейский.etymology: Formed with the adjective suffix -ский from Европа ('Europe'), via Latin Europa from Ancient Greek Εὐρώπη (Eurṓpē).

еда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ѣда / яда ('food, meal, eating'), from Proto-Slavic *ěda, derived from *ěsti (Russian есть 'to eat', from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed- 'to eat').

единственный.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic единъствьнъ ('single, sole, unique'), derived from единъство ('unity, oneness'), from единъ ('one, sole', Proto-Slavic *edinъ; compare native один).

единый.etymology: Adopted with Old Church Slavonic initial е- (compare native East Slavic один 'one') from ѥдинъ ('one, single, sole, united'), from Proto-Slavic *jedinъ.

ездить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ѣздити ('to ride, travel repeatedly or habitually'), the indeterminate/iterative verb of motion paired with ехать, derived from езда ('riding, journey', from Proto-Slavic *ězda / *ězditi).

history.meaning: to ride, travel back and forth
to travel, go by vehicle (multidirectional / habitual)

еле.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic еле / ели ('hardly, barely, as much as'), from Proto-Slavic *jeli / *jele, formed from the relative pronominal stem *je- + particle *-li / *-le (compare едва 'hardly').

ерунда.etymology: Emerged in 19th-century Russian seminary, student, and journalistic slang meaning 'nonsense, rubbish, trifle'. Commonly traced by Vasmer and Chernykh to Russian Orthodox seminary jargon adapting Latin gerundium ('the gerund', a grammatical topic notorious among schoolboys for tedious rules), possibly blended with dialectal ерунда / еранда ('watered-down kvass, weak brew, idler').

если.etymology: Shortened in Early Modern Russian (16th–17th centuries, alongside older ежели) from Old East Slavic есть ли ('is it that...?, whether it be'), combining есть ('is', 3rd person singular of быти 'to be') with the interrogative particle ли ('whether').

history.meaning: is it that?, whether it is

естественно.etymology: Adverb and parenthetical word derived from естественный ('natural'), from естество ('nature, essence').

естественный.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -енный from естество ('nature, essence, being'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ѥстьство ('being, nature', a calque of Greek οὐσία 'essence, being', formed from ѥсть 'is', third-person singular of быти 'to be' + -ьство).

есть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ѣсти ('to eat'), from Proto-Slavic *jěsti, continuing the ancient Proto-Indo-European athematic verb *h₁édti ('eats', root *h₁ed-), directly cognate with English eat, Latin edere, and Lithuanian ėsti.
есть.notes: A homonym **есть** ('there is / there are') comes from Old East Slavic ѥсть (3rd person singular of быть 'to be', cognate with Latin est and English is).

ехать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ѣхати (present ѣду, ѣдеши), from Proto-Slavic *ěxati (present stem *ěd-), continuing Proto-Indo-European *yeh₂- ('to go, travel, ride on horseback or in a cart'), directly cognate with Lithuanian jóti ('to ride on horseback') and Sanskrit yāti ('goes, travels, rides').

history.meaning: to ride, travel by vehicle or horse

ехать.notes: Present tense uses the stem **ед-**: **я еду, ты едешь, они едут**.

ещё.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic еще (Old Church Slavonic ѥще, 'still, yet, more'), from Proto-Slavic *ješčě / *ješče. Vasmer explains it most plausibly as a compound of a temporal/demonstrative stem *je- with an comparative or emphatic particle.
ещё.notes: Always pronounced with stressed **ё** (*ye-shchó*), even when printed without the two dots as *еще*.

жаба.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жаба ('toad'), from Proto-Slavic *žaba ('toad, frog'), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷēbʰ- ('slimy creature, toad'; cognate with Old Prussian gabawo 'toad' and Middle Low German quappe).

жабры.etymology: Plural noun (singular жабра) denoting fish gills, recorded in Russian from the 17th–18th centuries; connected by Vasmer with dialectal жабра ('jaws, gill') and Proto-Slavic *žębra / *žabra ('jaw, gill, mouth cavity').

жадина.etymology: Common-gender colloquial noun formed with the expressive personal suffix -ина from жадный ('greedy, stingy', from Proto-Slavic *žędьnъ).

жадность.etymology: Formed with the abstract noun suffix -ость from жадный ('greedy, avid, eager', originally 'thirsty, craving', inherited from Old East Slavic жадьныи, from Proto-Slavic *žędьnъ, derived from *žędja 'thirst, craving', Russian жажда).

жадный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жадьныи ('thirsty, craving, eager'), from Proto-Slavic *žędьnъ, derived from the same nasal-vowel root as жажда ('thirst, craving', Old Church Slavonic жѧжда, Proto-Slavic *žędja, cognate with Lithuanian pasigendù 'to miss, long for'). Originally meaning 'thirsty, hungering for' (still its meaning in Polish żądny 'eager for'), in Russian жадный specialized to mean 'greedy, stingy'.

жалеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жалѣти and Proto-Slavic *žalěti ('to grieve, feel pity, spare, regret'), derived from жаль (*žalь 'grief, sorrow, pity').

history.meaning: to pity, feel sorry for; to regret; to spare

жалкий.etymology: Formed with the adjective suffix -кий from жаль ('pity, sorrow'), inherited from Old East Slavic жаль ('grief, compassion'), from Proto-Slavic *žalь ('pain, grief, pity').

жалко.etymology: Impersonal predicate and adverb formed from the neuter short form of жалкий ('pitiful, pathetic; originally evoking pity or sorrow'), derived from жаль ('pity, grief, sorrow'), inherited from Old East Slavic жаль and Proto-Slavic *žalь ('sharp pain, grief').

history.meaning: it is a pity; (with dative + accusative) to feel sorry for

жалоба.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жалоба ('grief, lamentation, complaint'), formed with the suffix -оба from жаль ('pity, sorrow, grief', from Proto-Slavic *žalь).

жаловать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жаловати and Proto-Slavic *žalovati ('to feel affection or compassion for, show favour, reward'), built on the same root as жаль and жалеть; survives in modern Russian chiefly in the greeting Добро пожаловать! ('Welcome!') and in 'to favour, be fond of'.

history.meaning: to show mercy, bestow a grant or favour

rootFamily.gloss: to grant; to come/visit (in Добро пожаловать)

жаловаться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed from жаловать ('to feel pity for, favor', in Old East Slavic жаловати 'to grieve for, show compassion or favor'), derived from жаль ('grief, pity', Proto-Slavic *žalovati).

жалость.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жалость ('grief, compassion, pity'), formed with the abstract suffix -ость from жаль ('sorrow, pity', Proto-Slavic *žalostь).

жаль.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жаль ('grief, sorrow, pity, compassion'; originally a feminine i-stem noun), from Proto-Slavic *žalь, built on the lengthened grade of *želěti ('to grieve, feel pain or longing for', modern Russian жалеть, cognate with Lithuanian gėla 'sharp pain, grief'). Used today chiefly as an impersonal predicate ('it is a pity, I feel sorry').

жанр.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French genre ('kind, sort, artistic style or category'), from Latin genus (stem gener-, 'birth, race, kind, sort').

жар.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жаръ ('glowing coals, intense heat, fever'), from Proto-Slavic *žarъ (with *ž- from palatalization of *gēros before a front vowel), a lengthened-grade noun from the Proto-Indo-European root *gʷʰer- ('to burn, be hot'; cognate with гореть 'to burn', горячий 'hot', греть 'to warm', and Ancient Greek θερμός).

жареный.etymology: Adjectival passive participle of жарить ('to fry, roast'), derived in Russian from жар ('heat, glowing embers', Proto-Slavic *žarъ).

жарить.etymology: Formed in Russian as a denominative verb in -ить from жар ('fierce heat, glowing coals', Old East Slavic жаръ, Proto-Slavic *žarъ, ablaut-related to гореть 'to burn'): literally 'to cook over fierce heat or embers'.

жаркий.etymology: Formed with the adjective suffix -кий from жар ('heat, hot coals'), inherited from Old East Slavic жаръ ('glowing heat, fire'), from Proto-Slavic *žarъ (lengthened o-grade of *gorěti 'to burn', PIE *gʷʰōr-).

жарко.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicative derived from жаркий ('hot'), from жар ('heat', Proto-Slavic *žarъ).

жать.etymology: In the sense 'to press, squeeze' (1sg. жму), inherited from Old East Slavic жати (1sg. жьму), from Proto-Slavic *žęti (*žьmǫ), from Proto-Indo-European *gem- ('to grip, press, squeeze together'; cognate with ком 'lump' and Ancient Greek γέμω 'to be full').

жвачка.etymology: Colloquial contraction of жевачка ('cud; chewing gum'), derived from жевать (жую, 'to chew'), inherited from Old East Slavic жьвати, from Proto-Slavic *žьvati ('to chew'; cognate with English chew).

ждать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жьдати, from Proto-Slavic *žьdati ('to wait, expect'), cognate with Lithuanian geĩsti ('to desire, long for'). The old short yer vowel ь disappeared in weak position, leaving the consonant cluster жд-.

же.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic же ('indeed, but, the very same'), from Proto-Slavic *že, an enclitic emphatic and contrastive particle cognate with Sanskrit ha / gha and Ancient Greek γε.

жевать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жевати / жьвати and Proto-Slavic *žьvati ('to chew'), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵyewh₁- ('to chew'), directly cognate with English chew and German kauen.

желание.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic желание (reinforced by Old Church Slavonic желаниѥ), the verbal noun of желать ('to wish, desire', from Proto-Slavic *želati).

history.stage: Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic

желательно.etymology: Adverb and predicative derived from желательный ('desirable'), formed from желать ('to wish, desire', Old East Slavic желати / желѣти, Proto-Slavic *želati).

желать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic желати (and Old Church Slavonic желати / желѣти 'to wish, desire, grieve for'), from Proto-Slavic *želati / *želěti ('to long for, desire'), related to жаль ('grief, longing, pity') from a root meaning 'sharp longing or ache'.

желающий.etymology: Substantivized present active participle of желать ('to wish, desire', Proto-Slavic *želati), denoting anyone who wishes to participate or volunteer.

history.meaning: person wishing to, volunteer, interested party

желе.etymology: Culinary borrowing from French gelée ('jelly, culinary aspic; frost'), feminine past participle of geler ('to freeze, congeal'), from Latin gelare ('to freeze', from gelu 'frost, ice').

железный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic желѣзьныи, relational adjective formed with -ный from железо ('iron', from Proto-Slavic *želězo).

железо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic желѣзо ('iron'), from Proto-Slavic *želězo ('iron'), shared with Baltic (Lithuanian geležis 'iron'), an ancient Wanderwort for smelted iron.

железяка.etymology: Colloquial expressive augmentative noun formed with the suffix -яка from железо ('iron', Proto-Slavic *želězo), meaning a heavy or awkward hunk of metal.

history.meaning: hunk of metal, piece of scrap iron (colloquial)

желток.etymology: Formed from жёлтый 'yellow' + noun suffix -ок: literally 'the yellow part' of an egg, parallel to белок ('egg white', from белый 'white').
желток.notes: Fleeting о drops in oblique forms: желток -> желтка, желтков.

желудок.etymology: Inherited from Old Russian желудъкъ ('stomach, gizzard'), originally a diminutive with -ок of жёлудь (Old East Slavic желудь 'acorn', Proto-Slavic *želǫdь), named from the acorn-like shape of a bird's muscular gizzard.

жемчужина.etymology: Singulative noun formed with the suffix -ина ('a single pearl') from жемчуг ('pearls' collectively), borrowed in Old East Slavic (жьмчугъ / зьмчугъ) via Kipchak or Old Turkic jänčü / jinčü from Middle Chinese 珍珠 (trjen-tsju, 'precious pearl').

жена.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жена ('woman, wife'), from Proto-Slavic *žena, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷḗn ('woman, wife'; cognate with Ancient Greek γυνή, English queen, and Sanskrit gnā).

женатик.etymology: Colloquial noun formed with the personal suffix -ик from женатый ('married, of a man'), derived from жена ('wife', Proto-Slavic *žena).

женатый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic женатыи ('having a wife, married'), formed with the possessive adjective suffix -атый from жена ('wife, woman', Proto-Slavic *ženatъ, from *žena, PIE *gʷḗn).

женить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic женити ('to provide with a wife, marry off'), from Proto-Slavic *ženiti, denominative verb from *žena ('wife, woman', PIE *gʷḗn).

жениться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic женитися ('to take a wife, get married'), reflexive of женити ('to provide with a wife', Proto-Slavic *ženiti sę).

history.meaning: to get married (of a man or couple)

жених.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic женихъ ('bridegroom, suitor'), formed with the expressive masculine suffix -их from жена ('woman, wife', from Proto-Slavic *žena) / жениться ('to marry').

женский.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic женьскыи, formed with suffix -ский from жена ('woman, wife'), from Proto-Slavic *ženьskъ (from *žena 'woman, wife', PIE *gʷénh₂).

женщина.etymology: Formed in Russian (attested from the 16th–17th centuries) with the suffix -щина from женский ('female, women's', adjective from жена 'woman, wife', Proto-Slavic *žena), originally a collective noun ('womankind') before becoming the singular word for 'woman' as жена narrowed to 'wife'.

женщина-повар.etymology: Compound appositional noun combining женщина ('woman', formed with -щина from женский 'female', from жена 'woman, wife') + повар ('cook, chef', from варить 'to boil, cook', Proto-Slavic *povarъ).

жертва.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic жрьтва ('offering, sacrifice'), from Proto-Slavic *žьrtva, built with suffix *-tva on the verb *žьrti ('to offer sacrifice, praise solemnly'), cognate with Lithuanian girti ('to praise') and Sanskrit gṛṇāti ('calls, praises').

жертвовать.etymology: Derived with the verbal suffix -овать from жертва ('sacrifice, offering'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жрьтва ('sacrifice'), from Proto-Slavic *žьrtva (from *žьrti 'to offer sacrifice, praise', PIE *gʷerH-).

жест.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French geste and Polish gest from Latin gestus ('bodily movement, posture, gesture'), derived from gerere ('to carry, bear, comport oneself').

history.meaning: carriage, movement of the body, gesture

жестковатый.etymology: Formed within Russian from жёсткий ('hard, tough, stiff', from Proto-Slavic *žestъkъ) + the attenuative adjective suffix -оват- ('somewhat, rather, -ish').

жестокий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жестокыи (and Old Church Slavonic жесточь / жестокъ), originally meaning physically 'hard, stiff, rigid, unyielding' (a sense still preserved in its paronym жёсткий 'hard, stiff, tough', as in жёсткий матрас or жёсткое мясо). Derived from Proto-Slavic *žestъ / *žestokъ ('hard, stiff'); in standard Russian, жёсткий kept the physical sense 'hard, stiff', while жестокий specialized in the moral sense 'hard-hearted, cruel, fierce, severe'.

жестоко.etymology: Adverb formed from жестокий ('cruel, harsh, severe', originally 'hard, stiff, rigid'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *žestokъ (extended with *-okъ from *žestъ 'hard, stiff').

жесть.etymology: Borrowed from a Turkic word for sheet metal or brass — compare Tatar җиз and Kazakh жез ('brass, copper alloy') — and adapted in Russian for thin tinned sheet iron.

жестяной.etymology: Material adjective formed with the suffix -яной from жесть ('tinplate, thin sheet iron'), which was borrowed from Turkic *jez ('brass, sheet metal').

history.meaning: tinplate → tin, made of tinplate (жестяная банка 'tin can')

жечь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жечи (1st sg. жьгу), from Proto-Slavic *žeťi (*žegti), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ- ('to burn', with assimilation *dʰ-gʷʰ- > *gʷʰ-gʷʰ-).

живее.etymology: Comparative degree in -ее of живой ('alive, lively') and живо ('lively, briskly', from Proto-Slavic *živъ 'alive'); widely used in everyday speech as an urgent exhortation meaning 'quicker! look lively!'.

живо.etymology: Adverb formed from the neuter short form of живой ('alive, lively, brisk'), inherited from Old East Slavic живъ, from Proto-Slavic *živъ ('alive, living'), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós ('alive'; compare Latin vīvus, Lithuanian gývas, Sanskrit jīvá-, and English quick).

живой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic живыи ('alive, living, lively'), from Proto-Slavic *živъ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós ('alive'; cognate with Latin vivus, Lithuanian gyvas, and English quick).

живот.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic животъ ('life, living creature, property; belly'), from Proto-Slavic *životъ ('life'), formed with suffix -от from *živъ ('alive', Russian живой); the shift from 'life, vital organs' to 'belly, abdomen' occurred in East Slavic.

животное.etymology: Substantivized neuter singular of the adjective животный ('living, animate'), formed from archaic and Old East Slavic животъ ('life; living creature', Proto-Slavic *životъ, built on *živъ 'alive'), calquing Ancient Greek ζῷον (zôion, 'living being, animal').

history.stage: Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic

животное.notes: Because животное originated as a neuter adjective, it declines like an adjective in all cases (животного, животному, животные).

жидкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жидъкыи and Proto-Slavic *židъkъ ('liquid, runny, thin, pliant'), related to жижа ('slush, broth, liquid').

жизненно.etymology: Adverbial form of жизненный ('vital, relating to life'), derived from жизнь ('life'), from Old East Slavic жизнь, from Proto-Slavic *žiznь, formed from *žiti ('to live', from PIE *gʷeyh₃-).

жизнь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жизнь / Old Church Slavonic жизнь ('life'), from Proto-Slavic *žiznь, formed with the archaic action/state suffix *-znь from *žiti ('to live', Russian жить).

жилец.etymology: Formed in Russian with the personal noun suffix -ец from the participial/adjectival stem жил- of жить ('to live, reside', Proto-Slavic *žiti).

жильё.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic жилье, formed with the collective/place suffix -ьё from жилой ('inhabited, residential', historically the past participle жилъ of жить 'to live, dwell', from Proto-Slavic *žiti).

жирный.etymology: Derived from жир ('fat, grease') + the relational adjective suffix -ный; жир is inherited from Old East Slavic жиръ ('pasture, abundance, rich food, fat'), from Proto-Slavic *žirъ, a derivative of *žiti ('to live').

житель.etymology: Derived from жить ('to live, dwell', from Proto-Slavic *žiti) + the agent noun suffix -тель, modeled on Old Church Slavonic житель ('inhabitant, dweller').

жить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жити (present живу), from Proto-Slavic *žiti, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃w- ('to live'), cognate with Latin vīvō, Ancient Greek βίος, Sanskrit jīvati, and English quick (in its older sense 'living').

житься.etymology: Impersonal reflexive verb formed in Russian from жить ('to live', Proto-Slavic *žiti) + -ся, used with a dative experiencer (как вам живётся? 'how is life going for you?').

history.meaning: to live -> for life to go (impersonally)

жонглировать.etymology: Borrowed from French jongler ('to juggle', via German jonglieren), from Old French jogler ('to perform tricks, jest'), from Latin ioculārī ('to jest, joke'), from iocus ('joke, pastime'), adapted with -ировать.

жребий.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жрѣбии ('lot, tally stick'; compare native East Slavic жеребей), from Proto-Slavic *žerbьjь ('notched piece of wood cast in drawing lots'), related to *žerbo ('incision, cut').

жулик.etymology: Derived with the suffix -ик from Russian dialectal/argot жуль ('knife, thief, sharpster') and жулить ('to cut, whittle, filch, cheat at games'), connected with Proto-Slavic *žuliti ('to rub, chafe, squeeze, scrape').

history.meaning: sharp knife, cheat / to filch, cheat

жульен.etymology: Borrowed from French julienne ('julienne soup or finely shredded vegetables', from the personal name Julien/Julienne, from Latin Iūliānus); in Russian culinary usage, extended to mushrooms or poultry baked in cream and cheese in a small cocotte.

журнал.etymology: Borrowed from French journal ('daily newspaper, journal, logbook'), substantivized from Old French jornel ('daily'), from Late Latin diurnālis ('daily'), from Latin diēs ('day').

журналист.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century from French journaliste ('writer for a periodical or newspaper'), derived from journal ('daily newspaper, diary'), from Old French jornal and Late Latin diurnālis ('daily'), from Latin diēs ('day').

журналистка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the feminine suffix -ка from журналист ('journalist'), which was borrowed from French journaliste (from journal 'daily newspaper', ultimately from Latin diurnālis 'daily').

жутко.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate from жуткий ('eerie, uncanny, terrifying'), derived from Russian dialectal жуть ('dread, eerie terror'); the deeper etymology of жуть is uncertain (Vasmer notes proposed links to heavy oppressive weather or burning/chilling sensations).

history.meaning: dread -> eerie, terrible -> eerily; terribly, awfully

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: жуткий

жучок.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ок (with к > ч palatalization) from жук ('beetle, bug', inherited from Proto-Slavic *žukъ, of onomatopoeic origin from the buzzing sound *žū-); in the 20th century, also used as a semantic calque of English bug ('covert listening device').

жюльен.etymology: Borrowed from French julienne (in French cuisine, vegetables cut into thin strips, from the personal name Julien / Jules); in Russian restaurant cuisine, specialized to denote mushrooms or poultry baked in cream or béchamel sauce under a cheese crust in a small cocotte.

жюри.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century as an indeclinable neuter noun from French jury ('panel of competition judges or jurors'), itself borrowed from English jury (from Anglo-Norman juree 'sworn inquiry', Latin iūrāre 'to swear an oath').

history.meaning: panel of judges, jury (in a contest)

жюри.notes: In Russian, жюри refers to a panel of judges at a contest, festival, or competition (whereas a courtroom trial jury is суд присяжных).

жёлтый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жълтъ / жълтыи ('yellow'), from Proto-Slavic *žьltъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰl̥h₃-tós ('yellow, greenish-yellow', from *ǵʰelh₃- 'to shine, be yellow or green'), directly cognate with Lithuanian geltas ('yellow'), Latin helvus, and English yellow and gold.

жёсткий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic жьстъкыи / жестокии ('hard, stiff, rough, severe'), from Proto-Slavic *žestъkъ / *žьstъkъ ('hard, stiff, firm').

жёстко.etymology: Adverbial form of жёсткий ('hard, tough, harsh'), inherited from Old East Slavic жестъкъ, from Proto-Slavic *žestъkъ ('hard, stiff, severe').

за.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic за, from Proto-Slavic *za ('behind, beyond, after, in exchange for'). While common to all Slavic languages, its exact pre-Slavic Indo-European etymology remains debated; Vasmer compares Lithuanian už / ažù ('behind, for').

забавно.etymology: Adverbial form of забавный ('amusing, funny'), derived from забава ('amusement, pastime', originally 'delay, occupation'), from забавить (prefix за- + бавить 'to detain, keep occupied', causative of быть 'to be', Proto-Slavic *baviti).

забег.etymology: Deverbal noun from забежать ('to run in, start running'), formed from the prefix за- + бег ('running, race', from Proto-Slavic *běgъ).

забегаловка.etymology: Colloquial Russian derivative formed from забегать ('to drop in briefly, pop in', from за- + бегать 'to run', Proto-Slavic *běgati) + the colloquial noun suffix -ловка, literally a place one runs into for a quick meal or drink.

забегать.etymology: Formed with the prefix за- ('in, by on the way') + бегать ('to run', from Proto-Slavic *běgati), meaning 'to run in briefly, drop by'.

забежать.etymology: Formed from the prefix за- ('in, by the way') + бежать ('to run'), inherited from Old East Slavic бѣжати, from Proto-Slavic *běžati, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰegʷ- ('to flee, run').

забеременеть.etymology: Formed from the inchoative prefix за- ('begin to, become') + беременеть ('to become pregnant'), from беременная ('pregnant'), derived from Old Church Slavonic брѣмѧ / East Slavic беремя ('burden, load', Proto-Slavic *bermę, from *bьrati 'to bear').

забирать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of забрать ('to take away, pick up, collect'), formed from the prefix за- and -бирать, the iterative stem (with lengthened zero-grade vowel -ир-) of брать ('to take', from Proto-Slavic *bьrati / *birati).

history.meaning: to take away, pick up, collect

забить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic забити, formed from the prefix за- ('in, shut, to completion') + бить ('to beat, strike, drive in', from Proto-Slavic *biti).

history.meaning: to drive in by striking, beat
to hammer in; to score a goal

заблестеть.etymology: Inceptive perfective verb formed from prefix за- ('begin to') + блестеть ('to shine, gleam, sparkle'). The base verb descends from Proto-Slavic *blьstěti ('to flash, glitter'), from PIE *bhles- ('to shine'). The prefix за- marks the moment when a surface catches the light and begins to sparkle.

заблокировать.etymology: Formed from the perfective prefix за- + блокировать ('to block, blockade'), borrowed via German blockieren and French bloquer ('to obstruct, blockade', from Middle Dutch blok 'log, block').

заблудиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed from prefix за- ('off course, astray'), блудить ('to wander, roam', Proto-Slavic *blǫditi 'to wander, err', from PIE *bhlendh- 'to glimmer dimly, wander blindly'), and reflexive -ся. It is cognate with English blend and blind (via the PIE sense of 'clouded vision, losing one's bearings').

history.meaning: to see dimly, wander off course
to lose one's way, get lost

cognates.meaning: unable to see (from the same PIE root)

заблуждаться.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic заблуждати сѧ ('to wander astray, err'), imperfective of заблудити, from prefix за- ('astray') + блудити ('to wander, err', from Proto-Slavic *blǫditi).

заболевание.etymology: Verbal noun in -ние formed from заболевать ('to fall ill', imperfective of заболеть, built from inchoative за- + болеть 'to be sick, ache', Proto-Slavic *bolěti).

history.meaning: to fall ill -> illness, disease, medical condition

заболеть.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the inceptive prefix за- ('beginning of a state') and болеть ('to be ill, hurt'), derived from боль ('pain, illness', from Proto-Slavic *bolь).

history.meaning: to fall ill, get sick; to start hurting

забор.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic заборъ ('wooden stockade, enclosure'), formed from prefix за- ('behind, enclosing') + the root *bor- of брать ('to take, gather', originally boards or logs fitted into slotted posts to enclose a yard).

забота.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic забота ('care, anxiety, concern'), connected by Vasmer with зобать ('to peck, eat, gnaw', Old Church Slavonic зобати, Proto-Slavic *zobati), developing metaphorically from 'that which gnaws at one's heart' to 'worry, care'.

заботиться.etymology: Denominal reflexive verb formed with -ить + -ся from забота ('care, concern').

заботливый.etymology: Derived from забота ('care, concern, worry', from Old East Slavic забота, connected with зобати 'to peck, eat, fret') + the adjective suffix -ливый ('inclined to').

забрать.etymology: Formed by prefixing за- ('away, into one's possession') to брать ('to take', from Old East Slavic брати, Proto-Slavic *bьrati, PIE *bʰer-).

history.meaning: to pick up, take away, collect (perfective)

забраться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed from prefix за- ('into, up onto') + брать ('to take', inherited from Old East Slavic брати, Proto-Slavic *bьrati) + reflexive particle -ся.

забронировать.etymology: Perfective formed with за- from бронировать ('to reserve, book'), derived from twentieth-century administrative Russian броня ('official exemption or quota reservation'), a figurative extension of броня ('protective armour, coat of mail', from Old East Slavic броня): reserving something 'armours' or shields it from being taken by others.
забронировать.notes: In modern speech, забронировать / забронировать means 'to book (a table, room, or ticket)', whereas бронировать means 'to clad in armour'.

заброшенный.etymology: Past passive participle of забросить ('to throw far away, abandon, neglect'), formed from prefix за- ('beyond, away') + бросить ('to throw', from Proto-Slavic *brositi).

забывать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic забывати and Proto-Slavic *zabyvati ('to forget'), imperfective of забыть (*zabyti, formed from *za- 'behind, away' + *byti 'to be': literally 'to let something slip behind or out of one's awareness').

забытый.etymology: Past passive participle of забыть ('to forget'), inherited from Old East Slavic забыти, from Proto-Slavic *zabyti (prefix *za- 'behind, away' + *byti 'to be').

забыть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic забыти ('to forget'), from Proto-Slavic *zabyti, formed from *za- ('beyond, behind, away') + *byti ('to be'), i.e. 'to let slip behind/out of one's being or awareness'.

завал.etymology: Deverbal noun from завалить ('to heap up, block, overwhelm'), formed from prefix за- + валить ('to topple, heap, roll', from Proto-Slavic *valiti).

завалить.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('over, shut') + валить ('to topple, heap up, roll'), inherited from Old East Slavic валити, from Proto-Slavic *valiti.

history.meaning: to bury in, overload; to fail

заварить.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('begin, steep') + варить ('to boil, cook, brew'), inherited from Old East Slavic варити, from Proto-Slavic *variti ('to boil, cook').

заварочный.etymology: Formed in Russian with the adjectival suffix -ный from заварка ('tea brewing; dry tea leaves or strong tea concentrate'), derived from заварить ('to brew, steep in boiling water', built on за- + варить 'to boil'). Especially common in заварочный чайник ('brewing teapot', which holds strong tea essence in traditional two-pot Russian tea service).

history.form: заварить ('to steep in boiling water') → заварка → заварочный

morphemes.meaning: noun suffix (-ка with mobile vowel о and к → ч)

заведение.etymology: Verbal noun formed from завести ('to lead in; to establish, set up, found'), built from за- + вести ('to lead', Proto-Slavic *vesti). In the 18th century, заведение acquired the institutional sense 'something set up or established: an educational institution, public house, restaurant, or establishment' (учебное заведение, питейное заведение).

завезти.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('in, by the way') + везти ('to transport, convey by vehicle'), inherited from Old East Slavic везти, from Proto-Slavic *vezti, from PIE *weǵʰ-.

завернуть.etymology: Formed from the prefix за- ('around, in') + вернуть / вертеть ('to turn, twist, roll', from Proto-Slavic *vьrtěti).

history.meaning: to wrap up; to turn a corner, drop by

завести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic завести ('to lead behind or in'), formed from prefix за- ('behind, in, starting an action') + вести ('to lead', from Proto-Slavic *vesti). Later extended to winding up a clockwork mechanism, starting an engine, or acquiring a pet/habit.

history.meaning: to lead in, slip under; to wind up (a clock), start up

завестись.etymology: Reflexive form of завести ('to lead in, wind up, start up'), from prefix за- + вести ('to lead', inherited from Old East Slavic вести, Proto-Slavic *vesti) + -сь.

history.meaning: to start up (of an engine); to get worked up

заветный.etymology: Derived from завет ('covenant, testament, sacred precept') + adjective suffix -ный; завет comes from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic завѣтъ, from Proto-Slavic *zavětъ (*za- + *větъ 'counsel, pact', related to вещать 'to proclaim').

завещание.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic завѣщаниѥ ('testament, injunction'), verbal noun from завѣщати ('to bequeath, command'), derived from завѣтъ ('covenant, will', Proto-Slavic *zavětъ).

завидно.etymology: Predicative short neuter and adverb of завидный ('enviable'), derived from зависть / завидеть ('envy / to look askance at', from Proto-Slavic *zaviděti, built on *za- + *viděti 'to see', compare Latin invidere).

завидовать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic завидовати ('to envy, begrudge'), derived from зависть / завидѣти ('to look askance at, envy'), formed from the prefix за- and видѣти ('to see, look at', Russian видеть, Proto-Slavic *zaviděti). Exact structural and semantic parallel to Latin invidēre ('to look upon with malice, envy', from in- + vidēre).

history.meaning: to look askance/covetously at → to envy
to envy, be jealous of (+ dat.)

зависеть.etymology: Formed in literary Russian from за- + висеть ('to hang', from Proto-Slavic *visěti) as a semantic calque of Latin dēpendēre and French dépendre ('to hang from -> to depend on').

history.meaning: to hang from; to depend on

зависнуть.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('into a fixed state') + виснуть ('to hang, droop'), from Proto-Slavic *visnǫti, inchoative of *visěti ('to hang').

завод.etymology: Deverbal noun from заводить / завести ('to set up, establish, wind up, start'), formed from за- + водить ('to lead', Proto-Slavic *voditi), denoting first an 'establishment, breeding stud, or ironworks' and then a 'factory, plant, or clockwork mechanism'.

заводить.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of завести, formed from prefix за- + водить ('to lead, conduct', iterative of вести, from Proto-Slavic *voditi).

history.meaning: to start up, wind up, acquire

заводиться.etymology: Reflexive form of заводить ('to wind up, start up, acquire'), formed from prefix за- + водить ('to lead', Proto-Slavic *voditi) + -ся.

history.meaning: to start up; to get worked up

завоёвывать.etymology: Imperfective of завоевать ('to conquer, win over'), formed from за- + воевать ('to wage war, fight', from Proto-Slavic *vojevati, built on *vojь 'warrior') + the imperfectivizing suffix -ывать.

history.meaning: to conquer; to win (trust, a prize, an audience)

завтра.etymology: Formed within East Slavic from the Old East Slavic prepositional phrase за утро ('into the morning, for the next morning'), combining за + утро ('morning'). As the unstressed vowel u reduced to v before tr, заутра contracted into завтра.

завтрак.etymology: Formed within East Slavic from the prepositional phrase за утро ('for/in the morning') with suffix -ок (compare dialectal заутрок), parallel to завтра ('tomorrow', originally 'into the next morning'). The initial cluster simplified in speech into завтрак.

завтракать.etymology: Denominal verb formed with -ать from завтрак ('breakfast', originally заутрокъ 'morning meal', formed from за утро 'in the morning', Proto-Slavic *za utra).

завтрашний.etymology: Temporal adjective formed with the suffix -шний from завтра ('tomorrow'), itself a univerbation of Old East Slavic за утра ('in the morning', from за + утро, Proto-Slavic *za utra).

завхоз.etymology: Early Soviet syllabic abbreviation (сложносокращённое слово) of заведующий хозяйством ('manager of household/facilities'), combining заведующий ('head, manager') and хозяйство ('household, supplies, physical plant').

завязать.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('fast, shut') + вязать ('to tie, bind'), inherited from Old East Slavic вѧзати, from Proto-Slavic *vęzati; the colloquial sense 'to quit (a habit)' comes from tying shut a sack or bundle when finishing a job.

завязка.etymology: Deverbal noun in -ка from завязать ('to tie up; to initiate a plot or conversation; in slang, to quit drinking'), formed from за- + вязать ('to tie, bind', from Proto-Slavic *vęzati).

history.meaning: to tie up -> tie-string; dramatic opening of a plot; (slang) sobriety

завязка.notes: In colloquial Russian, быть в завязке means 'to be on the wagon / abstaining from alcohol'.

завязывать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of завязать ('to tie up; to quit'), formed with the imperfectivizing suffix -ыва- from за- + вязать (Proto-Slavic *vęzati 'to tie, bind').

загадать.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('ahead, in mind') + гадать ('to guess, divine, surmise'), inherited from Old East Slavic гадати, from Proto-Slavic *gadati ('to guess, speak, think').

history.meaning: to make (a wish); to set (a riddle)

загадочно.etymology: Adverbial form of загадочный ('mysterious, enigmatic'), derived from загадка ('riddle, enigma'), from загадать (prefix за- + гадать 'to guess, divine', Proto-Slavic *gadati).

загадочный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from загадка ('riddle, enigma, mystery'), derived from загадать ('to pose a riddle, think of', from за- + гадать 'to guess, divine', Proto-Slavic *gadati).

загипсовать.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('cover, encase') + гипсовать ('to apply plaster/gypsum'), derived from гипс ('gypsum, plaster of Paris', borrowed via German Gips from Latin gypsum, from Ancient Greek γύψος).

history.meaning: to put in a plaster cast

заглянуть.etymology: Formed from the prefix за- ('in, behind, briefly') + глянуть ('to glance, look', semelfactive of глядеть, from Proto-Slavic *ględěti).

history.meaning: to look in, peek in, drop by

загнать.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('into; to exhaustion') + гнать ('to drive, chase'), inherited from Old East Slavic гънати, from Proto-Slavic *gъnati, from PIE *gʷʰen- ('to strike, drive').

заговорить.etymology: Inchoative perfective formed from the prefix за- ('begin to') + говорить ('to speak, talk', inherited from Old East Slavic говорити, from Proto-Slavic *govoriti).

history.meaning: to start talking, begin to speak

загонять.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of загнать, formed from prefix за- + гонять ('to drive or chase repeatedly', iterative of гнать, from Proto-Slavic *ganjati / *goniti).

загораживать.etymology: Imperfective of загородить ('to fence off, block, obstruct'), formed from за- ('across, blocking') + городить ('to enclose with a fence', from Proto-Slavic *gorditi) + -ивать.

history.meaning: to fence off -> to block, obstruct (a view or passage)

загородить.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('shut, behind a barrier') + городить ('to fence, enclose'), inherited from Old East Slavic городити, from Proto-Slavic *gorditi, denominative from *gordъ ('enclosure, fence, town').

history.meaning: to build a fence or enclosure

заготовка.etymology: Deverbal noun from заготовить ('to prepare in advance, lay in supplies'), formed from prefix за- + готовить ('to prepare', from готовый 'ready', Proto-Slavic *gotovъ) + suffix -ка.

заготовщик.etymology: Agent noun formed from заготовить / заготовка ('advance preparation, procurement', from готовый 'ready', Proto-Slavic *gotovъ) + the occupational suffix -щик.

загранпаспорт.etymology: Twentieth-century Russian stump compound (syllabic abbreviation) of заграничный паспорт ('foreign-travel passport'), from заграничный ('beyond the border', from за- + граница 'border') + паспорт (via French passeport from Italian passaporto).

загреметь.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('begin to; fall noisily into') + греметь ('to thunder, rattle, clatter'), from Old East Slavic гремѣти, from Proto-Slavic *greměti (related to гром 'thunder'); colloquially 'to land noisily in prison or hospital'.

history.meaning: to rumble; (colloquial) to land in jail/hospital

загримировать.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix за- + гримировать ('to apply theatrical make-up'), from грим ('stage make-up'), borrowed from French grimer ('to make up an actor, paint wrinkles'), from Italian grimo ('wrinkled, old').

загрузить.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('into, full') + грузить ('to load, submerge'), derived from груз ('load, cargo, weight'), connected with Old East Slavic грузнути ('to sink') and Proto-Slavic *grǫziti ('to plunge, weight down').

загс.etymology: Early Soviet acronym (introduced in December 1917) of запись актов гражданского состояния ('registration of acts of civil status', i.e. civil registry office for births, marriages, and deaths).

history.meaning: registration of acts of civil status

загуститель.etymology: Derived from загустить ('to thicken, make dense', from prefix за- + густить, from густой 'thick, dense', Proto-Slavic *gǫstъ) + the agent/substance suffix -тель.

зад.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic задъ ('back part, rear'), from Proto-Slavic *zadъ ('back, rear'), originally a compound of preposition *za ('behind') + root *dъ (from PIE *dʰeh₁- 'to put, place', i.e. 'what is placed behind').

задавать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of задать ('to set, assign a task; to pose a question'), formed from the prefix за- and давать ('to give', iterative of дать, from Proto-Slavic *davati).

задавить.etymology: Perfective verb formed from completive за- + давить ('to press, crush, strangle', inherited from Proto-Slavic *daviti).

задание.etymology: Verbal noun formed with the suffix -ние from задать ('to assign, set a task', from за- + дать 'to give'). Denotes something assigned to be done: a school assignment, work task, or special mission.

задать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic задати, from Proto-Slavic *zadati, formed from prefix *za- ('ahead, before') + *dati ('to give', from PIE *deh₃-).

history.meaning: to ask (a question); to set (a task)

задаться.etymology: Reflexive form of задать ('to set, assign'), from prefix за- + дать ('to give', Proto-Slavic *dati) + -ся, developing the idiomatic sense 'to turn out well, succeed' (especially in negative constructions like день не задался).

задача.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from задать ('to give out, assign, pose [a question or task]'), from the prefix за- + дача ('giving', from дать 'to give', Proto-Slavic *dati).

задвинуть.etymology: Formed from the prefix за- ('behind, in, shut') + двинуть ('to move, slide', from Proto-Slavic *dvignǫti).

history.meaning: to push in (a drawer or bolt), shove behind; (slang) to sideline or deliver a speech

задержание.etymology: Verbal noun from задержать ('to detain, hold back, arrest'), formed from prefix за- + держать ('to hold', from Old East Slavic дьржати, Proto-Slavic *dьržati) + suffix -ние.

задержанный.etymology: Past passive participle of задержать ('to detain, delay, arrest'), from prefix за- + держать ('to hold', Proto-Slavic *dьržati); also substantivized as a noun meaning 'detainee'.

задержать.etymology: Formed with prefix за- from держать ('to hold, keep'), inherited from Old East Slavic дьржати, from Proto-Slavic *dьržati ('to hold fast').

history.meaning: to detain; to delay, hold back

задержаться.etymology: Reflexive form of задержать ('to hold back, detain, delay', from за- + держать 'to hold', Proto-Slavic *dьržati) + -ся.

history.meaning: to be delayed, linger, stay late

задерживать.etymology: Imperfective of задержать ('to hold back, delay, detain'), formed with the iterative suffix -ивать from за- + держать ('to hold', from Proto-Slavic *dьržati).

задерживаться.etymology: Reflexive imperfective of задержать ('to detain, delay'), formed from prefix за- + держивать (imperfective stem from держать 'to hold', Proto-Slavic *dьržati) + -ся.

задеть.etymology: Formed by prefixing за- ('against, in passing') to деть ('to put, place, do', from Old East Slavic дѣти, Proto-Slavic *děti, continuing PIE *dʰeh₁- 'to put, do'). Literally 'to catch or brush against something in passing', and figuratively 'to touch a nerve, offend slightly'.

history.meaning: to brush against, bump; to hurt someone's feelings

задний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic задьнии ('back, rear, hinder'), formed with the spatial adjective suffix -ний from зад ('back, rear part', from Proto-Slavic *zadъ).

задолбаться.etymology: Colloquial reflexive perfective verb formed from prefix за- ('to exhaustion') + долбать ('to peck, hammer, pound repeatedly', expressive derivative of долбить 'to chisel, hollow out', Proto-Slavic *dьlbiti) + -ся.

history.meaning: to get fed up, wear oneself out

задохнуться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed from prefix за- + дохнуть ('to breathe, gasp'), from Proto-Slavic *dъxnǫti ('to breathe', ablaut grade of *duxъ 'breath, spirit' and *dyxati 'to breathe', PIE *dʰwes-) + -ся.

задремать.etymology: Formed from the inchoative prefix за- ('begin to') + дремать ('to doze, slumber', inherited from Old East Slavic дрѣмати, Proto-Slavic *drěmati, cognate with Latin dormīre 'to sleep').

задумать.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('in advance, into mind') + думать ('to think'), inherited from Old East Slavic думати, from Proto-Slavic *dumati (from *duma 'thought, counsel').

history.meaning: to plan, conceive, have in mind

задуматься.etymology: Reflexive form of задумать, formed from prefix за- ('become absorbed in') + думать ('to think', Proto-Slavic *dumati) + -ся.

задумчивый.etymology: Derived from the stem of задуматься ('to become absorbed in thought', from за- + думать, Proto-Slavic *dumati) + the adjective suffix -чивый ('inclined to').

задушить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic задушити ('to strangle, suffocate, choke'), formed from the perfective prefix за- + душить ('to choke, strangle', causative derived from дух / душа 'breath, soul', Proto-Slavic *dušiti).

заезжать.etymology: Imperfective of заехать, formed from за- ('in, stopping by on the way') + -езжать (the iterative stem corresponding to ехать 'to ride, drive', from Proto-Slavic *ězditi).

history.meaning: to drop in on the way, drive in; to move in

заесть.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('into, after') + есть ('to eat, bite'), inherited from Old East Slavic ѣсти, from Proto-Slavic *ěsti (PIE *h₁ed-); the mechanical sense 'to jam, get stuck' arises from gears or parts biting and catching.

history.meaning: to eat after; to jam, get stuck

заехать.etymology: Formed from the prefix за- ('in, making a brief detour on the way') + ехать ('to go by vehicle, ride', from Old East Slavic ѣхати, Proto-Slavic *ěxati).

history.meaning: to drop by, stop in (by vehicle); to drive into

заждаться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed with the circumfix за-...-ся ('to do for a very long time, grow tired of doing') + ждать ('to wait', from Old East Slavic жьдати, Proto-Slavic *žьdati).

history.meaning: to wait a long time, grow tired of waiting

зажечь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic зажечи (Proto-Slavic *zažeťi), formed from inchoative за- ('begin to, set') + жечь ('to burn', Proto-Slavic *žeťi, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ- 'to burn').

history.meaning: to light, ignite; (colloquial) to party hard, rock the floor

зажечься.etymology: Reflexive and inchoative form of зажечь ('to light, ignite'), formed with -ся from за- + жечь ('to burn', inherited from Old East Slavic жечи, from Proto-Slavic *žeťi).

history.meaning: to light up, catch fire, come on

зажигалка.etymology: Derived from зажигать ('to light, ignite', imperfective of зажечь, from за- + жечь, Proto-Slavic *žegti 'to burn') + the instrument noun suffix -лка.

зажигать.etymology: Imperfective of зажечь ('to light, kindle, switch on'), inherited from Old East Slavic зажигати, formed from за- + -жигать (iterative of жечь 'to burn', from Proto-Slavic *žigati / *žeťi).

зажиточный.etymology: Derived from older/dialectal зажиток ('wealth, property earned by living and working'), from зажить ('to earn by living/working', from за- + жить 'to live', Proto-Slavic *žiti) + adjective suffix -очный.

заигрывать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed from prefix за- ('begin, entice into') + игрывать (iterative of играть 'to play', inherited from Old East Slavic играти, Proto-Slavic *jьgrati).

history.meaning: to flirt with, play up to

заика.etymology: Deverbal noun from заикаться ('to stutter, stammer'), formed from prefix за- + икать ('to hiccup, utter repeated short sounds', onomatopoeic Proto-Slavic *jьkati).

заикаться.etymology: Derived from заика ('stutterer') / икать ('to hiccup, utter spasmodic sounds'), formed with prefix за- from onomatopoeic Proto-Slavic *jьkati ('to hiccup, sob, stammer').

заинтересованный.etymology: Past passive participle of заинтересовать ('to interest, spark interest in'), formed from prefix за- + интересовать, from интерес ('interest', borrowed via German Interesse or French intérêt from Medieval Latin interesse).

заинтересоваться.etymology: Reflexive form of заинтересовать ('to spark interest'), from prefix за- + интересовать (from интерес 'interest', ultimately from Latin interesse) + -ся.

зайка.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from заяц (stem зай-, 'hare', inherited from Old East Slavic заяць, from Proto-Slavic *zajęcь).

зайти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic заити ('to go behind, set [of the sun], drop in'), formed from the prefix за- ('behind, in on the way') + идти ('to go, walk', from Proto-Slavic *jьti).

history.meaning: to drop in, step in; to set

зайчик.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -чик from заяц ('hare', from Proto-Slavic *zajęcь).

зайчонок.etymology: Derived from заяц ('hare', from Old East Slavic заяць, Proto-Slavic *zajęcь) + the young-animal diminutive suffix -онок (with palatalization ц > ч).

заказ.etymology: Deverbal noun from заказать ('to order, commission; in older Russian also to command or forbid'), built on prefix за- + казать ('to show, say, order', from Proto-Slavic *kazati).

history.meaning: to commission, order → an order, commission

заказать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic заказати (originally 'to forbid, command, instruct beforehand', later 'to place an order'), formed from the prefix за- + казать ('to show, say, order', from Proto-Slavic *kazati).

заказной.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ной from заказ ('order, commission'), deverbal noun of заказать.

заказчик.etymology: Agent noun derived from заказать / заказ ('order, commission', originally 'injunction, prohibition', from за- + казать 'to show, order', Proto-Slavic *kazati) + the agent suffix -чик.

заказывать.etymology: Imperfective of заказать ('to order, commission, book'), formed with the suffix -ывать from за- + казать.

закалка.etymology: Deverbal noun in -ка from закалить ('to temper glowing metal by quenching it in water; figuratively to toughen up the body or character'), formed from за- + калить ('to heat red-hot, temper', Proto-Slavic *kaliti).

history.meaning: to temper, toughen -> tempering; physical or moral toughness

закалка.notes: Often heard in человек старой закалки ('a person of the old school / old-fashioned toughness').

заканчивать.etymology: Imperfective of закончить ('to finish, complete'), formed from за- + кончать / кончить ('to end', derived from конец 'end', Proto-Slavic *konьcь) + the imperfectivizing suffix -ивать.

morphemes.meaning: end (from конец with о -> а in -ивать)

заканчиваться.etymology: Imperfective of закончиться ('to end, finish'), formed with the iterative suffix -ивать and reflexive -ся from за- + кончить (from конец 'end', Proto-Slavic *konьcь).

history.meaning: to end, come to an end

закат.etymology: Deverbal noun from закатиться ('to roll behind, set [of the sun]'), built from prefix за- ('behind, beyond the horizon') + катить ('to roll', Proto-Slavic *kotiti). Russian pictures the sun as a golden wheel rolling down behind the horizon at the close of day, just as восход pictures it walking upward at dawn.

history.meaning: to roll behind the horizon → sunset

закатать.etymology: Formed with the prefix за- ('up, into a roll') + катать ('to roll', iterative of катить, from Old East Slavic катити and Proto-Slavic *katiti).

history.meaning: to roll up (sleeves); to seal jars

заклеить.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('shut, over') + клеить ('to glue, paste'), denominative verb from клей ('glue'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъlějь ('glue, gum, resin').

history.meaning: to seal, glue shut, tape shut

заклинить.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('fast, tight') + клинить ('to wedge'), denominative from клин ('wedge'), inherited from Old East Slavic клинъ, from Proto-Slavic *klinъ ('wedge, peg').

history.meaning: to wedge tight, jam, seize up

заключаться.etymology: Reflexive imperfective of заключать ('to enclose, conclude, contain'), borrowed from or modeled on Old Church Slavonic заключати (from за- + ключити 'to lock, hook', from ключ 'key, hook', Proto-Slavic *ključь) + -ся.

history.meaning: to consist in, lie in; to be concluded

заключение.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic заключениѥ ('enclosing, imprisonment'), verbal noun from заключити ('to lock up', from ключ 'key', Proto-Slavic *ključь); the sense 'conclusion, inference, report' is a semantic calque of Latin conclūsiō.

заключить.etymology: Borrowed from or modeled on Old Church Slavonic заключити ('to lock up, shut in'), from prefix за- + ключити (from ключ 'key, bolt', Proto-Slavic *ključь); the senses 'to conclude (an agreement, an inference)' calque Latin conclūdere.

history.meaning: to enclose; to conclude, enter into

закодироваться.etymology: Reflexive perfective of закодировать ('to encode'), from за- + кодировать (from код 'code', via French code from Latin cōdex); in late-Soviet medical usage (introduced by A. R. Dovzhenko in the 1980s), 'to undergo psychological/aversion therapy against alcoholism'.

history.meaning: to get coded (treated against alcohol addiction)

закон.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic законъ / Old Church Slavonic законъ ('custom, law, faith'), from Proto-Slavic *zakonъ, formed from *za- + *konъ ('beginning, boundary, established order'; compare искони 'from the beginning').

законный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic законьныи, formed with suffix -ный from закон ('law, custom'), derived from за- + кон ('beginning, boundary, established order', Proto-Slavic *zakonъ).

закончить.etymology: Formed from the perfective prefix за- + кончить ('to finish, end'), derived from конец ('end', from Proto-Slavic *konьcь).

закончиться.etymology: Reflexive and intransitive form of закончить ('to finish') formed with the enclitic -ся.

history.meaning: to end, come to an end

закопать.etymology: Formed from the prefix за- ('in, covered over') + копать ('to dig', inherited from Old East Slavic копати, from Proto-Slavic *kopati).

history.meaning: to bury, fill in a hole

закричать.etymology: Formed from the inchoative prefix за- ('begin to, burst out') + кричать ('to shout, cry out', inherited from Proto-Slavic *kričati).

закрутить.etymology: Formed from the prefix за- ('tightly; begin to') + крутить ('to twist, turn, whirl', inherited from Old East Slavic крутити, Proto-Slavic *krǫtiti).

history.meaning: to screw tight, twist, curl; (colloquial) to start a whirlwind romance

закрывать.etymology: Imperfective verb paired with закрыть ('to close, shut, cover over'), formed with prefix за- + крывать (iterative of крыть 'to cover', from Proto-Slavic *kryti).

закрываться.etymology: Reflexive and middle/intransitive verb formed from закрывать ('to close, shut', built on за- + крыть 'to cover', Proto-Slavic *kryti) + -ся.

history.meaning: to close -> to close (intransitive), shut down

закрытый.etymology: Adjectival passive participle of закрыть ('to close, shut, cover'), formed from the prefix за- and крыть ('to cover, roof', inherited from Old East Slavic крыти, Proto-Slavic *kryti).

закрыть.etymology: Formed by prefixing за- ('shut, over') to крыть ('to cover', from Old East Slavic крыти, Proto-Slavic *kryti). Literally 'to cover over', which in Russian became the everyday verb 'to close, shut' (a door, window, book, or shop).

закрыться.etymology: Reflexive form of закрыть ('to cover, close, shut'), formed from prefix за- + крыть ('to cover', inherited from Old East Slavic крыти, Proto-Slavic *kryti) + -ся.

закупать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of закупить, formed from prefix за- ('in advance, in bulk') + купать (imperfective stem of купить 'to buy', inherited from Proto-Slavic *kupiti, an early borrowing from Gothic kaupōn 'to trade', from Latin caupō).

history.meaning: to buy in bulk, stock up

закупить.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('in advance, in bulk') + купить ('to buy'), inherited from Old East Slavic купити, from Proto-Slavic *kupiti (borrowed from Gothic kaupōn 'to trade', ultimately from Latin caupō 'merchant, innkeeper').

закупка.etymology: Deverbal noun derived from закупить / закупать ('to buy in bulk, procure', from за- + купить, Proto-Slavic *kupiti) + the noun suffix -ка.

закусить.etymology: Formed from за- + кусить ('to bite', from Old East Slavic кусити, Proto-Slavic *kǫsiti): literally 'to bite into', and specifically in Russian dining culture 'to follow a drink with a bite of food, or have a quick snack'.

history.meaning: to bite down on; to have a bite to eat (especially after a drink)

rootFamily.gloss: to have a snack / chase a drink with food (imperfective)

закуска.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Russian with the suffix -ка from закусить ('to take a bite of food, especially after a drink', from за- + кусить 'to bite', Proto-Slavic *kǫsiti).

history.meaning: to take a bite -> appetizer, cold starter, snack

rootFamily.gloss: to have a bite to eat

закуска.notes: In Russian menus, холодные закуски and горячие закуски are the cold and hot starter courses.

закусывать.etymology: Imperfective of закусить ('to bite into; to eat a snack after a drink of alcohol'), formed from prefix за- ('into, after') + кусывать (iterative of кусать 'to bite', from Proto-Slavic *kǫsati).

history.meaning: to have a bite; to chase a drink with food

зал.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (originally feminine зала, later masculine зал) via German Saal and French salle ('large hall, reception room'), from Frankish *sal / Old High German sal ('hall, single-room dwelling').

заладить.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('begin and persist in') + ладить ('to tune, arrange, repeat in a set rhythm'), denominative from лад ('harmony, order, manner', from Proto-Slavic *ladъ).

history.meaning: to keep on saying, harp on

залезать.etymology: Imperfective of залезть ('to climb onto or into'), formed from за- ('onto, into') + лезать (the iterative stem of лезть 'to climb, crawl', inherited from Proto-Slavic *lězti).

history.meaning: to climb up onto, get inside

залезть.etymology: Formed from prefix за- ('into, onto') + лезть ('to climb, crawl'), inherited from Old East Slavic лѣзти, from Proto-Slavic *lězti ('to crawl, climb').
