изумительный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -тельный from изумить ('to amaze, astonish'), literally 'to take someone out of their mind with wonder' (built on prefix из- 'out of' + ум 'mind, wit', from Proto-Slavic *umъ).

history.meaning: out of + mind → to astonish → amazing, exquisite, wonderful

изучать.etymology: Imperfective of изучить ('to study thoroughly, master'), formed from the prefix из- ('thoroughly, out') + учить ('to learn, teach', from Proto-Slavic *učiti).

изучить.etymology: Formed from prefix из- ('thoroughly, to the end') + учить ('to teach, learn'), inherited from Old East Slavic учити, from Proto-Slavic *učiti (from PIE *h₁ewk- 'to become accustomed').

изысканный.etymology: Past passive participle of изыскать ('to seek out, select carefully'), from Old Church Slavonic изискати (prefix из- + искати 'to seek', Proto-Slavic *jьskati); the sense 'refined, exquisite' calques French recherché and Latin exquīsītus ('sought out').

изюм.etymology: Borrowed from a Turkic language (compare Tatar йөзем, Kipchak and Crimean Tatar üzüm, Turkish üzüm 'grapes, raisins'), from Proto-Turkic *üŕüm ('grape').

икать.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьkati ('to hiccup, sob'), an onomatopoeic formation imitating the spasmodic sound of a hiccup (ик).

икра.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic икра ('fish roe, caviar; calf of the leg'), from Proto-Slavic *jьkra ('roe, spawn; rounded mass'), cognate with Lithuanian ikrai ('fish roe, spawn').

икринка.etymology: Singulative and diminutive noun formed with the compound suffix -ин-ка from икра ('roe, spawn, caviar', inherited from Old East Slavic икра, from Proto-Slavic *jьkra).

history.meaning: single fish egg, grain of caviar

или.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic или ('or'), from Proto-Slavic *ili, compounded from the connective conjunction *i ('and, even') + the interrogative/alternative particle *li ('whether, or').

иллюзия.etymology: Borrowed via German Illusion or French illusion (and Polish iluzja) from Latin illūsiō ('mockery, deceit, illusion'), from illūdere ('to play with, mock, deceive', from in- + lūdere 'to play').

иллюстрировать.etymology: Borrowed from German illustrieren ('to illustrate'), from Latin illustrare ('to light up, illuminate, elucidate'), derived from illustris ('bright, clear', from in- + lustrare).

ильич.etymology: Russian masculine patronymic meaning 'son of Ilya', formed with the inherited Slavic patronymic suffix -ич (Proto-Slavic *-itjь) from the given name Илья, which entered Old East Slavic via Byzantine Greek Ἠλίας (Ēlías) from Hebrew Ēliyyāhū ('My God is Yahweh').

имбирный.etymology: Relational adjective derived from имбирь ('ginger') + the adjective suffix -ный.

имбирь.etymology: Borrowed (attested in 16th-century Russian as инбирь, имберь) via German Ingwer / Middle High German ingewer and Polish imbir from Medieval Latin zingiber, from Ancient Greek ζιγγίβερις, ultimately from Middle Indic / Sanskrit śṛṅgavera (of Dravidian origin).

именинник.etymology: Derived from именины ('name day, saint's day; later also birthday', derived from имя, gen. имени 'name', Proto-Slavic *jьmę, PIE *h₁nómn̥) + the person suffix -ник.

именинница.etymology: Formed in Russian with the feminine suffix -ница (corresponding to masculine именинник) from именины ('name day, feast day of one's patron saint; in modern everyday speech, birthday'), a plural derivative of имя (stem имен-, 'name', Proto-Slavic *jьmę).
именинница.notes: Historically celebrated a person's saint's name day (день ангела / именины), but in modern secular Russian именинник and именинница are the everyday words for the person celebrating their birthday.

именно.etymology: Adverbialized short neuter of именной ('by name, nominal, specific'), derived from имя (stem имен-, 'name', inherited from Old East Slavic имя, from Proto-Slavic *jьmę), literally 'by name, specifically'.

иметь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic имѣти (and Old Church Slavonic имѣти), from Proto-Slavic *iměti ('to have, hold'), a stative verb built on the same Indo-European root as *jęti ('to take', compare Latin emō 'to take, buy'). Unlike Western European languages, Russian generally expresses everyday possession with у меня есть rather than иметь, reserving иметь for abstract and formal collocations.
иметь.notes: Used chiefly in set phrases such as **иметь право** ('to have the right'), **иметь в виду** ('to mean, have in mind'), and **иметь значение** ('to matter').

иметься.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive verb formed in Russian from иметь ('to have, possess', from Old East Slavic имѣти, Proto-Slavic *jьměti) + -ся: 'to be had, be available, exist'.

history.meaning: to have -> to be available, exist, be present

имидж.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English image ('public persona, look, reputation'), from Old French image, from Latin imāgō ('likeness, representation').

император.etymology: Borrowed (officially adopted as the title of Peter the Great in 1721) from Latin imperātor ('commander-in-chief, emperor'), agent noun from imperāre ('to command, rule', from in- + parāre 'to order, prepare').

импровизация.etymology: Borrowed via French improvisation or German Improvisation from Italian improvvisazione, from improvvisare ('to improvise'), from Latin imprōvīsus ('unforeseen, unexpected', from in- 'not' + prōvīsus 'foreseen').

импровизированный.etymology: Participial adjective from импровизировать ('to improvise'), ultimately from Italian improvvisare and Latin imprōvīsus ('unforeseen, impromptu').

history.meaning: to compose or perform on the spur of the moment

импровизировать.etymology: Borrowed via German improvisieren and French improviser from Italian improvvisare ('to compose or perform extempore'), from improvviso ('unforeseen, sudden'), from Latin imprōvīsus.

имущество.etymology: Derived with the suffix -ство from имущий ('having, possessing'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic имѫщии, present active participle of имѣти ('to have', from Proto-Slavic *jьměti).

имя.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic имя (genitive имене; Old Church Slavonic имѧ), from Proto-Slavic *jьmę ('name'), continuing the ancient Proto-Indo-European neuter n-stem *h₁nómn̥ ('name'), cognate with English name, Latin nōmen, Ancient Greek ὄνομα, and Sanskrit nāman.
имя.notes: One of the ten Russian neuter nouns in **-мя** that keep their ancient *-en-* stem in oblique cases: **имени, именем, имена**.

иначе.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic инако / иначе ('otherwise, in another way'), comparative/adverbial formation from инъ / иной ('other, another'), from Proto-Slavic *inъ ('one, other', cognate with Latin ūnus and English one).
иначе.notes: Both stress patterns are accepted in standard Russian: **иначе** and **иначе** (with **так или иначе** 'one way or another' always stressed on the middle syllable).

инвалид.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (originally referring to disabled war veterans, on the model of Paris's Hôtel des Invalides) from French invalide ('infirm, disabled soldier'), from Latin invalidus ('weak, infirm, powerless'), formed from in- ('not') + validus ('strong, healthy', from valēre 'to be strong').

history.meaning: disabled veteran → person with a disability

инвестировать.etymology: Borrowed via German investieren (and English invest) from Medieval Latin investīre ('to clothe in the insignia of office; later to employ capital'), from Latin in- + vestīre ('to clothe', from vestis 'garment').

history.meaning: to clothe in office; to invest

инвестиция.etymology: Borrowed via German Investition from Neo-Latin investītiō ('investment of capital; originally investiture'), derived from Medieval Latin investīre ('to clothe, invest').

инвестор.etymology: Borrowed from English investor (or via German Investor), agent noun from invest, ultimately from Medieval Latin investīre ('to clothe; to put capital into').

ингредиент.etymology: Borrowed via German Ingrediens / Ingredienz or French ingrédient from Latin ingrediēns, ingredientis ('that which enters into a mixture'), present active participle of ingredī ('to go into, enter', from in- + gradī 'to step').

индейка.etymology: Derived from earlier индейская курица ('Indian hen', via Polish indyk / indyjka), from Medieval Latin gallīna Indica ('Indian hen', from Latin Indicus 'of India'), because the American bird was originally thought to come from the Indies.

индивидуальный.etymology: Borrowed via French individuel and German individuell from Medieval Latin individuālis ('indivisible, individual'), from Latin individuus ('indivisible', from in- 'not' + dividuus 'divisible', calquing Ancient Greek ἄτομος).

индия.etymology: Borrowed via Byzantine Greek Ἰνδία and Latin India from Ancient Greek Ἰνδός ('the Indus River; an Indian'), borrowed via Old Persian Hinduš from Sanskrit सिन्धु (síndhu 'river, the Indus').

индюк.etymology: Borrowed via Polish indyk (adapted with the East Slavic suffix -юк), from Medieval Latin (gallus) Indicus ('Indian rooster'), named when the newly discovered Americas were identified with the Indies.

инженер.etymology: Borrowed via German Ingenieur and French ingénieur from Old French engigneor ('designer of war engines, builder'), from Medieval Latin ingeniātor, from Latin ingenium ('innate talent, clever device').

инициал.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth–nineteenth century via German Initial / Initiale and French initiale from Late Latin initiālis ('pertaining to the beginning', as in littera initiālis 'first letter'), derived from Classical Latin initium ('entrance, beginning'), from inīre ('to go into, enter upon', in- + īre 'to go').

history.meaning: initial letter of a word or name

инициал.notes: Most often encountered in the plural инициалы — in Russian official style, the two capital letters of a person's given name and patronymic accompanying the surname, or two initials carved on a personal keepsake.

инициатива.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century via French initiative from Medieval Latin initiātīva, derived from Latin initiāre ('to begin, originate', from initium 'beginning, entrance').

иногда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic иногда ('at another time, sometimes'), from Proto-Slavic *jьnogda, compounded from the pronominal stem *inъ ('other, another', the same root preserved in иной 'other' and один 'one') + the temporal adverbial suffix *-gda (compare когда 'when', всегда 'always').

иностранец.etymology: Derived from иностранный ('foreign, of another country', from иной 'other' + страна 'country, land') + the person suffix -ец.

иностранный.etymology: Compound adjective formed from иной ('other, another', from Proto-Slavic *jьnъ) + страна ('country, land', Church Slavonic form corresponding to East Slavic сторона, Proto-Slavic *storna) + suffix -ный.

инспектировать.etymology: Borrowed via German inspizieren / inspektieren from Latin inspectāre ('to look into, examine, inspect'), frequentative of inspicere (from in- 'into' + specere 'to look').

инспектор.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Inspektor or Polish inspektor from Latin inspector ('observer, overseer, examiner'), from inspicere ('to look into, examine').

инспекция.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish inspekcja or German Inspektion from Latin inspectio ('looking into, examination, oversight'), derived from inspicere ('to look into, examine').

институт.etymology: Borrowed via German Institut and French institut from Latin institūtum ('established custom, arrangement, educational or legal institution'), from instituere ('to set up, establish, instruct').

инструкция.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish instrukcja or German Instruktion from Late Latin instructio ('arrangement, teaching, direction'), derived from Latin instruere ('to build, prepare, furnish, instruct').

инструмент.etymology: Borrowed via German Instrument or Polish instrument from Latin instrumentum ('tool, implement, equipment'), derived from instruere ('to build, equip, furnish').

инсульт.etymology: Borrowed from medical Latin insultus ('attack, fit, apoplectic stroke'), verbal noun from insultāre / insilīre ('to leap upon, attack', from in- 'upon' + salīre 'to leap').

history.meaning: leaping upon; medical attack or stroke

интеллигентный.etymology: Derived in 19th-century Russian from интеллигент / интеллигенция ('cultured, educated person/class'), borrowed via German intelligent / Intelligenz and Polish inteligencja from Latin intellegēns ('understanding, discerning', from intellegere).

интервью.etymology: Borrowed from English interview, from Early Modern French entrevue ('face-to-face meeting'), verbal noun from s'entrevoir ('to see each other', from entre- 'between, mutually' + voir 'to see', Latin vidēre).

интерес.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Interesse or Polish interes from Medieval Latin interesse ('compensation, concern, importance'), the substantivized infinitive of Latin interesse ('to be between, make a difference, concern').

интересно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate formed from интересный ('interesting'), built on интерес ('interest, curiosity, importance'), borrowed in the Petrine era via German Interesse or French intérêt from Medieval Latin interesse ('what matters, is of importance', from Latin inter- + esse 'to be between, make a difference').
интересно.notes: At the start of a question, **Интересно, ...** idiomatically means 'I wonder...' (*Интересно, где ключ?* 'I wonder where the key is?').

интересный.etymology: Formed with the Russian adjectival suffix -ный from интерес ('interest'), borrowed in the Petrine era via German Interesse (or French intérêt) from Medieval Latin interesse ('to be of importance, make a difference; compensation').

history.meaning: to be between, make a difference, matter

интересовать.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (modeled on French intéresser and German interessieren) from интерес ('interest') + the verbal suffix -овать, ultimately from Latin interesse ('to be between, make a difference, concern, be of importance').

history.meaning: to concern, be of importance → to interest

интересоваться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed in Russian from интересовать ('to interest', derived from интерес 'interest', modeled on French s'intéresser and German sich interessieren) + -ся.

history.meaning: to interest -> to be interested in, inquire about

интернет.etymology: Borrowed in the 1990s from English Internet, shortened from internetwork ('interconnected network of computer networks'), formed from the Latin prefix inter- ('between, among') + English network.

интерьер.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French intérieur ('inside, interior space or design'), from Latin interior ('inner, nearer', comparative of intra 'within').

интим.etymology: Colloquial Russian back-formation (clipping) from интимный ('intimate', as in интимные отношения 'intimate relations' or интимная обстановка 'intimate setting'), ultimately from Latin intimus ('inmost').

интимный.etymology: Borrowed via French intime and German intim from Latin intimus ('innermost, deepest, closest'), superlative adjective formed from the root of in / intrā ('within').

интрига.etymology: Borrowed via French intrigue (and German Intrige) from Italian intrigo ('tangle, plot, scheme'), deverbal from intrigare ('to entangle'), from Latin intrīcāre ('to entangle, perplex', from in- + trīcae 'hindrances, tricks').

интрижка.etymology: Diminutive formed in Russian with suffix -ка (and velar palatalization г > ж) from интрига ('intrigue; secret love affair', from French intrigue).

инфаркт.etymology: Borrowed as a medical term via German Infarkt from New Latin infarctus ('blockage of blood supply to an organ causing tissue death'), from Latin infarcīre ('to stuff into, plug, obstruct').

cognates.meaning: tissue death from blocked blood supply

инфекция.etymology: Borrowed via German Infektion or French infection from Late/Medieval Latin infectiō ('staining, dyeing; contagion'), from inficere ('to dip in, stain, taint, corrupt', from in- + facere 'to make, put').

инфицировать.etymology: Borrowed via German infizieren from Latin inficere ('to dip into, stain, taint, infect', from in- 'in' + facere 'to make, put').

информатор.etymology: Borrowed via German Informator (or Polish informator) from Latin īnfōrmātor ('shaper, instructor'), agent noun from īnfōrmāre ('to give form to, instruct, inform', from in- + fōrma 'form').

информация.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish informacja or German Information from Latin īnfōrmātiō ('outline, concept, instruction, explanation'), derived from īnfōrmāre ('to shape, fashion, instruct, educate', from in- 'into' + fōrma 'form, shape').

history.meaning: to give form to, instruct → concept, instruction

информированный.etymology: Participial adjective from информировать ('to inform'), borrowed via German informieren and Polish informować from French informer and Latin īnfōrmāre ('to shape, instruct, inform').

инцидент.etymology: Borrowed via French incident and German Inzident from Medieval Latin incidēns (gen. incidentis, 'an occurrence, event'), substantivized present participle of Latin incidere ('to fall upon, happen', from in- + cadere 'to fall').

ирландия.etymology: Borrowed via New Latin / Western European Irlandia from English Ireland, compound of Old Irish Ériu ('Ireland', from Proto-Celtic *Φīwerjū 'fertile land') + Germanic land ('land').

ироничный.etymology: Derived from ирония ('irony', from Ancient Greek εἰρωνεία) + the adjective suffix -ичный.

ирония.etymology: Borrowed via Latin īrōnīa (and French ironie / German Ironie) from Ancient Greek εἰρωνεία ('dissimulation, feigned ignorance, Socratic irony'), from εἴρων ('dissembler, one who says less than he thinks').

искатель.etymology: Agent noun formed with the suffix -тель from искать ('to seek, look for, search'), inherited from Old East Slavic искати and Proto-Slavic *jьskati (cognate with English ask and Lithuanian ieškoti 'to seek').

искать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic искати (present ищу, ищеши), from Proto-Slavic *jьskati ('to look for, seek'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *h₂eys-sk̂é- ('to seek, search for'), directly cognate with English ask, German heischen, Lithuanian ieškóti ('to search'), and Sanskrit iccháti ('seeks, wishes').
искать.notes: Conjugates with **щ** throughout the present tense: **я ищу, ты ищешь, они ищут**.

исключительный.etymology: Derived from исключить ('to exclude, make an exception') + the adjective suffix -тельный, with the sense 'exceptional, extraordinary' calquing French exceptionnel.

исключить.etymology: Formed from prefix ис- (из- 'out of') + ключить (from ключ 'key, bolt', Proto-Slavic *ključь), coined as the antonym of включить ('to include, shut in') and calquing Latin exclūdere ('to shut out, exclude').

искра.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic искра, from Proto-Slavic *jьskra ('spark, flash'), built on a root meaning 'to gleam, flash' (related to *ěsnъ 'clear, bright').

искренне.etymology: Adverb formed from искренний ('sincere, heartfelt'), which goes back to Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic искрьнии ('near, neighboring, close, intimate'), derived from the archaic adverb/preposition искрь ('near, close by'). The deeper origin of *jьz-krь connects to *krai / *krь ('edge, side', compare край): originally 'standing right beside one, close at hand', whence 'intimate, open-hearted, sincere'.

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

искренний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic искрьнии / Old Church Slavonic искрьнь (originally 'near, neighboring, close, intimate', hence 'heartfelt, sincere'), derived from the archaic adverb/preposition искрь ('near, close by', from из + крь / корень 'root, edge').

искренность.etymology: Formed in Russian with the abstract noun suffix -ость from искренний ('sincere, candid'), which goes back to Old Church Slavonic искрьнь ('near, neighbourly, intimate, genuine', derived from the archaic Slavic adverb искрь 'close by, near').

искусственный.etymology: Derived from искусство ('art, skill, craftsmanship', from Old Church Slavonic искусьство 'experience, trial, skill', from искусъ 'test, trial', Proto-Slavic *jьzkusъ, from Gothic kausjan 'to test, taste') + suffix -енный.

искусство.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic искоусьство ('trial, test, experience, mastery, skill'), formed with the suffix -ство from искоусъ ('trial, test, probation') and искоусити ('to test, try', from Proto-Slavic *jьzkusiti; *kusiti is an early borrowing from Gothic kausjan 'to taste, test, try', cognate with English choose). From 'tested mastery and skill', in the 18th century искусство acquired the aesthetic sense 'fine art' (on the model of German Kunst and French art).

испания.etymology: Borrowed via Byzantine Greek Ἱσπανία and Latin Hispānia ('the Iberian Peninsula, Spain'), usually traced to Phoenician/Punic ʾī-šāpān ('coast/island of hyraxes') or a pre-Roman Iberian toponym.

испанский.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ский from Испания ('Spain', from Latin Hispānia).
испанский.notes: The colloquial idiom испанский стыд ('Spanish shame') means acute secondhand embarrassment on someone else's behalf (calqued from Spanish vergüenza ajena).

испачкать.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix ис- (из- 'thoroughly') + пачкать ('to soil, daub, smear', an expressive East Slavic verb related to dialectal пакать and Polish paciać 'to daub in mud').

испачкаться.etymology: Reflexive form of испачкать ('to soil, stain'), formed from prefix ис- + пачкать ('to dirty, smear') + -ся.

испечь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic испечи, formed from the perfective prefix ис- / из- + печь ('to bake, roast', from Proto-Slavic *peťi, from Proto-Indo-European *pekʷ- 'to cook').

испечься.etymology: Intransitive/middle reflexive form of испечь ('to bake through to completion'), built from prefix из-/ис- ('out, thoroughly') + печь ('to bake', Proto-Slavic *pekti, PIE *pekw- 'to cook, ripen') + reflexive -ся. Adding -ся shifts the verb from what the baker does ('to bake a tart') to what the pastry itself undergoes ('to finish baking in the oven'). It is cognate with English cook and Sanskrit pacati.

cognates.meaning: to prepare food by heat (via Latin coquere from *pekw-)

испоганить.etymology: Formed from prefix ис- (из- 'thoroughly') + поганить ('to defile, pollute'), from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic поганыи ('pagan, ritually unclean, foul', borrowed via Greek or Romance from Latin pāgānus 'country-dweller; pagan').

исполнение.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic испълнениѥ ('filling up, fulfillment'), verbal noun from испълнити ('to fill completely, fulfill', from prefix из- + пълнити, from пълнъ 'full', Proto-Slavic *pьlnъ).

исполнитель.etymology: Derived from исполнить ('to fulfill, execute, perform', from Old Church Slavonic испълнити 'to fill, fulfill', from пълнъ 'full', Proto-Slavic *pьlnъ) + the agent suffix -тель.

исполнить.etymology: Adopted with Old Church Slavonic prefix из- / ис- (from испълнити 'to fill up, accomplish, fulfil'), formed from ис- ('out, completely') + полнить ('to fill', from полный 'full', Proto-Slavic *pъlnъ). Literally 'to fill to the brim, bring to completion'.

исполнять.etymology: Imperfective of исполнить ('to fulfill, carry out, perform'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic испълняти (prefix из- + пълняти 'to fill', from пълнъ 'full', Proto-Slavic *pьlnъ).

исполняться.etymology: Reflexive form of исполнять ('to fill, fulfill'), from Old Church Slavonic испълняти сѧ ('to be filled, be completed, come true', from пълнъ 'full', Proto-Slavic *pьlnъ).

history.meaning: to come true, be fulfilled; to turn (an age)

использовать.etymology: Biaspectual verb formed from the prefix из- / ис- ('out') + пользовать ('to benefit, use, treat'), derived from польза ('use, benefit, advantage'), which goes back to Old East Slavic польга / польза ('ease, relief, benefit'), from Proto-Slavic *polьga (built on the root *lьg- 'light, easy', as in лёгкий 'light, easy' and льгота 'privilege, relief').

испортить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix из- / ис- ('out, completely') and портить ('to spoil, ruin, damage'). The base verb портить (attested in Old Russian портити) is derived by Vasmer from портъ ('piece of cut cloth, coarse garment', preserved in портной 'tailor'), originally meaning 'to cut or tear cloth to shreds, mar, ruin'.

history.meaning: cut piece of cloth → to cut up, mar, spoil

испортиться.etymology: Reflexive-intransitive verb formed from испортить ('to spoil, ruin, damage', from completive ис- + портить 'to spoil, mar') + -ся.

history.meaning: to ruin, spoil -> to go bad, spoil, deteriorate

испорченный.etymology: Past passive participle of испортить ('to spoil, ruin, damage'), formed from prefix ис- (из-) + портить ('to spoil, damage', from Old East Slavic пъртити, originally 'to cut or slash cloth', from пъртъ 'piece of cloth').

исправить.etymology: Borrowed from or modeled on Old Church Slavonic исправити ('to straighten out, set right, correct'), formed from из- / ис- ('out') + правити ('to make straight, direct', from правъ / правый 'straight, right', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

исправиться.etymology: Reflexive form of исправить ('to set straight, correct'), borrowed from or modeled on Old Church Slavonic исправити (prefix из- + правити 'to make straight, direct', from правый 'straight, right', Proto-Slavic *praviti) + -ся.

исправление.etymology: Verbal noun in -ение from исправить ('to straighten out, correct, reform'), built from ис- ('out') + править ('to direct, make straight', derived from правый 'straight, right', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

исправлять.etymology: Imperfective of исправить ('to fix, correct, straighten out'), formed from ис- ('out') + правлять / править ('to make straight, set right', from правый 'right, straight', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

испуг.etymology: Deverbal noun from испугать ('to frighten, startle'), formed from prefix ис- (из-) + пугать ('to scare, startle', an East Slavic expressive verb related to dialectal пужать).

испуганный.etymology: Past passive participle of испугать ('to frighten, startle'), formed from the prefix ис- + пугать ('to scare, frighten').

испугать.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix ис- (из-) + пугать ('to scare, frighten, startle', an East Slavic verb related to dialectal пужать).

испугаться.etymology: Reflexive form of испугать ('to frighten, startle') with the enclitic -ся, formed from the prefix ис- + пугать ('to scare, frighten').

испытание.etymology: Verbal noun from испытать ('to test, try out, experience'), from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic испытати (prefix из- 'out, thoroughly' + пытати 'to ask, inquire, test', Proto-Slavic *pytati) + -ние.

испытательный.etymology: Derived from испытать ('to test, examine, try out', from из- + пытать, Proto-Slavic *pytati) + the adjective suffix -тельный.

испытать.etymology: Adopted with Old Church Slavonic prefix из- / ис- (from испытати 'to search out, test thoroughly, experience'), built on ис- ('out, thoroughly') + пытать ('to inquire, test, try', from Proto-Slavic *pytati).

history.meaning: to test, try out; to experience

испытывать.etymology: Imperfective of испытать ('to test, try out, experience'), inherited from Old East Slavic испытати / Old Church Slavonic испытати, formed from ис- ('out, thoroughly') + пытать ('to ask, inquire, test', from Proto-Slavic *pytati).

исследование.etymology: Verbal noun from исследовать ('to investigate, examine, research'), formed from prefix ис- (из- 'out, thoroughly') + следовать ('to follow a track', from след 'footprint, track', Proto-Slavic *slědъ), calquing Latin investīgātiō ('tracking out').

исследовать.etymology: Formed from the Church Slavonic prefix ис- (из- 'out, thoroughly') + следовать ('to follow a track, trace', derived from след 'track, footprint', Proto-Slavic *slědъ), literally 'to track out thoroughly, investigate'.

истерика.etymology: Borrowed via medical Latin hystericus, German Hysterik, and French hystérique from Ancient Greek ὑστερικός ('suffering in the womb, hysterical'), from ὑστέρα ('womb, uterus', from PIE *údteros), reflecting the ancient medical belief that hysteria was caused by disturbances of the uterus.

истерить.etymology: Colloquial Russian denominative verb derived from истерика ('hysterics, tantrum', ultimately from Ancient Greek ὑστερικός).

history.meaning: to throw a fit, get hysterical

истеричка.etymology: Colloquial feminine person noun derived from истерик / истерика ('hysterical person / hysterics', from Ancient Greek ὑστερικός) + suffix -ка (with к > ч).

истина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic истина ('truth, reality, authenticity'), derived from истый (Old East Slavic истъ 'true, real, exact, same', from Proto-Slavic *jьstъ) + the abstract noun suffix -ина.

историк.etymology: Borrowed via Polish historyk or German Historiker from Latin historicus and Ancient Greek ἱστορικός (historikós, 'historical; scholar of history'), from ἱστορία (historía, 'inquiry, narrative, history').

исторический.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -еский from история ('history, story') or borrowed via Latin historicus from Ancient Greek ἱστορικός (historikós, 'historical').

история.etymology: Borrowed via Polish historia or directly from Byzantine/Ancient Greek ἱστορία (historía, 'inquiry, knowledge obtained by investigation, narrative, history'), from ἵστωρ (hístōr, 'wise man, witness, knower', from PIE *weyd- 'to see, know').

источник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic источьникъ / Old Church Slavonic источьникъ ('water spring, fountainhead, source'), formed with -ник from исток ('outflow, source of a river', from из- 'out' + ток 'flow', Proto-Slavic *jьztokъ < *teťi 'to flow').

исходный.etymology: Derived from исход ('going out, departure, origin, outcome', from Old Church Slavonic исходъ, calquing Ancient Greek ἔξοδος, from prefix из- + ходъ 'going, motion', Proto-Slavic *xodъ) + adjective suffix -ный.

исчезать.etymology: Imperfective of исчезнуть ('to disappear, vanish'), borrowed/adapted from Old Church Slavonic исчезати / исчезнѫти (Proto-Slavic *jьzčeznǫti, formed from *jьz- 'out, away' + *čeznǫti 'to fade, dwindle, vanish').

исчезнуть.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic изчезнути ('to vanish, disappear'), from Proto-Slavic *jьzčeznǫti, formed from *jьz- ('out, away') + *čeznǫti ('to fade away, dwindle, vanish').

исчерпать.etymology: Borrowed/adapted from Old Church Slavonic исчрьпати ('to ladle out to the bottom, drain completely'), formed from completive ис- ('out completely') + черпать ('to scoop, ladle, draw water', inherited from Proto-Slavic *čьrpati).

history.meaning: to exhaust, use up, settle completely (инцидент исчерпан)

итак.etymology: Univerbation of the conjunction и ('and') + the adverb так ('so, thus', from Proto-Slavic *tako), literally 'and so, thus'.

италия.etymology: Borrowed via Byzantine Greek Ἰταλία and Latin Ītalia ('Italy'), from Oscan Víteliú ('land of young cattle/calves', cognate with Latin vitulus 'calf').

итальянский.etymology: Adjective formed with suffix -ский from Италия ('Italy') / итальянец ('Italian'), from Italian italiano, derived from Latin Italia ('Italy').

итог.etymology: Univerbation (attested from the 17th–18th centuries in chancery arithmetic) of the phrase и того ('and of that [in total]', written at the bottom of a column of figures; compare modern итого 'in total'), combining и ('and') + того (genitive singular of то 'that').

йога.etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit योग (yóga 'yoking, union, spiritual and physical discipline'), from the verbal root युज् (yuj 'to yoke, join, concentrate', from PIE *yewg-, cognate with Russian иго 'yoke').

йогурт.etymology: Borrowed via Western European languages (French yoghourt / yaourt, German Joghurt, English yogurt) from Turkish yoğurt ('curdled milk, yogurt'), related to yoğun ('thick, dense') and yoğurmak ('to knead, thicken').

к.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic къ ('to, toward'), from Proto-Slavic *kъ(n), which Vasmer compares with Indo-Iranian particles such as Sanskrit kám ('toward, for the benefit of', used with the dative). Its original final nasal survives before third-person pronouns (к нему, к ней).
к.notes: Always governs the dative case: подойти к окну ('walk up to the window'), к утру ('by morning'); becomes ко before clusters (ко мне).

кабак.etymology: Attested in Russian since the 16th century ('crown tavern'); traced by Vasmer either to Low German kabacke ('ramshackle hut, pothouse') or to Turkic qabaq ('hollow gourd, vessel; wayside inn, tavern'), possibly through a convergence of both.

кабачок.etymology: Diminutive in -ок of regional/older кабак ('pumpkin, squash'), borrowed from Turkic (compare Tatar, Crimean Tatar, and Kipchak qabaq, Turkish kabak 'pumpkin, gourd, squash').

кабель.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from Dutch kabel or Low German kabel ('heavy ship's hawser; later insulated electrical cable'), from Old French cable (Norman/Picard), from Late Latin capulum ('halter, lasso, rope', from capere 'to hold, seize').

кабинет.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via German Kabinett and French cabinet ('small private room, study, closet for valuables'), diminutive of cabane / cabine ('small chamber, cabin').

кабинка.etymology: Diminutive formed with suffix -ка from кабина ('cabin, booth, compartment'), borrowed via French cabine and German Kabine from English cabin (from Old French cabane 'hut, small room').

каблук.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th–17th centuries from Turkic kabluk / kapluk (compare Turkish kaplık 'cover, heel-piece', derived from kaplamak 'to cover, encase').

кавалер.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish kawaler, German Kavalier, and French cavalier from Italian cavaliere ('horseman, knight, courtly gentleman escorting a lady'), from Late Latin caballārius (derived from caballus 'horse').

history.meaning: knight of an order; dancing partner, lady's escort, suitor

кадр.etymology: Borrowed from French cadre ('square picture frame; core framework of officers/personnel; single frame on a filmstrip'), from Italian quadro and Latin quadrum ('square', from quattuor 'four').

history.meaning: frame, border; staff framework; film frame
film shot/frame; staff member (plural кадры 'personnel'); (colloquial) quite a character

каждый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic каждыи / кожьдыи (Old Church Slavonic къжьдо, 'each, every'), from Proto-Slavic *kъžьdo, compounded from the interrogative pronoun *kъ- ('who, which') + the emphatic particle *-žьdo.

казаться.etymology: Reflexive form of казать ('to show', from Old East Slavic казати, Proto-Slavic *kazati 'to point out, show'): literally 'to show oneself as', hence 'to seem, appear'.

казахстан.etymology: Compound toponym formed from казах ('Kazakh', from Turkic qazaq 'free man, independent steppe rider') + the Persian geographical suffix -стан (-stān 'land, country', from Indo-Iranian *stāna-, PIE *steh₂- 'to stand').

казино.etymology: Borrowed via French casino from Italian casino ('country villa, social club, gambling house'), diminutive of casa ('house'), from Latin casa ('cottage, house').

как.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic како ('how, as'), from Proto-Slavic *kako, a pronominal manner adverb built on the Indo-European interrogative-relative root *kʷo- (cognate with Latin quō, English how and who, and Lithuanian kaĩp).

как-нибудь.etymology: Indefinite adverb formed from как ('how', inherited from Old East Slavic како, Proto-Slavic *kako) + the indefinite particle -нибудь (contracted from Old East Slavic ни буди 'be it whatever').

как-то.etymology: Indefinite adverb formed by attaching the indefinite enclitic particle -то (historically the neuter demonstrative pronoun то 'that') to как ('how', from Proto-Slavic *kako).

history.meaning: somehow, sort of; once, one day

какао.etymology: Borrowed via German Kakao and French cacao from Spanish cacao, borrowed from Classical Nahuatl cacahuatl ('cocoa beans', ultimately from Mixe-Zoquean *kakawa).

каков.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic каковъ ('of what kind, what sort of'), from Proto-Slavic *kakovъ, formed from interrogative-relative *kakъ ('what kind') + suffix *-ovъ.

какой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic какыи / какои ('what kind of, which'), from Proto-Slavic *kakъ, an adjectival derivative of the interrogative stem *ka- / *kъ- (Proto-Indo-European *kʷo-; compare Latin quālis 'of what kind').

history.meaning: what kind of, what a, which

какой-нибудь.etymology: Indefinite pronoun formed from какой ('what kind of, which', from Proto-Slavic *kakъ) and the indefinite enclitic particle -нибудь, historically the univerbated phrase ни будь ('be it whatever it may', from ни + будь, the 2nd sg. imperative of быть 'to be').

какой-то.etymology: Formed in Russian by attaching the indefinite enclitic particle -то (originally the neuter demonstrative то 'that') to the interrogative determiner какой ('what kind of, which'), expressing 'some kind of, a certain (specific but unidentified)'.

калейдоскоп.etymology: Borrowed via French kaléidoscope from English kaleidoscope, coined in 1817 by Scottish physicist Sir David Brewster from Ancient Greek καλός (kalós, 'beautiful') + εἶδος (eîdos, 'form, shape') + -σκόπιον ('instrument for viewing').

кальян.etymology: Borrowed via Turkic (compare Turkish/Azerbaijani qəlyan) from Persian قلیان (qalyān, 'water pipe, hookah'), itself derived from Arabic غَلَيَان (ḡalayān, 'boiling, bubbling', from غَلَى ḡalā 'to boil, bubble').

камбала.etymology: Borrowed in northern Russian from a Finnic language (compare Finnish kampela and Karelian kambala 'flounder, flatfish').

каменеть.etymology: Inchoative verb formed with the suffix -еть ('to become...') on the historical consonant stem камен- of камень ('stone', inherited from Old East Slavic камы, genitive камене, from Proto-Slavic *kamy).

history.meaning: stone → to turn to stone, harden like stone

каменный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic каменьныи ('made of stone, masonry'), formed from the stem камен- of камень ('stone', from Proto-Slavic *kamy, genitive *kamene) + the adjectival suffix -ный.

камень.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic камы (accusative/oblique камень, which generalized to the nominative), from Proto-Slavic *kamy (genitive *kamene, 'stone'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *h₂éḱmō ('stone, sharp rock'), cognate with Lithuanian akmuõ ('stone'), Ancient Greek ἄκμων ('anvil'), Sanskrit áśman ('stone'), and English hammer (originally 'stone tool').

камера.etymology: Borrowed via German Kamera / Kammer and Polish kamera from Latin camera ('vaulted room, arched chamber'), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, 'anything with an arched cover, vaulted chamber'). In Russian, камера preserves both the older architectural sense ('vaulted cell, prison cell, tire inner tube') and the modern sense ('photographic or video camera', shortened from camera obscura 'dark chamber').

history.meaning: chamber, prison cell; camera (from camera obscura)

кампания.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from French campagne ('open country; military operations in the field during a season'), from Late Latin campania ('level country, plain'), derived from Latin campus ('field').

камушек.etymology: Colloquial variant of камешек, diminutive of камень ('stone'), inherited from Old East Slavic камы (gen. камене), from Proto-Slavic *kamy, from PIE *h₂éḱmō ('stone, sharp rock').

камчатский.etymology: Relational adjective derived from Камчатка ('the Kamchatka River and Peninsula', recorded in the 17th century and traditionally linked to the Cossack explorer Ivan Kamchaty, from камчатый 'damask-patterned', from камка 'damask silk') + suffix -ский.

канал.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Dutch kanaal, German Kanal, or French canal from Latin canālis ('water-pipe, groove, canal, channel', derived from canna 'reed').

канализация.etymology: Borrowed via French canalisation or German Kanalisation ('channeling, sewer system'), derived from canaliser ('to channel, lay pipes', from canal, Latin canālis).

кандидат.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Kandidat or Polish kandydat from Latin candidātus ('one clothed in white'), derived from candidus ('shining white'). In ancient Rome, office-seekers wore a bleached white toga (toga candida) in the Forum to symbolize purity and integrity.

history.meaning: gleaming white → office-seeker wearing a white toga

кандидатура.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via German Kandidatur or French candidature, formed with the Medieval Latin office/status suffix -ūra from Latin candidātus ('candidate, office-seeker dressed in a white toga').

капать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic капати ('to drip, fall in drops'), from Proto-Slavic *kapati, an expressive/imitative verb capturing the sound of falling liquid drops.

капелька.etymology: Double diminutive formed in Russian from капля ('drop', from Proto-Slavic *kapľa, derived from onomatopoeic *kapati 'to drip') + the diminutive suffix -елька (-к-а).

history.meaning: drop -> tiny drop, a tiny bit

morphemes.meaning: noun stem (from капля with fleeting е)

капелька.notes: Ни капельки ('not a single tiny drop') means 'not in the slightest / not at all'.

капитан.etymology: Borrowed via Polish kapitan from Late Latin capitaneus 'chief, commander', formed on Latin caput 'head'.

капля.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic капля ('drop of liquid'), from Proto-Slavic *kapja (with epenthetic l after labial p), derived from the expressive verb *kapati ('to drip, fall in drops', modern Russian капать).

каприз.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French caprice ('sudden whim, fancy'), from Italian capriccio (originally 'sudden shudder or fright, as if one's hair stood on end like a hedgehog', from capo 'head' + riccio 'hedgehog, curl', later associated with capra 'goat' and its frisky leaps).

капсула.etymology: Borrowed from Latin capsula 'small box or chest', a diminutive of capsa 'box, case for scrolls'. Through French and Italian cousins of capsa, it is a distant doublet of касса and кассета.

капуста.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic капуста, from Proto-Slavic *kapusta ('cabbage'), an early borrowing blending Medieval Latin compos(i)ta ('pickled greens, sauerkraut', compare Italian composta) with Latin caput / caputium ('head [of cabbage]').

капусточка.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed with suffix -очка from капуста ('cabbage', from Proto-Slavic *kapusta).

капучино.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from Italian cappuccino ('espresso with steamed milk foam'), literally 'Capuchin friar' (from cappuccio 'hood, cowl', because the reddish-brown color of espresso mixed with milk resembled the habit worn by friars of the Capuchin order, and via Viennese Kapuziner coffee).

history.meaning: hood → Capuchin friar → espresso with foamed milk

кара.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кара ('punishment, chastisement, strife'), deverbal from карать ('to punish, rebuke', from Proto-Slavic *kara / *karati).

карамельно-сливочный.etymology: Compound culinary adjective formed in Russian from карамельный ('caramel', from карамель, borrowed via French caramel from Spanish caramelo) + linking vowel -о- + сливочный ('creamy', derived from сливки 'cream', originally the top layer poured or skimmed off milk, from сливать 'to pour off').

карандаш.etymology: Borrowed in the sixteenth or seventeenth century from Turkic *qara tas ('black stone, black slate, graphite'), a compound of kara 'black' + tas 'stone', with an intrusive -н- in Russian pronunciation.
карандаш.notes: Writing in pencil takes the instrumental case in Russian: написать карандашом 'to write in pencil'.

караоке.etymology: Borrowed in the late twentieth century from Japanese カラオケ (karaoke), a compound of 空 (kara, 'empty') + オケ (oke, clipped from オーケストラ ōkesutora, borrowed from English orchestra): literally 'empty orchestra' (instrumental backing without a live lead singer).

карась.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic карась ('crucian carp'), a widespread European fish name (compare Polish karaś, Middle Low German karas, German Karausche, Lithuanian karõsas) of ancient Wanderwort or substrate origin.

карате.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from Japanese 空手 (karate, literally 'empty hand'), compound of 空 (kara 'empty') + 手 (te 'hand').

каратист.etymology: Derived from карате ('karate', from Japanese 空手 karate) + the agent suffix -ист.

караулить.etymology: Denominative verb from караул ('guard, sentry, watch'), borrowed into Old East Slavic (караулъ) from Turkic qaravul / qaraul ('watchman, sentry, patrol', from Mongolic qara'ul, derived from qara- 'to look, watch').

карбонара.etymology: Borrowed from Italian (pasta alla) carbonara ('carbonara pasta'), derived from carbonaro ('charcoal burner', from Latin carbōnārius, from carbō 'coal, charcoal').

кардиган.etymology: Borrowed from English cardigan ('knitted buttoned jacket or sweater without a collar'), named after James Brudenell, 7th Earl of Cardigan (1797–1868), a British commander in the Crimean War whose troops wore knitted woollen waistcoats.

каре.etymology: Borrowed from French carré ('square; military square formation; four of a kind in card games; rack of lamb'), substantivized past participle of carrer ('to square'), from Latin quadrātus ('squared', from quattuor 'four').

history.meaning: square; four of a kind (cards); rack of meat
four of a kind; bob haircut; rack (of lamb)

карета.etymology: Borrowed via Polish kareta (and German Karrete) from Northern Italian carretta ('light carriage, cart'), diminutive of carra / Latin carrus ('four-wheeled wagon', of Gaulish origin *karros).

каркать.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *karkati ('to caw, croak'), an onomatopoeic verb imitating the harsh call кар! of a crow or raven; because a raven's croaking was folklorically regarded as an omen of disaster, каркать came to mean 'to predict bad luck, jinx things' (Не каркай! 'Don't jinx it!').

history.meaning: to caw, croak; (colloquial) to jinx by predicting misfortune

rootFamily.gloss: to jinx, bring about bad luck by talking about it

карма.etymology: Borrowed via nineteenth- and twentieth-century European philosophical literature from Sanskrit कर्मन् (kárman, nominative kárma, 'deed, action, work; moral law of cause and effect'), from the Proto-Indo-European root *kʷer- ('to make, do').

карман.etymology: Recorded in Russian from the 16th–17th centuries (earlier meaning 'money pouch, purse hung at the belt'), borrowed from Turkic karman ('purse, pocket', attested across Kipchak and Volga Turkic languages).

карманный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from карман ('pocket'), borrowed into Russian from Turkic karman ('purse, money-pouch, pocket').

карп.etymology: Borrowed via Middle Low German karpe, German Karpfen, or Polish karp from Medieval Latin carpa ('Danube carp').

карпаччо.etymology: Borrowed from Italian carpaccio ('dish of thinly sliced raw beef or fish'), coined in Venice in 1950 by Giuseppe Cipriani and named after the Venetian Renaissance painter Vittore Carpaccio for the signature red and white tones of his paintings.

карта.etymology: Borrowed via Polish karta and German Karte from Latin charta ('sheet of papyrus, paper, document') and Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, 'leaf of papyrus').

картина.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) from Italian cartina ('fine paper, small sheet, print'), a diminutive of carta ('paper, card, chart'), from Latin charta and Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, 'sheet of papyrus'). In Russian, картина expanded from an engraving or print on paper to any painting, picture, or motion picture.

картинка.etymology: Diminutive formed in Russian with the suffix -ка from картина ('painting, picture'), which was borrowed in the Petrine era from Italian cartina ('fine paper, small print', diminutive of carta 'paper, card').

картограф.etymology: An international scholarly compound combining карта 'map, chart' + Greek-derived -граф 'one who writes or draws' (from graphein 'to write, draw').

картография.etymology: Borrowed from French cartographie, a scholarly compound formed from Ancient Greek khartes ('sheet of papyrus, map') + -graphia ('drawing, writing').

картонный.etymology: Formed in Russian with the relational suffix -ный from картон ('cardboard, pasteboard'), borrowed via French carton (or German Karton) from Italian cartone ('heavy paper, pasteboard', augmentative of carta 'paper, card' with suffix -one).

картофель.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from German Kartoffel, dissimilated from earlier Tartuffel, from Italian tartufolo ('truffle', diminutive of tartufo, from Vulgar Latin *terrae tūfer 'earth tuber', from Latin tūber 'lump, swelling').

картофельный.etymology: Relational adjective derived from картофель ('potato', from German Kartoffel) + the adjective suffix -ный.

карточка.etymology: Formed in Russian as the diminutive (with suffix -очка) of карта ('card, chart, map'), borrowed via Polish karta / German Karte from Latin charta and Ancient Greek χάρτης ('leaf of papyrus, sheet of paper'). While карта means a geographical map or playing card (and bank card), карточка names an index card, business card, postcard, or bank/metro card.

history.meaning: small card, index card, bank card

карточный.etymology: Derived from карточка / карта ('playing card, card', borrowed via Polish karta and German Karte from Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτης 'sheet of papyrus') + suffix -ный.

картошка.etymology: Colloquial and everyday collective/diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from картофель ('potatoes'), borrowed in the 18th century from German Kartoffel (earlier Tartuffel, altered by dissimilation of t-t > k-t from Italian tartufolo 'little truffle', because potato tubers grow underground like truffles).

карцер.etymology: Borrowed via German Karzer ('university, school, or military detention cell') from Latin carcer ('enclosure, prison, dungeon'; compare German Kerker and English incarcerate).

карьера.etymology: Borrowed from French carrière ('racecourse, rapid course, professional career'), from Italian carriera ('carriage road, racecourse'), from Vulgar Latin *(via) carrāria ('wagon road', from Latin carrus).

карьерный.etymology: Relational adjective derived from карьера ('career', from French carrière) + the adjective suffix -ный.

касаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of касать ('to touch'), inherited from Old East Slavic касатисѧ, iterative (with lengthened root vowel -a-) of коснуться ('to touch'), from Proto-Slavic *kasati sę (related to *česati 'to comb, scratch').

history.meaning: to concern, to apply to; to touch

касса.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via German Kasse from Italian cassa ('money chest, strongbox, cash desk'), from Latin capsa ('box, case for scrolls or money', related to capere 'to hold').

кассовый.etymology: Formed in Russian with the relational suffix -овый from касса ('cash desk, checkout, ticket office', borrowed via German Kasse from Italian cassa). Frequently heard in кассовый чек ('cash-register receipt') and кассовый аппарат ('cash register').

кастинг.etymology: Borrowed in the late twentieth century from English casting ('selection of actors or models for roles in a film, show, or advertisement'), verbal noun of to cast ('to assign roles', originally from Old Norse kasta 'to throw').

history.meaning: auditioning and selecting performers for roles

кастрюля.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via German Kastrol, a regional variant of Kasserolle, which comes from French casserole 'saucepan' (a diminutive of casse 'pan').

катануть.etymology: Colloquial single-action (semelfactive) verb formed in Russian from катать ('to roll, take for a drive', inherited from Proto-Slavic *katati / *kotati) + the suffix -нуть.

history.meaning: to roll -> to roll once; (slang) to dash off a complaint or go for a quick spin

катастрофа.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French catastrophe or German Katastrophe and Late Latin catastrophē from Ancient Greek καταστροφή (katastrophḗ, 'overturning, sudden turn of events, tragic dénouement'), compounded from κατά ('down') + στροφή ('a turning', from στρέφω 'to turn').

катать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic катати, from Proto-Slavic *katati ('to roll, wheel about', iterative-intensive alongside *kotiti 'to roll', Russian катить).

history.meaning: to roll; to take for a ride

кататься.etymology: Reflexive form of катать ('to roll, drive around', from Proto-Slavic *katati) + -ся.

history.meaning: to roll; to ride, skate, ski

категорически.etymology: Adverbial form of категорический ('categorical, unconditional'), derived from категория ('category', from Ancient Greek κατηγορία).

категория.etymology: Borrowed via Late Latin catēgoria (and German Kategorie / French catégorie) from Ancient Greek κατηγορία ('accusation, assertion, philosophical category', from κατηγορέω 'to speak against, predicate', from κατά + ἀγορεύω).

катин.etymology: Possessive adjective formed with the suffix -ин from Катя ('Katya'), affectionate hypocoristic of the feminine given name Екатерина ('Catherine', from Greek Αἰκατερίνη).

катушка.etymology: Derived from катать / катить ('to roll, wind', from Proto-Slavic *katati / *kotiti) + the instrument noun suffix -ушка.

кафе.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French café ('coffee; coffeehouse, café'), which entered French via Italian caffè and Ottoman Turkish kahve from Arabic qahwa. Indeclinable neuter noun in Russian (pronounced with hard or semi-soft ф and stressed final -е: [kɐˈfɛ]).

кафе-памятник.etymology: Compound noun formed in Russian from кафе ('café', borrowed from French café 'coffee; coffeehouse') + памятник ('monument, memorial, heritage site', derived from память 'memory', Proto-Slavic *pamętь).

кафешка.etymology: Colloquial Russian diminutive formed with suffix -шка from кафе ('café'), borrowed from French café ('coffee; coffeehouse', via Italian caffè and Turkish kahve from Arabic qahwa).

качаться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive form of качать ('to rock, swing, sway'), formed with -ся. The verb качать is an iterative formation on the East Slavic stem как- / кач- (related to катить 'to roll', Proto-Slavic *kotiti), originally describing a back-and-forth rocking or rolling motion like a cradle, boat, or suspended lantern.

history.meaning: to roll → to rock back and forth

качественно.etymology: Adverbial form of качественный ('qualitative; of high quality'), derived from качество ('quality', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic качьство, a calque of Ancient Greek ποιότης and Latin quālitās, from какъ 'of what kind').

history.meaning: qualitatively; to a high standard, well

качество.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic качьство ('quality, nature, sort'), formed as a calque of Ancient Greek ποιότης (poiótēs, coined by Plato from ποῖος 'of what kind?', just as Cicero coined Latin quālitās from quālis 'of what kind?'), built from the Slavic interrogative pronoun какъ ('of what kind, how', Russian какой) + the abstract suffix -ьство (-ство), with palatalization of к > ч.

каша.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic каша ('porridge, cooked grain'), from Proto-Slavic *kaša ('porridge, gruel'), cognate with Lithuanian košė ('porridge, mash', from kirti / košti 'to strain, filter').

кашлять.etymology: Denominative verb from кашель ('cough'), inherited from Old East Slavic кашьль, from Proto-Slavic *kašьlь ('cough', from onomatopoeic PIE *kʷeh₂s- 'to cough'; cognate with Lithuanian kosulỹs, Sanskrit kāsa, English cough).

каштан.etymology: Borrowed via Polish kasztan and German Kastanie from Latin castanea ('chestnut'), from Ancient Greek καστανέα ('chestnut tree and nut').

каяться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic каяти сѧ ('to repent, regret, blame oneself'), reflexive of Proto-Slavic *kajati ('to avenge, punish, pay a penalty'), from PIE *kʷoy-eh₂- (root *kʷey- 'to pay, atone', cognate with Greek ποινή and Russian цена).

history.meaning: to exact or pay a penalty

квадрат.etymology: Borrowed via German Quadrat or Polish kwadrat from Latin quadratum ('a square'), substantivized neuter of quadratus ('squared, four-cornered', from quattuor 'four').

квадратный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from квадрат ('square'), borrowed via German Quadrat and Polish kwadrat from Latin quadrātum ('square', from quattuor 'four').

квалификация.etymology: Borrowed via German Qualifikation or French qualification from Medieval Latin quālificātiō, from quālificāre ('to attribute a quality to, qualify', from Latin quālis 'of what kind' + facere 'to make').

квартал.etymology: Borrowed via German Quartal ('quarter of a year, urban district') from Medieval Latin quartale ('fourth part, quarter'), derived from Latin quartus ('fourth').

квартира.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish kwatera and German Quartier ('billet, lodging, quarters') from French quartier and Latin quartārius ('fourth part, quarter of a town or camp where soldiers were billeted').

history.meaning: fourth part, district → military quarters, lodging

квартирка.etymology: Diminutive formed in Russian with the suffix -ка from квартира ('apartment, flat'), which was borrowed in the Petrine era via German Quartier and Polish kwatera from French quartier ('quarter of a town, soldiers' billet', from Latin quartārius 'fourth part').

квартплата.etymology: A Soviet-era syllabic abbreviation (stump compound) of квартирная плата ('apartment payment, rent'), combining квартира ('apartment, flat', borrowed via Polish kwatera and German Quartier from French quartier) and плата ('payment, fee', from Proto-Slavic *platiti).

history.meaning: rent, monthly utility and housing bill

квиты.etymology: Predicative plural adjective (used in мы с тобой квиты 'we are even / quits'), borrowed in the eighteenth–nineteenth centuries via German quitt ('even, free of debt') and French quitte ('discharged of debt'), from Medieval Latin quītus / Latin quiētus ('at rest, cleared of a claim').

квота.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th or early 20th century via German Quote or English quota from Medieval Latin quota (short for quota pars 'how great a part, proportional share'), from Latin quot ('how many').

кедровый.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -овый from кедр ('cedar; Siberian pine'), borrowed via Old Church Slavonic кедръ from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros, 'cedar, juniper').

кетчуп.etymology: Borrowed from English ketchup, which entered seventeenth-century English via Malay kicap from Hokkien / Southern Min Chinese 膎汁 (kê-chiap, 'brine of pickled fish or shellfish'); tomato ketchup developed later in nineteenth-century English and American cookery.

кивать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кивати, from Proto-Slavic *kyvati ('to nod, shake the head, beckon'), iterative of *kynǫti ('to nod, toss').

кивнуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective of кивать ('to nod, beckon'), inherited from Old East Slavic кывати / кивати, from Proto-Slavic *kyvati ('to nod, shake the head, sway').

кидать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кидати, from Proto-Slavic *kydati ('to throw, fling, cast', iterative counterpart of *kynǫti 'to throw, toss', Russian кинуть).

кидаться.etymology: Reflexive form of кидать ('to throw, fling', from Proto-Slavic *kydati) + -ся.

history.meaning: to throw things at; to rush, lunge at

килограмм.etymology: Borrowed from French kilogramme, coined during the French Revolution (1795) from Greek χίλιοι (khílioi, 'thousand') + γράμμα (grámma, 'small weight, gram').

километр.etymology: Borrowed from French kilomètre (introduced in 1795 with the metric system), formed from kilo- ('one thousand', from Ancient Greek χίλιοι) + mètre ('meter', from Ancient Greek μέτρον 'measure').

кинжал.etymology: Borrowed via North Caucasian or Turkic languages (compare Kumyk къынжал qınjal, Kabardian къамэ / хъанджал, Georgian ხანჯალი xanǯali) from Arabic خَنْجَر (ḵanjar, 'curved double-edged dagger'), with dissimilation of final -r to -l.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: кинжал

кинза.etymology: Borrowed into Russian culinary usage from Georgian ქინძი (kindzi, 'fresh coriander, cilantro').
кинза.notes: In Russian kitchens, кинза refers to the fresh green leaves (cilantro), while кориандр usually refers to the dried seeds.

кино.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century from German Kino, a clipping of Kinematograph (compare French cinématographe, coined by the Lumière brothers in the 1890s), from Ancient Greek κίνημα (kínēma, 'movement', from κινέω 'to move') + γράφω (gráphō, 'to write, record').
кино.notes: Indeclinable neuter noun in Russian: **пойти в кино**, **смотреть старое кино**.

кинокритик.etymology: Compound formed from кино- ('cinema, film', clipped from кинематограф, from Ancient Greek κίνημα 'movement') + критик ('critic', via German Kritiker / French critique from Latin criticus, Ancient Greek κριτικός 'able to judge').

кинорежиссёр.etymology: Compound formed from кино- ('cinema, film', from Ancient Greek κίνημα 'movement') + режиссёр ('stage or film director', borrowed via German Regisseur from French régisseur 'manager, director', from régir 'to direct, govern', Latin regere).

кинотеатр.etymology: Compound formed from кино- ('cinema, film', from кинематограф, Ancient Greek κίνημα 'movement') + театр ('theater', via French théâtre and Latin theātrum from Ancient Greek θέατρον 'place for viewing').

кинуть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кинути and Proto-Slavic *kynǫti ('to throw, cast, nod'), semelfactive verb in -нуть paired with кидать (*kydati 'to throw, fling'); in late twentieth-century Russian slang it developed the figurative sense 'to scam, cheat out of money, ditch'.

history.meaning: to throw, toss; (slang) to scam, abandon

киоск.etymology: Borrowed via French kiosque (or German Kiosk) from Ottoman Turkish köşk ('garden pavilion, summerhouse'), itself from Persian کوشک (kūšk, 'palace, portico, pavilion').

кипеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кыпѣти ('to boil, bubble, seethe'), from Proto-Slavic *kypěti, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷūp- ('to boil, seethe, smoke'; cognate with Latin cupere 'to desire passionately' and Sanskrit kúpyati 'bubbles up, becomes angry').

кипятиться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed from кипятить ('to boil [transitively]', built on кипеть 'to boil, seethe', Proto-Slavic *kypěti) + -ся: literally 'to boil oneself', and figuratively in everyday speech 'to get worked up, fume, lose one's temper'.

history.meaning: to boil -> to be boiled; (colloquial) to get hot under the collar, fume

кипяток.etymology: Formed in East Slavic with the noun suffix -ок from an old present participle stem кипят- of кипеть ('to boil, bubble', from Old East Slavic кипѣти, Proto-Slavic *kypěti, continuing PIE *kwep- 'to boil, seethe, steam'; cognate with Lithuanian kūpėti 'to boil over' and Latin cupiō): literally 'boiling liquid, boiling water'.

кира.etymology: Russian feminine given name Кира, borrowed via Church Slavonic from Ancient Greek Κύρα (Kýra, 'mistress, lady'), feminine counterpart of Κῦρος (Kŷros, 'lord, master', also linked in Greek tradition with the Persian royal name Kūruš / Cyrus).

киргиз.etymology: Borrowed from Turkic (Kyrgyz кыргыз qırğız, attested in the 8th-century Orkhon inscriptions as Old Turkic Qïrqïz), traditionally linked in Turkic etymology to qïrq ('forty', i.e. 'the forty tribes').

киргизский.etymology: Relational adjective derived from киргиз ('Kyrgyz') + the adjective suffix -ский.

кирпич.etymology: Borrowed from Turkic — compare Turkish kerpic, Tatar кирпеч, and Kazakh кірпіш ('sun-dried or fired clay brick') — attested in East Slavic since late medieval building accounts.
кирпич.notes: Stress stays on the ending throughout its declension: кирпич, кирпича, кирпичи, кирпичей.

кирпичный.etymology: Formed in Russian with the relational/material suffix -ный from кирпич ('brick', borrowed into Old Russian in the 14th–15th centuries from Turkic kerpič 'sun-dried or kilned clay brick').

кисленький.etymology: Affectionate and attenuative adjective formed with suffix -енький from кислый ('sour', inherited from Old East Slavic кислыи, from Proto-Slavic *kyslъ, from *kysnǫti 'to turn sour, ferment').

кислинка.etymology: Formed with the nuance suffix -инка ('a slight touch or trace of a quality') from кислый ('sour, tart', from Proto-Slavic *kyslъ): 'a pleasant touch of tartness or acidity'.

кислить.etymology: Intransitive taste verb formed with -ить from кислый ('sour, tart', from Proto-Slavic *kyslъ), following the productive Russian pattern for flavour nuances (compare горчить 'to taste slightly bitter').

history.meaning: sour → to taste sour, have a tart edge

кислота.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic кислота ('sourness'), derived from кислый ('sour', Proto-Slavic *kyslъ) + suffix -ота; the chemical sense 'acid' calques Latin acidum, French acide, and German Säure.

кислый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кислыи ('sour, fermented, acidic'), originally a past active l-participle of киснуть ('to turn sour, ferment', from Proto-Slavic *kysnǫti / *kyslъ).

кисточка.etymology: Diminutive of кисть ('cluster, tuft of bristles, paintbrush, hand') formed with the double diminutive suffix -оч-ка. Russian кисть descends from Old East Slavic кисть and Proto-Slavic *kystь ('tuft, bunch of herbs or bristles, cluster of berries'). Because early brushes were bound tufts of bristles or flax, кисточка became the everyday word for both an artist's paintbrush and a baker's pastry brush.

history.meaning: small brush (paint or pastry brush), tassel

кисть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кысть / кисть ('tuft, bunch, cluster, brush, hand'), from Proto-Slavic *kystь ('tuft, bunch of bristles or twigs, cluster').

history.meaning: paintbrush; cluster; hand (from wrist to fingers)

кит.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic китъ ('whale, sea monster') from Byzantine/Ancient Greek κῆτος (pronounced kítos in Byzantine Greek, 'whale, huge sea monster').

китаец.etymology: Derived with the ethnonymic suffix -ец from Китай ('China'), inherited from Old East Slavic Китаи, borrowed via Turkic (Qïtay) and Mongolic from the name of the Khitan people (契丹), who ruled northern China as the Liao dynasty (907–1125).

китайский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with -ский from Китай ('China'), which entered Old East Slavic via Turkic Qïtay from the ethnonym of the Khitan (契丹 Qìdān), the nomadic people who ruled northern China as the Liao dynasty (907–1125) and also gave medieval European Cathay.
китайский.notes: Compare the colloquial idiom китайская грамота ('Chinese writing'), meaning something impossibly complicated ('it's all Greek to me').

китель.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from German Kittel ('smock, work tunic, uniform jacket'), from Middle High German kittel.

кишка.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кишька, from Proto-Slavic *kyšьka ('gut, intestine, stuffed casing').

кишмиш.etymology: Borrowed via Turkic (compare Tatar, Uzbek, and Azeri kişmiş) from Persian کشمش (kešmeš 'currants, small seedless grapes and raisins').

клавиша.etymology: Borrowed via Polish klawisz ('key of a musical instrument') from Medieval Latin clavis ('key of an organ or clavichord', in Classical Latin 'key, bolt').

клад.etymology: Native East Slavic noun built on the root of класть ('to lay, put, stow away'): literally something laid away in a secret spot for safekeeping, hence 'buried treasure, hoard'.

кладбище.etymology: Derived with locative suffix -бище from класть (кладу, 'to lay, place, bury'; compare Old Russian кладьбище), originally 'place where bodies (or timber stacks) are laid to rest', from Proto-Slavic *klasti.

кладовка.etymology: Colloquial univerbation with suffix -ка of кладовая (комната) ('storage room, pantry'), from кладовой ('for storing'), built on класть / клад ('to lay, store away / stored goods', from Proto-Slavic *klasti).

кланяться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кланятися ('to bow down, greet reverently'), from Proto-Slavic *klanjati sę, lengthened-grade iterative of *kloniti sę ('to bend, incline', from PIE *ḱley- 'to lean').

клапан.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from German Klappen, plural of Klappe ('flap, lid, hinged valve'), related to klappen ('to clap, fold, click shut').

класс.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Klasse and French classe from Latin classis ('one of the six property divisions of Roman citizens; fleet, army; school class, rank, category'). In colloquial modern Russian, класс! is also used as an exclamation meaning 'top-class, cool, awesome!'.

классика.etymology: Borrowed via German Klassik ('classical antiquity, classic works') from Latin classicus ('belonging to the highest class of citizens, first-rate, model', from classis 'class, division').

классический.etymology: Borrowed via German klassisch and French classique (adapted with the Russian adjective suffix -еский) from Latin classicus ('of the first class, exemplary, standard', from classis).

классно.etymology: Adverb formed from the adjective классный ('first-rate, cool', originally 'pertaining to a class or rank'), derived from класс ('class, grade, high quality'), borrowed in the 18th century via German Klasse and French classe from Latin classis ('division of citizens, class').

классный.etymology: Formed in Russian with the adjectival suffix -ный from класс ('school class, grade, category', borrowed via German Klasse and French classe from Latin classis); in twentieth-century school and youth speech, 'high-grade, first-class' generalized into 'great, cool, awesome'.

кластер.etymology: Borrowed in the second half of the 20th century (first in astronomy, physics, and computing, later in economics and regional policy) from English cluster ('bunch, group of similar things growing or held together'), from Old English clyster ('bunch, cluster').

класть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic класти (present кладу, кладеши), from Proto-Slavic *klasti (stem *klad-, 'to lay, place, stack, load'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *kl̥h₂d- ('to lay timber, stack, load'; cognate with Lithuanian klóti 'to spread, lay' and English lade / load). Serves as the suppletive imperfective partner of perfective положить ('to put, lay').

клевать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic клевати, from Proto-Slavic *klьvati ('to peck', related to клюв 'beak', from PIE *k(e)lew- / *glewbʰ- 'to tear, peck, carve').

клевер.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from Low German klēver (or Dutch klaver / English clover), from Proto-West Germanic *klaibrō ('clover', literally 'sticky plant', related to kleben 'to stick').

клеить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic клѣити, from Proto-Slavic *kъlějiti ('to glue'), denominative verb from *kъlějь ('glue, tree resin, gum', Russian клей).

клей.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic клеи ('glue, tree resin'), from Proto-Slavic *kъlejь ('glue, gum'), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- / *gley- ('clay, sticky substance'; cognate with Ancient Greek κόλλα 'glue').

клеймо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic клеимо ('brand mark on livestock, craftsman's hallmark, seal'), considered by Vasmer an early borrowing from Old Norse kleima ('to smear, dab, mark') or Middle Low German.

history.meaning: brand, hallmark; stigma, mark of shame

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: клеймо

клептомания.etymology: Borrowed from French kleptomanie (coined around 1816 by Swiss physician André Matthey), a neo-classical compound of Ancient Greek κλέπτω ('to steal') + μανία ('madness, compulsion').

клетка.etymology: Diminutive formed with suffix -ка from клеть ('storehouse, timber frame, room'), inherited from Old East Slavic клѣть, from Proto-Slavic *klětь ('woven or timber enclosure, storehouse, cell').

клешня.etymology: Derived in East Slavic from the root of клещи ('pincers, tongs'), from Proto-Slavic *klěšča ('tongs, pincers'), related to *klěsnǫti ('to pinch, squeeze together').

history.meaning: claw, pincer (of a crab or lobster)

клещ.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic клѣщь, from Proto-Slavic *klěščь ('tick'), built on the same root as *klěšča / *klěšči (Russian клещи, 'pincers, tongs') and *klěščiti ('to pinch, clamp'), naming the arachnid after its pinching mouthparts.

клиент.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century via German Klient or French client from Latin cliēns (genitive clientis, 'dependent, follower under the protection of a Roman patrician patron', later 'legal client, customer'), related to clināre ('to lean on') or cluēre ('to hear, obey').

history.meaning: plebeian under a patron's protection; legal client

клизма.etymology: Borrowed via medical Latin clysma (and German Klysma) from Ancient Greek κλύσμα ('liquid used for washing out, enema'), derived from κλύζω ('to wash, drench, rinse out').

клиника.etymology: Borrowed via French clinique and German Klinik from Late Latin clīnicē, from Ancient Greek κλινική (τέχνη) ('bedside medical practice'), from κλίνη ('bed, couch', from κλίνω 'to lean, recline').

клинок.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from Dutch klink or German Klinge ('sword blade', originally named from the metallic ring of tempered steel) and adapted with the Russian suffix -ок by folk-etymological association with native клин ('wedge').

history.meaning: blade (of a knife, dagger, or sword)

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: клинок

клип.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English (video) clip ('short excerpt cut from a film; music video'), from clip ('to cut, trim with shears', from Old Norse klippa).

кличка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the noun suffix -ка from кличать / кликать ('to call, cry out, name', inherited from Proto-Slavic *klikati; compare клич 'call, cry').

history.meaning: call -> pet's name; nickname, underworld alias

кличка.notes: In standard Russian, animals have a кличка ('pet name') rather than a human имя, and among people кличка refers to a street, school, or criminal nickname.

клон.etymology: Borrowed via English clone (and German Klon, introduced in 1903 by botanist H. J. Webber) from Ancient Greek κλών ('twig, slip, shoot used for plant propagation', from κλάω 'to break off').

history.meaning: asexually propagated group or organism; clone

клонить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic клонити, from Proto-Slavic *kloniti ('to bend, incline, bow'), o-grade causative-iterative from PIE *ḱley- ('to lean, incline'; cognate with Greek κλίνω and Latin clīnāre).

history.meaning: to incline, bend; to make drowsy

клоун.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from English clown ('comic stage rustic, jester, circus clown'), which entered 16th-century English (originally meaning 'clod, boor, country bumpkin') from Low German or Scandinavian (compare Icelandic klunni 'clumsy, boorish fellow' and Low German Klönne).

клоунада.etymology: Derived from клоун ('clown', borrowed in the 19th century from English clown 'rustic, jester, circus clown') + the suffix -ада (after French-derived theatrical nouns such as буффонада, арлекинада).

клуб.etymology: Borrowed in the late 18th century from English club ('social association, society of members meeting periodically'), which developed in 17th-century England from club ('thick stick, cudgel', from Old Norse klubba) via the notion of a 'knot or gathering of people' sharing expenses.
клуб.notes: Russian has a homonym клуб ('ball of smoke, puff', plural клубы), which is a native Slavic word related to клубок ('ball of yarn').

клубника.etymology: Derived in Russian from клубный / клуб ('round ball, globular cluster', inherited from Old East Slavic клубъ 'ball, sphere', from Proto-Slavic *klǫbъ) + the berry suffix -ника, named for the round, ball-like shape of the fruit.

клубничный.etymology: Formed in Russian with the relational suffix -ный (with к → ч) from клубника ('garden strawberry'), itself derived in Russian from клуб ('round ball, globe, clew', from Proto-Slavic *klǫbъ) because of the round, globular shape of the ripe berry.

ключ.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ключь, from Proto-Slavic *kľučь ('hook, wooden bolt, key'), belonging to an Indo-European family for curved bolts and locks (compare Latin clāvis 'key' and claudō 'to close'). In Russian the same word denotes a door key, a musical clef, and a mechanic's wrench.

ключик.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ик from ключ ('key'), which is inherited from Old East Slavic ключь, from Proto-Slavic *kľučь ('hook, wooden bolt, key'), from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂u- ('hook, peg, key'; cognate with Latin clāvis 'key').

клюшка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of dialectal клюка ('crooked stick, hooked staff, crutch'), inherited from Old East Slavic клюка ('hook, crooked stick'), from Proto-Slavic *kljuka ('hook, bend').

history.meaning: hooked stick; hockey stick, golf club

клякса.etymology: Borrowed from German Klecks 'blot, splatter of ink', from klecksen 'to blot, splash', adapted into Russian as a feminine -а noun.
клякса.notes: Поставить кляксу means 'to make an ink blot' when writing with a dip nib or fountain pen.

клясться.etymology: Reflexive form of клясть ('to curse, execrate'), inherited from Old East Slavic кляти / клятися (1st sg. кльнуся), from Proto-Slavic *klęti sę ('to swear an oath', literally 'to call down a curse upon oneself if one's word is false').

history.meaning: to bind oneself by a curse → to swear an oath

книга.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кънига (often plural кънигы 'letters, scroll, book'), from Proto-Slavic *kъniga. Its ultimate pre-Slavic origin is uncertain: Vasmer discusses proposed wanderword routes through Turkic from East Asian or Near Eastern terms for scrolls without a single proven path.

книжка.etymology: Diminutive of книга ('book') formed with the suffix -ка (with regular palatalization г → ж). The base noun книга comes from Old East Slavic кънига and Proto-Slavic *kъniga ('scroll, writing, book').
книжка.notes: Besides being a warm everyday word for a book, книжка is the standard term for small official booklets such as трудовая книжка ('employment record book') and зачётная книжка ('student gradebook').

книжный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кънижьныи ('relating to books or scripture, learned'), formed with the suffix -ный from книга ('book', from Proto-Slavic *kъňiga).

кнопка.etymology: Formed with the Russian suffix -ка from кноп ('small knob, knot, button'), borrowed in the Petrine era from German Knopf or Dutch knoop ('button, knob, knot', cognate with English knob).

history.meaning: push-button; drawing pin, thumbtack; snap fastener

кнопочка.etymology: Diminutive formed with suffix -очка from кнопка ('push-button, thumbtack, snap fastener'), borrowed with suffix -ка from Middle Low German knōp or German Knopf ('knob, button, stud', from Proto-Germanic *knaupaz).
