князь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кънязь ('prince, ruler'), from Proto-Slavic *kъnędzь, an early borrowing from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz ('king, head of a clan', from *kunją 'kin, family'; cognate with English king and German König).

кобура.etymology: Borrowed (compare Polish kobura) via Turkic (Turkish kubur 'cylindrical case, quiver, pistol holster on a saddle', Tatar kubura), from Arabic qubūr or Turkic-Mongolic qubur ('tube, case, quiver').

кованый.etymology: Verbal adjective in -ный formed from ковать ('to forge metal, hammer on an anvil, shoe a horse'), inherited from Old East Slavic ковати and Proto-Slavic *kovati ('to strike, forge', cognate with Lithuanian kauti 'to strike, forge' and English hew).

коварный.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic коварьнъ ('skillful, artful; crafty, insidious'), derived from archaic коварь ('blacksmith, metal-forger', built on ковать 'to forge, hammer metal', Proto-Slavic *kovati): the meaning shifted from 'skillfully forged' to 'forging plots, treacherous'.

ковать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ковати, from Proto-Slavic *kovati ('to forge, hammer metal, shoe a horse'), from Proto-Indo-European *kewh₂- ('to strike, hew, forge'; cognate with Lithuanian káuti, Latin cūdere, English hew).

коврик.etymology: Formed in Russian as the diminutive of ковёр ('carpet, rug', with mobile vowel ё dropping in oblique and derived forms: ковра, коврик) + suffix -ик. Old East Slavic ковьръ is traced by Vasmer to an early Volga Bulgar / Turkic borrowing (*käbär / *kävir 'woven carpet').

ковёр.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ковьръ ('carpet, rug, tapestry'), borrowed from an Old Turkic / Volga Bulgar form *käwür / *käbir (compare Chuvash кавир kavir 'carpet' and Kipchak kövüz).

когда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic къгда ('when', Old Church Slavonic къгда), from Proto-Slavic *kъgda, formed from the interrogative stem *kъ- ('what, which') + the temporal suffix *-gda (compare всегда 'always' and иногда 'sometimes').

когда-либо.etymology: Indefinite adverb formed in Russian from когда ('when', from Proto-Slavic *kъgda) + the indefinite enclitic particle -либо ('ever, any', historically reduced from любо 'pleasing, whichever one likes').

history.meaning: when + ever -> ever, at any time

когда-нибудь.etymology: Indefinite temporal adverb formed from когда ('when', from Old East Slavic къгда, Proto-Slavic *kъgda) + the indefinite enclitic particle -нибудь (from ни будь 'be it whenever it may', 2nd sg. imperative of быть 'to be').

history.meaning: whenever it may be → someday, one day, ever

когда-то.etymology: Indefinite temporal adverb formed from когда ('when', inherited from Old East Slavic къгда, from Proto-Slavic *kъgda) + the indefinite enclitic particle -то.

history.meaning: once, at some time in the past

кое-кто.etymology: Indefinite pronoun formed in Russian from the prefix кое- (fossilized form of the pronoun кой 'which, some', Proto-Slavic *kъjь) + кто ('who', Proto-Slavic *kъto).

history.meaning: someone (often implying the speaker knows who), a few people

кое-кто.notes: When used with a preposition, the preposition splits the compound: у кое-кого or кое у кого ('at someone's place').

кое-что.etymology: Indefinite pronoun formed from the prefix кое- (historically the neuter singular кое of the archaic interrogative/relative pronoun коий 'which', Proto-Slavic *kъjь) + что ('what', Proto-Slavic *čьto). Typically implies something specific that the speaker knows about but chooses not to name yet ('something, a thing or two').

кожа.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кожа ('goat-skin, hide, leather, human skin'), from Proto-Slavic *koža, derived with the possessive/material suffix *-ja (where *z + *j > ж) from *koza ('goat', modern Russian коза): originally 'goat-skin', then generalized across Slavic to any animal hide, leather, or skin.

кожаный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кожаныи ('made of leather or hide'), formed from кожа ('skin, hide, leather', from Proto-Slavic *koža) + the material suffix -аный.

козырь.etymology: Attested in Russian since the 17th century (also meaning 'high standing collar'); of uncertain origin, connected by Vasmer either with Turkic forms (compare Chuvash küzər 'trump') or with коза ('goat', via goatskin collar trim).

козёл.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic козьлъ ('he-goat, billy goat'), from Proto-Slavic *kozьlъ, a masculine derivative formed with suffix *-ьlъ from *koza ('goat', Russian коза).

кой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кыи / кои ('who, which, what'), from Proto-Slavic *kъjь, compound of the interrogative stem *kъ- (from PIE *kʷo-) + the pronominal stem *jь; preserved in modern Russian in set phrases such as ни в коем случае.

history.meaning: which (archaic; ни в коем случае 'by no means')

кокон.etymology: Borrowed from French cocon ('silkworm cocoon'), from Occitan cocon ('eggshell; cocoon'), diminutive of coca ('shell'), from Late Latin coccum ('berry, shell').

кокос.etymology: Borrowed via German Kokos / Dutch kokos and French coco from Spanish and Portuguese coco ('coconut', originally 'grinning face, bogeyman', because the three pores at the base of the shell resemble a face).

коктейль.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth–twentieth centuries from English cocktail ('mixed drink', literally 'cock's tail').

кола.etymology: Borrowed via English cola (and French/German Kola) from a West African name (Temne an-kola, Mandinka kolo) for the caffeine-bearing kola nut (Cola acuminata), used to flavor cola soft drinks.

колбаса.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кълбаса (attested in a twelfth-century Novgorod birchbark document) and Proto-Slavic *kъlbasa ('sausage'); etymologists debate whether it is an early borrowing from Turkic (compare Turkish külbastı 'grilled meat') or a native Slavic formation related to колоб ('round lump').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: колбаса

колбаска.etymology: Diminutive formed in Russian with the suffix -ка from колбаса ('sausage', from Old East Slavic кълбаса).

коленка.etymology: Colloquial singulative/diminutive formed with suffix -ка from колено ('knee; joint'), inherited from Old East Slavic колѣно, from Proto-Slavic *kolěno ('knee, joint', from PIE *kʷel- 'to turn, bend').

колено.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic колѣно ('knee; joint; generation, tribe'), from Proto-Slavic *kolěno ('knee, joint, bend'), related to *kolo ('wheel') from the notion of bending/turning.

колесо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic коло (genitive колесе, plural колеса, 'wheel, circle'), from Proto-Slavic *kolo (stem *koles-), continuing Proto-Indo-European *kʷékʷlos ('wheel, circle', a reduplicated noun from *kʷel- 'to turn, revolve'), directly cognate with English wheel, Ancient Greek κύκλος (whence cycle), and Sanskrit cakrá.

колечко.etymology: Diminutive of кольцо ('ring') formed with suffix -ко (with palatalization ц → ч and fleeting vowel е). Russian кольцо is itself an old diminutive of коло ('wheel, circle', Proto-Slavic *kolo, from PIE *kwelo- 'to turn, wheel'). Through that Indo-European root it is directly cognate with English wheel, cycle, and collar.

количество.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic количьство ('quantity, amount, size'), a calque of Ancient Greek ποσότης ('quantity'), derived from коликъ ('how much, how great', from Proto-Slavic *kolikъ) + suffix -ьство.

коллега.etymology: Borrowed via German Kollege or Polish kolega from Latin collega ('partner in office, fellow magistrate'), formed from com- ('together') + legare ('to depute, commission, choose').

колледж.etymology: Borrowed from English college, from Old French college, from Latin collēgium ('association of colleagues, guild, corporation'), from collēga ('partner in office', from com- + legere 'to choose, deputize').

коллектив.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th or early 20th century from German Kollektiv ('group working together, collective'), from French collectif and Latin collectivus ('gathered together', from colligere 'to gather, collect').

коллектор.etymology: In the financial sense 'debt collector', borrowed in the post-Soviet period from English collector (short for debt collector). Earlier technical senses ('sewer main, electrical commutator') came via German Kollektor and French collecteur from Late Latin collector ('gatherer'), from Latin colligere ('to gather together').

history.meaning: to gather together → gatherer, tax collector

коллекция.etymology: Borrowed via Polish kolekcja, German Kollektion, or French collection from Latin collectiō ('a gathering together'), from colligere ('to gather, assemble', from com- + legere 'to gather, choose').

колокольня.etymology: Formed in Russian with the place-noun suffix -ня from колокол ('church bell'), inherited from Old East Slavic колоколъ, from Proto-Slavic *kolkolъ (an ancient reduplicated onomatopoeic word *kal-kal- for a ringing bell).

колокольчик.etymology: Diminutive of колокол ('large church or tower bell') formed with suffix -чик. Russian колокол descends from Old East Slavic колоколъ and Proto-Slavic *kolkolъ ('bell'), an ancient reduplicated sound-symbolic noun from PIE *kalg- / *klag- ('to resound, clang, ring'), cognate with Latin calare ('to call out, proclaim') and Sanskrit kalakala ('confused ringing sound').

колония.etymology: Borrowed via Polish kolonia or German Kolonie from Latin colōnia ('settlement, farmstead'), derived from colōnus ('settler, farmer', from colere 'to cultivate, inhabit'); in Soviet and modern Russian legal usage (исправительная колония) it became the standard term for a correctional prison facility.

колонка.etymology: Diminutive formed with suffix -ка from колонна ('column, pillar'), borrowed via French colonne and Italian colonna from Latin columna ('pillar, post, column').

колонна.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via French colonne or Italian colonna from Latin columna ('pillar, architectural column').

history.meaning: architectural column; marching or vehicle column

колоть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic колоти and Proto-Slavic *kolti ('to stab, prick, split, chop', showing regular East Slavic pleophony -оло- from *-ol- between consonants; compare Old Church Slavonic клати), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₂- ('to strike, pierce').

history.meaning: to prick, sting, stab; to chop (firewood or sugar)

колпак.etymology: Attested in Old Russian from the 15th century for a tall pointed felt cap or crown; borrowed from Turkic qalpaq ('tall felt or fur cap'; compare Turkish kalpak, Kazakh қалпақ, and Tatar калпак). In modern Russian, колпак denotes a tall chef's toque (поварской колпак), a nightcap, a fool's cap, or a protective glass/lamp dome.

колье.etymology: Borrowed from French collier ('necklace, collar'), from Old French colier, from Latin collāre ('neckband, collar'), from collum ('neck').

кольцо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кольце ('ring'), diminutive formed with the suffix *-ьce from коло ('wheel, circle', from Proto-Slavic *kolo, cognate with колесо 'wheel' and Ancient Greek κύκλος).

коляска.etymology: Derived in East Slavic or borrowed via Polish kolaska ('light wheeled carriage'), diminutive of коляса ('carriage', originally plural of колесо 'wheel', inherited from Old East Slavic колесо, Proto-Slavic *kolo, stem *koles- 'wheel', PIE *kʷékʷlos).

ком.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *komъ ('lump, clod, ball'), derived from an Indo-European root meaning 'to press, squeeze together' (related to Russian комкать 'to crumple' and dialectal комить 'to press into a ball', and compared by Vasmer with Lithuanian kãmanos).
ком.notes: Plural is комья (nominative plural комья, genitive plural комьев). Famous in the proverb Первый блин комом ('The first pancake comes out as a lump').

кома.etymology: Borrowed via medical Latin coma from Ancient Greek κῶμα ('deep, trance-like sleep, lethargy', related to κεῖμαι 'to lie down').

команда.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Kommando and French commande ('order, military detachment, crew'), from Medieval Latin commenda / Vulgar Latin *commandare ('to entrust, order').

командир.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via German Kommandeur / kommandieren from French commandeur ('commander'), derived from commander ('to command, order'), from Vulgar Latin *commandāre (a blend of Latin commendāre 'to entrust' and mandāre 'to order').

командировка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with suffix -ка from командировать ('to dispatch on an official mission'), borrowed in the Petrine era from German kommandieren ('to command, detail on duty'), from French commander (Vulgar Latin *commandāre).

командование.etymology: Verbal noun in -ание from командовать ('to command'), borrowed in the Petrine era via German kommandieren / Polish komenderować from French commander (from Late Latin commandāre 'to entrust, order').

командовать.etymology: Borrowed via Polish komendować or formed in Russian from команда ('command, detachment') + the verbal suffix -овать, ultimately from French commander.

комар.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic комаръ, from Proto-Slavic *komarъ ('mosquito, gnat'), an onomatopoeic formation from the buzzing root *kom-.

комбинатор.etymology: Borrowed via German Kombinator / French combinateur from Late Latin combīnātor ('one who combines'); the colloquial Russian sense 'clever schemer, wheeler-dealer' was popularized by Ilf and Petrov's character Ostap Bender («великий комбинатор»).

комбинация.etymology: Borrowed via Polish kombinacja and German Kombination from Late Latin combīnātiō ('joining two by two'), from combīnāre ('to combine', from com- 'together' + bīnī 'two by two').

комедия.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century via Polish komedia and German Komödie from Latin comoedia, from Ancient Greek κωμῳδία (kōmōidía, 'comedy'), a compound of κῶμος (kômos, 'revel, festival procession') and ᾠδή (ōidḗ, 'song, ode').

комиссия.etymology: Borrowed via Polish komisja and German Kommission from Medieval/Classical Latin commissiō ('entrusting, charge, committee'), from committere ('to bring together, entrust', from com- + mittere 'to send').

комитет.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via French comité and German Komitee from English committee ('body of persons to whom a matter is committed'), from Anglo-Norman committer and Latin committere ('to entrust, commit').

комментарий.etymology: Borrowed via German Kommentar or directly from Latin commentārium / commentārius ('notebook, memoir, explanatory notes'), derived from commentārī ('to reflect upon, expound', intensive of comminīscī 'to devise, call to mind').

коммерческий.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -еский from коммерция ('commerce, trade'), borrowed via German Kommerz / French commerce from Latin commercium ('trade, traffic, merchandise', from com- + merx 'wares').

коммуналка.etymology: A colloquial Soviet-era univerbation formed with the suffix -ка from коммунальная квартира ('communal apartment'), where several families shared a single kitchen and bathroom. Коммунальный comes from French communal, from Latin commūnis ('common, shared').

коммунальный.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ный from French communal ('belonging to a commune or shared community'), from Late Latin commūnālis (built on Latin commūnis 'common, shared').

коммунистка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the feminine suffix -ка from коммунист ('communist'), borrowed from French communiste (derived from commun 'common, shared', Latin commūnis).

комната.etymology: Borrowed via Polish and Czech komnata from Old High German kemināta, ultimately from Medieval Latin camīnāta ('a room heated by a fireplace', from Latin camīnus 'hearth, stove'). In older Russian architecture it originally meant a warm, heated chamber, before broadening to any indoor room.

history.meaning: room with a hearth or stove

комната.notes: In hotels, an individual guest room is usually called **номер**, while **комната** names a room in a house or flat.

комнатка.etymology: Diminutive formed in Russian with the suffix -ка from комната ('room', originally 'heated room with a stove or fireplace', borrowed via Polish komnata from Medieval Latin camīnāta).

комнатный.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ный from комната ('room', borrowed via Polish komnata from Medieval Latin camīnāta 'room with a fireplace').

комочек.etymology: Affectionate double diminutive formed with the suffix -ек from комок ('small lump, ball'), itself the diminutive of ком ('lump, clod, ball', from Proto-Slavic *komъ).

history.meaning: lump → small lump → tiny lump, little ball

компания.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish kompania, German Kompanie, or French compagnie from Vulgar Latin *compānia ('fellowship of sharing bread'), from Latin com- ('with') + pānis ('bread').

компас.etymology: Borrowed via German Kompass (and Dutch kompas) from Italian compasso 'divider, mariner's compass', derived from Late Latin compassare 'to pace out, measure around' (com- + passus 'step, pace').
компас.notes: Standard everyday Russian stresses the first syllable ком- in компас.

компетентный.etymology: Borrowed via German kompetent and French compétent (adapted with -ный) from Latin competēns ('fitting, suitable, qualified'), present participle of competere ('to meet, coincide, be qualified', from com- + petere 'to seek, aim at').

комплекс.etymology: Borrowed via German Komplex from Latin complexus ('encompassing, interconnected whole'), past participle of complectī ('to embrace, plait or weave together').

комплект.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (initially meaning a 'full complement of troops') via Polish komplekt or German Komplekt from Latin complētus ('filled up, complete'), past participle of complēre ('to fill up', from com- + plēre 'to fill').

комплимент.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via German Kompliment and French compliment from Italian complimento ('act of courtesy, polite expression of praise'), from Spanish cumplimiento ('fulfillment of courtesy'), derived from Latin complēre ('to fill up, complete, fulfill one's polite duty'). In restaurant usage, комплимент от шефа (blended with French/English complimentary) also denotes a free appetizer from the chef.

history.meaning: compliment; complimentary dish from the chef

композитор.etymology: Borrowed via German Kompositor / Polish kompozytor from Latin compositor ('one who puts together, arranger, maker'), derived from componere ('to put together, compose').

компот.etymology: Borrowed from French compote ('stewed fruit'), from Old French composte ('mixture, fruit preserve'), from Latin composita ('things put together', feminine past participle of compōnere 'to put together').

компромат.etymology: 20th-century Soviet bureaucratic/KGB syllabic abbreviation of компрометирующий материал ('compromising material'), from компрометировать ('to compromise, discredit', via German kompromittieren / French compromettre) + материал.

компромисс.etymology: Borrowed via French compromis and German Kompromiss from Latin comprōmissum ('mutual promise to abide by an arbitrator's decision'), neuter past participle of comprōmittere (from com- + prōmittere 'to promise').

компьютер.etymology: Borrowed in the second half of the 20th century from English computer, an agent noun from compute, which goes back via French computer to Latin computāre ('to reckon, sum up, calculate', from com- 'together' + putāre 'to reckon, consider').

компьютерный.etymology: Relational adjective formed in late twentieth-century Russian with the suffix -ный from компьютер ('computer'), borrowed from English computer (from compute, Latin computāre 'to reckon, calculate').

комфорт.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from English comfort ('domestic ease, convenience'), from Old French confort ('solace, support, strength'), from Late Latin confortāre ('to strengthen greatly', from com- + fortis 'strong').

комфортно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate in -о from комфортный ('comfortable'), derived from комфорт ('comfort'), borrowed in the nineteenth century from English comfort (via Old French confort from Late Latin confortāre 'to strengthen, console').

кон.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic конъ ('beginning, limit, turn, order; stake in a game'), from Proto-Slavic *konъ ('beginning, boundary, row', an o-grade formation from the root *čen- / *kъn- also seen in начать 'to begin' and конец 'end').

конверт.etymology: Borrowed from French couvert 'envelope, cover; place setting', originally the past participle of couvrir 'to cover' (from Latin cooperire), with an intrusive н added in Russian pronunciation.

кондитер.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (earlier кандитор) from German Konditor ('pastry chef, confectioner'), which was adapted in Renaissance German from Latin condītor ('one who seasons, preserves, or pickles food and fruit'), from condīre ('to season, spice, preserve in sugar').

history.meaning: to season, preserve → maker of preserves and sweets

кондитерский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with -ский from кондитер ('confectioner, pastry chef'), borrowed in the eighteenth century from German Konditor ('pastry cook'), from Latin condītor ('one who seasons, preserves, or prepares delicacies', from condīre 'to season, preserve in sugar or spices').

кондиционер.etymology: Borrowed in the twentieth century (modeled on French conditionneur and English air conditioner) from the stem of Latin condiciō ('condition, state'): an appliance that regulates the temperature and humidity of indoor air.

history.meaning: air conditioner; hair or fabric conditioner

конец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic коньць ('end, limit, tip'), from Proto-Slavic *konьcь, formed with the suffix *-ьcь from *konъ ('beginning, limit, boundary').

конечно.etymology: Adverb from the short neuter of конечный ('final, ultimate, conclusive'), derived from конец ('end, limit', from Old East Slavic коньць, Proto-Slavic *konьcь). Originally 'ultimately, conclusively, in the end', it developed into the conversational affirmative 'of course, certainly' (pronounced [kɐˈnʲeʂnə], 'канешно', with чн > шн).
конечно.notes: In the meaning 'of course', the cluster **чн** is pronounced **шн** (*канешно*).

конина.etymology: Derived from конь ('horse', inherited from Old East Slavic конь, from Proto-Slavic *konjь) + the meat-denoting noun suffix -ина.

конкретно.etymology: Adverb in -о from конкретный ('concrete, specific'), borrowed via French concret and German konkret from Latin concrētus ('grown together, condensed, solid, tangible', past participle of concrescere).

history.meaning: specific, concrete -> specifically, concretely; (slang) seriously, totally

конкретный.etymology: Borrowed via German konkret and French concret (adapted with -ный) from Latin concrētus ('grown together, condensed, solid, tangible'), past participle of concrēscere ('to grow together, solidify', from com- + crēscere 'to grow').

конкурент.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from German Konkurrent ('competitor, rival'), from Latin concurrēns (genitive concurrentis), present participle of concurrere ('to run together, clash, compete', from com- 'together' + currere 'to run').

конкурс.etymology: Borrowed via German Konkurs and French concours ('competition, competitive examination', originally 'a running together of candidates') from Latin concursus ('running together, assembly', from concurrere).

конный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic коньныи, from Proto-Slavic *konjьnъ, relational adjective derived from *konjь ('horse', Russian конь) + suffix *-ьnъ.

консистенция.etymology: Borrowed via Polish konsystencja or German Konsistenz from Medieval Latin consistentia ('firmness, density, texture'), derived from Latin consistere ('to stand firm, hold together').

конспирация.etymology: Borrowed via Polish konspiracja or German Konspiration from Latin conspīrātiō ('breathing together, secret plot, conspiracy'); in nineteenth- and twentieth-century Russian underground and intelligence usage it specialized to mean 'clandestine tradecraft, maintaining secrecy and cover'.

консультация.etymology: Borrowed via Polish konsultacja or German Konsultation from Latin consultātiō ('deliberation, seeking of expert advice'), from consultāre ('to take counsel, consult').

контакт.etymology: Borrowed via German Kontakt or French contact from Latin contāctus ('a touching, touch'), derived from contingere, contāctum ('to touch, border on', from com- + tangere 'to touch').

контора.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Dutch kantoor and Low German Kontor ('counting house, merchant's office') from French comptoir ('counting table, counter, agency', from Late Latin computātōrium, built on computāre 'to count').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: контора

контрабанда.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via French contrebande or Italian contrabbando ('smuggling, goods imported in defiance of an official edict'), from Medieval Latin contrābannum (contrā 'against' + bannum 'proclamation, ban').

history.meaning: action contrary to an official ban

контракт.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Kontrakt, Dutch contract, or Polish kontrakt from Latin contractus ('drawing together; agreement, bargain'), from contrahere ('to draw together, conclude an agreement', from com- + trahere 'to draw').

контролировать.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from German kontrollieren (or formed in Russian with -ировать from контроль), from French contrôler ('to verify against a duplicate register, supervise'), from Old French contrerolle ('counter-roll, duplicate ledger used to verify accounts', from contre- + rolle 'scroll, roll').

контроль.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century via French contrôle (or German Kontrolle) from Old French contrerolle ('duplicate register or roll kept to verify the first'), from Medieval Latin contrārotulus (contrā- 'against' + rotulus 'little wheel, scroll, roll').

history.meaning: duplicate scroll used to audit accounts

контрольная.etymology: Substantivized feminine adjective clipped from контрольная работа ('verification paper, school test'), formed with -ный from контроль ('checking, verification'), borrowed from French contrôle (from Old French contrerôle 'duplicate register kept to verify accounts').

history.meaning: test paper -> school test, written exam

конфета.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century (earlier конфекты) via German Konfekt and Polish konfekty from Italian confetto ('candied fruit, sweetmeat, sugar plum'), from Medieval Latin confectum ('something prepared, medicinal preserve or sweetmeat compounded by an apothecary'), neuter past participle of Latin conficere ('to put together, prepare').

конфетка.etymology: Diminutive formed with suffix -ка from конфета ('candy, sweet'), borrowed via German Konfekt and Italian confetto ('sweetmeat, sugared confection') from Medieval Latin confectum ('something prepared', from Latin conficere 'to prepare').

конфиденциально.etymology: Adverbial form of конфиденциальный ('confidential'), borrowed via French confidentiel and German konfidentiell from Latin cōnfīdentia ('trust, confidence', from cōnfīdere 'to trust fully', from com- + fīdere).

конфликт.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via German Konflikt from Latin cōnflīctus ('a striking together, collision, clash'), verbal noun from cōnflīgere ('to strike together, contend', from com- 'together' + flīgere 'to strike').

концепция.etymology: Borrowed via Polish koncepcja, German Konzeption, or French conception from Latin conceptiō ('comprehending, conceiving, formulation'), from concipere ('to take in, conceive', from com- + capere 'to take').

концерт.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Konzert and French concert from Italian concerto ('musical performance, harmony, agreement'), derived from concertāre ('to bring into agreement, harmonize; in Latin, to contend, strive together').

концертный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from концерт ('concert'), borrowed via German Konzert / French concert from Italian concerto ('musical performance, harmony').

концовка.etymology: Formed in Russian from конец (oblique stem конц-, 'end', from Proto-Slavic *konьcь) + the noun suffix -овка: the closing part or finale of a story, performance, or game.

кончаться.etymology: Reflexive and intransitive form of кончать ('to finish, end', iterative of кончить, from конец 'end', Proto-Slavic *konьcь) + -ся.

history.meaning: to end, come to an end

кончено.etymology: Predicative short neuter past passive participle of кончить ('to finish, end'), inherited from Old East Slavic коньчити, from Proto-Slavic *konьčiti (denominative from *konьcь 'end', Russian конец).

кончик.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -чик from конец ('end, tip', with loss of -ец / merger with -чик), inherited from Old East Slavic коньць and Proto-Slavic *konьcь ('end, tip, beginning').

history.meaning: end → very tip, point (кончик носа, кончик пера)

кончиться.etymology: Reflexive and intransitive form of кончить ('to finish, bring to an end', from конец 'end', Proto-Slavic *konьcь) + -ся.

конь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic конь ('horse, steed'), from Proto-Slavic *konjь ('horse', typically reconstructed as *komnь and connected with комонь 'warhorse' or Celtic/Indo-European equine terms).

коньяк.etymology: Borrowed from French cognac, named after the town of Cognac in southwestern France (Charente department), where the double-distilled wine brandy has been produced since the 17th century.

history.meaning: town in Charente → brandy from Cognac

коньячок.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed with suffix -ок (and к > ч) from коньяк ('cognac'), borrowed from French cognac, named after the town of Cognac in southwestern France.

конюшня.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic конюшьня ('horse stable'), derived from конюх ('groom, stableman', from конь 'horse', Proto-Slavic *konjuxъ) + the place suffix -ня (with х > ш).

координация.etymology: Borrowed via French coordination and German Koordination from Medieval/Neo-Latin coordinātiō ('arranging in the same rank or order'), from co- ('together') + Latin ōrdinātiō ('arrangement', from ōrdō 'order, row').

копать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic копати and Proto-Slavic *kopati ('to dig, delve, strike the ground'), from the Proto-Indo-European root *(s)kep- ('to cut, chop, dig').

history.meaning: to dig; (figurative) to dig up dirt on someone, investigate

копаться.etymology: Reflexive form of копать ('to dig'), inherited from Old East Slavic копати, from Proto-Slavic *kopati ('to dig, strike', from PIE *(s)kep- 'to cut, chop, dig') + -ся.

history.meaning: to dig around, rummage; to dawdle

копейка.etymology: Shortened from копейная деньга ('lance coin'), introduced during the monetary reform of Elena Glinskaya (mother of Ivan the Terrible) in 1534–1535. The new silver wire coins minted in Moscow depicted the Grand Prince on horseback holding a lance (**копьё**, from Old East Slavic копие, Proto-Slavic *kopьje 'spear, lance'), distinguishing them from older coins showing a saber.

history.meaning: silver coin stamped with a rider holding a lance (копьё)

копилка.etymology: Formed in Russian from the verb копить ('to save up, accumulate') + the instrument/container suffix -лка (historically past participle -л- + noun suffix -ка), literally 'a container for saving up coins'.

history.meaning: to save up → money box, piggy bank

копировать.etymology: Borrowed via German kopieren (and Polish kopiować) from Medieval Latin cōpiāre ('to transcribe, reproduce in plenty'), from Latin cōpia ('abundance, plenty; transcript, copy').

копить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic копити ('to gather, amass'), from Proto-Slavic *kopiti ('to heap up, gather together'), a denominative verb from *kopa ('heap, stack, shock of grain', preserved in Russian копа and копна 'haystack').

history.meaning: heap, stack → to heap up, amass

копия.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish kopia or German Kopie from Medieval Latin copia ('transcript, reproduction', in Classical Latin 'abundance, plenty, ample supply', via the phrase copiam describendi facere 'to grant permission to transcribe').

копчёный.etymology: Past passive participle / verbal adjective of коптить ('to cure food in smoke, emit soot'), derived from копоть ('soot, lampblack, thick smoke', inherited from Proto-Slavic *kopъtь).

history.meaning: to cure in smoke -> smoked (meat, fish, or cheese)

morphemes.meaning: smoke, soot (from коптить with т -> ч)

копыто.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic копыто, from Proto-Slavic *kopyto ('hoof'), derived with the instrument/body-part suffix *-yto from *kopati ('to dig, paw the ground, strike with the foot').

кораблик.etymology: Diminutive of корабль ('ship, vessel') formed with the masculine diminutive suffix -ик. Old East Slavic корабль entered early Slavic from Byzantine Greek karabion, diminutive of karabos ('light ship, vessel'), preserving the archaic epenthetic -л- after labial б. In Russian кораблик is the classic word for a folded paper boat or small model sailing vessel.

cognates.meaning: light sailing ship (from the same Greek source)

корабль.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic корабль ('ship'), borrowed at an early date (with epenthetic ль after labial б) from Byzantine/Ancient Greek κάραβος / καράβιον ('light ship; originally horned beetle, crab').

коралловый.etymology: Relational and colour adjective formed from коралл ('coral') with suffix -овый. The noun коралл entered Russian via German Koralle and Polish koral from Latin corallium and Ancient Greek korallion ('red Mediterranean coral'). Like English coral, коралловый describes both marine coral and a warm pinkish-orange sunset hue.

корвалол.etymology: Soviet pharmaceutical trade name coined in 1960 at the Kyiv Chemical-Pharmaceutical Plant as an analogue of Valocordin, formed from Latin cor ('heart') + val(eriana) ('valerian', from valēre 'to be strong') + -ол.

кореец.etymology: Derived with the ethnonymic suffix -ец from Корея ('Korea'), borrowed via Western European Corea / Korea from the name of the Korean Goryeo dynasty (高麗 Koryŏ, 918–1392).

корень.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic корень, from Proto-Slavic *korenь (nom. *kory, gen. *korene 'root'), cognate with Lithuanian kẽras ('old tree stump, bush').

кореш.etymology: Russian colloquial/slang noun ('pal, close friend'), originally 19th-century argot; usually explained as an expressive clipping with suffix -ш of коренной (товарищ) ('root/true comrade', from корень 'root').

корешок.etymology: Diminutive in -ок of корень ('root', with stem remodeling корн- → кореш- before -ок), inherited from Old East Slavic корень and Proto-Slavic *korenь ('root'). Extended in bookbinding and stationery to the 'spine' of a book or the 'stub' of a receipt.

history.meaning: root → little root; spine (of a book), ticket stub

корж.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from Ukrainian корж 'flat dry cake, baked disc of dough', used in Russian baking for each baked pastry layer of a layered cake or tart base.

корзина.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic корзина ('wicker basket'), derived from dialectal корз ('woven bark or osier basket'; compare Swedish korg 'basket') or related to корь / кора ('bark, bast strip stripped for weaving').

корзинка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from корзина ('basket').

корзиночка.etymology: Double diminutive formed with the suffix -очка from корзинка / корзина ('basket'); also used in culinary Russian for a shortcrust pastry tartlet shaped like a small basket.

коридор.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French corridor or German Korridor from Italian corridore ('long gallery or passage for running through'), derived from correre ('to run', from Latin currere).

корица.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic корица (Proto-Slavic *korica), a diminutive of кора 'tree bark' — literally 'little bark', because cinnamon sticks are dried rolls of inner bark.
корица.notes: The Russian adjective коричневый 'brown' comes directly from корица ('cinnamon-coloured')!

коричневый.etymology: Formed in 18th-century Russian with suffix -евый from коричный ('cinnamon-coloured'), derived from корица ('cinnamon', itself a diminutive of кора 'bark of a tree', from Proto-Slavic *kora): literally 'bark-cinnamon coloured', which became the standard modern Russian word for 'brown'.

корка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of кора ('tree bark, rind, outer shell'), inherited from Old East Slavic кора and Proto-Slavic *kora ('bark, peel', cognate with Latin corium 'hide, leather, rind').

history.meaning: bark → bread crust, citrus peel, rind

корм.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кърмъ and Proto-Slavic *kъrmъ ('food, fodder, nourishment, provisions').

кормить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кърмити ('to feed, nourish'), from Proto-Slavic *kъrmiti, a denominative verb built on *kъrmъ ('fodder, food, nourishment', Russian корм).

кормиться.etymology: Reflexive form of кормить ('to feed, nourish'), inherited from Old East Slavic кърмити, from Proto-Slavic *kъrmiti (denominative from *kъrmъ 'fodder, food', Russian корм) + -ся.

history.meaning: to eat, feed on, make a living

коробка.etymology: Formed in East Slavic with the diminutive suffix -ка from короб ('bast basket, hamper, crate', from Old East Slavic коробъ, Proto-Slavic *korbъ, related to Latin corbis 'basket'). Originally a small woven bast container, коробка came to name any cardboard, wooden, or metal box.

коробочка.etymology: Double diminutive formed with suffix -очка from коробка / короб ('bast basket, box'), inherited from Old East Slavic коробъ, from Proto-Slavic *korbъ ('basket, box'; cognate with Latin corbis 'basket' and German Korb).

корова.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic корова (with East Slavic pleophony -оро- corresponding to Old Church Slavonic крава), from Proto-Slavic *korva ('cow'), from PIE *ḱr̥h₂-weh₂ ('horned animal', from *ḱerh₂- 'horn'; cognate with Lithuanian kárvė and Latin cervus 'stag').

коровка.etymology: Diminutive formed in Russian with the suffix -ка from корова ('cow', inherited from Old East Slavic корова, Proto-Slavic *korva with East Slavic pleophony -оро-, cognate with Latin cervus 'horned stag').
коровка.notes: Appears in божья коровка ('ladybug', literally 'God's little cow') and as the name of Russia's classic milk-cream fudge sweet («Коровка»).

королева.etymology: Inherited from Late Old East Slavic королева ('queen'), originally a possessive adjective in -ева ('the king's [wife]') formed from король ('king', Proto-Slavic *korľь, derived from the name of the Frankish emperor Charlemagne, Karl / Carolus Magnus).

королевский.etymology: Relational adjective derived from король ('king', from Proto-Slavic *korljь) + the possessive-relational suffix -евский.

королевство.etymology: Formed with the realm/abstract suffix -ство from королев / королевский ('royal, king's'), derived from король ('king', Proto-Slavic *korľь, from the name of Charlemagne, Frankish Karl).

король.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic король (with East Slavic pleophony -оро-), from Proto-Slavic *korljь ('king'), borrowed from the Old High German name Karl ('Charlemagne, Charles the Great', 742–814).

короткий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic коротъкыи ('short', showing East Slavic pleophony -оро-; compare Old Church Slavonic кратъкъ, preserved in краткий 'brief'), from Proto-Slavic *kortъkъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- ('to cut off'), cognate with English short, German kurz, and Latin curtus.

коротко.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic коротъко ('shortly, briefly', with East Slavic pleophony -оро-), from Proto-Slavic *kortъko, adverb of *kortъkъ (Russian короткий 'short', from PIE *(s)ker- 'to cut').

короче.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic короче, the comparative degree of короткий ('short', Old East Slavic коротъкыи, from Proto-Slavic *kortъkъ, comparative *kortje, with East Slavic ч from *tj). In colloquial Russian, короче (short for короче говоря 'speaking more briefly') is ubiquitous as the discourse filler 'in short, anyway, long story short'.

rootFamily.gloss: to stop (Church Slavonic root variant крат-)

корочка.etymology: Double diminutive formed with the suffix -очка from корка ('crust, rind, peel'), itself a diminutive of кора ('bark, rind', from Proto-Slavic *kora).

корпоратив.etymology: Late 20th-century colloquial Russian noun formed by ellipsis/clipping from корпоративный вечер / корпоративный праздник ('corporate party'), from корпоративный ('corporate', from Latin corporātīvus / corporātiō, from corpus 'body').

корпус.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via German Korpus from Latin corpus ('body, frame, structure, substance', from PIE *kwerp- 'body, form'). In Russian корпус denotes the resonant wooden body or case of a piano or violin, the outer case of a pocket watch, the hull of a ship, or a separate building wing on a university campus. It is a direct cognate of English corps, corpse, and corporation.

history.meaning: body/case of an instrument, hull, building wing

коррупционер.etymology: Derived in Russian from коррупция ('corruption', from Latin corruptiō) + the French-modeled agent suffix -онер (on the pattern of функционер, коалиционер).

коррупция.etymology: Borrowed via Polish korupcja and German Korruption from Latin corruptiō ('spoiling, seduction, bribery'), from corrumpere ('to destroy, spoil, bribe', from com- + rumpere 'to break').

коршун.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кършунъ ('kite, bird of prey'), of uncertain further etymology (connected by some scholars with Bulgarian кърша 'to tear, break' or an early steppe borrowing).

косметика.etymology: Borrowed via French cosmétique and German Kosmetik from Ancient Greek κοσμητική (τέχνη) ('the art of dress and adornment'), from κοσμητικός ('skilled in adorning'), from κόσμος ('order, ornament').

космический.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ический from космос ('cosmos, outer space'), borrowed from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, 'order, ornament, the ordered universe') and κοσμικός (kosmikós).

космонавт.etymology: Coined in mid-20th-century Russian (building on spaceflight pioneer Ari Sternfeld's 1930s term космонавтика / French cosmonautique and established globally in April 1961 with Yuri Gagarin's orbital flight) from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, 'universe, cosmos') + ναύτης (naútēs, 'sailor, navigator').

коснуться.etymology: Semelfactive perfective verb in -нуть-ся paired with касаться ('to touch'), inherited from Old East Slavic коснути and Proto-Slavic *kosnǫti ('to touch, brush against'), related by o-grade ablaut to чесать ('to scratch, comb', from *česati).

history.meaning: to touch, brush against (takes genitive case)

коснуться.notes: Like *касаться*, *коснуться* governs the genitive case: *коснуться руки* ('to touch a hand').

костин.etymology: Russian possessive adjective formed with the suffix -ин from Костя, the everyday diminutive of the masculine given name Константин ('Constantine', from Latin Cōnstantīnus 'steadfast, constant').

косточка.etymology: Diminutive formed with suffix -очка from кость ('bone; fruit stone'), inherited from Old East Slavic кость, from Proto-Slavic *kostь (from PIE *kóst-i-s 'bone, rib').

history.meaning: little bone; fruit pit or stone

костыль.etymology: Formed in East Slavic with the tool/object suffix -ыль from кость ('bone', Proto-Slavic *kostь) or the related dialectal verb костить / костылять ('to hobble, peg'): a wooden walking crutch or a heavy L-headed iron railway spike.

history.meaning: crutch; iron spike; (programming slang) quick-and-dirty workaround

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: костыль

кость.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кость, from Proto-Slavic *kostь ('bone'), from Proto-Indo-European *kóst-i-s ('bone, rib'; cognate with Latin costa 'rib' and os 'bone').

костюм.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century from French costume ('customary dress, attire, suit'), which was borrowed from Italian costume ('custom, habit, style of dress'), from Vulgar Latin *cōnsuētūmen (from Classical Latin cōnsuētūdō 'custom, habit').

костюмер.etymology: Borrowed from French costumier ('costume maker, wardrobe master'), derived from costume ('costume, dress', from Italian costume 'custom, habit, dress', from Latin cōnsuētūdō).

костюмчик.etymology: Diminutive formed with suffix -чик from костюм ('suit, costume'), borrowed from French costume, from Italian costume ('custom, fashion, dress', from Latin cōnsuētūdō 'custom, habit').

костёр.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic костьръ (gen. костъра, 'woodpile, stack of logs, tower'), from Proto-Slavic *kostьrъ ('heap, stack of wood'), which shifted in Russian from 'stacked pile of firewood' to 'bonfire'.

косяк.etymology: Derived from косой ('slanting, oblique, crooked', from Proto-Slavic *kosъ) + noun suffix -як (originally 'something set at an angle: doorjamb, wedge-shaped flock of birds or school of fish'; in colloquial slang, 'something gone awry, a blunder or screw-up').

кот.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic котъ ('tomcat'), from Proto-Slavic *kotъ ('cat'), an early European wanderwort borrowed from Late Latin cattus ('domestic cat', likely of Afroasiatic/Nubian origin).

котельная.etymology: Substantivized feminine relational adjective formed from котельный ('boiler [adj.]'), derived from котёл ('cauldron, boiler, kettle', inherited from Old East Slavic котьлъ, from Proto-Slavic *kotьlъ, an early borrowing via Gothic *katils from Latin catillus / catinus 'bowl, deep pot').

котик.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed with the suffix -ик from кот ('tomcat, cat'), which is inherited from Old East Slavic котъ, from Proto-Slavic *kotъ ('cat'), an early European wanderwort matching Late Latin cattus.
котик.notes: Very common in Russian as a tender pet name ('honey, baby') as well as for a cat or a fur seal (морской котик).

котлета.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French côtelette ('rib chop, cutlet'), a diminutive of côte ('rib, side'), from Latin costa ('rib'). In 19th-century Russian cookery the meaning shifted from a bone-in rib cut to a pan-fried cake or patty of minced meat, poultry, or fish.

котлетка.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed with suffix -ка from котлета ('cutlet, patty'), borrowed from French côtelette ('rib chop'), diminutive of côte ('rib'), from Latin costa ('rib').

который.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic которыи ('which of two, which'), from Proto-Slavic *kotorъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *kʷóteros ('which of two', built with the comparative contrast suffix *-tero- on the interrogative stem *kʷo-), directly cognate with English whether, Ancient Greek πότερος, Sanskrit katará, and Lithuanian katràs.
который.notes: Still preserves its older interrogative sense in time expressions: **Который час?** ('What time is it?').

котёл.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic котьлъ ('cauldron, copper kettle'), from Proto-Slavic *kotьlъ, an early Slavic borrowing from Gothic *katils / katilē ('kettle, cauldron', ancestor of English kettle and German Kessel), itself borrowed by Germanic peoples from Latin catīnus / catillus ('deep cooking bowl, dish').

котёнок.etymology: Derived from кот ('tomcat', inherited from Old East Slavic котъ, from Proto-Slavic *kotъ, an early borrowing from Late Latin cattus) + the young-animal suffix -ёнок.

кофе.etymology: Vasmer traces кофе to English coffee or Dutch koffie, and the wider European word family ultimately to Arabic qahwa. He records the older Russian variants кофей and кофий. The immediate borrowing route is therefore presented as an alternative, not a settled single path.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: кофе

кофе.notes: In formal Russian, кофе is masculine and indeclinable: чёрный кофе, крепкий кофе. The stress stays on the first syllable.

кофе-брейк.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English coffee break ('short break for coffee and refreshments during a workday or conference'), compound of coffee (ultimately from Arabic qahwa) + break.

кофеин.etymology: Borrowed via German Koffein (coined in 1820 by chemist Friedlieb Ferdinand Runge as Kaffein) and French caféine, from Kaffee / café ('coffee') + the chemical alkaloid suffix -in (-ин).

кофейный.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ный from the older declinable stem кофей ('coffee', modern кофе, borrowed via Dutch koffie or English coffee, ultimately from Arabic qahwa).
кофейный.notes: Preserves the final -й of the older Russian form кофей (also seen in кофейня 'coffee shop' and кофейник 'coffee pot').

кофейня.etymology: Derived from the stem of кофей / кофейный ('coffee', borrowed in the Petrine era via Dutch koffie from Turkish kahve and Arabic qahwa) + the place suffix -ня (compare Polish kawiarnia).

кофемашина.etymology: Modern Russian compound noun (calquing German Kaffeemaschine / Italian macchina da caffè) formed by combining кофе ('coffee') + машина ('machine, appliance').

кофеёк.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed with suffix -ёк from older/colloquial кофей ('coffee', variant of кофе, borrowed via Dutch koffie from Turkish kahve and Arabic qahwa).

history.meaning: a bit of coffee, nice cup of coffee

кофта.etymology: Borrowed (via Polish kofta or Baltic German) from Early Modern Swedish kofta / Low German kuft ('short coat or jacket'), generally traced to an adaptation of Turkic/Persian kaftan (кафтан).

кошелёк.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ёк from кошель ('woven bag, pouch, purse'), inherited from Old East Slavic кошель, derived from кош ('woven basket', from Proto-Slavic *košь).

кошка.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кошька ('female cat'), a derivative in -ка either from *kotjьka (from котъ 'cat', Proto-Slavic *kotъ) or from кочка.

кошмар.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French cauchemar ('nightmare, oppressive dream'), a compound of Old French caucher ('to trample, press down upon', from Latin calcāre 'to tread with the heel') and mare ('night-goblin, incubus', from Germanic/Dutch mare, cognate with the second element of English nightmare).

коэффициент.etymology: Borrowed via French coefficient and German Koeffizient from New Latin coefficiēns (coined in late 16th-century algebra by François Viète), from co- ('together') + Latin efficiēns ('producing, effecting', from efficere).

краб.etymology: Borrowed via German Krabbe or Dutch krab (and English crab), from Proto-Germanic *krabbō ('crab, crawling crustacean').

крабовый.etymology: Relational adjective derived from краб ('crab', borrowed via German Krabbe or Dutch krab from Middle Low German krabbe) + the adjective suffix -овый.

кража.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кража ('theft', with East Slavic ж from *dj; compare Old Church Slavonic кражда), from Proto-Slavic *kradja, deverbal noun from *krasti (1st sg. *kradǫ 'to steal', Russian красть).

край.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic край and Proto-Slavic *krajь ('cut edge, border, rim'), derived with the o-grade ablaut from the verbal root of кроить ('to cut out, shape'). From the physical edge of an object or garment, the sense extended to a frontier or administrative region.
край.notes: Takes the stressed locative ending -ю after в and на: на краю стола ('on the edge of the table').

крайне.etymology: Adverb formed from the adjective крайний ('extreme, outermost'), which is derived from край ('edge, border, extreme limit'), inherited from Old East Slavic краи and Proto-Slavic *krajь ('edge, cut border', related to кроить 'to cut out').

крайний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic краинии ('situated at the edge, outermost'), from Proto-Slavic *krajьnъjь, relational adjective formed from *krajь ('cut edge, border, rim'), itself an o-grade noun linked to *krojiti ('to cut, slice out').

history.meaning: extreme, endmost, last in a row

крайний.notes: Appears constantly in по крайней мере ('at least', literally 'by the outermost measure'), в крайнем случае ('in an emergency / as a last resort'), and queue etiquette Кто крайний? ('Who is last in line?').

крайность.etymology: Derived from крайний ('extreme, outermost', from край 'edge, border, rim', Old East Slavic краи, Proto-Slavic *krajь, related to *krojiti 'to cut') + the abstract noun suffix -ость.

кран.etymology: Borrowed in the early eighteenth century from Dutch kraan ('crane; tap, spigot') or Low German, where a barrel tap or faucet was named by metaphor after the long curved neck and beak of a crane bird.

краса.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic краса and Proto-Slavic *krasa ('beauty, splendour, bright colour, ornament'), the root noun from which both красивый ('beautiful') and красный ('red', originally 'beautiful, fair') developed.

красавец.etymology: Derived in East Slavic with the masculine personal suffix -ец from краса / красавый ('beauty, handsome', from Proto-Slavic *krasa 'beauty').

красавица.etymology: Formed in Russian with the feminine suffix -ица from красавец ('handsome man') and the older adjective красавый ('beautiful, comely'), derived from краса ('beauty'), from Old East Slavic краса and Proto-Slavic *krasa ('beauty, colour, ornament').

красавчик.etymology: Colloquial and affectionate derivative formed in Russian with the diminutive suffix -чик from красавец ('handsome man', from краса 'beauty').

history.meaning: handsome man -> good-looking guy, charmer; (colloquial praise) legend, good job!

красиво.etymology: Formed as the short neuter and adverbial form of красивый ('beautiful, handsome'), derived from краса ('beauty, adornment', Proto-Slavic *krasa) with the suffix -о.

красивый.etymology: Formed in East Slavic with the suffix -ивый from краса ('beauty, splendour', from Proto-Slavic *krasa). As older красный ('beautiful, bright') specialized into the colour word 'red' during the Middle Russian period, красивый took over the primary meaning 'beautiful, handsome'.

краситель.etymology: Formed in Russian with the agent/instrument suffix -тель from красить ('to paint, dye, color'), derived from краса ('beauty, bright color', in Old East Slavic especially 'red or bright color', from Proto-Slavic *krasa).

history.meaning: to dye, color → dye, coloring agent

красить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic красити and Proto-Slavic *krasiti, originally meaning 'to adorn, beautify, embellish' (from *krasa 'beauty, bright colour'), which specialized in Russian to 'to apply paint or dye'.
красить.notes: First-person singular shows consonant mutation с -> ш: я крашу ('I paint').

краска.etymology: Formed in Russian with the suffix -ка from красить ('to colour, paint, dye, adorn'), derived from краса ('beauty, bright colour', from Proto-Slavic *krasa).

красно-золотой.etymology: Compound colour adjective joining красно- (from красный 'red', originally 'beautiful, bright', Proto-Slavic *krasьnъ) + золотой ('golden', from золото 'gold', Proto-Slavic *zolto).

красный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic красьныи ('beautiful, fair, bright'), derived from краса ('beauty', from Proto-Slavic *krasa). In Russian, starting in the 15th–16th centuries, 'beautiful, radiant' specialized into the primary colour word 'red' (replacing older червлёный and багряный), while the older sense 'beautiful' survives in Красная площадь ('Red/Beautiful Square') and красивый.

красота.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic красота and Proto-Slavic *krasota ('beauty, splendour'), formed from краса (*krasa 'beauty') + the abstract noun suffix -ота.

красотка.etymology: Derived from красота ('beauty', from краса 'beauty, ornament', Proto-Slavic *krasa) + the feminine person suffix -ка.

красочно.etymology: Adverbial form of красочный ('colorful, vivid'), derived from краска ('paint, dye, color', from краса / красный, Proto-Slavic *krasa).

красть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic красти (1sg. краду), from Proto-Slavic *krasti (*kradǫ, 'to steal'), an ancient Slavic verb whose deeper Indo-European connections remain uncertain (Vasmer notes comparisons with Old Irish crod 'booty, cattle' as tentative).

краткий.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кратъкъ ('short, brief'; compare native East Slavic pleophonic короткий), from Proto-Slavic *kortъkъ ('short', from PIE *(s)ker- 'to cut').

креативно.etymology: Adverbial form of креативный ('creative'), borrowed in the late 20th century from English creative (from Latin creātīvus, from creāre 'to create').

креативный.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English creative (and German kreativ), from Medieval/New Latin creātīvus, derived from Latin creāre ('to create, bring forth, produce').

креветка.etymology: Borrowed from French crevette ('shrimp, prawn') and adapted to Russian feminine declension with -ка; French crevette comes from Norman dialect crevette / Old French chevrette ('little she-goat', diminutive of chèvre from Latin capra, comparing a shrimp's long antennae and darting leaps to a kid goat).

кредит.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Kredit and French crédit from Italian credito ('trust, commercial credit, loan'), from Latin crēditum ('something entrusted, a loan'), neuter past participle of crēdere ('to believe, trust, entrust').

крем.etymology: Borrowed from French crème ('cream, custard, cosmetic cream'), which blends Late Latin chrisma ('anointing oil, ointment', from Greek khrisma) with Gaulish *krama ('milk cream').
крем.notes: In Russian, fresh liquid dairy cream for coffee or cooking is сливки, whereas крем refers to whipped cake filling or cosmetic cream.

крем-суп.etymology: Culinary compound modeled on French soupe à la crème / English cream soup, combining крем ('cream', from French crème) and суп ('soup', from French soupe).

history.meaning: thick puréed soup enriched with cream

кремовый.etymology: Relational and colour adjective formed with the suffix -овый from крем ('cream, custard, frosting'), borrowed from French crème ('cream', from Late Latin chrisma 'unguent' blended with Gaulish *crama 'cream').

крепиться.etymology: Reflexive form of крепить ('to strengthen, fasten'), inherited from Old East Slavic крѣпити, from Proto-Slavic *krěpiti (denominative from *krěpъ / *krěpъkъ 'strong, firm', Russian крепкий) + -ся.

history.meaning: to hold on, stay strong; to be fastened

крепкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic крѣпъкъ / крѣпъкыи ('strong, firm, sturdy, steadfast'), from Proto-Slavic *krěpъkъ, an extension in *-ъkъ of *krěpъ ('strong, solid'), cognate with Old Norse hræfa ('to endure') and Welsh craff ('firm, strong'). Used for sturdy objects, strong tea or coffee (крепкий кофе, крепкий чай), and sound sleep (крепкий сон).

крепко.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic крѣпъко, the adverbial and short neuter form of крепкий ('strong, firm, sturdy', Proto-Slavic *krěpъkъ).
крепко.notes: Used idiomatically in крепко спать ('to sleep soundly').

крепость.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic крѣпость ('strength, firmness; stronghold, fortress'), derived from крѣпыи (крепкий 'strong, firm', Proto-Slavic *krěpъ) + abstract suffix -ость.

кресло.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кресло / кръсло ('armchair, seat frame'), from Proto-Slavic *kreslo ('chair with a back or arms, wooden frame').

крестоносец.etymology: Compound noun calquing Medieval Latin crucifer ('cross-bearer'), formed from крест ('cross', Old East Slavic крьстъ, Proto-Slavic *krьstъ) + linking vowel -о- + -носец ('bearer', from носить 'to carry, wear'): a medieval knight who sewed a cloth cross onto his garment for the Crusades.

крещение.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic крьщениѥ ('baptism, christening', with Church Slavonic щ from *tj), verbal noun from крьстити ('to baptize, mark with a cross'), from крьстъ ('cross, Christ', Proto-Slavic *krьstъ, borrowed from Old High German Christ, from Latin Chrīstus, Ancient Greek Χριστός 'anointed one').

кривляться.etymology: Reflexive iterative verb derived from кривить ('to bend, twist, distort'), from кривой ('crooked, wry', from Proto-Slavic *krivъ) + -ся.

history.meaning: to make faces, grimace, clown around

криво.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krivo, the adverbial and short neuter form of кривой ('crooked, curved, askew', Proto-Slavic *krivъ, cognate with Lithuanian kreivas 'crooked').

кривой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кривыи, from Proto-Slavic *krivъ ('crooked, bent, curved'; cognate with Lithuanian kreĩvas and Latvian krievs, from PIE *(s)krey- 'to turn, bend').

криворукий.etymology: Compound adjective formed from кривой ('crooked', Proto-Slavic *krivъ) + linking vowel -о- + рука ('hand, arm', Proto-Slavic *rǫka), literally 'crooked-handed'.

кризис.etymology: Borrowed via German Krisis and Latin crisis from Ancient Greek κρίσις (krísis, 'turning point in a disease, decision, judgment'), derived from κρίνω (krínō, 'to separate, decide, judge').

history.meaning: medical or political turning point, crisis

крик.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic крикъ ('shout, cry, clamour'), from Proto-Slavic *krikъ, an expressive/imitative noun built on the Indo-European root *(s)kreyk- ('to shriek, cry out'; cognate with Lithuanian krykštauti 'to shriek' and English shriek / screech).

криминал.etymology: Borrowed via German Kriminal- and Polish kryminał from Medieval Latin crīminālis ('pertaining to crime'), from Latin crīmen (gen. crīminis, 'judicial charge, indictment, offense, crime').

критик.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Kritiker or French critique from Latin criticus, itself from Ancient Greek κριτικός (kritikós, 'able to discern or judge'), derived from κρίνω (krínō, 'to separate, decide, judge').

history.meaning: judge of literature or art, critic

критиковать.etymology: Borrowed via Polish krytykować (and German kritisieren / French critiquer), derived from critique ('criticism, critic'), via Latin criticus from Ancient Greek κριτικός ('able to discern or judge', from κρίνω 'to separate, judge').

критический.etymology: Borrowed via German kritisch and French critique (adapted with the Russian suffix -еский) from Latin criticus, from Ancient Greek κριτικός ('decisive, critical, able to judge', from κρίνω 'to judge, decide').

кричать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кричати (present кричу, кричиши), from Proto-Slavic *kričati ('to shout, cry out'), formed with suffix *-ěti (where *k + *ě > чa) from the root of крик ('shout, cry', Proto-Slavic *krikъ).

кровавый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кръвавыи, from Proto-Slavic *krъvavъ ('bloody, blood-stained'), derived from *kry (gen. *krъve 'blood', Russian кровь, from PIE *krewH-) + suffix *-avъ.

кроватка.etymology: Diminutive formed with suffix -ка from кровать ('bed'), inherited from Old East Slavic кровать, borrowed from Byzantine Greek κραββάτι(ον), from Ancient Greek κράββατος ('couch, pallet, low bed').

кровать.etymology: Borrowed into Old East Slavic кровати / кровать from Byzantine Greek κράββατος (krábbatos, genitive κραββάτου; Modern Greek κρεβάτι, 'bedstead, couch').

кровь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кры (accusative кръвь, which replaced the old nominative, just as in любовь and церковь), from Proto-Slavic *kry (genitive *krъve, 'blood'), from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂- ('raw flesh, clotted blood, gore'; compare Lithuanian kraũjas 'blood', Sanskrit kravíṣ- 'raw flesh', Latin cruor 'blood from a wound' / crūdus 'raw', and English raw).

крокодил.etymology: Known in Old East Slavic as коркодилъ and reshaped in modern Russian after Latin crocodīlus and Ancient Greek κροκόδειλος (krokódeilos, originally 'lizard of the stone wall', applied by Greek travellers in Egypt to the Nile crocodile).

крокодилий.etymology: Possessive adjective formed with suffix -ий from крокодил ('crocodile'), borrowed via Church Slavonic крокодилъ (Old East Slavic коркодилъ) and Latin crocodīlus from Ancient Greek κροκόδειλος ('lizard; Nile crocodile').

крокодиловый.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -овый from крокодил ('crocodile').

кролик.etymology: Borrowed via Polish królik ('rabbit', literally 'little king'), a partial calque of Middle High German küniclîn (modern German Kaninchen), which reshaped Latin cunīculus ('rabbit') by folk etymology after künic ('king').

кроме.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кромѣ ('outside, apart from, except'), frozen locative singular of крома ('edge, border, partition, crust of bread'), from Proto-Slavic *kroma ('edge, border, cut-off piece').

history.meaning: on the outside, apart from, except

крошечный.etymology: Derived in Russian from крошка ('crumb, tiny bit', diminutive of кроха 'crumb', Proto-Slavic *kroxa) with the adjectival suffix -ечный (with ш from х): literally 'crumb-sized, tiny'.

крошка.etymology: Diminutive formed with suffix -ка (and х > ш) from кроха ('crumb, tiny bit'), inherited from Old East Slavic кроха, from Proto-Slavic *kroxa ('crumb, bit', related to *kruxъ 'piece' and *krъšiti 'to crumble').

круассан.etymology: Borrowed from French croissant ('crescent; crescent-shaped flaky pastry'), originally the present participle of croître ('to grow, wax, as the waxing crescent moon'), from Latin crēscere ('to grow'). The Viennese crescent roll (Kipferl) was popularized in Paris in the 19th century as the croissant.

круг.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кругъ ('circle, disk, wheel'), from Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ ('circle, ring'), cognate with Proto-Germanic *hringaz (the ancestor of English ring and German Ring).

кругло.etymology: Formed as the short neuter and adverbial derivative of круглый ('round', from Proto-Slavic *krǫglъ, built on *krǫgъ 'circle').

круглосуточно.etymology: Adverbial form of круглосуточный ('round-the-clock, 24-hour'), compound derived from круглые сутки ('a full 24-hour day'), from круглый ('round, whole', Proto-Slavic *krǫglъ) + сутки ('24-hour period', originally 'junction of day and night').

history.meaning: around the clock, 24 hours a day

круглый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic круглыи (Old Church Slavonic крѫглъ, 'round'), from Proto-Slavic *krǫglъ, derived with the adjectival suffix *-lъ from *krǫgъ ('circle, disk, ring', modern Russian круг, related to Proto-Germanic *hringaz 'ring').

круговой.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -овой from круг ('circle'), from Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ.

кругом.etymology: Adverb and preposition lexicalized from the instrumental singular of круг ('circle'), inherited from Old East Slavic кругъ, from Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ ('circle, ring').

кружиться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive form of кружить ('to circle, whirl, spin'), a denominative verb formed from круг ('circle, wheel, disk', with г > ж before -и-), inherited from Old East Slavic кругъ and Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ ('circle, ring', cognate with Old Norse hringr and English ring).

history.meaning: circle → to move in a circle
to spin, whirl; (голова кружится) to feel dizzy

кружка.etymology: Borrowed in Middle Russian (via Polish kruż and diminutive krużka) from Middle High German krūse ('earthenware jug, mug, tankard', related to English cruse).
кружка.notes: Note stress contrast: кружка ('mug') vs. кружка (genitive singular of кружок, 'small circle').

кружок.etymology: Diminutive formed with suffix -ок (and г > ж) from круг ('circle', inherited from Old East Slavic кругъ, from Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ); the sense 'study group, hobby club' calques German Kreis and French cercle.

крупнейший.etymology: Superlative/elative form in -ейший of крупный ('large, major; originally coarse-grained'), derived from крупа ('groats, coarse grain', from Proto-Slavic *krupa).

крупно.etymology: Adverbial form of крупный ('large, big, coarse'), derived from крупа ('groats, coarse grain', from Proto-Slavic *krupa).

history.meaning: coarsely; on a large scale, big time

крупный.etymology: Derived with the adjectival suffix -ный from крупа ('groats, coarse crushed grain', from Old East Slavic крупа and Proto-Slavic *krupa 'coarse grain, lump, hailstone'): originally 'coarse-grained, consisting of large granules' (as in крупная соль 'coarse salt'), then 'large, big, major'.

history.meaning: large, big; coarse (of salt, sand, grain)

крутить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic крутити and Proto-Slavic *krǫtiti ('to twist, twirl, turn'), a causative-iterative verb related to *krǫtъ ('twisted, steep', Russian крутой).

крутиться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of крутить ('to twist, twirl, turn'), inherited from Old East Slavic крутити and Proto-Slavic *krǫtiti ('to twist, whirl, turn').

history.meaning: to turn → to spin, revolve, turn

круто.etymology: Adverb and short neuter form of крутой ('steep, sharp, hard-boiled; stern; cool, awesome'), inherited from Old East Slavic круто, from Proto-Slavic *krǫto ('tightly twisted, steeply, severely').

крутой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic крутъ ('steep, swift, stern'), from Proto-Slavic *krǫtъ ('twisted, tightly wound, steep, severe'), originally related to *krǫtiti ('to twist, whirl', Russian крутить). From 'tightly twisted, steep, hard-boiled (яйцо вкрутую)' developed the senses 'stern, tough' and modern colloquial 'cool, awesome'.

крушить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic крушити, from Proto-Slavic *krušiti ('to break into pieces, crumble, smash', causative/denominative from *kruxъ 'lump, fragment').

крыло.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic крило / крыло, from Proto-Slavic *kridlo ('wing'), formed with the instrument suffix *-dlo from PIE *(s)krey- ('to turn, move in an arc, skim').

крылышко.etymology: Diminutive formed with suffix -ышко from крыло ('wing', from Proto-Slavic *kridlo).

крыльцо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic крыльце ('little wing; entrance porch'), originally a diminutive of крыло ('wing', Proto-Slavic *kridlo) applied to the projecting roofed side-flight of steps attached like a wing to a wooden house.

крыса.etymology: Attested in Russian from the 16th–17th centuries (earlier крыса / криса; compare dialectal кртыса and Lithuanian kirstùkas 'shrew'). Vasmer connects it with the Proto-Slavic root *krt- / *krys- ('to gnaw, cut, burrow', related to крот 'mole' and Lithuanian kir̃sti 'to cut, bite'). In Russian criminal and prison slang, крыса also means a 'mole, traitor who steals from or informs on his own group'.

крыть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic крыти ('to cover, roof, hide'), from Proto-Slavic *kryti ('to cover'), cognate with Lithuanian krūti / krauti ('to pile up, stack, cover').

крыша.etymology: Formed in East Slavic from крыть ('to cover, roof', from Old East Slavic крыти, Proto-Slavic *kryti) with the rare noun suffix -ша (compare польша/крыша). Literally 'that which covers a house'.

крышка.etymology: Formed in Russian as a diminutive and instrument noun from крыша ('roof, covering') and the verbal root of крыть ('to cover', Proto-Slavic *kryti): 'a small cover or lid'.

крючок.etymology: Diminutive of крюк 'hook' with suffix -ок. Old East Slavic крюкъ was borrowed from Old Norse krokr 'hook, bend' (the same Scandinavian source that gave English crook).

крёстный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic крьстьныи ('relating to the baptismal cross'), formed with -ный from крест ('cross; baptism', Proto-Slavic *krьstъ); in крёстный отец ('godfather', or substantivized крёстный) and крёстная мать ('godmother') it denotes kinship through baptism.
крёстный.notes: Pronounced with ё in the baptismal sense (крёстный отец 'godfather'), whereas крестный with е is used in church phrases like крестный ход ('procession of the cross').

кстати.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase к стати ('to the proper fit, proportion, or occasion'), from the preposition к ('to') and the dative singular of стать ('form, build, stature, fitting moment', derived from стать 'to stand, become', Proto-Slavic *statь). From meaning 'fittingly, at an opportune moment' (это очень кстати), it also grammaticalized into the discourse marker 'by the way, speaking of which'.

history.meaning: to the proper fit or occasion, opportunely

кто.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic къто ('who'), from Proto-Slavic *kъto, formed from the Indo-European interrogative stem *kʷo- / *kʷú- ('who', cognate with English who, Latin quī, Lithuanian kàs, and Sanskrit kás) extended with the demonstrative particle *-to.

кто-нибудь.etymology: Formed in Russian by attaching the indefinite enclitic particle -нибудь (originally a clause ни будь 'be it whoever it may be', from ни + imperative будь of быть 'to be') to the interrogative pronoun кто ('who').

кто-то.etymology: Formed in Russian by attaching the indefinite enclitic particle -то (historically the neuter demonstrative pronoun то 'that') to the interrogative pronoun кто ('who'), creating an indefinite pronoun for a specific but unidentified person ('someone, somebody').
кто-то.notes: Use **кто-то** when a real person is involved whose identity you don't know (*Кто-то звонит* 'Someone is ringing'); use **кто-нибудь** for 'anyone at all' in questions or requests.

кубик.etymology: Formed in Russian from куб ('cube') with the masculine diminutive suffix -ик; куб was borrowed via German Kubus or French cube from Latin cubus and Ancient Greek kybos ('six-sided die, cube').
кубик.notes: Used for toy building blocks (детские кубики), dice, and diced food (нарезать кубиками 'to cut into small cubes').

кувалда.etymology: Borrowed via Belarusian or Ukrainian ковадло and Polish kowadło ('blacksmith's anvil', from Proto-Slavic *kovadlo, built on *kovati 'to forge' + instrument suffix *-dlo), undergoing consonant metathesis (-дл- -> -лд-) and shifting in Russian from 'anvil' to 'heavy two-handed blacksmith's sledgehammer'.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: кувалда

кувшин.etymology: Recorded in East Slavic from the 15th–16th centuries. Vasmer connects it with an eastern trade borrowing (compare Tatar and Chuvash küpšä / küvšän 'wooden or clay vessel' or Persian kūza) or with Baltic relatives (Lithuanian kaušìnis 'dipper, ladle', from káušas 'wooden scoop', the source of Russian ковш).

куда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic куды / куда ('whither, where to'), from Proto-Slavic *kǫda / *kuda, a directional adverb built on the interrogative stem *k- ('what, where', PIE *kʷo-) + directional suffix *-da (correlative with туда 'there' and сюда 'here').

куда-нибудь.etymology: Indefinite adverb formed from куда ('whither, where to', from Proto-Slavic *kǫda) + the indefinite particle -нибудь (contracted from ни буди 'whatever it may be', 2nd/3rd sg. imperative of быть 'to be').

куда-то.etymology: Indefinite directional adverb formed in Russian from куда ('where to, whither', from Old East Slavic куда and Proto-Slavic *kǫda) + the indefinite enclitic particle -то (historically the neuter demonstrative pronoun то, Proto-Slavic *to).

кудесник.etymology: Derived with the personal agent suffix -ник from Old East Slavic кудесъ (plural кудеса, 'sorcery, magic charms, wonders'), an unpalatalized/ablaut relative of чудо (stem чудес-, Proto-Slavic *čudo 'wonder, miracle').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: кудесник

кудри.etymology: Plural of archaic singular кудря, inherited from Proto-Slavic *kǫdŕa ('curl, lock of curly hair', with regular development of nasal *ǫ > Russian у; compare Polish kędzior 'curl').

кукарекать.etymology: Onomatopoeic verb derived from the interjection кукареку ('cock-a-doodle-doo', imitating a rooster's crow) + verbal suffix -ать.

кукловод.etymology: Compound noun formed from кукла ('puppet, doll', borrowed from Byzantine Greek κούκλα 'doll') + linking vowel -о- + the stem of водить ('to lead, guide', from Proto-Slavic *voditi).

кулак.etymology: Inherited from late Old East Slavic кулакъ ('fist'), borrowed from a Turkic language (compare Turkic qol 'arm, hand' and derivatives in -aq).

кулинарный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from кулинар / кулинария ('culinary art, cookery'), borrowed in the 19th century via German kulinarisch / French culinaire from Latin culīnārius ('pertaining to the kitchen'), from culīna ('kitchen').

кулон.etymology: Borrowed from French coulant ('sliding neck ornament, pendant on a chain'), substantivized present participle of couler ('to flow, slide, glide'), from Latin cōlāre ('to strain, filter').

history.meaning: sliding gem or pendant on a neck ribbon

культура.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century via German Kultur and French culture from Latin cultūra ('tilling, cultivation; education and refinement of the mind'), derived from colere ('to till, cultivate, tend, inhabit').

культурно.etymology: Adverbial form of культурный ('cultured, civilized, polite'), derived from культура ('culture'), borrowed via German Kultur from Latin cultūra ('tilling, cultivation, education', from colere).

культурный.etymology: Formed from культура ('culture, cultivation') with the adjectival suffix -ный. Russian культура was borrowed via German Kultur from Latin cultura ('tilling, cultivation, refinement of the mind'), from colere ('to tend, cultivate, inhabit', PIE *kwel- 'to move around, tend'). In conversational Russian культурный means not only 'cultural' (as in heritage), but also 'civilized, orderly, well-mannered'.

купидон.etymology: Borrowed via French Cupidon from Latin Cupīdō (gen. Cupīdinis, 'Cupid, Roman god of love; literally passionate desire'), derived from cupere ('to desire, long for').

купить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic купити ('to buy, trade'), from Proto-Slavic *kupiti, an early Slavic borrowing from Gothic kaupōn ('to trade, traffic, buy'; compare German kaufen and English cheap, originally 'market, bargain'), which Germanic peoples had borrowed from Latin caupō ('innkeeper, small retailer, wine-merchant').

купюра.etymology: Borrowed from French coupure ('cut, excision; detached printed banknote or bond'), derived from couper ('to cut', from coup 'blow, cut').

history.meaning: cut; printed banknote of a given denomination

курган.etymology: Borrowed into Old East Slavic (курганъ) from Kipchak/Polovtsian Turkic qurğan ('fortified mound, earthwork, burial tumulus', derived from Turkic qur- 'to build, erect, fortify').

history.meaning: ancient burial mound, tumulus, memorial hill

cognates.meaning: prehistoric steppe burial mound (borrowed from Russian)

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: курган

куриный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the animal-possessive suffix -иный from кура / куры ('hen, chickens'), inherited from Old East Slavic кура / куръ ('rooster'), from Proto-Slavic *kurъ / *kura, of onomatopoeic origin imitating a bird's crowing.
