курить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic курити and Proto-Slavic *kuriti ('to make smoke, burn incense, smoulder, distil'); when tobacco entered Russia in the seventeenth century, курить табак ('to burn/smoke tobacco') became its dominant everyday sense.

курица.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic курица ('hen, chicken'), formed with the feminine suffix -ица from куръ ('rooster, cock', preserved in курятник 'henhouse' and the proverb попасть как кур во щи), from Proto-Slavic *kurъ ('rooster'), an onomatopoeic formation imitating the bird's crowing.

куропатка.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic куропатка (altered by folk etymology after лапка / патка from older куропъть / куроптва), from Proto-Slavic *kuropъty ('partridge', compound of *kurъ 'rooster, fowl' + *pъta 'bird', literally 'hen-bird').

курочка.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed with suffix -очка from кура / курица ('hen, chicken'), inherited from Old East Slavic кура / курица, feminine of куръ ('rooster', from onomatopoeic Proto-Slavic *kurъ).

курс.etymology: Borrowed via German Kurs, Dutch koers, and French cours from Latin cursus ('running, course, direction, voyage'), from currere ('to run'); the idiom быть в курсе ('to be in the know') calques French être au courant.

history.meaning: course, exchange rate; (в курсе) in the know

куртка.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from Polish kurtka ('short jacket'), diminutive of kurta, which came from Latin curtus ('short, shortened, cropped').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: куртка

курьер.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (first recorded in 1701) via German Kurier or Polish kurier from French courrier and Italian corriere ('messenger, runner'), derived from Latin currere ('to run').

курящий.etymology: Present active participle of курить ('to smoke; originally to burn incense, make smoke'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *kuriti ('to smoke, smolder'), used as an adjective and noun ('smoker').

кусать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кусати and Proto-Slavic *kǫsati ('to bite', iterative of *kǫsiti, with nasal *ǫ > Russian у), related to кусок ('bitten-off piece, morsel').

кусаться.etymology: Reflexive form of кусать ('to bite'), inherited from Old East Slavic кусати, from Proto-Slavic *kǫsati (iterative of *kǫsiti 'to bite, take a piece', related to кусок 'piece') + -ся.

history.meaning: to bite, be in the habit of biting

кусок.etymology: Formed with the diminutive suffix -ок from older Russian кус ('bite, morsel, piece'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *kǫsъ ('bitten-off piece'), which belongs to the same root as кусать ('to bite', Proto-Slavic *kǫsati).
кусок.notes: Drops the fleeting vowel -о- in all oblique forms: кусок -> куска, куску.

кусочек.etymology: Double diminutive formed in Russian with suffix -ек from кусок ('piece, bit, slice', itself formed with -ок from older кус 'bite, morsel', Old East Slavic кусъ, from Proto-Slavic *kǫsъ 'bitten-off piece', related to кусать 'to bite', cognate with Lithuanian kąsti 'to bite').

куст.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic кустъ and Proto-Slavic *kǫstъ ('bush, shrub, dense cluster of stems', with nasal *ǫ > у), connected by Vasmer with Lithuanian kuokštas ('tuft, handful, bush').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: куст

кухня.etymology: Vasmer records кухня from 1717, with поварня used earlier. He traces the borrowing through Polish and Czech to an Old High German word for kitchen, ultimately from Latin coquina. The Russian word belongs to a much-travelled European kitchen-word family.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: кухня

кухонный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from кухня ('kitchen', inserting a fleeting о inside the stem кухн-), which entered Russian in the early eighteenth century via Polish kuchnia and Old High German kuchina from Late Latin coquīna ('kitchen').

куча.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic куча and Proto-Slavic *kuča ('heap, stack, haycock').

history.meaning: pile, heap; (colloquial) a ton of, lots of

кушать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic кушати / покушати ('to taste, try, test, experience'), from Proto-Slavic *kušati (iterative of *kusiti 'to taste, try', an early borrowing from Gothic kausjan 'to taste, test', from the same root as вкус 'taste' and искусство). From 'tasting or sampling food and drink', кушать became a polite or deferential verb for 'to eat' (traditionally used when inviting guests to eat — Кушайте, пожалуйста! — or when speaking to children).

history.meaning: to eat (polite invitation or with children)

кушать.notes: In careful standard Russian, adults usually say **я ем** (from **есть**) about themselves rather than *я кушаю*, reserving **кушать** for polite invitations (**Кушать подано!**, **Кушайте!**) and children.

лаборатория.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin laboratorium 'workshop, place of scientific work', built on Latin laborare 'to work, take pains' from labor 'toil, effort'.

лавка.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лавъка, diminutive of лава ('long wooden bench along a wall or outside a house', from Proto-Slavic *lava, cognate with Lithuanian lóva 'bedstead'). Because medieval merchants displayed their wares on wooden benches in the market rows, лавка came to mean both 'wooden bench' and 'small shop, stall'.

history.meaning: wooden bench; market stall, small shop

ладить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ладити and Proto-Slavic *laditi ('to put in order, bring into harmony'), a denominative verb from лад (*ladъ 'harmony, peace, order, musical mode').

history.meaning: order, harmony -> to make harmonious, arrange
to get along well with; to tune or mend

ладно.etymology: Originally the short neuter and adverbial form of ладный ('harmonious, well-fitted, in good order'), derived from лад ('harmony, peace, agreement; musical mode', Proto-Slavic *ladъ).

ладонь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic долонь (via metathesis д-л -> л-д in Russian) and Proto-Slavic *dolnь ('palm of the hand, flat surface'), related to *dolъ ('hollow, valley, bottom') from the cupped hollow of the open hand.
ладонь.notes: Notice how Ukrainian долоня and Polish dłoń keep the original d...l consonant order, whereas Russian swapped them to ладонь.

ладошка.etymology: Colloquial diminutive formed with suffix -ка from ладоша / ладонь ('palm of the hand'), inherited from Old East Slavic долонь (with metathesis д-л > л-д), from Proto-Slavic *dolnь ('palm, flat surface', related to дол 'valley').

лажануться.etymology: Colloquial/slang reflexive perfective verb formed with suffix -нуться from лажать / лажа ('blunder, bum note, falsehood').

лажать.etymology: Colloquial/slang verb (originally musicians' and underworld argot meaning 'to play out of tune, lie, bungle'), derived from лажа ('lie, bum note, blunder', connected with dialectal and argot derivatives of лгать / ложь 'lie').

history.meaning: to mess up, blunder, play false

лазанья.etymology: Borrowed from Italian lasagna (plural lasagne 'flat pasta sheets, layered baked pasta dish'), from Vulgar Latin *lasania, from Latin lasanum ('cooking pot'), from Ancient Greek λάσανον ('trivet, stand for a pot').

лазарет.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Lazarett and French lazaret from Italian lazzaretto ('Venetian quarantine hospital'), a blend of Santa Maria di Nazareth (the Venetian island where a plague hospital was established in 1423) with Saint Lazarus (Лазарь, patron saint of lepers and the sick).

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: лазарет

лазить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лазити, from Proto-Slavic *laziti ('to climb, crawl about'), lengthened o-grade iterative counterpart of *lězti ('to climb, crawl', Russian лезть).

лайк.etymology: Borrowed in the early 21st century from English like (the social-media approval button and count), from Old English līcian ('to please, be like or suitable').

лайкнуть.etymology: Twenty-first-century internet Russian verb formed from лайк ('a social-media like', borrowed from English like) + the single-action verbal suffix -нуть.

history.meaning: a 'like' -> to click 'like' on a post or photo

лак.etymology: Borrowed in the early eighteenth century via German Lack or Dutch lak from Italian lacca ('resinous varnish'), which traces back through Medieval Latin and Arabic lakk to Prakrit and Sanskrit lakṣā ('lac insect; red resinous shellac').

лактоза.etymology: Borrowed from French lactose (coined in 19th-century chemistry by Jean-Baptiste Dumas), formed from Latin lac (stem lact-, 'milk') + the chemical sugar suffix -ose (-оза).

лампа.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via German Lampe (or French lampe) from Latin lampas ('torch, oil lamp'), from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, 'torch, beacon'), derived from λάμπω ('to shine').

лампочка.etymology: Formed in Russian as the diminutive (with suffix -очка) of лампа ('lamp', borrowed via German Lampe / French lampe from Ancient Greek λαμπάς 'torch, lamp'). Originally 'a small icon-lamp or oil lamp', and since the late 19th century the standard everyday word for an electric lightbulb.

ланч.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English lunch ('midday meal', shortened from luncheon).

лапа.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лапа, from Proto-Slavic *lapa ('paw, broad flat hand or foot'; cognate with Lithuanian lópa 'paw', Latvian lãpa, and Gothic lofa 'palm of the hand').

лариса.etymology: Russian feminine given name Лариса, borrowed via Church Slavonic from Ancient Greek Λάρισα (Lárisa), the name of the ancient Thessalian city and of the early Christian martyr Saint Larissa, often connected in Greek folk tradition with λάρος ('seagull').

history.meaning: city in Thessaly; Christian saint's name

ласково.etymology: Adverbial form of ласковый ('affectionate, tender, gentle'), derived from ласка ('caress, affection, kindness', from Old East Slavic ласка, Proto-Slavic *laska).

ласковый.etymology: Derived from ласка ('caress, tenderness, kindness', inherited from Old East Slavic ласка, from Proto-Slavic *laska) + the adjective suffix -овый.

ласточка.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ластовица / ласточька, from Proto-Slavic *lastovica / *lastъka ('swallow'), formed from the root *lasta ('swallow', connected with fluttering flight).

латте.etymology: Borrowed from Italian (caffè) latte ('espresso with steamed milk', literally 'coffee milk'), from latte ('milk'), from Latin lac (acc. lactem 'milk').

латунный.etymology: Formed in Russian with the relational suffix -ный from латунь ('brass'), which entered Russian in the 17th century via German Latun or Italian/French laton / laiton ('brass, latten', from Medieval Latin lātonem).

латунь.etymology: Borrowed via Middle High German latūn ('brass') from Old French laton (modern French laiton 'brass'), generally traced via Medieval Latin or Romance to Arabic lāṭūn ('copper, brass').

лацкан.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from German Latz / Lätzchen ('bib, flap, folded breast-piece of a coat'), diminutive of Middle High German laz ('flap, cord,elace'), which itself came from Old French laz and Latin laqueus ('noose, snare, lace'). In Russian tailoring terminology лацкан settled as the standard word for the folded front lapel of a suit jacket or overcoat.

левый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣвый and Proto-Slavic *lěvъ ('left, originally curved or awkward'), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂iwos, cognate with Latin laevus and Ancient Greek laios ('left').

легально.etymology: Adverbial form of легальный ('legal'), borrowed via German legal and French légal from Latin lēgālis ('pertaining to the law', from lēx, gen. lēgis 'law').

легальный.etymology: Borrowed via German legal and French légal (adapted with suffix -ный) from Latin lēgālis ('pertaining to the law, lawful'), derived from lēx (gen. lēgis 'law').

легенда.etymology: Borrowed via German Legende or Polish legenda from Medieval Latin legenda ('things to be read', originally narratives of saints' lives appointed to be read aloud at church services, from Latin legere 'to read'); in twentieth-century intelligence jargon it also came to mean an undercover operative's fabricated biography ('cover story').

history.meaning: legend; map key; undercover cover story

легко.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic легъко ('lightly, easily'), short neuter singular and adverb of лёгкий ('light in weight; easy', from Proto-Slavic *lьgъkъ, continuing PIE *h₁lengʷʰ-u- 'light, nimble'; cognate with English light, Latin levis, and Sanskrit laghú). Pronounced [lʲɪxˈko] ('лехко').

легковерный.etymology: Compound adjective formed from легко ('easily', from лёгкий 'light, easy', Proto-Slavic *lьgъkъ) + верить / вера ('belief, trust', Proto-Slavic *věra) + -ный, calquing German leichtgläubig and French crédule.

легкомысленно.etymology: Adverb in -о from легкомысленный ('light-minded, frivolous, reckless'), a compound calquing German leichtsinnig / French léger d'esprit, built from лёгкий ('light in weight') + linking vowel -о- + мысль ('thought, mind').

ледяной.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ледяныи ('made of ice, ice-cold'), formed with the material suffix -яной from лёд ('ice', stem лед-, from Old East Slavic ледъ, Proto-Slavic *ledъ, cognate with Lithuanian lẽdas 'ice').

лежать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лежати (present лежу, лежиши), from Proto-Slavic *ležati ('to be lying down'), a stative verb in *-ěti built on the Proto-Indo-European root *legʰ- ('to lie down'), directly cognate with English lie, German liegen, and Latin lectus ('bed').
лежать.notes: Russian uses **лежать** for any object resting flat on a surface (*ключи лежат на столе* 'the keys are on the table').

лезвие.etymology: Derived in East Slavic (older Russian лезвеё / лезвие) from the root of лезть ('to climb, penetrate, work its way in', Proto-Slavic *lězti): originally the sharp edge of an axe or knife wedge that 'enters' the wood.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: лезвие

лезть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣзти (present лѣзу), from Proto-Slavic *lězti ('to climb, crawl, creep'), cognate with Latvian lēzēt ('to slide, creep') and Old Prussian līse ('crawls'). In colloquial Russian, лезть also means 'to barge in, meddle, stick one's nose into' (не лезь не в своё дело).

history.meaning: to climb, reach into; to intrude, meddle

лейка.etymology: Derived from the present/imperative stem лей- of лить ('to pour', inherited from Old East Slavic лити, from Proto-Slavic *liti) + the instrument suffix -ка.

лейтенант.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th–18th century via German Leutnant from French lieutenant ('deputy, officer acting in place of a superior'), a compound of lieu ('place', from Latin locus) + tenant ('holding', present participle of tenir 'to hold', from Latin tenēre), literally 'place-holder'.

лекарственный.etymology: Derived from лекарство ('medicine, remedy', from лекарь 'healer, physician', from Proto-Slavic *lěkarjь, from *lěkъ 'cure, medicine', an early borrowing from Gothic lēkeis 'physician') + suffix -енный.

лекарство.etymology: Derived with suffix -ство from лекарь ('healer, physician'), inherited from Old East Slavic лѣкарь, from Proto-Slavic *lěkarь (derived from *lěkъ 'medicine, cure', an early borrowing from Gothic lēkeis 'physician').

лекция.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via Polish lekcja or German Lektion from Latin lēctiō ('a reading aloud, academic discourse'), derived from legere ('to read').

ленивый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣнивыи, from Proto-Slavic *lěnivъ ('lazy, sluggish'), derived from *lěnь ('laziness, sloth', Russian лень) + the adjective suffix *-ivъ.

лента.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лента ('woven strip of bast, linen ribbon'), which Vasmer connects with an early Slavic derivative or borrowing related to лён ('flax, linen', Proto-Slavic *lьnъ, or Latin linteum 'linen cloth, strip').

лентяй.etymology: Formed in Russian from лень ('laziness, sloth', inherited from Proto-Slavic *lěnь) + the expressive personal noun suffix -тяй.

лень.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣнь ('laziness, sloth'), from Proto-Slavic *lěnь, abstract noun from the adjective *lěnъ ('slow, idle, lazy'; cognate with Lithuanian lė̃nas 'slow, calm' and Latin lēnis 'gentle, slow').

леопард.etymology: Borrowed via Western European languages and Latin leopardus from Ancient Greek λεόπαρδος ('leopard'), compound of λέων ('lion') + πάρδος ('panther, pard'), from the ancient belief that the leopard was a cross between a lion and a panther.

лепесток.etymology: Diminutive in -ок of dialectal and older Russian лепест ('leaf, petal, thin flap'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *lepestъ ('leaf, petal, flake'), built on an expressive Balto-Slavic root *lep- ('to flutter, peel, leaf'; compare лист and Lithuanian lapas 'leaf').

history.meaning: leaf, flap → flower petal; thin flake (of almonds or pastry)

лепет.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лепетъ and Proto-Slavic *lepetъ ('babble, murmur, fluttering sound'), built on the onomatopoeic root *lep- imitating soft, indistinct lip movements.

лепить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣпити and Proto-Slavic *lěpiti ('to stick, smear, mould out of clay or wax'), a causative/factitive verb ablaut-related to льнуть and липнуть (*lьpěti 'to cling, stick').

history.meaning: to mould, sculpt (dumplings, clay, snowmen); to stick on

лес.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣсъ and Proto-Slavic *lěsъ ('woodland, forest, timber'). Vasmer compares Old English lēah ('woodland glade, clearing', modern English -ley in place names and meadow lea).
лес.notes: Takes the stressed locative -у after в: в лесу ('in the woods').

лесбиянка.etymology: Derived with the feminine person suffix -ка from лесбиянин / лесбийский ('Lesbian, of Lesbos'), via French lesbienne and Latin Lesbius from Ancient Greek Λέσβιος ('inhabitant of the island of Lesbos, home of the poet Sappho').

леска.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of older Russian леса ('plaited fishing line or wicker fish-weir'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *lěsa ('plaited wattling, braided cord').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: леса

лестница.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣствица / лѣстница, from Proto-Slavic *lěstvica, built on the verb лезть (*lězti, 'to climb'). Literally 'something for climbing'; the middle т is silent in modern pronunciation ('lesnitsa').

летать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣтати, from Proto-Slavic *lětati ('to fly repeatedly or in various directions'), lengthened-grade iterative of *letěti ('to fly', Russian лететь).

лететь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic летѣти and Proto-Slavic *letěti ('to fly, move swiftly through the air'). Represents the unidirectional ('flying in one direction right now') partner of летать.
лететь.notes: First-person singular has т -> ч mutation: я лечу, ты летишь.

летний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣтьнии (Proto-Slavic *lětьnьjь), the relational adjective derived from лето ('summer; year') with the soft adjectival suffix -ний.

history.meaning: relating to summer or the year

лето.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣто and Proto-Slavic *lěto ('warm season, summer; year'). Because Slavic peoples counted time by warm seasons, the plural лета still serves as the genitive plural ('years') of год (пять лет 'five years').

летом.etymology: Grammaticalized instrumental singular of лето ('summer; in Old East Slavic also year'), inherited from Old East Slavic лѣто, from Proto-Slavic *lěto ('warm season, summer, year').

летопись.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣтопись ('yearly chronicle, annals'), a compound calque of Byzantine Greek χρονογραφία: formed from лѣто ('summer; year', Proto-Slavic *lěto) + linking -о- + -пись (from писать 'to write').

лечение.etymology: Verbal noun formed with the suffix -ение from лечить ('to treat medically, heal'), inherited from Old East Slavic лѣчити, from Proto-Slavic *lěčiti ('to cure, heal'), derived from *lěkъ ('medicine, remedy'; compare Gothic lēkeis 'physician').

лечить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣчити ('to heal, cure, treat'), from Proto-Slavic *lěčiti, a denominative verb from *lěkъ ('medicine, remedy, healing charm'; preserved in лекарство 'medicine', Polish lek 'medicine', and Czech lék). Most etymologists (including Vasmer) trace *lěkъ to an early borrowing from Gothic lēkeis ('physician, healer'; compare Old English lǣċe 'physician', archaic English leech). In modern Russian slang, лечить кого-то also means 'to lecture, feed tall tales, try to talk someone into something'.

history.meaning: to treat medically; (slang) to lecture, spin a yarn

лечиться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed from лечить ('to treat medically, heal', from Old East Slavic лѣчити, Proto-Slavic *lěčiti, built on *lěkъ 'medicine, cure', an early Proto-Slavic borrowing from Germanic *lēkijaz 'healer, physician') + -ся.

history.meaning: to treat -> to undergo medical treatment, take a cure

лечь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лечи (future лягу, ляжеши; past леглъ > лёг; Old Church Slavonic лещи), from Proto-Slavic *legti ('to lie down', with nasal infix *lęg- in the present/future stem), continuing Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- ('to lie down', cognate with English lie and lay).
лечь.notes: Future tense uses the stem **ляг- / ляж-**: **я лягу, ты ляжешь, они лягут**; past tense **он лёг, она легла**.

лжец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic лъжьць ('liar'), derived from лъжь (ложь 'lie, falsehood; lying', from Proto-Slavic *lъžь, from *lъgati 'to lie') + the agent suffix -ец (*-ьcь).

ли.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ли and Proto-Slavic *li, an enclitic interrogative and disjunctive particle ('whether, or') placed immediately after the focused word in a yes/no question.
ли.notes: Always stands second in its clause, right after the word being questioned: Знаешь ли ты? ('Do you know?').

либо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic либо ('or, either'), phonetically reduced in unstressed position from любо ('as you please, pleasing', short neuter of любыи 'dear, pleasing', from Proto-Slavic *ljubъ, PIE *lewbʰ- 'to love, desire').

ливень.etymology: East Slavic derivative formed from the stem of лить / ливать ('to pour', from Proto-Slavic *liti) + the noun suffix -ень.

лидер.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth–twentieth centuries from English leader ('head of a political party, movement, or sporting race', derived from the verb to lead).

rootFamily.gloss: to lead, be in the lead

лизнуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective verb formed with suffix -нуть from лизать ('to lick'), inherited from Old East Slavic лизати, from Proto-Slavic *lizati, from PIE *leyǵʰ- ('to lick').

history.meaning: to give a lick, lick once

ликвидировать.etymology: Borrowed via German liquidieren from Medieval Latin liquidāre ('to make clear, settle accounts, wind up an estate or business', from Latin liquidus 'clear, fluid'); in twentieth-century Russian its meaning broadened from 'winding up an enterprise' to 'abolishing, eradicating, or eliminating'.

history.meaning: to wind up a business; to eliminate

лимон.etymology: Borrowed via Early Modern European trade routes (Italian limone or German Limone) from Arabic laymūn and Persian līmūn ('citrus fruit, lemon'), ultimately of South Asian origin.

лимонад.etymology: Borrowed via German Limonade and French limonade from Italian limonata ('lemon drink'), derived from limone ('lemon', borrowed via Arabic laymūn from Persian līmūn).

лимонный.etymology: Formed in Russian from лимон ('lemon') with the relational adjectival suffix -ный.

лимончик.etymology: Diminutive formed with suffix -чик from лимон ('lemon'), borrowed via Italian limone / Greek λεμόνι / Turkish limon from Arabic laymūn and Persian līmūn.

лимузин.etymology: Borrowed from French limousine ('enclosed luxury car; originally a hooded cloak worn by shepherds in the Limousin region of central France, named after the city of Limoges').

линейка.etymology: Derived in Russian from линия ('line', via Polish linijka) with the suffix -ейка: originally a ruled guide line, and hence the straight-edged ruler used to draw or measure lines.

линия.etymology: Borrowed via Polish linia or German Linie from Latin līnea ('linen thread, plumb line, drawn stroke'), itself derived from līnum ('flax, linen', because builders snapped a taut linen string to mark a straight line).

липа.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic липа and Proto-Slavic *lipa ('linden, lime tree'), derived from the Proto-Slavic root *lip- ('to stick, adhere') after the tree's sticky, mucilaginous inner bark (bast) and sweet sap.
липа.notes: The German city name Leipzig comes from the Slavic name Lipsk ('place of linden trees').

липкий.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lipъkъ ('sticky, adhesive'), built on the verbal root of льнуть / липнуть ('to stick, cling', Proto-Slavic *lьpěti / *lipnǫti).

липовый.etymology: Derived from липа ('linden tree') with the adjectival suffix -овый: 'relating to or made from linden (such as linden-blossom tea, honey, or soft carving wood)'.
липовый.notes: In colloquial Russian, липовый also acquired the slang sense 'fake, forged' (from soft linden wood used to carve counterfeit seals).

липучка.etymology: Formed in colloquial Russian with the suffix -учка from липнуть / липкий ('to stick, sticky', inherited from Proto-Slavic *lьpěti / *lьpnǫti): originally flypaper or a sticky plant bur, and in modern everyday Russian a Velcro hook-and-loop fastener (застёжка-липучка).

history.meaning: to stick -> sticky strip, flypaper, Velcro

лирика.etymology: Borrowed via German Lyrik or French lyrique from Latin lyricus and Ancient Greek lyrikos ('sung to the lyre, lyric poetry'), from lyra ('lyre'). Beyond its literary meaning of 'lyric poetry', colloquial Russian uses лирика (especially in без лирики or никакой лирики) to mean 'emotional sentimentality, poetic mush' as opposed to practical action.

history.meaning: lyre → poetry sung to the lyre

лист.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic листъ and Proto-Slavic *listъ ('tree leaf; flat sheet'), cognate with Lithuanian laiškas ('leaf; letter'). In modern Russian the two meanings split their plurals: листья for tree leaves and листы for sheets of paper or metal.

history.meaning: leaf; sheet of paper or metal

лист.notes: Plural is листья for leaves on trees, but листы for sheets of paper or baking trays.

листать.etymology: Denominative verb formed in Russian from лист ('leaf of a tree; sheet or page of paper', inherited from Old East Slavic листъ and Proto-Slavic *listъ).

history.meaning: sheet, page → to leaf through, turn pages

листик.etymology: Diminutive formed in Russian with the suffix -ик from лист ('leaf of a plant; sheet of paper', inherited from Old East Slavic листъ, Proto-Slavic *listъ).

history.meaning: leaf; sheet of paper -> little leaf; small slip or sheet of paper

листок.etymology: Formed in Russian from лист ('leaf; sheet of paper') with the masculine diminutive suffix -ок: 'a small leaf' or 'a slip/sheet of paper'.
листок.notes: Drops the fleeting -о- in declined forms: листок -> листка.

листочек.etymology: Double diminutive formed with -ек from листок ('small leaf; sheet of paper', with к → ч before -ек), itself the diminutive in -ок of лист ('leaf; sheet of paper', from Old East Slavic листъ and Proto-Slavic *listъ).

history.meaning: leaf, sheet → small leaf; slip of paper

литература.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via Polish literatura or German Literatur from Latin litterātūra ('writing, grammar, learning, scholarship'), derived from littera ('letter of the alphabet; plural litterae, written works').

литр.etymology: Borrowed from French litre (introduced in 1795 in the French metric system from older French litron, a grain measure), via Medieval Latin litra from Ancient Greek λίτρα (lítra, a Sicilian unit of weight and volume).

лить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лити and Proto-Slavic *liti ('to pour, cast molten metal'), from Proto-Indo-European *leyH- ('to pour, flow', cognate with Lithuanian lieti 'to pour').

лифт.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th / early 20th century from British English lift ('elevator'), from the verb lift ('to raise', from Old Norse lypta, Proto-Germanic *luftijaną).

лифчик.etymology: Diminutive formed with suffix -чик from лиф ('bodice, waist of a garment'), borrowed from Dutch lijf or Low German līf ('body; bodice, waist', cognate with German Leib 'body').

лицевой.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -евой from лицо ('face; front or right side of cloth, a building, or a page'), inherited from Old East Slavic лице and Proto-Slavic *lice ('face, cheek, outward appearance').

history.meaning: face, front → front, facing, obverse (лицевая сторона 'front side')

лицо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лице and Proto-Slavic *lice ('face, cheek, outward appearance, person'), originally a diminutive or derivative of *likъ ('visage, countenance, image', preserved in Russian лик).

лично.etymology: Adverbial form in -о of личный ('personal'), derived from лицо ('face, person', from Old East Slavic лице and Proto-Slavic *lice).

личность.etymology: Coined in 18th-century Russian from личный ('personal', from лицо 'face, person', Proto-Slavic *lice) + the abstract noun suffix -ость, as a calque of German Persönlichkeit and French personnalité.

личный.etymology: Derived from лицо ('face; person, individual', Old East Slavic лице, Proto-Slavic *lice) with palatalization of ц > ч before the adjectival suffix -ный. As лицо developed the legal and grammatical sense 'person, individual' (influenced by Old Church Slavonic translating Greek πρόσωπον), личный came to mean 'personal, private, individual'.

лишать.etymology: Imperfective of лишить ('to deprive, bereave'), inherited from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic лишити, from Proto-Slavic *lišiti (denominative from *lixъ 'left over, deprived, bad', Russian лихой).

лишаться.etymology: Reflexive form of лишать ('to deprive', from Proto-Slavic *lišiti / *lišati) + -ся.

лишение.etymology: Borrowed from or modeled on Old Church Slavonic лишениѥ ('deprivation, loss, want'), verbal noun from лишити ('to deprive', from Proto-Slavic *lišiti).

лишить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лишити and Proto-Slavic *lišiti ('to deprive of, bereave, leave without'), derived from the adjective *lixъ (archaic Russian лихой 'bereft, excessive, odd, evil').

history.meaning: left over, bereft -> to deprive of
to deprive of, strip of (rights, a licence, an inheritance)

лишний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лижьнии / лишнии ('exceeding, superfluous, extra'), derived from лихо / лихой ('excess, surplus, over-measure', from Proto-Slavic *lixъ 'left over, excessive, odd-numbered', continuing PIE *leykʷ-s-o- from *leykʷ- 'to leave over'; cognate with Ancient Greek λείπω and Latin linquō / reliquus).

morphemes.meaning: excess, left over (from лихо, with х → ш)

лишь.etymology: Restrictive particle shortened from older Russian and Old East Slavic лише ('more, beyond; only'), originally the comparative form of *lixъ ('excessive, remaining over beyond a limit', related to лишний 'extra' and лишить 'to deprive').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: лишь

лоб.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лъбъ (genitive лъба, 'skull, crown of the head, forehead'), from Proto-Slavic *lъbъ (in West Slavic 'skull, head', as in Polish łeb), connected by Vasmer with Proto-Indo-European *lewp- ('peeled bark, shell, skull-cap').
лоб.notes: Has a fleeting **о** that drops in all oblique forms: **лоб**, but **на лбу**, **со лба**.

лобби.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English lobby ('hotel entrance hall, foyer; political pressure group originally meeting in the parliamentary lobby'), from Medieval Latin lobia / laubia ('covered gallery', of Frankish origin *laubijā).

лобовой.etymology: Relational adjective derived from лоб (gen. лба, 'forehead', inherited from Old East Slavic лъбъ 'skull, forehead', from Proto-Slavic *lъbъ) + suffix -овой.

ловить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ловити ('to hunt, catch, fish'), from Proto-Slavic *loviti, a denominative verb from *lovъ ('hunting, catch, prey').

ловкость.etymology: Derived from ловкий ('deft, agile, adroit', originally 'skilled at catching/hunting', derived from лов / ловить 'to catch, hunt', Proto-Slavic *lovъ) + the abstract noun suffix -ость.

ловушка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the instrument/noun suffix -ушка from ловить ('to catch, hunt, trap', from Old East Slavic ловити, Proto-Slavic *loviti, derived from ловъ 'hunt, catch').

логика.etymology: Borrowed via Latin logica (and German Logik / Polish logika) from Ancient Greek λογική (τέχνη) ('the art of reasoning'), from λογικός ('pertaining to speech or reason'), from λόγος ('word, speech, reason').

логический.etymology: Borrowed via German logisch / Latin logicus (adapted with the Russian suffix -еский) from Ancient Greek λογικός ('pertaining to reason or speech', from λόγος 'word, reason').

логично.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate from логичный ('logical, consistent'), derived from логика ('logic'), borrowed via Latin logica from Ancient Greek λογική (logikḗ, 'the art of reasoning'), built on λόγος (lógos, 'word, reason, account').

логичный.etymology: Formed in Russian with the adjective suffix -ный from логика ('logic', or adapted from French logique / German logisch), ultimately from Ancient Greek λογικός (logikós, 'of speech or reason'), derived from λόγος (lógos, 'word, reckoning, reason').

логотип.etymology: Borrowed via French logotype or German Logotyp (and English logotype), coined in early nineteenth-century typography from Ancient Greek λόγος (lógos, 'word') + τύπος (túpos, 'impression, cast type'): originally a single piece of metal type cast with a whole word or emblem, later a company logo.

лодка.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лодъка, diminutive of лодья (ладья 'boat, ship'), from Proto-Slavic *oldi / *oldьja ('dugout canoe, boat'; cognate with Lithuanian aldijà and Old Norse alda 'wave, trough').

ложечка.etymology: Diminutive formed in Russian with the suffix -ечка from ложка ('spoon', inherited from Old East Slavic лъжька, Proto-Slavic *lъžьka / *lъžica).
ложечка.notes: Also appears in the anatomical phrase под ложечкой ('in the pit of the stomach', e.g., сосёт под ложечкой 'a hollow, anxious feeling in the pit of one's stomach').

ложиться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of ложить ('to lay, place'), inherited from Old East Slavic ложитисѧ, from Proto-Slavic *ložiti sę ('to lay oneself down', causative of *ležati 'to lie').

history.meaning: to lie down, go to bed

ложка.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лъжька ('spoon'), from Proto-Slavic *lъžьka (diminutive of *lъga). Vasmer compares Albanian lugë ('spoon') and traces the root to carving or hollowing out wood (wooden spoons were traditional across Rus').

ложный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лъжьныи and Proto-Slavic *lъžьnъ ('false, untruthful'), formed with the adjectival suffix -ный from ложь ('lie, falsehood', Old East Slavic лъжь, Proto-Slavic *lъžь, cognate with English lie and German Lüge).

ложь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лъжь ('lie, falsehood'), from Proto-Slavic *lъžь, a feminine i-stem noun derived from the root of лгать ('to lie', Old East Slavic лъгати, Proto-Slavic *lъgati), from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ- ('to tell a lie'; exact cognate with German Lüge and English lie).

лом.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ломъ ('breaking, windfall timber, pry bar, scrap'), a deverbal o-grade noun from ломить / ломать ('to break, fracture'), from Proto-Slavic *lomъ. As a tool, a лом is a heavy iron bar for breaking ice, stone, or prying.

history.meaning: breaking; heavy pry bar; broken pieces

ломать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ломати, iterative of ломить ('to break'), from Proto-Slavic *lomati / *lomiti ('to break, fracture', o-grade of an older verb preserved in OCS лємити).

ломаться.etymology: Formed in Russian by adding the reflexive-intransitive clitic -ся to ломать ('to break', Proto-Slavic *lomati, iterative of *lomiti): 'to break on its own, break down, get out of order'.

ломбард.etymology: Borrowed via German Lombard and French lombard ('pawnbroker's shop'), named after medieval Italian bankers and moneylenders from Lombardy (Italian Lombardia, from Late Latin Langobardia 'land of the Lombards').

ломтик.etymology: Diminutive in -ик of ломоть (genitive ломтя, 'cut or broken slice of bread'), derived from ломить / ломать ('to break off'), from Proto-Slavic *lomъtь ('broken-off piece').

лопата.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лопата, from Proto-Slavic *lopata ('shovel, spade, broad paddle'), derived with suffix *-ata from *lopa ('broad flat blade'; cognate with Lithuanian lópeta 'spade').

лосось.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лосось, from Proto-Slavic *lososь ('salmon'), from Proto-Indo-European *laḱs- ('salmon, trout'; cognate with Lithuanian lašišà, German Lachs, Old English leax).

лось.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лось, from Proto-Slavic *olsь ('elk, moose'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ól-ḱ-i-s ('elk, deer'; cognate with Old Norse elgr, German Elch, English elk, and related to Russian олень).

лотерейный.etymology: Relational adjective derived from лотерея ('lottery', borrowed via French loterie and Dutch loterij from Italian lotteria, from lotto 'lot, share', of Germanic origin *hlaut-) + suffix -ный.

лотерея.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via French loterie, German Lotterie, or Dutch loterij from Italian lotteria, built on lotto ('lot, share, prize', of Frankish origin *hlot, cognate with English lot).

лошадь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лошадь (attested since 1111, alongside diminutive лоша), borrowed from a Turkic word for a pack-horse or gelding (compare Tatar/Kipchak alaša 'gelding, workhorse', or *alaša at 'pack-horse', adapted with the East Slavic suffix -адь).

луг.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лугъ and Proto-Slavic *lǫgъ ('low-lying riverside meadow, water-meadow, grove', with regular East Slavic denasalization of *ǫ > у; compare Polish łęg 'water-meadow').

лужица.etymology: Diminutive in -ица of лужа ('puddle, pool'), inherited from Old East Slavic лужа, from Proto-Slavic *luža ('puddle, marshy pool', related to *lugъ 'water-meadow').

лузер.etymology: Borrowed in the late twentieth century as a colloquial slang noun from English loser ('one who loses or fails chronically', agent noun from to lose).

лук.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лукъ and Proto-Slavic *lukъ ('onion, leek'), an early pan-Slavic borrowing from Proto-Germanic *laukaz ('leek, garlic, onion', the ancestor of English leek and German Lauch).
лук.notes: A collective singular in Russian (резать лук 'to chop onions'); a homonym лук ('bow for arrows') is a native Slavic word from *lǫkъ ('bend, curve').

луковый.etymology: Relational adjective derived from лук ('onion', inherited from Old East Slavic лукъ, from Proto-Slavic *lukъ, an early borrowing from Proto-Germanic *laukaz 'leek, onion') + suffix -овый.

луна.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic луна ('moon'), from Proto-Slavic *luna ('moon, moonlight'), from Proto-Indo-European *lewk-s-neh₂ ('the shining one', from *lewk- 'light, bright'; exact cognate with Latin lūna).

луч.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лучь ('ray of light, beam; resinous pine torch'), from Proto-Slavic *lučь, continuing the Proto-Indo-European root *lewk- ('bright, light, shine'), cognate with Latin lūx ('light') and English light.

лучше.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лучше / луче ('better'), the comparative adverb and predicate counterpart of лучший ('better, best'), serving as the suppletive comparative of хорошо ('well') and хороший ('good').

лучший.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лучшии / лучии ('better, best'), originally a comparative/superlative adjective from a Proto-Slavic stem *luč- ('hitting the mark, fitting, auspicious'; compare получить 'to receive' and случай 'chance, occasion'). Serves as the suppletive superlative ('best') and comparative ('better') of хороший ('good').

лыжа.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лыжа ('ski, snowshoe'), from a Proto-Slavic root *lyz- / *lyž- ('to glide, slide, slip'; compare Russian лызнуть 'to slip away').

лысина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лысина ('bald spot, white blaze on an animal's forehead'), derived from лысый ('bald', from Proto-Slavic *lysъ, from PIE *lewk-s-o- 'shining, white') + suffix -ина.

лысый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic лысыи ('bald; having a white forehead blaze'), from Proto-Slavic *lysъ ('bald, bare, gleaming'), derived from the Proto-Indo-European root *lewk- ('light, bright, shining'; compare луч 'ray' and луна 'moon'), originally describing a shining bare scalp or a white blaze on an animal's forehead.

cognates.meaning: having a white blaze on the forehead

льгота.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic льгота and Proto-Slavic *lьgota ('ease, relief from taxes or duties, exemption'), formed with the abstract suffix -ота from the root *lьg- ('light, easy', seen in лёгкий < *lьgъkъ 'light' and польза < Old East Slavic польга 'benefit'): literally 'a lightening of one's burden'.

cognates.meaning: grace period, deadline (originally tax-free period for new settlers)

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: льгота

льняной.etymology: Material adjective formed from лён ('flax, linen', genitive льна with fleeting vowel ё) + suffix -яной. Russian лён descends from Old East Slavic льнъ and Proto-Slavic *lьnъ ('flax'), from PIE *lino- ('flax'). It is directly cognate with English linen, line (originally a spun flaxen cord), and Latin linum.

льстить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic льстити and Old Church Slavonic льстити ('to deceive, cajole, flatter'), derived from лесть ('flattery; in older Slavic, guile or deceit'), from Proto-Slavic *lьstь, an early borrowing from Proto-Germanic *listiz ('cunning, skill, craft', compare German List).

любезно.etymology: Adverb from the short neuter of любезный ('kind, obliging, gracious, dear'), borrowed from Church Slavonic любезьныи ('beloved, affectionate, courteous'), built on the root of любовь / любить ('love / to love', from Proto-Slavic *ľubъ).

любезный.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic любезьнъ ('beloved, dear, kind'), formed from obsolete любезнь ('love, affection', compare болезнь from боль), derived from любить / милый ('to love', Proto-Slavic *ľubъ).

любимый.etymology: Originally the present passive participle formed with suffix -им-ый from любить ('to love, like', from Proto-Slavic *ľubiti): literally 'being loved, beloved', and in everyday usage 'favourite' (любимый кофе 'favourite coffee').

любитель.etymology: Derived from любить ('to love, be fond of', inherited from Old East Slavic любити, from Proto-Slavic *ljubiti, PIE *lewbʰ-) + agent suffix -тель; the sense 'amateur, enthusiast' calques French amateur and German Liebhaber.

любить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic любити (present люблю, любиши), from Proto-Slavic *ľubiti ('to love, hold dear'), a denominative verb from *ľubъ ('dear, pleasing'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ- ('to care for, desire, love'), directly cognate with English love, German lieben, Latin lubet / libīdō, and Sanskrit lúbhyati.

любоваться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed in East Slavic from любовать (built on любый / любовь 'dear, pleasing, love', Proto-Slavic *ľubъ) + -ся: 'to take pleasure in looking at, gaze admiringly upon'.

history.meaning: to admire, feast one's eyes on

любоваться.notes: Takes the instrumental case of the person or view being admired: любоваться закатом ('to admire the sunset').

любовник.etymology: Formed with the personal noun suffix -ник from любовный ('amorous, relating to love'), derived from любовь ('love', Old East Slavic любы, oblique stem любъв-, Proto-Slavic *ľuby).

любовница.etymology: Feminine counterpart of любовник ('lover'), formed with the feminine agent suffix -ница from любовный ('amorous, of love'), derived from любовь ('love', Old East Slavic любы / любовь, Proto-Slavic *ľuby).

любовь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic любы (accusative любовь, which replaced the old nominative, just as in кровь and морковь), from Proto-Slavic *ľuby (genitive *ľubъve, 'love, affection'), from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ- ('to care, desire, love'; cognate with English love, German Liebe, and Sanskrit lúbhyati 'desires').
любовь.notes: When used as a common noun ('love'), the vowel **о** is fleeting in oblique cases (**любви**, **любовью**); in the female given name **Любовь**, the **о** is retained throughout (**у Любови**).

любой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic любыи ('dear, pleasing, whichever one pleases'), from Proto-Slavic *ľubъ ('dear, beloved', cognate with любить 'to love' and English lief / love). From phrases like на любой выбор ('whichever pleases you') it grammaticalized into the determiner 'any'.

любопытно.etymology: Adverb and predicate from любопытный ('curious, inquisitive; interesting'), an East Slavic compound of любо- ('fond of, eager to', from *ľubъ 'dear, fond') + пытать ('to inquire, question, probe, test', from Proto-Slavic *pytati; compare вопрос / попытка): literally 'eager to inquire'.

любопытный.etymology: Compound adjective formed from любо- ('fond of, eager', from любый / любить, Proto-Slavic *ljubъ) + the stem of пытать ('to ask, inquire, investigate', from Proto-Slavic *pytati) + suffix -ный, literally 'eager to inquire'.

любопытство.etymology: Formed in Russian with the abstract noun suffix -ство from любопытный ('curious, inquisitive'), a compound of любо- ('fond of', from любый / любить) + пытать ('to ask, inquire, probe', Proto-Slavic *pytati): literally 'eagerness to inquire and find out'.

любящий.etymology: Adjectival present active participle of любить ('to love'), from Old East Slavic любити, from Proto-Slavic *ľubiti ('to love'), derived from *ľubъ ('dear, beloved').

люкс.etymology: Borrowed from French luxe ('luxury, elegance'), from Latin luxus ('excess, extravagance, luxury').

люстра.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French lustre ('chandelier; luster, gloss'), from Italian lustro, from Latin lūstrāre ('to illuminate, brighten').

ля.etymology: Borrowed via Italian and French musical solfège from the sixth syllable of Guido d'Arezzo's 11th-century hymn Ut queant laxis, where the phrase Labii reatum ('guilt of the lips') began on the sixth degree of the hexachord. In Russian musical usage, ля is an indeclinable neuter noun naming the pitch A (440 Hz above middle C), as in ля минор ('A minor').

history.meaning: sixth solfège syllable in Guido d'Arezzo's hymn

cognates.meaning: sixth note of the solfège scale

лёгкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic льгъкыи and Proto-Slavic *lьgъkъ ('light in weight; easy'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ-u-s, cognate with English light and Latin levis.
лёгкий.notes: Pronounced [лёхкий], with г devoicing and spirantizing to [х] before к.

лёд.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ледъ and Proto-Slavic *ledъ ('ice'), with exact Baltic cognates in Lithuanian ledas and Latvian ledus ('ice').
лёд.notes: Drops the vowel ё -> ь in oblique forms: лёд -> льда, на льду ('on the ice').

м.etymology: The fourteenth letter of the Russian Cyrillic alphabet (named эм in modern Russian, and мыслѣте 'think!' in the traditional Old Church Slavonic acrostic alphabet), adapted from the Greek letter mu (Μ, μ), ultimately from Phoenician mem ('water').

history.meaning: the letter M; standard abbreviation for метр ('metre') or минута

маг.etymology: Borrowed via Latin magus and Ancient Greek μάγος (mágos, 'Magian priest, magician, wizard'), from Old Persian maguš.

магазин.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via French magasin (or German Magazin / Italian magazzino, originally 'storehouse, warehouse, granary') from Arabic makhāzin (مخازن, plural of makhzan 'storehouse, treasury', from khazana 'to store up'). In 19th-century Russian магазин shifted from a wholesale storehouse to a retail shop or store (while English magazine specialized in a periodical 'storehouse' of articles).

магия.etymology: Borrowed via Polish magia or directly from Latin magia, from Ancient Greek μαγεία (mageía, 'magic, sorcery'), derived from μάγος (mágos, 'magician').

history.meaning: theology of the Magi; magic, sorcery

магнат.etymology: Borrowed via Polish magnat or German Magnat from Late Latin magnās, magnātis ('great man, nobleman'), derived from Latin magnus ('great, large').

магнитный.etymology: Derived from магнит ('magnet') + adjectival suffix -ный; магнит comes via Ancient Greek μαγνῆτις λίθος (magnêtis líthos, 'stone of Magnesia').

магнитофон.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-twentieth century from German Magnetophon (originally the 1935 trademark of the German electronics company AEG for the first magnetic tape recorder), compounded from Ancient Greek μαγνήτης (magnḗtēs, 'magnet') + φωνή (phōnḗ, 'sound, voice').

мадам.etymology: Borrowed from French madame ('madam, Mrs.'), originally Old French ma dame ('my lady'), from Latin mea domina.

мажор.etymology: Borrowed through French majeur and Italian maggiore ('major musical mode'), from Latin maior ('greater', comparative of magnus 'great'), referring to the larger third interval in a major scale.

мазать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мазати (1sg. мажу), from Proto-Slavic *mazati ('to smear, grease, anoint'), from Proto-Indo-European *mag- ('to knead, smear, press'; cognate with Ancient Greek μάσσω 'to knead' and English make).

мазохист.etymology: Borrowed from German Masochist, coined from the surname of Austrian writer Leopold von Sacher-Masoch (1836–1895) + agent suffix -ist.

май.etymology: Inherited via Old East Slavic маи and Old Church Slavonic маи from Byzantine Greek Maïos and Latin Māius (mēnsis) ('the month of May'), named after the Italic earth and growth goddess Maia.

майка.etymology: Likely adapted in the early 20th century from French maillot ('knitted jersey, sports shirt, swimsuit', from maille 'mesh') with the Russian noun suffix -ка.

майонез.etymology: Borrowed from French mayonnaise ('mayonnaise'), traditionally traced to Port Mahón (Minorca) after its capture by the Duc de Richelieu in 1756, though alternative derivations within French also exist.

майор.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century via German Major (and Polish major) from Spanish mayor / French major, shortened from sergeant-major, ultimately from Latin maior ('greater, senior', comparative of magnus 'great').

майский.etymology: Formed in Russian from май ('May') with the relational adjectival suffix -ский.

макака.etymology: Borrowed via French macaque from Portuguese macaco ('monkey'), itself borrowed from a Bantu language of Central Africa (cf. Kongo makaku).

макароны.etymology: Borrowed via French macaroni or German Makaroni from Italian maccheroni (southern Italian maccaroni, 'dumplings, pasta'), probably from Medieval Greek μακαρωνία.

макать.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *makati ('to dip in liquid'), a lengthened-grade iterative/causative related to *moknǫti ('to get wet') and *mokrъ ('wet').

макияж.etymology: Borrowed from French maquillage ('makeup'), verbal noun from maquiller ('to put on makeup; originally to disguise or fake').

максимально.etymology: Adverb in -о formed from максимальный ('maximal, maximum'), derived via German maximal from Latin maximus ('greatest, largest', superlative of magnus 'great').

history.meaning: maximal -> maximally, as much as possible

максимум.etymology: Borrowed via German Maximum from Latin maximum ('the greatest amount'), neuter singular of maximus ('greatest', superlative of magnus 'great, large').

маленький.etymology: Formed in East Slavic as an expressive diminutive adjective from малый ('small, little', from Old East Slavic малъ, Proto-Slavic *malъ; compare Gothic smals and English small) with the affectionate suffix -еньк-ий. In everyday Russian маленький largely displaced малый as the standard long-form word for 'small'.

маленько.etymology: Colloquial adverb formed from маленький ('little, small'), diminutive of малый ('small'), from Proto-Slavic *malъ.

малина.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *malina ('raspberry'), formed with the berry suffix -ина from a colour root connected by Vasmer with Latin mulleus ('reddish, purple-red'), Lithuanian mėlynas ('blue, dark'), and Sanskrit malina ('dark-coloured, stained').

мало.etymology: Adverb and quantifier formed from the neuter short form of малый ('small, little'), inherited from Old East Slavic мало / малъ, from Proto-Slavic *malъ ('small, little'). Vasmer compares Gothic smals ('small'), Ancient Greek μῆλον ('small cattle, sheep'), and Latin malus.

малой.etymology: Colloquial substantivized adjective preserving the end-stressed East Slavic nominative singular малой of малый ('small, young', inherited from Proto-Slavic *malъ): 'the young one, kid, youngest son or brother'.

history.meaning: small, young -> youngster, kid, little brother

малость.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic малость, formed with the abstract noun suffix -ость from малый ('small, little', Proto-Slavic *malъ); in colloquial speech also used adverbially to mean 'a little bit, slightly'.

history.meaning: trifle, small bit; (colloquial adv.) a bit

малый.etymology: Substantivized use ('young fellow, lad') of the adjective малый ('small, young'), inherited from Old East Slavic малъ, from Proto-Slavic *malъ ('small').

малыш.etymology: Formed in Russian with the expressive noun suffix -ыш from малый ('small, little'), inherited from Old East Slavic малъ and Proto-Slavic *malъ ('small').

малышка.etymology: Derived from малыш ('little child, toddler') + feminine/diminutive suffix -ка, from малый ('small', Proto-Slavic *malъ).

мальчик.etymology: Derived in Russian with the diminutive suffix -чик from малец ('lad, youngster'), itself built on малый ('small, young', Proto-Slavic *malъ): literally 'a little one, young lad'.

мальчишка.etymology: Expressive/colloquial diminutive formed in Russian from мальчик ('boy', itself a diminutive of малый 'small, lad', Proto-Slavic *malъ) with the suffix -ишка.

history.meaning: small -> boy -> young lad, kid, urchin

мальчишник.etymology: Derived from мальчик / мальчишка ('boy, lad', from малый 'small, young') + suffix -ник, denoting a pre-wedding party of the groom with his male friends.

мама.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mama ('mother, mum'), originating in universal nursery speech reduplicating the bilabial syllable ma-, parallel to Latin mamma, Greek mammē, and English mama.

мамин.etymology: Possessive adjective formed from мама ('mum, mother', from Proto-Slavic nursery word *mama) + possessive suffix -ин.

мамка.etymology: Derived from мама ('mum, mother', from Proto-Slavic *mama) + colloquial/diminutive suffix -ка; historically also used for a wet nurse.

мамочка.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed in Russian with the suffix -очка from мама ('mum, mother', inherited from Proto-Slavic *mama).
мамочка.notes: In the plural exclamation Мамочки! ('Mommies!'), it is used colloquially for 'Goodness gracious! / Oh my gosh!'.

мамуля.etymology: Affectionate colloquial diminutive formed in Russian from мама ('mum, mother') + the endearing kinship suffix -уля (compare папуля, бабуля, дедуля).

манатки.etymology: Colloquial plural noun of uncertain origin; Vasmer connects it with dialectal манатка ('rag, garment') and манатья ('monastic mantle', from Byzantine Greek μανδύας).

манго.etymology: Borrowed via European languages (English mango, Portuguese manga) from Malay mangga, ultimately from Tamil மாங்காய் (māṅkāy) or Malayalam māṅṅa.

манера.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish maniera or German Manier from French manière ('manner, way'), from Vulgar Latin *manuāria, derived from Latin manus ('hand').

манипулировать.etymology: Borrowed from German manipulieren or French manipuler ('to handle, manipulate'), from Medieval Latin manipulāre, from Latin manipulus ('handful', from manus 'hand').

мансарда.etymology: Borrowed from French mansarde ('attic room beneath a sloped mansard roof'), named after the 17th-century French classical architect François Mansart (1598–1666), who popularized steep double-pitched roofs with habitable dormer rooms in Paris.

маньяк.etymology: Borrowed from French maniaque ('maniac'), from Late Latin maniacus, from Ancient Greek μανιακός (maniakós, 'mad, frantic'), derived from μανία (manía, 'madness, obsession').

марать.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *marati ('to soil, smear, dirty'), related to dialectal мара ('mist, delusion') and Indo-European roots meaning 'to smear, darken, stain'.

маринованный.etymology: Past passive participle / verbal adjective formed from мариновать ('to marinate, pickle in a seasoned vinegar brine').
маринованный.notes: In Russian cuisine, маринованные огурцы / грибы are pickled with vinegar, whereas солёные огурцы / грибы are cured by salt-brine lacto-fermentation without vinegar.

мариновать.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via German marinieren and French mariner from Italian marinare ('to pickle in brine, preserve like sea-fish'), derived from Latin marīnus ('of the sea, briny', from mare 'sea').

history.meaning: of the sea -> to pickle in sea-brine
to marinate, pickle; (colloquial) to keep someone waiting endlessly

марионетка.etymology: Borrowed from French marionnette ('puppet, marionette'), a diminutive of Marion (itself a diminutive of the name Marie), adapted with Russian suffix -ка.

марка.etymology: Borrowed via German Marke 'mark, token, stamp' from French marque, of Germanic origin (akin to mark 'sign, boundary'). Used in Russian both for a postage stamp (почтовая марка) and for a brand or make.

маркетинг.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English marketing, verbal noun from to market (ultimately from Latin mercātus 'trade, market').

маркетинговый.etymology: Derived in modern Russian from маркетинг ('marketing', from English marketing) + adjectival suffix -овый.

марс.etymology: Borrowed from Latin Mārs (genitive Mārtis), the Roman god of war and the fourth planet from the Sun.

history.meaning: Roman god of war; planet Mars

марсианский.etymology: Derived from марсианин ('Martian', modeled on French martien / Latin Mārtiānus from Mārs) + adjectival suffix -ский.

март.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic and Old East Slavic мартъ from Byzantine Greek μάρτιος (mártios), from Latin (mēnsis) Mārtius ('month of Mars, the Roman god of war and agriculture').

марш.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Marsch from French marche ('marching, walk') and the military command marche! ('forward march!'), from marcher ('to walk, march').

маршрут.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from German Marschroute ('line of march, planned itinerary'), a compound of Marsch ('march') + Route ('road, route'), both originally from French.
маршрут.notes: Everyday Russian uses маршрут for bus and tram lines as well as walking or travel itineraries.

маска.etymology: Borrowed via French masque or German Maske from Italian maschera ('mask'), from Medieval Latin masca or Arabic مسخرة (maskhara, 'buffoon, mockery').

маскировка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Russian with the suffix -ка from маскировать ('to mask, disguise, camouflage'), borrowed via German maskieren from French masquer ('to put on a mask, conceal', from masque 'mask').

history.meaning: to disguise -> disguise, military camouflage, concealment

маскирующий.etymology: Present active participle of маскировать ('to mask, disguise, camouflage', borrowed from French masquer / German maskieren, built on маска 'mask').

history.meaning: to mask, camouflage -> camouflaging, concealing, disguising

масло.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic масло ('butter, oil'), from Proto-Slavic *maslo (< *maz-slo), built from мазать ('to spread, smear, anoint') plus suffix *-slo: literally 'something spread on bread'.

массаж.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French massage ('therapeutic rubbing and kneading of the body'), derived from masser ('to massage', traced to Arabic مَسَّ massa 'to touch, feel, stroke' or Ancient Greek μάσσω 'to knead').

массажист.etymology: Derived from массаж ('massage', borrowed from French massage) + agent suffix -ист.

мастер.etymology: Attested since Old East Slavic мастеръ (alongside маисторъ), borrowed via Middle Low German or Byzantine Greek maïstōr from Latin magister ('chief, teacher, master craftsman', built on magis 'more').

мастер-класс.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century as a compound calque/loan from English master class, combining мастер ('master') and класс ('class').

мастерская.etymology: Substantivized feminine adjective from мастерская (комната / палата) ('craftsman's or artist's room'), derived from мастер ('master craftsman, artisan'), which entered Old East Slavic (мастеръ / маисторъ) via Byzantine Greek μαΐστωρ or Middle Low German mēster from Latin magister ('master, teacher, chief').

мастерство.etymology: Formed in Russian from мастер ('master craftsman, expert') + the abstract noun suffix -ство. Мастер is attested in Old East Slavic as мастеръ / маистеръ, borrowed from Middle Low German mēster or Byzantine Greek μαΐστωρ, ultimately from Latin magister ('chief, teacher, master').

масштаб.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from German Maßstab ('measuring rod, scale'), a compound of Maß ('measure') and Stab ('staff, rod').

матвей.etymology: Traditional Russian vernacular form of the masculine name Матфей, borrowed via Church Slavonic and Byzantine Greek Ματθαῖος (Matthaîos) from Hebrew Mattityāhū (מַתִּתְיָהוּ, 'gift of God'). East Slavic speakers regularly replaced the unfamiliar Greek sound θ (fita) with в or ф.

математика.etymology: Borrowed via Polish matematyka or Latin mathēmatica from Ancient Greek μαθηματική (τέχνη) (mathēmatikḗ, 'mathematical science'), from μάθημα (máthēma, 'learning, study').

материал.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Material or Polish materiał from Late Latin māteriāle / Classical Latin māteriālis ('belonging to matter/timber'), derived from māteria ('building timber, substance, matter').

материально.etymology: Adverb formed from материальный ('material, financial') + adverbial suffix -о.

материальный.etymology: Borrowed via Polish materialny or German material from Late Latin māteriālis ('of matter, material'), from Latin māteria ('matter, substance'), adapted with Russian suffix -ный.

материться.etymology: Derived from the oblique stem матер- of мать ('mother', Proto-Slavic *mati) + verbal suffix -ить + reflexive -ся, originally referring to uttering maternal profanity (мат).

матовый.etymology: Derived with the adjectival suffix -овый from мат ('matte, unpolished surface'), borrowed from German matt or French mat ('dull, lustreless, frosted').

матрас.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via Dutch matras or German Matratze from Italian materasso, ultimately from Arabic مطرح (maṭraḥ, 'place where cushions are thrown, floor mat').

матч.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th century from English match ('sports contest, game between two matched sides'), from Middle English macche ('equal, opponent, counterpart, contest'), from Old English ġemæcca ('mate, companion, equal').

мать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мати (accusative матерь, which gave the modern nominative мать, while the ancient consonant stem -ер- is preserved in all oblique cases: матери, матерью, матерей), from Proto-Slavic *mati (genitive *matere), from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr ('mother'; compare Sanskrit mātṛ, Ancient Greek μήτηρ, Latin māter, Lithuanian mótė, German Mutter, and English mother).

мафия.etymology: Borrowed via Western European languages from Italian (specifically Sicilian) mafia, documented in 1860s Palermo in the sense 'boldness, swagger; criminal secret society' (often traced to Sicilian mafiusu 'bold, swaggering', probably from Arabic maḥyāṣ 'boasting, bragging').

махать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic махати (present машу, машеши), from Proto-Slavic *maxati ('to wave, swing, brandish'), related to мах ('a swing, stroke') and мановение ('a nod or wave of the hand').

махинация.etymology: Borrowed via German Machination or Polish machinacja from Latin māchinātiō ('contrivance, artifice, plot'), derived from māchinārī ('to contrive, scheme') and māchina ('device, engine, stratagem'), from Ancient Greek μηχανή / Doric μαχανά (mākhaná).

махнуть.etymology: Semelfactive verb formed from махать ('to wave') + suffix -нуть, from Proto-Slavic *maxnǫti / *maxati ('to wave, swing').

машина.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via German Maschine or French machine ('engine, apparatus') from Latin māchina ('device, contrivance'), itself borrowed from Doric Greek μαχανά (mākhanā, Attic μηχανή). In 20th-century everyday Russian машина became the standard word for a car (автомобиль).

машинист.etymology: Borrowed from German Maschinist or French machiniste, or formed in Russian from машина ('machine, locomotive engine') + suffix -ист.

машинка.etymology: Diminutive of машина ('machine, engine; car'), formed with the suffix -ка. Base noun машина was borrowed in the Petrine era via German Maschine / French machine from Latin māchina ('device, engine, contrivance'), from Doric Greek μαχανά (mākhaná, Attic μηχανή mēkhanḗ). While машина in everyday Russian came to mean a full-sized 'car, automobile', the diminutive машинка denotes either a 'toy car' or a small household/office appliance (стиральная машинка 'washing machine', пишущая машинка 'typewriter', машинка для стрижки 'hair clippers').

маэстро.etymology: Borrowed from Italian maestro ('master, teacher, musical conductor'), inherited from Latin magister ('master, chief, director').

маячить.etymology: Derived from маяк ('beacon, landmark, lighthouse') + verbal suffix -ить, originally meaning 'to signal or appear in the distance like a beacon'.

мгновение.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мъгновениѥ ('wink of an eye, instant'), verbal noun from мъгнѫти ('to blink, wink'), from Proto-Slavic *mъgnǫti (related to миг).

мебель.etymology: Borrowed in the early eighteenth century via German Möbel from French meuble ('piece of furniture, movable property'), from Latin mōbilis ('movable', because furniture consists of the movable goods of a house).
мебель.notes: A collective feminine singular noun in Russian (новая мебель 'new furniture').

медаль.etymology: Borrowed via French medaille from Italian medaglia 'coin, medallion', going back to Late Latin medalia 'small coin worth half a denarius' (related to Latin medius 'middle, half').

медальон.etymology: Borrowed from French médaillon ('medallion, locket'), from Italian medaglione, augmentative of medaglia ('medal').

медведь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic медвѣдь, from Proto-Slavic *medvědь, an ancient hunter's taboo compound of *medъ ('honey') and *ěsti (stem *ěd-, 'to eat'), literally 'honey-eater'.

медвежий.etymology: Possessive adjective formed from медведь ('bear', Proto-Slavic *medvědь) + suffix -ий (Proto-Slavic *medvědьjь).

медийный.etymology: Derived in late 20th-century Russian from медиа ('mass media', from English media / Latin medium) + adjectival suffix -ный.

медик.etymology: Borrowed via Polish medyk or German Medikus from Latin medicus ('physician, healer'), derived from medērī ('to heal, cure').

медикаментозно.etymology: Medical adverb in -о formed from медикаментозный ('pharmaceutical, involving medication'), derived via French médicamenteux and German medikamentös from Latin medicāmentōsus (from medicāmentum 'drug, remedy', built on medērī 'to heal').

медитация.etymology: Borrowed via Polish medytacja or directly from Latin meditātiō ('contemplation, reflection'), from meditārī ('to ponder, meditate').

медицина.etymology: Borrowed via Polish medycyna from Latin medicīna (ars) ('the healing art, medicine'), derived from medicus ('physician').

медицинский.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ский from медицина ('medicine'), borrowed via Polish medycyna from Latin medicīna (ars) ('the art of healing', from medicus 'physician').

медленно.etymology: Formed as the adverbial derivative in -о of медленный ('slow').

медленный.etymology: Derived from the verb медлить ('to linger, delay, tarry', Old East Slavic мьдлити, Proto-Slavic *mьdьlъ 'slow, sluggish, weak'): originally 'lingering, unhurried', hence 'slow'.

медный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мѣдьныи, the relational adjective derived from медь ('copper', Proto-Slavic *mědь) with the suffix -ный.

медовый.etymology: Relational adjective derived from мёд ('honey') + suffix -овый. Russian мёд descends from Old East Slavic медъ and Proto-Slavic *medъ ('honey, mead'), from PIE *medhu- ('honey, sweet fermented honey drink'). It is a direct cognate of English mead, Sanskrit madhu ('honey, sweet'), and Ancient Greek methy.

медсестра.etymology: Twentieth-century syllabic compound (сложносокращённое слово) contracted from медицинская сестра ('medical sister, nurse'), which replaced pre-revolutionary сестра милосердия ('Sister of Mercy', a calque of French sœur de la charité).

медуза.etymology: Borrowed via scientific New Latin Medūsa (given by Carl Linnaeus in 1752 to free-swimming jellyfish because their trailing tentacles recalled the snake-haired Gorgon) from Ancient Greek Μέδουσα (Médousa, literally 'guardian, female ruler', from μέδω 'to protect, rule over').

между.etymology: Borrowed in its Church Slavonic form между (with Church Slavonic жд < *dj; compare native East Slavic межи and межа 'boundary strip'), originally the old dual locative of Proto-Slavic *medja ('boundary, border strip between two fields'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos ('middle'), cognate with Latin medius and English mid / middle.

мексиканский.etymology: Derived from Мексика ('Mexico', from Spanish México, of Nahuatl origin) + adjectival suffix -ан-ский.

мел.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мѣлъ ('chalk, fine white limestone'), from Proto-Slavic *mělъ ('finely ground powder, chalk'), built on the verbal root of молоть ('to grind, mill', Proto-Slavic *melti) and мелкий ('fine, small').
мел.notes: Takes the partitive genitive мелу or мела and locative в мелу ('covered in chalk').

мелисса.etymology: Borrowed via botanical Latin melissa from Ancient Greek μέλισσα (mélissa 'honeybee', derived from μέλι 'honey'), because the fragrant lemon-scented herb attracts bees (hence its traditional name 'bee balm' or 'lemon balm').

мелкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мѣлъкыи and Proto-Slavic *mělъkъ ('finely ground, small-grained, shallow'), derived from the same root *měl- ('crushed, ground fine') as мел ('chalk') and молоть ('to grind').
мелкий.notes: Describes both small-grained or small-sized things (мелкий песок 'fine sand', мелкий дождь 'fine drizzle') and shallow water (мелкая река).

мелко.etymology: Adverb and predicative form of мелкий ('small, fine-grained, shallow'), inherited from Old East Slavic мѣлъкъ ('fine, crushed'), from Proto-Slavic *mělъkъ, related to *mělъ ('chalk, fine sand', Russian мел) and *melti ('to grind', Russian молоть).

history.meaning: small, shallow → finely; it is shallow

мелодия.etymology: Borrowed via German Melodie or French mélodie from Late Latin melōdia and Ancient Greek melōidía ('singing, choral song, tune'), a compound of mélos ('limb; musical phrase, song') + ōidḗ ('song, ode').

меломан.etymology: Borrowed from French mélomane ('music lover'), compounded from Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos, 'song, melody') and μανία (manía, 'passion, enthusiasm').

мелочь.etymology: Derived in Russian from мелкий ('small, fine, petty') with the feminine abstract/collective noun suffix -очь (with к -> ч palatalization): 'small items, small change (coins), or a minor trifle'.

мелькнуть.etymology: Semelfactive verb formed from мелькать ('to flash, gleam briefly') + suffix -нуть, related to Russian мельком ('in passing, briefly').

менеджер.etymology: Borrowed from English manager, agent noun from to manage (ultimately from Italian maneggiare 'to handle', from Latin manus 'hand').

менее.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мьнѣе / Old Church Slavonic мьнѣѥ ('less'), comparative degree of *mьnьjь ('smaller, lesser'), from Proto-Slavic *mьn- (cognate with Latin minor, minus).

меньше.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мьньше and Proto-Slavic *mьnьje ('less, smaller'), the suppletive comparative of малый / маленький ('small') and мало ('little'), from Proto-Indo-European *mey- ('small, lessen'), cognate with Latin minus and English minish.

меню.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French menu ('detailed list of dishes, bill of fare'), originally a noun use of the adjective menu ('small, finely detailed'), from Latin minūtus ('small, minute').

менять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мѣняти ('to exchange, swap, change'), from Proto-Slavic *měňati, built on *měna ('exchange, barter, change'), from Proto-Indo-European *mey- ('to change, exchange', cognate with Latin mūnus / commūnis and Latvian mainīt 'to exchange').

меняться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of менять ('to change, exchange, barter'), inherited from Old East Slavic мѣняти, iterative of мѣнити ('to exchange', from мена 'exchange', Proto-Slavic *měna).

history.meaning: to change, alter; to trade places/items

мера.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мѣра ('measure, standard, moderation'), from Proto-Slavic *měra ('measure'), descending from Proto-Indo-European *méh₁-reh₂, built on the root *meh₁- ('to measure'; compare Latin mētior and Sanskrit mātrā).
мера.notes: Spelled мѣра with historical yat (ѣ) until the 1918 orthographic reform; anchors idioms like по крайней мере ('at least'), в меру ('in moderation'), and принять меры ('to take action').

мерзавец.etymology: Formed in Russian with the masculine personal suffix -ец from an older adjective мерзавый / мерзкий ('vile, loathsome, abominable', originally 'causing a cold shudder, freezing', from Proto-Slavic *mьrzъkъ, built on the same root *mьrz- as мёрзнуть 'to freeze' and мороз 'frost').

мерзкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мьрзъкыи ('loathsome, abominable, vile'), derived from Proto-Slavic *mьrzъkъ (from *mьrzěti 'to cause a chill of revulsion, be loathsome', related to *mьrznǫti 'to freeze').

history.meaning: causing a shudder of revulsion, loathsome

мерить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мѣрити, from Proto-Slavic *měriti ('to measure'), denominative verb from *měra ('measure', Russian мера).

мероприятие.etymology: Coined in early 20th-century official Russian as a compound of мера ('measure, step') + linking vowel -о- + приятие / принятие ('taking, adoption', from принять меры 'to take measures').

месиво.etymology: Formed in East Slavic with the mass/substance noun suffix -иво from месить ('to knead, mix, trample mud', inherited from Proto-Slavic *měsiti): originally mashed grain and bran mixed for livestock, and more broadly any thick mush, slop, or muddy mess.

history.meaning: to knead, mix -> mash, mush, slop

месить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мѣсити and Proto-Slavic *měsiti ('to mix, knead dough or clay'), cognate with Lithuanian maišyti ('to mix, stir') and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *meyk- ('to mix', cognate with Latin miscēre and English mix).
месить.notes: First-person singular has с -> ш mutation: я мешу тесто ('I knead the dough').

местечко.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ечко from место ('place, spot', inherited from Old East Slavic мѣсто, Proto-Slavic *město); historically in western regions of the Russian Empire it also served as a calque of Polish miasteczko ('small market town, shtetl').

history.meaning: place -> cosy little spot; (historical) small market town

местечко.notes: Тёплое местечко ('a warm little spot') is a classic idiom for a cushy, lucrative job.

местный.etymology: Derived from место ('place, locality', Proto-Slavic *město) with the relational adjectival suffix -ный: 'belonging to this place, local'.
местный.notes: The consonant -т- is silent in standard pronunciation: pronounced [месный], spelled местный.

место.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мѣсто ('place, spot, site, town'), from Proto-Slavic *město ('dwelling place, spot', in West Slavic 'city, town', as in Polish miasto and Czech město), continuing Balto-Slavic *maista- (cognate with Lithuanian miẽstas 'town, city' and minti / maitìnti 'to dwell, feed').

месть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мьсть ('vengeance, retribution'), from Proto-Slavic *mьstь ('revenge, recompense'), from Proto-Indo-European *mit-ti- ('exchange, requital', related to Sanskrit mithás 'mutually' and Latin mūtuus).

месье.etymology: Borrowed from French monsieur ('sir, Mr.'), originally a contraction of Middle French mon sieur ('my lord', from Latin meus senior).

месяц.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мѣсяць and Proto-Slavic *měsęcь ('moon; calendar month'), from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s ('moon, month'), a distant cognate of English moon and month and Latin mēnsis.
месяц.notes: Means both a calendar month and the crescent moon in the night sky.

металл.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via German Metall or French métal and Latin metallum ('mine, quarry; mineral, metal') from Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon, 'mine, quarry, metal ore').

металлический.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ический from металл ('metal'), borrowed via German Metall / French métal from Latin metallum and Ancient Greek μέταλλον ('mine, quarry; mineral, metal').

метель.etymology: Formed in Russian with the noun suffix -ель from мести (present stem мет-, 'to sweep, whirl, blow snow across the ground', inherited from Proto-Slavic *mesti): literally 'sweeping, swirling snow'.

метод.etymology: Borrowed via French méthode and German Methode from Latin methodus and Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos, 'pursuit of knowledge, systematic way of inquiry'), from μετά ('after, along') + ὁδός ('way, road').

методика.etymology: Borrowed via German Methodik or New Latin methodica from Ancient Greek μεθοδική (methodikḗ), from μέθοδος (méthodos, 'pursuit of knowledge, method').

метр.etymology: Borrowed from French mètre ('metre', introduced during the French Revolution as the base unit of length), from Ancient Greek métron ('measure, rule').

метро.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from French métro, a clipping of chemin de fer métropolitain ('metropolitan railway', first opened in Paris in 1900), from Late Latin mētropolitānus and Ancient Greek μητρόπολις (mētrópolis, 'mother-city, capital').
