метро.notes: Indeclinable neuter noun in Russian: ехать на метро ('to go by metro'), станция метро ('metro station').

меч.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мечь / мьчь and Proto-Slavic *mьčь ('double-edged sword'), shared with Gothic mēkeis and Old English mēce; considered an ancient migratory weapon word borrowed into both Slavic and Germanic from a third source (often sought in the Caucasus or ancient Near East).

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: меч

мечеть.etymology: Attested in Old Russian chronicles and travel accounts from the 14th–15th centuries (as мечеть / мизгить), borrowed via Volga Bulgar or Kipchak Turkic mäčät / mäčit from Arabic مَسْجِد (masjid, 'mosque', literally 'place of prostration in prayer', from sajada 'to bow down, prostrate oneself'; the same Arabic word gave Spanish mezquita and English mosque).

мечта.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic мьчьта ('vision, phantom, imagination, daydream'; native Old East Slavic had мьчьтъ), from Proto-Slavic *mьčьta, built on the root *mьknǫti / *mьčati ('to flash, glimmer, flit before the eyes'; compare мерцать 'to glimmer' and маячить). Originally 'a fleeting apparition', it acquired its warm modern Russian sense 'cherished daydream, aspiration' in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.
мечта.notes: Russian distinguishes **мечта** (a waking daydream or life aspiration) from **сон** (a dream seen while sleeping).

мечтать.etymology: Derived from мечта ('daydream, cherished wish, vision'), adopted via Old Church Slavonic мьчьта ('phantasm, vision, imagination'), from Proto-Slavic *mьčьta, built on the root *mьk- / *mьg- ('to flicker, gleam, flash before the eyes'; compare мигать 'to blink, twinkle').

мешать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мѣшати and Proto-Slavic *měšati ('to mix, stir; to confuse, get in the way'), the iterative-durative derivative of *měsiti (Russian месить 'to knead'). From 'to mix up or muddle someone's work' arose the sense 'to disturb, hinder (+ dative)'.

history.meaning: to mix, stir; to confuse, hinder
to stir (with accusative); to disturb, hinder (with dative)

мешать.notes: With a direct object in the accusative it means 'to stir' (мешать суп); with a person in the dative it means 'to bother, get in the way of' (не мешай мне).

мешаться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed from мешать ('to mix, stir; to hinder, interfere') + -ся, from Proto-Slavic *měšati ('to mix, confuse').

history.meaning: to mix; to get in the way
to get in the way, get underfoot

мешок.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мѣшькъ, originally a diminutive formed with -ок (< *-ьkъ) from мѣхъ / мех ('skin bag, wineskin, bellows, fur pelt'), from Proto-Slavic *měxъ ('hide bag, pelt'), cognate with Lithuanian maĩšas ('sack, bag').

мешочек.etymology: Double diminutive formed with -ек from мешок ('bag, sack', with к → ч before -ек), itself a derivative in -ок of Old East Slavic мѣхъ ('animal skin, wineskin, fur bag', from Proto-Slavic *měxъ).

history.meaning: bag, sack → small pouch, little bag

миг.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *migъ ('blink of an eye, instant'), deverbal from *migati (Russian мигать 'to blink, wink, flash'): literally 'the time it takes to blink an eye'.

history.meaning: to blink -> blink of an eye, instant

мигалка.etymology: Colloquial instrument noun formed from мигать ('to blink, flash', from Proto-Slavic *migati) + suffix -лка.

мигать.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *migati ('to blink, wink, flash'), related to Baltic words such as Lithuanian migti ('to fall asleep, close the eyes') and мгла ('mist, dimness').

cognates.meaning: to close the eyes, fall asleep

мигом.etymology: Adverbialized instrumental singular of миг ('instant, blink of an eye'), derived from Proto-Slavic *migъ / *migati ('to blink').

history.meaning: in a flash, in no time

мигрант.etymology: Borrowed via German Migrant or English migrant from Latin migrāns (stem migrant-), present active participle of migrāre ('to move from one place to another, depart').

миграционный.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ный from миграция ('migration'), borrowed from Latin migrātiō ('removal, change of habitation'), from migrāre ('to move from one place to another').

мидия.etymology: Borrowed from Modern Greek μύδι (mýdi, plural μύδια mýdia, 'mussel'), from Ancient Greek μύδιον (mýdion), diminutive of μῦς (mûs, 'mouse; mussel').

микроб.etymology: Borrowed from French microbe, coined in 1878 by surgeon Charles Sédillot from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, 'small') + βίος (bíos, 'life').

микрофон.etymology: Borrowed via French microphone or English microphone, a scientific compound of Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, 'small, faint') + φωνή (phōnḗ, 'sound, voice').

миксер.etymology: Borrowed in the twentieth century from English mixer ('kitchen appliance for beating and mixing; rotating-drum concrete mixer truck', agent/instrument noun from to mix).

миленький.etymology: Affectionate diminutive adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -енький from милый ('dear, sweet, nice', inherited from Proto-Slavic *milъ).
миленький.notes: In the idiom как миленький ('like a darling'), it means someone will comply meekly and without fuss.

миленько.etymology: Adverb formed from миленький ('cute, sweet'), diminutive of милый ('dear, nice'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *milъ.

милиция.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish milicja or German Miliz from Latin mīlitia ('military service, soldiery, citizen force', from mīles 'soldier'); adopted in 1917 for the Soviet civil police force (renamed полиция in Russia in 2011).

history.meaning: militia; Soviet and post-Soviet police force

миллиард.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French milliard ('one thousand million, 10⁹'), coined in sixteenth-century French from million ('million') with the augmentative suffix -ard.

миллиграмм.etymology: Borrowed from French milligramme, formed from the metric prefix milli- (from Latin mīlle 'thousand') + gramme ('gram').

миллиметр.etymology: Borrowed from French millimètre ('one-thousandth of a metre'), compounded from Latin mille ('thousand') + French mètre ('metre').

миллион.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via French million or German Million from Italian milione (attested in the 13th–14th centuries, famously in Marco Polo's Il Milione), an augmentative of mille ('thousand', from Latin mīlle), literally 'a great thousand' (1,000 × 1,000).

миллионер.etymology: Borrowed from French millionnaire ('millionaire'), derived from million ('million', from Italian milione).

мило.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мило, the short neuter and adverbial form of милый ('dear, sweet, kind', Proto-Slavic *milъ, cognate with Lithuanian mielas 'dear, sweet').

милостыня.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic милостыни / Old Church Slavonic милостꙑни ('compassion, charity, alms'), from Proto-Slavic *milostyňi, derived from *milostь ('mercy, grace', from *milъ 'dear').

милость.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic милость (reinforced by Old Church Slavonic милость), from Proto-Slavic *milostь ('grace, mercy, kindness, affection'), formed from *milъ (Russian милый, 'dear, sweet') + the abstract noun suffix *-ostь.

history.stage: Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic

милость.notes: Preserved in traditional polite formulas such as Милости просим! ('Welcome! We kindly invite you in!') and Скажите на милость ('Pray tell / goodness gracious').

милый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic милъ / милыи ('dear, sweet, lovable, gentle'), from Proto-Slavic *milъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *meyl- / *meyH- ('gentle, mild, dear, peaceful'), directly cognate with Lithuanian mýlas / mielas ('dear, sweet'), Latin mītis ('mild, gentle'), and peace-root мир.

мильфей.etymology: Borrowed from French mille-feuille ('layered puff pastry', literally 'thousand-leaf', from mille 'thousand' + feuille 'leaf, sheet').

мимика.etymology: Borrowed via German Mimik or directly from Ancient Greek μιμική (τέχνη) (mimikḗ, 'the art of mime and facial expression'), from μῖμος (mîmos, 'mime, actor').

мимо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мимо and Proto-Slavic *mimo ('passing by, past'), originally a fossilized adverbial form built on the verbal root of миновать ('to pass by, elapse', Proto-Slavic *minǫti).
мимо.notes: Takes the genitive case when used as a preposition: пройти мимо дома ('to walk past the house').

миндаль.etymology: Entered Russian via Old Church Slavonic мигдалъ and Polish migdal from Latin amygdalus and Ancient Greek amygdale 'almond', with the consonant cluster reshaping smoothly to миндаль in East Slavic.

cognates.meaning: almond (via Old French almande from the same Latin word)

миндаль.notes: Used as a collective masculine singular noun in culinary Russian: жареный миндаль 'roasted almonds'.

миндальный.etymology: Formed in Russian from миндаль ('almond') with the adjectival suffix -ный. Russian миндаль was borrowed via Polish migdał or Middle Greek mandyla from Ancient Greek amygdálē ('almond', the same Greek word that gave English almond and amygdala).

cognates.meaning: almond (from Greek amygdalē via Latin and French)

минестроне.etymology: Borrowed from Italian minestrone ('thick vegetable soup'), augmentative of minestra ('soup', from minestrare 'to serve, dish up', from Latin ministrāre).

минимум.etymology: Borrowed via German Minimum from Latin minimum ('the smallest amount or degree'), neuter singular of minimus ('smallest, least').

министерство.etymology: Derived in the early 19th century from министр ('minister') + suffix -ство, modeled on French ministère ('ministry').

министр.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish minister, German Minister, or French ministre from Latin minister ('attendant, servant, official'), related to minor ('lesser').

минор.etymology: Borrowed via Italian minore or French mineur from Latin minor ('lesser, smaller'); used as a musical term for a minor key and figuratively for a gloomy or melancholic mood.

минус.etymology: Borrowed via German Minus from Latin minus ('less'), neuter comparative of parvus ('small, little').

минута.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via German Minute or French minute from Medieval Latin pars minūta prīma ('first small division [of an hour]'), the feminine past participle of Latin minuō ('to lessen, make small').

history.meaning: first small part (one-sixtieth of an hour)

минутка.etymology: Formed in Russian as the affectionate diminutive (with suffix -ка) of минута ('minute', borrowed in the early 18th century from Medieval Latin minūta 'small division of an hour'). Often used in polite requests: Одну минутку! ('Just a moment!').

минутный.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ный from минута ('minute'), borrowed in the Petrine era from Medieval Latin minūta (pars) ('small division of an hour', from Latin minūtus 'small, minute').

history.meaning: first small division (1/60 of an hour)

минуточка.etymology: Affectionate double diminutive of минута ('minute'), formed from минутка + -очка. Минута was borrowed in the Petrine era from Medieval Latin minūta (pars minūta prīma, 'first small division of an hour'), from Latin minūtus ('small, diminished').
минуточка.notes: Frequently used in the polite request Минуточку! ('Just a moment, please!').

мир.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic миръ ('peace, concord; village community; the universe, world'), from Proto-Slavic *mirъ ('peace, world order'), cognate with Lithuanian mieras ('peace') and Sanskrit mitrá ('friend, alliance'). In pre-1918 orthography the two senses were artificially distinguished as миръ ('peace') and міръ ('world, community'), though both descend from the same Slavic word.
мир.notes: The proverb *Мир тесен* literally means 'The world is cramped/narrow' — i.e., 'It's a small world!'.

мирить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мирити and Proto-Slavic *miriti ('to make peace, reconcile'), a denominal verb built on мир ('peace, concord', Proto-Slavic *mirъ).

мириться.etymology: Reflexive and reciprocal verb formed with -ся from мирить ('to reconcile, make peace between'), a denominative verb from мир ('peace'), inherited from Old East Slavic миръ and Proto-Slavic *mirъ ('peace, concord').

history.meaning: to make peace, reconcile; to put up with

мирно.etymology: Adverb formed from мирный ('peaceful') + -о, derived from мир ('peace'), from Proto-Slavic *mirъ ('peace').

миска.etymology: Formed as the diminutive of older Russian миса ('bowl, basin, tureen'), borrowed via Polish misa or directly from Vulgar Latin mēnsa ('table; dish of food served on a table').

миссия.etymology: Borrowed via Polish misja or German Mission from Latin missiō ('a sending, dispatch, mission'), from mittere ('to send').

мистический.etymology: Borrowed via German mystisch or French mystique (adapted with suffix -еский) from Latin mysticus, from Ancient Greek μυστικός (mystikós, 'secret, mystic').

митинг.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from English meeting ('public assembly, political rally', verbal noun of to meet); in Russian it specialized specifically to mean an outdoor political rally or protest demonstration.
митинг.notes: False friend in business contexts: an office or business meeting in Russian is встреча or совещание, whereas митинг is a political rally or street demonstration.

мишка.etymology: Diminutive of the personal name Михаил / Миша ('Michael') + suffix -ка, traditionally used in Russian folk speech as an affectionate or euphemistic nickname for a bear (медведь) because of initial sound similarity.

мишленовский.etymology: Derived from Мишлен (French Michelin, the surname of brothers André and Édouard Michelin, who founded the Michelin restaurant guide in 1900) + Russian adjectival suffix -овский.

младенец.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic младеньць ('infant, young child'), exhibiting South Slavic мл- for East Slavic молод-; from Proto-Slavic *moldьnьcь, derived from *moldъ ('young, tender').

младший.etymology: Adopted with the South Slavic / Church Slavonic root vocalism млад- (compare native East Slavic молод- in молодой 'young'), representing the comparative/superlative stem of Proto-Slavic *moldъ ('young, tender').

мнение.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мьнѣниѥ ('opinion, thought'), a verbal noun built on мьнѣти (Russian мнить, 'to think, suppose, deem'), from Proto-Slavic *mьněti, from Proto-Indo-European *men- ('to think, call to mind'; cognate with English mind and Latin mēns).

многие.etymology: Plural of долгая форма многие / многий ('many a, numerous'), inherited from Old East Slavic мъногыи, from Proto-Slavic *mъnogъ ('much, many'; compare Gothic manags, English many).

много.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мъного ('much, many'), the short neuter singular and quantitative adverb of мъногыи ('many, numerous'), from Proto-Slavic *mъnogъ, closely related to Proto-Germanic *managaz (English many, German manch).

многовато.etymology: Attenuative adverb formed in Russian with the suffix -овато ('a bit too, somewhat') from много ('much, many', inherited from Proto-Slavic *mъnogo).

многое.etymology: Substantivized neuter singular of многий ('much, many'), inherited from Old East Slavic мъногое, from Proto-Slavic *mъnogъ ('much, many').

многоходовочка.etymology: Colloquial diminutive of многоходовка ('multi-move combination', originally a chess term formed from много 'many' + ход 'move' + -овка) + diminutive suffix -очка.

множество.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мъножьство / Old Church Slavonic мъножьство ('multitude, great number'), formed from многий (*mъnogъ 'many, much', with г -> ж palatalization) + the collective/abstract suffix -ество.

мобильник.etymology: Colloquial univerbation formed in the 1990s from мобильный телефон ('mobile telephone') + noun suffix -ник.

мобильный.etymology: Borrowed via French mobile or German mobil from Latin mōbilis ('movable, agile', from movēre 'to move'), adapted with the Russian adjectival suffix -ный.

могила.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic могила ('burial mound, grave') and Proto-Slavic *mogyla ('earthen mound, hill, tumulus, grave').

мода.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Mode or directly from French mode ('fashion, custom, manner'), from Latin modus ('measure, manner, way').

модель.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via French modèle or German Modell from Italian modello ('pattern, mold, model'), from Vulgar Latin *modellus, diminutive of Latin modulus / modus ('measure').

модельер.etymology: Derived in Russian on a French model from модель ('fashion model, design') + agent suffix -ьер (cf. French modéliste / modeleur).

модно.etymology: Adverb formed from модный ('fashionable') + adverbial suffix -о.

можно.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мощьно / можьно ('it is possible, one has the power to'), originally the short neuter singular of можьныи ('possible, mighty'), formed from мочь ('to be able, can; power', from Proto-Slavic *mogti, with *g + *ьn > жн). Functions as the everyday impersonal modal predicate 'one may, it is possible, may I?'.

history.meaning: to be able → it is possible

мозг.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мозгъ ('brain, bone marrow') and Proto-Slavic *mozgъ ('marrow, brain'), from Proto-Indo-European *mosgʰos ('marrow, brain', cognate with German Mark and English marrow).

мозговой.etymology: Derived from мозг ('brain, marrow', inherited from Proto-Slavic *mozgъ) + adjectival suffix -овой.

мой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мои (f. моя, n. мое), from Proto-Slavic *mojь ('my, mine'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *meyos, an adjectival possessive built on the first-person singular oblique pronoun stem *me- (cognate with Latin meus and Old Prussian mais).

мокасины.etymology: Borrowed via English moccasin or French mocassin from a Virginia Algonquian language (Powhatan mockasin, 'shoe').

мокрый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мокрыи and Proto-Slavic *mokrъ ('wet, damp'), related to мочить ('to wet, soak') and мокнуть ('to get wet').

молекула.etymology: Borrowed via French molécule from New Latin mōlēcula ('minute particle'), a scientific diminutive formed from Latin mōlēs ('mass, bulk').

молекулярный.etymology: Derived from молекула ('molecule') + suffix -ярный (modeled on French moléculaire).

молить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic молити ('to ask, implore, pray'), from Proto-Slavic *moliti ('to entreat, pray').

молиться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic молитися ('to pray'), reflexive of молити ('to implore, pray'), from Proto-Slavic *moliti sę.

молния.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мълния (Old Church Slavonic млънии, 'lightning'), from Proto-Slavic *mъlniji, continuing Proto-Indo-European *ml̥dʰ-ni- ('lightning bolt, Thor's hammer'; cognate with Old Prussian mealde 'lightning' and Welsh mellt 'lightning'). In the 20th century, застёжка-молния ('lightning fastener', shortened to молния) became the standard Russian word for a zipper.

молодец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic молодьць ('young man, brave warrior, gallant youth'), formed from молодъ / молодой ('young', displaying East Slavic pleophony -оло- from Proto-Slavic *moldъ) + the masculine noun suffix -ец. In folk poetry, добрый молодец meant a 'strapping, valiant youth', which generalized into an exclamation of praise ('well done! good job!').

молодожёны.etymology: Compound noun formed from молодой ('young', Proto-Slavic *moldъ) + linking vowel -о- + жена ('wife', plural жёны, Proto-Slavic *žena).

молодой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic молодъ / молодыи ('young, tender', showing East Slavic pleophony -оло-; compare Old Church Slavonic младъ), from Proto-Slavic *moldъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *ml̥dú- ('soft, tender, young'), cognate with Latin mollis ('soft'), Sanskrit mṛdú ('soft, delicate'), and English mild.

молодость.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic молодость, derived from молодой ('young', from Proto-Slavic *moldъ) + abstract noun suffix -ость.

молодуха.etymology: Colloquial and folk derivative formed in East Slavic with the feminine suffix -уха from молодой ('young', from Old East Slavic молодыи, Proto-Slavic *moldъ with East Slavic pleophony -оло-): traditionally a recently married young peasant woman, now colloquially any young woman.

history.meaning: young -> young married woman, young woman

молодые.etymology: Substantivized plural of the adjective молодой ('young', inherited from Old East Slavic молодыи, Proto-Slavic *moldъ), used traditionally to refer to a newly married couple.

молодёжь.etymology: Collective noun formed in Russian from молодой ('young', inherited from Old East Slavic молодыи, Proto-Slavic *moldъ) + the collective/abstract suffix -ёжь.
молодёжь.notes: Singular-only feminine collective noun in Russian: современная молодёжь ('modern youth').

молоко.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic молоко (showing East Slavic pleophony -оло-; compare Old Church Slavonic млѣко and Polish mleko), from Proto-Slavic *melko. Vasmer compares Proto-Germanic *meluk- (English milk, German Milch), noting that scholars debate whether Slavic borrowed the word early from Germanic or shared an older western Indo-European root.

молоток.etymology: Diminutive in -ок of молот ('heavy sledgehammer'), inherited from Old East Slavic молотъ (with East Slavic pleophony -оло-) and Proto-Slavic *moltъ ('hammer, mallet'), derived from the same root as молоть ('to grind, crush', Proto-Indo-European *melh₂-, cognate with Latin malleus 'hammer, mallet'). Eventually молоток became the everyday Russian word for a hand hammer.

молоточек.etymology: A double diminutive built in Russian from молоток ('hammer', itself a diminutive of молот 'sledgehammer, mallet', Proto-Slavic *moltъ) + -ек (with к -> ч): 'a little hammer', such as a felt-covered piano hammer.

morphemes.meaning: first diminutive suffix (-ок with к -> ч)

молотый.etymology: Past passive participle of молоть ('to grind, mill'), inherited from Old East Slavic молоти (with regular East Slavic pleophony -оло-) and Proto-Slavic *melti ('to grind', from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂-, cognate with Latin molere and English mill / meal).

history.meaning: to grind → ground, finely milled (молотый кофе 'ground coffee')

молочник.etymology: Formed in Russian from молочный ('milk, dairy', from молоко 'milk', Proto-Slavic *melko) with the noun suffix -ник: 'a vessel for serving milk or cream, milk jug'.

молочный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic молочьныи, derived from молоко ('milk', from Proto-Slavic *melko) + adjectival suffix -ный.

молча.etymology: Present adverbial participle (деепричастие) of молчать ('to be silent, keep quiet') lexicalized as an adverb ('silently, without a word'). Молчать comes from Old East Slavic мълчати, from Proto-Slavic *mъlčati ('to fall silent').

молчание.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мълчание / Old Church Slavonic млъчаниѥ ('silence'), verbal noun from молчать ('to be silent', from Proto-Slavic *mьlčati).

молчать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мълчати and Proto-Slavic *mъlčati ('to keep silent, be still'), originally a stative verb in *-ěti built on *mъlk- (seen in замолкнуть 'to fall silent').

мольберт.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century among Academy artists from German Malbrett ('painting board, easel'), a compound of malen ('to paint', from Old High German malon 'to mark, colour') + Brett ('board, plank'). In Russian studio and café usage, мольберт refers to the three-legged wooden easel used either by painters or to display menus and seating charts.

history.meaning: to paint + board → painter's board, easel

момент.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via German Moment or French moment from Latin mōmentum ('movement, impulse, brief particle of time', contracted from *movimentum), derived from movēre ('to move').

моментально.etymology: Adverb in -о formed from моментальный ('instantaneous'), derived from момент ('moment, instant', borrowed via German Moment and French moment from Latin mōmentum 'movement, brief space of time').

history.meaning: moment -> instantaneous -> instantly, in a flash

монастырь.etymology: Borrowed in the Old East Slavic period (attested from the 11th century as манастырь / монастырь) from Byzantine Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion, 'hermitage, monastery'), from μοναστήρ / μοναχός (monakhós, 'monk, solitary'), derived from μόνος (mónos, 'alone, solitary').

монета.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish moneta from Latin moneta 'mint; coined money', named after the temple of Juno Moneta on the Capitoline Hill in Rome, beside which silver coins were struck.

history.meaning: epithet of Juno; the Roman mint; coin

cognates.meaning: place where coins are struck (early Germanic loan from Latin moneta)

монетка.etymology: Diminutive of монета ('coin') + suffix -ка; монета was borrowed via Polish moneta from Latin monēta ('mint, coin', from the temple of Iūnō Monēta in Rome).

монстр.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from French monstre ('monster, prodigy'), from Latin mōnstrum ('divine portent, unnatural creature, monster', derived from monēre 'to warn').

history.meaning: monster, beast; giant/powerhouse in a field

мораль.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French morale ('ethics, morality; moral of a fable'), substantive use of the feminine of moral, from Latin mōrālis ('pertaining to manners or morals'), coined by Cicero from mōs, mōris ('custom, habit, character').

history.meaning: morality, morals; moral of a story

морально.etymology: Adverb formed from моральный ('moral, mental') + adverbial suffix -о.

моральный.etymology: Borrowed via French moral or German moralisch from Latin mōrālis ('relating to morals or character', from mōs, mōris 'custom, habit'), adapted with Russian suffix -ный.

морг.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French morgue ('mortuary where unidentified bodies were laid out for viewing', originally the name of the Paris Morgue at the Grand Châtelet prison, where prison warders 'eyed' or inspected incoming prisoners, related to Middle French morguer 'to look solemnly at').

морда.etymology: Attested in East Slavic and Polish (morda) for an animal's snout or muzzle (and vulgarly a human face); its deeper pre-Slavic origin is uncertain (Vasmer reviews hypotheses connecting it with a root meaning 'to snarl, grimace' or an Iranian loan).

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: морда

море.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic море and Proto-Slavic *morje ('sea'), from Proto-Indo-European *móri ('sea, body of standing water'), cognate with Latin mare ('sea'), German Meer, and English mere / marine.

морепродукты.etymology: Twentieth-century compound plural noun formed from море ('sea', inherited from Proto-Slavic *moŕe) + продукты ('foodstuffs, products', from Latin prōductum): literally 'sea products', corresponding to English seafood and French fruits de mer.

history.meaning: sea + foodstuffs -> seafood (especially shellfish, shrimp, squid, and mussels)

морж.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century via northern Russian dialects from a Sámi language (cf. Kildin Sámi moršša 'walrus').

морковка.etymology: Formed in Russian from морковь ('carrot, carrots') with the suffix -ка: used colloquially both for a single carrot and for carrots collectively.

морковь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мъркы (accusative мъркъвь) and Proto-Slavic *mъrky ('wild carrot, root vegetable'), an early prehistoric cognate or shared Wanderwort with Proto-Germanic *murhōn ('wild carrot, parsnip', modern German Möhre 'carrot').
морковь.notes: Like many former Slavic *-ū-stem nouns (such as свекровь, любовь, церковь), its modern nominative singular морковь comes from the old accusative form.

мороженое.etymology: Substantivized neuter singular of мороженый ('frozen'), passive participle of морозить ('to freeze'), derived from мороз ('frost', from Proto-Slavic *morzъ).

морочить.etymology: Derived from морок / морока ('darkness, gloom, delusion, bewilderment', East Slavic pleophonic form of Proto-Slavic *morkъ) + verbal suffix -ить.

морской.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic морьскыи ('sea, marine, maritime'), formed from море ('sea', from Proto-Slavic *morje, continuing PIE *móri 'sea, body of water'; cognate with Latin mare, French mer, and English mere/marine) + the relational suffix -ской.

морщиться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of морщить ('to wrinkle, crease, pucker'), derived from морщина / морск ('wrinkle, fold, pucker', from Proto-Slavic *morščiti).

history.meaning: to wrinkle → to wince, pucker up one's face (e.g. from sourness)

моряк.etymology: Agent noun derived from море ('sea') with the masculine person suffix -як. Russian море descends from Old East Slavic море and Proto-Slavic *morje ('sea'), from PIE *mori- ('body of water, sea, lake'). It is a direct cognate of Latin mare (whence English marine and mariner), German Meer, and Old English mere.

москвич.etymology: Formed in Russian from Москва ('Moscow', Old East Slavic Москы / Москва) + the Slavic resident/origin suffix -ич (Proto-Slavic *-itjь, denoting a native or inhabitant of a city).

history.meaning: native or inhabitant of Moscow, Muscovite

москвичка.etymology: Derived from москвич ('Muscovite', from Москва 'Moscow') + feminine inhabitant suffix -ка.

московский.etymology: Adjective formed with suffix -ский from Москва ('Moscow', Old East Slavic Москы, stem Москов-), named after the Moskva River (from an early Balto-Slavic hydronym *Mask-(u)va 'marshy, damp river').

мост.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мостъ ('bridge; timber-paved street'), from Proto-Slavic *mostъ. Vasmer connects it most plausibly with метать ('to throw, lay across': logs laid across water or mud), an older sense still visible in мостовая ('cobblestone or paved roadway').

мостик.etymology: Diminutive formed in Russian with the suffix -ик from мост ('bridge', inherited from Old East Slavic мостъ, Proto-Slavic *mostъ).

history.meaning: bridge -> small footbridge; ship's bridge (капитанский мостик); gymnastic bridge

мостовая.etymology: A substantivized feminine adjective (originally мостовая улица 'paved or timber-decked street') derived from мост ('bridge; timber or stone street paving', Proto-Slavic *mostъ). In medieval Rus', muddy streets were paved with split logs laid like a bridge deck (мостить улицу).

morphemes.meaning: feminine adjectival ending used as a noun

мотать.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *motati ('to wind, reel, shake'), an iterative formation related to *mesti ('to throw, sweep').

history.meaning: to wind; (slang) to serve a sentence

мотель.etymology: Borrowed in the twentieth century from American English motel, coined in 1925 in California as a blend of motor + hotel ('roadside hotel for motorists').

мотор.etymology: Borrowed in the late nineteenth century via German Motor from Latin motor ('mover, one that imparts motion'), an agent noun from movēre ('to move').

мотоцикл.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century from French motocycle ('motorcycle'), formed from moto- (from moteur 'motor', Latin motor) + cycle ('bicycle', from Greek κύκλος 'wheel').

мотоциклист.etymology: Borrowed from French motocycliste or formed in Russian from мотоцикл ('motorcycle') + agent suffix -ист.

мохито.etymology: Borrowed in the late twentieth century from Cuban Spanish mojito ('Havana cocktail of white rum, lime, mint, sugar, and soda water'), diminutive of mojo ('Cuban citrus-garlic seasoning sauce', from mojar 'to wet, moisten').

мочалка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the instrument suffix -лка from мочалить ('to shred soaked linden bark into fibres'), derived from мочало ('soaked bast fibre', itself from мочить 'to soak, steep in water', Proto-Slavic *močiti): traditional Russian bath scrubbers were made from bundles of soaked linden bast.

history.meaning: to soak -> soaked linden bast -> bast bath scrubber, washcloth, loofah

мочь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мочи (present могу, можеши; Old Church Slavonic мощи), from Proto-Slavic *mogti ('to be able, have power'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *megʰ- ('to be able, have power'), directly cognate with English may and might and German mögen.

мошенник.etymology: Derived from Old Russian мошна ('pouch, money bag, purse', from Proto-Slavic *mošьna) + agent suffix -ник; originally denoted a pickpocket who cut or stole purses.

мошенница.etymology: Feminine form of мошенник ('con artist, swindler', from мошна 'purse') formed with the feminine agent suffix -ица.

мощный.etymology: Formed in Russian with the adjectival suffix -ный from мощь ('might, power'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мощь (showing the South Slavic reflex *tj -> щ, corresponding to native East Slavic мочь, from Proto-Slavic *moťь 'power', built on *moťi 'to be able').

мраморный.etymology: Derived from мрамор ('marble', borrowed via Old Church Slavonic мраморъ from Latin marmor and Ancient Greek μάρμαρος) + adjectival suffix -ный.

мрачный.etymology: Derived from мрак ('darkness, gloom', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мракъ, from Proto-Slavic *morkъ) + adjectival suffix -ный.

мрачняк.etymology: Colloquial slang noun formed in late twentieth-century Russian with the expressive suffix -няк from мрачный ('gloomy, dark, bleak'), itself derived from Church Slavonic мракъ ('darkness, gloom', corresponding to East Slavic морок from Proto-Slavic *morkъ).

history.meaning: gloomy, dark -> utter gloom, downer, depressing atmosphere

мстить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мьстити, from Proto-Slavic *mьstiti ('to take vengeance'), denominative verb from *mьstь ('vengeance', Russian месть).

мудрец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мудрьць, derived from мудрый ('wise', from Proto-Slavic *mǫdrъ) + agent noun suffix -ец.

мудрость.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мудрость and Old Church Slavonic мѫдрость (Proto-Slavic *mǫdrostь), formed with the abstract noun suffix -ость from мудрый (*mǫdrъ 'wise, sage', from the Indo-European root *mendʰ- 'to direct one's mind, be alert').

мудрый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мудрыи and Proto-Slavic *mǫdrъ ('wise, sage, thoughtful'), from Proto-Indo-European *mndʰ-ró-s ('mindful, awake, wise'), cognate with Lithuanian mandras ('wide-awake, clever') and Ancient Greek manthánō ('to learn').

муж.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мужь (and Old Church Slavonic мѫжь 'man, husband'), from Proto-Slavic *mǫžь ('man, male, husband'), from Proto-Indo-European *mon-gʷ-yo- / *man-u- ('man'; compare Sanskrit mányate / mánu-, German Mann, and English man).

мужественный.etymology: Derived from мужество ('courage, fortitude, manliness') + adjectival suffix -енный (cf. Old Church Slavonic мѫжьствьнъ).

мужество.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мужьство / Old Church Slavonic мѫжьство ('manliness, courage'), derived from муж ('man, husband', Proto-Slavic *mǫžь) + abstract suffix -ство.

мужик.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мужикъ (attested from the 13th–14th centuries), formed with the diminutive/expressive suffix -ик from мужь / муж ('man, husband', Proto-Slavic *mǫžь). Historically denoting a commoner or peasant man as opposed to a nobleman, in modern colloquial Russian мужик means 'guy, bloke' or 'a tough, real man'.

мужской.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мужьскыи ('manly, men's, male, masculine'), formed with the relational suffix -ской from муж ('man, husband', Old East Slavic мужь, from Proto-Slavic *mǫžь, continuing PIE *mónu-gʷʰ-o- 'man', cognate with English man, German Mann, and Sanskrit mánu).

мужчина.etymology: Formed in East Slavic from муж ('man, husband', Proto-Slavic *mǫžь) with the suffix -чина (via мужьскъ 'male, manly'): originally a collective noun ('menfolk'), which shifted to a single adult man while retaining first-declension -а endings.
мужчина.notes: Pronounced [мущина]; grammatically masculine despite its -а ending (молодой мужчина).

музыка.etymology: Borrowed via Polish muzyka and Latin mūsica from Ancient Greek mousikḗ (tékhnē) ('the art of the Muses — poetry and music'), derived from Moûsa ('Muse').
музыка.notes: The stress on the first syllable (музыка) reflects transmission through Polish via Latin, rather than directly from Greek.

музыкальный.etymology: Borrowed via Polish muzykalny or German musikalisch (adapted with Russian -ный), built on музыка ('music') and Medieval Latin mūsicālis.

музыкант.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Musikant or Polish muzykant from Late Latin mūsicans (genitive mūsicantis, 'playing music'), from Latin mūsica ('music').

мука.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мука ('flour'), from Proto-Slavic *mǫka ('flour, meal'), from the Indo-European root *menk- ('to knead, crush, press'; cf. мякнуть 'to soften', мять 'to knead').

мультиварка.etymology: Modern Russian compound coined in the 2000s from мульти- ('multi-', from Latin multus 'many') + -варка ('cooker', from варить 'to boil, cook', on the model of скороварка and пароварка).

мультик.etymology: Colloquial clipping and diminutive in -ик of мультипликационный фильм / мультфильм ('animated film', literally 'multiplication film', so called in early twentieth-century cinema because animation required multiplying/reproducing thousands of sequential frames, from Latin multiplicātiō).

мускат.etymology: Borrowed via German Muskat or French muscat from Old Provençal muscat ('having a musky aroma; nutmeg; muscat grape'), from Late Latin muscus ('musk').

мусор.etymology: Attested in Russian with the original sense 'broken plaster, rubble, sweepings, refuse'. Vasmer notes that its origin is uncertain: he compares dialectal мусарить ('to befoul, dirty') and мура ('dust, rubbish'), as well as a possible connection with dialectal бусор ('rubbish, debris') or Greek μουτζούρα ('smudge, soot').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: мусор

мусорка.etymology: Colloquial univerbation formed with the suffix -ка from мусорный бак / мусорный ящик ('garbage bin'), derived from мусор ('rubbish, trash, builder's debris', attested in Russian since the sixteenth–seventeenth centuries).

history.meaning: garbage / trash bin -> trash bin, dumpster

мусорный.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ный from мусор ('garbage, rubbish, debris', attested in Middle Russian; Vasmer discusses a possible connection with dialectal мусора 'soot, dirt, residue' or a Greek loan).

мутить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мутити, from Proto-Slavic *mǫtiti ('to stir up, make murky, agitate'), related to мутный ('turbid, cloudy').

history.meaning: to stir up, make muddy, trouble
to stir up; (slang) to scheme, be up to something

муха.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic муха, from Proto-Slavic *muxa ('fly'), from Proto-Indo-European *mūs- / *muHs- (cognate with Latin musca and Ancient Greek μυῖα).

мучить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мучити ('to torment, torture'), a denominative verb from мука ('torment, torture, agony'; note stress **мука**, distinct from **мука** 'flour', though both share the same root!), from Proto-Slavic *mǫka ('torment; flour', originally 'crushing, kneading, pressing', from PIE *menk- 'to knead, crush', cognate with Lithuanian mìnkyti 'to knead dough').

мучиться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мучитися, reflexive of мучити ('to torment, torture'), from Proto-Slavic *mǫčiti (derived from *mǫka 'torment, suffering').

мучной.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ной (and regular к -> ч palatalization) from мука ('flour, meal', inherited from Old East Slavic мука, Proto-Slavic *mǫka 'flour', originally 'something crushed or kneaded soft', ablaut-related to мять 'to knead, press').

history.meaning: flour -> flour-based, farinaceous (substantivized neuter мучное 'pastries, starchy baked goods')

мы.etymology: An inherited Slavic first-person plural pronoun, recorded in Old Church Slavonic as мы. Vasmer compares Baltic relatives, including Lithuanian mes. He discusses possible reshaping of the pronoun by analogy with other grammatical forms; that detail is a proposed historical explanation rather than a simple borrowing story.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: мы

мыло.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мыло ('soap'), from Proto-Slavic *mydlo, formed from the verb *myti ('to wash', modern Russian мыть) + the Proto-Slavic instrument suffix *-dlo (which regularly simplified to -ло in East Slavic; compare Polish mydło and Czech mýdlo): literally 'a washing-substance'.

rootFamily.gloss: to wash one's face and hands

мыльный.etymology: Derived from мыло ('soap', Proto-Slavic *mydlo, an instrument noun in *-dlo from мыть 'to wash') with the adjectival suffix -ный: 'soapy, relating to soap'.

мыслить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мыслити, from Proto-Slavic *mysliti ('to think'), denominative verb from *myslь ('thought', Russian мысль).

мысль.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мысль and Proto-Slavic *myslь ('thought, idea, intention'), related to Lithuanian mausti ('to ache for, yearn') and Ancient Greek mŷthos ('speech, thought, story').

мыть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мыти and Proto-Slavic *myti ('to wash with water'), cognate with Lithuanian maudyti ('to bathe') and Latvian maut ('to swim, immerse').

rootFamily.gloss: to wash one's face and hands

мыть.notes: Present tense stem alternates ы -> о: я мою, ты моешь, они моют.

мычать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мычати, from Proto-Slavic *myčati ('to low, moo, bellow'), of onomatopoeic origin (*myk- / *mū- imitating cattle sounds).

мышеловка.etymology: Compound noun formed in Russian from мышь ('mouse', inherited from Proto-Slavic *myšь) + linking vowel -е- + -ловка ('trap, catcher', from ловить 'to catch', Proto-Slavic *loviti).
мышеловка.notes: Famous in the Russian proverb Бесплатный сыр бывает только в мышеловке ('Free cheese is found only in a mousetrap').

мышка.etymology: Formed with the diminutive suffix -ка from мышь ('mouse', Proto-Slavic *myšь, from Proto-Indo-European *mūs 'mouse', cognate with English mouse, Latin mūs, and Sanskrit mūṣ).

мышца.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic мышьца ('muscle, arm', originally 'little mouse', diminutive of мышь 'mouse', Proto-Slavic *myšь), an ancient anatomical metaphor shared with Ancient Greek μῦς and Latin mūsculus ('little mouse -> muscle'), comparing the ripple of a flexed biceps under the skin to a darting mouse.

мышь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мышь, from Proto-Slavic *myšь ('mouse'), from Proto-Indo-European *múHs ('mouse'), directly cognate with English mouse, German Maus, Latin mūs, Ancient Greek μῦς, and Sanskrit mūṣ.

мэр.etymology: Borrowed from French maire ('mayor, head of a municipality'), from Latin māior ('greater, elder, superior', comparative of magnus 'great').

мэрия.etymology: Borrowed from French mairie ('town hall, mayor's office'), derived from maire ('mayor'), which comes from Latin maior ('greater, senior official').

cognates.meaning: head of a city (from the same Old French source)

мюзикл.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-20th century from English musical (shortening of musical comedy).

мягкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мягъкыи ('soft, tender, pliable', Old Church Slavonic мѧгъкъ), from Proto-Slavic *mękъkъ (with voicing кк > гк before a velar), continuing Proto-Indo-European *menk- ('to knead, press soft'; cognate with мука 'flour' and Lithuanian mìnkyti 'to knead dough'). Pronounced [mʲæxʲkʲɪj] ('мяхкий').
мягкий.notes: The cluster **гк** is pronounced **хк** (*мяхкий*), just like in **лёгкий** (*лёхкий*).

мягко.etymology: Adverbial form in -о of мягкий ('soft, gentle'), from Old East Slavic мягъко and Proto-Slavic *mękъko (with dissimilation of *k-k to гк).
мягко.notes: Pronounced [мяхка], with г devoicing and spirantizing to [х] before к.

мякиш.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -иш from мягкий (historically мякъкыи 'soft', from Proto-Slavic *mękъkъ): literally 'the soft inner part' of a loaf of bread or cake, as opposed to the crust (корка).

history.meaning: soft → soft inside crumb of baked bread or cake

мякоть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мякоть, from Proto-Slavic *mękъtь ('soft part'), derived from *mękъkъ ('soft', Russian мягкий).

мясник.etymology: Formed in East Slavic from мясной / мясо ('meat, flesh', Old East Slavic мясо, Proto-Slavic *męso) + the occupational agent suffix -ник.

мясной.etymology: Relational adjective inherited from Old East Slavic мясьныи, formed with the suffix -ной from мясо ('meat, flesh'), from Proto-Slavic *męso (cognate with Lithuanian mėsà, Sanskrit māṃsá-, and Gothic mimz).

мясо.etymology: An inherited Slavic word for meat or flesh. Vasmer records it across the Slavic languages and compares Baltic and Indo-Iranian relatives. It belongs to an older inherited word family rather than being a recent Russian borrowing.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: мясо

мясо.notes:
- Common collocations: *жареное мясо* (fried meat), *куриное мясо* (chicken meat).
- Genitive plural *мяс* is rare; the word is mostly used in the singular.

мясокомбинат.etymology: A Soviet-era industrial compound combining мясо ('meat', inherited from Proto-Slavic *męso) + linking vowel -о- + комбинат ('integrated industrial plant, combine', borrowed via German Kombinat from Late Latin combīnātus 'joined together').

мясорубка.etymology: Compound instrument noun formed from мясо ('meat', Proto-Slavic *męso) + linking vowel -о- + рубить ('to chop, mince', Proto-Slavic *rǫbiti) + suffix -ка.

мята.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *męta, an early borrowing from Latin menta 'mint' (with nasal *ę regularly yielding Russian я), which comes from Ancient Greek minthe.

cognates.meaning: aromatic herb (early borrowing from Latin menta)

мята.notes: Comparing Polish mięta (preserving the nasal vowel) with Russian мята nicely illustrates the regular Slavic sound law *ę -> я.

мятный.etymology: Formed in Russian with the relational suffix -ный from мята ('mint'), which entered Old East Slavic (мята / мѧта) from Latin menta ('mint', before the loss of Slavic nasal vowels turned men- into мѧ- > мя-), ultimately from Ancient Greek μίνθη (mínthē).

мять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мяти, from Proto-Slavic *męti (1sg *mьnǫ, 'to press, knead, crumple'), cognate with Lithuanian minti ('to tread, trample').

мяч.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мячь ('ball'), from Proto-Slavic *męčь ('soft/stuffed ball'), derived from the nasal root *męk- seen in мягкий ('soft', Proto-Slavic *mękъkъ) and мять ('to knead, squeeze').

мёд.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic медъ ('honey; fermented honey-wine, mead'), from Proto-Slavic *medъ, continuing one of the oldest Proto-Indo-European words, *médʰu ('honey, sweet fermented mead'), directly cognate with English mead, Lithuanian medùs ('honey'), Ancient Greek μέθυ ('wine'), and Sanskrit mádhu ('honey, sweet drink').
мёд.notes: Takes the locative ending **-у** when speaking of being in or coated with honey (**в меду**), and gave its name to the bear (**медведь**, literally 'honey-eater / honey-knower').

мёрзнуть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мьрзнути and Proto-Slavic *mьrznǫti ('to freeze, congeal with cold'), built with the inchoative suffix *-nǫti on the zero-grade of the root *merz- (whose o-grade gave *morzъ > Russian мороз 'frost').

мёртвый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic мьртвыи and Proto-Slavic *mьrtvъ ('dead'), from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥twós ('dead', built on *mer- 'to die'), directly cognate with Latin mortuus ('dead') and Sanskrit mṛtá.

на.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic на, from Proto-Slavic *na ('on, onto, at'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *h₂enō / *h₂no ('on, up along'), cognate with Ancient Greek ἀνά ('up, upon'), Gothic ana, and English on.
на.notes: Uses the prepositional case for location (на столе 'on the table') and the accusative for direction (на стол 'onto the table').

набег.etymology: Deverbal noun from набежать / набегать ('to run upon, swoop down on', formed from на- 'upon, against' + бег / бежать 'run', Proto-Slavic *běgъ): a sudden foray or raid.

набежать.etymology: Formed from the prefix на- ('onto; in a crowd or quantity') + бежать ('to run', from Proto-Slavic *běžati).

набирать.etymology: Imperfective partner of набрать ('to gather, collect, dial'), formed from prefix на- ('up, a quantity of') + -бирать (the lengthened-grade iterative stem *birati of брать 'to take, gather', from Proto-Slavic *bьrati, PIE *bʰer-). Used for gathering berries or water (набирать воду) and for dialling a phone number (набирать номер).

history.meaning: to gather, fill; to dial (a number) or type

набираться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of набраться, formed from набирать ('to gather, collect', from на- + iterative -бирать of брать 'to take') + reflexive suffix -ся.

набить.etymology: Formed from the prefix на- ('onto, to fullness, in quantity') + бить ('to beat, strike', inherited from Proto-Slavic *biti).

history.meaning: to stuff, fill; to break a quantity of; to beat up

наблюдатель.etymology: Agent noun derived from наблюдать ('to observe, watch', from на- + *bljudati, related to блюсти 'to guard, watch') + suffix -тель.

наблюдательный.etymology: Formed in Russian with the adjectival suffix -тельный from наблюдать ('to observe, watch').

history.meaning: to observe -> observant, sharp-eyed; supervisory (наблюдательный совет)

наблюдать.etymology: Imperfective of соблюсти / наблюсти, formed from на- + блюдать / блюсти ('to watch over, guard, keep', inherited from Old East Slavic блюсти, Proto-Slavic *bľusti, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- 'to be awake, be aware', cognate with будить 'to wake' and Sanskrit bódhati).

наблюдаться.etymology: Reflexive and passive form of наблюдать ('to observe, supervise', from на- + iterative stem of блюсти 'to watch, guard', Proto-Slavic *bljusti) + -ся.

history.meaning: to be observed; to be under medical care

наблюдение.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ение from наблюдать ('to observe, watch over, supervise'), built from на- ('upon, over') + the Slavic root of блюсти ('to guard, watch, keep', Old East Slavic блюсти, Proto-Slavic *bľusti), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- ('to be awake, aware'; cognate with будить 'to wake' and Sanskrit buddha 'awakened').

набор.etymology: Deverbal noun from набрать ('to gather, collect, assemble'), formed from prefix на- + -бор (o-grade root of брать 'to take', Proto-Slavic *bьrati).

набрасываться.etymology: Imperfective of наброситься ('to pounce on, fall upon'), formed from на- ('onto') + -брасывать (iterative of бросать 'to throw') + reflexive -ся.

history.meaning: to throw oneself upon, pounce on

набрать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from cumulative на- ('up, in a quantity') + брать ('to take'), inherited from Old East Slavic бьрати, from Proto-Slavic *bьrati, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- ('to carry, bear'). The sense 'to dial a telephone number' (набрать номер) developed from 'to pick out / compose characters or digits' (as in typesetting, набрать текст).

history.meaning: to gather up, take in quantity
to gather, accumulate; to dial (a number)

набраться.etymology: Reflexive of набрать ('to gather, collect'), formed from prefix на- + брать ('to take', Proto-Slavic *bьrati) + -ся.

history.meaning: to accumulate; to gain (courage/experience); (colloq.) to get drunk

наваливаться.etymology: Imperfective of навалиться ('to lean heavily on, pile on'), formed from prefix на- ('onto') + -валивать (iterative of валить 'to topple, heap', Proto-Slavic *valiti) + -ся.

наверное.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase на верное ('for certain, as a sure thing', combining на + neuter accusative of верный 'true, sure, reliable', from вера 'truth, faith'). In the 19th century наверное still meant 'for certain, surely', before softening in conversational usage (as 'surely' often does) to 'probably, most likely'.

наверняка.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase на верняка ('as a dead certainty, for sure'), built from на + colloquial/hunting noun верняк ('a sure thing, a sure shot', derived from верный 'true, sure, unerring', from вера 'truth, faith'). Unlike наверное (which softened to 'probably'), наверняка kept the strong meaning 'for sure, certainly'.

history.meaning: as a sure thing → for sure, certainly

наверх.etymology: Univerbation of the directional prepositional phrase на верх ('onto the top, upward'), combining the preposition на ('onto') with the accusative singular of верх ('top, upper part', from Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ).

наверху.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase на верху ('on the top, on the upper floor'), combining the preposition на ('on') with верху, the locative singular (-у) of верх ('top, upper part', from Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ).

навес.etymology: Deverbal noun from навесить ('to hang or suspend overhead'), formed from prefix на- ('over, above') + весить ('to hang', from Proto-Slavic *věsiti). Denotes a roofed shelter, awning, or canopy projecting over an entrance or courtyard.

history.meaning: to hang overhead → overhanging roof, canopy

навести.etymology: Perfective verb inherited from Old East Slavic навести (1st sg. наведу), formed from the prefix на- ('onto, upon') and вести ('to lead, conduct', from Proto-Slavic *vesti). Used both literally ('to direct, aim, lead onto; to build a bridge across') and in common idioms such as навести порядок ('to put in order, tidy up') and навести справки ('to make inquiries').

history.meaning: to direct, aim; to establish (навести порядок)

навестить.etymology: Derived from prefix на- + вестить ('to bring word, inquire after', from весть 'news, message', Proto-Slavic *věstь), which developed the meaning 'to call upon, visit'.

наводить.etymology: Imperfective of навести, formed from prefix на- ('onto, toward') + водить ('to lead, conduct', from Proto-Slavic *voditi).

history.meaning: to lead onto, direct, bring about

навоз.etymology: Deverbal noun from навозить ('to cart onto a field'), from prefix на- + воз / возить ('to cart, haul', Proto-Slavic *vozъ); originally 'that which is hauled onto the fields as fertilizer'.

history.meaning: carting on; load carted onto a field

наврать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from cumulative prefix на- + врать ('to lie, fib, babble', from Proto-Slavic *vьrati).

навредить.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix на- + вредить ('to harm, injure', derived from вред 'harm', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врѣдъ, Proto-Slavic *verdъ).

навсегда.etymology: Formed in Russian by fusing the directional preposition на ('for, onto') with всегда ('always'): 'for always, forever, for good'.

навык.etymology: Deverbal noun from навыкнуть ('to grow accustomed to, acquire practice in'), formed from на- + the Proto-Slavic root *vyk- (*vyknǫti 'to learn by habit, get used to', cognate with Lithuanian jùnkti 'to become accustomed' and related by ablaut to учить 'to teach/learn').

history.meaning: to get accustomed → acquired habit, skill

навязать.etymology: Formed from prefix на- ('onto') + вязать ('to tie, bind', from Proto-Slavic *vęzati); the figurative sense 'to impose, force upon' comes from 'tying something onto someone'.

history.meaning: to tie on; to impose, force on

нагадить.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix на- + гадить ('to soil, defile, do a dirty trick'), derived from гад ('reptile, vermin, loathsome creature', from Proto-Slavic *gadъ).

history.meaning: to make a mess; to do a dirty trick

наглеть.etymology: Inchoative verb in -еть formed in Russian from наглый ('impudent, brazen, insolent'), which goes back to Old East Slavic наглыи and Proto-Slavic *naglъ (originally 'sudden, abrupt, headlong', a sense preserved in Polish nagły 'sudden', shifting in Russian to 'pushy, brazen').

history.meaning: brazen, impudent -> to grow insolent, get cheeky

нагло.etymology: Adverb formed from наглый ('impudent, brazen'). In Old East Slavic наглъ and Proto-Slavic *naglъ the word meant 'sudden, abrupt, headlong, violent' (a meaning still kept in Polish nagły 'sudden'); in Russian 'acting headlong without restraint' shifted to 'brazen, insolent'.

наглость.etymology: Formed in Russian with the abstract noun suffix -ость from наглый ('impudent, brazen, insolent', from Proto-Slavic *naglъ 'sudden, headlong, rash').

наглотаться.etymology: Formed from cumulative prefix на- + глотать ('to swallow', from Proto-Slavic *glъtati) + satiative reflexive suffix -ся ('to swallow a large amount of').

наглый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic наглыи ('sudden, headlong, impetuous'), from Proto-Slavic *naglъ ('sudden, abrupt, rash', compare Polish nagły 'sudden, abrupt, urgent' and Czech náhlý 'sudden'). In Russian, the meaning shifted from acting with 'headlong abruptness' (preserved in нагрянуть) to acting with 'brazen, shameless impudence'.

нагнетать.etymology: Imperfective of нагнести ('to press, compress, pump in'), formed from prefix на- + гнетать (iterative of гнести 'to press, oppress', from Proto-Slavic *gnesti).

history.meaning: to pump in, pressurize; to stir up tension

наговаривать.etymology: Imperfective of наговорить, formed from на- ('upon, against') + говаривать (iterative of говорить 'to speak, talk'); constructed with на + accusative (наговаривать на кого-либо) it means 'to speak falsely against, slander, malign'.

history.meaning: to speak -> to slander, malign; to record voice; to recite a charm

rootFamily.gloss: to say a lot; to slander (perfective)

наговорить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from the cumulative prefix на- ('in a large quantity, a lot of') + говорить ('to speak, talk', inherited from Old East Slavic говорити and Proto-Slavic *govoriti).

history.meaning: to say a lot of (often too much); to slander

награда.etymology: Formed as a deverbal noun from наградить ('to reward, endow'), combining Old Church Slavonic initial на- + -град- (from Proto-Slavic *gorditi 'to build up, enclose, replenish'; compare город and преграда) and reinforced semantically by Polish nagroda ('reward, recompense').

наградить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic наградити ('to reward, compensate; originally to build up, replenish'), showing South Slavic -град- (from Proto-Slavic *gorditi).

наградной.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ной from награда ('reward, decoration, medal').

history.meaning: reward, award -> commendation, awarded as an honour (наградное оружие)

награждать.etymology: Imperfective of наградить ('to reward, decorate'), borrowed/adapted from Old Church Slavonic награждати / наградити (showing South Slavic -ра- and *dj -> жд, originally 'to build up, replenish, compensate', from на- + градити 'to build, enclose').

history.meaning: to reward, award, confer a decoration

нагрев.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from нагреть / нагревать ('to heat up, warm'), built from на- + греть ('to warm, heat', inherited from Proto-Slavic *grěti).

history.meaning: to heat up -> heating, heat level

нагреваться.etymology: Reflexive-intransitive verb formed from нагревать ('to heat up', imperfective of нагреть, from на- + греть 'to warm', Proto-Slavic *grěti) + -ся.

history.meaning: to heat (trans.) -> to heat up, get hot (intrans.)

нагружать.etymology: Imperfective of нагрузить ('to load, burden'), formed from prefix на- ('onto') + гружать (iterative of грузить 'to load', from груз 'cargo, weight').

нагрузка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from нагрузить / нагружать ('to load, burden', from груз 'load') + noun suffix -ка.

нагуливать.etymology: Imperfective of нагулять ('to acquire by walking or grazing, work up an appetite'), formed from cumulative prefix на- + -гуливать (iterative of гулять 'to walk, stroll').

history.meaning: to walk / to gain by walking
to work up (an appetite), put on (weight)

нагулять.etymology: Formed from the cumulative prefix на- ('acquire or build up by doing an action') + гулять ('to walk, stroll outdoors'): most commonly in нагулять аппетит ('to work up an appetite by walking in the fresh air').

history.meaning: to stroll -> to work up (an appetite, rosy cheeks) by walking

над.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic надъ ('above, over'), from Proto-Slavic *nadъ, historically an extension of the preposition *na ('on, upon') with the spatial suffix *-dъ (parallel to *podъ 'under' and *perdъ 'in front of').
над.notes: Governs the instrumental case: лампа над столом ('the lamp above the table'); becomes надо before consonant clusters (надо мной).

надавить.etymology: Formed from the prefix на- ('on, upon') + давить ('to press, squeeze, weigh down', inherited from Proto-Slavic *daviti).

history.meaning: to press down on; (figurative) to put pressure on someone

надевать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic надѣвати (Proto-Slavic *naděvati), the imperfective of надеть ('to put on clothes or accessories'), formed from на- ('onto') + девать / деть ('to put, place', Proto-Slavic *děti).
надевать.notes: Usage rule: надевать что-то (на себя) ('to put an item of clothing on'), vs. одевать кого-то ('to dress someone').

надежда.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic надежда ('hope, reliance'), showing the characteristic South Slavic reflex -жд- from Proto-Slavic *dj (compare the native East Slavic root in надёжный 'reliable'), formed from на- ('upon') + *děti ('to put, place'): literally 'putting one's trust upon something'.

наделать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from cumulative prefix на- ('a quantity of') + делать ('to do, make', from Proto-Slavic *dělati).

history.meaning: to make a lot of; to commit, cause (trouble)

надеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic надѣти, from Proto-Slavic *naděti ('to put on, place upon'), formed from the prefix *na- ('on, onto') and *děti ('to put, place', Russian деть, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- 'to put, do').
надеть.notes: Standard Russian distinguishes **надеть** ('to put an item of clothing on oneself': *надеть пальто, надеть очки*) from **одеть** ('to dress a person': *одеть ребёнка*).

надеяться.etymology: Inherited via Old Church Slavonic and Old East Slavic надѣятися ('to hope, rely on'), built on the prefix на- + дѣяти ('to do, place') + -ся: originally 'to place oneself or one's trust upon something'.

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic
history.meaning: to place one's trust in, hope

надзор.etymology: Deverbal noun from надзирать / надзреть ('to oversee, watch over'), formed from над- ('over, above') + the o-grade root -зор of зреть ('to look, see', Proto-Slavic *zьrěti / *zorъ), corresponding in structure to Latin supervīsiō and German Aufsicht.

history.meaning: to watch over -> supervision, oversight, surveillance

надо.etymology: Shortened in East Slavic from older надобѣ ('it is necessary, needed'), historically the locative phrase на добѣ ('at the right time, in season, fittingly') from доба ('fitting time, usefulness', related to добрый and удобный).

history.meaning: at the right time -> it is needed

надоедать.etymology: Imperfective of надоесть ('to bore, weary, pester'), historically formed from prefix над- (надо-) + есть / ясти ('to eat', Proto-Slavic *ěsti), literally 'to eat away at someone'.

надоесть.etymology: Formed from the prefix над- / надо- ('over, upon, to excess') and есть ('to eat', Old East Slavic ѣсти, Proto-Slavic *ěsti, from PIE *h₁ed-). Literally 'to eat away at someone, gnaw at someone to excess', whence 'to bore to death, make someone sick and tired of something' (мне это надоело).

history.meaning: to gnaw at, eat away at
to bore, get on someone's nerves, make sick and tired of (+ dat.)

надолго.etymology: Adverb formed by univerbation of the prepositional phrase на долго ('for a long time'), combining the preposition на ('for') with долго ('long', from Proto-Slavic *dъlgo).

history.meaning: for a long time, for long

надпись.etymology: Formed as a prefixal-stem noun from надписать ('to write upon, superscribe', from над- 'above, upon' + писать 'to write'): 'something written on a surface, an inscription, caption, or label'.

history.meaning: to write on top of, inscribe

надрыв.etymology: Deverbal noun from надорвать / надрывать ('to tear slightly; to strain excessively'), formed from prefix над- ('partially, on the surface') + рыв- (from рвать 'to tear', Proto-Slavic *rъvati).

надумать.etymology: Formed from the resultative prefix на- + думать ('to think', from дума 'thought, counsel', Proto-Slavic *dumati): 'to arrive at a decision after thinking, make up one's mind'.

history.meaning: to decide, think up, make up one's mind

надуться.etymology: Reflexive of надуть ('to inflate, puff up'), formed from prefix на- + дуть ('to blow', from Proto-Slavic *duti) + -ся; the sense 'to sulk, pout' comes from puffing out one's cheeks or lips.

history.meaning: to puff up; to sulk, pout

надёжно.etymology: Adverb formed from надёжный ('reliable, secure', derived from East Slavic надёжа 'hope, reliance', corresponding to Church Slavonic надежда) + -о.

надёжность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from надёжный ('reliable, trustworthy, sturdy'), the native East Slavic counterpart (with ж from *dj and ё before a hard consonant) of Church Slavonic надежда ('hope, reliance', from на- + деть 'to place trust upon').

надёжный.etymology: Derived in Russian from the native East Slavic noun надёжа ('hope, reliance, mainstay', the East Slavic counterpart of Church Slavonic надежда 'hope', from Proto-Slavic *nadědja) with the adjectival suffix -ный: 'worthy of trust, reliable, secure'.

наедине.etymology: Adverb formed by univerbation of the Old Church Slavonic / older Russian prepositional phrase на ѥдинѣ ('in one, alone by oneself'), from на + the locative singular of единъ ('one, single, alone', Proto-Slavic *jedinъ).

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

наесться.etymology: Formed from cumulative prefix на- + есть ('to eat', from Proto-Slavic *ěsti) + satiative reflexive suffix -ся ('to eat to full satisfaction').

наехать.etymology: Formed from prefix на- ('onto, into') + ехать ('to ride, drive', from Proto-Slavic *ěxati); in colloquial slang, 'to confronting or laying into someone' metaphors running into them.

history.meaning: to run into; (slang) to lay into, confront

нажарить.etymology: Formed from cumulative prefix на- ('a quantity of') + жарить ('to fry, roast', derived from жар 'heat, embers', Proto-Slavic *žarъ).

history.meaning: to fry up a quantity of

нажать.etymology: Formed from на- ('onto, down upon') + жать ('to press, squeeze', Proto-Slavic *žęti, 1sg жму): 'to press down on (a button, lever, or pedal)'.
нажать.notes: Future tense uses the nasal-derived -м- stem: я нажму, ты нажмёшь ('I will press').

наждачный.etymology: Derived with the suffix -ный from наждак ('emery, corundum abrasive'), borrowed into Russian via Ottoman Turkish or Kipchak Turkic nacdak / naždak from Persian naxčak and Arabic naxec ('emery stone').
наждачный.notes: Most commonly encountered in наждачная бумага ('sandpaper, emery paper').

нажимать.etymology: Imperfective of нажать ('to press'), formed from prefix на- ('onto') + -жимать (iterative of жать 'to squeeze, press', from Proto-Slavic *žęti / *žimati).

нажраться.etymology: Formed from cumulative prefix на- + жрать ('to devour, gorge', from Proto-Slavic *žьrati) + satiative reflexive suffix -ся; colloquially extended from 'to gorge oneself' to 'to get blind drunk'.

history.meaning: to gorge oneself; (slang) to get hammered

назад.etymology: Univerbation of the Old East Slavic prepositional phrase на задъ ('onto the back part, backward'), combining the directional preposition на with the accusative singular of зад ('back, rear part', from Proto-Slavic *zadъ). Used both spatially ('back, backward') and temporally after a duration ('ago': пять минут назад).

названивать.etymology: Iterative verb formed from prefix на- + -званивать (frequentative of звонить 'to ring, call', from звон 'ringing sound', Proto-Slavic *zvonъ).

название.etymology: Verbal noun formed from назвать ('to call by name, name, title'), built from prefix на- + звать ('to call', from Old East Slavic зъвати, Proto-Slavic *zъvati). Names the title of a book, hotel, street, or object (whereas a person's given name is имя).

history.meaning: name (of a thing, place, or book), title

назвать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic назьвати ('to call by name, summon'), formed from the prefix на- and звать ('to call', Old East Slavic зъвати, Proto-Slavic *zъvati, cognate with Sanskrit hváyati 'calls, invokes').

назло.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase на зло ('for evil, to spite'), from на ('for, onto') + зло ('evil, harm, spite', from Proto-Slavic *zъlo).

назначать.etymology: Imperfective of назначить ('to appoint, designate, set'), formed from prefix на- + -значать (from значить 'to mark, signify', derived from знак 'sign, mark').

назначение.etymology: Verbal noun formed from назначить ('to appoint, designate, assign', from на- + значить) + suffix -ение.

назначить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix на- and значить ('to mark, signify, mean'), derived from знак ('sign, mark', from Proto-Slavic *znakъ, built on *znati 'to know'). Literally, 'to put a mark on, designate for a role or time', whence 'to appoint (to a post), set (a date/meeting), or prescribe (treatment)'.

history.meaning: to appoint, designate, set (a time), prescribe

называть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic называти (Proto-Slavic *nazyvati), the imperfective of назвать ('to call by name, name'), formed from на- + звать ('to call', Proto-Slavic *zъvati) with lengthened root vowel *ъ -> *y.

называться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive/passive verb formed from называть ('to call, name', imperfective of назвать, with lengthened root vowel -ы- from Proto-Slavic *nazyvati, built on *zъvati 'to call'). Means 'to be called, have the name/title of'.

rootFamily.gloss: name, title (of an object, book, restaurant)

наивный.etymology: Borrowed in the late 18th century from French naïf (feminine naïve, 'natural, artless, naive'), inherited from Latin nātīvus ('inborn, natural'), adapted with Russian adjectival suffix -ный.

найти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic наити ('to come upon, walk onto, find'), from Proto-Slavic *naiti, formed from the prefix *na- ('onto, upon') + *iti ('to walk, go', modern Russian идти). Literally 'to walk right onto something, come across it', which became the standard Slavic verb 'to find' (parallel to Latin invenīre 'to come upon').

history.meaning: to walk upon, come across → to find

найтись.etymology: Perfective reflexive/passive form of найти ('to find', literally 'to come upon by walking', from на- 'onto, upon' + йти / идти 'to go', Old East Slavic наити, Proto-Slavic *najьti). With -сь, найтись means 'to be found, turn up' (and figuratively 'to find the right words, not be at a loss').

rootFamily.gloss: to be located; to be found (impf.)

наказание.etymology: Verbal noun from наказать ('to punish; in older Russian, to instruct, admonish'), formed from на- + казать ('to show, order', Proto-Slavic *kazati) + -ание.

наказанный.etymology: Past passive participle (used adjectivally) of наказать ('to punish', from на- + казать 'to show, admonish', Proto-Slavic *nakazati).

наказать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic наказати ('to instruct, admonish, teach a lesson'), formed from the prefix на- and казати ('to show, point out, speak', Proto-Slavic *kazati). Up to the 18th century, наказать meant 'to instruct, give orders' (preserved in наказ 'mandate, instruction to a deputy'); from 'teaching someone a stern lesson', it shifted in modern Russian to 'to punish'.

наказывать.etymology: Imperfective of наказать ('to punish; originally to instruct, order'), formed from prefix на- + -казывать (iterative of казать 'to show, declare', Proto-Slavic *kazati).

накатить.etymology: Formed from prefix на- ('onto') + катить ('to roll', from Proto-Slavic *kotiti); colloquially used for knocking back a shot of alcohol.

history.meaning: to roll onto; (colloq.) to have a drink

накачивать.etymology: Imperfective of накачать ('to pump up, inflate'), formed from prefix на- + -качивать (iterative of качать 'to rock, pump').

накладка.etymology: Formed in Russian from накладывать / наложить ('to lay on top, superimpose', from на- 'on' + класть 'to lay, put') + the noun suffix -ка. Originally denoting a physical overlay, patch, or hairpiece, it acquired the colloquial figurative sense 'an unintended overlap, mix-up, hitch'.

history.meaning: to lay on top, overlap → overlay; mix-up, hitch

наклейка.etymology: Deverbal object noun formed in Russian with the suffix -ка from наклеить ('to glue on, stick on'), built from на- ('onto') + клеить ('to glue', from клей 'glue', Proto-Slavic *klejь).

history.meaning: to stick on -> sticker, pasted label

наклон.etymology: Deverbal noun from наклонить ('to tilt, incline, bend'), formed from prefix на- + клон (from клонить 'to incline, bend', Proto-Slavic *kloniti).

наклонить.etymology: Formed with the prefix на- ('downward, toward') + клонить ('to incline, bend, tilt'), inherited from Old East Slavic клонити and Proto-Slavic *kloniti.

наклониться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of наклонить ('to tilt, bend down'), formed with prefix на- ('onto, downward') + клонить ('to incline, bend, bow', from Proto-Slavic *kloniti).

history.meaning: to tilt → to lean down, bend over

наклонять.etymology: Derived as the imperfective of наклонить ('to tilt, incline, bend downward'), formed from на- ('toward, down') + клонить ('to incline, bow', Proto-Slavic *kloniti).

наконец.etymology: Formed in Russian by univerbation of the prepositional phrase на конец ('to the end, at the end'), from на ('to, at') + конец ('end', Proto-Slavic *konьcь).

наконец-то.etymology: Formed in Russian from наконец ('finally, at last', a univerbation of the prepositional phrase на конец 'at the end', from конец 'end', Proto-Slavic *konьcь) + the emphatic particle -то, expressing relief or long-awaited completion.

накопить.etymology: Formed from the cumulative prefix на- ('amass a quantity of') + копить ('to save up, hoard, accumulate', derived from копа 'heap, stack, threescore', inherited from Proto-Slavic *kopa).

history.meaning: heap, stack -> to heap up, amass

накопиться.etymology: Reflexive of накопить ('to accumulate, save up'), formed from cumulative prefix на- + копить ('to amass, hoard', from копа 'heap, stack', Proto-Slavic *kopa) + -ся.

накормить.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix на- ('to satiety, fully') from кормить ('to feed, nourish'), derived from корм ('fodder, food'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъrmiti.

накосячить.etymology: Colloquial slang perfective verb formed with на- from косячить ('to botch, blunder, mess up'), derived from косяк ('something skewed or awry; a blunder', built on косой 'crooked, askew, slanted', Proto-Slavic *kosъ).

history.meaning: askew -> blunder -> to mess up, screw up

накраситься.etymology: Reflexive of накрасить ('to paint, dye'), formed from prefix на- + красить ('to color, paint, adorn', from краса 'beauty, color', Proto-Slavic *krasa) + -ся.

history.meaning: to put on makeup, dye one's hair

накричать.etymology: Formed from the prefix на- ('upon, at', governing на + accusative) + кричать ('to shout, yell', inherited from Proto-Slavic *kričati).

history.meaning: to yell at, scold loudly (накричать на кого-либо)

накрутить.etymology: Formed from prefix на- ('onto, in quantity') + крутить ('to twist, wind, turn', inherited from Proto-Slavic *krǫtiti).

history.meaning: to wind onto; to inflate, pile on

накручивать.etymology: Imperfective of накрутить ('to wind up, inflate'), formed from prefix на- + -кручивать (iterative of крутить 'to twist, wind', Proto-Slavic *krǫtiti).

history.meaning: to wind up; (colloq.) to agitate, work up

накрывать.etymology: Imperfective of накрыть ('to cover'), formed from prefix на- ('over, onto') + -крывать (iterative of крыть 'to cover', from Proto-Slavic *kryti).

накрыть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic накрыти, formed from prefix на- ('over, onto') + крыть ('to cover', from Proto-Slavic *kryti).

накрыться.etymology: Reflexive of накрыть ('to cover', from на- + крыть 'to cover', Proto-Slavic *kryti) + -ся; in colloquial slang, 'to break down, fall through' (as if covered over and finished).

history.meaning: to cover oneself; (slang) to break down, fall through

накушаться.etymology: Formed from cumulative prefix на- + кушать ('to eat, taste', from Proto-Slavic *kušati / *kusiti 'to taste, try') + satiative reflexive suffix -ся.

history.meaning: to eat one's fill; (ironic) to get drunk

наладиться.etymology: Reflexive-intransitive derivative of наладить ('to put in order, adjust, set right', formed from на- + ладить 'to arrange harmoniously', built on лад 'harmony, order', Proto-Slavic *ladъ) + -ся.

history.meaning: order, harmony -> to put in order
to set right -> to work out, come right, improve

налаживать.etymology: Imperfective of наладить ('to adjust, put in order, establish'), formed from prefix на- + -лаживать (iterative of ладить 'to arrange, make harmonious', from лад 'harmony, order', Proto-Slavic *ladъ).

history.meaning: order, harmony / to put in order

налаживаться.etymology: Imperfective of наладиться ('to work out, get sorted'), formed from налаживать ('to set right, adjust', from на- + ладить 'to put in order', with regular д -> ж palatalization) + -ся.

history.meaning: to get sorted out, start going well (Жизнь налаживается!)

morphemes.meaning: order, harmony (from лад with д -> ж)

налево.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase на лево ('to the left'), combining the directional preposition на with the short neuter accusative of левый ('left', from Old East Slavic лѣвыи, Proto-Slavic *lěvъ, continuing PIE *leh₂iwós 'left, curved'; directly cognate with Latin laevus and Ancient Greek λαιός 'left').

history.meaning: to the left, on the left

налегать.etymology: Imperfective of налечь ('to lean heavily on'), formed from prefix на- ('onto') + -легать (iterative of лечь 'to lie down', from Proto-Slavic *lěgati).

history.meaning: to lean on; to go heavy on (food, work)

наливать.etymology: Imperfective partner of налить ('to pour, fill by pouring'), formed from prefix на- ('in, onto') + ливать (iterative of лить 'to pour', from Old East Slavic лити, Proto-Slavic *liti, cognate with Lithuanian lìeti 'to pour').

налить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic налити (future налью, past налил), formed from prefix на- ('into, onto') + лить ('to pour', from Proto-Slavic *liti, continuing Balto-Slavic *lei- 'to pour, flow'; cognate with Lithuanian lìeti 'to pour' and lytùs 'rain').

наличные.etymology: Substantivized plural of наличный (as in наличные деньги 'cash money'), formed from the phrase на лицо ('present in person, physically before one's face/eyes', built on на + лицо 'face, presence'): originally 'goods or coins physically on hand for inspection', as opposed to credit or bills of exchange.
