history.meaning: present before one's eyes → ready money on hand, cash

наличный.etymology: Derived from the prepositional phrase на лицо ('present in person, visible before one's eyes, on hand'), built on на ('on') + лицо ('face, person, actual presence', Proto-Slavic *lice).

history.meaning: present on the spot, on hand

наловить.etymology: Formed from cumulative prefix на- ('a quantity of') + ловить ('to catch, hunt', from Proto-Slavic *loviti, from *lovъ 'hunt, catch').

налоговая.etymology: Colloquial substantivized feminine adjective from налоговая инспекция / служба ('tax inspection / service'); налоговый derives from налог ('tax', from наложить 'to impose, lay upon').

налогоплательщик.etymology: Compound noun formed in Russian (calquing German Steuerzahler) from налог ('tax, assessment', originally 'that which is laid upon', deverbal from наложить) + linking vowel -о- + плательщик ('payer', from платить 'to pay').

намекать.etymology: Imperfective of намекнуть ('to hint, allude'), formed from prefix на- + -мекать (related to смекать 'to grasp, figure out', from Proto-Slavic *mьkati / *mekati).

намекнуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective of намекать ('to hint, imply'), formed with the suffix -нуть.

намерен.etymology: Predicative short adjective from Old Church Slavonic намѣренъ ('aimed at, intended'), past passive participle of намѣрити ('to measure out, aim at, intend', from на- + мѣрити 'to measure').

намечаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of наметиться, formed from намечать ('to mark out, plan', from на- + метить 'to mark, aim', derived from мета 'mark, target') + -ся.

history.meaning: to be planned, be in the offing

намного.etymology: Formed by fusing the preposition на ('by [a margin]') with много ('much, a lot'): literally 'by a lot, much (+ comparative)'.
намного.notes: Used before comparatives: намного лучше ('much better'), намного проще ('far simpler').

намокнуть.etymology: Formed in Russian from the prefix на- ('to a resulting state') + мокнуть ('to get wet', built on the root of мокрый 'wet', Proto-Slavic *mokrъ).
намокнуть.notes: Past tense drops the suffix -ну-: он намок, она промокла.

намёк.etymology: Deverbal noun back-formed from намекать / намекнуть ('to hint, imply').

нанести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нанести ('to bring upon, lay on'), formed from prefix на- ('onto, upon a surface') + нести ('to carry, bring', from Proto-Slavic *nesti). Used for brushing on glaze/paint, plotting marks on a map, or paying a visit.

history.meaning: to apply, brush on (glaze, paint), mark (on a map)

нанимать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic наимати and Proto-Slavic *najьmati ('to hire, rent', imperfective of нанять < *najęti), formed from на- + имать ('to take', Proto-Slavic *jьmati): literally 'to take on (a worker or lodging for pay)'.

history.meaning: to take on -> to hire, rent

наниматься.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of наняться ('to take a job, hire oneself out'), formed from нанимать ('to hire, rent', from на- + -нимать / ять 'to take', Proto-Slavic *najьmati) + -ся.

history.meaning: to get hired, take a job

наносить.etymology: Imperfective of нанести, formed from на- ('onto, upon') + носить ('to carry, bring', iterative of нести, from Proto-Slavic *nositi).

history.meaning: to apply (a layer of cream or paint); to inflict (a blow, damage, or insult); to pay (a visit)

нанять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic наяти (наиму, 'to hire, rent, take on'), from Proto-Slavic *na-jęti ('to take on for pay', from *jęti 'to take').

history.meaning: to hire, to employ; to rent

наоборот.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase на оборот ('onto the reverse turn/side'), combining на with оборот ('turn, rotation, reverse side', native East Slavic pleophonic form from Proto-Slavic *ob-vortъ, built on *vьrtěti 'to turn').

history.meaning: on the contrary, the other way round, vice versa

наорать.etymology: Colloquial perfective verb formed from prefix на- ('at, onto') + орать ('to yell, shout', from Proto-Slavic *orati 'to shout, bawl').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — орать (to shout)

наотрез.etymology: Adverb formed by univerbation of the prepositional phrase на отрез ('as if cutting clean off'), from на + отрез ('a clean cut-off', deverbal from отрезать 'to cut off', Proto-Slavic *otrězati).

history.meaning: to cut off -> clean cut -> flatly, point-blank (especially in отказаться наотрез 'to refuse point-blank')

нападающий.etymology: Substantivized present active participle of нападать ('to attack', from на- 'upon' + падать 'to fall', Proto-Slavic *padati); adopted in twentieth-century sporting terminology as a semantic calque of English forward / attacker.

напарник.etymology: Formed in Russian from на паре ('in a pair, working as a pair') — from на- + пара ('pair', borrowed via German Paar / Polish para from Latin paria 'equal things, pair') + the person suffix -ник: 'one who works in a pair with another, work partner, teammate'.

напасть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic напасти and Proto-Slavic *napasti ('to fall upon, attack'), formed from на- ('upon, against') + пасть ('to fall', Proto-Slavic *pasti).

напевать.etymology: Formed in Russian from на- ('lightly, in a low or casual way') + певать (iterative of петь 'to sing', Proto-Slavic *pěti): 'to hum, croon, sing softly to oneself'.

напечатать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix на- from печатать ('to stamp with a seal, print, type'), derived from печать ('seal, stamp, printing press', Old East Slavic печать, Proto-Slavic *pečatь).

написанный.etymology: Past passive participle of написать ('to write'), formed with resultative prefix на- + писать ('to write') + participial suffix -нн-. Писать continues Old East Slavic пьсати and Proto-Slavic *pьsati ('to trace, paint, write'), from Proto-Indo-European *peyk̂- ('to mark, incise, paint').
написанный.notes: Long attributive forms keep double нн (написанный от руки адрес), whereas short predicate forms drop to a single н (тут написано, открытка написана).

написать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic написати ('to write, paint'), formed as the standard perfective of писать ('to write') by adding the prefix на- ('on a surface, to completion').

history.meaning: to write down, paint on a surface

напиток.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic напитокъ, formed with the noun suffix -ок from напить / напиться ('to drink one's fill', passive participle напитый), built from the prefix на- and пить ('to drink', Proto-Slavic *piti).

напиться.etymology: Formed from the saturative prefix на- ('to one's fill, to excess') + пить ('to drink', inherited from Old East Slavic пити, Proto-Slavic *piti, PIE *peh₃-) + the reflexive postfix -ся, which together express doing an action to satiety ('to drink one's fill of water') or excess ('to get drunk').

history.meaning: to drink one's fill; to get drunk

напихать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from cumulative prefix на- ('in quantity, to fullness') + пихать ('to shove, stuff, push', from Proto-Slavic *pьxati / *pixati).

наплевать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix на- ('onto') + плевать ('to spit', from Proto-Slavic *pľьvati); used figuratively and predicatively to mean 'to not care at all'.

history.meaning: to spit on; not to care

напоить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic напоити and Proto-Slavic *napojiti ('to give to drink'), formed from completive на- + поить ('to give to drink, water', Proto-Slavic *pojiti, the o-grade causative of *piti 'to drink').

history.meaning: to drink -> to cause to drink -> to give a drink
to give someone a drink (e.g. tea); to get someone drunk

наполнить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic напълнити, formed from prefix на- + полнить ('to fill', from полный 'full', Proto-Slavic *pьlnъ).

наполнять.etymology: Imperfective of наполнить ('to fill'), formed from prefix на- + -полнять (from полный 'full', Proto-Slavic *pьlnъ).

наполовину.etymology: Formed by fusing the preposition на ('to the extent of') with the accusative singular половину of половина ('half', derived from пол 'half', Proto-Slavic *polъ).

напоминать.etymology: Imperfective of напомнить ('to remind'), formed from prefix на- + поминать ('to mention, remember', related to помнить 'to remember', from Proto-Slavic *pomьniti).

напомнить.etymology: Formed in Russian from на- ('onto, into awareness') + помнить ('to remember', Proto-Slavic *pomьniti, from *mьněti 'to think, keep in mind'): 'to bring back to someone's memory, remind'.

напоследок.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase на последок ('for the end, at the close'), from на + последок ('remnant, end', derived from после 'after', Proto-Slavic *poslědъ).

history.meaning: for the last, at the end

направить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic направити (Proto-Slavic *napraviti 'to make straight, guide, direct'), formed from на- ('toward') + править ('to direct, steer, make straight', from правый 'straight, right').

направление.etymology: Verbal noun in -ение from направить ('to direct, guide, refer'), built from на- + править ('to steer, direct, make straight', derived from правый 'straight, right', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

history.meaning: to direct, refer -> direction, trend; medical or official referral slip

направлять.etymology: Imperfective of направить ('to direct, guide, send'), formed from prefix на- + -правлять (from править 'to guide, steer, straighten', from правый 'straight, right', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

направляться.etymology: Reflexive of направлять ('to direct, guide') + -ся ('to direct oneself, head toward').

направо.etymology: Formed in East Slavic by fusing the directional preposition на ('to') with the short neuter accusative право of правый ('right', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

history.meaning: to the right, on the right

например.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase на пример ('for an example, after the model of'), formed from the preposition на ('for, onto') + пример ('example, model'), which is derived from примерить ('to try on, measure against', from при- + мерить 'to measure', built on мера 'measure', Proto-Slavic *měra).

напролёт.etymology: Adverb formed by univerbation of the prepositional phrase на пролёт ('straight through in a single flight'), from на + пролёт ('flight straight through', from пролететь 'to fly through', built on лететь 'to fly', Proto-Slavic *letěti).

history.meaning: straight through -> all through without stopping, on end (всю ночь напролёт 'all night long')

напроситься.etymology: Formed from prefix на- + просить ('to ask, beg', from Proto-Slavic *prositi) + reflexive suffix -ся ('to get oneself invited; to ask for trouble').

history.meaning: to invite oneself; to ask for it

напротив.etymology: Compound preposition and adverb formed from на ('on, at') + против ('opposite, against', from Proto-Slavic *protivъ).

history.meaning: opposite, across from; on the contrary

напрягать.etymology: Imperfective of напрячь ('to tense, strain'), from prefix на- + *pręgti ('to harness, stretch, pull taut', cf. Old Church Slavonic напрѧшти, упряжь).

history.meaning: to strain, tense; (colloq.) to bother, stress out

напрягаться.etymology: Reflexive of напрягать ('to strain, tense', from Proto-Slavic *napręgti) + -ся.

напряжённый.etymology: Past passive participle / verbal adjective of напрячь ('to strain, tense, stretch tight'), formed from на- + прячь ('to harness, draw tight, stretch', from Proto-Slavic *pręťi, seen in упряжка 'team harness').

history.meaning: to stretch tight, draw a bow
to strain, tense -> tense, strained, intense

напрямую.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase на прямую (дорогу / линию) ('onto the straight road/line'), from на + feminine accusative of прямой ('straight, direct', Proto-Slavic *prěmъ).

напугать.etymology: Perfective counterpart of пугать ('to scare, frighten'), formed with the prefix на- and the expressive East Slavic verb пугать (compare dialectal пуга 'whip; owl' and Ukrainian пугач 'eagle owl', from an onomatopoeic cry *pug- used to startle birds or animals).

нарезать.etymology: Formed from the cumulative prefix на- ('in a quantity, into pieces') and резать ('to cut, slice'), inherited from Old East Slavic рѣзати and Proto-Slavic *rězati ('to cut, carve', cognate with Lithuanian rėžti 'to cut, incise'). Note that stress distinguishes aspect: perfective **нарезать** ('to slice up') vs. imperfective **нарезать**.

нарезка.etymology: Formed in Russian as an action and result noun from нарезать ('to slice up, cut into pieces', from на- + резать 'to cut') with the suffix -ка.

history.meaning: slicing; platter of sliced food (cold cuts, cheese)

нарисованный.etymology: Past passive participle of нарисовать ('to draw, paint'), formed from prefix на- + рисовать ('to draw', borrowed via Polish rysować from Middle High German rīzen 'to incise, draw').

нарисовать.etymology: Formed in Russian by adding the perfectivizing prefix на- ('onto a surface, to completion') to рисовать ('to draw').

наркоз.etymology: Borrowed via German Narkose from Ancient Greek νάρκωσις (nárkōsis, 'numbing, stupor, torpor'), derived from ναρκόω ('to benumb, deaden', from νάρκη 'numbness, torpor').

народ.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic народъ ('people, multitude, lineage'), from Proto-Slavic *narodъ, a deverbal noun formed from *naroditi ('to give birth to in numbers, beget, produce'), from *na- + *roditi ('to give birth', Russian родить). Literally, 'that which has been born or grown up together, a generation or people'.

народный.etymology: Relational adjective inherited from Old East Slavic народьныи, formed from народ ('people, nation', from Proto-Slavic *narodъ) + the adjectival suffix -ный.

наружу.etymology: Formed by univerbation of the prepositional phrase на ружу ('to the outside, into open view'), from Old East Slavic ружь ('outward appearance, open air, outside', related to обнаружить 'to uncover, detect').
наружу.notes: Indicates motion outward (выйти наружу 'to come out'), whereas снаружи indicates location ('on the outside').

нарушать.etymology: Imperfective of нарушить ('to violate, break, disturb'), borrowed/adapted from Old Church Slavonic нарушати / нарушити ('to break down, destroy, transgress'), formed from на- + рушить ('to pull down, demolish, break', Proto-Slavic *rušiti).

history.meaning: to violate, break (a law, rule, silence, or peace)

нарушение.etymology: Verbal noun formed from нарушить ('to break, violate, disturb'), built from на- + рушить ('to break down, tear down, shatter', from Proto-Slavic *rušiti). Just as English speaks of 'breaking' a law or rule, Russian uses нарушить / нарушение for the 'breach or violation' of a rule, law, or order.

history.meaning: to break (a rule/peace) → violation, breach, infringement

нарушить.etymology: Formed from prefix на- + рушить ('to break down, destroy, disturb', inherited from Proto-Slavic *rušiti).

нарушиться.etymology: Reflexive and intransitive form of нарушить ('to break, violate, disrupt') + -ся.

нарываться.etymology: Imperfective of нарваться ('to dash oneself onto a sharp obstacle or ambush; colloquially to ask for trouble, provoke a fight'), formed from на- ('onto, against') + рываться (iterative of рваться 'to rush, lunge, tear forward', from рвать 'to tear', Proto-Slavic *rъvati) + -ся.

history.meaning: to run into an ambush -> (colloquial) to ask for trouble, push one's luck

нарываться.notes: Often heard in the colloquial warning Ты нарываешься! ('You're asking for trouble! / You're pushing it!').

насильно.etymology: Adverb formed from насильный ('forced, violent'), derived from насилие / на силу ('by force', from сила 'strength, force', Proto-Slavic *sila).

насквозь.etymology: Adverb formed in Russian from prefix на- + сквозь ('through, right through'), inherited from Old East Slavic сквозѣ and Proto-Slavic *skvozě ('through an opening or gap').

history.meaning: right through, all the way through

насколько.etymology: Adverb and conjunction formed by univerbation of the prepositional phrase на сколько ('to how much, by how much'), from на + сколько ('how much, how many', Proto-Slavic *kolьko).

history.meaning: to what extent, how much; as far as (насколько я знаю 'as far as I know')

насладиться.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic насладитися ('to take delight in, enjoy'), formed from на- + сладити ('to make sweet, delight', showing South Slavic слад- for East Slavic солод-, Proto-Slavic *soldъ 'sweet').

наслаждаться.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic наслаждатися, imperfective of насладитися ('to delight in, enjoy'), exhibiting the South Slavic *dj > жд reflex from Proto-Slavic *soldъ ('sweet').

наследие.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic наслѣдие ('inheritance, heritage'), built on на- + слѣдъ ('track, footprint', Proto-Slavic *slědъ): literally 'that which follows in a predecessor's footsteps'.

наследница.etymology: Feminine form of наследник ('heir', from наследовать 'to inherit, follow in the footsteps of', derived from след 'footprint, track', Proto-Slavic *slědъ) + suffix -ница.

наследство.etymology: Derived from наследить / наследовать ('to succeed, inherit', literally 'to step into the tracks of', from на- + след 'track, footprint', Proto-Slavic *slědъ) + suffix -ство.

насмотреться.etymology: Formed from cumulative prefix на- + смотреть ('to look, watch', from Proto-Slavic *smotriti) + satiative reflexive suffix -ся ('to watch to one's fill').

history.meaning: to see enough of, have one's fill of looking

наснимать.etymology: Formed from cumulative prefix на- ('a large quantity of') + снимать ('to take off; to photograph, film').

history.meaning: to take off; to photograph, film
to film or photograph a lot of

наставник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic наставьникъ ('guide, teacher, preceptor, spiritual mentor', calquing Ancient Greek ἐπιστάτης and καθηγητής), formed with the agent suffix -ник from наставити ('to set on the right path, instruct', from на- + ставить 'to set, place').

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

настойчиво.etymology: Adverb in -о formed from настойчивый ('persistent, insistent'), derived from настоять / настаивать ('to insist, stand firm upon', from на- 'upon' + стоять 'to stand', Proto-Slavic *stojati).

history.meaning: to stand firm on -> insistent -> persistently, insistently

настольный.etymology: Formed in Russian from the prepositional phrase на столе ('on the table'), combining prefix на- ('on') + стол ('table, desk', from Proto-Slavic *stolъ) + adjectival suffix -ный: 'meant to stand or be used on a table or desk' (настольная лампа 'desk lamp', настольная игра 'board game').

настоятель.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic настоѩтель ('overseer, superior, prior'), a calque of Ancient Greek ἐπιστάτης / προεστώς ('one who stands over'), from настояти ('to stand over, preside') + agent suffix -тель.

настоящий.etymology: Borrowed in its Church Slavonic participial form настоящии (with -щ- from *tj), the present active participle of настояти ('to stand upon, be present at hand', built on на- + стоять 'to stand'). First meant 'currently standing before us, present' (настоящее время 'present tense'), and from 'actually present' developed the everyday sense 'real, genuine, authentic'.

настраивать.etymology: Imperfective of настроить ('to tune a musical instrument, configure equipment, put someone in a mood'), formed from на- + строить ('to build, arrange, put in order', from строй 'order, harmony, tuning', Proto-Slavic *strojiti) + -ивать.

history.meaning: to tune (an instrument); to adjust, configure; to predispose emotionally

morphemes.meaning: order, tune (from строить with о -> а)

настрогать.etymology: Formed from cumulative prefix на- ('a quantity of') + строгать ('to plane, shave wood, slice thinly', from Proto-Slavic *strugati).

history.meaning: to slice up, whittle a quantity of

настроение.etymology: Verbal noun from настроить ('to tune a musical instrument; to attune, put in a frame of mind'), built from на- + строить ('to arrange, order, build', from Proto-Slavic *strojiti). Just as German Stimmung ('mood') comes from stimmen ('to tune an instrument'), Russian настроение shifted from 'the tuning of strings' to a person's emotional 'mood, frame of mind'.

history.meaning: tuning of a musical instrument → emotional attunement, mood

настроить.etymology: Formed from на- ('into proper order') + строить ('to build, arrange, order', Proto-Slavic *strojiti, from *strojь 'order, array, tuning'): 'to put an instrument into tune' or 'to configure, set up'.

history.meaning: to tune (an instrument); to set up, configure

cognates.meaning: to tune (an instrument); put in a mood

настрой.etymology: Deverbal noun from настроить ('to tune a musical instrument, put in a certain mood or frame of mind'), formed from на- + строить ('to arrange, tune', from строй 'order, harmony', Proto-Slavic *strojь).

настройка.etymology: Derived in Russian from настроить ('to tune; to set up, configure') with the action/object noun suffix -ка.

history.meaning: tuning (of a piano or violin); adjustment, setting

наступать.etymology: Imperfective of наступить, formed from на- ('onto, upon') + ступать ('to step, tread'), inherited from Old East Slavic наступати, from Proto-Slavic *nastǫpati (*na- + *stǫpati 'to step'). From 'to step onto' came both 'to advance (militarily)' and 'to set in, arrive (of a season, night, or event)'.

history.meaning: to step on; to advance; to set in

rootFamily.gloss: to step on; to set in (pf)

наступить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic наступити ('to step upon, advance; to come upon'), formed from the prefix на- ('on, onto') and ступить ('to step, tread', from Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti). Has two primary uses in modern Russian: physical ('to step on something', наступить на ногу) and temporal ('to come, set in, arrive', of seasons, times of day, or events: наступила зима).

history.meaning: to step on; to set in
to step on (+ на); to come, arrive (of time/events)

настырный.etymology: Colloquial adjective derived from dialectal настыриться ('to persist stubbornly') and стыр / стырить ('to quarrel, stick out; peg, pole'), of expressive Slavic origin.

насчёт.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase на счёт ('onto the account of'), combining the preposition на with счёт ('count, reckoning, account', from Proto-Slavic *sъčьtъ, related to считать 'to count'). Grammaticalized as a conversational preposition (+ genitive) meaning 'about, regarding, concerning'.

насыпать.etymology: Formed from на- ('into, onto, filling') + сыпать ('to pour or strew dry, granular substances such as flour, sugar, or sand', Proto-Slavic *sypati).
насыпать.notes: Russian distinguishes налить ('to pour liquids') from насыпать ('to pour dry goods like flour, salt, or sugar'). Also note the stress pair: насыпать (imperfective) vs. насыпать (perfective).

натворить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the cumulative prefix на- ('in a quantity') and творить ('to create, make, do'), inherited from Old East Slavic творити and Proto-Slavic *tvoriti ('to form, shape, make', related to тварь 'creature'). In modern colloquial Russian, натворить specialized in a negative or ironic sense: 'to do something bad, cause a mess or trouble' (Что ты натворил? 'What have you done?!').

history.meaning: to do/make (especially mischief, trouble, or a mess)

натирать.etymology: Imperfective of натереть ('to rub on, polish, grate, chafe'), formed from на- + тирать (the iterative stem of тереть 'to rub, grate', inherited from Proto-Slavic *terti / *tirati).

history.meaning: to rub with ointment, polish (a floor), grate (cheese), chafe (a blister)

наткнуться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed from на- ('onto, against') + ткнуть ('to poke, thrust, jab', semelfactive of тыкать, from Proto-Slavic *tъknǫti) + -ся: literally 'to strike or impale oneself upon something unexpectedly', hence 'to stumble across, bump into'.

history.meaning: to strike against; to stumble upon, run into by chance

натренироваться.etymology: Formed from cumulative/completive prefix на- + тренироваться ('to train, practice', from тренировать, borrowed via German trainieren or French entraîner from English train).

натура.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish natura from Latin nātūra ('birth, nature, character, disposition'), derived from nāscī (past participle nātus, 'to be born').

натуральный.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish naturalny or German natural from Latin nātūrālis ('by birth, natural, genuine'), derived from nātūra ('nature', from nāscī 'to be born').

наука.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic наука ('learning, instruction, skill'), from Proto-Slavic *nauka, derived from *naučiti ('to teach', from the Indo-European root *euk- 'to become accustomed, learn').

научить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic научити, formed from the perfective prefix на- and учить ('to teach', from Proto-Slavic *učiti, causative of the PIE root *h₁ewk- 'to become accustomed, learn').

history.meaning: to teach (someone: acc. + чему: dat. or infinitive)

научиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed by adding -ся ('oneself') to научить ('to teach'), from Old East Slavic научити, built from на- + учить ('to teach', Proto-Slavic *učiti, causative of the PIE root *h₁ewk- 'to become accustomed'). Literally, 'to teach oneself, acquire a skill'.

научный.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ный (and regular к -> ч palatalization) from наука ('science, scholarship, learning', inherited from Proto-Slavic *nauka, built on the root *uk- / *uč- of учить 'to teach, learn').

нахамить.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix на- + хамить ('to behave boorishly, be rude'), derived from хам ('boor, cad', from the biblical name Ham / Хам, Noah's son who disrespected his father).

нахвататься.etymology: Formed with the cumulative prefix на- ('in quantity, a lot of') + хватать ('to grab, snatch, catch', Proto-Slavic *xvatati) + reflexive -ся, meaning 'to pick up or accumulate (habits, words, or superficial knowledge)'.

находить.etymology: Imperfective partner of найти ('to find'), inherited from Old East Slavic находити, formed from на- ('upon, onto') + ходить ('to walk, go', Proto-Slavic *xoditi) — literally 'to come upon, walk onto something' (just like Latin invenīre 'to come upon, find').

находиться.etymology: Reflexive of находить ('to come upon, find', imperfective of найти, built from на- 'upon' + ходить 'to walk, go'). Literally 'to be found (in a place)' — compare French se trouver — which became the standard Russian verb 'to be located, be situated'.

history.meaning: to be found → to be located, be situated

находка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the noun suffix -ка from находить ('to find, come across', built on на- + ходить). Denotes a found object, a lucky discovery, or a lost-and-found item (бюро находок 'lost-and-found office').

history.meaning: something found, lucky find, lost property

находчивый.etymology: Formed with the adjectival suffix -чивый from находить / находка ('to find, hit upon a solution / a clever find'), built on на- ('upon') + ходить ('to go, walk'): 'quick at finding a solution, resourceful'.

history.meaning: to find / a find → resourceful, quick-witted

национальный.etymology: Borrowed via French national or German national (derived from Latin nātiō 'birth, tribe, nation') and adapted with the Russian adjectival suffix -ный.

начало.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic начало and Proto-Slavic *načęlo ('beginning, origin'), formed with the neuter noun suffix *-lo from *načęti (Russian начать 'to begin').

начальник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic начальникъ (and Old Church Slavonic начѧльникъ 'founder, leader, chief'), formed from начало ('beginning, command, authority', from начать 'to begin', Proto-Slavic *načęti) + the agent suffix -ник.

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

начальница.etymology: Feminine form of начальник ('boss, chief, commander', derived from начало 'beginning, authority', Proto-Slavic *načęlo) + feminine agent suffix -ница.

начальство.etymology: Collective and abstract noun formed with the suffix -ство from начальный / начальник ('head, chief, superior'), derived from начало ('beginning; command, authority', Old East Slavic начало, Proto-Slavic *načęlo, from *načęti 'to begin').

начатое.etymology: Substantivized neuter singular of начатый ('begun, started'), the past passive participle of начать ('to begin, start', inherited from Old East Slavic начати, Proto-Slavic *načęti).

history.meaning: started -> that which has been started (довести начатое до конца 'to finish what one started')

начать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic начати (future начну, past начал; Old Church Slavonic начѧти), from Proto-Slavic *načęti ('to begin, start'), formed from prefix *na- + *čęti ('to begin, initiate', from PIE *kʷen- / *ken- 'to arise, begin anew'; related to конец 'end', originally 'extremity, tip', and искони 'from the beginning').
начать.notes: The historical nasal vowel *ę* appears as **-а-** in the infinitive and past (**начать, начал**) and as **-н-** before a vowel in the future (**начну, начнёшь, начнут**).

начаться.etymology: Perfective intransitive/reflexive verb formed by adding -ся to начать ('to begin, start'), inherited from Old East Slavic начати, from Proto-Slavic *načęti ('to begin', from *na- + *čęti, related to конец 'end').

начеку.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase на чеку ('on watch, on guard'), from на + locative of dialectal/obsolete чек ('watch, guard, expectation', related to чекать 'to wait, watch out for', Proto-Slavic *čekati).

начинание.etymology: Verbal noun formed from начинать ('to begin, initiate', from Proto-Slavic *načinati, related to *načęti 'to begin') + suffix -ание.

начинать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic начинати and Proto-Slavic *načinati ('to begin'), the imperfective counterpart of начать (*načęti), showing the ancient Indo-European ablaut alternation between nasal *-čę- (in начать) and lengthened *-čin- (in начинать). The root *čęti is cognate with конец ('end'), originally denoting either extremity of a span.

начинаться.etymology: Formed in Russian as the reflexive and intransitive counterpart of начинать ('to begin') with the suffix -ся. Начинать continues Proto-Slavic *načinati, an imperfective built on *načęti (from *na- + *čęti 'to begin, set in motion', sharing an older root with конец 'end' and кончать 'to finish').

начинка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Russian with the suffix -ка from начинить ('to fill, stuff [a pie, dumpling, or pastry]'), built from на- + чинить ('to arrange, prepare, fill', from чин 'order, arrangement', Proto-Slavic *činiti).

history.meaning: to stuff, fill -> pie or dumpling filling, stuffing

наш.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нашь (f. наша, n. наше), from Proto-Slavic *našь ('our, ours'), formed from the first-person plural pronoun stem *na- / *no- (seen in oblique нас, нам; compare Latin nōs) + possessive suffix *-sjь (with *sj > ш).

нашинковать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix на- + шинковать ('to shred, slice finely', borrowed via Polish szynkować or Ukrainian шинкувати, from German).

не.etymology: The negative particle не is inherited from older Slavic, rather than being a recent borrowing. Vasmer compares negative forms across the Indo-European languages, including Latin ne- and Baltic ne. The Russian particle also appears in word formation, but a prefixed word may develop a meaning of its own.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: не

неадекватный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('not, in-') + адекватный ('adequate, appropriate; colloquially, sane, reasonable', from Latin adaequātus 'equalized, matched').

небедный.etymology: Formed by litotes from negative prefix не- ('not') + бедный ('poor', from беда 'misfortune, need', Proto-Slavic *bědьnъ).

небезопасно.etymology: Adverb formed from negative prefix не- ('not') + безопасно ('safe, safely', from без 'without' + опасный 'dangerous', from опасаться 'to fear, beware').

неблагодарный.etymology: Formed with negative prefix не- ('un-') from благодарный ('grateful, thankful'), derived from Old Church Slavonic благодарити ('to give thanks', calquing Greek εὐχαριστεῖν, from благо 'good' + дар 'gift').

небо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic небо and Proto-Slavic *nebo ('sky, heaven'), an ancient Proto-Indo-European neuter *-es-stem (*nébʰos 'cloud, mist, sky'), cognate with Ancient Greek néphos ('cloud'), Latin nebula ('mist'), and Sanskrit nábhas ('cloud, sky').
небо.notes: Preserves its ancient *-es-stem in the plural небеса ('the heavens, skies').

небольшой.etymology: Formed in Russian by prefixing negative не- ('not, un-') to большой ('big, large', from Old East Slavic большии 'bigger, greater'), yielding a litotes meaning 'small, modest-sized'.

небрежный.etymology: Derived via Church Slavonic from небрѣщи ('to neglect, disregard') and небрѣжение ('neglect'), formed from не- ('not') + брѣщи ('to care for, guard', South Slavic cognate of East Slavic беречь, Proto-Slavic *bergti).

неважно.etymology: Formed with negative не- ('not') + важно ('importantly; it is important'), from важный ('weighty, important', borrowed via Polish ważny from Old High German wāga 'weight, scales').

history.meaning: not important → never mind, it does not matter; (colloquial) poorly

неверный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic невѣрьныи / Old Church Slavonic невѣрьнъ, formed from negative prefix не- ('un-, not') + верный ('faithful, true, correct', from вера 'faith', Proto-Slavic *věra).

невероятно.etymology: Adverbial and predicate form in -о of невероятный ('incredible, improbable'), formed with negative не- + вероятный ('probable, likely', literally 'capable of being taken on trust', a Church Slavonic-modelled compound of вера 'faith, belief' + яти 'to take', calquing German wahrscheinlich / Latin vērīsimilis).

невероятный.etymology: Formed from the negative prefix не- ('not') + вероятный ('probable, believable'), which was borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вѣроѩтьнъ ('credible, worthy of belief', a compound of вѣра 'faith, belief' + ѩти 'to take', calquing Ancient Greek πιθανός): literally 'not able to be taken on faith, unbelievable'.

невесело.etymology: Adverb formed from negative prefix не- ('not') + весело ('merrily, cheerfully', from весёлый 'merry, cheerful', Proto-Slavic *veselъ).

невеста.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic невѣста and Proto-Slavic *nevěsta ('bride, newlywed daughter-in-law'), most widely explained by etymologists as *ne- ('not') + *věsta ('known', verbal adjective from *věděti 'to know'): a protective taboo name ('the unknown woman') for a bride entering her husband's household from another clan so as not to expose her to hostile spirits.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: невеста

невестка.etymology: Derived with suffix -ка from невеста ('bride', in older and dialectal Slavic also 'daughter-in-law, sister-in-law'), from Proto-Slavic *nevěsta, generally explained as a taboo compound meaning 'the unknown woman' (entering the husband's family), from *ne- + *věděti ('to know').

history.meaning: bride, new wife in the clan

невидимый.etymology: Inherited via Old Church Slavonic невидимъ, formed from negative prefix не- ('in-, un-') + видимый ('visible', present passive participle of видеть 'to see', Proto-Slavic *viděti).

невинный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic невиньныи / Old Church Slavonic невиньнъ, formed from negative prefix не- ('un-, without') + винный (from вина 'guilt, fault', Proto-Slavic *vina).

невкусно.etymology: Adverb formed from невкусный ('not tasty') + -о (or negative prefix не- + вкусно 'tastily').

невкусный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + вкусный ('tasty', from вкус 'taste', derived from Proto-Slavic *vъkusъ / *kusiti 'to taste').

невозможно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate formed from невозможный ('impossible'), built with the negative prefix не- on возможный ('possible'), which derives from Old Church Slavonic възмощи / возмочь ('to be able, have the power to', from въз- + мощи / мочь 'to be able, can', Proto-Slavic *moťi).

невозможный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('im-, not') + возможный ('possible', from возмочь 'to be able', from мочь 'can, to be able', Proto-Slavic *mogti).

невредимый.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic невредимъ ('unharmed, inviolable'), formed from negative не- + вредити ('to harm, injure', from вредъ 'harm, damage') + the participial-adjectival suffix -имъ. Note the Church Slavonic non-pleophonic root вред- beside native East Slavic вередить.
невредимый.notes: Often paired in the set phrase *цел и невредим* ('safe and sound').

невыгодный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('un-') + выгодный ('profitable, advantageous', from выгода 'benefit, profit').

невыезд.etymology: Formed with the negative prefix не- ('non-') from выезд ('departure, exit by vehicle, trip out'), a deverbal noun from выехать ('to drive out, depart', from вы- + ехать 'to go by vehicle', Proto-Slavic *ěxati). Used almost exclusively in the legal formula **подписка о невыезде** ('signed undertaking not to leave town pending trial or investigation').

невыносимый.etymology: Formed in Russian from the negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + выносимый ('bearable', present passive participle of выносить 'to bear, endure, tolerate', from вы- + носить 'to carry').

невыполнимый.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('un-') + выполнимый ('feasible, doable', from выполнить 'to fulfill, carry out', from полный 'full').

негде.etymology: Negative predicative adverb formed from negative/existential prefix не- (Old East Slavic нѣ- < *ne je 'there is not') + где ('where', from Proto-Slavic *kъde).

негодяй.etymology: Derived from негожий / негодный ('unfit, good-for-nothing', from не- + годиться 'to be suitable, fit', Proto-Slavic *goditi) + expressive personal noun suffix -яй; in the 18th century it also denoted a recruit unfit for military service.

недавно.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('not') + давно ('long ago', from давний 'long-standing, ancient', Proto-Slavic *davьno).

недалеко.etymology: Formed with negative prefix не- ('not') from далеко ('far, far away'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *daleko.

недаром.etymology: Univerbated adverb formed from negative не ('not') + даром ('for nothing, in vain, gratis'), originally the instrumental singular of дар ('gift', Proto-Slavic *darъ, from PIE *deh3- 'to give'). Because даром shifted from 'as a free gift' to 'for nothing, without reason', недаром literally means 'not without good reason'—idiomatically 'no wonder' or 'not for nothing'.

history.meaning: gift → as a gift, for nothing
not in vain, with good reason, no wonder

недвижимость.etymology: Formed with the abstract noun suffix -ость from недвижимый ('immovable'), which entered Russian law in the Petrine era (недвижимое имение / имущество) as a calque of French biens immeubles / Latin rēs immōbilis ('immovable property, real estate'), built on не- ('not') + двигать ('to move').

неделька.etymology: Diminutive of неделя ('week; originally Sunday, the day of rest', from Proto-Slavic *neděľa, literally 'not-doing', from *ne + *dělati 'to do, work') + suffix -ка.

неделя.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic недѣля ('Sunday, day of rest; seven-day week'), from Proto-Slavic *nedělja, a compound of *ne ('not') + *dělati ('to do, work'): literally 'no-working day' (Sunday). In Russian, the church word воскресение ('Resurrection') took over the meaning 'Sunday', while неделя shifted to name the whole seven-day week.

недовольный.etymology: Formed in Russian from the negative prefix не- ('not, dis-') + довольный ('satisfied, pleased'), which derives from доволь / вдоволь ('enough, sufficiency'), from до- ('up to') + воля ('will, wish', Proto-Slavic *voľa).

недоеденный.etymology: Past passive participle of недоесть ('to not finish eating'), formed from the prefix недо- ('incompletely, under-') + есть ('to eat', from Proto-Slavic *ěsti).

недолгий.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('not') + долгий ('long', inherited from Proto-Slavic *dьlgъ).

недолго.etymology: Adverb formed from negative prefix не- ('not') + долго ('for a long time', from долгий 'long', Proto-Slavic *dьlgъ).

недолюбливать.etymology: Formed from the prefix недо- ('insufficiently, less than fully') + -любливать (iterative stem of любить 'to love', from Proto-Slavic *ľubiti).

history.meaning: to not be fond of, dislike

недооценивать.etymology: Imperfective of недооценить ('to underestimate, undervalue'), formed from prefix недо- ('under-, insufficiently') + оценивать ('to evaluate, appraise', from цена 'price, value', Proto-Slavic *cěna).

недооценить.etymology: Formed in Russian with the compound prefix недо- ('insufficiently, under-') + оценить ('to value, appraise, assess', built on цена 'price, value', Proto-Slavic *cěna).

history.meaning: to assess, value -> to underestimate, undervalue

недопонимание.etymology: Formed from the prefix недо- ('incomplete, partial') + понимание ('understanding', verbal noun from понимать 'to understand').

history.meaning: mutual misunderstanding, lack of full understanding

недопустимый.etymology: Formed in Russian from the negative prefix не- ('not, in-') + допустимый ('permissible, admissible'), originally the present passive participle of допустить ('to allow, admit', from до- 'up to' + пустить 'to let go', Proto-Slavic *pustiti).

недоразумение.etymology: Formed from the compound prefix недо- ('insufficiently, mis-') + разумение ('understanding, comprehension', verbal noun from разуметь 'to understand', built on разум 'reason, mind', Proto-Slavic *orzumъ), likely modelled on Polish nieporozumienie or German Missverständnis.

rootFamily.gloss: of course, it stands to reason

недорогой.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('not') + дорогой ('expensive, dear', inherited from Proto-Slavic *dorgъ).

недостаток.etymology: Derived from недостать / недоставать ('to be lacking, fall short', from не- + достать 'to suffice, reach') + noun suffix -ок.

недостача.etymology: Derived from недостать / недоставать ('to be short of, fall short') with the noun suffix -ча (modeled on nouns like сдача and подача).

недоступный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('in-, un-') + доступный ('accessible, available', from доступ 'access', from доступить 'to step up to, reach').

недосып.etymology: Colloquial zero-suffixed deverbal noun from недосыпать ('to not get enough sleep'), formed from prefix недо- ('insufficiently') + спать / -сыпать ('to sleep', Proto-Slavic *sъpati).

нежнее.etymology: Comparative degree of нежный ('tender, gentle, delicate') and нежно ('tenderly'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *něžьnъ (derived from *něga 'pampering, tenderness, comfort').

нежнейший.etymology: Superlative form of нежный ('tender, gentle', derived from нега 'bliss, comfort, pampering', Proto-Slavic *něga) + superlative suffix -ейший.

нежно.etymology: Adverb formed from нежный ('tender, gentle, delicate'), inherited from Old East Slavic нѣжьныи, derived from нѣга / нега ('comfort, pampering, bliss'), from Proto-Slavic *něga.

нежность.etymology: Formed with the abstract noun suffix -ость from нежный ('tender, gentle, delicate'), which is derived from нега ('blissful comfort, pampered ease, softness', inherited from Proto-Slavic *něga).

нежный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нѣжьныи and Proto-Slavic *něžьnъ ('tender, delicate, pampered'), derived from нега ('bliss, comfort, tender care', Proto-Slavic *něga).

незабываемый.etymology: Formed with negative prefix не- ('un-') + забываемый (present passive participle of забывать 'to forget', built on за- + бывать / быть 'to be'). Literally 'not able to be forgotten, unforgettable'.

независимый.etymology: Calque of French indépendant (or German unabhängig), formed from negative prefix не- ('in-, non-') + зависимый ('dependent', from зависеть 'to depend', literally 'to hang from').

незаконно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate in -о from незаконный ('illegal, unlawful'), formed from negative не- ('not, il-') + законный ('legal, lawful', from закон 'law', Proto-Slavic *zakonъ).

history.meaning: lawful -> unlawful -> illegally; it is illegal

незаменимый.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('in-, un-') + заменимый ('replaceable', from заменить 'to replace, substitute', derived from мена 'exchange', Proto-Slavic *měna).

незаметно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate in -о from незаметный ('inconspicuous, imperceptible'), formed from negative не- ('not') + заметный ('noticeable', from заметить 'to notice').

незамужний.etymology: Derived from the negated phrase не замужем ('unmarried [of a woman]', literally 'not behind a husband', from за + муж 'husband', Proto-Slavic *mǫžь) + adjectival suffix -ний.

незнакомец.etymology: Built transparently from не- 'un-, not' + знакомец 'acquaintance' (from знакомый 'familiar, known' + person suffix -ец, ultimately from знать 'to know').

незнакомый.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('un-') + знакомый ('familiar, acquainted', from знакомить 'to acquaint', related to знак 'sign' and знать 'to know').

неизбежный.etymology: Borrowed/adapted from Church Slavonic неизбѣжьнъ ('inescapable, unavoidable'), formed from negative не- ('not') + избежать ('to escape, flee out of, avoid', from из- 'out' + бежать 'to run, flee', Proto-Slavic *běžati) + -ный.

неизвестно.etymology: Predicative adverb formed from неизвестный ('unknown', from не- + известный 'known, famous', derived from весть 'news, knowledge', Proto-Slavic *věstь).

неизвестный.etymology: Formed from the negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + известный ('known, well-known', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic извѣстьнъ, built on вѣсть 'news, knowledge').
неизвестный.notes: The middle -т- is silent in standard pronunciation: [неизвесный].

неинтересно.etymology: Adverb formed from negative prefix не- ('un-, not') + интересно ('interesting, interestingly', from интерес 'interest', borrowed via German Interesse from Latin interesse).

неисправимый.etymology: Formed in Russian from the negative prefix не- ('not, in-') + исправимый ('corrigible, reparable', present passive participle of исправить 'to correct, reform', built on правый 'right, straight').

некачественный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('non-, low-') + качественный ('of good quality', from качество 'quality', a Church Slavonic calque of Latin quālitās from какъ 'what kind').

некий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нѣкыи / Old Church Slavonic нѣкъи ('some, a certain'), from Proto-Slavic *někъjь, compounded from indefinite prefix *ně- and interrogative pronoun *kъjь ('who, which').

некогда.etymology: Formed from the negative predicative prefix не- ('there is no...') + когда ('when', Proto-Slavic *kъgda): with stressed некогда it means 'there is no time (to do something)'; with unstressed некогда it means 'once upon a time, formerly'.
некогда.notes: Takes a dative logical subject + infinitive: Мне некогда ждать ('I have no time to wait').

некого.etymology: Negative predicative pronoun (stressed on the prefix: некого, lacking a nominative case), formed by univerbation of Old East Slavic не (ѥсть) кого ('there is not [anyone] whom [to...]'), combining negative не with кого, the genitive/accusative of кто ('who', Proto-Slavic *kъto).

history.meaning: there is nobody to (with infinitive: некого послать 'there is nobody to send')

некого.notes: Prepositions are placed between не and the pronoun: не с кем поговорить ('there is nobody to talk to'), не у кого спросить ('there is nobody to ask').

некоторый.etymology: Indefinite pronoun/adjective formed with prefix не- (Old East Slavic нѣ-, from Proto-Slavic *ně- 'some, a certain') + который ('which', from Proto-Slavic *kotorъ).

некрасивый.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('un-') + красивый ('beautiful, handsome', derived from краса 'beauty', Proto-Slavic *krasa).

некуда.etymology: Negative pronominal adverb formed from stressed negative particle не- ('there is not') + куда ('whither, where to', from Proto-Slavic *kǫda).

некультурно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate in -о from некультурный ('uncultured, ill-mannered'), formed from negative не- ('not, un-') + культурный ('cultured, polite', derived from культура 'culture', Latin cultūra).

history.meaning: cultured -> uncultured -> in an uncultured way; it is bad manners

неласковый.etymology: Formed from the negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + ласковый ('affectionate, gentle, tender'), derived from ласка ('caress, affection', inherited from Proto-Slavic *laska).

нелегал.etymology: Back-formed in Russian by clipping the adjective suffix from нелегальный ('illegal, clandestine', from не- 'not' + легальный 'legal', from Latin lēgālis). First used in late Imperial and Soviet intelligence/revolutionary jargon for an underground operative living under false papers, and later extended to an undocumented migrant.

history.meaning: illegal, clandestine → underground agent; undocumented worker

нелегально.etymology: Adverb formed from нелегальный ('illegal', from negative prefix не- + легальный 'legal', borrowed via German legal or French légal from Latin lēgālis) + -о.

нелегко.etymology: Adverb formed from negative prefix не- ('not') + легко ('easily, easy', from лёгкий 'light, easy', inherited from Proto-Slavic *lьgъkъ).

нелепо.etymology: Adverb formed from нелепый ('absurd, awkward'), inherited from Old East Slavic нелѣпыи ('unfitting, unseemly, ugly'), from negative prefix не- + obsolete лѣпый ('fitting, comely, beautiful', Proto-Slavic *lěpъ).

нелепый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нелѣпыи and Old Church Slavonic нелѣпъ ('unseemly, unfitting, absurd'), formed from negative не- ('not') + archaic лепый (*lěpъ 'handsome, fitting, fair', preserved in великолепный 'magnificent' and Czech lepý 'comely'): originally 'unbecoming, ill-fitting', later 'absurd, ridiculous'.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: лепый

неловкий.etymology: Formed in Russian from the negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + ловкий ('deft, agile, adroit', derived from лов / ловить 'to catch, hunt', Proto-Slavic *lovъ): literally 'not deft at catching', hence both physically 'clumsy' and socially 'awkward, embarrassing'.

неловко.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicative form of неловкий ('awkward, clumsy, uncomfortable'), formed from не- ('not') + ловкий ('deft, adroit, handy; comfortable'), originally 'good at catching', derived from лов ('hunt, catch') and ловить ('to catch', Proto-Slavic *loviti).

нельзя.etymology: Univerbation of Old East Slavic не льзѣ ('it is not possible, there is no freedom/ease'), combining the negative particle не with льзѣ, the dative-locative singular of an old noun льга ('ease, freedom, benefit', from Proto-Slavic *lьga, related to лёгкий 'light, easy' and preserved in льгота 'privilege, exemption').

history.meaning: it is not permitted / not possible

немедленно.etymology: Adverb formed from the adjective немедленный ('immediate, unhesitating'), built with the negative prefix не- on медленный ('slow'), historically a participle related to медлить ('to delay, tarry', from Proto-Slavic *mьdьlъ 'slow, sluggish').

неметь.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *něměti ('to become mute or numb'), derived from *němъ ('mute, dumb', Russian немой).

history.meaning: to go numb; to become speechless

немец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нѣмьць and Proto-Slavic *němьcь ('foreigner speaking an unintelligible tongue; specifically a German'), formed with the personal suffix -ец from немой (*němъ 'mute, dumb, unable to speak intelligibly [i.e., in Slavic]', in contrast to *slověne 'those who speak clearly, Slavs').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: немец

немецкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нѣмьчьскыи ('foreign, Western European, German'), formed from нѣмьць / немец ('German; in medieval Rus', any foreigner speaking an unintelligible Western tongue'), derived with the suffix *-ьcь from нѣмъ / немой ('mute, dumb, unable to speak intelligibly', Proto-Slavic *němъ). Early Slavs contrasted themselves — словене, 'people of the intelligible word (слово)' — with their western neighbors, *němьci ('those who cannot speak [our language]').

history.meaning: mute → speaker of an unintelligible tongue, Germanic neighbor

немного.etymology: Formed in Russian by prefixing не- ('not') to много ('much, a lot'): literally 'not much', i.e. 'a little, some, slightly'.

немножко.etymology: Diminutive adverb formed with suffix -ко from немного ('a little, not much'), compound of не- ('not') + много ('much, many', from Proto-Slavic *mъnogo).

немой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нѣмыи, from Proto-Slavic *němъ ('mute, dumb, speaking indistinctly'), of expressive origin.

немыслимый.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('un-') + мыслимый ('thinkable, conceivable', present passive participle of мыслить 'to think', from мысль 'thought', Proto-Slavic *myslь).

ненавидеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ненавидѣти (and Old Church Slavonic ненавидѣти 'to hate'), from Proto-Slavic *nenaviděti, formed with the negative prefix *ne- on *naviděti ('to look gladly upon, favor'), itself from *na- ('upon') + *viděti ('to see, look at', Russian видеть). Literally, 'not to bear looking at someone' (compare Latin invidia 'envy', from in- + vidēre).

history.meaning: to be unable to look upon → to hate

ненависть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ненависть, from Proto-Slavic *nenavistь ('hatred'), abstract noun from *nenaviděti ('to hate', literally 'not to look gladly upon', from *ne + *naviděti, root *viděti 'to see').

ненадолго.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('not') + надолго ('for a long time', from на + долго 'long').

history.meaning: for a short time, not for long

ненадёжный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('un-') + надёжный ('reliable, trustworthy', derived from надёжа 'hope, reliance', East Slavic counterpart of надежда).

ненасытный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ненасытьныи / Old Church Slavonic ненасытьнъ ('insatiable'), formed from negative prefix не- + насытить ('to satiate', from сытый 'full, sated', Proto-Slavic *sytъ).

ненормальный.etymology: Formed with the negative prefix не- ('non-, un-') + нормальный ('normal', borrowed via French normal / German normal from Latin normalis 'made according to a carpenter's square, regular', from norma 'rule, norm').

необдуманный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('un-') + обдуманный ('thought-out, considered', past passive participle of обдумать 'to think over', from думать 'to think').

необходимость.etymology: Formed in Russian with the abstract noun suffix -ость from необходимый ('necessary, essential, indispensable').

необходимый.etymology: Formed from the negative prefix не- ('not') + обходимый ('bypassable', present passive participle of обходить 'to walk around, bypass, do without'): literally 'that which cannot be bypassed or dispensed with'.

history.meaning: to bypass -> impossible to bypass, indispensable, necessary

необыкновенный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('un-, extra-') + обыкновенный ('ordinary, usual', derived from обыкновение 'custom, habit', from обыкнуть 'to become accustomed').

необычно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate in -о from необычный ('unusual'), formed from negative не- ('not, un-') + обычный ('usual, customary', derived from обычай 'custom', Proto-Slavic *obyčajь).

history.meaning: usual -> unusual -> unusually; it is unusual

необычный.etymology: Formed in Russian from the negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + обычный ('usual, ordinary'), which is derived from обычай ('custom, habit', Old East Slavic обычаи, Proto-Slavic *obvyčajь, built on *ob- + the root *vyk- 'to grow accustomed').

неодетый.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('un-') + одетый ('dressed', past passive participle of одеть 'to dress, clothe', from Proto-Slavic *oděti).

неожиданно.etymology: Adverb in -о formed from неожиданный ('unexpected'), built from negative не- ('not, un-') + ожиданный (passive participle of ожидать 'to expect, await', from ждать 'to wait', Proto-Slavic *žьdati).

неожиданность.etymology: Abstract noun formed from неожиданный ('unexpected', from не- + ожидать 'to wait for, expect', from ждать 'to wait') + suffix -ость.

неожиданный.etymology: Formed in Russian from the negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + ожиданный ('expected'), passive participle of ожидать ('to await, expect'), built on о- + ждать ('to wait', inherited from Old East Slavic жьдати, Proto-Slavic *žьdati).

неопытный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('in-, un-') + опытный ('experienced', from опыт 'experience, trial', derived from пытать 'to test, try').

неплохо.etymology: Formed in Russian as the predicate and manner adverb of неплохой ('not bad, fairly good'), combining negative не- ('not') with плохо ('badly'), from плохой ('bad').

неплохой.etymology: Litotic adjective formed from negative prefix не- ('not') + плохой ('bad, poor', from Proto-Slavic *ploxъ).

непобедимый.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic непобѣдимъ ('invincible, unconquerable'), formed from negative prefix не- + побѣдити ('to conquer, defeat', from побѣда 'victory').

непогода.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic непогода, formed from negative/pejorative prefix не- + погода ('weather, originally favorable weather', from Proto-Slavic *pogoda, related to *godъ 'suitable time').

неполный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('in-, un-') + полный ('full, complete', inherited from Proto-Slavic *pьlnъ).

непонятно.etymology: Adverb and predicative formed from непонятный ('unclear, incomprehensible') + -о.

непонятный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('in-, un-') + понятный ('understandable, clear', from понять 'to grasp, understand', Proto-Slavic *pojęti).

неправда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic неправьда ('injustice, falsehood, untruth'), formed with the negative prefix не- and правда ('truth, justice', derived from правый 'right, true, straight', Proto-Slavic *pravьda).

неправильно.etymology: Adverb formed with the negative prefix не- from правильно ('correctly, rightly'), derived from правильный ('correct, right') and правило ('rule'), ultimately from правый ('straight, right', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

неправильный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('in-, un-') + правильный ('correct, regular', from правило 'rule, straightedge', derived from правый 'right, straight', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

неправый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic неправыи ('unjust, crooked, wrong'), formed with the negative prefix не- and правый ('right, straight, just', from Proto-Slavic *pravъ). In modern Russian, it is used almost exclusively in the short predicate forms **неправ / неправа / неправы** ('wrong, mistaken': ты неправ 'you are wrong').

непредсказуемый.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('un-') + предсказуемый ('predictable', from предсказать 'to foretell, predict', a calque of Latin praedīcere from пред- 'fore-' + сказать 'to say').

неприветливый.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('un-') + приветливый ('friendly, welcoming, affable', derived from привет 'welcome, greeting').

непривычно.etymology: Adverb formed from непривычный ('unaccustomed, unfamiliar', from не- + привычный 'familiar, habitual', from привыкнуть 'to get used to') + -о.

неприлично.etymology: Adverb formed from неприличный ('indecent, improper', from не- + приличный 'decent, fitting', derived from лик / лицо 'face, appearance') + -о.

неприступный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('in-, un-') + приступный ('accessible, approachable', from приступить 'to approach; to storm a fortress', from ступить 'to step').

неприятно.etymology: Adverb and predicative formed from неприятный ('unpleasant', from не- + приятный 'pleasant, agreeable', from приять 'to receive favorably', Proto-Slavic *prijęti) + -о.

неприятность.etymology: Formed with the abstract noun suffix -ость from неприятный ('unpleasant, disagreeable'), from не- ('not') + приятный ('pleasant, agreeable', from Old Church Slavonic приятъ 'accepted, welcome', past passive participle of приятии 'to receive, accept').

неприятный.etymology: Formed in Russian from the negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + приятный ('pleasant, agreeable'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic приѩтьнъ ('acceptable, welcome, pleasing'), derived from приѩти (Russian принять, 'to receive, accept', from *pri- + *jęti 'to take').

непросто.etymology: Adverb formed from непростой ('not simple, complex') + -о (or negative prefix не- + просто 'simply, easily').

непростой.etymology: Litotic adjective formed from negative prefix не- ('not') + простой ('simple, ordinary', inherited from Proto-Slavic *prostъ).

непрофессионально.etymology: Adverb formed from непрофессиональный ('unprofessional', from не- + профессиональный 'professional', from профессия 'profession', Latin professiō) + -о.

неравный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('un-') + равный ('equal', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic равьнъ, corresponding to native East Slavic ровный, from Proto-Slavic *orvьnъ).

нерв.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Nerv or French nerf from Latin nervus ('sinew, tendon, nerve'), cognate with Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron).

нервировать.etymology: Borrowed from German nervieren or derived in Russian from нерв ('nerve') + verbal suffix -ировать.

history.meaning: to make nervous, get on someone's nerves

нервничать.etymology: Formed in 19th-century Russian with the colloquial behavioral verb suffix -ничать from нервный ('nervous'), itself derived from нерв ('nerve'), borrowed via German Nerv / French nerf from Latin nervus ('sinew, tendon, nerve').

history.meaning: nervous → to act nervously, fret, worry

morphemes.meaning: to behave in a certain manner

нервный.etymology: Adjective formed with suffix -ный from нерв ('nerve'), borrowed via German Nerv or French nerf from Latin nervus ('sinew, tendon, bowstring, nerve', cognate with Greek νεῦρον).

нереально.etymology: Adverb formed from нереальный ('unreal, unrealistic', from не- + реальный 'real', from Late Latin reālis) + -о.

нерентабельный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('un-') + рентабельный ('profitable, cost-effective', borrowed from German rentabel, from French rente 'income, return').

неровно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate in -о from неровный ('uneven, crooked'), formed from negative не- ('not, un-') + ровный ('even, flat, straight', inherited from Proto-Slavic *orvьnъ).

неровный.etymology: Formed from the negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + ровный ('even, flat, level, straight'), inherited from Old East Slavic ровьныи, from Proto-Slavic *orvьnъ ('level, flat, equal'; compare Old Church Slavonic равьнъ and Russian равный).

нерусский.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('non-') + русский ('Russian', from Old East Slavic русьскыи, derived from Русь 'Rus').

несвежий.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('not') + свежий ('fresh', inherited from Proto-Slavic *svěžь).

несерьёзно.etymology: Adverb formed from negative prefix не- ('not') + серьёзно ('seriously', from серьёзный 'serious', borrowed from French sérieux, from Medieval Latin sēriōsus).

несерьёзный.etymology: Formed in Russian from the negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + серьёзный ('serious'), which was borrowed in the eighteenth century from French sérieux (from Late Latin sēriōsus, built on Latin sērius 'earnest, grave').

несколько.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нѣколько / нѣсколько, formed from the indefinite prefix не- (historically нѣ- from Proto-Slavic *ně-, 'some, a certain') + сколько ('how much, how many', from Proto-Slavic *koli / *koliko 'how much', with initial с- from *sь-koliko).

нескоро.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('not') + скоро ('soon, quickly', from скорый 'fast, quick', inherited from Proto-Slavic *skorъ).

history.meaning: not soon, not for a long time

нескромность.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('im-, in-') + скромность ('modesty', derived from скромный 'modest, unassuming', borrowed via Polish skromny).

несложно.etymology: Adverb formed from несложный ('not complicated, simple', from не- + сложный 'complex, compound', from сложить 'to put together') + -о.

несомненно.etymology: Adverb formed from несомненный ('undoubted, certain', from не- + сомнение 'doubt', via Church Slavonic съмьнѣниѥ from мьнѣти 'to think, suppose') + -о.

несоответствие.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('non-, in-') + соответствие ('correspondence, conformity', derived from соответствовать 'to correspond', from со- 'with' + ответ 'answer').

несправедливо.etymology: Adverb formed with negative prefix не- from справедливо ('justly, fairly'), from справедливый ('just, fair', borrowed via Polish sprawiedliwy, ultimately built on правда 'truth, justice', Proto-Slavic *pravьda).

несправедливый.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('un-') + справедливый ('fair, just', borrowed via Polish sprawiedliwy, derived from правда 'truth, justice', Proto-Slavic *pravьda).

нести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нести, from Proto-Slavic *nesti ('to carry'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *h₁neḱ- ('to reach, take, carry'), cognate with Lithuanian nèšti ('to carry'), Ancient Greek ἐνεγκεῖν ('to bring, bear'), and Sanskrit náśati ('attains').
нести.notes: Unidirectional verb of motion ('carrying on foot in one direction'), paired with multidirectional *носить*.

несуществующий.etymology: Formed from the negative prefix не- ('non-, not') + существующий ('existing', present active participle of существовать 'to exist', derived from существо 'being, creature, essence', built on the Old Church Slavonic present participle сѫщь 'being' of быти 'to be').

несчастный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('un-') + счастный / счастье ('good fortune, happiness', from Proto-Slavic *sъčęstьje, a compound of *sъ- 'good' + *čęstь 'part, share, lot').

несчастье.etymology: Formed from the negative prefix не- ('lack of, bad') + счастье ('happiness, good fortune', from Proto-Slavic *sъčęstьje, built on *sъ- 'good, with' + *čęstь 'part, share, lot').

нет.etymology: Contracted from Old East Slavic нѣту / нѣтъ ('there is not'), itself a fusion of the Proto-Slavic negative phrase *ne je tu ('is not here': negative particle *ne + *jestь 'is' + locative *tu 'there/here'). Because it originally contained the verb 'is', нет means both 'no' in replies and 'there is no' (+ genitive).

нетерпеливый.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('im-, un-') + терпеливый ('patient', derived from терпеть 'to endure, be patient', from Proto-Slavic *tьrpěti).

нетерпение.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('im-, lack of') + терпение ('patience, endurance', verbal noun from терпеть 'to endure, tolerate', from Proto-Slavic *tьrpěti).

нетрадиционный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('non-, un-') + традиционный ('traditional', from традиция 'tradition', borrowed from Latin trāditiō 'handing down').

нетрудно.etymology: Adverb formed from negative prefix не- ('not') + трудно ('hard, difficult', from трудный 'difficult', derived from труд 'labor, toil', Proto-Slavic *trudъ).

нету.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нѣту ('there is not'), an ancient contraction of не єсть ту ('is not here/there', with the archaic locative adverb ту 'there'); standard Russian нет shortened the final vowel.

history.meaning: is not here, there is no

неуверенность.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('in-, lack of') + уверенность ('confidence, certainty', from уверенный 'confident, assured', derived from вера 'faith, belief').

неувязочка.etymology: Colloquial diminutive of неувязка ('inconsistency, hitch, snag', formed from не- + увязать 'to tie together, coordinate', from вязать 'to tie', Proto-Slavic *vęzati) + suffix -очка.

неудача.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('un-, mis-') + удача ('good luck, success', derived from удаться 'to turn out well, succeed', from дать 'to give', Proto-Slavic *dati).

неудачник.etymology: Derived from неудача ('failure, bad luck') / неудачный ('unlucky') + personal agent suffix -ник.

неудачно.etymology: Adverb in -о formed from неудачный ('unsuccessful, unlucky, ill-chosen'), built from negative не- ('un-') + удачный ('successful', from удача 'success, good luck', derived from удаться 'to turn out well').

неудачный.etymology: Derived from неудача ('failure, bad luck') + adjectival suffix -ный (or negative prefix не- + удачный 'successful, lucky').

неудивительно.etymology: Predicative adverb formed from negative prefix не- ('not') + удивительно ('surprising, surprisingly', from удивить 'to amaze, surprise', derived from диво 'wonder, marvel', Proto-Slavic *divo).

неудобно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicative form of неудобный ('inconvenient, uncomfortable, awkward'), formed from не- ('not, un-') + удобный ('convenient, comfortable'), which is built on у- + доба ('fitting time, suitability, opportune moment', Proto-Slavic *doba, cognate with English dapper and German tapfer).

неудобство.etymology: Formed with the abstract noun suffix -ство from неудобный ('inconvenient, uncomfortable'), built from negative не- ('in-, un-') + удобный ('convenient, comfortable', derived from Proto-Slavic *udobь 'at a fitting time or manner', built on *doba 'fitting time').

неужели.etymology: Formed in Russian by fusing не ('not') + уже ('already', older уж / уже) + the interrogative particle ли: literally 'is it not already so that...?', expressing surprise or disbelief ('really?, can it really be?').

неуместный.etymology: Formed from the negative prefix не- ('in-, not') + уместный ('appropriate, fitting, in its proper place', derived from the prepositional phrase у места 'at the right place', built on место 'place', Proto-Slavic *město).

history.meaning: in place -> appropriate -> inappropriate, out of place

неуместный.notes: The middle -т- is silent in standard pronunciation: [неумесный].

неумеха.etymology: Colloquial common-gender noun formed with the expressive person suffix -ха from не уметь ('not to know how', from не + уметь 'to know how, be able', inherited from Proto-Slavic *uměti).

history.meaning: not to know how -> bungler, all-thumbs person

неумно.etymology: Adverb formed from negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + умно ('cleverly, wisely', from умный 'smart, wise', derived from ум 'mind, intellect', Proto-Slavic *umъ).

неустойка.etymology: Derived from не устоять (в слове / договоре) ('to fail to stand by one's word or contract', from устоять 'to stand firm, hold out', root стоять 'to stand') + noun suffix -ка.

history.meaning: to fail to hold firm, default

нефтяной.etymology: Derived from нефть ('crude oil, petroleum', borrowed via Ottoman Turkish neft from Persian نفت naft) + adjectival suffix -яной.

нехороший.etymology: Formed in Russian from the negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + хороший ('good').

нехорошо.etymology: Formed in Russian from the negative prefix не- ('not') + хорошо ('well, good'), the adverb and short neuter form of хороший ('good'), from Old East Slavic хорошии.

history.meaning: not + well/good → not good, wrong, unwell

нечаянно.etymology: Adverb in -о from нечаянный ('unintended, accidental, unexpected'), formed from negative не- ('not, un-') + чаянный, the past passive participle of archaic чаять ('to expect, hope for, wait for', from Old East Slavic чаяти, Proto-Slavic *čajati): literally 'unlooked-for, unforeseen'.

нечего.etymology: Negative predicative pronoun (stressed on the first syllable: **нечего**, literally 'there is nothing [to do]') inherited from Old East Slavic нечего, contracted from *не есть чего ('there is not of what', where не is fused with the lost present copula *е / есть and чего is the genitive of что 'what', Proto-Slavic *čьto). Distinct in stress and meaning from **нечего / ничего** ('nothing').

history.meaning: there is nothing (to); no point in (+ infinitive)

нечего.notes: Followed by an infinitive (with an optional dative subject): **Мне нечего сказать** ('I have nothing to say'), **Нечего делать** ('There's nothing to do').

нечем.etymology: Negative predicative pronoun in the instrumental case (stressed on the prefix: нечем, corresponding to genitive нечего), formed by univerbation of не (есть) чем ('there is nothing with which [to...]'), from negative не + чем, the instrumental singular of что ('what', Proto-Slavic *čьto).

history.meaning: nothing (to do something with: мне нечем платить 'I have nothing to pay with')

нечестно.etymology: Adverb formed with negative prefix не- ('un-, not') from честно ('honestly, fairly'), derived from честный ('honest, honorable'), from честь ('honor', Proto-Slavic *čьstь).

нечестный.etymology: Formed from negative prefix не- ('dis-, un-') + честный ('honest, honorable, fair', derived from честь 'honor', from Proto-Slavic *čьstь).

неясно.etymology: Adverb and predicative formed from неясный ('unclear, vague', from negative prefix не- + ясный 'clear, bright', Proto-Slavic *jasnъ) + -о.

ни.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ни ('not even, neither, nor'), from Proto-Slavic *ni, formed by combining the Indo-European negative particle *ne ('not') with the emphatic/connective particle *i ('even, also'): literally 'not even'.

нигде.etymology: Negative locative adverb inherited from Old East Slavic никъдѣ, formed from the negative prefix ни- and где ('where', Old East Slavic къдѣ, from Proto-Slavic *kъde).

ниже.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ниже and Proto-Slavic *niže ('lower, below'), the comparative of низкий ('low') and низко, built on *nizъ ('bottom, down', with z + j -> ž).

нижний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нижьнии (Proto-Slavic *nižьnьjь), the relational positional adjective formed from низ ('bottom, lower part') with the soft adjectival suffix -ний (with з -> ж).

низ.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic низъ ('down, bottom, low ground'), from Proto-Slavic *nizъ ('bottom, downward'), continuing a Proto-Indo-European spatial stem *ni- ('down, below', cognate with English beneath and German nieder).

низкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic низькыи, from Proto-Slavic *nizъkъ, formed with the adjectival suffix *-ъkъ from *nizъ ('bottom, low place, down'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ni- ('down'; compare English beneath and German nieder).

cognates.meaning: lower (from the same PIE spatial root *ni-)

низко.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic низько, the short neuter and adverbial form of низкий ('low', Proto-Slavic *nizъkъ, derived from *nizъ 'down, bottom').

никак.etymology: Negative adverb formed from the negative prefix ни- and как ('how', from Old East Slavic како, Proto-Slavic *kako).

history.meaning: in no way, by no means, not at all

никакой.etymology: Formed by adding the negative prefix ни- ('not even one, no') to какой ('what kind of, which'): 'no ... whatsoever, none at all'.

history.meaning: none at all, no kind of

никакой.notes: When used with a preposition, ни splits off in front of the preposition: ни в коем случае / ни по какой причине ('for no reason at all').

никогда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic никъгда ('never'), from Proto-Slavic *nikъgda, formed by prefixing the negative particle *ni ('not even') to *kъgda ('when', modern Russian когда).

никто.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic никъто ('nobody, no one'), from Proto-Slavic *nikъto, compounded from the negative particle *ni ('not even') + the interrogative pronoun *kъto ('who').
никто.notes: With a preposition, the word splits in three: **ни у кого** ('nobody has'), **ни с кем** ('with nobody').

никуда.etymology: Negative directional adverb formed from the negative prefix ни- and куда ('where to, whither', from Old East Slavic кудѣ / куда, Proto-Slavic *kǫdě).
никуда.notes: Russian distinguishes location (**нигде** 'nowhere, in no place') from direction of motion (**никуда** 'to nowhere': *я никуда не пойду*).

никчёмный.etymology: Colloquial adjective formed by univerbation of the phrase ни к чему ('for nothing, to no purpose', from ни + к + dative чему of что 'what') + adjectival suffix -ный.

history.meaning: to no purpose, good for nothing

нитка.etymology: Formed with the diminutive/singulative suffix -ка from нить ('thread, filament'), inherited from Old East Slavic нить, from Proto-Slavic *nitь ('thread'), from Proto-Indo-European *sney- ('to spin, twist, sew'; cognate with Lithuanian nýtis 'heddle', German nähen 'to sew', and English needle).

ниточка.etymology: Affectionate double diminutive of нить ('thread'), formed via нитка ('thread') + diminutive suffix -очка.

нить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нить, from Proto-Slavic *nitь ('thread'), from the Proto-Indo-European root *(s)nēi- ('to spin, twist thread', cognate with English needle and German nähen 'to sew').

нифига.etymology: Colloquial univerbation of ни фига ('not a fig, nothing at all'), from negative particle ни + genitive singular of фиг / фига ('fig; rude thumb-between-fingers gesture signifying nothing', ultimately from Latin fīcus 'fig').

ничто.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ничьто ('nothing'), from Proto-Slavic *ničьto, compounded from the negative particle *ni ('not even') + the interrogative pronoun *čьto ('what').
ничто.notes: Most often encountered in its genitive/accusative form **ничего** (pronounced *ничево*).

ничья.etymology: Substantivized feminine singular of the negative possessive pronoun ничей ('nobody's, belonging to neither side', formed from ни- + чей 'whose', Proto-Slavic *čьjь), originally modifying игра ('nobody's game') or партия ('nobody's match').
ничья.notes: Declines like the feminine pronoun чья: сыграть вничью ('to play to a draw'), закончиться ничьей ('to end in a tie').

ниша.etymology: Borrowed as an architectural term from French niche ('wall recess'), from Old French nichier 'to make a nest', going back to Latin nidus 'nest' (distant Indo-European cousin of Russian гнездо and English nest).

нищета.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нищета / Old Church Slavonic нищета ('poverty, destitution'), derived from нищий ('poor, destitute, beggar', Proto-Slavic *niščь) + abstract suffix -ета.

но.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нъ / но ('but'), from Proto-Slavic *nъ, which Vasmer traces to an old Indo-European adversative and temporal particle *nu ('now, well, on the other hand').

новенькая.etymology: Substantivized feminine form of новенький ('brand-new; newcomer'), diminutive of новый ('new', from Proto-Slavic *novъ).

новенький.etymology: Diminutive adjective formed from новый ('new', inherited from Old East Slavic новыи, Proto-Slavic *novъ) + suffix -енький.

новинка.etymology: Derived from новина ('something new; newly plowed land', from новый 'new', Proto-Slavic *novъ) + diminutive/concrete suffix -ка.

history.meaning: new thing, fresh crop or land
