новичок.etymology: Formed in East Slavic from новыи / новый ('new') via the stem нович- (or older новикъ 'newcomer, new recruit') + the expressive diminutive-agent suffix -ок: literally 'a newly arrived person or beginner'.
новичок.notes: Drops the fleeting vowel -о- in all oblique forms: *новичок → новичка, новичку*.

новоселье.etymology: Compound noun formed from новый ('new', Proto-Slavic *novъ) + linking vowel -о- + селить / село ('settlement, dwelling', Proto-Slavic *selo) + suffix -ье, denoting a new home and the celebration of moving into it.

новость.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic новость ('newness, novelty, tidings'), from Proto-Slavic *novostь, an abstract noun formed from *novъ ('new') + *-ostь ('-ness'). From the quality of being new it came to mean a newly reported event or piece of news.

новый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic новъ, from Proto-Slavic *novъ, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos ('new'), cognate with English new, German neu, French neuf/nouveau, Latin novus, and Ancient Greek νέος.

нога.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нога and Proto-Slavic *noga ('foot, leg'). Outside Slavic, its exact cognate is Lithuanian nagas ('fingernail, claw, hoof', Russian ноготь 'nail'), showing an ancient semantic shift within Slavic from 'claw/hoof' to the whole leg and foot.
нога.notes: Covers both 'leg' and 'foot' in Russian. Accusative singular shifts stress to the stem: ногу; nominative plural is ноги.

ноготь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ногъть, from Proto-Slavic *nogъtь ('fingernail, claw'), formed with suffix *-ъtь from the same Proto-Indo-European root *h₃nogʰ- ('nail, claw, hoof') as нога ('foot, leg').

нож.etymology: Нож is an inherited Slavic word, recorded as ножь in Old Russian and Old Church Slavonic. Vasmer connects its historical root with заноза, вонзить and пронзить: words involving a splinter, piercing or thrusting into something. That connection gives the knife word a history associated with a pointed or piercing object.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: нож

ножик.etymology: Diminutive of нож ('knife', inherited from Proto-Slavic *nožь, related to *nьziti 'to stab, pierce') + diminutive suffix -ик.

ножка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of нога ('foot, leg', with regular velar palatalization г → ж before -к-), inherited from Old East Slavic ножька and Proto-Slavic *nožьka. Used both for a small foot and for the supporting leg or stem of a chair, table, or glass.

history.meaning: foot, leg → little foot; furniture leg

ножницы.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ножьницѣ, plural instrument noun derived from нож ('knife', Proto-Slavic *nožь) + suffix -ницы, originally denoting a pair of hinged blades.

ноль.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Null ('zero') from Italian nulla / Medieval Latin nulla (figura) ('no figure, cipher'), feminine of Latin nūllus ('not any, none'); Russian uses both ноль (in everyday speech and sports scores) and нуль (in technical and mathematical idioms like с нуля 'from scratch').

номер.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (via German Nummer or Dutch nummer) from Latin numerus / Italian numero ('number'). In 19th-century Russian inns and hotels, номер ('a numbered room') became the standard everyday word for a hotel room.

норвежский.etymology: Derived from Норвегия ('Norway', from Medieval Latin Norvegia, from Old Norse Norðrvegr 'northern way') + adjectival suffix -ский (with velar palatalization г > ж).

норка.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic норька ('mink'), derived from нора ('burrow, den, hole', from Proto-Slavic *nora, related to нырять 'to dive, duck into a hole') + suffix -ка.

норма.etymology: Borrowed via German Norm or Polish norma from Latin norma ('carpenter's square, rule, pattern, standard').

нормально.etymology: Adverbial and predicate form in -о of нормальный ('normal, standard'), derived from норма ('norm, standard, rule'), borrowed via German Norm / Polish norma from Latin norma ('carpenter's square, rule, standard'). In everyday spoken Russian, нормально commonly means 'fine, OK, doing well'.

нормальный.etymology: Borrowed via German normal or French normal and adapted with the Russian adjectival suffix -ный, ultimately from Latin normālis ('made according to the carpenter's square, regular'), from norma ('carpenter's square, rule, standard').

нос.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic носъ and Proto-Slavic *nosъ ('nose; beak; prow'), from the o-grade of Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s- ('nose'), cognate with English nose, Latin nāsus, and Sanskrit nāsā.

history.meaning: nose; spout of a kettle; bow of a ship

нос.notes: Takes the stressed locative -у after в and на: на носу ('on the nose; just around the corner').

носик.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ик from нос ('nose; prow, beak, spout'), inherited from Old East Slavic носъ and Proto-Slavic *nosъ (cognate with English nose and Latin nāsus).

history.meaning: nose → little nose; pouring spout (of a kettle or teapot)

носить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic носити ('to carry repeatedly, bear, wear'), from Proto-Slavic *nositi, the o-grade iterative/multidirectional counterpart of нести (*nesti 'to carry in one direction', from PIE *h₁neḱ-). Just like English wear / bear or French porter, carrying clothes on the body became the standard verb 'to wear'.

history.meaning: to carry (one way) → to carry habitually, wear

носиться.etymology: Reflexive of носить ('to carry, bear', multidirectional verb from Proto-Slavic *nositi) + -ся ('to carry oneself around rapidly, rush about').

носок.etymology: Diminutive of нос ('nose; toe or tip of footwear', from Proto-Slavic *nosъ) + suffix -ок; shifted from 'toe of a boot or stocking' to 'short stocking, sock'.

history.meaning: little nose; toe of a shoe; sock

нота.etymology: Borrowed via Polish nota or German Note from Latin nota ('written mark, sign, musical character, cipher'), related to nōscere ('to come to know, recognize').
нота.notes: In the plural, **ноты** regularly means 'sheet music' (*играть по нотам* 'to play from sheet music').

нотариус.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Notarius from Latin notārius ('shorthand writer, clerk, notary'), derived from nota ('mark, sign, note').

нотный.etymology: Formed in Russian from нота ('musical note') with the adjectival suffix -ный; нота was borrowed via Polish nota from Latin nota ('written mark, sign, musical note').
нотный.notes: Used in collocations like нотная тетрадь ('music manuscript notebook') and нотный лист ('sheet of music').

ноутбук.etymology: Borrowed in the 1990s from English notebook (computer) ('portable folding personal computer the size of a paper notebook').
ноутбук.notes: In Russian, ноутбук (often shortened colloquially to ноут) is the universal word for any laptop computer, while a paper notebook is блокнот or тетрадь.

ночевать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ночевати ('to pass the night'), derived from ночь ('night'), from Proto-Slavic *nočevati (from *noťь 'night', PIE *nókʷts).

ночка.etymology: Diminutive of ночь ('night', inherited from Old East Slavic ночь, from Proto-Slavic *noktь) + diminutive suffix -ка.

ночлег.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ночьлѣгъ, from Proto-Slavic *noktьlěgъ, a compound of *noktь ('night', ночь) and *lěgъ ('lying down, lodging', related to лечь 'to lie down').

history.meaning: place or act of lying down for the night

ночлежка.etymology: Colloquial univerbation formed with the suffix -ка from ночлежный дом ('night-lodging house, doss-house'), derived from ночлег ('overnight lodging', an East Slavic compound of ночь 'night' + лечь / лежать 'to lie down', Proto-Slavic *noťьlěgъ).

history.meaning: night + lying down -> place to sleep for the night

ночной.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ночьныи (Proto-Slavic *noktьnъ), the relational adjective derived from ночь ('night', Proto-Slavic *noktь) with the suffix -ной.

ночь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ночь (Old Church Slavonic нощь), from Proto-Slavic *noktь, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts ('night'), cognate with English night, German Nacht, French nuit, Latin nox, and Lithuanian naktìs.

нравиться.etymology: Formed in Russian as the reflexive of нравить ('to please, suit someone's disposition'), derived from нрав ('character, disposition, temper', borrowed in its Church Slavonic non-pleophonic form нравъ alongside native East Slavic норовъ, from Proto-Slavic *norvъ): literally 'to match someone's disposition or taste'.

history.meaning: to suit one's taste, please, be liked

нравиться.notes: The person who likes something stands in the dative case, while the thing liked is the grammatical subject: **Мне нравится эта комната** ('This room pleases me / I like this room').

нравоучение.etymology: Compound noun coined in eighteenth-century literary Russian (calquing German Sittenlehre and Latin doctrīna mōrum) from нравы ('morals, customs, character', plural of Church Slavonic нравъ, corresponding to native East Slavic норов from Proto-Slavic *norvъ) + linking vowel -о- + учение ('teaching, instruction').

history.meaning: moralizing lecture, sermon, moral of a fable

ну.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ну ('well!, now then!, come on!'), from Proto-Slavic *nu, an ancient Indo-European discourse and prompting particle related to *nyně ('now'; compare English now, German nun, Latin nunc, and Lithuanian nù 'well!').

ну-ка.etymology: Colloquial hortatory particle formed from the interjection/particle ну ('well, come on', inherited from Proto-Slavic *nu, cognate with English now and Latin nunc) + the enclitic particle -ка (shortened from тка / тако, used with imperatives to soften or urge an immediate action).

history.meaning: come on, let's see, go on

ну-ну.etymology: Reduplication of the expressive Slavic particle and interjection ну ('well, come on, now', Proto-Slavic *nu, PIE *nu 'now'), used in Russian either with skeptical, ironic intonation ('yeah, right; we'll see about that') or soothingly ('there, there').

нуждаться.etymology: Derived from нужда ('need, want, necessity', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic нужда, corresponding to Old East Slavic нужа, from Proto-Slavic *nuda) + verbal suffix -ать + reflexive -ся.

history.meaning: to need, be in need of

нужнее.etymology: Comparative degree of нужный ('needed, necessary', from нужда / нужа 'need', Proto-Slavic *nudьnъ) formed with the comparative suffix -ее.

нужно.etymology: Neuter short-form predicate and adverbial form of нужный ('necessary, needed'), derived from нужда / нужа ('need, necessity, compulsion', from Old East Slavic нужа / Old Church Slavonic нѫжда and Proto-Slavic *nǫdja).

history.meaning: needed → (it is) necessary, one needs to

нужный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нужьныи ('necessary, urgent, pressing'), derived from нужа / нужда ('need, necessity, compulsion'), from Proto-Slavic *nudja, related to нудить ('to compel, urge').
нужный.notes: Most often heard in its short neuter forms **нужно** ('one needs to') and **нужен / нужна / нужны** ('is needed').

нынешний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нынѣшьнии, derived from ныне ('now, at present', from Proto-Slavic *nyně) + adjectival suffix -шний.

нынче.etymology: Colloquial contraction of older Russian нынеча ('today, nowadays'), formed from ныне ('now', from Proto-Slavic *nyně) + emphatic enclitic particle -ча / -че.

ныть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ныти (1sg. ною, 'to ache dully, pine, despair'), from Proto-Slavic *nyti ('to ache, languish, grow weary'; preserved in унывать 'to lose heart, be despondent'), cognate with Lithuanian niaũti. From 'to ache with a dull, persistent pain' developed the everyday colloquial sense 'to whine, complain'.

history.meaning: to ache dully; to whine, complain

нюанс.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French nuance ('shade of color, subtle difference'), from nuer ('to shade'), derived from nue ('cloud', from Popular Latin *nūba / Latin nūbēs).

нянчиться.etymology: Reflexive of нянчить ('to nurse, look after a child'), derived from нянька / няня ('nanny, nursemaid', from nursery word *ňaňa) + -ся.

о.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic о / объ and Proto-Slavic *o(b) ('around, against, concerning'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂mbʰi ('around, on both sides'), cognate with Ancient Greek amphí and Latin ob.
о.notes: Uses the variant об before words beginning with a vowel sound (а, о, у, э, и): думать о работе, but думать об осени.

оазис.etymology: Borrowed via German Oase or French oasis from Late Latin oasis, from Ancient Greek ὄασις (óasis, 'fertile spot in the Libyan desert'), ultimately of Ancient Egyptian origin (wḥꜣt).

оба.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic оба, from Proto-Slavic *oba ('both'), continuing the Proto-Indo-European dual pronoun/numeral *h₂ébʰoh₁ ('both'), directly cognate with Lithuanian abù, Ancient Greek ἄμφω, Latin ambō, and the second element of English both and German beide.
оба.notes: Preserves an ancient gender distinction: **оба** (stem *обо-*) is used with masculine and neuter nouns, while **обе** (stem *обе-*) is used with feminine nouns.

обалдеть.etymology: Colloquial perfective verb formed from prefix о- + балдеть ('to become dazed, go crazy'), derived from балда ('heavy sledgehammer; blockhead, daze').

history.meaning: heavy hammer, blockhead / to become dazed

обаятельный.etymology: Derived from обаять ('to charm, bewitch, enchant'), originally formed from prefix о- ('around') + баять ('to speak, tell tales, cast spells with words', from Proto-Slavic *bajati).

обвести.etymology: Formed from об- ('around') + вести ('to lead, draw a line', Proto-Slavic *vesti): 'to lead or draw a line around something, to circle or outline'.
обвести.notes: Conjugates with the dental stem вед-: я обведу, ты обведёшь; past tense обвёл, обвела.

обвинение.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ение from обвинить ('to accuse, charge, blame'), built from об- ('around, upon') + винить ('to blame'), derived from вина ('fault, guilt, blame', inherited from Old East Slavic вина and Proto-Slavic *vina).

history.stage: Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic

обвинить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic обвинити, formed from prefix об- + винить ('to blame, accuse', derived from вина 'guilt, fault', from Proto-Slavic *vina).

обвинять.etymology: Imperfective of обвинить ('to blame, accuse'), formed from prefix об- + -винять (from вина 'guilt, fault', Proto-Slavic *vina).

обвиняться.etymology: Reflexive and passive form of обвинять ('to accuse, blame') + -ся.

обворовать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix об- ('around, thoroughly') + воровать ('to steal', derived from вор 'thief').

обвязать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix об- ('around, on all sides') + вязать ('to tie, bind, knot'). The base verb descends from Old East Slavic вязати and Proto-Slavic *vęzati ('to tie, bind'), from PIE *h2enǵh- ('to tie tightly, constrict'). Adding об- specifies wrapping a cord or ribbon all the way around an object or ring.

обговариваться.etymology: Imperfective passive/reflexive of обговорить ('to discuss, stipulate in advance'), formed from prefix об- ('about, around') + -говаривать (iterative of говорить 'to speak') + -ся.

history.meaning: to be discussed, be agreed on

обед.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic обѣдъ and Proto-Slavic *obědъ ('midday meal, dinner'), a prefixal derivative of *ob- ('around, at') + *ěsti ('to eat', Russian есть). Originally it denoted both the main meal of the day and the midday time around which it was eaten.

обедать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic обѣдати ('to dine, eat the main midday meal'), from Proto-Slavic *obědati, a denominative verb built on *obědъ (Russian обед, 'dinner, lunch'), which is a compound of *ob- ('around, at') + *ěd- ('eating', from *ěsti 'to eat').

обеденный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -енный from обед ('lunch, dinner'), inherited from Old East Slavic обѣдъ, from Proto-Slavic *obědъ ('mealtime, time around eating', from *ob- + *ěsti 'to eat').
обеденный.notes: Common in обеденный стол ('dining table') and обеденный перерыв ('lunch break').

обезболивающее.etymology: Substantivized neuter present active participle of обезболивать ('to relieve pain, anesthetize'), formed from о- + без- ('without') + боль ('pain', Proto-Slavic *bolь).

обезьяна.etymology: Attested in Old Russian travel accounts (such as Afanasy Nikitin's 15th-century Journey Beyond Three Seas) as абезьяна / обезьяна, borrowed via Persian بوزینه (būzīna, 'monkey, ape') or Arabic/Turkish abuzine.

обеспеченный.etymology: Adjectival past passive participle of обеспечить ('to provide for, make secure'), formed from о- + без- ('without') + печа ('care, worry', related to печься 'to care, worry', Proto-Slavic *peča), literally 'made free from worry or want'.

обеспечить.etymology: Formed in Russian from о- + без- (spelled обес- before voiceless п) + the root of archaic печа ('care, worry, anxiety, trouble', Old East Slavic печа, Proto-Slavic *peča, also seen in беспечный 'carefree' and опека 'guardianship'): originally 'to free someone from material worry or want', whence 'to provide for, secure, ensure'.

history.meaning: to free from material worry -> to provide for, supply, ensure

обеспечить.notes: Although modern speakers often mentally associate обеспечить with печь ('stove'), its historical root is печа ('care, worry', related to печаль 'sorrow' and печься 'to care about').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: беспечный

обесточить.etymology: 20th-century technical verb formed on the privative pattern о- + без- ('without') + ток ('electric current', literally 'flow', from течь 'to flow', Proto-Slavic *tokъ) + -ить.

history.meaning: to de-energize, cut off the power

обещание.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic обѣщаниѥ ('promise, vow'), a verbal noun from обѣщати (modern обещать 'to promise'), showing the South Slavic reflex -щ- from Proto-Slavic *tj in *ob-větjati, built on *ob- + *větъ ('solemn word, declaration, counsel'; compare обет 'vow' and ответ 'answer').

обещанный.etymology: Past passive participle of обещать ('to promise'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обѣщати ('to promise, vow', from Proto-Slavic *obvěščati, derived from *ob- + *věščati 'to speak solemnly').

обещать.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic обѣщати ('to promise, vow'), derived from обѣтъ ('vow, solemn promise', Proto-Slavic *obvětъ, built on *ob- + *větъ 'speech, counsel, pact', as in совет 'advice, council' and ответ 'answer').

morphemes.meaning: speak, vow (*vět- + *-j- -> щ in Church Slavonic)

обещать.notes: Notice the Church Slavonic sound change *tj -> щ in обещать (from обет 'vow').

обжарка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from обжарить / обжаривать ('to sear, roast, fry on all sides', from об- + жарить 'to fry, roast', derived from жар 'heat') + noun suffix -ка.

history.meaning: to fry or roast on all sides

обжигать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed from prefix об- ('around, on the surface') + iterative stem -жигать (alternating with жечь 'to burn', Proto-Slavic *žegti / *žьgati, from PIE *dhegwh- 'to burn'). Its present active participle обжигающий ('scalding, burning-hot') is widely used for freshly baked pans, tea, or icy wind. It is cognate with English day and fever (via PIE *dhegwh-).

обжиматься.etymology: Colloquial reciprocal-reflexive verb formed from обжимать ('to squeeze or press all around', imperfective of обжать, built from об- 'around' + жимать / жать 'to press, squeeze', Proto-Slavic *žęti / *žimati) + -ся.

history.meaning: to squeeze around -> (colloquial) to hug tightly, cuddle, neck in corners

обида.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic обида ('wrong, injury, insult'), from Proto-Slavic *obida, derived from the verb *obviděti (Old East Slavic обидѣти, Russian обидеть 'to offend, wrong'), literally 'to look past, overlook, slight someone' (from *ob- 'around, past' + *viděti 'to see', with simplification *bv > *b).

history.meaning: to look past, slight → wrong, offense

обидеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic обидѣти ('to wrong, injure, offend'), from Proto-Slavic *obiděti, reduced by haplology/dissimilation from *ob-viděti ('to look past, overlook, slight', from *ob- 'around, past' + *viděti 'to see', Russian видеть). From 'looking past someone with disregard', the meaning developed into 'to wrong, hurt, offend'.

history.meaning: to look past, slight → to wrong, offend

обидеться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed by adding -ся to обидеть ('to offend, hurt'), inherited from Old East Slavic обидѣти, from Proto-Slavic *obiděti (reduced from *ob-viděti 'to look past, slight').

обидно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate continuing the short neuter singular of обидный ('hurtful, offensive, disappointing'), derived from обида ('offence, hurt, wrong', inherited from Old East Slavic обида, Proto-Slavic *obida, contracted from *ob-viděti 'to look past, overlook, slight').

history.meaning: to look past, slight -> offence, injury
offence -> hurtful -> it is hurtful, it's a shame

обижать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of обидеть ('to offend, hurt, wrong'), continuing Old East Slavic обижати (with East Slavic ж from Proto-Slavic *dj; compare Church Slavonic обиждати), formed from *ob- ('around, past') + *viděti ('to see', Russian видеть). Originally *ob-viděti meant 'to look past someone, overlook, slight, treat with disregard', which developed into 'to wrong, offend, hurt'.

history.meaning: to overlook, slight → to wrong, offend

обижаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive verb formed from обижать ('to offend, hurt'), continuing Old East Slavic обижати, from Proto-Slavic *obiděti / *obidjati (reduced from *ob-viděti 'to look past, slight').

обиженный.etymology: Past passive participle (used adjectivally) of обидеть ('to offend, wrong'), from Old East Slavic обидѣти, from Proto-Slavic *obviděti (literally 'to look past, overlook, slight', from *ob- + *viděti 'to see').

обколоть.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix об- ('around, all over') + колоть ('to prick, pierce, inject; to chop', inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolti).

history.meaning: to inject all around; to chip around

облажаться.etymology: Colloquial slang verb formed from prefix об- + лажать ('to blunder, play a false note, mess up', from slang лажа 'blunder, falsehood') + reflexive suffix -ся.

обламывать.etymology: Imperfective of обломать / обломить ('to break off around; in slang, to spoil someone's plans or pleasure'), formed from prefix об- + -ламывать (iterative of ломать 'to break', Proto-Slavic *lomiti).

history.meaning: to break off; (slang) to spoil, turn down, let down

областной.etymology: Derived from область ('region, province', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic область 'power, domain, province', from *ob- + *vold-ti 'to rule', cognate with East Slavic волость) + adjectival suffix -ной.

область.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic область ('power, authority, domain, province'), reflecting Proto-Slavic *ob-vold-tь with South Slavic liquid metathesis (-ла-), whereas native East Slavic pleophony produced волость ('rural district; old princely authority'), built on *volděti ('to rule, possess').

history.meaning: administrative region (oblast); field or sphere of knowledge

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: область

облегчение.etymology: Verbal noun in -ение formed on облегчить ('to lighten, ease, relieve', modeled on Old Church Slavonic обльгъчити), built from об- + лёгкий ('light in weight, easy', Proto-Slavic *lьgъkъ): literally 'a making lighter of a burden'.
облегчение.notes: Pronounced [аблихчение], with *г* softening to a [х]-like fricative before *ч*, just as in *лёгкий*.

обливаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of облиться ('to pour over oneself'), formed from prefix об- ('over, around') + -ливать (iterative of лить 'to pour', Proto-Slavic *liti) + -ся.

history.meaning: to pour over oneself; (fig.) to bleed/stream

облизать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic облизати and Proto-Slavic *oblizati, formed from the prefix об- ('all around, all over') + лизать ('to lick', Proto-Slavic *lizati, from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵʰ- 'to lick', cognate with English lick and Latin lingere).

history.meaning: to lick -> to lick all over
to lick clean, lick all over

облизать.notes: Famous in the culinary praise Пальчики оближешь! ('You'll lick your fingers! / Finger-licking good!').

облить.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix об- ('around, over') + лить ('to pour', inherited from Proto-Slavic *liti).

обложка.etymology: Formed in Russian from обложить ('to lay around, wrap, cover') + -ка: literally the protective outer wrap laid around the pages of a book or notebook.

обман.etymology: Deverbal noun from обмануть ('to deceive, cheat'), formed from the prefix об- ('around') and the Proto-Slavic root *man- ('to beckon, lure, delude', as in манить 'to lure, entice' and Lithuanian monai 'delusion, sorcery').

обманутый.etymology: Past passive participle of обмануть ('to deceive, cheat'), formed from prefix об- + мануть / манить ('to beckon, lure, delude', from Proto-Slavic *maniti).

обмануть.etymology: Formed with the prefix об- ('around') on the Proto-Slavic root *maniti ('to beckon, lure, delude, trick'; compare манить 'to beckon, entice' and Lithuanian monai 'witchcraft, delusion'). The consonant cluster -бм- simplified from *об-мануть, literally 'to lure around, delude with false appearances'.

обманщик.etymology: Agent noun formed in Russian with the suffix -щик from обман ('deceit, trickery') / обмануть ('to deceive, cheat', built on the Proto-Slavic root *man- 'to lure, delude').

обманывать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of обмануть ('to deceive, cheat'), formed with the imperfectivizing suffix -ыва- on the stem обман- (from об- 'around' + Proto-Slavic *maniti 'to lure, delude, trick').

обмен.etymology: Deverbal noun from обменять ('to exchange, swap'), formed from prefix об- + мена / менять ('exchange / to change, swap', from Old East Slavic мѣна and Proto-Slavic *měna).

обмениваться.etymology: Imperfective of обменяться ('to exchange'), formed from prefix об- + -менивать (iterative of менять 'to change, exchange', from мена 'exchange', Proto-Slavic *měna) + reciprocal suffix -ся.

history.meaning: to exchange with one another, swap

обменять.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix об- ('around, mutually') + менять ('to change, exchange'), derived from мена ('exchange, barter', Proto-Slavic *měna, from PIE *mey- 'to change, exchange, go past'). Through that Indo-European root of reciprocal exchange, it is cognate with Latin mutare ('to change') and English mutual and commute.

обменяться.etymology: Perfective reciprocal verb formed from prefix об- + менять ('to change, exchange', from мена 'exchange', Proto-Slavic *měniti) + -ся.

обморок.etymology: Formed from prefix об- + морок ('darkness, clouding of consciousness, stupor', East Slavic pleophonic reflex of Proto-Slavic *morkъ 'darkness, gloom').

обмыть.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix об- ('around, over') + мыть ('to wash', inherited from Proto-Slavic *myti); colloquially used for celebrating a new purchase or event over drinks ('wetting' it).

history.meaning: to wash; (colloq.) to celebrate with a drink

обнаглеть.etymology: Formed with the perfective prefix об- from наглеть ('to grow insolent'), from наглый ('impudent, brazen'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *naglъ ('sudden, impetuous, bold').

обнаружить.etymology: Formed in Russian from об- + наружу ('outward, into the open', from на- + the archaic noun ружь 'outside, open view, surface', related to снаружи 'on the outside'): literally 'to bring out into the open, uncover, detect'.

history.meaning: to bring into the open, reveal

обнимать.etymology: Imperfective of обнять ('to embrace, clasp around'), inherited from Old East Slavic объимати, formed from prefix об- ('around') + имать / ять ('to take, grasp', from Proto-Slavic *ob-jьmati).

обниматься.etymology: Reciprocal verb formed with -ся from обнимать ('to embrace, hug'), the imperfective of обнять (Old East Slavic объѩти, from *ob- 'around' + *jęti / *jьmati 'to take, grasp', where the initial н- of -нимать arose by rebracketing after prefixes ending in -н, such as вън-ѩти).

history.meaning: to hug → to hug each other

обновить.etymology: Formed with the prefix об- from новить ('to make new'), derived from новый ('new'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *novъ (from Proto-Indo-European *néwos).

обнять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic обьяти / обняти ('to embrace, clasp around'), formed from the prefix об- ('around') and яти ('to take, grasp', Proto-Slavic *obъjęti, with epenthetic -н- generalized from nasal prefixes into the infinitive обнять and present обниму, while the past tense обнял preserves the older nasal-free stem).

обняться.etymology: Reciprocal reflexive of обнять ('to embrace, hug'), inherited from Old East Slavic объятися, from Proto-Slavic *obъjęti ('to clasp around, embrace', from *ob- + *jęti 'to take') + -ся.

обогнать.etymology: Formed from the prefix обо- ('around, past', expanding from об- before the historic yer cluster in *gъnati) + гнать ('to drive, chase', from Proto-Slavic *gъnati): literally 'to drive/run around and ahead of someone', hence 'to overtake, outstrip'.
обогнать.notes: Conjugates with the alternating present/future stem *обгон-*: *я обгоню, ты обгонишь, они обгонят*.

обогреватель.etymology: Agent/instrument noun in -тель formed from обогревать ('to warm up, heat'), prefixed with обо- from греть ('to warm'), from Proto-Slavic *grěti ('to warm, heat').

обожать.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic обожати ('to deify, worship as a god', used as a calque of French adorer 'to adore'), formed from о- + бог ('god', with г -> ж) + -ать.

обозвать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix обо- (об-) + звать ('to call, name', inherited from Proto-Slavic *zъvati).

обозначиться.etymology: Reflexive of обозначить ('to mark, designate, indicate', from prefix обо- + значить 'to mark, signify', derived from знак 'sign') + -ся.

history.meaning: to become visible; (colloq.) to show oneself, make contact

обойти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic обити / обоити ('to walk around'), formed with the prefix об- / обо- ('around') + йти / идти ('to go on foot, walk', from Proto-Slavic *jьti).

history.meaning: to walk around, bypass, make the rounds of

обойтись.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed from обойти ('to walk around, bypass', from обо- 'around' + идти 'to go', Proto-Slavic *iti) + -ся. From 'to go around an obstacle' developed the senses 'to get by without something' (обойтись без), 'to cost' (обойтись в сумму), and 'to turn out all right' (всё обошлось).

history.meaning: to get around, manage without; to turn out

обокрасть.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix обо- (об-) + красть ('to steal', inherited from Proto-Slavic *krasti).

обомлеть.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix обо- (об-) + млеть ('to grow numb, faint, become stupefied', from Proto-Slavic *mьlěti).

оборона.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic оборона ('defense, protection'), East Slavic pleophonic form of Proto-Slavic *ob-borna ('warding off, defense', from *borniti 'to fight, defend', Russian боронить).

оборот.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic оборотъ ('turn, rotation, reverse side'), showing native East Slavic pleophony (-оро-) from Proto-Slavic *obvortъ (from *ob- 'around' + *vortiti 'to turn', Russian воротить / вертеть).

morphemes.meaning: turn (from *vort- with East Slavic -оро- and loss of v after b)

rootFamily.gloss: on the contrary, the other way round

оборотный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from оборот ('turn, rotation, reverse side'), built on prefix об- + ворот ('turning', native East Slavic pleophonic form of Proto-Slavic *vortъ, from *vьrtěti 'to turn').

history.meaning: turn, reverse → reverse, back (оборотная сторона 'reverse/back side')

morphemes.meaning: turn (ворот, with simplification of бв → б)

оборудование.etymology: Verbal noun formed from оборудовать ('to equip, fit out with tools and machinery'), built with the prefix об- on the archaic noun орудие / орудъ ('tool, instrument, implement, affair', from Proto-Slavic *orǫdьje 'tool, business, gear'; compare Polish orędzie and Old High German arunti 'errand').

history.meaning: to fit out with tools → equipment, machinery

обострение.etymology: Verbal noun from обострить ('to sharpen, aggravate, make acute', formed from об- + острить, from острый 'sharp, acute', Proto-Slavic *ostrъ) + suffix -ение.

обрабатывать.etymology: Imperfective of обработать ('to work, cultivate, process'), formed from prefix об- + -рабатывать (iterative of работать 'to work', from работа 'work').

обрадовать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix об- + радовать ('to gladden, make happy', derived from рад 'glad', from Proto-Slavic *radъ).

обрадоваться.etymology: Formed in Russian from об- (perfectivizing prefix) + радоваться ('to rejoice, be glad', derived from рад 'glad', Proto-Slavic *radъ).
обрадоваться.notes: Takes the dative case for what delights you: обрадоваться подарку ('to be delighted with the gift').

образ.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic образъ ('carved figure, icon, form, image, manner'), from Proto-Slavic *ob-razъ ('something struck or carved out', from *ob- + *razъ / *raziti 'to strike, cut').

образец.etymology: Derived with the suffix -ец from образ ('form, image, pattern'), inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic образъ ('carved figure, form, manner'), from Proto-Slavic *ob-razъ (from *ob- + *raziti 'to strike, carve').

образно.etymology: Adverb formed from образный ('figurative, vivid', derived from образ 'image, form, figure', from Proto-Slavic *oborzъ, from *ob- + *rězati 'to carve, cut') + -о.

образование.etymology: Verbal noun from образовать ('to form, shape, educate'), a calque on German Bildung ('formation, education') built on образ ('form, image'), from Proto-Slavic *obrazъ.

образоваться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of образовать ('to form, shape, organize'), derived from образ ('form, shape, image', from Proto-Slavic *obrazъ).

history.meaning: to form, take shape; (colloq.) to work itself out

образцовый.etymology: Adjective formed with -овый from образец ('sample, model'), itself derived from образ ('form, image, pattern', from Proto-Slavic *obrazъ).

обратить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обратити ('to turn, convert'), showing South Slavic -рат- (corresponding to East Slavic воротить) from Proto-Slavic *obvortiti ('to turn around', from *ob- + *vortiti).

обратиться.etymology: Reflexive of обратить ('to turn', from Old Church Slavonic обратити, Proto-Slavic *obvortiti) + -ся ('to turn oneself toward someone, address, apply').

обратно.etymology: Adverb from the short neuter of обратный ('reverse, return'), borrowed from Church Slavonic обратьныи (with South Slavic -ра- instead of East Slavic -оро- as in оборот), formed from обратити ('to turn back, turn around', from Proto-Slavic *ob-vortiti, built on *vьrtěti 'to turn').

rootFamily.gloss: on the contrary, the other way round

обратный.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic обратьнъ ('turning back, reverse'), derived from обратити ('to turn around', Proto-Slavic *obvortiti).

обращать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обращати ('to turn, convert'), imperfective of обратити, from Proto-Slavic *ob-vortiti ('to turn around', with South Slavic metathesis *vort- > врат-/вращ-), from *vьrtěti ('to turn').

обращаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of обращать ('to turn, direct'), from Old Church Slavonic обращати (Proto-Slavic *ob-vortiti 'to turn around'), developing the senses 'to turn toward someone, address' and 'to handle, treat'.

history.meaning: to address, turn to; to treat, handle

обращение.etymology: Verbal noun in -ение from обращать / обратиться ('to turn, address, treat'), from Old Church Slavonic обращение ('turning, conversion'), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *ob-vortiti.

обрезать.etymology: Formed from prefix об- ('around, off') + резать ('to cut, slice', inherited from Proto-Slavic *rězati).

обрезок.etymology: Derived from обрезать ('to trim, cut off', from об- + резать 'to cut') + noun suffix -ок, denoting a cut-off scrap or trimming.

обрести.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обрѣсти ('to find, discover, obtain'), from Proto-Slavic *obrěsti (from *ob- + *rěsti 'to come upon, encounter', cf. встретить).

обронить.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix об- + ронить ('to drop, shed', from Proto-Slavic *roniti, causative of *rinǫti 'to rush, fall').

обрубок.etymology: Derived from обрубить ('to chop off around, lop', from об- + рубить 'to chop, hew', Proto-Slavic *rǫbiti) + noun suffix -ок.

обручальный.etymology: Derived from обручать / обручить ('to betroth with a ring'), itself from обруч ('bracelet, ring, hoop', from Proto-Slavic *obrǫčь, a compound of *ob- 'around' + *rǫka 'hand').

обряд.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic обрядъ ('order, arrangement, custom, ceremony'), deverbal from обрядить ('to arrange, prepare', from об- + ряд 'order, row', Proto-Slavic *obrędъ).

обследование.etymology: Verbal noun formed from обследовать ('to examine, inspect, survey') + suffix -ование.

обследовать.etymology: Formed from prefix об- ('around, thoroughly') + следовать ('to follow, investigate', derived from след 'track, trace', Proto-Slavic *slědъ).

обслуживание.etymology: Verbal noun formed from обслуживать ('to serve, wait on, maintain', from об- + служить 'to serve') + suffix -ание.

обслуживать.etymology: Imperfective of обслужить ('to serve, attend to'), formed from prefix об- + -служивать (iterative of служить 'to serve', from слуга 'servant', Proto-Slavic *služiti).

обслужить.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix об- + служить ('to serve', inherited from Old East Slavic служити, Proto-Slavic *služiti).

обстановка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from обставить / обставлять ('to set around, furnish, surround', from об- + ставить 'to place, set', Proto-Slavic *staviti) + suffix -ка.

обстоятельство.etymology: Coined in the 18th century (featured in Trediakovsky and Lomonosov, on the model of Old Church Slavonic обстояние) as a structural calque of Latin circumstantia / French circonstance ('that which stands around an event: a circumstance'), formed from об- ('around', Latin circum-) + стоять ('to stand', Latin stāre) + -тельство.

обсудить.etymology: Formed with prefix об- ('around, thoroughly') from судить ('to judge, reason about'), inherited from Old East Slavic обсудити, from Proto-Slavic *ob-sǫditi (from *sǫdъ 'judgment').

history.meaning: to judge, consider from all sides

обсуждать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обсѫждати (imperfective of обсѫдити / обсудить 'to judge from all sides, deliberate upon, discuss'), showing the Old Church Slavonic reflex -жд- for Proto-Slavic *dj (compare native East Slavic осужать), formed from об- ('around, from all sides') + судить ('to judge', from суд 'judgment, court', Proto-Slavic *sǫdъ).

обсуждаться.etymology: Reflexive/passive form in -ся of обсуждать ('to discuss, deliberate'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обсуждати ('to judge, examine'), from Proto-Slavic *ob-sǫditi, from *sǫdъ ('judgment').

обсушить.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix об- ('all around, on the surface') + сушить ('to dry'), causative of сухой ('dry', Proto-Slavic *suxъ, from PIE *saus- 'dry, parched'). While высушить means to dry something out completely, обсушить specifically means to dry off the outer surface moisture—such as patting washed berries dry with a linen towel. It is cognate with English sear and Greek auios.

history.meaning: to dry off on all sides, pat dry

обсчитать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix об- (expressing error or cheating in an action) + считать ('to count, calculate', from Proto-Slavic *sъčitati).

обувь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic обувь ('footwear'), from Proto-Slavic *obuvь, a collective feminine noun derived from *obuti ('to put on footwear', Russian обуть), combining the prefix *ob- ('around') + the ancient Balto-Slavic root *-u- / *auti ('to wrap or clothe the feet'; compare Lithuanian aũti 'to put on shoes' and Russian разуть 'to take off shoes').
обувь.notes: Used as a collective singular noun in Russian (*удобная обувь* 'comfortable shoes').

morphemes.meaning: around (as an historical prefix fused with the root)

обустраиваться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of обустроиться ('to get settled, arrange one's surroundings'), formed from prefix об- + устраивать ('to arrange, establish', from устроить / строй 'order, structure') + -ся.

обучать.etymology: Imperfective of обучить ('to teach, instruct, train'), formed from prefix об- + учить ('to teach', from Proto-Slavic *učiti).

обучение.etymology: Verbal noun from обучить / обучать ('to teach, train', from об- + учить, Proto-Slavic *učiti) + suffix -ение.

обходительный.etymology: Adjective in -тельный formed from обходиться ('to treat, deal with people, behave toward'), itself from обходить ('to go around'), from Proto-Slavic *ob-xoditi.

обходить.etymology: Imperfective of обойти ('to walk around, bypass'), formed from prefix об- ('around') + ходить ('to walk, go', inherited from Proto-Slavic *xoditi).

обходиться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of обойтись, formed from обходить ('to go around, deal with', from об- + ходить) + -ся.

history.meaning: to cost; to manage without; to treat

общаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive/reciprocal verb formed from общать (Old Church Slavonic обьщати 'to make common, share, associate with'), derived from общий ('common, shared', from Proto-Slavic *obьťь, built on *ob 'around'). Literally, 'to share company or conversation with others'.

history.meaning: to communicate, talk with, socialize, hang out

общественный.etymology: Adjective in -енный formed from общество ('society, community'), derived from общий ('common, shared'), an Old Church Slavonicism from Proto-Slavic *obьťь ('common, around').

общество.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic обьщьство ('community, fellowship, sharing'), formed from обьщь (Russian общий, 'common, shared', Proto-Slavic *obьťь, from *ob- 'around') + the abstract/collective suffix -ство. In the 18th century it was also used as a semantic calque of French société ('society, association').

общий.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обьщь ('common, shared, general'), where -щ- is the South Slavic reflex of Proto-Slavic *tj (compare native East Slavic вобче / вообще). Derived from Proto-Slavic *obьťь ('around, shared by those around'), formed from the preposition/prefix *ob ('around, about').

общительный.etymology: Adjective in -тельный formed from общаться ('to communicate, associate') / общить ('to make common, unite'), from общий ('common, shared'), via Old Church Slavonic from Proto-Slavic *obьťь.

объединять.etymology: Imperfective of объединить ('to unite'), formed from prefix объ- + единить ('to unite', derived from единый 'one, single, united', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ѥдинъ, Proto-Slavic *jedinъ).

объект.etymology: Borrowed via German Objekt or Polish obiekt from Medieval Latin obiectum ('something thrown before the mind, object'), neuter past participle of Latin obicere ('to throw before, present'), from ob- + iacere ('to throw').

history.meaning: thing presented to the mind or senses

объективный.etymology: Borrowed via German objektiv or French objectif from Medieval Latin obiectivus ('relating to an object'), formed with Russian adjectival suffix -ный.

объявить.etymology: Formed from prefix объ- + явить ('to show, manifest, reveal', from Proto-Slavic *javiti, related to явь 'waking reality').

объявиться.etymology: Reflexive of объявить ('to announce, reveal', from объ- + явить, Proto-Slavic *javiti) + -ся ('to reveal oneself, show up').

объявление.etymology: Verbal noun from объявить ('to make known, declare, announce'), formed from prefix об- + явить ('to show, reveal, manifest', inherited from Proto-Slavic *aviti).

объявлять.etymology: Imperfective of объявить ('to declare, announce'), formed with prefix об- and stem явить ('to show, manifest'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *aviti ('to reveal, make known').

объявляться.etymology: Imperfective of объявиться and passive of объявлять ('to announce, declare', from объ- + являть) + -ся.

history.meaning: to be announced; to turn up

объяснение.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ение from объяснить ('to explain, make clear'), built from объ- ('around, thoroughly') + яснить ('to make clear'), from ясный ('clear, bright, distinct', inherited from Old East Slavic ясьныи, Proto-Slavic *jasnъ).

объяснительная.etymology: Substantivized feminine adjective from объяснительная записка ('explanatory note'), derived from объяснить ('to explain', from ясный 'clear').

объяснить.etymology: Formed from the prefix об- ('around, thoroughly', spelled with hard sign ъ before iotated я) + яснить, a causative verb built on ясный ('clear, bright', from Proto-Slavic *jasnъ): literally 'to make thoroughly clear'.

объяснять.etymology: Imperfective of объяснить ('to explain, make clear'), formed from prefix объ- + яснить (derived from ясный 'clear, bright', from Proto-Slavic *jasnъ).

объём.etymology: Deverbal noun from объять (present stem объим- / обым-, 'to embrace, encompass'), from Proto-Slavic *obъjьmъ (from *ob- 'around' + *jęti 'to take, grasp').

обыграть.etymology: Formed with the prefix об- ('around, out-') from играть ('to play'), inherited from Old East Slavic играти, from Proto-Slavic *jьgrati ('to play, dance').

обыкновенный.etymology: Derived from обыкновение ('custom, habit, wont') and the older verb обыкнуть ('to grow accustomed'), built from об- + the Proto-Slavic root *vyk- (*vyknǫti 'to learn by habit, get used to', with *bv > *b after prefix *ob-).

обыскать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix об- ('around, thoroughly') + искать ('to search, look for', from Proto-Slavic *jьskati, with regular shift и > ы after a hard consonant prefix).

обыскивать.etymology: Imperfective of обыскать ('to search, frisk'), formed from prefix об- + -ыскивать (iterative of искать 'to look for', Proto-Slavic *jьskati).

обычно.etymology: Formed as the adverbial derivative in -о of обычный ('usual, customary'), derived from обычай ('custom, habit', Old East Slavic обычаи, from *ob- + *vyknǫti 'to get used to, learn by habit', as in привыкнуть).

обычный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic обычьныи, from Proto-Slavic *obyčьnъ ('customary, habitual'), derived from *obykъ / *obyčajь (Russian обычай 'custom, habit'), which combines *ob- ('around') + the root *vyk- / *uč- ('to get used to, learn'; compare привыкнуть 'to get used to' and учить 'to teach/learn').
обычный.notes: Historically, the *в* of the root *вык-* dropped after labial *б* (*об-вык- → обык-*).

обязанность.etymology: Abstract noun formed from обязанный ('obliged, bound', past passive participle of обязать 'to bind, oblige') + suffix -ость.

обязанный.etymology: Adjectival passive participle of обязать ('to bind around; to oblige, place under a duty'), borrowed in its Old Church Slavonic prefixal form об-язати (where East Slavic had обвязать), from *ob- ('around') + *vęzati ('to tie, bind', Russian вязать). Literally, 'bound by obligation' (paralleling Latin obligātus from ligāre 'to bind').

обязательно.etymology: Adverb from the short neuter of обязательный ('obligatory, binding, without fail'), derived from обязать ('to bind by duty, oblige'), historically formed with Church Slavonic об- (for обв-) + вязать ('to tie, bind', from Proto-Slavic *vęzati): literally 'in a binding way'.

обязательный.etymology: Derived from обязать ('to bind, oblige', historically from об- + вязать 'to tie, bind', Proto-Slavic *obvęzati) + adjectival suffix -тельный.

обёртка.etymology: Formed in Russian from обёртывать / обернуть ('to wrap around') + the noun suffix -ка, built on the prefix об- ('around') and the Slavic root *vьrt- ('to turn, wind'; compare вертеть 'to turn, twirl'). Just as in обычный, the initial *в* of the root simplified after *б* (*об-верт- → обёрт-*).

овечка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from овца ('sheep', with regular alternation ц → ч and fleeting vowel е), which is inherited from Old East Slavic овьца, from Proto-Slavic *ovьca (diminutive of *ovь), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ówis ('sheep'; cognate with English ewe, Latin ovis, and Sanskrit ávi).

овощ.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic овощь ('fruit, garden produce', compare native Old East Slavic овочь) from Proto-Slavic *ovoktь ('growing fruit or crop'), often connected by Vasmer with the Indo-European root *h₂weg- ('to grow, increase', as in Latin augēre and English wax).
овощ.notes: A classic Slavic 'false friend': in Polish (owoc) and Czech (ovoce) the word still means 'fruit', whereas in Russian овощи narrowed to 'vegetables'.

овощной.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian from овощ ('vegetable') + -ной. Овощ was adopted via Old Church Slavonic овощь ('fruit, growing produce', compare native East Slavic dial. овок), from Proto-Slavic *ovotjь, which Vasmer connects with words for growth and swelling.

овца.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic овьца, from Proto-Slavic *ovьca ('sheep'), a diminutive of *ovь, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ówis ('sheep'; compare Latin ovis, Sanskrit ávi-, English ewe).

оглушить.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix о- + глушить ('to deafen, muffle, stun', derived from глухой 'deaf', from Proto-Slavic *gluxъ).

history.meaning: to deafen; to stun, knock out

оглядываться.etymology: Imperfective of оглянуться ('to look back, look around'), formed from prefix о- ('around') + -глядывать (iterative of глядеть 'to look', Proto-Slavic *ględěti) + -ся.

огнетушитель.etymology: Compound instrument noun formed from огонь (stem огн-, 'fire', Proto-Slavic *ognь) + connecting vowel -е- + тушитель ('extinguisher', from тушить 'to extinguish, put out', Proto-Slavic *tušiti).

ого.etymology: Expressive Slavic interjection ого! (compare Ukrainian ого, Polish oho, German oho), formed by reduplicating the vocalic exclamation о! with an intervocalic breathy [ɣ] or [h] sound to express surprise, admiration, or impression at size or scale ('whoa!', 'oh my!').

оголять.etymology: Imperfective of оголить ('to bare, strip, expose'), formed from prefix о- + голить (derived from голый 'bare, naked', from Proto-Slavic *golъ).

огонь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic огнь and Proto-Slavic *ognjь ('fire'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ngʷnis ('fire'), a famous ancient sacred word cognate with Sanskrit agní ('fire; the fire god Agni'), Latin ignis ('fire', whence English ignite), and Lithuanian ugnis.
огонь.notes: Drops the fleeting vowel -о- in all oblique forms: огонь -> огня, на огне ('on the stove heat').

огонёк.etymology: Diminutive of огонь ('fire, light', inherited from Old East Slavic огнь, from Proto-Slavic *ogňь, from PIE *h₁n̥gʷnis) + diminutive suffix -ёк.

ограбить.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix о- from грабить ('to rob, plunder'), originally 'to seize, rake away', from Proto-Slavic *grabiti ('to seize, snatch, rake').

оградка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of ограда ('fence, enclosure'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ограда (compare East Slavic огорода), from Proto-Slavic *ob-gorda, from *gorditi ('to enclose, fence').

ограниченный.etymology: Past passive participle (used adjectivally) of ограничить ('to limit, bound, restrict'), formed from prefix о- + граница / гранить ('border, boundary', from грань 'border, edge', Proto-Slavic *granь).

ограничить.etymology: Formed with prefix о- and verbal suffix -ить from граница ('border, boundary'), itself derived from грань ('edge, boundary, landmark'), from Proto-Slavic *granь.

огромный.etymology: Derived from the Slavic root гром- ('thunder', as in гром 'thunder' and громить 'to smash, crash'). Originally meaning 'thunderous, stunning, awe-inspiring in scale' (compare Polish ogromny 'huge, vast'), the meaning shifted from auditory force to visual and physical immensity.

огрызок.etymology: Formed with suffix -ок from огрызть ('to gnaw around'), from о- ('around') + грызть ('to gnaw, bite'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *gryzti ('to gnaw').

огузок.etymology: Derived from prefix о- + гуз / гузно ('rump, buttocks, tail end', inherited from Proto-Slavic *guzъ) + noun suffix -ок; originally 'rump piece of meat or hide', and used in kitchen slang for a rookie or kitchen boy.

history.meaning: rump cut of meat or fur; (slang) runt, rookie

огурец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic огурьць, borrowed from Byzantine Greek ἄγουρος (ágouros, 'unripe, green [cucumber]', from Ancient Greek ἄωρος 'untimely, unripe') + Slavic diminutive suffix -ец.

одеваться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of одевать ('to dress, clothe'), imperfective of одеть, from Proto-Slavic *ob-děti ('to put around, clothe'), from *děti ('to put, place').

history.meaning: to get dressed, to dress oneself

одежда.etymology: Borrowed in its Old Church Slavonic form одежда ('clothing, garment, attire'), showing the South Slavic reflex -жд- for Proto-Slavic *dj (compare native East Slavic одёжа), from Proto-Slavic *odedja, derived from *oděti ('to clothe, wrap around', Russian одеть), formed from *o(b)- ('around') + *děti ('to put, place', PIE *dʰeh₁-).

morphemes.meaning: put, clothe (Church Slavonic stem of одеть)

rootFamily.gloss: to put on (an item of clothing)

одержать.etymology: Borrowed via Church Slavonic одрьжати ('to hold fast, contain, prevail'), formed from prefix о- + держать ('to hold', from Proto-Slavic *dьržati).

одетый.etymology: Past passive participle of одеть ('to dress, clothe'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *odětъ.

одеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic одѣти, from Proto-Slavic *oděti ('to clothe, wrap around'), formed from *ob- ('around') + *děti ('to put, place', Russian деть).

одеться.etymology: Reflexive of одеть ('to dress, clothe', from Proto-Slavic *oděti) + -ся ('to dress oneself').

одеяло.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic одѣяло ('cloak, covering, blanket'), from Proto-Slavic *odědlо / *odějalo, formed with the instrument/object suffix -ло from одѣяти / одевать ('to clothe, cover', from *o(b)- 'around' + *děti 'to put, lay'). Literally 'that with which one covers oneself'.

один.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic одинъ (alongside Church Slavonic единъ), from Proto-Slavic *edinъ / *odinъ ('one, alone'), compounded from an intensifying particle *ed- / *od- plus *inъ ('one, single, another', from Proto-Indo-European *óynos, cognate with English one, German ein, and Latin ūnus).

один-один.etymology: Score-keeping phrase repeating the cardinal numeral один ('one', inherited from Old East Slavic одинъ / единъ, from Proto-Slavic *edinъ / *jedinъ), used literally in sports and figuratively in conversation when two sides are tied at one point each ('one-all').

одинаково.etymology: Formed as the adverbial derivative in -о of одинаковый ('identical, the same'), built on один ('one', Proto-Slavic *edinъ / *odinъ) with the suffixes -ак- and -овый.

history.meaning: identically, in the same way, equally

одинаковый.etymology: Formed in East Slavic with the adjectival suffix -овый from одинакий ('single, identical, of one kind'), built on один ('one', from Proto-Slavic *odinъ / *edinъ) + the qualitative suffix -ак- (compare двоякий 'twofold').

history.meaning: one → of one and the same kind, identical

одиннадцатый.etymology: Ordinal numeral derived from одиннадцать ('eleven'), a contraction of Old East Slavic одинъ на десяте ('one upon ten', Proto-Slavic *jedinъ na desęte).

одиннадцать.etymology: Inherited via contraction from the Old East Slavic phrase одинъ на десяте ('one on [top of] ten', Proto-Slavic *jedinъ na desęte). The unstressed second element на десяте wore down in pronunciation to the suffix -надцать used in all Russian teen numerals (11–19).
одиннадцать.notes: Spelled with double -нн- because the final -н of один meets the initial н- of на десяте.

одинокий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic одиногии / одинокыи, formed with suffix -окий from один ('one, alone'), from Proto-Slavic *edinъ / *odinъ ('one').

одиноко.etymology: Adverb and predicative formed from одинокий ('lonely, solitary, single', derived from один 'one, alone', Proto-Slavic *jedinъ + suffix -окий) + -о.

одиночество.etymology: Formed in Russian with the abstract noun suffix -ество from одинокий ('alone, solitary, single', with к → ч before -е-), which is built on один ('one, alone', from Old East Slavic одинъ, Proto-Slavic *jedinъ) + -окий.

однажды.etymology: Formed in Russian from the feminine/archaic stem одна- of один ('one', Old Church Slavonic единажды) with the multiplicative adverbial suffix -жды (from Old Church Slavonic шьды, related to шествие 'going, step'): literally 'one time, once, one day'.

одновременно.etymology: Adverb formed from одновременный ('simultaneous'), a compound calque (modeled on German gleichzeitig / French simultané) from один ('one') + время (stem времен-, 'time') + -но.

одноклассник.etymology: Compound noun formed from одно- (from один 'one, same') + класс ('class, school grade', from Latin classis via French/German) + agent suffix -ник.

одноклассница.etymology: Feminine form of одноклассник ('classmate', compounded from один 'one, same' + класс 'school class' + -ник) + suffix -ница.

одноклеточный.etymology: Biological compound formed from один ('one') + клетка ('cell, cage') + adjectival suffix -ный; used figuratively in colloquial slang to mean 'primitive, dim-witted'.

одноместный.etymology: Compound adjective formed from один ('one') + место ('place, seat, berth', Proto-Slavic *město) + adjectival suffix -ный.

одобрить.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic одобрити ('to approve, deem good'), a denominal verb built from о- + добрый ('good', Proto-Slavic *dobrъ) + -ить: literally 'to declare good, give one's approval to'.

одобрять.etymology: Imperfective verb paired with одобрить ('to approve, endorse'), formed with prefix о- from добрый ('good, kind', from Proto-Slavic *dobrъ): literally 'to deem good, pronounce favourable'.

одолеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic одолѣти, from Proto-Slavic *odolěti ('to overcome, prevail over'), derived from *o- + *doľa ('share, lot, upper hand', Russian доля).

одолжение.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ение from одолжить ('to lend; to oblige, do a favour'), derived from долг ('debt, obligation', Old East Slavic дългъ, Proto-Slavic *dъlgъ). Originally meaning 'a loan' or 'placing someone in one's debt by a kindness', it settled in expressions like сделать одолжение ('to do a favour').

одолжить.etymology: Derived (with influence from Polish obdłużyć) from prefix о- + должить (from долг 'debt, loan', inherited from Proto-Slavic *dъlgъ).

одуматься.etymology: Formed from prefix о- + думать ('to think', from Proto-Slavic *dumati) + reflexive suffix -ся ('to bethink oneself, reconsider').

history.meaning: to come to one's senses, think better of it

ожидание.etymology: Verbal noun formed from ожидать ('to wait for, expect', from prefix о- + -жидать, iterative of ждать 'to wait', Proto-Slavic *žьdati) + suffix -ание.

ожидать.etymology: Formed with prefix о- from ждать (жду, iterative -жидать, 'to wait for'), inherited from Old East Slavic ожидати, from Proto-Slavic *ob-židati (from *žьdati 'to wait').

озарение.etymology: Verbal noun from озарить ('to illuminate, light up'), formed from prefix о- + зарить (derived from заря 'dawn, glow', Old Church Slavonic зарѩ, Proto-Slavic *zaŕa) + suffix -ение.

озвереть.etymology: Perfective inchoative verb formed from prefix о- + звереть ('to become like a wild beast', derived from зверь 'wild animal, beast', from Proto-Slavic *zvěrь).

озвучить.etymology: Coined in 20th-century Russian from prefix о- + звук ('sound', from Proto-Slavic *zvǫkъ) + verbal suffix -ить; originally a cinema term meaning 'to add sound/voiceover to a film', later extended to 'to voice, announce publicly'.

history.meaning: to dub, add sound to; to voice, announce

озеро.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic озеро (with regular East Slavic change of initial je- > o- before a front vowel; compare Old Church Slavonic ѥзеро and Polish jezioro), from Proto-Slavic *ezero ('lake'), closely cognate with Lithuanian ẽžeras and Latvian ezers ('lake').
озеро.notes: Nominative plural shifts the vowel and stress: озеро → озёра.

ознакомиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive formed with prefix о- and -ся from знакомить ('to acquaint'), derived from знакомый ('familiar, acquainted'), from знать ('to know', Proto-Slavic *znati).

означать.etymology: Imperfective of означить ('to mark, signify'), formed from prefix о- + -значать (from значить 'to mean, signify', derived from знак 'sign, mark').

ой.etymology: An inherited Slavic primary interjection (Proto-Slavic *ojь), attested across East, West, and South Slavic as a natural vocalic exclamation of sudden surprise, alarm, pain, or mild dismay ('oh!', 'oops!').

ой-ой.etymology: Formed by expressive reduplication of the primary Slavic interjection ой ('oh!, ouch!'), conveying mild alarm, sympathy, or sudden discomfort.

ой-ой-ой.etymology: Formed by triple reduplication of the interjection ой ('oh!, ouch!'), expressing heightened dismay, concern, or playful reproach ('oh dear!, oh no!').

оказать.etymology: Formed from prefix о- + казать ('to show, display', inherited from Proto-Slavic *kazati), originally meaning 'to show, manifest' (as in showing help, honor, or resistance).

оказаться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed from оказать ('to show, render'), built from the prefix о- and казать ('to show, appear', Old East Slavic казати, Proto-Slavic *kazati). With the reflexive suffix -ся, оказаться literally means 'to show oneself to be', whence 'to turn out to be' or 'to find oneself in a place'.

history.meaning: to turn out to be; to find oneself (somewhere)

оказывать.etymology: Imperfective of оказать ('to render, show'), formed from prefix о- + -казывать (iterative of казать 'to show', from Proto-Slavic *kazati).

оказываться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of оказывать ('to show, render'), imperfective of оказать, formed from о- + казать ('to show'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *kazati ('to show, point out').

history.meaning: to turn out to be, prove to be

окаянный.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic окаѩнъ ('wretched, pitiable, accursed'), past passive participle of окаѩти ('to pity, lament, condemn', from о- + каяти 'to censure, repent', Proto-Slavic *kajati).

океан.etymology: Borrowed via Old East Slavic окиянъ / океанъ from Byzantine Greek ὠκεανός (ōkeanós, 'the great outer sea, ocean'), personified in antiquity as the Titan Oceanus.

окей.etymology: 20th-century borrowing from English okay / OK, originating in 1839 American newspaper slang (initialism for 'oll korrect', a humorous spelling of 'all correct').

окно.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic окно, from Proto-Slavic *okъno, derived from *oko ('eye', from PIE *h₃ekʷ-). Like English window (from Old Norse vindauga, 'wind-eye'), Slavic named a window as the 'eye' of a house wall.

око.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic око, from Proto-Slavic *oko ('eye'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- ('to see; eye', cognate with Latin oculus and Lithuanian akis).

околачиваться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of околотиться, formed from prefix о- + -колачивать (iterative of колотить 'to beat, knock about', from Proto-Slavic *koltiti) + -ся; colloquially 'to knock about, hang around idly'.

около.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic около ('around, near'), adverbialized accusative/locative formed from о- ('around') + коло ('wheel, circle, ring', from Proto-Slavic *kolo 'wheel, circle').

окончательный.etymology: Derived from окончание / окончить ('to finish, bring to an end', from о- + кончить 'to end', derived from конец 'end', Proto-Slavic *konьcь) + adjectival suffix -тельный.

окончить.etymology: Formed with perfective prefix о- from кончить ('to finish, end'), derived from конец ('end'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *konьcь ('end, limit').

окоп.etymology: Deverbal noun from окопать ('to dig around, entrench'), formed from prefix о- ('around') + копать ('to dig', inherited from Proto-Slavic *kopati).

окошко.etymology: Affectionate/everyday diminutive in -ко of окно ('window', via earlier/dialectal оконо / окошно), inherited from Proto-Slavic *okno, which was derived from *oko ('eye') because early windows were round 'eye-holes' in a timber wall.

окрошка.etymology: Culinary noun derived from окрошить ('to crumble or chop into small pieces'), formed from prefix о- + крошить ('to crumble, dice', from кроха 'crumb', Proto-Slavic *kroxa) + suffix -ка.

history.meaning: okroshka (cold diced soup with kvass or kefir)

окружать.etymology: Imperfective of окружить ('to surround, encircle'), formed from prefix о- + кружить (from круг 'circle', inherited from Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ).

окружить.etymology: Formed with prefix о- ('around') from кружить ('to circle'), derived from круг ('circle, ring'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ ('circle').

октава.etymology: Borrowed via Italian ottava or Polish oktawa from Medieval Latin octāva ('interval of an eighth'), feminine of Latin octāvus ('eighth', from octō 'eight', distant Indo-European cognate of Russian восемь).

history.meaning: eighth (musical interval spanning eight scale degrees)

окупаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of окупиться ('to pay for itself, recoup its cost'), formed from prefix о- + купать / купить ('to buy, redeem', from Proto-Slavic *kupiti) + -ся.

history.meaning: to pay for itself, pay off

окурок.etymology: Derived from окурить ('to smoke off/around', from о- + курить 'to smoke', Proto-Slavic *kuriti) + noun suffix -ок, denoting a leftover smoked stub.

оленина.etymology: Formed in Russian from олень ('deer, stag, reindeer') + the meat-denoting suffix -ина (compare говядина 'beef', баранина 'lamb/mutton'). Олень is inherited from Old East Slavic олень, from Proto-Slavic *elenь ('stag, deer'), cognate with Lithuanian élnis and Ancient Greek ἔλαφος.

оливка.etymology: Derived with suffix -ка from олива ('olive tree, olive'), borrowed via Polish oliwa or German Olive from Latin olīva ('olive'), itself an early loan from archaic Greek *ἐλαίϝα (elaíwa).

оливковый.etymology: Adjective formed with -овый from оливка ('olive'), borrowed via Polish oliwka or German Olive from Latin olīva ('olive, olive tree'), itself an early borrowing from Greek ἐλαία (elaía).

олигарх.etymology: Borrowed via German Oligarch or French oligarque from Ancient Greek ὀλιγάρχης (oligárkhēs, 'member of an oligarchy'), from ὀλίγος (olígos, 'few, little') + ἄρχω (árkhō, 'to rule').

олимпиада.etymology: Borrowed via French olympiade or Latin Olympias from Ancient Greek Ὀλυμπιάς (Olympiás, 'Olympiad, period between Olympic Games; the Olympic Games'), from Ὀλυμπία ('Olympia').

омар.etymology: Borrowed from French homard ('lobster'), from Old Norman houmar, borrowed from Old Norse humarr ('lobster').

омерзительно.etymology: Adverb formed from омерзительный ('revolting, disgusting'), derived from омерзить / омерзеть ('to disgust, become loathsome'), from Proto-Slavic *mьrzěti ('to be loathsome, freeze/shudder'; compare мерзкий).

омлет.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th centuries from French omelette ('omelette'), altered in Middle French from earlier alemette / alumelle ('thin metal blade, flat pancake'), ultimately from Latin lāmella ('thin plate', diminutive of lāmina).

он.etymology: An inherited Slavic pronoun, recorded in Old Russian and Old Church Slavonic as онъ. Its older demonstrative sense connects “he” with “that one”; Vasmer compares other Slavic forms and Lithuanian anas, meaning that one or he.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: он

он.notes: Many simple prepositions require an initial н- in the third-person oblique forms: у него, к нему, с ним, о нём. Check the construction rather than adding н- after every preposition.

он-то.etymology: Compound form consisting of the third-person masculine pronoun он ('he', from Old East Slavic онъ, Proto-Slavic *onъ) + the emphatic enclitic particle -то (from the demonstrative pronoun тот 'that').

она.etymology: Она belongs to the inherited Slavic demonstrative-pronoun family also seen in он and оно. Vasmer records the feminine form она in Old Russian and Old Church Slavonic and compares feminine forms in the other Slavic languages. The older connection with pointing to that person survives behind its everyday meaning she.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: он (including она)

онеметь.etymology: Perfective of неметь ('to grow mute or numb'), formed from prefix о- + неметь (derived from немой 'mute, dumb', from Proto-Slavic *němъ).

history.meaning: to go numb; to be struck dumb

они.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic они (masculine plural; feminine plural онѣ > оне merged into они in modern Russian), from the Proto-Slavic distal demonstrative pronoun *onъ ('that one, he'; plural *oni 'those ones, they').

оно.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic оно, from Proto-Slavic *ono, the neuter singular of the demonstrative and third-person pronoun *onъ ('that one; he'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *h₂enós ('that one yonder'; compare Lithuanian anàs).

опа-на.etymology: Expressive colloquial interjection formed from оп / опа (an exclamation accompanying a sudden jump, catch, or surprise, compare гоп) + the demonstrative/emphatic particle -на ('there, take that!').

history.meaning: exclamation of sudden action or surprise

опаздывать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of опоздать ('to be late, arrive late'), formed with root vowel lengthening (о > а) and the imperfective suffix -ыва- from поздно / поздний ('late', Old East Slavic поздо, Proto-Slavic *pozdъ).

history.meaning: to be running late, be late (imperfective)

опасно.etymology: Adverb formed from опасный ('dangerous'), originally 'cautious, watchful', derived from опасать ('to guard, beware'), from о- + пасти ('to herd, guard, watch over'), from Proto-Slavic *pasti.

опасность.etymology: Formed with the abstract suffix -ость from опасный ('dangerous', in older Russian also 'cautious, watchful'), derived from опасаться ('to beware, fear') and the root of пасти ('to herd, guard, watch over', Proto-Slavic *pasti, from PIE *peh₂- 'to protect'). The sense shifted from 'requiring caution' to 'fraught with danger'.

опасный.etymology: Derived from опасаться ('to beware, be on one's guard, fear') and archaic опасъ ('caution, guard, protection'), built from о- ('around') + пасти ('to herd, guard, watch over', from Proto-Slavic *pasti, PIE *peh₂- 'to protect, tend'). Originally опасный meant 'watchful, cautious, circumspect'; by the 18th century it shifted from the person exercising caution to the situation requiring caution ('fraught with danger, dangerous').

rootFamily.gloss: thank you (from спаси Бог, same root пас-)

опекать.etymology: Derived from опека ('guardianship, care, wardship', shared with Polish opieka), formed from prefix о- + пека / печа ('care, concern', related to печься 'to care for', Proto-Slavic *peča).

history.meaning: to look after, take care of

оператор.etymology: Borrowed via German Operator or French opérateur from Late Latin operātor ('worker, performer'), agent noun from Latin operārī ('to work, operate'), from opus ('work').

операционная.etymology: Substantivized feminine adjective clipped from операционная палата / комната ('operating room'), from операционный ('surgical, operating'), derived from операция ('surgical operation', borrowed via German Operation and French opération from Latin operātiō 'work, operation').
операционная.notes: Declines as a feminine adjective even though it functions as a noun: в операционной ('in the operating room').

операция.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via Polish operacja or German Operation from Latin operātiō ('work, performance, activity'), derived from operārī ('to work, labor') and opus ('work').

опергруппа.etymology: 20th-century syllabic abbreviation of оперативная группа ('operational group, field task force'), combining оперативный ('operational', from Latin operātīvus) and группа ('group').

опереться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic оперетися, from Proto-Slavic *opereti sę ('to lean against, prop oneself'), formed from prefix *o(b)- + *perti (1sg *pьrǫ, 'to press, push, prop', Russian переть) + -ся.

оперировать.etymology: Borrowed via German operieren from Latin operārī ('to work, labor; perform an operation'), from opus, operis ('work'), adapted with the Russian verbal suffix -овать.

history.meaning: to operate on, to perform surgery

оплата.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from оплатить ('to pay for'), from о- + платить ('to pay'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *platiti ('to pay', originally with pieces of cloth, *platъ).

оплатить.etymology: Formed in Russian from о- ('around, completely') + платить ('to pay', Proto-Slavic *platiti): 'to pay for (a bill, fare, or purchase)'.
оплатить.notes: Usage contrast: оплатить takes a direct object in the accusative without a preposition (оплатить проезд, оплатить счёт), whereas заплатить takes за + accusative (заплатить за кофе).

оплачивать.etymology: Imperfective of оплатить ('to pay for'), formed from prefix о- + -плачивать (iterative of платить 'to pay', derived from плата 'payment', Proto-Slavic *platiti).

оплошность.etymology: Abstract noun derived from оплошный ('careless, negligent') and оплошать ('to blunder, be remiss'), from плохой / плошать ('bad, weak, careless', from Proto-Slavic *ploxъ) + -ость.

опоздание.etymology: Verbal noun formed from опоздать ('to be late', from prefix о- + поздно / поздний 'late', from Proto-Slavic *pozdь) + suffix -ание.

опоздать.etymology: Formed in Russian from о- + поздно ('late', Proto-Slavic *pozdьno, built on *pozdъ 'late', related to по- / после 'after'): 'to arrive or act too late, miss'.
опоздать.notes: Takes на + accusative for an event or transport: опоздать на поезд ('to miss / be late for the train'), опоздать на работу ('to be late for work').

опозорить.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix о- + позорить ('to disgrace, shame', derived from позор 'shame, disgrace; in older Slavic, public spectacle or view', from зреть 'to look, behold').

опора.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *opora ('support, prop'), deverbal noun with o-grade ablaut from *opereti ('to lean, prop', Russian опереть, root *per- 'to press, prop').

опохмелиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed from prefix о- + похмелиться ('to take a drink to relieve a hangover'), derived from похмелье ('hangover', from по- 'after' + хмель 'hops; intoxication', Proto-Slavic *xъmeľь).

history.meaning: to cure a hangover (with a drink)

оправдание.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ние from оправдать ('to justify, acquit, prove right'), built on о- + правда ('truth, justice, right', inherited from Old East Slavic правьда, derived from правый 'right, straight, just', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

history.stage: Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic

оправдать.etymology: Prefixed verb formed from о- + правда ('truth, justice, legal right', Old East Slavic правьда, from правый 'right, just', Proto-Slavic *pravъ): literally 'to declare right or innocent, clear of blame'.

history.meaning: to acquit; to justify, live up to

оправдывать.etymology: Imperfective of оправдать ('to acquit, justify, vindicate'), formed from prefix о- + правдать (from правда 'truth, justice, right', Proto-Slavic *pravьda).

history.meaning: to justify; to live up to

определить.etymology: Borrowed via Church Slavonic опрѣдѣлити ('to bound, define, determine, appoint'), formed from prefix о- + прѣдѣлъ ('boundary, limit', from *per- + *dělъ 'division').

определиться.etymology: Reflexive of определить ('to determine, define') + -ся ('to become defined; to settle on a decision').

history.meaning: to make up one's mind, decide

определять.etymology: Imperfective of определить ('to determine, define, identify', from предел 'boundary, limit').

опрос.etymology: Deverbal noun from опросить ('to question, poll, survey'), formed from prefix о- ('around') + просить ('to ask; in older Russian also to question, inquire', from Proto-Slavic *prositi).

оптимизация.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English optimization or French optimisation, derived from Latin optimus ('best', superlative of bonus 'good').

оптимизм.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French optimisme ('optimism', coined in 1737 in reference to Leibniz's doctrine of the 'best of all possible worlds'), from Latin optimus ('best').

оптовик.etymology: Derived with suffix -ик from оптовый ('wholesale'), from опт ('wholesale trade', as in оптом 'in bulk'), generally connected with общий ('common, shared') or Old East Slavic оpath/объть ('together, in full').

опубликовать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix о- + публиковать ('to publish, make public', borrowed via Polish publikować or German publizieren from Latin pūblicāre, from pūblicus 'public').

опускать.etymology: Formed as the imperfective counterpart of опустить ('to lower, let down, drop into'), from о- + пускать ('to let go, release', Proto-Slavic *puskati).

history.meaning: to lower, put down, drop in

опустить.etymology: Formed from о- + пустить ('to let go, release', Proto-Slavic *pustiti): 'to let something down, lower (one's hands, a lid, or a blind), or drop (a letter into a postbox)'.

history.meaning: to lower, put down, drop in

опустить.notes: First-person singular has ст -> щ mutation: я опущу, ты опустишь.

опутать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix о- ('around') + путать ('to tangle, fetter, bind', derived from путо / путы 'fetters, hobbles, ropes', from Proto-Slavic *pǫto).

опухнуть.etymology: Perfective verb formed from prefix о- ('around, all over') + пухнуть ('to swell, puff up', inherited from Proto-Slavic *puxnǫti, related to пух 'fluff, down').

опухоль.etymology: Derived from опухнуть ('to swell up', from пухнуть 'to swell', Proto-Slavic *puxnǫti) + noun suffix -оль.

опыт.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in East Slavic from опытать ('to test, examine, try out all around'), built on prefix о- + пытать ('to inquire, test, try', from Proto-Slavic *pytati). Covers both accumulated 'experience' and a scientific or culinary 'experiment, trial'.

опытный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from опыт ('experience, experiment, trial'), a deverbal noun from опытать ('to test, try out, assay'), built from о- + пытать ('to test, inquire, probe', from Proto-Slavic *pytati). Literally, 'tested by trial, possessing practical experience'.

опять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic опять ('back, again'), fused from the preposition о ('around, back') + пята ('heel', Proto-Slavic *pęta): literally 'turning back on one's heel, retracing one's steps' (compare вспять 'backwards').
