Grech from пар ('steam', Proto-Slavic *parъ) + linking vowel -о- + воз ('hauler, vehicle', from возить 'to haul, transport'): literally 'steam-hauler'.

пароль.etymology: Borrowed via German Parole from French parole ('word, watchword, password'), from Late Latin parabola ('comparison, speech, word'), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ).

парочка.etymology: Diminutive noun formed from пара ('pair, couple', borrowed via Polish para from Middle High German pār, from Latin pāria 'equals', neuter plural of pār 'equal') + diminutive suffix -очка.

партизан.etymology: Borrowed via French partisan ('member of a party or irregular military detachment') from northern Italian partigiano ('partner, member of a faction'), derived from parte ('part, side', from Latin pars).

history.meaning: member of a party; irregular fighter

партизанить.etymology: Denominative verb in -ить formed from партизан ('partisan, guerrilla fighter'), borrowed via French partisan from Italian partigiano ('member of a party or faction', from parte 'part, side').

history.meaning: supporter of a party; irregular fighter

партия.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish partia / German Partie from French partie ('part, share, batch of goods, match/game, political party'), originally the feminine past participle of partir ('to divide, share', from Latin partīrī, built on pars, partis 'part').

history.meaning: batch (of goods or baking); game (of chess); party

партнёр.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French partenaire or English partner (altered in Middle English from parcener 'joint heir, sharer', from Anglo-Norman parçonier, from Latin partītiō 'division, share').

парусник.etymology: Derived inside Russian from парусный ('sailing') / парус ('sail') with the noun suffix -ник. Old East Slavic парусъ ('sail') was borrowed in the Viking-Byzantine trade era from Byzantine Greek pharos ('linen cloth, sail, cloak'). In Russian парусник denotes any vessel propelled by sails.

morphemes.meaning: noun suffix denoting a vessel or agent

парусный.etymology: Relational adjective formed from парус ('sail') with the suffix -ный. Old East Slavic парусъ ('sail') entered early East Slavic navigation vocabulary from Byzantine Greek pharos ('heavy linen cloth, sail'). In Russian парусный корабль is the classic phrase for a tall sailing ship.

паршивый.etymology: Adjective formed with -ивый from парша ('scab, favus, mange'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *pьrša / *parša ('scaly skin disease, scab'), developing the figurative sense 'scabby, wretched, lousy'.

пас.etymology: Two converged homonyms: in card games ('я пас' = 'I pass'), from French je passe (from passer 'to pass'); in ball sports ('a pass'), borrowed in the 20th century from English pass (ultimately from the same French verb).

пасовать.etymology: Formed from French passer ('to pass', from Vulgar Latin *passāre, from Latin passus 'step') + -овать: in card games ('to pass one's turn' and figuratively 'to back down') via German passen / French je passe; in team sports ('to pass the ball') via English pass.

history.meaning: to pass (sports, cards); to back down

паспорт.etymology: Borrowed via German Paßport or Dutch paspoort from French passeport ('authorization to pass through a port or city gate'), from passer ('to pass') + port ('port, harbor' or porte 'gate').

history.meaning: document permitting passage through a port or gate

пассажир.etymology: Borrowed via German Passagier or Dutch passagier from French passager ('traveler, passenger'), derived from passage ('passage, journey').

пассажирский.etymology: Relational adjective formed from пассажир ('passenger', borrowed via German Passagier from French passager, from Italian passeggero, derived from passaggio 'passage') + suffix -ский.

паста.etymology: Borrowed via German Paste ('paste, ointment') and Italian pasta ('dough, pasta'), from Late Latin pasta ('dough, paste'), from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá, 'barley porridge').

пасть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пасти ('to fall, collapse'), from Proto-Slavic *pasti (1sg *padǫ), from Proto-Indo-European *ped- ('to step, stumble, fall').

пасха.etymology: Borrowed in the Old East Slavic period via Old Church Slavonic пасха from Byzantine Greek πάσχα (páskha, 'Passover; Easter'), from Aramaic פַּסְחָא (pasḥā) and Biblical Hebrew פֶּסַח (pésaḥ, 'Passover', from pāsaḥ 'to pass over, spare'). In Russian, Пасха denotes both the Christian holiday of Easter and the traditional pyramid-shaped sweetened quark/curd cheese dish prepared for Easter.

пасьянс.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French patience ('patience; solitaire card game requiring patience', from Latin patientia 'endurance, patience', from patī 'to suffer, endure').

пауза.etymology: Borrowed via German Pause from Latin pausa ('halt, stop, cessation'), itself from Ancient Greek παῦσις (paûsis, 'stopping, ceasing'), from παύω (paúō, 'to stop').

паук.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic паукъ, from Proto-Slavic *paǫkъ ('spider'), an archaic compound of prefix *pa- + *ǫkъ ('hook, curved leg', from PIE *h₂enk- 'to bend, curve').

паутина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic паучина / паутина, derived with suffix -ина from паук ('spider'), from Proto-Slavic *paǫkъ ('spider') / *paǫtina ('spiderweb').

пахнуть.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *paxnǫti ('to blow softly, puff, emit an odour'), an inchoative -нуть verb built on the expressive Slavic root *pax- / *pux- ('puff of air, breath, waft'; compare пахать in its older dialectal sense 'to fan, sweep, blow' and пух 'fluff, down').

history.meaning: to waft, blow → to give off a smell

пахнуть.notes: Takes the instrumental case for what something smells like: *пахнет свежим хлебом* ('it smells of fresh bread').

пацан.etymology: Colloquial word that entered standard slang from southern Russian/Ukrainian and Yiddish/Odessa argot in the late 19th–early 20th century; most widely traced either to Yiddish פּאָצן (potsn, diminutive of פּאָץ pots) or to southern dialectal пацюк ('piglet, rat', from interjection паць-паць).

пациент.etymology: Borrowed via German Patient or Polish pacjent from Latin patiēns, genitive patientis ('suffering, enduring; a patient under medical treatment', present participle of patī 'to suffer, undergo').

пачка.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via Polish paczka ('parcel, packet') from German Pack ('pack, bundle', related to English pack), adapted with the feminine diminutive/noun suffix -ка.

пачкать.etymology: Derived from an expressive Slavic root *pač- / *pat- ('to smear, splash mud'; compare Polish paćkać / paczkać 'to daub, smear, soil' and dialectal Russian пачкать 'to daub, smudge').

паштет.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from German Pastete ('pâté, meat pie, pastry'), from Medieval Latin pastāta / Old Italian pastata, derived from Late Latin pasta ('dough, paste'), from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá, 'barley porridge, salted mess of food').

history.meaning: dough, paste → dish baked in pastry

паяльник.etymology: Instrument noun in -ник formed from паять ('to solder'), of uncertain origin; Vasmer links it via *паяти ('to join, give to drink/quench metal') to поить ('to water') or спаять.

паясничать.etymology: Derived with verbal suffix -ничать from паяц ('buffoon, clown'), borrowed via French paillasse or German Bajazzo from Italian pagliaccio ('clown', literally 'straw mattress', from paglia 'straw', after the mattress-ticking costume of comic actors).

history.meaning: to clown around, to play the fool

певец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пѣвьць ('singer'), formed from the stem of петь ('to sing', Old East Slavic пѣти, Proto-Slavic *pěti) + agent suffix -ец (Proto-Slavic *pěvьcь).

певица.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пѣвица ('female singer'), feminine counterpart of певец ('singer', Proto-Slavic *pěvьcь, from *pěti 'to sing') formed with suffix -ица.

педаль.etymology: Borrowed via French pédale (and Italian pedale) from Latin pedālis ('pertaining to the foot'), derived from pēs, stem ped- ('foot', Indo-European cognate of Russian пешком 'on foot').

history.meaning: pedal (of a piano, bicycle, or car)

rootFamily.gloss: on foot (native Slavic cousin of Latin ped-)

педикюр.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th or early 20th century from French pédicure ('care of the feet and toenails', coined from Latin pēs, genitive pedis 'foot' + cūra 'care').

пекарня.etymology: Built in Russian from пекарь 'baker' + the place suffix -ня, from the Slavic verb печь 'to bake, roast'.
пекарня.notes: Genitive plural inserts a fleeting е: пекарен.

пекарь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пекарь (and reinforced by Polish piekarz), formed from the verbal root of печь ('to bake', stem пек-, Proto-Slavic *pekti) with the agent suffix -арь (from Proto-Slavic *-arь, an early borrowing from Latin -ārius).

пельмень.etymology: Borrowed via Ural regional Russian from Komi and Udmurt пельнянь (pel'n'an'), a Permic compound of pel' ('ear', describing the folded ear-like shape of the dumpling) + n'an' ('bread, dough') — literally 'ear-bread'.
пельмень.notes: Almost always used in the plural пельмени when referring to the dish; the singular пельмень denotes a single dumpling.

пемзочка.etymology: Diminutive formed from пемза ('pumice', borrowed via Polish pemza / German Bims, Middle High German bümez, from Late Latin pūmicem, from Latin pūmex 'pumice stone') + diminutive suffix -очка.

пена.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пѣна, from Proto-Slavic *pěna ('foam, froth'), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)poymneh₂ (cognate with Latin spūma, Sanskrit phéna, Old English fām 'foam').

пенальти.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century as a football term from English penalty (short for penalty kick, from Middle French pénalité, from Medieval Latin poenālitās, from Latin poena 'punishment, penalty').

пение.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic пѣние ('singing, vocal music'), verbal noun derived from пѣти ('to sing', Proto-Slavic *pěti).

пенсионер.etymology: Borrowed from French pensionnaire or German Pensionär ('recipient of a pension'), derived from pension (from Latin pēnsiō 'payment, weight').

пенсионерка.etymology: Feminine noun in -ка formed from пенсионер ('pensioner'), borrowed from French pensionnaire or German Pensionär (from Latin pēnsiō 'payment, allowance').

пенсия.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish pensja and German Pension from Latin pēnsiō ('payment, installment, allowance'), derived from pendere ('to weigh out silver, pay').
пенсия.notes: In Russian на пенсии means 'retired' (literally 'on a pension'), and выйти на пенсию means 'to retire'.

первый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пьрвыи ('first'), from Proto-Slavic *pьrvъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *pŕ̥h₂wos ('foremost, first', built on *per- 'forward, in front'), directly cognate with Sanskrit pūrva ('first, former'), Lithuanian pìrmas, and English first / fore.

перебегать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('across, over', from Proto-Slavic *per-) + бегать ('to run', from Old East Slavic бѣгати, Proto-Slavic *běgati).

перебивать.etymology: Imperfective of перебить ('to break across, interrupt'), formed with prefix пере- ('across, through') + бивать, iterative of бить ('to beat, strike', from Proto-Slavic *biti).

перебирать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('over, through one by one') + -бирать (iterative stem of брать 'to take', from Proto-Slavic *birati).

history.meaning: to sort through, take one by one

перебить.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('across, over') from бить ('to beat, strike'), inherited from Old East Slavic бити, from Proto-Slavic *biti.

перебор.etymology: Deverbal noun from перебрать / перебирать ('to take too much, exceed the limit, sort through'), from пере- ('over, excess') + брать ('to take', Proto-Slavic *bьrati).

переборщить.etymology: Colloquial perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('excessively, over-') + борщить (denominal verb from борщ 'borscht, beet soup'), originally meaning 'to pour too much borscht or overdo the ingredients in borscht' (blended in folk feel with перебор 'excess').

перебрать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('through one by one; in excess') + брать ('to take', from Old East Slavic брати, Proto-Slavic *bьrati).

history.meaning: to sort through; to take or drink too much

перевезти.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('across, over') from везти ('to convey by vehicle, transport'), inherited from Old East Slavic везти, from Proto-Slavic *vezti.

history.meaning: to transport, carry in a vehicle

перевернуть.etymology: Formed in Russian from пере- ('over, from one side to the other') + вернуть ('to turn', Proto-Slavic *vьrnǫti, related to вертеть 'to turn, spin'): 'to turn over, flip upside down or to the other side'.

перевернуться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('over') + вернуть ('to turn', from Old East Slavic вьрнути, Proto-Slavic *vьrnǫti) + reflexive particle -ся.

перевести.etymology: Formed from пере- ('across, from one side or language to another') + вести ('to lead', Proto-Slavic *vesti): 'to lead across (a street), transfer, translate (from one language to another), or catch one's breath (перевести дух)'.

history.meaning: to translate; to transfer; to lead across

перевести.notes: Notice how перевести ('to lead across -> translate') exactly parallels Latin trādūcere (trans 'across' + dūcere 'to lead' -> French traduire 'to translate').

перевод.etymology: Deverbal noun formed by zero-suffixation from переводить / перевести ('to lead across, transfer; to translate', from prefix пере- + водить / вести, Proto-Slavic *pervodъ); the sense 'translation' calques Latin trāductiō / French traduction.

переводить.etymology: Imperfective of перевести ('to lead across, transfer; to translate'), formed from пере- ('across') + водить ('to lead', from Proto-Slavic *voditi); the sense 'to translate' is a calque on Latin trānsferre / trādūcere.

history.meaning: to transfer, to move; to translate

переводчик.etymology: Agent noun formed from переводить ('to transfer; to translate', from prefix пере- + водить 'to lead', Proto-Slavic *voditi) + agent suffix -чик.

перевозить.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('across, over') + возить ('to convey, transport by vehicle', iterative of везти, from Proto-Slavic *voziti).

перевозка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from перевозить ('to transport across', from пере- + возить, Proto-Slavic *voziti) + nominal suffix -ка.

переворачиваться.etymology: Reflexive imperfective verb formed from переворачивать ('to turn over', secondary imperfective of переворотить, from prefix пере- + воротить 'to turn', Proto-Slavic *vortiti) + reflexive particle -ся.

переворот.etymology: Deverbal noun from переворотить ('to turn upside down, overturn'), formed from пере- ('over') + воротить ('to turn', East Slavic pleophonic form of Proto-Slavic *vortiti).

перевязать.etymology: Formed with the prefix пере- ('across, around, anew') + вязать ('to tie, bind'), from Old East Slavic вязати and Proto-Slavic *vęzati ('to tie, bind').

history.meaning: to tie up, bind across with string; to bandage

перевязочная.etymology: Substantivized feminine adjective from перевязочный ('bandaging, dressing'), derived from перевязка ('bandaging') / перевязать ('to bandage, bind around'), from пере- + вязать ('to tie, bind', Proto-Slavic *vęzati).

history.meaning: dressing room (in a clinic or hospital)

перегар.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with o-grade root vocalism (-гар) from перегореть / перегорать ('to burn through, distil completely', from prefix пере- + гореть 'to burn', Proto-Slavic *gorěti); originally a distilling term for spirits burned off in moonshine production, later applied to stale alcohol breath.

перегибать.etymology: Imperfective of перегнуть ('to bend over, bend too far'), formed with prefix пере- ('over, too much') from сгибать / гнуть ('to bend'), from Proto-Slavic *gъbnǫti ('to bend').

history.meaning: to overdo it (перегибать палку = to go too far)

переговаривать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('back and forth, over') + говаривать (frequentative of говорить 'to speak, talk', from Proto-Slavic *govoriti).

переговорить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('over, mutually') + говорить ('to speak, talk', from Old East Slavic говорити, Proto-Slavic *govoriti).

переговорщик.etymology: Agent noun formed from переговоры ('negotiations, talks', from переговорить 'to confer, discuss') + agent suffix -щик.

переговоры.etymology: Plural deverbal noun formed from переговорить / переговариваться ('to talk back and forth, confer', from prefix пере- + говорить 'to speak', Proto-Slavic *govoriti).

history.meaning: to talk back and forth, confer

перед.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic передъ ('front; in front of'), showing regular East Slavic pleophony -ере- beside Old Church Slavonic прѣдъ, from Proto-Slavic *perdъ ('front, forepart'), related to *per- ('forward, through') and cognate with Lithuanianankstis / pir̃mas ('first, foremost').
перед.notes: Takes the instrumental case (*перед домом* 'in front of the house', *перед работой* 'just before work'). Expands to **передо** before clusters like *мной* (*передо мной*).

передавать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the prefix пере- ('across, from one to another') + давать ('to give', iterative of дать, from Proto-Slavic *davati).

history.meaning: to hand over, pass along, transmit

передать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic передати ('to hand over, pass across, transmit'), formed from the native East Slavic prefix пере- ('across, over', Proto-Slavic *per-) + дать ('to give', Proto-Slavic *dati). Used both physically ('pass the salt, hand over a key') and communicatively ('pass on a message, send regards: передать привет').

history.meaning: to pass on, hand over, convey (perfective)

morphemes.meaning: across, over from one to another

передача.etymology: Derived with suffix -ча from передать ('to hand over, transmit, broadcast'), formed from пере- ('across, over') + дать ('to give', from Proto-Slavic *dati).

передвинуть.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('across, to another place') + двинуть ('to move', semelfactive of двигать, from Proto-Slavic *dvignǫti).

history.meaning: to move, shift to another place

переделать.etymology: Formed in Russian from пере- ('over again, anew, differently') + делать ('to do, make'): 'to redo, remake, remodel, or convert'.

переделка.etymology: Derived in Russian from переделать ('to redo, remodel, alter') with the action/result noun suffix -ка.

переделывать.etymology: Secondary imperfective verb formed from переделать ('to redo, alter', from prefix пере- 'over, anew' + делать 'to do, make', Proto-Slavic *dělati) + imperfective suffix -ывать.

передержанный.etymology: Past passive participial adjective formed from передержать ('to hold or keep too long, overcook', from prefix пере- 'excessively' + держать 'to hold, keep', Proto-Slavic *dьržati).

передержать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('too long, excessively') + держать ('to hold, keep', from Old East Slavic дьржати, Proto-Slavic *dьržati).

history.meaning: to overcook, keep (on the heat) too long

передерживать.etymology: Secondary imperfective verb formed from передержать ('to keep too long, overcook', from prefix пере- + держать, Proto-Slavic *dьržati) + imperfective suffix -ивать.

передний.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic передьнии, showing native East Slavic pleophony (-ере-) from Proto-Slavic *perdьnьjь ('situated in front'), derived from перед ('front; before') with the soft positional suffix -ний.

передумать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix пере- (indicating redoing or altering a previous state) and думать ('to think', from Old East Slavic думати, Proto-Slavic *dumati). Literally, 'to think over again in a different way', i.e., 'to change one's mind'.

переедание.etymology: Verbal noun formed from переедать ('to overeat', from prefix пере- 'excessively' + едать, iterative of есть 'to eat', Proto-Slavic *ěsti) + abstract suffix -ние.

переезд.etymology: Formed as a prefixal-stem noun from переехать ('to move, travel across, relocate', from пере- 'across, to a new place' + ехать / ездить 'to ride, drive'): both 'moving house, relocation' and 'a railway level crossing'.

переезжать.etymology: Imperfective of переехать ('to cross by vehicle, move residence'), formed with prefix пере- ('across, over') from езжать / ездить ('to ride, travel', from Proto-Slavic *ězditi).

history.meaning: to move (house), to relocate; to cross

переехать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix пере- ('across, from one place to another') and ехать ('to go by vehicle, travel', from Old East Slavic ѣхати, Proto-Slavic *ěxati). Means 'to cross by vehicle, run over' or 'to move to a new home, apartment, or city'.

history.meaning: to ride across, move to another place

morphemes.meaning: across, from one place to another

пережарить.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('over, excessively') from жарить ('to fry, roast'), derived from жар ('heat, embers'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *žarъ ('glowing heat').

переживать.etymology: Imperfective of пережить, formed from пере- ('through, across, over') + живать (iterative of жить 'to live'): originally 'to live through an experience or hardship', from which modern Russian developed the everyday intransitive meaning 'to worry, fret, take things to heart'.

history.meaning: to live through, experience deeply → to worry, fret

переживать.notes: *Не переживай!* is one of the warmest and most common Russian ways to say 'Don't worry!'

пережить.etymology: Formed from the prefix пере- ('through, across, beyond') + жить ('to live', Proto-Slavic *žiti): literally 'to live all the way through a trial or beyond someone else', hence 'to survive, endure, outlive'.

перезагрузить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('again, anew') + загрузить ('to load; in computing, to boot', from за- + грузить 'to load', from груз 'cargo'); used in computing as a calque of English reboot / reload.

перезванивать.etymology: Secondary imperfective verb formed from перезвонить ('to ring again, call back by phone', from prefix пере- + звонить 'to ring', from звон 'peal', Proto-Slavic *zvoniti) + suffix -ивать.

перезвонить.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('again, back') from звонить ('to ring, call by telephone'), derived from звон ('ringing, peal'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *zvonъ ('sound, ringing').

перейти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic переити (Proto-Slavic *perjьti 'to walk across'), formed from пере- ('across, over to') + идти ('to walk, go'): 'to cross (a street or bridge)' or 'to switch over to'.
перейти.notes: Future tense: я перейду, ты перейдёшь; past tense: перешёл, перешла.

переключатель.etymology: Instrumental agent noun formed with suffix -тель from переключать ('to switch over'), which combines prefix пере- ('across, from one position to another') with the root of ключ ('key, latch, switch', Proto-Slavic *ključь, from PIE *klew- 'hook, bolt, key', cognate with Latin clavis and English close). Literally 'that which switches from one setting to another', it denotes an oven dial or electrical switch.

history.meaning: to switch over → switch, selector dial

morphemes.meaning: across, from one setting to another

переключить.etymology: Perfective verb formed by prefix substitution with пере- ('over, to another setting') after включить ('to switch on, include', derived from ключ 'key, switch', Proto-Slavic *kľučь).

переключиться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of переключить ('to switch over'), formed with prefix пере- from включить / ключ ('key, switch'), from Proto-Slavic *kľučь ('hook, key, bolt').

history.meaning: to switch over, to shift focus

переколотить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with distributive/exhaustive prefix пере- ('all one after another') + колотить ('to beat, pound, smash', from Old East Slavic колотити, Proto-Slavic *koltiti, causative/iterative of *kolti 'to split, strike').

перекормить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('excessively, over-') + кормить ('to feed', from Old East Slavic кърмити, Proto-Slavic *kъrmiti, from *kъrmъ 'food, fodder').

перекрасить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('again, in a different color') + красить ('to paint, dye', originally 'to adorn', from краса 'beauty, color', Proto-Slavic *krasiti).

перекрыть.etymology: Formed from пере- ('across, blocking') + крыть ('to cover', Proto-Slavic *kryti): 'to cover over completely, roof over' and hence 'to dam, block off, or shut off (water, gas, or a road)'.

history.meaning: to shut off (water, gas), block, roof over

перекрыть.notes: Conjugates like крыть: я перекрою, ты перекроешь ('I will shut off').

перекупить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('over, outbidding another') + купить ('to buy', from Old East Slavic купити, Proto-Slavic *kupiti).

history.meaning: to buy up; to lure away by paying more

перекур.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Russian from перекурить ('to take a break for a smoke'), built from the prefix пере- ('between, during a pause') + курить ('to smoke', originally 'to make smoke, burn incense', Proto-Slavic *kuriti).

history.meaning: to pause for a smoke → smoke break, short work break

перекурить.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('in an interval, briefly') from курить ('to smoke'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *kuriti ('to make smoke, kindle').

history.meaning: to smoke, have a smoke break

перекус.etymology: Deverbal noun formed by zero-suffixation from перекусить ('to bite in two; colloquially to grab a quick bite to eat'), from prefix пере- + кусать ('to bite', Proto-Slavic *kǫsati).

history.meaning: to bite through; to have a quick bite

перекусить.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('across; briefly in between') from кусить ('to bite'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *kǫsiti ('to bite, taste a piece').

history.meaning: to bite through; to have a bite to eat, grab a snack

переложить.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('across, from one place to another') from ложить ('to lay, put'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *ložiti ('to lay, place').

перелом.etymology: Deverbal noun formed by zero-suffixation from переломить ('to break in two, fracture'), from prefix пере- ('across, in two') + ломить ('to break', Proto-Slavic *lomiti).

переломать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with distributive prefix пере- ('many or all things') + ломать ('to break', from Proto-Slavic *lamati, iterative of *lomiti).

переманить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('over to one's side') + манить ('to beckon, lure, entice', from Old East Slavic манити, Proto-Slavic *maniti).

перемена.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic перемѣна ('change, alternation, replacement'), formed from prefix пере- + мена ('exchange, change', Proto-Slavic *měna, PIE *mey- 'to exchange').

перемешивать.etymology: Imperfective of перемешать ('to mix thoroughly, stir up'), formed with prefix пере- from мешать ('to mix, stir'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *měšati ('to mix, knead').

перемирие.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic перемирие ('truce, temporary peace'), formed from prefix пере- ('across an interval') + мир ('peace', Proto-Slavic *mirъ) + suffix -ие.

перенервничать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('excessively') + нервничать ('to be nervous, fret', from нервный 'nervous', derived from нерв 'nerve', borrowed via German Nerv / French nerf from Latin nervus).

history.meaning: to get overly nervous, get worked up

перенести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic перенести (Proto-Slavic *pernesti), formed from пере- ('across, to another place or time') + нести ('to carry', Proto-Slavic *nesti): 'to carry across, move, or reschedule/postpone to another date'.

history.meaning: to move, carry over; to reschedule; to endure

переносить.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('across, over; through') + носить ('to carry', iterative of нести, from Old East Slavic носити, Proto-Slavic *nositi).

history.meaning: to move, carry over; to postpone; to bear

переночевать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('through the duration of') + ночевать ('to spend the night', derived from ночь 'night', Old East Slavic ночь, Proto-Slavic *nočь).

history.meaning: to spend the night, stay overnight

переодеваться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive verb formed from пере- ('re-, anew, changing from one to another') + одеваться ('to dress oneself'), built on одевать / одеть ('to clothe', from о- 'around' + деть 'to put, place', Proto-Slavic *děti).

переодеться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of переодеть ('to change clothes'), formed with prefix пере- ('anew, differently') from одеть ('to dress'), from Proto-Slavic *ob-děti.

перепарковать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('to another spot, anew') + парковать ('to park a vehicle', borrowed from English park).

перепел.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic перепелъ, from Proto-Slavic *perpelъ ('quail'), a reduplicated onomatopoeic formation imitating the bird's call or fluttering wings (compare *pьrpati).

перепелиный.etymology: Relational and possessive adjective formed from перепел ('quail', Old East Slavic перепелъ, from Proto-Slavic *perpelъ, an onomatopoeic reduplication imitating the bird's call) + animal-adjective suffix -иный.

переперчить.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('excessively, too much') from перчить ('to pepper'), derived from перец ('pepper'), from Old East Slavic пьпьрь (via Greek πέπερι from Sanskrit pippalī).

history.meaning: to over-pepper, put too much pepper

переписать.etymology: Formed with the prefix пере- ('over again, anew, from one sheet to another') + писать ('to write', from Old East Slavic писати and Proto-Slavic *pьsati).

переписка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from переписываться / переписать ('to exchange letters, correspond; to copy out', from prefix пере- + писать 'to write', Proto-Slavic *pьsati) + nominal suffix -ка.

history.meaning: to correspond by letter or message

переписывать.etymology: Secondary imperfective verb formed from переписать ('to rewrite, copy out', from prefix пере- + писать 'to write', Proto-Slavic *pьsati) + imperfective suffix -ывать.

переписываться.etymology: Reciprocal-reflexive verb formed from переписывать ('to write back and forth', from пере- + писать, Proto-Slavic *pьsati) + reflexive particle -ся.

history.meaning: to correspond, write to each other

переплёт.etymology: Deverbal noun from переплести ('to interweave, bind a book by sewing and lacing the gatherings onto cords'), formed from prefix пере- ('across, together') + плести ('to plait, weave, braid', from Proto-Slavic *plesti).

history.meaning: to lace and bind book pages → bookbinding, hard cover

перепутанный.etymology: Formed as the past passive participle and adjective of перепутать ('to tangle up, mix up, confuse'), built from пере- + путать ('to tangle, fetter, confuse', derived from путо 'hobble, tether, fetter', Proto-Slavic *pǫto).

перепутать.etymology: Formed with perfective prefix пере- from путать ('to tangle, confuse'), derived from путо ('fetters, hobble, cord'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *pǫto ('bond, fetter').

перепутье.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic перепутие ('crossroads, fork in a road'), formed from prefix пере- ('across') + путь ('way, road', Proto-Slavic *pǫtь) + neuter suffix -ье (*-ьje).

перепёлка.etymology: Feminine noun formed from перепел ('quail', Old East Slavic перепелъ, Proto-Slavic *perpelъ, an onomatopoeic reduplicated formation imitating the bird's call) + suffix -ка.

перерабатывать.etymology: Secondary imperfective verb formed from переработать ('to process, rework; to work overtime', from prefix пере- + работать 'to work', Proto-Slavic *orbota) + suffix -ывать.

перерезать.etymology: Verb formed with prefix пере- ('across, in two') + резать ('to cut', from Old East Slavic рѣзати, Proto-Slavic *rězati).

переругаться.etymology: Reciprocal perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('with one another, all around') + ругать ('to scold, abuse', Old East Slavic ругати, Proto-Slavic *rǫgati) + reflexive particle -ся.

history.meaning: to quarrel, fall out with each other

перерыв.etymology: Deverbal noun from перервать / перерывать ('to tear across, interrupt, pause'), formed from пере- ('across') + рвать ('to tear', Proto-Slavic *rъvati).

переселить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('across, to a new place') + селить ('to settle, house', derived from село 'settlement, village', Proto-Slavic *selo).

переселиться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed from переселить ('to relocate, resettle', from пере- + селить, Proto-Slavic *seliti) + reflexive particle -ся.

переселять.etymology: Imperfective verb formed from переселить ('to relocate, resettle', from пере- + селить, Proto-Slavic *seliti) + imperfective suffix -ять.

пересмотр.etymology: Deverbal noun from пересмотреть ('to look over again, review, revise'), formed from пере- ('anew') + смотреть ('to look, examine', Proto-Slavic *sъmotriti).

переснять.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('again, anew') + снять ('to take off; to photograph or film', from Old East Slavic съняти, Proto-Slavic *sъnęti).

пересоленный.etymology: Past passive participial adjective formed from пересолить ('to oversalt', from prefix пере- 'excessively' + солить 'to salt', derived from соль 'salt', Proto-Slavic *solь).

history.meaning: to put too much salt in

пересолить.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('excessively, too much') from солить ('to salt'), derived from соль ('salt'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *solь ('salt').

history.meaning: oversalt, put too much salt in

пересохнуть.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('completely, excessively') + сохнуть ('to dry, become dry', from Proto-Slavic *sъxnǫti, related to сухой 'dry', *suxъ).

переспать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('through the night; together') + спать ('to sleep', from Old East Slavic съпати, Proto-Slavic *sъpati).

history.meaning: to sleep overnight; to sleep with (someone)

переставать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with prefix пере- + ставать (imperfective of стать 'to stand, become, stop', from Old East Slavic переставати, Proto-Slavic *perstavati).

переставить.etymology: Formed with the prefix пере- ('across, to another place, anew') + ставить ('to put, set, stand', from Proto-Slavic *staviti).

history.meaning: to move, shift to another spot, rearrange

переставлять.etymology: Imperfective of переставить ('to move to another place, rearrange'), formed from пере- ('across, over') + ставить ('to place, set upright', from Proto-Slavic *staviti).

перестановка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from переставить / переставлять ('to move to another place, rearrange', from prefix пере- + ставить 'to place, set', Proto-Slavic *staviti) + nominal suffix -ка.

перестараться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('excessively, too much') + стараться ('to try hard, endeavor', from Proto-Slavic *starati sę).

history.meaning: to overdo it, try too hard

перестать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic перестати ('to stop, cease'), formed from the prefix пере- ('across, over, through') and стать ('to stand, come to a halt', from Proto-Slavic *stati).

history.meaning: to come to a stop, cease

перестирать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('all one after another; or again') + стирать ('to wash laundry', originally 'to rub off', from Proto-Slavic *sъtirati).

пересчитать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with prefix пере- ('again; one by one') + считать ('to count', from Old East Slavic съчитати, Proto-Slavic *sъčitati).

пересчитывать.etymology: Secondary imperfective verb formed from пересчитать ('to recount, count all', from пере- + считать) + imperfective suffix -ывать.

переть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic перети (пьру, 'to press, push, prop'), from Proto-Slavic *perti ('to press, push, carry forcefully'), from Proto-Indo-European *per-.

переулок.etymology: Formed in East Slavic from пере- ('across, connecting between') + улка / улица ('street', originally 'narrow passage, opening'): a short side street or lane running across between two main streets.
переулок.notes: Drops the fleeting -о- in all oblique forms: переулок -> в переулке ('in the side street').

перехватить.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('across, intercepting') from хватить ('to seize, grab'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *xvatiti ('to snatch, grasp').

history.meaning: to intercept, to grab, to take over

переход.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic переходъ (Proto-Slavic *perxodъ), a prefixal-stem noun derived from переходить / перейти ('to walk across, pass over', from пере- 'across' + ход 'going, walk').

переходить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic переходити (Proto-Slavic *perxoditi), formed from пере- ('across, over') + ходить ('to walk, go'): the imperfective of перейти ('to cross a street; to move on or switch to').

перец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic перьць ('pepper'), formed with the Slavic noun suffix *-ьcь from early Slavic *pьpьrь, borrowed via Latin piper or Byzantine Greek πέπερι (péperi) ultimately from Sanskrit पिप्पली (pippalī, 'long pepper').

history.meaning: pepper (spice or bell/chili pepper); (slang) guy, fellow

перечеркнуть.etymology: Perfective semelfactive verb formed with prefix пере- ('across') + черкнуть ('to draw a line, stroke', from черта / черкать 'line, stroke', Proto-Slavic *čьrtati / *čьrkati).

перечить.etymology: Derived from перек / поперёк ('across, athwart'), inherited from Old East Slavic перекы ('across, against'), from Proto-Slavic *perkъ ('transverse, contrary', compare Old Church Slavonic прѣкъ).

перила.etymology: Plural-only derivative built on the Slavic root of переть / опереться ('to press, lean, support oneself') with the instrument suffix -ило: literally 'the bars one leans on for support' along stairs or a bridge.
перила.notes: Always plural in modern standard Russian: держаться за перила ('to hold on to the railing').

период.etymology: Borrowed via French période / German Periode (and earlier via Church Slavonic) from Latin periodus, from Ancient Greek περίοδος ('going around, circuit, cycle of time', from περί 'around' + ὁδός 'way').

перо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic перо ('feather, wing, quill'), from Proto-Slavic *pero, built on the Proto-Indo-European root *per- / *pet- ('to fly, wing'; cognate with Ancient Greek πτερόν 'feather, wing' and English feather). Because goose quills were for centuries the standard writing instrument, перо also came to mean a metal pen nib.

персона.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish persona and German Person from Latin persōna ('actor's mask, character in a play, personage, human being', likely from Etruscan phersu 'mask').

персонаж.etymology: Borrowed from French personnage ('character in a play or novel, personage'), derived from personne ('person'), from Latin persōna ('actor's mask, character, person').

персонал.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from German Personal ('staff, body of employees'; compare French personnel), substantivized from Late Latin persōnālis ('pertaining to persons'), from Latin persōna ('person, character, mask').

персонально.etymology: Adverb formed from персональный ('personal, individual', borrowed via Polish personalny / French personnel from Late Latin persōnālis, from Latin persōna 'person') + adverbial suffix -о.

перспектива.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Perspektive and French perspective from Medieval Latin perspectīva (ars) ('the science of optics and visual perspective'), from Latin perspicere ('to look through, see clearly', from per- 'through' + specere 'to look').

перспективный.etymology: Adjective formed with -ный from перспектива ('perspective, future prospect'), borrowed via French perspective / German Perspektive from Medieval Latin perspectiva (ars) ('optical science, view through'), from Latin perspicere ('to look through').

перстень.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пьрстьнь ('finger ring set with a gem'), from Proto-Slavic *pьrstьnь, derived from *pьrstъ ('finger', Old East Slavic пьрстъ).

перчатка.etymology: Inherited from Old Russian персчатка / перщатка ('glove with separate fingers', as opposed to рукавица 'mitten'), derived from перст ('finger'), from Proto-Slavic *pьrstъ ('finger').

перьевой.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -евой from the collective/plural stem перья ('feathers, nibs', singular перо, from Proto-Slavic *pero 'feather'). Used especially in перьевая ручка ('fountain pen, nib pen').

history.meaning: feather, nib → feather, nib (перьевая ручка 'fountain pen')

песня.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пѣснь / пѣсня and Proto-Slavic *pěsnь ('song'), formed with the archaic Slavic action-noun suffix *-snь from the verbal root of петь ('to sing', Proto-Slavic *pěti).
песня.notes: Genitive plural inserts a fleeting е: много песен ('many songs').

песок.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пѣсъкъ and Proto-Slavic *pěsъkъ 'sand', related to Indo-European words for crushed grit and dust (compare Sanskrit pamsu 'crumbling soil, sand').
песок.notes: Drops the fleeting vowel -о- in all oblique forms: песок -> песка, на песке.

петербург.etymology: Everyday shortened form of Санкт-Петербург (Saint Petersburg), founded by Tsar Peter the Great in May 1703 and named in Dutch/German style (Sankt-Pieterburch / Sankt-Petersburg) after his patron saint, the Apostle Peter (from Greek Πέτρος 'rock, stone') + Germanic -burg ('fortress, city').

петля.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic петля ('noose, loop, snare, buttonhole') and Proto-Slavic *pętlja, generally connected by Vasmer and Trubachev with the nasal root *pęti ('to stretch, pull taut, fasten', compare распять and путо), or with early Germanic *fatilaz ('strap, band'). From a cord loop it extended to a metal door hinge.

history.meaning: loop, buttonhole; door or cabinet hinge

петля.notes: Genitive plural inserts a fleeting е: дверных петель ('of door hinges').

петрушка.etymology: Borrowed via Polish pietruszka (adapted from Czech petrzel and Middle High German petersilje), ultimately from Latin petroselinum and Ancient Greek petroselinon, literally 'rock celery' (petra 'rock' + selinon 'celery'). Reshaped in Russian to match familiar -ушка nouns.

петух.etymology: Formed in East Slavic from the stem of петь ('to sing, crow', Old East Slavic пѣти, Proto-Slavic *pěti) + expressive agent suffix -ух (displacing older пѣтель 'rooster'), literally 'the singer / crower'.

петь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пѣти and Proto-Slavic *pěti (present tense *pojǫ 'I sing'), originally meaning 'to celebrate in song, chant, praise'.

morphemes.meaning: sing (alternating with поj- in present tense)

cognates.meaning: to crow (of a rooster; archaic 'to sing')

петь.notes: Present tense uses the o-grade stem поj-: я пою, ты поёшь, они поют.

печаль.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic печаль ('sorrow, grief, care, affliction'), from Proto-Slavic *pečalь ('burning grief, care'), derived from *pekti ('to burn, bake, torment').

печально.etymology: Adverb and predicative short neuter form of печальный ('sad, sorrowful', from печаль 'sorrow, grief', Proto-Slavic *pečalь).

печальный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic печальныи ('sorrowful, grieving'), formed from печаль ('sorrow, grief', Proto-Slavic *pečalь) + adjectival suffix -ный.

печатать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic печатати ('to seal, stamp with a signet; later to print type'), derived from печать ('seal, stamp, brand', Proto-Slavic *pečatь, originally 'branding iron', from *pekti 'to burn, bake').

печатный.etymology: Derived in Russian from печать ('seal, stamp; printing press, print', Proto-Slavic *pečatь) with the adjectival suffix -ный: 'printed (as opposed to handwritten), press'.
печатный.notes: Used in писать печатными буквами ('to write in block / printed letters').

печать.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pečatь, originally meaning a heated branding iron used to stamp livestock or wax, derived from the same root as печь 'to bake, burn, scorch'. From 'brand, seal' it expanded to 'printing press' and 'print'.

печень.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic печень ('liver'), from Proto-Slavic *pečenь ('liver', originally 'that which is roasted for food', derived from *pekti 'to roast, bake', Russian печь; compare Lithuanian kepenys 'liver' from kepti 'to bake').

печенье.etymology: Formed as a verbal noun in -енье from печь ('to bake', passive participle печёный 'baked', Proto-Slavic *pekti): originally 'the act of baking' or 'baked goods', which specialized to 'biscuits, cookies, small pastries'.
печенье.notes: Usually used as an uncountable collective singular in Russian: домашнее печенье ('homemade cookies').

печенька.etymology: Colloquial singulative and diminutive noun formed from печенье ('cookies, biscuits, baked pastry', derived from печь 'to bake', Proto-Slavic *pekti) + diminutive suffix -ка.

печка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of печь ('stove, oven'), inherited from Old East Slavic печь, from Proto-Slavic *pečь ('oven, stove, cave'), derived from *pekti ('to bake, roast').

печь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic печь, where both the feminine noun печь ('oven, masonry stove', from Proto-Slavic *pektь) and the verb печь ('to bake', from *pekti) continue Proto-Indo-European *pekʷ- ('to cook, bake', cognate with Latin coquō).

печься.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic печися and Old Church Slavonic пещи сѧ ('to be baked; figuratively to burn with care or concern for someone'), reflexive of печь ('to bake, scorch', Proto-Slavic *pekti, PIE *pekʷ-).

history.meaning: to bake; to trouble oneself, care for
to care about, worry; to bake
to care about, look after; to bake

печёночный.etymology: Adjective formed with -ный from печёнка / печень ('liver'), inherited from Old East Slavic печень, from Proto-Slavic *pečenь ('liver', originally 'that which is roasted', from *pekti 'to roast').

печёный.etymology: Participial adjective inherited from Old East Slavic печеныи ('baked, roasted'), from Proto-Slavic *pečenъ, past passive participle of *pekti ('to bake, roast').

пешком.etymology: Fossilized instrumental singular of an old noun/adjective пешок (diminutive of пеший 'on foot, pedestrian'), from Proto-Slavic *pěšь ('going on foot'), derived with *-x- from the Proto-Indo-European root *ped- ('foot'; compare Latin pēs, pedis and English pedal).

пещера.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пещера ('cave, cavern', showing South Slavic щ from *ktj; compare native East Slavic печера), from Proto-Slavic *pektjera, derived from *pektь ('oven, hollow rock', from *pekti 'to bake').

пианино.etymology: Borrowed from Italian pianino, a diminutive of piano with the suffix -ino, so literally 'a little piano'. Russian uses it for the upright piano found in homes; the grand piano is рояль. Like other borrowed nouns in -о, it never changes its ending.
пианино.notes: Indeclinable: играть на пианино, у пианино, с пианино.

пианист.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French pianiste ('pianist'), derived from piano (shortened from Italian pianoforte 'soft-loud').

пианистка.etymology: Feminine agent noun formed in Russian from пианист ('pianist', from French pianiste) + feminine suffix -ка.

пиар.etymology: Borrowed in the 1990s from the English initialism PR (/piːˈɑːr/), standing for public relations (from Latin pūblicus 'public' + relātiō 'relation, report').

пивко.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed from пиво ('beer', originally 'any beverage or drink', from Proto-Slavic *pivo, derived from *piti 'to drink') + neuter diminutive suffix -ко.

пивник.etymology: Colloquial noun formed from пивной ('beer [adj.]', from пиво 'beer', Proto-Slavic *pivo) + suffix -ник (denoting a beer hall/pub or a beer drinker/brewer).

пивной.etymology: Relational adjective formed from пиво ('beer', from Old East Slavic пиво, Proto-Slavic *pivo, from *piti 'to drink') + adjectival suffix -ной.

пиво.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пиво ('drink, beverage; beer, ale'), from Proto-Slavic *pivo, formed from *piti ('to drink', Russian пить) with the neuter noun suffix *-vo. Originally meaning any 'drink, potion', across most Slavic languages *pivo specialized to mean 'beer'.

пиджак.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from English pea jacket (originally a sailor's heavy short coat, itself from Dutch pijjekker 'coat of coarse wool'). In Russian the word shifted to mean an ordinary suit jacket or blazer.

пик.etymology: Borrowed via French pic ('mountain peak, sharp point') or English peak, ultimately from a Western Romance/Pre-Roman expressive root *pīkk- ('sharp point, pike').

пикник.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French pique-nique (or via English picnic, itself from French), a late 17th-century French rhyming compound of piquer ('to pick, peck at food') + nique ('trifle, small thing').

history.meaning: social meal where each guest contributes or dines outdoors

пилить.etymology: Denominal verb formed from пила ('saw', from Old East Slavic пила, Proto-Slavic *pila, an early borrowing from Proto-Germanic *fīlō 'file, saw'); the figurative sense 'to nag' likens incessant scolding to monotonous sawing.

пилот.etymology: Borrowed via French pilote and German Pilot from Italian pilota ('helmsman, steersman'), altered from Old Italian pedota, from Medieval Greek *πηδώτης ('rudder-man', from Ancient Greek πηδόν 'oar blade, helm').

пилюля.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via Polish pilula and German Pillule from Latin pilula ('little ball, globule, medicinal pill', diminutive of pila 'ball').

пинать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пинати ('to kick, push, spur'), from Proto-Slavic *pinati, iterative of *pęti ('to stretch, strike, kick', PIE *(s)pen-).

пинаться.etymology: Reflexive imperfective verb formed from пинать ('to kick', from Proto-Slavic *pinati) + reflexive particle -ся (denoting habitual or mutual kicking).

history.meaning: to kick (about or at one another)

пинок.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from пинать / пнуть ('to kick', from Proto-Slavic *pinati / *pьnǫti) + singulative suffix -ок.

пинцет.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from French pincette ('small tongs, tweezers'), diminutive of pince ('plier, grip'), from pincer ('to pinch, grip between two points').

пир.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пиръ ('feast, banquet, drinking party'), from Proto-Slavic *pirъ, formed from the root of *piti ('to drink', PIE *peh₃(y)-) + archaic nominal suffix *-rъ.

пирамида.etymology: Borrowed via German Pyramide or Latin pyramis, pyramidis from Ancient Greek πυραμίς (puramís, 'Egyptian pyramid'), itself from Egyptian pꜣ-mr ('the pyramid, tomb') or folk-etymologized in Greek from πυραμίς ('wheat cake').

пират.etymology: Borrowed via German Pirat and French pirate from Latin pīrāta, from Ancient Greek πειρατής ('sea robber, brigand', literally 'attacker, adventurer', from πειράω 'to attempt, assault', from πεῖρα 'trial, attempt').

пирог.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пирогъ, from Proto-Slavic *pirogъ, formed from *pirъ ('feast, banquet', itself derived from пить 'to drink'). Originally пирог named special festive stuffed bread baked for guests at a celebration.

пирожное.etymology: Substantivized neuter singular of the adjective пирожный ('pertaining to pie or pastry'), derived from пирог ('pie, festive baked loaf'), which comes from Old East Slavic пирогъ, derived from пиръ ('feast, banquet', Proto-Slavic *pirъ, related to пить 'to drink').
пирожное.notes: In Russian, торт is a large whole multi-layered cake for sharing, whereas пирожное is a single-serving pastry or cake.

пирожок.etymology: Diminutive formed from пирог ('pie, pasty', from Old East Slavic пирогъ 'festive loaf or filled pie', Proto-Slavic *pirogъ, derived from *pirъ 'feast') + diminutive suffix -ок.

писатель.etymology: Agent noun formed with the suffix -тель from писать ('to write', originally 'to paint, decorate with marks', from Old East Slavic писати, Proto-Slavic *pьsati, from PIE *peys- / *pik- 'to carve, mark, paint').

писать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic писати (present пишу, пишеши; Old Church Slavonic пьсати), from Proto-Slavic *pьsati (originally 'to paint, trace designs, adorn with colour', then 'to write'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *peyk̂- ('to mark, incise, paint'; cognate with Latin pingō / pictūra, whence English picture and paint).

history.meaning: to write (also 'to paint' in писать картину)

писать.notes: In artistic usage, Russian still says **писать картину маслом** ('to paint a picture in oils'), preserving the ancient meaning 'to paint'.

пистолет.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century via German Pistole and French pistolet. Remarkably, the European word goes back to a Slavic source: 15th-century Hussite Czech píšťala ('whistle, flute; early hand-cannon', from Proto-Slavic *piščalь, native Russian пищаль), which passed into German Pitschale / Pistole and French pistolet before returning to Russian.

пистолетик.etymology: Diminutive formed from пистолет ('pistol', borrowed via French pistolet and German Pistole from Czech píšťala 'whistle, pipe, early hand-cannon', from Proto-Slavic *piščalь) + diminutive suffix -ик.

письмо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic письмо, from Proto-Slavic *pisьmo ('writing, inscription, letter'), derived from писать (*pьsati, originally 'to paint, trace designs, write', cognate with Latin pingō 'to paint').

питание.etymology: Verbal noun from питать ('to nourish, feed'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic питати ('to nourish, rear'), from Proto-Slavic *pitati ('to feed, nourish', related to *piťa 'food').

питаться.etymology: Reflexive imperfective verb formed from питать ('to feed, nourish', from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic питати, Proto-Slavic *pitati 'to nourish', PIE *peyt- 'food, fat') + reflexive particle -ся.

питер.etymology: Colloquial clipping of Санкт-Петербург ('Saint Petersburg', founded in 1703 by Peter the Great and originally named Sankt-Piter-Burch after Dutch Sint-Pietersburch 'Saint Peter's fortress', preserving the Dutch vowel -и- of Pieter).

пить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пити, from Proto-Slavic *piti ('to drink'), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃(i)- ('to drink'; compare Ancient Greek πίνω, Sanskrit píbati, and Latin bibō / pōtus).

rootFamily.gloss: to drink up; to have a drink

пицца.etymology: 20th-century borrowing from Italian pizza ('flatbread baked with toppings'), attested in Medieval Latin (997 CE in Gaeta) as pizza, likely from Lombardic bizzo / pizzo ('mouthful, flatbread') or Greek πίττα (pítta, 'pie, cake').

пища.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пища ('food, nourishment', showing South Slavic щ from Proto-Slavic *tj; compare native East Slavic пича), from Proto-Slavic *pitja, derived from *pitati ('to feed, nourish').

пищеварение.etymology: Compound noun coined in the 18th century as a loan translation of Latin dīgestiō / Ancient Greek πέψις ('cooking of food in the stomach'), formed from пища ('food') + -е- + варение ('boiling, cooking', from варить 'to boil, cook', Proto-Slavic *variti).

пищевой.etymology: Adjective in -евой formed from пища ('food, nourishment'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пища (with щ < *tj, compare native East Slavic пича), from Proto-Slavic *pitja ('food, nourishment').

плав.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плавъ ('swimming, floating, navigation'), from Proto-Slavic *plavъ, long o-grade derivative of *pluti ('to float, swim, sail', PIE *plew-); preserved mainly in idioms like на плаву ('afloat').

плавать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плавати, iterative-durative of плыть ('to swim, float, sail'), from Proto-Slavic *plavati (lengthened grade of *pluti, from Proto-Indo-European *plew- 'to flow, float').

плавно.etymology: Adverb formed from плавный ('smooth-flowing, fluid', originally 'floating smoothly on water', derived from плав / плавать 'to float, swim', Proto-Slavic *plavъ) + adverbial suffix -о.

плавочки.etymology: Diminutive plural of плавки ('swimming briefs/trunks'), formed in the 20th century from плавать ('to swim', from Proto-Slavic *plavati).

плакат.etymology: Borrowed from German Plakat ('poster, placard'), from Dutch plakkaat / Middle French placard ('notice posted on a wall'), from plaquer ('to plate, stick flat on').

плакать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плакати and Proto-Slavic *plakati ('to weep, lament; originally to beat one's breast in mourning'), from Proto-Indo-European *plāk- ('to strike flat, beat the chest in grief'), cognate with Latin plangere ('to beat the breast, lament', whence French plaindre and English plaintive) and Lithuanian plakti ('to beat, whip').

history.meaning: to strike, beat the breast in grief

плакать.notes: Present tense shows к -> ч palatalization throughout: я плачу, ты плачешь, они плачут (stress on the first syllable: я плачу 'I cry' vs. я плачу 'I pay').

пламенный.etymology: Adjective formed from пламя (stem пламен-, 'flame'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пламѩ (compare native East Slavic полымя), from Proto-Slavic *polmę ('flame').

пламя.etymology: Adopted with the South Slavic / Church Slavonic liquid metathesis плам- (compare native Old East Slavic поломя) from Proto-Slavic *polmę ('flame, blaze'), an ancient neuter *-men-stem built on the same root as палить ('to burn, scorch') and пепел ('ash').
пламя.notes: Belongs to the small neuter -мя declension (alongside имя, время, семя): genitive/dative/prepositional пламени, instrumental пламенем.

план.etymology: Borrowed in the early eighteenth century via French plan and German Plan ('flat drawing, ground plan, scheme'), where architectural plan ('ground-floor projection') blended Latin plānus ('flat, level surface') with planta ('sole of the foot; footprint of a building').

планетарий.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century via German Planetarium from New Latin planetārium ('device or theater projecting the movements of planets and stars', from Late Latin planēta 'planet', from Ancient Greek πλανήτης 'wanderer').

планировать.etymology: Derived in Russian from план ('plan') with the borrowed verbal suffix -ировать (after German planen / French planifier): 'to draw up a plan, schedule, or design'.
планировать.notes: A homonym планировать ('to glide in the air', from French planer) has fixed stress on -и-, whereas планировать ('to make a plan') is stressed on the same syllable in modern standard Russian.

плановый.etymology: Relational adjective formed from план ('plan, schedule, layout', borrowed in the 18th century via German Plan from French plan 'ground plan, flat projection', from Latin plānus 'flat, level') + adjectival suffix -овый.

плантатор.etymology: Borrowed via German Plantator or Polish plantator from Latin plantātor ('planter, one who plants', from plantāre 'to plant'; historically used for colonial plantation owners).

планшет.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French planchette ('small flat board, surveyor's plane-table'), diminutive of planche ('plank, board', from Late Latin planca). First used in Russian for a cartographer's drawing board or officer's map-case, and in the 21st century adopted (via планшетный компьютер) for a touchscreen tablet.

плата.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плата ('payment, fee') or back-formed from платить ('to pay', Proto-Slavic *platiti, originally 'to pay using pieces of linen cloth *platъ').

платить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic платити ('to pay'), from Proto-Slavic *platiti, a denominative verb built on *platъ ('piece of cloth, linen'). In early medieval Slavic trade, standardized pieces of woven linen cloth served as a medium of exchange and currency (compare Czech platit 'to pay' and plátno 'linen').

history.meaning: piece of linen cloth (used as currency) → to pay

платный.etymology: Adjective formed with -ный from плата ('pay, fee') / платить ('to pay'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *platiti ('to pay').

платок.etymology: Diminutive noun formed from Old East Slavic платъ ('piece of linen cloth, kerchief', from Proto-Slavic *platъ 'piece of cloth') + diminutive suffix -ок.

платформа.etymology: Borrowed from French plateforme ('flat raised surface, railway platform'), a compound of Middle French plate ('flat', feminine of plat) + forme ('form, shape').

платье.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic платие (originally a collective neuter noun meaning 'garments, clothes in general', a sense preserved in верхнее платье 'outerwear' and платяной шкаф 'wardrobe'), derived from платъ ('piece of woven cloth, kerchief', from Proto-Slavic *platъ). Narrowed in modern everyday usage to 'a woman's dress'.

платёж.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic платежь ('payment'), formed from платить ('to pay', Proto-Slavic *platiti, originally 'to pay with pieces of linen cloth *platъ') + nominal suffix -ёж (*-ežь).

плебей.etymology: Borrowed via German Plebejer or Polish plebejusz from Latin plēbēius ('belonging to the common people, plebeian'), derived from plēbs ('the common people of ancient Rome').

плевать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пльвати (present плюю), from Proto-Slavic *pľьvati ('to spit'), an ancient onomatopoeic Indo-European verb (*spjew- / *pjew-; compare Lithuanian spiáuti, Latin spuō, Gothic speiwan, and English spew). In colloquial Russian, мне плевать (на что-то) means 'I couldn't care less, I don't give a spit about it'.

плеваться.etymology: Reflexive imperfective verb formed from плевать ('to spit', from Old East Slavic пльвати / плювати, Proto-Slavic *pľьvati, from onomatopoeic PIE *(s)pyew- 'to spit') + reflexive particle -ся.

history.meaning: to spit (repeatedly); to spit in disgust

плед.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from English plaid ('checkered tartan cloak or travel blanket worn in Scotland', from Scottish Gaelic plaide 'blanket, mantle').

племянник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic племеньникъ ('kinsman, member of the same tribe/clan; nephew'), formed with suffix -ник from племя (stem племен-, 'tribe, clan, family', Proto-Slavic *plemę).

племянница.etymology: Formed with the feminine suffix -ица from племянник ('nephew', in Old East Slavic 'tribesman, kinsman'), derived from племя ('tribe, clan, kinsfolk', Old East Slavic племѧ, Proto-Slavic *plemę).

пленник.etymology: Derived with suffix -ник from плен ('captivity'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плѣнъ ('booty, captivity', compare native East Slavic полон), from Proto-Slavic *pelnъ.

плесень.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плѣснь ('mold, mildew'), from Proto-Slavic *plěsnь ('mold, grey coating', related to *plěšь 'bald or pale patch', from PIE *pel- 'pale, grey').

плескаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of плескать ('to splash, lap, slosh'), inherited from Old East Slavic плескати and Proto-Slavic *pleskati, an onomatopoeic root imitating the sound of slapping water or clapping hands.

history.meaning: to splash → to splash about, lap (of water)

плеснуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective verb corresponding to плескать ('to splash, lap, clap', from Old East Slavic плескати, Proto-Slavic *pleskati, of onomatopoeic origin) + semelfactive suffix -нуть.

history.meaning: to splash once; to pour a little

плечо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плече and Proto-Slavic *pleťe ('shoulder, upper back'), formed from *plet-je ('broad, flat shoulder blade area'), from Proto-Indo-European *plat- / *pleth₂- ('flat, broad', cognate with Ancient Greek platýs 'broad, flat' and English flat / plate).
плечо.notes: Notice how *tj gave ч in East Slavic плечо (compare Old Church Slavonic плеще with щ). Nominative plural is плечи, genitive plural плеч.

плита.etymology: Inherited via Old East Slavic плита ('flat stone slab, paving flag, brick') from Byzantine Greek plítha / Ancient Greek plínthos ('fired brick, squared stone slab, plinth'). In modern Russian it denotes both a heavy stone or concrete slab and a kitchen cooking stove (originally a cast-iron top plate set over a brick hearth).

cognates.meaning: squared base slab of a column (from Greek plinthos)

плитка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of плита ('flat stone slab, flagstone, cooker range'), borrowed early into Old East Slavic плита from Byzantine and Ancient Greek πλίνθος ('fired brick, squared tile, flat slab'). Used for a ceramic tile, a small hotplate, or a moulded bar of chocolate.

плов.etymology: Borrowed via Turkic languages of the Caucasus and Central Asia (compare Azerbaijani plov, Uzbek palov, Turkish pilav) from Persian پلو (polow / palāv 'cooked rice dish'), ultimately from Sanskrit पुलाव / पलल (pulāka 'lump of boiled rice').

плод.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плодъ and Old Church Slavonic плодъ ('fruit, offspring, produce'), from Proto-Slavic *plodъ ('fruit, yield'), related to племя ('tribe, seed') and расплодиться ('to multiply').

пломба.etymology: Borrowed via German Plombe ('lead seal; dental filling') from French plomb ('lead, lead seal'), from Latin plumbum ('lead').

плоский.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плоскыи and Proto-Slavic *ploskъ ('flat, level, broad'), built with the suffix *-skъ on the root *plo- / *plat- ('broad, flat', also seen in плечо 'shoulder' and пласт 'flat layer').

плоско.etymology: Formed as the short neuter and adverbial form in -о of плоский ('flat', Proto-Slavic *ploskъ).

плот.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плотъ ('wattle fence, raft'), from Proto-Slavic *plotъ ('wattled structure, fence, raft bound together'), ablaut-grade noun from *plesti ('to plait, weave, bind').

плотно.etymology: Adverbial form in -о of плотный ('dense, tight, snug'), from Old East Slavic плътьныи.

плотный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плътьныи ('compact, stout, corporeal'), derived from плъть ('flesh, body; compact woven fence', from Proto-Slavic *plъtь, related to плести 'to plait, weave tightly together').

history.meaning: closely woven structure, flesh → compact, dense

плохо.etymology: Deadjectival adverb formed from плохой ('bad'), originally the neuter short form of the adjective. Inherited from Old East Slavic плохъ ('simple, poor, weak, bad'), from Proto-Slavic *ploxъ, whose deeper Indo-European connections remain uncertain (Vasmer compares possible links to words for 'timid, startled' or 'flat, bare').
плохо.notes: Used both as a manner adverb (он плохо готовит) and as an impersonal predicate with a dative experiencer (мне плохо 'I feel unwell').

плохой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плохыи ('simple, weak, poor, bad'), from Proto-Slavic *ploxъ ('timid, weak, scanty, bad'). Vasmer notes that its deeper pre-Slavic connections are uncertain, comparing possible links to words for 'flattened, worn down' or 'frightened, skittish' (compare переполох 'alarm').
плохой.notes: Comparative form is suppletive or palatalized: **хуже** ('worse').

площадка.etymology: Formed in Russian as the diminutive of площадь ('square, flat open area') with the suffix -ка. Площадь comes from Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic площадь ('flat open space, plaza'), ultimately tied to плоский ('flat').
площадка.notes: Covers a staircase landing (*лестничная площадка*), a children's playground (*детская площадка*), and a viewing platform (*смотровая площадка*).

площадь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic площадь ('open town square, level space'), borrowed or adapted from Old Church Slavonic площадь, a derivative of плоскъ ('flat, level', with sk + j -> šč): originally 'a broad, flat open space in a town'.

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

плыть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плыти (present плыву, older плову), from Proto-Slavic *plyti / *pluti ('to float, swim, sail'), from Proto-Indo-European *plew- ('to flow, float, swim'; compare Ancient Greek πλέω 'to sail', Sanskrit plávate 'floats, swims', Latin pluere 'to rain', and English flow / float).

history.meaning: to swim, float, sail (in one direction)

плюнуть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плюнути ('to spit once'), from Proto-Slavic *pľunǫti, semelfactive of *pľьvati ('to spit', from onomatopoeic PIE *(s)pyew-).

плюс.etymology: Borrowed via German Plus / French plus from Latin plūs ('more'), used in European arithmetic since the Renaissance for addition ('+') and extended in everyday Russian to mean 'an advantage' or 'plus, in addition to'.

плюх.etymology: Expressive Russian sound-symbolic interjection imitating the flat slap and splash of a heavy or wide object landing in water or mud. From the same onomatopoeic stem плюх- (related to плескать 'to splash', Proto-Slavic *plьskati) Russian also forms the colloquial verbs плюхать and плюхнуться ('to plop or flop down').

плюшевый.etymology: Relational adjective formed from плюш ('plush fabric', borrowed via German Plüsch from French peluche 'plush, shag fabric', from Old French peluchier 'to pluck', ultimately from Latin pilus 'hair') + adjectival suffix -евый.

плющ.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плющь and Proto-Slavic *pljuščь ('ivy'). Etymologists debate its deeper source: Vasmer notes connections with *pljuti ('to spit, ooze') after the plant's bitter sap, or with root-clusters meaning 'to creep, entwine, cling'.

пляж.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French plage ('sea beach, gently sloping shore', via Italian piaggia from Late Latin plagia 'coast, flat slope', from Ancient Greek πλάγια 'flanks, sides').

плясать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плясати ('to dance'), from Proto-Slavic *plęsati ('to dance', either connected with *pleskati 'to clap, stamp' or an early borrowing from Gothic plinsjan 'to dance').

плёнка.etymology: Diminutive of older Russian плена ('thin skin, membrane'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *pelna ('membrane, husk, skin'). Derived from the Proto-Indo-European root *pel- ('skin, hide, film'), which is also the source of Latin pellis ('skin') and English film, fell, and pelt. In the twentieth century, the word expanded from biological membranes to photographic film and magnetic recording tape.

пнуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective verb formed from the zero-grade stem *pьn- of Proto-Slavic *pęti / iterative *pinati ('to stretch, strike, kick', PIE *(s)pen-) + semelfactive suffix -нуть.

по.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic по ('along, over, after, according to'), from Proto-Slavic *po, continuing Proto-Indo-European *po / *pos ('after, along, by'; compare Lithuanian põ 'after, under, through' and Latin po- in pōnō).
по.notes: Takes the dative in its most common spatial and communicative uses: идти по улице ('walk along the street'), говорить по телефону ('talk on the phone').

по-арабски.etymology: Adverb formed with circumfix по-...-ски from арабский ('Arabic, Arabian', from араб 'Arab', borrowed via Western European languages and Greek Ἄραψ from Arabic عَرَب 'Arabs').

по-братски.etymology: Adverb formed with circumfix по-...-ски from братский ('brotherly, fraternal'), derived from брат ('brother'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *bratrъ / *bratъ (from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr).

по-бретонски.etymology: Adverb formed with circumfix по-...-ски from бретонский ('Breton'), from French breton ('of Brittany, France').

history.meaning: Breton, in the Breton culinary style

по-бургундски.etymology: Culinary and manner adverb formed with circumfix по-...-ски from бургундский ('Burgundian', from Бургундия 'Burgundy', via French Bourgogne / Medieval Latin Burgundia, named after the Germanic Burgundians).

по-быстрому.etymology: Colloquial adverb formed with prefix по- and dative ending -omu from быстрый ('fast, quick'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *bystrъ ('swift, clear-flowing').

по-вашему.etymology: Adverb formed from preposition по- and the dative neuter singular of ваш ('your'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *vašь ('your').

по-дижонски.etymology: Culinary adverb formed with circumfix по-...-ски from дижонский ('of Dijon', from the French city of Dijon, renowned for mustard production, from Latin Dīviō, accusative Dīviōnem).

history.meaning: city in Burgundy famous for mustard

по-другому.etymology: Adverb formed in Russian from the prefix по- ('in the manner of, according to') + the dative singular другому of другой ('other, another, different', inherited from Old East Slavic другыи 'second, other', from Proto-Slavic *drugъ).

по-дружески.etymology: Adverb formed with circumfix по-...-ски from дружеский ('friendly', derived from друг 'friend', Old East Slavic другъ, Proto-Slavic *drugъ).

по-итальянски.etymology: Adverb formed with the circumfix по-...-ски ('in the language or manner of') from итальянский ('Italian'), derived from Италия ('Italy', from Latin Italia).

history.meaning: Italian (adj) → in Italian, in the Italian style

morphemes.meaning: in the language or style of

по-любому.etymology: Colloquial adverb formed from preposition по + dative singular любому of любой ('any, whichever', originally 'pleasing to one's choice', from Old East Slavic любыи 'dear, pleasing', Proto-Slavic *ľubъ).

history.meaning: definitely, in any case, either way

по-моему.etymology: Parenthetical adverbial phrase formed from the preposition по ('according to, in the manner of') + моему, the dative singular masculine/neuter of мой ('my, mine', Old East Slavic мои, Proto-Slavic *mojь), with ellipsis of мнению ('according to my opinion').

history.meaning: according to my (opinion) → in my opinion; my way

по-мужски.etymology: Adverb formed with the circumfix по-...-ски ('in the manner of') from мужской ('masculine, men's'), derived from муж ('man, husband', inherited from Old East Slavic мужь, Proto-Slavic *mǫžь).

history.meaning: masculine, men's → like a man, man-to-man

по-настоящему.etymology: Adverb formed with prefix по- and dative ending -ему from настоящий ('present, real, genuine'), originally present active participle of настоять ('to stand firm, be present'), from Proto-Slavic *stojati.

по-новому.etymology: Adverb formed with prefix по- and dative ending -ому from новый ('new'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *novъ ('new').

по-парижски.etymology: Adverb formed with circumfix по-...-ски from парижский ('Parisian', from Париж 'Paris', ultimately from French Paris).

по-прежнему.etymology: Adverb formed from the prefix по- ('according to, as') + the dative singular прежнему of прежний ('former, previous'), derived from Old Church Slavonic прѣжде (Russian прежде, 'before, formerly', comparative of *perdъ 'in front, before').

по-разному.etymology: Adverb formed from preposition по + dative singular разному of разный ('different, various', derived from розный, from Proto-Slavic *orzьnъ 'apart, separate').

по-русски.etymology: Adverb formed with circumfix по-...-ски from русский ('Russian'), inherited from Old East Slavic русьскыи ('pertaining to Rus'').

по-соседски.etymology: Adverb formed with circumfix по-...-ски from соседский ('neighborly'), derived from сосед ('neighbor'), from Proto-Slavic *sǫsědъ ('one who sits/dwells together', from *sǫ- + *sěděti).

по-старому.etymology: Adverb formed with prefix по- and dative ending -ому from старый ('old'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *starъ ('old').

history.meaning: as before, in the old way

по-твоему.etymology: Adverb formed from preposition по ('according to') + dative singular masculine/neuter твоему of possessive pronoun твой ('your, thy', Old East Slavic твои, Proto-Slavic *tvojь).

по-флорентийски.etymology: Adverb formed with circumfix по-...-ски from флорентийский ('Florentine', of Florence / Firenze, Italy), calquing culinary French à la florentine (typically prepared with spinach and Mornay sauce).

по-флотски.etymology: Adverb formed with circumfix по-...-ски from флотский ('naval, navy's', from флот 'fleet, navy', borrowed under Peter the Great from Dutch vloot / French flotte); famous in culinary use for макароны по-флотски ('navy-style pasta with minced meat').

по-французски.etymology: Adverb formed with the circumfix по-...-ски ('in the language or manner of') from французский ('French'), derived from француз ('Frenchman', borrowed in the 17th century via Polish Francuz from Italian francese / French Français).

history.meaning: French (adj) → in French, in the French style

morphemes.meaning: in the language or style of

по-хорошему.etymology: Adverb formed from preposition по + dative singular хорошему of хороший ('good', Old East Slavic хорошии).

по-человечески.etymology: Adverb formed with circumfix по-...-ски from человеческий ('human', from человек 'human being, person', Old East Slavic человѣкъ, Proto-Slavic *čelověkъ).

по-честному.etymology: Adverb formed with prefix по- and dative ending -ому from честный ('honest, fair'), derived from честь ('honor'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *čьstь ('honor, respect').

поаккуратнее.etymology: Attenuative comparative adverb formed in Russian with prefix по- ('a little more') + аккуратнее, comparative of аккуратный ('careful, neat, tidy'), borrowed in the early eighteenth century via German akkurat (and Polish akuratny) from Latin accūrātus ('prepared with care'), from ad- + cūra ('care, attention').
поаккуратнее.notes: Watch the false friend with English accurate: Russian аккуратно / поаккуратнее means 'gently, neatly, watch your step!' (for example when carrying heavy boxes through a doorway).

поаплодировать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with delimitative prefix по- ('a little, for a while') + аплодировать ('to applaud', borrowed from French applaudir, from Latin applaudere 'to clap the hands in approval', from ad- + plaudere 'to clap').

history.meaning: to applaud, give a round of applause

побаловать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with attenuative prefix по- ('a little') + баловать ('to pamper, spoil, indulge', from Old East Slavic баловати, traditionally connected to балий 'healer, charmer', from *bajati 'to speak, charm, tell').

побегать.etymology: Delimitative verb formed with prefix по- ('for a while') from бегать ('to run around'), iterative of бежать ('to run'), from Proto-Slavic *běgati.

побегушки.etymology: Expressive plural noun formed from побегать ('to run about for a while', from по- + бегать 'to run', Proto-Slavic *běgati) + colloquial plural suffix -ушки; used chiefly in быть на побегушках ('to be an errand boy / gofer').

победа.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic побѣда ('victory, conquest'), a deverbal noun from побѣдити / победить ('to vanquish, overcome, defeat'), built on бѣда ('distress, compulsion, calamity', Russian беда, Proto-Slavic *běda). Originally 'the overcoming or subjugation of an adversary by force'.

победитель.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic побѣдитель ('victor, conqueror, winner'), formed with the agent suffix -тель from побѣдити (modern победить 'to conquer, win'), built on по- + бѣда (modern беда 'calamity, distress', originally 'compulsion, overcoming by force', from Proto-Slavic *běda).
