The verb continues Old East Slavic терти and Proto-Slavic *terti ('to rub, grate'), from the Proto-Indo-European root *terh₁- ('to rub, turn, bore'). It is cognate with Latin terere ('to rub, wear away') and English throw and thread.

cognates.meaning: to rub, wear out (source of English attrition, trite)
to hurl (from PGmc *þrāwaną 'to twist, turn' < PIE *terh₁-)

поужинать.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from ужинать ('to have supper/dinner'), derived from ужин ('evening meal', originally 'midday/south meal'), from Old East Slavic ужинъ, derived from югъ / угъ ('south, midday sun', Proto-Slavic *jugъ).

поумнеть.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix по- + умнеть ('to grow smarter, become wiser'), derived from умный ('smart, wise', from ум 'mind, intellect', from Proto-Slavic *umъ).

поухаживать.etymology: Formed from delimitative prefix по- ('for a while') + ухаживать ('to look after, tend; to court, woo', iterative derived from у- + ходить 'to go, walk', from Proto-Slavic *xoditi).

history.meaning: to court or look after for a while

поучительный.etymology: Derived from поучить / поучать ('to instruct, teach, edify', from по- + учить 'to teach', from Proto-Slavic *učiti) + adjectival suffix -тельн-ый.

поучиться.etymology: Delimitative/perfective verb formed with prefix по- from учиться ('to learn, study'), reflexive of учить ('to teach'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *učiti.

пофантазировать.etymology: Formed from delimitative prefix по- ('a bit, for a while') + фантазировать ('to fantasize, daydream', borrowed via German phantasieren from Late Latin phantasiare, from Ancient Greek φαντασία 'imagination').

history.meaning: to fantasize, daydream for a while

похвала.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic похвала ('praise, laudation'), deverbal from похвалити ('to praise', from по- + Proto-Slavic *xvaliti, from *xvala 'praise').

похвалить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic похвалити (Proto-Slavic *poxvaliti), formed from the perfectivizing prefix по- + хвалить ('to praise', from хвала 'praise', Proto-Slavic *xvala).

похвастаться.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from хвастаться ('to boast, brag'), derived from хвастать, from Proto-Slavic *xvastati ('to babble, brag', of expressive/onomatopoeic origin).

похитить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic похитити ('to snatch away, seize, abduct', corresponding to East Slavic похватить), formed from по- + Proto-Slavic *xytiti ('to snatch, catch, seize').

похищать.etymology: Imperfective of похитить, borrowed from Old Church Slavonic похищати ('to snatch away, abduct'), with the Church Slavonic reflex -щ- (*tj) from Proto-Slavic *poxytjati (*po- + *xytiti 'to seize').

похлопать.etymology: Formed with the perfective/attenuative prefix по- ('a little, briefly') and хлопать ('to clap, pat, slam'). The base verb is of expressive, onomatopoeic Proto-Slavic origin (*xlopati, imitating the sound of a flat slap or clap). It parallels similar imitative Slavic verbs such as топать ('to stamp') and шлёпать ('to slap, splash').

похмелье.etymology: Prepositional-suffixal derivative formed from по ('after') + хмель ('hops; intoxication', from Old East Slavic хмѣль, Proto-Slavic *xъmelь) + neuter suffix -ье, literally 'the condition after intoxication'.

походу.etymology: Colloquial adverbialization of the prepositional phrase по ходу ('along the course [of events], by the look of things'), from по ('along, by') + ход ('course, movement', from Proto-Slavic *xodъ).

похоже.etymology: Neuter short form and adverb of похожий ('similar, resembling'), derived from походить ('to take after, resemble', from по- + ходить 'to walk, go'). Used both as a predicate ('it looks like, it is similar') and as a parenthetical discourse marker ('it seems, apparently').

history.meaning: similar → alike; it seems, looks like

похожий.etymology: Derived from походить ('to resemble, take after, go along someone's path'), built from the prefix по- ('along, after') and ходить ('to walk, go', Proto-Slavic *xoditi), with the alternation д > ж before the adjectival suffix -ий. Literally, 'walking in the same way, taking after'.

history.meaning: taking after in gait/manner → similar, resembling

похоронить.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from по- + хоронить ('to bury', in older and dialectal Russian 'to hide, keep safe, guard'), inherited from Old East Slavic хоронити ('to guard, keep, hide, bury'), from Proto-Slavic *xorniti (the native East Slavic pleophonic counterpart of Old Church Slavonic хранити / хранить 'to keep, preserve').

history.meaning: to hide away, lay to rest, bury

похороны.etymology: Plural-only noun derived from похоронить ('to bury, inter'), from по- + хоронить ('to bury; originally to guard, keep safe, hide', East Slavic pleophonic form of Proto-Slavic *xorniti).

похудеть.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix по- + худеть ('to grow thin, lose weight'), derived from худой ('thin, lean; bad', inherited from Proto-Slavic *xudъ 'thin, meager, poor').

похуже.etymology: Attenuative comparative form derived from prefix по- ('a bit, somewhat') + хуже ('worse', comparative of худой 'bad', from Proto-Slavic *xudje).

поцеловать.etymology: Perfective counterpart of целовать ('to kiss'), formed with the prefix по- from Old East Slavic цѣловати ('to greet, wish good health; to kiss'), derived from цѣлъ / целый ('whole, hale, healthy', Proto-Slavic *cělъ).

history.meaning: whole, hale → to wish health in greeting, kiss

поцеловаться.etymology: Perfective reciprocal verb formed from по- + целоваться ('to kiss each other'), from целовать ('to kiss'), inherited from Old East Slavic цѣловати ('to greet, wish good health, kiss'), derived from цѣлыи (Russian целый, 'whole, hale, unharmed', Proto-Slavic *cělъ).

history.meaning: whole, hale → to wish health, greet with a kiss

поцелуй.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from the imperative stem of поцеловать ('to kiss'), from по- + целовать ('to kiss, greet', originally 'to wish someone whole/healthy'), derived from целый ('whole, intact', Proto-Slavic *cělъ).

почва.etymology: Developed from earlier Russian подчва / почва ('sole of footwear; ground underfoot, underlying layer'), formed from prefix под- ('under') + root *čьva (related to чобот 'boot, shoe').

почему.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase по чему ('along/by what?, on account of what?'), combining the preposition по with чему, the dative singular of что ('what', from Old East Slavic чьто).

почему-то.etymology: Indefinite adverb formed in Russian from почему ('why', univerbation of по чему 'by what, on account of what', from по + dative чему of что 'what') + the indefinite enclitic particle -то ('some-').

почерк.etymology: Formed in Russian as a zero-suffixed noun from почеркнуть / почёркивать ('to trace a line, dash off with a pen'), built on по- + черкать ('to scribe, scratch lines'), from the Slavic root *čьrt- / *čьrk- ('incised line, stroke'; compare черта 'line, trait' and очерк 'sketch, essay').

history.meaning: to trace strokes → handwriting, script style

почесать.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from чесать ('to scratch, comb'), inherited from Old East Slavic чесати, from Proto-Slavic *česati ('to comb, scratch, strip').

починить.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing prefix по- + чинить ('to repair, mend, put in order', derived from чин 'order, rank, proper arrangement', Proto-Slavic *činъ): 'to fix, mend, repair'.

history.meaning: order -> to arrange, put in order

почистить.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing prefix по- + чистить ('to clean, brush, peel', Proto-Slavic *čistiti, derived from чистый 'clean, pure', Proto-Slavic *čistъ).
почистить.notes: First-person singular shows ст -> щ mutation: я почищу, ты почистишь.

почитать.etymology: Delimitative perfective formed with prefix по- ('for a while, a little') from читать ('to read'), inherited from Old East Slavic читати, iterative of чьсти ('to read, count, honor', Proto-Slavic *čitati).

почка.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пъчька / почка ('bud, swelling; kidney'), diminutive of archaic *пъка ('swelling, bulge'), from Proto-Slavic *pъkati ('to swell, burst open, bud').

почта.etymology: Borrowed in the late seventeenth century via Polish poczta from Italian posta ('relay station where fresh horses are stationed; mail service'), originally the feminine past participle of Latin pōnere (posita 'placed, stationed').
почта.notes: Takes на for both 'at the post office' (на почте) and 'by mail / email' (отправить по почте).

почтальон.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via French postillon (and Italian postiglione 'post-rider, mail coachman'), reshaped in Russian under the influence of почта ('mail, post').

почтение.etymology: Verbal noun from почтить ('to honor, respect'), inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic почьтение ('respect, reverence'), from по- + чьсти ('to honor, revere', Proto-Slavic *čьsti).

почти.etymology: Originated in Russian as the frozen singular imperative почти ('reckon! consider it as!') of почесть / почитать ('to reckon, count, consider', from по- + честь / читать 'to count, reckon, read', Proto-Slavic *čisti).Saying 'reckon it a hundred' (*почти сто*) grammaticalized into the adverb 'almost, nearly'.

почувствовать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from по- + чувствовать ('to feel, sense'), derived from чувство ('feeling, sense', Old East Slavic чувьство, built on the verb чуять / чути 'to sense, perceive, hear', Proto-Slavic *čuti).

почём.etymology: Adverbialized prepositional phrase formed from по ('at the rate of, for') + чём (locative singular of что 'what', from Proto-Slavic *čьto), literally 'at what price each?'.

history.meaning: for how much, at what price

почётный.etymology: Derived with the adjectival suffix -ный from почёт ('honor, esteem, respect'), an action noun from почитать / почесть ('to honor, esteem, count as'). The root descends from Proto-Slavic *čьt- / *čisti ('to count, read, honor'), from the Proto-Indo-European root *kʷeyt- ('to notice, observe, respect'). It belongs to the same root family as Russian честь ('honor') and читать ('to read').

пошевелить.etymology: Formed from the attenuative/perfective prefix по- ('a little') + шевелить ('to move slightly, stir, wiggle', an expressive East Slavic verb often linked by Vasmer with ковылять / шевелить).
пошевелить.notes: Often takes the instrumental case of a body part: пошевелить пальцами ('to wiggle one's fingers/toes').

пошире.etymology: Formed in Russian by adding the attenuative prefix по- ('a little, nicely') to шире ('wider', comparative of широкий 'wide', Proto-Slavic *širokъ).

history.meaning: a little wider, nice and wide

пошляк.etymology: Derived from пошлый ('vulgar, banal, commonplace'; originally in Old Russian пошьлыи 'customary, old-established, traditional', from пойти / пошёл 'having gone since old times') + agent suffix -як.

пошлёпать.etymology: Formed from delimitative/perfective prefix по- + шлёпать ('to slap, smack, splash'), an expressive verb of onomatopoeic origin imitating the sound of a flat slap or splash.

history.meaning: to slap a bit; to slap down cards

пошутить.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from шутить ('to joke, jest'), derived from шут ('jester, fool'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *šutъ.

history.meaning: to joke, to make a joke

пощада.etymology: Deverbal noun from пощадить ('to spare, show mercy'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пощада / пощадѣти (with Church Slavonic щ from *skj/*stj), from по- + Proto-Slavic *ščęděti ('to spare').

пощадить.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix по- + щадить ('to spare, have mercy on'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пощадѣти / щадѣти, from Proto-Slavic *ščęděti ('to spare, be thrifty with').

поэзия.etymology: Borrowed via Polish poezja or German Poesie from Latin poēsis, from Ancient Greek ποίησις (poíēsis, 'making, creation, poetry'), from ποιέω (poiéō, 'to make, compose').

поэт.etymology: Borrowed via French poète or German Poet from Latin poēta, from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs, 'maker, creator, poet'), agent noun from ποιέω ('to make, compose').

поэтому.etymology: Formed in Russian by fusing the preposition по ('along, by reason of, on account of') with этому, the dative singular of этот ('this'): literally 'by this, on account of this', hence 'therefore, that is why'.

появиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed with the prefix по- from явиться ('to appear, show oneself'), derived from явить ('to show, manifest'), from Old East Slavic явити and Proto-Slavic *javiti ('to make visible, reveal', from *javъ 'awake, manifest, open', as in наяву 'in waking life', cognate with Sanskrit āvíṣ 'openly, before the eyes').

history.meaning: manifest, visible → to show oneself, appear

появление.etymology: Verbal noun derived from появиться ('to appear, show up'), formed from prefix по- + явиться (from явить 'to show, manifest', from Proto-Slavic *javiti) + suffix -ение.

появляться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive verb derived from появиться ('to appear'), from prefix по- + являться (from Proto-Slavic *javľati, iterative of *javiti 'to show, reveal', related to *javь 'reality, wakefulness') + -ся.

пояс.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic поясъ ('belt, girdle'), from Proto-Slavic *pojasъ, deverbal from *pojasati ('to gird', from *po- + *jasati, from Proto-Indo-European *yeh₃s- 'to gird').

поясница.etymology: Derived from пояс ('belt, waist', from Proto-Slavic *pojasъ) + anatomical/locative noun suffix -ница, denoting the part of the back around which a belt is worn.

правда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic правьда ('truth, justice, law code' — famously in Русская правда, the 11th-century Kievan legal code), from Proto-Slavic *pravьda, formed from *pravъ ('straight, right, just, true') + the abstract suffix *-ьda.

rootFamily.gloss: to tuck in, make a bed

правдоподобно.etymology: Adverb derived from правдоподобный ('plausible, verisimilar'), a compound calque (modeled on Latin verisimilis / German wahrscheinlich) from правда ('truth') + -о- + подобный ('similar, like').

правдоподобность.etymology: Abstract noun derived from правдоподобный ('plausible, verisimilar', compound of правда 'truth' + подобный 'similar, like') + abstract noun suffix -ость.

правее.etymology: Comparative form in -ее of правый ('right, on the right-hand side'), inherited from Old East Slavic правыи ('straight, right, just'), from Proto-Slavic *pravъ.

правило.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic правило ('straightedge, ruler, canon, rule'), formed with the instrument suffix -ло from правити ('to make straight, guide, govern', from правый 'straight, right', Proto-Slavic *pravъ). Like English rule and ruler, it originally meant a carpenter's straightedge before signifying a principle or regulation.

history.meaning: straight, right → to guide, straighten → straightedge, rule

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

правильно.etymology: Adverb formed from правильный ('correct, right, proper'), derived from правило ('rule, straightedge, rudder'), itself built with the instrument suffix -ло on правый ('straight, right, just', from Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

правильный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from правило ('rule, straightedge, guide'), derived from правый ('straight, right, just', from Proto-Slavic *pravъ). Literally, 'conforming to the rule or straight line'.

правитель.etymology: Agent noun in -тель formed from править ('to rule, govern, steer, direct'), derived from правый ('straight, right'), from Proto-Slavic *praviti ('to make straight, guide, rule').

право.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic право ('right, justice, law'), substantivized neuter singular of правыи / правый ('straight, right, just, true'), from Proto-Slavic *pravъ ('straight, right'). Parallels the semantic development of German Recht and French droit ('straight → right, law').

православный.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic православьнъ ('Orthodox'), a compound calque of Byzantine Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos, 'having right belief / glorifying rightly'), combining правый ('right, true', translating Greek ὀρθός orthós) + славить / слава ('glory, praise', translating Greek δόξα dóxa).

правосудие.etymology: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic and Old East Slavic правосудиѥ ('justice, righteous judgment', calquing Ancient Greek δικαιοκρισία), from правый ('right, just', *pravъ) + -о- + суд ('judgment, court', *sǫdъ) + -ие.

правота.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic правота ('uprightness, justice, correctness'), formed from правый ('right, true, just', from Proto-Slavic *pravъ) + abstract noun suffix -ота.

правый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic правыи and Proto-Slavic *pravъ ('straight, direct, true, just; right-hand'), from Proto-Indo-European *pro-wo-s ('forward-facing, straight', built on *pro 'forward'). Because the right hand was regarded as the 'straight, proper' hand, правый came to mean both 'correct, in the right' and 'right-hand'.
правый.notes: As a short predicate (ты прав, она права, вы правы), it always means 'you are right / correct'.

праздник.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic праздьникъ 'feast day, holiday', derived from праздьнъ ('unoccupied, free from everyday labour', from Proto-Slavic *porzdьnъ): a day set free from ordinary work for celebration.
праздник.notes: The middle consonant -д- is silent in everyday pronunciation (pronounced [празник], spelled праздник).

праздничный.etymology: Relational and qualitative adjective formed with the suffix -ный from праздник ('holiday, celebration', with к → ч before -н-), adopted from Old Church Slavonic праздьникъ ('feast day', from праздьнъ 'unoccupied, free from work').
праздничный.notes: Like *праздник*, the middle -д- is silent in standard speech: pronounced [празничный].

празднование.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic праздьнованиѥ ('celebration, keeping a feast'), verbal noun from праздьновати ('to celebrate') + -ние.

праздновать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic праздьновати ('to keep a holiday, celebrate, be idle'), derived from праздьнъ ('empty, idle, festive', corresponding to East Slavic порожний, from Proto-Slavic *porzdьnъ).

history.meaning: to be idle; to celebrate a feast

практиковать.etymology: Formed from практика ('practice', borrowed via Polish praktyka or German Praktik from Late Latin practica, from Ancient Greek πρακτική 'practical work', from πράσσω 'to do, act') + verbal suffix -овать.

практически.etymology: Adverb formed from практический ('practical'), borrowed via German praktisch / French pratique from Late Latin practicus, from Ancient Greek πρακτικός (praktikós, 'fit for action, practical', from πράσσω 'to do, act').

прапорщик.etymology: Derived in 17th-century Russian from прапор ('banner, standard, ensign', from Church Slavonic прапоръ 'banner, flag', a reduplicated derivative of *per-/*por- 'to fly, flutter', cognate with перо) + agent suffix -щик.

прачечная.etymology: Substantivized feminine adjective from прачечный, derived from прачка ('laundress, washerwoman'), diminutive of archaic прачька / праля, from Proto-Slavic *pьrati ('to beat laundry with a wash-beetle, wash clothes').

превратить.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic прѣвратити ('to turn over, overturn, transform'), showing the South Slavic prefix and root vocalism прѣ-врат- (compare native East Slavic пере-ворот- in перевернуть), from Proto-Slavic *pervortiti ('to turn across/over').

morphemes.meaning: across, over (Church Slavonic counterpart of пере-)

превратить.notes: First-person singular shows the Church Slavonic mutation т -> щ: я превращу; takes в + accusative (превратить воду в пар).

превратиться.etymology: Reflexive of превратить ('to turn into, transform'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣвратити ('to overturn, convert, transform', from прѣ- 'over, across' + вратити 'to turn', from Proto-Slavic *vertiti) + -ся.

превращать.etymology: Imperfective of превратить, borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣвращати ('to overturn, transform'), with Church Slavonic прѣ- and -щ- (*tj) from Proto-Slavic *pervertjati.

превращаться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive form in -ся of превращать ('to transform, turn into'), adopted with Church Slavonic vocalism (пре- 'across, over' + вращать 'to turn', corresponding to native East Slavic пере- + ворочать, from Proto-Slavic *vortiti).

history.meaning: to transform → to turn into, be transformed into

предавать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдавати (imperfective of прѣдати 'to hand over, deliver up, betray', with non-pleophonic прѣ- < *per-), from Proto-Slavic *per-dati ('to give over').

history.meaning: to hand over, deliver up, betray
to betray, to be unfaithful to

преданно.etymology: Adverb derived from преданный ('devoted, loyal', originally past passive participle of предать / предаться 'to give oneself over to, dedicate oneself', from Old Church Slavonic прѣдати 'to hand over, entrust').

преданность.etymology: Abstract noun derived from преданный ('devoted, loyal', from предать / предаться 'to devote oneself to', from Old Church Slavonic прѣдати) + abstract suffix -ость.

преданный.etymology: Past passive participle of предать ('to hand over, commit oneself wholly to someone'), from Old Church Slavonic прѣданъ ('given over, devoted'), from Proto-Slavic *per-dati ('to give over').

предатель.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдатель ('betrayer, traitor, Judas'), formed with the agent suffix -тель from прѣдати / предать ('to hand over, deliver up to an enemy, betray'), a compound of прѣ- ('over, across') + дати ('to give', Russian дать; compare Latin trāditor 'traitor' from trāns-dare 'to hand over').

предательство.etymology: Derived from предатель ('traitor, betrayer', from предать 'to hand over, betray', from Old Church Slavonic прѣдати, from прѣ- + дати 'to give', Proto-Slavic *dati) + suffix -ство.

предать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдати ('to hand over, deliver up, betray', calquing Greek προδίδωμι / Latin trādere), formed with non-pleophonic prefix прѣ- (< *per-) + дати ('to give', Proto-Slavic *dati).

history.meaning: to hand over, deliver up, betray

предварительный.etymology: Derived from предварить ('to forestall, precede, anticipate', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъварити 'to go before, anticipate', from прѣдъ 'before' + варити 'to go ahead, precede') + suffix -тельн-ый.

предвзятый.etymology: Formed in the 19th century as a calque (modeled on French préconçu or German voreingenommen) from prefix пред- ('before, in advance') + взятый ('taken', past passive participle of взять, from Proto-Slavic *vъzęti).

предвидеться.etymology: Reflexive/passive form of предвидеть ('to foresee', a calque of Latin praevidere or French prévoir), formed from prefix пред- ('before, in advance') + видеть ('to see', from Proto-Slavic *viděti) + -ся.

предвыборный.etymology: Adjective formed with prefix пред- ('before, pre-') and suffix -ный from выборы ('elections'), plural of выбор ('choice, election'), from выбрать ('to choose out', Proto-Slavic *bьrati).

предел.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдѣлъ ('boundary, border, limit', corresponding to East Slavic передел), formed from прѣ- ('across, over', *per-) + дѣлъ ('division, part', from *děliti 'to divide').

предельно.etymology: Adverb derived from предельный ('utmost, extreme, limit'), formed from предел ('limit, boundary', from Old Church Slavonic прѣдѣлъ) + adjectival suffix -н- + -о.

предлагать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдълагати ('to lay before, set forth, offer'), formed from the Church Slavonic prefix прѣдъ- ('before, in front of', East Slavic перед-) and -лагати (iterative of ложити 'to lay, place'). Literally, 'to lay something before someone' (an exact structural parallel to Latin prōpōnere 'to propose').

предлог.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдълогъ ('placing before; preposition; pretext', calquing Ancient Greek πρόθεσις), from прѣдъ- ('before') + -логъ (ablaut noun from *ložiti / *legti 'to lay, lie').

предложение.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъложение ('setting forth, presentation, offering'), the verbal noun of прѣдъложити / предложить ('to lay before, offer, propose'). In the 18th century, Russian grammarians (such as Lomonosov) also used it to calque Latin prōpositiō ('grammatical clause/sentence, logical proposition').

предложить.etymology: Adopted with the Church Slavonic prefix пред- ('before, in front of', corresponding to native East Slavic перед-) + ложить ('to lay, place', Proto-Slavic *ložiti), a calque pattern parallel to Latin prōpōnere ('to set before someone, propose'): literally 'to lay before someone for consideration'.

history.meaning: to set before, lay out, propose

предмет.etymology: Calqued in the 18th century (via Polish przedmiot) from Latin obiectum ('something thrown or set before the mind or senses'), from пред- ('before', Latin ob-) + мет- (метать 'to throw, cast', Proto-Slavic *metati).

предоплата.etymology: Modern compound noun formed from prefix пред- ('before, in advance') + оплата ('payment', from оплатить 'to pay for', from о- + платить 'to pay', from Proto-Slavic *platiti).

предоставить.etymology: Formed with Church Slavonic prefix пред- ('before') + оставить ('to leave, let remain', from о- + ставить 'to place, set', from Proto-Slavic *staviti), literally 'to place or leave before someone at their disposal'.

history.meaning: to provide, place at someone's disposal

предохранитель.etymology: Formed in Russian from предохранить ('to guard in advance, protect against danger', from пред- 'before, in advance' + охранить 'to guard, protect') with the instrument suffix -тель: literally 'a advance-protector', hence a safety catch or an electrical fuse that blows to protect wiring.

предполагаемый.etymology: Present passive participle of предполагать ('to suppose, presume, assume'), formed with Old Church Slavonic prefix пред- ('before, fore-') + полагать ('to lay, suppose', from Proto-Slavic *polagati), calquing Latin suppōnere / German voraussetzen.

предполагать.etymology: Formed in bookish Russian from Old Church Slavonic prefix пред- ('before, fore-') + полагать ('to lay, suppose, think', Proto-Slavic *polagati), calquing Latin suppōnere / German voraussetzen.

предположить.etymology: Calqued from Latin supponere / French supposer (or Ancient Greek ὑποτίθημι), formed from prefix пред- ('before, in advance') + положить ('to lay, place, posit', from по- + ложить, Proto-Slavic *ložiti).

предпочитать.etymology: Imperfective of предпочесть ('to prefer, esteem above others'), formed from prefix пред- ('before, ahead of') + почитать ('to honor, esteem, consider', from по- + Proto-Slavic *čьtati / *čisti 'to count, honor').

предприниматель.etymology: Calque on French entrepreneur or German Unternehmer, formed from предпринимать ('to undertake', from пред- 'before' + принимать 'to take') + agent suffix -тель.

history.meaning: one who undertakes a business venture

предпринимать.etymology: Imperfective of предпринять ('to undertake'), coined in the 18th century from the Church Slavonic prefix пред- ('before, fore-') + принимать ('to take, accept') as a morphological calque of German unternehmen and French entreprendre ('to undertake').

предродовой.etymology: Compound adjective formed from prefix пред- ('before, pre-') + родовой ('relating to childbirth or delivery', derived from роды 'childbirth', from Proto-Slavic *rodъ 'birth, lineage').

председатель.etymology: Calque on Latin praeses (from praesidēre 'to sit in front, preside') and German Vorsitzender, formed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъсѣдати ('to sit in front, preside') + agent suffix -тель.

history.meaning: one who sits in front, presiding officer

предсказание.etymology: Verbal noun in -ание from предсказать ('to foretell, predict'), modelled with the Church Slavonic prefix пред- ('before, in advance', calquing Latin prae-dicere) + сказать ('to say, tell', from Proto-Slavic *sъkazati).

предсказуемый.etymology: Present passive participle of предсказывать ('to predict, foretell', calquing Latin praedicere), formed from prefix пред- ('before, fore-') + сказывать ('to tell, say', from Proto-Slavic *sъkazati) + -емый.

представитель.etymology: Formed from представить ('to place before, present, represent', a calque pattern matching Latin repraesentāre and German vorstellen) with the agent suffix -тель: 'one who represents others, a representative or spokesperson'.

представить.etymology: Formed with the Church Slavonic prefix пред- ('before, in front of') + ставить ('to place, set, stand', Proto-Slavic *staviti): literally 'to place before someone' (hence 'to present, introduce') or 'to set before one's mind' (hence 'to imagine, picture', calquing German sich vorstellen).

представиться.etymology: Reflexive of представить ('to present, introduce; to imagine'), formed from prefix пред- ('before') + ставить ('to place, set', from Proto-Slavic *staviti) + -ся ('to present oneself').

представление.etymology: Verbal noun from представить ('to present, perform, imagine', from пред- + ставить 'to place before', influenced by Latin repraesentatio and German Vorstellung) + suffix -ение.

представлять.etymology: Formed as the imperfective of представить ('to place before, present, introduce; to picture before one's mind'), built with the Old Church Slavonic prefix пред- ('before, in front of') + ставить ('to set, place', with labial epenthesis в -> вл in the imperfective). Its sense 'to imagine' (представлять себе) calques German sich vorstellen ('to place before oneself').

предстоять.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъстояти ('to stand before, be imminent'), formed from прѣдъ- ('before, in front of') + стояти ('to stand', Proto-Slavic *stojati).

history.meaning: to lie ahead, be in store

предупредить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдоупрѣдити ('to go ahead of, forestall, anticipate'), formed from прѣдъ- ('before') + оу- + прѣдити ('to go in front', from предъ / перед 'in front', Proto-Slavic *perdъ). In the 18th century, influenced by French prévenir ('to go before → to forewarn, notify in advance'), it acquired the modern meaning 'to warn'.

history.meaning: to forestall → to warn, notify in advance

предупреждать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of предупредить ('to warn, notify in advance; to prevent'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдоупрѣждати (showing the Church Slavonic reflex -жд- for Proto-Slavic *dj), built on предъ / перед ('before, in front').

history.meaning: to warn, notify in advance; to forestall

предупреждающий.etymology: Present active participle of предупреждать ('to warn, forestall'), borrowed with Church Slavonic vocalism (пред- 'before, in advance' + у- + преждать 'to go ahead of, anticipate', from передить / перед 'front', Proto-Slavic *perdъ).

предупреждение.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ение from предупредить ('to warn, forestall, prevent'), built from Church Slavonic пред- ('before, ahead') + упредить ('to forestall, anticipate', from the root of перед 'in front, before', Proto-Slavic *perdъ).

history.meaning: to forestall, warn → warning, advance notice

предчувствие.etymology: Formed as a calque on French pressentiment or German Vorgefühl from пред- ('before, fore-') + чувствие / чувство ('feeling, sense', from Proto-Slavic *čuvьstvo, from *čuti 'to feel, perceive').

прежде.etymology: Borrowed in its Church Slavonic form прежде (with non-pleophonic пре- and -жд- from Proto-Slavic *-dj-; compare native Old East Slavic переже), from Proto-Slavic *perdje, the comparative adverb of *perdъ ('front, before'; Russian перед): literally 'more to the front, earlier, before'.

прежний.etymology: Adjective formed from прежде ('before, formerly'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣжде (with жд < *dj; compare native East Slavic переже), comparative of *perdъ ('front, before').

history.meaning: former, previous, the same as before

презент.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via Polish prezent or German Präsent from French présent ('gift, present'), from Old French present ('something offered in someone's presence'), from Latin praesens.

президент.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century, initially for heads of state colleges and academies, later for heads of republic states) via German Präsident and French président from Latin praesidēns (genitive praesidentis, 'presiding officer, governor'), present participle of praesidēre ('to sit before, preside over, guard', from prae- 'before' + sedēre 'to sit').

history.meaning: to sit in front / preside → presiding head

преимущество.etymology: Derived from Old Church Slavonic прѣимущии ('superior, preeminent', active participle of прѣимѣти 'to have in excess, surpass', from прѣ- 'beyond, over' + имѣти 'to have', Proto-Slavic *jьměti) + suffix -ство.

прекрасно.etymology: Formed as the short neuter and adverbial derivative in -о of прекрасный ('wonderful, beautiful, fine').

прекрасный.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic прѣкрасьнъ ('surpassingly beautiful, splendid'), formed with the intensive prefix пре- (from Old Church Slavonic прѣ- 'across, beyond, very') + красный in its original Slavic meaning 'beautiful, fair' (Proto-Slavic *krasьnъ, before красный shifted to 'red' in Russian).
прекрасный.notes: Preserves the ancient Slavic meaning of красный ('beautiful'), also seen in Красная площадь ('Red [originally Beautiful] Square').

прекратить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣкратити ('to cut short, abridge, terminate'), formed from the prefix прѣ- (East Slavic пере-) and кратити ('to shorten', from кратъкъ 'short', East Slavic короткий, from Proto-Slavic *kortъkъ). Literally, прекратить means 'to cut short'.

history.meaning: to cut short, bring to an end

прекращать.etymology: Imperfective of прекратить ('to stop, cut short, terminate'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣкращати / прѣкратити ('to shorten, cut off', from прѣ- + кратити 'to shorten', from кратъкъ 'short', Proto-Slavic *kortъkъ).

прекращаться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive form of прекращать ('to stop, cease', from Old Church Slavonic прѣкращати 'to cut short, end', derived from кратъкъ 'short', Proto-Slavic *kortъkъ) + -ся.

прелестно.etymology: Adverb derived from прелестный ('charming, delightful', from прелесть 'charm, allure; in Old Church Slavonic прѣльсть deception, temptation') + -но.

прелесть.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣльсть ('deception, delusion, seduction, temptation'), from прѣ- + льсть ('deceit, cunning, flattery', from Proto-Slavic *lьstь, an early borrowing from Gothic lists 'craft, wile'); softened in 18th-century Russian to 'captivating charm, delight'.

премия.etymology: Borrowed via German Prämie or Polish premia from Latin praemium ('reward, prize, profit', originally 'what is taken before others', from prae- 'before' + emere 'to take').

преодолеть.etymology: Formed with Church Slavonic prefix пре- ('across, over', Old Church Slavonic прѣ-) + одолеть ('to overpower, prevail over', from о- + доля 'share, lot, fate', from Proto-Slavic *doľa).

препарат.etymology: Borrowed via German Präparat from Latin praeparatum ('something prepared'), neuter past passive participle of praeparare ('to prepare, make ready'), from prae- ('before') + parare ('to make ready').

преподаватель.etymology: Agent noun formed with the suffix -тель from преподавать ('to teach, lecture', in Church Slavonic and older Russian 'to hand over, transmit, impart'), built from пре- ('across, over') + подавать ('to give, serve', from дать 'to give', Proto-Slavic *dati).

преподавать.etymology: Imperfective of преподать ('to impart, give, teach'), formed with Old Church Slavonic prefix пре- + по- + давать ('to give', Proto-Slavic *davati), developing the specialized sense 'to lecture, teach a subject'.

history.meaning: to teach (at a school or university)

преподносить.etymology: Imperfective of преподнести ('to present, offer solemnly; to spring a surprise'), formed from Church Slavonic prefix пре- + подносить ('to bring up, present', from под- + носить 'to carry', Proto-Slavic *nositi).

прервать.etymology: Formed with Old Church Slavonic prefix пре- ('across, through', corresponding to native пере-) from рвать ('to tear, break'), from Proto-Slavic *rъvati.

прерваться.etymology: Reflexive of прервать ('to interrupt, break off', formed with Church Slavonic prefix пре- 'across, through' + рвать 'to tear, break', from Proto-Slavic *rъvati) + -ся.

прерывать.etymology: Imperfective of прервать ('to interrupt, break off'), formed with Church Slavonic prefix пре- ('across, through', corresponding to East Slavic пере-) + рывать (iterative of рвать 'to tear', from Proto-Slavic *rъvati).

пресечение.etymology: Verbal noun from пресечь ('to cut across, cut off, put a stop to'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣсѣчение, from прѣ- ('across') + сѣщи ('to cut, hew', Proto-Slavic *sěkti).

преследовать.etymology: Formed with Church Slavonic prefix пре- ('through, after', likely influenced by Polish prześladować) + следовать ('to follow', from след 'track, footprint', from Proto-Slavic *slědъ).

пресный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic прѣсьнъ / Old Church Slavonic прѣснъ ('unleavened, fresh'), from Proto-Slavic *prěsnъ ('fresh, unleavened, unfermented'), cognate with Lithuanian prėskas ('unleavened, sweet, unfermented').

пресс-конференция.etymology: Twentieth-century compound calque of English press conference (or German Pressekonferenz), combining пресса ('the press, print media', from French presse, ultimately from Latin pressare 'to press') + конференция ('conference', from Medieval Latin conferentia).

престижный.etymology: Derived from престиж ('prestige', borrowed in the 19th century from French prestige 'aura, glamour; originally illusion, conjuring trick', from Latin praestigium 'delusion,jugglery') + adjectival suffix -ный.

престол.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣстолъ ('throne, altar table'), formed from прѣ- + столъ ('table, seat, throne', from Proto-Slavic *stolъ, related to *stьlati 'to spread' / *stati 'to stand').

преступление.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣстѫплениѥ ('transgression, stepping across a forbidden line'), verbal noun from прѣстѫпити (Russian преступить, 'to step over, transgress, violate the law', from пре- 'across' + ступить 'to step', Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti).

преступник.etymology: Agent noun in -ник derived from преступить ('to step across, transgress, violate the law'), formed with Old Church Slavonic prefix пре- ('across, over') + ступить ('to step', Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti).

претендент.etymology: Borrowed via German Prätendent or French prétendant from Medieval/Modern Latin praetendens (genitive praetendentis), present active participle of praetendere ('to stretch forth, put forward a claim').

претендовать.etymology: Borrowed via Polish pretendować or German prätendieren from French prétendre / Latin praetendere ('to stretch before, hold out, lay claim to', from prae- 'before' + tendere 'to stretch').

претензия.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish pretensja or German Prätention from Medieval Latin praetēnsiō ('stretching forth, assertion of a right, claim'), from Latin praetendere ('to hold out before, lay claim').

преувеличивать.etymology: Imperfective of преувеличить ('to exaggerate, overstate'), formed from the Church Slavonic prefix пре- ('over, excessively') + увеличивать ('to increase, magnify', built on у- + великий 'great, large', Proto-Slavic *velikъ).

преувеличить.etymology: Formed from Church Slavonic intensive prefix пре- ('over, excessively') + увеличить ('to enlarge, increase', from у- + величить 'to make great, magnify', derived from великий 'great, large', Proto-Slavic *velikъ).

префект.etymology: Borrowed via French préfet or German Präfekt from Latin praefectus ('overseer, governor, prefect'), noun use of the past passive participle of praeficere ('to set over, put in charge', from prae- 'before, over' + facere 'to make, put').

history.meaning: one placed in charge, governor, prefect

префектура.etymology: Borrowed via German Präfektur or French préfecture from Latin praefectura ('office or jurisdiction of a prefect'), derived from praefectus ('prefect, governor').

history.meaning: office or district of a prefect

при.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic при and Proto-Slavic *pri ('at, by, near, in the presence of'), from Proto-Indo-European *prey / *preh₂i, closely related to Lithuanian prie ('at, by, near') and Latin prae ('before, in front of').

history.meaning: near, in the presence of, during the reign of
by, attached to, in the presence of, during

при.notes: Always governs the prepositional case: при свете лампы ('by the light of a lamp'), при входе ('at the entrance').

прибавка.etymology: Derived from прибавить / прибавлять ('to add, increase', formed from prefix при- 'to, in addition' + бавить, causative of быть 'to be', from Proto-Slavic *baviti 'to cause to be, prolong, add') + noun suffix -ка.

прибежать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb inherited from Old East Slavic прибѣжати, formed from при- ('to, arrival') + бежать ('to run', from Proto-Slavic *běžati, from PIE *bʰegʷ- 'to flee, run').

history.meaning: to come running, arrive at a run

приберечь.etymology: Formed with the prefix при- ('aside, in reserve') and беречь ('to guard, keep safe'). The base verb comes from Old East Slavic беречи and Proto-Slavic *bergti ('to guard, care for'), showing East Slavic pleophony (-ере- from *-er-). It derives from the Proto-Indo-European root *bʰergʰ- ('to keep safe, protect, bury'), making it cognate with English bury and borrow.

прибираться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive verb from прибрать ('to put in order, tidy up', from prefix при- + брать 'to take, gather', from Proto-Slavic *bьrati) + -ся.

прибить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic прибити ('to nail on, beat down'), formed from prefix при- ('to, against') + бить ('to beat, strike', from Proto-Slavic *biti).

history.meaning: to fasten by striking, beat down
to nail up; (colloquial) to strike dead, kill

приближаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of приблизиться ('to approach, draw near'), formed from prefix при- ('toward') + ближаться (from близкий / близ 'near, close', from Proto-Slavic *blizъ) + -ся.

приблизить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic приближити ('to bring near'), formed from prefix при- ('to, toward') + близить ('to bring near', derived from близ 'near', from Proto-Slavic *bliziti).

прибой.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with ablaut from прибить ('to beat against [the shore]', from prefix при- 'against, toward' + бить 'to beat, strike', Proto-Slavic *biti, ablaut grade *bojь).

history.meaning: to beat or wash against the shore

приболеть.etymology: Formed from attenuative prefix при- ('slightly, a bit') + болеть ('to be ill, ache', from боль 'pain, illness', from Proto-Slavic *bolěti).

history.meaning: to fall slightly ill, be a bit unwell

прибор.etymology: Deverbal noun from прибрать ('to fit together, arrange, put in order', from при- + брать 'to take'): originally 'a matched set of gear or tableware' (still used in столовый прибор 'cutlery, place setting'), and later 'instrument, gauge, device, apparatus'.

history.meaning: set of fittings, gear, place setting

прибрать.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from при- ('together, into order') + брать ('to take', inherited from Old East Slavic бьрати, Proto-Slavic *bьrati): 'to gather things into their proper places, tidy up, clean up'.

history.meaning: to tidy up, clean up; (colloq.) прибрать к рукам 'to take control of'

прибывать.etymology: Imperfective of прибыть ('to arrive; to increase, rise'), formed from prefix при- ('to, toward; in addition') + бывать (iterative of быть 'to be', from Proto-Slavic *byvati).

history.meaning: to be repeatedly, come to be

прибыль.etymology: Derived from прибыть ('to increase, accrue, be added', from prefix при- + быть 'to be', Proto-Slavic *byti) + archaic action/result noun suffix -ль (as in убыль).

прибыть.etymology: Formed with prefix при- ('to, arrival, addition') from быть ('to be'), inherited from Old East Slavic прибыти, from Proto-Slavic *pri-byti.

history.meaning: to come to be at a place, arrive, increase

привал.etymology: Deverbal noun from привалить ('to roll/lean against, moor a boat to shore, halt on a march to rest'), formed from при- ('to, against') + валить ('to roll, lean, throng', Proto-Slavic *valiti).

привезти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic привезти (Proto-Slavic *privezti), formed from the directional prefix при- ('arrival at a destination') + везти ('to convey by vehicle, haul', Proto-Slavic *vezti, cognate with Latin vehere and English wagon/way).

history.meaning: to bring by cart or boat

привезти.notes: Past tense drops the infinitive ending and vocalizes to ё in the masculine: привёз, привезла, привезли.

привести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic привести (Proto-Slavic *privesti), formed from при- ('to a destination') + вести ('to lead on foot', Proto-Slavic *vesti, stem вед-): 'to bring someone along on foot, lead to a place or result'.

history.meaning: to bring (leading someone); to lead to

привести.notes: Conjugates with the dental stem вед-: я приведу, ты приведёшь; past tense привёл, привела.

привет.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic привѣтъ ('friendly welcome, greeting, affable speech'), a deverbal noun from привѣтити ('to greet, welcome warmly'), built from prefix при- + *větъ ('speech, counsel, address', the same Proto-Slavic root seen in ответ 'answer' and совет 'advice'). In the 20th century Привет! became the standard informal greeting 'Hi! / Hello!'.

приветствовать.etymology: Formed with suffix -ствовать from привет ('greeting, welcome'), derived from при- + вет ('word, counsel, greeting', from Proto-Slavic *větъ; compare ответ, совет).

прививка.etymology: Derived from привить / прививать ('to graft a plant; to inoculate, vaccinate', literally 'to twist/entwine onto', from prefix при- + вить 'to twist, plait, wind', Proto-Slavic *viti) + noun suffix -ка.

привидение.etymology: Verbal noun from привидеться ('to appear in a vision or dream, seem'), formed from prefix при- + видеться (from видеть 'to see', Proto-Slavic *viděti) + suffix -ение.

history.meaning: to appear as a vision, seem

привинтить.etymology: Formed in Russian from при- ('fastening onto, attaching') + винтить ('to screw', derived from винт 'screw', borrowed via Polish gwint from German Gewinde 'screw thread'): 'to screw on, fasten with a screw'.

history.meaning: screw -> to screw on, attach with screws

привинтить.notes: First-person singular has т -> ч mutation: я привинчу, ты привинтишь.

привлечение.etymology: Verbal noun from привлечь ('to draw toward, attract, engage'), borrowed from or modeled on Old Church Slavonic привлѣчение / привлѣщи (corresponding to East Slavic приволочь, from при- + Proto-Slavic *velkti 'to drag, draw').

привлечь.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic привлѣщи ('to draw toward, attract', compare native East Slavic приволочь), from Proto-Slavic *pri-velkti ('to drag/draw toward').

приводить.etymology: Imperfective of привести ('to bring on foot, lead to'), inherited from Old East Slavic приводити, formed from при- ('to, arrival') + водить ('to lead', from Proto-Slavic *voditi).

history.meaning: to bring (a person); to lead to, cite

привозить.etymology: Imperfective of привезти ('to bring by vehicle, deliver'), inherited from Old East Slavic привозити, formed from при- ('to, arrival') + возить ('to convey by vehicle', from Proto-Slavic *voziti).

history.meaning: to bring by cart or boat

привокзальный.etymology: Prepositional-prefixal adjective formed from при ('by, near, adjacent to') + вокзал ('railway station', borrowed from English Vauxhall [Pleasure Gardens], which came to mean a concert pavilion and then a railway terminal in Russian) + suffix -ный.

привыкать.etymology: Imperfective of привыкнуть ('to get used to, grow accustomed'), formed from при- ('to') + the Proto-Slavic root *vyk- (*vyknǫti 'to learn by habit, become accustomed', cognate with Lithuanian jùnkti 'to get used to').

привыкнуть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic привыкнути, formed with prefix при- from выкнуть ('to learn, grow accustomed'), from Proto-Slavic *vyknǫti (from PIE *wuk- / *wewk-, related to учить 'to teach' and наука).

привычка.etymology: Noun in -ка derived from привыкнуть ('to get used to, become accustomed'), formed with prefix при- from выкнуть ('to learn by habit, grow accustomed'), from Proto-Slavic *vyknǫti (related to учить and навык).

привычный.etymology: Derived from привычка ('habit') / привыкнуть ('to get used to, become accustomed', formed from prefix при- + выкнуть 'to learn, get accustomed', from Proto-Slavic *vyknǫti, cognate with учить) + adjectival suffix -ный.

привязать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic привязати ('to tie to, bind, attach'), formed from prefix при- ('to, onto') + вязать ('to tie, bind', from Proto-Slavic *vęzati).

пригласительный.etymology: Derived from пригласить ('to invite', from prefix при- + гласить 'to call, voice', with Church Slavonic non-pleophonic глас 'voice' from Proto-Slavic *golsъ) + adjectival suffix -тельн-ый.

пригласить.etymology: Adopted with the South Slavic / Church Slavonic root vocalism -глас- (compare native East Slavic -голос- in голос 'voice') from пригласити ('to call to oneself, summon, invite'), formed from при- ('to') + гласить ('to call, sound', from глас 'voice', Proto-Slavic *golsъ).

morphemes.meaning: voice, call (Church Slavonic counterpart of голос)

пригласить.notes: First-person singular has с -> ш mutation: я приглашу, ты пригласишь.

приглашать.etymology: Borrowed with Old Church Slavonic non-pleophonic -глаш- (compare native голос 'voice') from приглашати, imperfective of пригласити ('to call to oneself, summon, invite'), from при- + гласъ ('voice, call', Proto-Slavic *golsъ).

history.meaning: to call toward oneself, summon, invite

приглашаться.etymology: Passive/reflexive form of приглашать ('to invite', imperfective of пригласить, from prefix при- + Old Church Slavonic stem глашати 'to call, proclaim', from Proto-Slavic *golsiti) + -ся.

приглашение.etymology: Verbal noun from пригласить / приглашать ('to invite', formed from prefix при- + Church Slavonic root глас- 'voice, call', from Proto-Slavic *golsъ) + suffix -ение.

приглядеть.etymology: Formed with prefix при- ('attentively, watching over') from глядеть ('to look'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *ględěti ('to look, gaze').

history.meaning: to look after, to keep an eye on

приглядеться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of приглядеть, formed from при- ('closely, accustomed to') + глядеть ('to look', Proto-Slavic *ględěti) + -ся.

history.meaning: to take a closer look, to observe closely

приглядывать.etymology: Imperfective of приглядеть ('to look after, keep an eye on'), formed from prefix при- + глядеть ('to look, gaze', from Proto-Slavic *ględěti) + imperfective suffix -ывать.

history.meaning: to keep an eye on, look after

приговор.etymology: Deverbal noun from приговорить ('to sentence, condemn; in Old Russian to decide by council, agree upon'), formed from prefix при- + говорить ('to speak, say', from Proto-Slavic *govoriti).

пригодиться.etymology: Formed from prefix при- + годиться ('to be suitable, fit, be of use', derived from год 'suitable time, year; in Proto-Slavic *godъ fitting time, pleasing thing') + -ся.

history.meaning: to come in handy, prove useful

пригонять.etymology: Imperfective of пригнать ('to drive in, bring by driving'), formed from prefix при- ('to, toward') + гонять ('to drive, chase', iterative of гнать, from Proto-Slavic *goniti / *gъnati).

history.meaning: to drive in, deliver by driving

приготовить.etymology: Formed with the perfective prefix при- + готовить ('to prepare, make ready; to cook'), derived from готовый ('ready', from Old East Slavic готовыи and Proto-Slavic *gotovъ).

history.meaning: to prepare, make ready; to cook (a dish or meal)

приготовиться.etymology: Reflexive of приготовить ('to prepare, make ready, cook'), formed from prefix при- + готовить ('to prepare', derived from готовый 'ready', from Proto-Slavic *gotovъ) + -ся.

приготовление.etymology: Verbal noun from приготовить ('to prepare, cook', from prefix при- + готовить 'to prepare', from готовый 'ready', Proto-Slavic *gotovъ) + suffix -ение.

приготовленный.etymology: Past passive participle of приготовить ('to prepare, cook'), formed from prefix при- + готовить ('to make ready, prepare', from Proto-Slavic *gotoviti).

пригреть.etymology: Formed from prefix при- + греть ('to warm, heat', inherited from Old East Slavic грѣти, from Proto-Slavic *grěti 'to warm', related to *gorěti 'to burn' and *žarъ 'heat').

history.meaning: to warm gently; to shelter, take in

придавать.etymology: Imperfective of придать ('to add, give, impart, attach [importance]'), formed from prefix при- ('to, in addition') + давать ('to give', iterative of дать, from Proto-Slavic *davati).

придавить.etymology: Formed from prefix при- ('down, against') + давить ('to press, squeeze, crush', inherited from Old East Slavic давити, from Proto-Slavic *daviti 'to press, strangle').

придираться.etymology: Imperfective of придраться ('to find fault with, pick on', literally 'to tear/snag onto someone'), formed from prefix при- + дирать (iterative stem of драть 'to tear, strip', from Proto-Slavic *dьrati) + -ся.

history.meaning: to fasten upon, find fault with
to pick on, cavil, find fault

придраться.etymology: Formed from prefix при- ('to, onto') + драть ('to tear, pull', from Proto-Slavic *dьrati) + reflexive suffix -ся, evolving from 'to snag or tear onto' to 'to seize upon a pretext, find fault with'.

history.meaning: to find fault with, pick on

придумать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix при- (indicating addition or mental attainment) and думать ('to think'), from Old East Slavic думати and Proto-Slavic *dumati (from *duma 'thought, counsel', an early borrowing from Gothic dōms 'judgment').

придумывать.etymology: Imperfective of придумать ('to think up, devise, invent'), formed with prefix при- from думать ('to think'), inherited from Old East Slavic думати, from Proto-Slavic *dumati.

придурок.etymology: Formed in Russian with the prefix при- ('slightly, touched') + the root of дурак / дурной ('fool / foolish', from Proto-Slavic *durъ 'stupefied, foolish') + the person suffix -ок; closely connected with придуриваться ('to play the fool').

приезд.etymology: Deverbal noun from приехать / приезжать ('to arrive by vehicle or horse'), formed from prefix при- ('to, toward') + езд (from ездить / ехать 'to ride, travel', from Proto-Slavic *ězdъ, *ěxati).

приезжать.etymology: Imperfective partner of приехать ('to arrive by vehicle'), formed from the arrival prefix при- + езжать (iterative stem of ездить / ехать 'to travel by vehicle, ride', from Proto-Slavic *ěxati / *ězditi).

morphemes.meaning: ride, travel by vehicle (ездить, with зд → зж)

приехать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic приѣхати, from Proto-Slavic *prijěxati, formed from the arrival prefix *pri- ('up to, arriving at') + *jěxati (Russian ехать 'to go by vehicle, ride').

history.meaning: to arrive (by horse, boat, or cart)

приехать.notes: Always implies arrival by transport (train, car, bus, bicycle), whereas **прийти** is arrival on foot.

прижать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic прижати ('to press against, squeeze'), formed from prefix при- ('to, against') + жать ('to press, squeeze', from Proto-Slavic *žęti 'to squeeze, compress').

приз.etymology: Borrowed via French prise ('capture, seized booty, prize') or German Prise / Preis, from Old French prise ('taking, seizure'), feminine past participle of prendre ('to take', from Latin prehendere), blended semantically with French prix ('price, reward', from Latin pretium).

призвание.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic призьваниѥ ('calling, summons, vocation', calquing Ancient Greek κλῆσις and Latin vocatio), verbal noun from призвать ('to call, summon', from при- + звать, Proto-Slavic *zъvati).

приземлиться.etymology: Twentieth-century aviation verb formed as a prefixal-suffixal derivative from при- ('to, onto') + земля ('earth, ground', from Proto-Slavic *zemľa) + verbal suffix -ить + -ся ('to touch down on the ground').

признавать.etymology: Imperfective of признать ('to recognize, acknowledge, confess'), formed with prefix при- from знать ('to know'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *znati.

признаваться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of признаться ('to confess, admit'), formed from prefix при- + знавать (iterative of знать 'to know, recognize', from Proto-Slavic *znati) + -ся.

признак.etymology: Formed from prefix при- + знак ('sign, mark, token', from Proto-Slavic *znakъ, derived from *znati 'to know, recognize'), probably influenced by Polish przyznak or Czech příznak.

признание.etymology: Verbal noun in -ние from признать ('to acknowledge, confess, recognize'), formed from при- + знать ('to know', Proto-Slavic *znati).

признательный.etymology: Adjective in -тельный formed from признавать / признать ('to acknowledge [a debt or kindness]'), calquing French reconnaissant ('grateful', literally 'recognizing'), built on знать ('to know').

признать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic признати ('to recognize, acknowledge'), formed from prefix при- + знать ('to know', from Proto-Slavic *znati).

признаться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed from признать ('to recognize, acknowledge'), built from the prefix при- and знать ('to know', from Proto-Slavic *znati, PIE *ǵneh₃-). With the reflexive suffix -ся, признаться means 'to acknowledge about oneself, confess, admit' (often in love: признаться в любви).

призрак.etymology: Borrowed from Church Slavonic призракъ ('appearance, vision, phantom'), formed from prefix при- + зракъ ('sight, look, form, image', with non-pleophonic зр- from Proto-Slavic *zorkъ, related to *zьrěti 'to look, see').

прийти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic приити / прити ('to come, arrive on foot'), formed from the prefix при- ('up to, arrival') + идти ('to walk, go', Old East Slavic ити, from Proto-Slavic *iti). Like идти, it takes its past tense (пришёл, пришла, пришли) from the suppletive stem *šьd-.

прийтись.etymology: Perfective reflexive/impersonal verb formed by adding -сь to прийти ('to come, arrive on foot', from при- + идти, Proto-Slavic *prijьti). From the concrete sense of two parts 'coming together into alignment, fitting' (прийтись по вкусу 'to suit one's taste'), the impersonal dative construction мне пришлось + infinitive developed the sense 'it fell to my lot to, I had to'.

history.meaning: to come to fit, fall to someone's lot
to fit; (impersonal + dat.) to have to

rootFamily.gloss: to have to (impf.); to be related to

приказ.etymology: Formed in Middle Russian as a prefixal-stem noun from приказать ('to order, command', from при- + казать 'to show, declare, instruct', Proto-Slavic *kazati). In Muscovite Rus', a приказ was also a central government chancellery executing the Tsar's orders.

приказать.etymology: Formed with prefix при- from казать ('to show, say, order'), inherited from Old East Slavic приказати ('to order, entrust'), from Proto-Slavic *pri-kazati.

прикалываться.etymology: Colloquial slang semantic development of прикалываться ('to pin onto oneself', imperfective of приколоться, from при- + колоть 'to prick, pin, stab', Proto-Slavic *kolti), which in late 20th-century youth slang came to mean 'to get a kick out of, crack jokes, mess around'.

history.meaning: to pin on; (slang) to tease, amuse
to joke around, kid, mess with

прикарманить.etymology: Colloquial prefixal-suffixal verb formed from при- ('to oneself') + карман ('pocket', borrowed from Turkic, cf. Tatar/Chagatai karman 'purse, pocket') + verbal suffix -ить ('to put into one's own pocket, appropriate').

прикасаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of прикоснуться ('to touch'), formed from prefix при- ('to') + касаться ('to touch', iterative of коснуться, from Proto-Slavic *kasati / *kosnǫti 'to touch').

history.meaning: to touch lightly, make contact with

приклеить.etymology: Formed from the attachment prefix при- ('onto, fast to') + клеить ('to glue, paste'), which is derived from клей ('glue, tree resin, birdlime', Proto-Slavic *kъlejь).

приключение.etymology: Verbal noun in -ение from приключиться ('to happen unexpectedly, befall'), built on prefix при- + ключиться ('to happen, fit together like a key or hook', from ключ 'hook, key', Proto-Slavic *kľučь). Originally 'an unexpected event or occurrence', then an 'adventure'.

history.meaning: to happen, befall → unexpected occurrence, adventure

приколоть.etymology: Formed from при- ('fastening onto') + колоть ('to prick, pierce, pin', Proto-Slavic *kolti): 'to pin on, fasten with a pin or clip'.

history.meaning: to pin on, fasten with a pin

прикольно.etymology: Colloquial adverb formed from прикольный ('cool, funny, amusing'), derived from the slang noun прикол ('joke, gag, fun thing'), itself a deverbal noun from приколоть ('to pin, fasten with a pin; in slang, to tease or crack a joke', built on при- + колоть 'to prick, pierce', Proto-Slavic *kolti).

history.meaning: to pin / crack a joke → gag, fun → cool, funny → cool, fun

прикольнуться.etymology: Semelfactive colloquial slang verb formed from приколоться / прикалываться ('to joke, pull a prank', originally 'to pin oneself to', from при- + колоть 'to prick, pin', Proto-Slavic *kolti) with suffix -ну- + -ся.

history.meaning: to pull a prank, make a joke

прикольный.etymology: Late 20th-century slang adjective formed with -ный from прикол ('joke, gag, fun thing'), deverbal noun from приколоть / прикалываться ('to pin; in slang, to crack jokes, needle, have fun'), from при- + колоть ('to prick, pin', Proto-Slavic *kolti).

прикончить.etymology: Formed with prefix при- ('completely, to the end') from кончить ('to finish, end'), derived from конец ('end'), from Proto-Slavic *konьcь.

history.meaning: to finish off, to kill, to bump off

прикрепить.etymology: Formed with prefix при- ('to, onto') from крепить ('to fasten, strengthen'), derived from крепкий ('strong, firm'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *krěpъ ('strong, firm').

history.meaning: to attach, to assign, to fasten

прикрутить.etymology: Formed from prefix при- ('to, onto') + крутить ('to twist, turn, wind', inherited from Old East Slavic крутити, from Proto-Slavic *krǫtiti 'to twist, whirl').

history.meaning: to screw on, fasten by twisting; to turn down

прикрывать.etymology: Imperfective of прикрыть ('to cover, shield, conceal'), formed from prefix при- + крывать (iterative of крыть 'to cover', from Proto-Slavic *kryti).

прикрытие.etymology: Verbal noun from прикрыть ('to cover, shield, conceal', from prefix при- + крыть 'to cover', from Proto-Slavic *kryti) + suffix -тие.

прикрыть.etymology: Formed with prefix при- ('slightly; protectively') from крыть ('to cover'), inherited from Old East Slavic крыти, from Proto-Slavic *kryti ('to cover, hide').

прилетать.etymology: Imperfective of прилететь ('to arrive by flying'), formed from prefix при- ('to, toward') + летать ('to fly', iterative of лететь, from Proto-Slavic *lětati / *letěti).

history.meaning: to fly in, arrive by plane

прилететь.etymology: Formed with prefix при- ('arrival') from лететь ('to fly'), inherited from Old East Slavic прилетѣти, from Proto-Slavic *pri-letěti ('to arrive by flying').

history.meaning: to fly to, arrive by air
to arrive (by air), to fly in

прилечь.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from attenuative при- ('for a short while, lightly') + лечь ('to lie down', inherited from Old East Slavic лечи, from Proto-Slavic *legti, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵʰ- 'to lie down', cognate with English lie and German liegen).

history.meaning: to lie down for a bit
to lie down (for a short rest)

прилипчивый.etymology: Adjective formed with suffix -чивый from прилипать / прилипнуть ('to stick to, cling to'), from при- ('to') + липнуть ('to stick, adhere', from Proto-Slavic *lьpnǫti / *lipati).

прилично.etymology: Adverb formed from приличный ('decent, proper, seemly'), originally 'fitting the face/person, suitable', from при- + лик / лицо ('face, appearance', Proto-Slavic *likъ).

приличный.etymology: Inherited via Old East Slavic приличьныи ('similar, fitting, seemly'), formed from при- + лик / лицо ('face, form, appearance', Proto-Slavic *likъ), shifting from 'matching in appearance, suitable' to 'decent, respectable, sizable'.

приложение.etymology: Verbal noun from приложить ('to lay beside, attach, apply'), formed from при- ('to, beside') + ложить ('to lay, place', Proto-Slavic *ložiti); the modern computing sense 'app' is a semantic calque of English application.

приложить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic приложити (Proto-Slavic *priložiti), formed from при- ('against, next to') + ложить ('to lay, place', Proto-Slavic *ložiti): 'to lay or press something flat against a surface, apply, or enclose/attach'.

прилёт.etymology: Deverbal noun from прилететь ('to arrive by flying'), formed from при- ('arrival') + лёт / лететь ('to fly', inherited from Proto-Slavic *letěti).

приманка.etymology: Derived from приманить / приманивать ('to lure, attract, beckon', from prefix при- + манить 'to beckon, lure, entice', from Proto-Slavic *maniti) + noun suffix -ка.

применить.etymology: Formed from prefix при- ('to') + менить ('to change, exchange, match to', derived from мена 'exchange, change', from Proto-Slavic *měniti 'to change, exchange'); originally meant 'to compare, adapt, match to' and hence 'to apply, put to use'.

history.meaning: to adapt, compare; to apply, use

пример.etymology: Deverbal noun from примерить ('to measure against, try on, match'), formed from prefix при- ('to, against') + мерить ('to measure', from мера 'measure', from Proto-Slavic *měra).

примерить.etymology: Formed from the prefix при- ('fitting to, matching against') + мерить ('to measure', from мера 'measure', Proto-Slavic *měra): literally 'to measure a garment or shoe against oneself', hence 'to try on'.

примерка.etymology: Action noun derived from примерить / примерять ('to try on clothes, measure for fit', from prefix при- + мерить 'to measure', from Proto-Slavic *měriti) + suffix -ка.

примерно.etymology: Adverb derived from примерный ('approximate; exemplary', from пример 'example, rough measure against something', derived from при- + мера 'measure', Proto-Slavic *měra) + -но.

примерный.etymology: Adjective formed with -ный from пример ('example, model; approximate measure'), derived from примерить ('to measure against, try on'), from при- + мера ('measure', Proto-Slavic *měra).

примета.etymology: Deverbal noun from приметить ('to notice, mark, observe'), formed from prefix при- + метить ('to mark, aim', derived from мета 'mark, target, sign', from Proto-Slavic *měta).

примирение.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic примирениѥ ('reconciliation, peacemaking'), verbal noun from примирить ('to reconcile', from при- + мир 'peace', Proto-Slavic *mirъ) + -ение.

примирительный.etymology: Derived from примирить ('to reconcile, make peace between', from prefix при- + мирить 'to reconcile', from мир 'peace', Proto-Slavic *mirъ) + adjectival suffix -тельн-ый.

примирить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic примирити ('to reconcile, make peace'), formed from prefix при- + мирить ('to make peace', from мир 'peace', from Proto-Slavic *mirъ).

примчаться.etymology: Formed from prefix при- ('to, toward') + мчаться ('to rush, speed along', from мчать 'to carry off swiftly', inherited from Old East Slavic мъчати, from Proto-Slavic *mъčati 'to push, drag, rush', related to *mъknǫti 'to move, dart').

принадлежать.etymology: Formed in Early Modern Russian (calquing Polish przynależeć and German angehören / zukommen) from при- + над- + лежать ('to lie', Proto-Slavic *ležati): literally 'to lie under/by someone's rightful domain', hence 'to belong to'.
принадлежать.notes: Takes the dative case: эта вещь принадлежит мне ('this thing belongs to me').

принести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic принести ('to bring by carrying'), formed from the arrival prefix при- + нести ('to carry on foot', from Proto-Slavic *nesti, from PIE *h₁neḱ- 'to reach, carry, obtain').

принимать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of принять ('to take, accept, receive'), inherited from Old East Slavic приимати, formed from the prefix при- ('to, towards') and -нимать (with epenthetic н- reanalyzed from prefixes ending in a nasal, from Old East Slavic имати 'to take', iterative of яти, Proto-Slavic *jьmati).

history.meaning: to receive, accept, take (medicine, guests, a shower, or a decision)

приносить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic приносити (Proto-Slavic *prinositi), the imperfective counterpart of принести ('to bring by carrying'), formed from при- ('to a place') + носить ('to carry', iterative of нести, Proto-Slavic *nositi).
приносить.notes: First-person singular has с -> ш mutation: я приношу, ты приносишь.

принтер.etymology: Late 20th-century borrowing from English printer, agent/instrument noun from print (from Old French preinte 'impression', from Latin premere 'to press').

принц.etymology: Borrowed via German Prinz from Old French prince ('prince, ruler, first citizen'), from Latin princeps ('first person, chief, sovereign', from primus 'first' + capere 'to take').

принцесса.etymology: Borrowed via German Prinzessin / French princesse ('princess'), formed from prince ('prince', from Latin princeps) + feminine suffix -esse.

принцип.etymology: Borrowed via German Prinzip or French principe from Latin principium ('beginning, foundation, fundamental rule'), derived from princeps ('first, chief', from primus 'first' + capere 'to take').

принципиально.etymology: Adverb derived from принципиальный ('principled, fundamental, a matter of principle', from принцип 'principle', borrowed from Latin principium 'beginning, foundation, principle') + -но.

принципиальность.etymology: Abstract noun in -ость formed from принципиальный ('principled, of principle'), derived from принцип (from Latin principium 'foundation, principle').

принципиальный.etymology: Derived from принцип ('principle', borrowed via German Prinzip or French principe from Latin principium 'beginning, origin, fundamental rule', from princeps 'first') + adjectival suffix -альн-ый (after Late Latin principalis / German prinzipiell).

принятие.etymology: Verbal noun from принять ('to take, accept, adopt'), inherited from Old East Slavic приняти, from Proto-Slavic *pri-jęti ('to take to oneself, receive', from *jęti 'to take').

принятый.etymology: Past passive participle of принять ('to take, accept, receive', inherited from Old East Slavic прияти, with epenthetic -н- after prepositions, from prefix при- + Proto-Slavic *jęti 'to take').

принять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic приятии / приняти, from Proto-Slavic *prijęti ('to take to oneself, receive, accept'), formed from the prefix *pri- ('to, toward') + *jęti ('to take, grasp', PIE *h₁em-), with the epenthetic -н- generalized from old prepositional combinations.

history.meaning: to accept, receive; to mistake for

принять.notes: In the construction *принять кого-то за кого-то*, it means 'to mistake someone for someone else'.

приобрести.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic приобрѣсти ('to find, gain, acquire'), formed from prefix при- + обрѣсти ('to find, discover', from *ob- + Proto-Slavic *rěsti 'to find, meet with').

приобретение.etymology: Verbal noun from приобрести ('to acquire, gain', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic приобрѣсти, from при- + обрѣсти 'to find, discover') + suffix -ение.

приобщить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic приобъщити ('to make a partaker, unite with, add to'), formed from при- + общий ('common, shared', from Proto-Slavic *obьťь).

history.meaning: to join to a whole, associate
to add, to attach (to a case file); to acquaint with

приостановить.etymology: Formed from attenuative prefix при- ('temporarily, somewhat') + остановить ('to stop, halt', from о- + становить 'to set, place, stand', from стан 'camp, stature, stand', Proto-Slavic *stanъ).

history.meaning: to set up, bring to a stand

припарковаться.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix при- + парковаться ('to park a vehicle', from парковать + -ся, derived from парк 'park, depot', ultimately from English to park / French parquer).

history.meaning: to leave a vehicle in a designated place

приписать.etymology: Formed with prefix при- ('in addition, onto') from писать ('to write'), inherited from Old East Slavic писати, from Proto-Slavic *pisati.

history.meaning: to ascribe, credit, add in writing

приписка.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -ка from приписать ('to add in writing, append a note'), built on prefix при- ('in addition, onto') + писать ('to write', from Proto-Slavic *pьsati).

history.meaning: to add in writing → postscript, added written note

приплыть.etymology: Formed from prefix при- ('to, toward') + плыть ('to swim, float, sail', inherited from Old East Slavic плыти, from Proto-Slavic *plyti, from Proto-Indo-European *plew- 'to flow, float, swim').

history.meaning: to arrive by swimming or sailing
to swim/sail in; (idiomatic) to reach a dead end

приподнять.etymology: Formed from attenuative prefix при- ('slightly, a little') + поднять ('to lift, raise', from под- + ять 'to take', from Proto-Slavic *podъjęti).

history.meaning: to lift slightly, raise a bit

припугнуть.etymology: Formed with attenuative prefix при- ('slightly, a little') from пугнуть ('to frighten, startle'), semelfactive of пугать ('to scare').

history.meaning: to scare a little, to give a fright

приработок.etymology: Derived from приработать ('to earn on the side, earn in addition', from prefix при- 'in addition' + работать 'to work', from работа 'work', Proto-Slavic *orbota) + noun suffix -ок.

природа.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic природа ('birth, origin, lineage, innate character') and reinforced as a calque on Latin nātūra (via Polish przyroda), formed from при- + род ('birth, kind, generation', from Proto-Slavic *rodъ).

history.meaning: that which is inborn, birth, nature

природный.etymology: Derived from природа ('nature, birth, origin', formed from prefix при- + род 'birth, kin, kind', from Proto-Slavic *rodъ, calquing Latin natura) + adjectival suffix -ный.

прирождённый.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прирожденъ (with жд < *dj), past passive participle of природити ('to beget, endow by birth'), from при- + родити ('to give birth', Proto-Slavic *roditi).

присаживаться.etymology: Reflexive imperfective formed with attenuative prefix при- ('for a moment, on the edge') from саживаться / садиться ('to sit down'), from Proto-Slavic *saditi ('to seat').

history.meaning: to take a seat, to sit down

присесть.etymology: Formed with attenuative prefix при- ('briefly, on the edge; or squatting down') from сесть (сяду, 'to sit down'), inherited from Old East Slavic сѣсти, from Proto-Slavic *sěsti.

history.meaning: to sit down (for a moment); to squat

прислать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic присълати (Proto-Slavic *prisъlati), formed from при- ('to the recipient') + слать ('to send', Proto-Slavic *sъlati): 'to send something so that it arrives here/there'.
прислать.notes: Future tense shows сл -> шл palatalization: я пришлю, ты пришлёшь, они пришлют.

прислушиваться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of прислушаться ('to listen closely, lend an ear, heed'), formed from prefix при- ('toward, closely') + слушать ('to listen', from Proto-Slavic *slušati) + -ива- + -ся.

присматривать.etymology: Imperfective of присмотреть ('to look after, keep an eye on'), formed from prefix при- + сматривать (iterative of смотреть 'to look, watch', from Proto-Slavic *sъmotriti).

history.meaning: to keep an eye on, look after

присмотр.etymology: Deverbal noun from присмотреть ('to look after, watch over'), formed with prefix при- ('attentively') from смотреть ('to look, watch', Proto-Slavic *sъmotriti).

присмотреть.etymology: Formed from prefix при- + смотреть ('to look, watch', inherited from Old East Slavic съмотрити, from Proto-Slavic *sъmotriti).

history.meaning: to look after, keep an eye on

присмотреться.etymology: Reflexive of присмотреть ('to look closely'), formed from prefix при- ('closely, attentively') + смотреть ('to look, watch', from Proto-Slavic *sъmotriti) + -ся ('to peer closely, get used to seeing').

history.meaning: to take a closer look, examine closely

присниться.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix при- + сниться ('to appear in a dream, be dreamed', derived from сон, genitive сна 'sleep, dream', from Proto-Slavic *sъnъ, from PIE *swep-no-s).

присоединиться.etymology: Reflexive of присоединить ('to join, unite with, annex'), formed from prefix при- ('to') + соединить ('to unite, join together', from со- + единый 'one, single', Old Church Slavonic ѥдинъ, Proto-Slavic *jedinъ) + -ся.

присоединяться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of присоединиться ('to join'), formed from prefix при- + соединяться ('to unite, join', derived from со- + единый 'one', from Old Church Slavonic ѥдинъ).

приспособленный.etymology: Past passive participle of приспособить ('to adapt, fit'), formed from при- + способ ('way, method, means', borrowed via Polish sposób or formed from пособь 'help, aid', related to поcобить and себе).

приставать.etymology: Imperfective of пристать ('to stick to, put in to shore, latch onto, pester'), formed with prefix при- ('to, against') from ставать / стать ('to stand', Proto-Slavic *stati).

history.meaning: to come to stand beside, stick to
to pester, to harass; to dock

приставка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with the suffix -ка from приставить ('to set against, attach, place beside'), built from при- ('to, beside') + ставить ('to put, set upright', from Proto-Slavic *staviti). In the 18th century Russian grammarians used приставка to calque Latin praefixum ('prefix'); in the late 20th century (from телеприставка / игровая приставка, an electronic unit attached to a TV set), it became the everyday word for a video game console or set-top box.

пристально.etymology: Adverb formed from пристальный ('intent, fixed, steadfast'), derived from пристать ('to stick to, cleave to, fix one's gaze on'), from при- + стать ('to stand', Proto-Slavic *stati).

history.meaning: to stand close to, cleave to

пристать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пристати ('to come to shore, join, stick to'), formed from prefix при- ('to, alongside') + стать ('to stand, come to a stop', from Proto-Slavic *stati).

history.meaning: to put in to shore, adhere, accost
to stick to; to pester, bother

пристрелить.etymology: Formed from prefix при- (indicating finishing off or killing, as in прибить) + стрелить ('to shoot', from стрела 'arrow, shot', from Proto-Slavic *strěla).

history.meaning: to shoot dead, finish off with a shot

пристроить.etymology: Formed from prefix при- ('to, onto, alongside') + строить ('to build, arrange, settle', inherited from Old East Slavic строити 'to arrange, order, build', from Proto-Slavic *strojiti).

history.meaning: to build on; to place, find a spot or job for
