ребро.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic ребро ('rib'), from Proto-Slavic *rebro ('rib, edge, side'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rebʰ- ('to arch over, roof, enclose', cognate with German Rippe and English rib).

ребята.etymology: Plural of ребёнок (historically дитя / робя), continuing Old East Slavic робята, the nominative plural of робя ('child, young servant'), from Proto-Slavic *orbę (genitive *orbęte), from the same root *orb- ('orphan, young servant, worker') as раб ('slave') and работа ('work'). The initial ре- (from earlier ро-) arose through vowel assimilation or dissimilation in Russian dialects.

ребёнок.etymology: Dissimilated in Russian (р...б from р...р) from earlier робёнок ('child'), formed with the young-being suffix -ёнок from Old East Slavic робя (plural робята → modern ребята 'children, guys, lads'), from Proto-Slavic *orbę ('orphan, minor, child dependent on the household', from the same Indo-European root *h₃órbʰos as работа 'work' and Latin orbus 'bereft').
ребёнок.notes: In standard Russian, the neutral plural of **ребёнок** is suppletive **дети** ('children'), while **ребята** means 'kids, guys, lads'.

реванш.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French revanche ('retaliation, return match, rematch'), deverbal from revancher / se revancher ('to take vengeance, pay back'), from Old French revengier, from Late Latin revindicare ('to lay claim to, avenge').

ревизор.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Revisor and Polish rewizor from Medieval/Modern Latin revisor ('inspector, auditor'), agent noun from Latin revidere (past participle revisus 'to look back at, re-examine, inspect').

ревнивый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ревьнивыи ('zealous, fervent; jealous'), derived from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic ревьнъ ('zealous') and ръвьнь ('zeal, ardor, rivalry', from Proto-Slavic *rъvьnъ) + suffix -ивый.

ревновать.etymology: Inherited via Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic رьвьновати ('to be zealous, emulate, be jealous'), derived from ревность / рьвьныи ('zealous, fervent'), from Proto-Slavic *rьvьnъ ('zealous, rivaling').

history.meaning: to be zealous, strive after, be jealous

ревность.etymology: Inherited via Old Church Slavonic and Old East Slavic рьвьность ('zeal, ardor, jealousy'), formed with suffix -ость from рьвьныи ('zealous, ardent'), from Proto-Slavic *rьvьnъ.

регион.etymology: Borrowed via German Region / French région or Polish region from Latin regio (genitive regionis 'direction, boundary line, district, region'), derived from regere ('to direct, rule, guide').

регистрация.etymology: Borrowed via Polish registracja / German Registration from Medieval Latin registratio ('recording in a register'), from registrare ('to record'), from Late Latin regesta ('list, register, things recorded', from Latin regerere 'to carry back, record').

регулярно.etymology: Adverb derived from регулярный ('regular', borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish regularny / German regulär from Late Latin regularis 'according to rule', from Latin regula 'straightedge, rule') + -но.

редактировать.etymology: Borrowed via German redigieren / Redaktion or French rédiger / rédaction, from Latin redigere, redāctum ('to drive back, bring into order, compile, edit'), adapted with Russian suffix -ировать.

history.meaning: to bring into order, arrange, edit

редактор.etymology: Borrowed in the late 18th–19th century via French rédacteur and German Redakteur from New Latin redāctor ('compiler, editor'), derived from Latin redāctus, past participle of redigere ('to bring back, reduce to order, compile', from red- 'back' + agere 'to drive, put').

редакция.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via French rédaction and German Redaktion ('editing, wording; editorial board/office'), from Late Latin redactio ('bringing back, reduction to order'), from Latin redigere (past participle redactus 'to drive back, bring into order, edit').

редкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рѣдъкыи ('sparse, thin, widely spaced; rare'), from Proto-Slavic *rědъkъ ('sparse, not dense, rare'), cognate with Lithuanian rẽtas ('sparse, thin, rare') and Latin rārus ('thinly spaced, rare'). Originally referring to physical spacing (e.g. редкий лес 'thin/sparse forest', as the antonym of густой and частый), it also developed the temporal/qualitative meaning 'uncommon, rare'.

редко.etymology: Adverb formed from редкий ('sparse, rare, thin'), inherited from Old East Slavic рѣдъкыи, from Proto-Slavic *rědъkъ ('spaced apart, sparse, rare').

редкость.etymology: Derived from редкий ('sparse, rare, uncommon', inherited from Old East Slavic рѣдъкыи, from Proto-Slavic *rědъkъ 'sparse, thin, rare') + abstract noun suffix -ость.

режим.etymology: Borrowed from French régime ('system of rule, regimen, operating mode'), from Latin regimen ('guidance, government, rule'), derived from regere ('to rule, direct').

history.meaning: form of government; prescribed routine or mode

режиссёр.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via German Regisseur from French régisseur ('manager, stage director'), derived from régir ('to direct, govern, manage'), from Latin regere ('to rule, direct').

резать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рѣзати and Proto-Slavic *rězati ('to cut, slice, carve'), cognate with Lithuanian rėžti ('to cut, incise, scratch').
резать.notes: Present tense shows з -> ж palatalization throughout: я режу, ты режешь, они режут.

резерв.etymology: Borrowed from French réserve ('something kept back, reserve force or supply'), deverbal noun from réserver ('to keep back, save'), from Latin reservāre ('to keep back, save up').

резиденция.etymology: Borrowed via Polish rezydencja and German Residenz from Medieval Latin residentia ('abode, official seat'), derived from Latin residens, present participle of residere ('to sit back, remain, reside', from re- + sedere 'to sit').

резина.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th centuries from Latin resina / French résine ('resin, gum', from Ancient Greek ῥητίνη 'pine resin'), originally in the phrase резина эластичная (translating New Latin resina elastica / French résine élastique 'elastic gum, caoutchouc, rubber').

резкий.etymology: Derived from резать ('to cut, slice, carve', inherited from Old East Slavic рѣзати, from Proto-Slavic *rězati) + adjectival suffix -кий; literally 'cutting, incisive, sharp'.

резко.etymology: Adverb formed from резкий ('sharp, cutting, abrupt'), derived with the suffix -кий from резать ('to cut, slice', from Proto-Slavic *rězati).

резной.etymology: Derived in Russian from резать ('to cut, carve in wood or stone', Proto-Slavic *rězati) with the adjectival suffix -ной: 'carved, fretwork, ornamented with woodcarving'.

результат.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French résultat or German Resultat from Medieval Latin resultātum ('outcome, effect'), substantivized neuter past participle of Latin resultāre ('to spring back, rebound, result from', frequentative of resilīre 'to leap back', from re- + salīre 'to leap').

резьба.etymology: Formed from резать ('to cut, carve, incise', Proto-Slavic *rězati) with the archaic Slavic action/result suffix -ьба: denotes both artistic wood or stone 'carving' (резьба по дереву) and the spiral 'thread' cut into a screw or bolt.

резюме.etymology: Borrowed from French résumé ('summary, abstract; curriculum vitae'), substantivized past participle of résumer ('to sum up, summarize'), from Latin resumere ('to take up again, recapitulate').

рейс.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from Dutch reis or Middle Low German reise / German Reise ('journey, trip, voyage'), from Old High German reisa ('departure, journey, military expedition'), related to reisen ('to travel, rise up to go').

рейтинг.etymology: Borrowed in the second half of the 20th century (initially in chess/sports rankings and later in political polling, television, and finance) from English rating ('assessment, ranking, poll standing'), derived from rate ('to estimate, value', from Old French rate and Latin rata pars 'reckoned share').

река.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рѣка and Proto-Slavic *rěka ('river'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reyH- ('to flow, stream, move'), a distant cousin of Latin rīvus ('stream, brook', whence English rival and river) and Sanskrit rīti ('stream, current').
река.notes: Nominative plural shifts stress to the stem: реки.

реквизит.etymology: Borrowed via German Requisit ('something required; theatrical prop') from Latin requisitum ('something needed or demanded'), neuter past passive participle of requirere ('to seek again, need, require', from re- + quaerere 'to seek').

реклама.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via German Reklame from French réclame ('editorial puff, commercial advertisement'), originally a typographical catchword or falconer's call-back, from Latin reclāmāre ('to call out again').

рекламный.etymology: Adjective formed with suffix -ный from реклама ('advertising, advertisement'), borrowed from French réclame (ultimately from Latin reclāmāre 'to cry out, call back').

рекомендация.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via Polish rekomendacja / German Rekommandation from Medieval Latin recommendatio ('recommendation, commending'), from recommendare ('to commend to someone's care', from re- + commendare).

рекомендовать.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish rekomendować and German rekommandieren from Medieval Latin recommendāre ('to commend to someone's care or favour'), built from Latin re- + commendāre ('to entrust, commit to care').

ректор.etymology: Borrowed via German Rektor or Polish rektor from Latin rēctor ('ruler, director, helmsman; in Medieval Latin, head of a university or school'), agent noun from regere ('to rule, guide').

history.meaning: guide, director, head of a university

ремень.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic ремень ('leather strap, thong, belt'), from Proto-Slavic *remenь ('strap, belt').

ремонт.etymology: Borrowed from French remonte, a noun from remonter 'to put back up, to set up again'. In Russian the word settled on the idea of putting things back in order, and today it is the everyday word both for fixing things and for renovating a flat.
ремонт.notes: У нас ремонт means 'we are renovating'. A false friend for French and English speakers: it never means 'remount'.

ремонтировать.etymology: Derived from ремонт ('repair, refurbishment; originally replacement of cavalry horses', borrowed in the 18th century from French remonte 'remounting of cavalry, supply of fresh horses', from remonter 'to mount again, refit') + verbal suffix -ировать.

history.meaning: to refit, put back together / replacement of mounts

рентабельность.etymology: Derived from рентабельный ('profitable, cost-effective', borrowed from German rentabel / French rentable, from rente 'income, yield, rent', from Vulgar Latin *rendita, from Latin reddere 'to give back, yield') + abstract suffix -ость.

рентабельный.etymology: Borrowed from German rentabel ('profitable, yielding a return') or French rentable, derived from Rente / rente ('income, revenue, yield', from Vulgar Latin *rendita 'what is rendered/returned').

рентген.etymology: Named after German physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen (1845–1923), who discovered X-rays (German Röntgenstrahlen) in 1895.

рентгеновский.etymology: Adjective formed with suffix -овский from рентген ('X-ray, roentgen'), named after German physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen (1845–1923), who discovered X-rays in 1895.

репертуар.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French répertoire ('catalog, inventory; theatrical repertoire'), from Late Latin repertorium ('inventory, list, catalog'), from Latin reperire (past participle repertus 'to find, discover').

репетировать.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century via German repetieren ('to repeat, rehearse a play or concert') from Latin repetere ('to seek again, go over again, repeat').

репетитор.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via German Repetitor / French répétiteur ('private tutor who reviews lessons with students'), from Late Latin repetitor ('one who repeats'), from Latin repetere ('to repeat, go over again').

репетиция.etymology: Borrowed via Polish repetycja or German Repetition from Latin repetitio ('a repeating, going over again'), derived from repetere ('to repeat, strike or seek again', from re- + petere).

репортаж.etymology: Borrowed from French reportage ('on-the-spot journalistic reporting'), derived from reporter ('reporter', itself borrowed by French from English reporter, from Old French reporter / Latin reportāre 'to carry back, report').

репутация.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish reputacja, German Reputation, or French réputation from Latin reputātiō ('reckoning, consideration, estimation'), from reputāre ('to reckon, think over').

ресепшен.etymology: Late 20th-century borrowing from English reception ('hotel front desk, reception area'), from Old French recepcion, from Latin receptio ('receiving, admission'), from recipere ('to receive').

history.meaning: front desk at a hotel or office

республика.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th–18th centuries via Polish rzeczpospolita / respublika and German Republik from Latin res publica ('public affair, commonwealth, state'), from res ('affair, thing') + publica (feminine of publicus 'public, of the people').

ресторан.etymology: Ресторан comes from French restaurant, either directly or through German Restaurant, according to Vasmer. The French word is connected with restaurer, to restore, refresh or strengthen. The ultimate French source is clear in this account; the immediate borrowing route into Russian is presented as an alternative.

history.meaning: the form behind the name of the establishment

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: ресторан

ресторанный.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ный from ресторан ('restaurant'), which was borrowed in the 19th century from French restaurant (originally 'a restorative meat bouillon', present participle of restaurer 'to restore one's strength', from Latin restaurāre).

реструктурировать.etymology: Late 20th-century borrowing modeled on English restructure / French restructurer, built on prefix ре- ('again') + структура ('structure', from Latin strūctūra 'building, arrangement', from struere 'to build').

ресурс.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French ressource ('means, resource, expedient'), from Old French resourse ('relief, recovery, spring upward'), feminine past participle of resourdre ('to rise again, spring up'), from Latin resurgere.

рехнуться.etymology: Colloquial verb derived with expressive suffix -хнуть from dialectal решить / решиться ума ('to lose one's mind, be deprived of reason', where решить alternates dialectally with лишить 'to deprive of') or from dialectal рех ('hole, gap, error').

history.meaning: (dialectal) to be deprived of one's mind
to lose one's mind, go nuts

рецепт.etymology: Borrowed via German Rezept from Latin receptum ('something received or taken'), tied to the Latin imperative recipe ('take!') written at the top of apothecary prescriptions and cookery formulas.
рецепт.notes: Just like German Rezept, Russian рецепт means both a kitchen recipe (рецепт пирога) and a doctor's prescription.

рецидив.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via German Rezidiv and French récidive ('relapse of an illness; repeat offense'), from Medieval/Legal Latin recidiva, from Latin recidivus ('falling back, returning, recurring'), from recidere ('to fall back', from re- + cadere 'to fall').

речной.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ной from река ('river', with regular palatalization к → ч before -н-), inherited from Old East Slavic рѣка and Proto-Slavic *rěka.

речь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рѣчь and Proto-Slavic *rěčь ('speech, word, discourse; matter'), a lengthened-grade feminine root-noun derived from the verb *rekti (Old East Slavic речи 'to speak, say', preserved in изречь). Notice how in Polish (rzecz) and Czech (věc) the sense 'what is spoken of, matter under discussion' became the general word for 'thing'.
речь.notes: Used in о чём идёт речь? ('what is being talked about / what is the subject?').

решать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of решить ('to decide, solve'), inherited from Old East Slavic рѣшати / рѣшити and Old Church Slavonic рѣшити ('to untie, loosen, set free, absolve'), from Proto-Slavic *rěšiti (cognate with Lithuanian rišti 'to tie, untie'). From 'untying a knot', the meaning shifted to 'solving a problem' and 'settling or deciding a question' (compare Latin solvere 'to loosen → solve' and dēcidere).

решаться.etymology: Reflexive/passive form in -ся of решать ('to decide, solve'), imperfective of решить, inherited via Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic рѣшити ('to untie, loosen, settle', Proto-Slavic *rěšiti).

history.meaning: to be resolved, to be sorted out; to decide

решающий.etymology: Present active participle of решать ('to decide, settle'), from Proto-Slavic *rěšiti ('to untie, settle, resolve'), used adjectivally in the sense 'decisive, crucial'.

решение.etymology: Formed as the verbal noun in -ение from решить ('to decide, solve', originally 'to untie, unbind, release a knot', from Proto-Slavic *rěšiti, cognate with Lithuanian rišti 'to tie, untie'). Just like Latin solvere ('to untie -> solve / resolve'), 'untying a knot' became the metaphor for solving a problem or reaching a decision.

решить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рѣшити and Old Church Slavonic рѣшити ('to untie, unbind, release, settle a question'), from Proto-Slavic *rěšiti ('to untie a knot, loosen, resolve'), cognate with Lithuanian rišti ('to tie, bind'). Just as Latin solvere meant 'to loosen, untie' before meaning 'to solve', Slavic *rěšiti moved from 'untying a knot' to 'solving a problem, deciding'.

решиться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of решить ('to decide, resolve'), from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic рѣшити ('to untie, settle', Proto-Slavic *rěšiti), meaning 'to make up one's mind, bring oneself to act'.

history.meaning: to make up one's mind, to dare

решённый.etymology: Past passive participle of решить ('to decide, settle, solve; originally in Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic рѣшити to untie, loosen, release', from Proto-Slavic *rěšiti).

решётка.etymology: Derived as a diminutive/object noun from решето ('sieve, riddle with a mesh of crossed strips', Proto-Slavic *rešeto): from the woven lattice of a sieve, решётка came to mean any lattice, grate, oven rack, metal grille, or fence railings.

history.meaning: sieve -> lattice, grate, grille, oven rack

ржать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ръжати ('to neigh, whinny'), from Proto-Slavic *rъžati ('to neigh'), from an onomatopoeic root *rъz- / *rъž- imitating the neighing or growling of animals.

ринг.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century from English ring ('enclosed arena for boxing or wrestling; originally a circle of spectators around boxers'), from Old English hring ('ring, circle').

history.meaning: circle of spectators; roped boxing enclosure

рис.etymology: Borrowed in the late 18th–19th centuries via Low German Rīs or Dutch rijst (replacing older Russian сарачинское пшено) from Old French ris, via Italian/Latin oryza from Ancient Greek ὄρυζα (óruza, ultimately of Indo-Aryan/Dravidian origin).

риск.etymology: Borrowed from French risque ('hazard, danger, risk'), from Italian risco / rischio (originally maritime insurance terminology for sailing near cliffs or hazards).

рисковать.etymology: Formed with suffix -овать from риск ('risk') or borrowed directly from French risquer ('to hazard, risk'), from Italian rischiare.

history.meaning: to risk, to take a risk

рисовать.etymology: Borrowed in the late seventeenth or early eighteenth century via Polish rysować ('to draw, sketch, score lines') from Middle High German rīzen / German reißen ('to incise, score, sketch with a stylus', cognate with English write and German Riss 'draft, sketch').

cognates.meaning: to form letters (originally 'to scratch/incise', same Germanic root *wrītaną)

рисовый.etymology: Derived from рис ('rice', borrowed in the 19th century via German Reis or Dutch rijs from Old French ris, from Italian riso, from Latin oryza, from Ancient Greek ὄρυζα, ultimately of Indo-Aryan/Dravidian origin) + adjectival suffix -овый.

рисунок.etymology: Borrowed in the late 17th or early 18th century from Polish rysunek ('drawing, sketch, outline'), which was formed with the German-derived suffix -unek (from -ung) on Polish rysować ('to draw, trace lines'), itself borrowed from Middle High German rīzen ('to incise, sketch, draw lines'; modern German reißen, Riss 'draft, plan', cognate with English write).
рисунок.notes: Drops the fleeting vowel -о- in all oblique forms: *рисунок → рисунка, на рисунке*.

ритм.etymology: Borrowed via French rythme or German Rhythmus from Latin rhythmus and Ancient Greek rhythmós ('measured flow, recurring beat, symmetry, proportion'), derived from rhéō ('to flow', cognate with Russian река / ринуться).

робкий.etymology: Derived from робеть ('to be timid, lose courage, quail'), formed from Old East Slavic робъ ('servant, slave; child, youth', East Slavic reflex of Proto-Slavic *orbъ 'orphan, bondservant, child') + adjectival suffix -кий.

робот.etymology: Borrowed in the 1920s from Czech robot ('artificial worker, automaton'), coined in 1920 by Karel Čapek (at his brother Josef Čapek's suggestion) in his play R.U.R. from Czech robota ('corvée, forced labor, drudgery'), from Proto-Slavic *orbota ('servitude, hard work').

ровесница.etymology: Feminine of ровесник ('person of the same age, peer'), inherited from Old East Slavic ровьсьникъ (dissimilated from *ровьстьникъ, derived from ровьнъ 'equal, even', Proto-Slavic *orvьnъ, + вьрста 'age, peer').

history.meaning: woman or girl of the same age

ровно.etymology: Adverb from the short neuter of ровный ('even, flat, level, straight'), from Old East Slavic ровьныи (showing East Slavic ров- from Proto-Slavic *orvьnъ; compare Old Church Slavonic равьнъ > Russian равный 'equal'). Means both 'evenly, smoothly' and, with numbers or clock times, 'exactly, on the dot' (ровно в восемь 'at eight sharp').

ровный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ровьныи ('level, flat, even, equal'), showing native East Slavic initial ро- from Proto-Slavic *orvьnъ (compare the Old Church Slavonic doublet равный 'equal' with initial ра-).

morphemes.meaning: level, even (East Slavic doublet of равн-)

ровный.notes: Illustrates the classic East Slavic ро- vs. South Slavic ра- split from Proto-Slavic *orC-: Russian ровный means physically 'even, flat, straight', while равный means abstractly 'equal'.

ровнять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ровьняти (Proto-Slavic *orvьnjati), a denominal verb derived from ровный ('even, flat, straight'): 'to make physically level, even, or straight'.

history.meaning: flat, even -> to make even, level
to level, make even or straight

ровнять.notes: Spelling rule: ровнять (with о) means 'to make physically smooth/even/straight', whereas равнять (with а) means 'to treat as equal / equate'.

рог.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic рогъ ('horn'), from Proto-Slavic *rogъ ('horn'), cognate with Lithuanian ragas ('horn') and Old Prussian ragis.

род.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic родъ ('birth, origin, kin, clan, kind'), from Proto-Slavic *rodъ, deverbal from *roditi ('to give birth, bear'), from PIE *h₃erdʰ- ('to grow high, increase', cognate with Latin arbor and Sanskrit ṛdhyati).

роддом.etymology: Early Soviet syllabic abbreviation of родильный дом ('maternity hospital, birthing home'), combining родильный ('maternity, birthing', from родить 'to give birth', Proto-Slavic *roditi) + дом ('house, home', Proto-Slavic *domъ).

родина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic родина ('family, clan, native land'), formed with the suffix -ина from род ('birth, family, kin, clan', from Proto-Slavic *rodъ, related to родить 'to give birth'). From 'one's native kin and birthplace' it expanded to 'homeland, motherland'.

родитель.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic родитель (and Old Church Slavonic родитель 'begetter, parent'), formed with the agent suffix -тель from родити / родить ('to give birth, beget', from Proto-Slavic *roditi).

родительский.etymology: Derived from родитель ('parent, begetter', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic родитель, agent noun from родити 'to give birth, beget', from Proto-Slavic *roditi) + adjectival suffix -ский.

родить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic родити ('to give birth, bear, beget'), from Proto-Slavic *roditi ('to bear, bring forth'), causative-iterative from the root of *rodъ ('birth, growth, kin').

родиться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic родитисѧ, reflexive of родить ('to give birth, bear, beget'), from Proto-Slavic *roditi sę ('to be born'), built on the root *rod- ('birth, growth, kin').

родной.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic родьныи (Proto-Slavic *rodьnъ), derived from род ('kin, family, birth, origin', Proto-Slavic *rodъ, built on родить 'to give birth, bear'): 'related by blood, native (city, language), or one's own dear'.

history.meaning: kin, birth -> of one's own kin, native

родовой.etymology: Derived from род ('kin, clan, family; birth', from Proto-Slavic *rodъ) and роды ('childbirth') + adjectival suffix -овой.

родственник.etymology: Formed with the agent/person suffix -ник from родственный ('related by blood or marriage'), derived from родство ('kinship') and род ('kin, clan, family, birth', from Proto-Slavic *rodъ).

morphemes.meaning: person belonging to a kinship relation

роды.etymology: Plural-only noun derived from the plural of род ('birth, generation', inherited from Old East Slavic родъ, from Proto-Slavic *rodъ, deverbal of *roditi 'to give birth').

рожать.etymology: Imperfective of родить ('to give birth'), inherited from East Slavic рожати (with East Slavic ж from Proto-Slavic *dj, corresponding to Church Slavonic раждати), from Proto-Slavic *rodjati.

рождаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of родиться ('to be born'), formed from the Church Slavonic stem рождати / раждати (with -жд- from Proto-Slavic *dj, from *rodjati 'to give birth') + reflexive suffix -ся.

рождение.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рождение ('birth, nativity'), the verbal noun of родити ('to give birth, bear', Proto-Slavic *roditi), exhibiting the Old Church Slavonic reflex -жд- for Proto-Slavic *dj (compare native East Slavic рожение).
рождение.notes: Most frequent in **день рождения** ('birthday', literally 'day of birth').

рожок.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ок (with regular palatalization г → ж) from рог ('horn'), inherited from Old East Slavic рогъ, from Proto-Slavic *rogъ ('horn', cognate with Lithuanian rãgas 'horn'). Named after its horn-like shape, рожок denotes a little horn, a shepherd's horn, a shoe-horn, or a wafer ice-cream cone.

роза.etymology: Borrowed via German Rose (and Polish róża) from Latin rosa ('rose'), an ancient Mediterranean word parallel to Ancient Greek ῥόδον (rhódon).

розетка.etymology: Borrowed with diminutive suffix -ка from French rosette ('little rose; rose-shaped architectural ornament, small saucer for jam, wall plate/socket'), diminutive of rose (from Latin rosa).

history.meaning: little rose; circular ornamental wall plate or saucer

розмарин.etymology: Borrowed via German Rosmarin and Polish rozmaryn from Latin rosmarinus (or ros marinus 'sea dew', folk-etymologized from earlier Latin ros maris, related to Ancient Greek ῥῶψ μυρίνης 'fragrant shrub').

розовый.etymology: Relational and colour adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -овый from роза ('rose'), borrowed via German Rose and Polish róża from Latin rosa ('rose').

розыгрыш.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from разыграть / разыгрывать ('to play out, raffle, draw lots; to play a practical joke on someone', with stressed prefix роз- from Proto-Slavic *orz- + играть 'to play', from *jьgra) + noun suffix -ыш.

history.meaning: prize draw, play-off; practical joke, prank

розыск.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with stressed prefix роз- (from Proto-Slavic *orz-) from разыскать / разыскивать ('to search out, investigate', from рас-/роз- + искать 'to seek, look for', from Proto-Slavic *jьskati).

history.meaning: official search, criminal investigation; wanted list

ролазин.etymology: Fictional or screen-coined pharmaceutical name (Ролазин) used in the television series, modeled on real medications ending in the chemical/pharmaceutical suffix -азин (-azine, such as ранолазин 'ranolazine' or хлорпромазин 'chlorpromazine', coined in 19th-century chemistry from French azote 'nitrogen' + -ine).

ролик.etymology: Diminutive in -ик of роль / роля ('roller, small wheel, scroll'), borrowed from German Rolle ('roll, scroll, pulley wheel, caster'), from Latin rotula ('little wheel', diminutive of rota); extended to 'reel of film, short video clip'.

ролл.etymology: Late 20th-century culinary borrowing from English roll (as in California roll, sushi roll, translating Japanese makizushi 'rolled sushi'), from Old French rolle ('scroll, roll'), from Latin rotulus ('little wheel, scroll').

роль.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Rolle from French rôle ('actor's part, role; originally the rolled parchment scroll on which an actor's lines were written'), from Old French rolle, from Medieval Latin rotulus ('scroll, little wheel').

history.meaning: scroll of lines; actor's part, role

рома.etymology: Hypocoristic (affectionate short form) of the Russian masculine given name Роман (Roman), which entered East Slavic via Byzantine Greek Rhōmanós from Latin Rōmānus ('a Roman, citizen of Rome').

роман.etymology: As a Russian masculine given name, Роман entered Old East Slavic via Byzantine Greek Ῥωμανός (Rhōmanós) from Latin Rōmānus ('Roman, citizen of Rome'). (The common noun роман 'novel, romance' is a separate 18th-century borrowing from French roman, from the same ultimate Latin source.)

романтик.etymology: Borrowed via German Romantiker or French romantique ('a romantic person or writer'), derived from роман ('chivalric romance, novel', from Old French romanz 'vernacular tale').

романтика.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from German Romantik ('Romanticism, romantic spirit or atmosphere'), ultimately from Old French romanz ('verse narrative in the vernacular Romance tongue, chivalric romance').

романтический.etymology: Derived with the suffix -еский from романтика / French romantique or German romantisch ('romantic, like in a chivalric romance'), from Old French romanz ('verse narrative in the vernacular Romance language').

романтично.etymology: Adverb formed from романтичный ('romantic'), derived from романтика / романтический, ultimately from French romantique (from Old French romanz 'vernacular chivalric romance').

романтичный.etymology: Derived from романтика ('romance, romantic spirit', borrowed via German Romantik / French romantique, ultimately from Old French romanz 'verse narrative in the vernacular Romance tongue') + adjectival suffix -ный.

history.meaning: chivalric tale written in Romance vernacular

ромашка.etymology: Diminutive reshaped with the suffix -ка from Middle Russian романовъ цвѣтъ or Polish rumianek ('chamomile'), ultimately from Medieval Latin anthemis romana ('Roman chamomile'), derived from Roma ('Rome').

ромашковый.etymology: Derived with the adjectival suffix -овый from ромашка ('chamomile, daisy'), which developed as a diminutive of older Russian романова трава / роман ('Roman herb', borrowed via Polish rumianek / roman from Medieval Latin anthemis romana 'Roman chamomile').

роскошно.etymology: Deadjectival adverb formed from роскошный ('luxurious, sumptuous') with the adverbial suffix -о.

роскошный.etymology: Derived with the adjectival suffix -ный from роскошь ('luxury, splendor'), borrowed or influenced via Polish rozkosz / Ukrainian розкіш (with East Slavic okanje prefix роз-) from Proto-Slavic *orzkošь ('abundance, sensual pleasure').

российский.etymology: Relational adjective formed from Россия ('Russia', the Hellenized Chancery form borrowed from Byzantine Greek Ῥωσία for Old East Slavic Русь) with the suffix -ский.

history.meaning: Russian (pertaining to the state of Russia)

рост.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ростъ ('growth, stature, interest on a loan'), from Proto-Slavic *orstъ, a deverbal noun from *orsti (modern Russian расти, 'to grow').

рот.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рътъ ('beak, snout, point, mouth'), from Proto-Slavic *rъtъ ('projecting tip, beak, mouth'), related to рыть ('to dig, root with the snout'). In Russian рот replaced the older Slavic word уста ('mouth, lips') in everyday speech.
рот.notes: Drops the fleeting о in oblique cases: **рот** → **рта**, and has the locative in -у: **во рту** ('in the mouth').

роялть.etymology: Subtitling lemmatization variant of роялти ('royalty payment, licensing fee'), borrowed in the late twentieth century from English royalty, from Old French roialté ('kingship, royal prerogative'), from Latin rēgālis ('royal, regal').

рояль.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French royal ('royal, kingly'), shortened from piano royal ('royal/grand piano'), from Old French roial, ultimately from Latin rēgālis ('royal, of a king').

рубашка.etymology: Originally a diminutive of рубаха 'shirt, tunic', from Old East Slavic рубъ 'coarse linen cloth, hem, cut piece', connected with рубить 'to cut, chop' — originally a garment cut from homespun cloth.
рубашка.notes: Although formed as a diminutive, рубашка is now the neutral everyday word for a button-up shirt.

рубин.etymology: Borrowed via German Rubin from Medieval Latin rubīnus ('ruby, red gemstone'), derived from Latin rubeus ('red, reddish'). The Latin adjective descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *h₁rewdʰ- ('red'). This makes рубин a distant Indo-European cousin of both English red / ruby and native Russian рдеть ('to glow red') and рыжий ('red-haired').

cognates.meaning: red gemstone (via Old French from Medieval Latin rubīnus)

рубить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рубити ('to chop, hew, cut down'), from Proto-Slavic *rǫbiti ('to chop, hem, notch'), derived from *rǫbъ ('edge, border, hem, cut').

рубль.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рубль (first attested in 13th-century Novgorod birchbark documents and chronicles), derived from рубить ('to chop, cut, notch', Proto-Slavic *rǫbiti). Historically it denoted a measured silver ingot either cut from a longer bar or marked with notches indicating weight, replacing the older гривна.

history.meaning: silver ingot of standard weight; rouble

рубль.notes: Declines with end stress throughout: *один рубль, два рубля, пять рублей*.

ругать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ругати ('to mock, jeer at, insult'), from Proto-Slavic *rǫgati ('to mock, scold', related to Old Church Slavonic рѫгъ 'mockery, derision').

ругаться.etymology: Formed by adding the reciprocal/intransitive postfix -ся to ругать ('to scold, abuse, swear at'), inherited from Old East Slavic ругати and Proto-Slavic *rǫgati ('to mock, jeer, scold', compare Old Church Slavonic рѫгати сѧ 'to mock').

history.meaning: to quarrel, argue; to swear, scold

rootFamily.gloss: to have an argument, fall out

ружьё.etymology: Evolved in 17th-century Russian (originally collective 'weapons, firearms', later a single gun/rifle) as a colloquial phonetic contraction of оружие ('weapon, arms'), from Proto-Slavic *orǫžьje.

руина.etymology: Borrowed via Polish ruina or German Ruine from Latin ruīna ('a rushing down, tumbling, collapse, ruin'), derived from the verb ruere ('to fall violently, collapse').

рука.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рука (Old Church Slavonic рѫка), from Proto-Slavic *rǫka ('hand, arm'), closely cognate with Lithuanian rankà ('hand, arm'), derived from the Balto-Slavic verb *renk- ('to gather, collect, pick up'; compare Lithuanian riñkti 'to gather'): literally 'the gatherer, picker'.
рука.notes: Like most Slavic languages, Russian uses the single word **рука** for both the hand and the whole arm.

рукав.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рукавъ and Proto-Slavic *rǫkavъ ('sleeve; branch channel of a river'), derived from рука ('arm, hand', Proto-Slavic *rǫka) with the suffix -ав: literally 'the garment part covering the arm'.
рукав.notes: Nominative plural has stressed ending -а: рукава ('sleeves').

руководитель.etymology: Formed with the agent suffix -тель from руководить ('to lead, guide, direct', a Church Slavonic calque of Greek χειραγωγέω 'to lead by the hand', from рука 'hand' + водить 'to lead').

history.meaning: to lead by the hand, guide

руководить.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic рѫководити ('to lead by the hand, guide'), a compound calque of Byzantine Greek χειραγωγέω (kheiragōgéō, from χείρ 'hand' + ἄγω 'to lead'), combining рука ('hand', Proto-Slavic *rǫka) + linking vowel -о- + водить ('to lead', Proto-Slavic *voditi).

history.meaning: to lead by the hand, guide

руководить.notes: Takes the instrumental case for the group or organization being led: руководить отделом ('to head a department').

руководство.etymology: Derived with suffix -ство from руководить ('to guide, lead, direct'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рѫководити ('to lead by the hand', a calque on Greek χειραγωγέω, from рука 'hand' + водить 'to lead').

history.meaning: to lead by the hand, guide

рукола.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from Italian rucola ('arugula, rocket'), a Northern Italian diminutive derived from Latin ērūca ('colewort, salad rocket').

рулет.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century via German Roulade / Rolle and French roulette / roulade from French rouler ('to roll up'), from Old French roler and Late Latin rotulus ('little wheel, scroll', diminutive of Latin rota 'wheel').

history.meaning: rolled meat or sponge-cake roulade, Swiss roll

рулетик.etymology: Diminutive in -ик of рулет ('rolled meat or pastry dish, roulade'), borrowed from French roulade or German Roulade / Rolle, from French rouler ('to roll up', from Late Latin rotulāre).

рулетка.etymology: Borrowed from French roulette ('little wheel', diminutive of roue 'wheel', from Latin rota 'wheel'). In Russian, рулетка refers both to a coiled spring-loaded measuring tape (which winds up on a small wheel inside its round case) and to a roulette wheel.

рулон.etymology: Borrowed from French rouleau (or adapted from German Rolle / French rouler) ('cylindrical roll of paper, fabric, or wallpaper'), ultimately derived from Diminutive Late Latin rotulus ('little wheel, scroll', from Latin rota 'wheel').

руль.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine naval era (with dissimilation р...р > р...л from earlier рурь) from Dutch roer ('ship's rudder, helm', cognate with German Ruder and English rudder).

рум-сервис.etymology: Borrowed in the late twentieth century from English room service, a compound of room (from Old English rūm 'space, chamber') and service (from Old French servise, from Latin servitium).

history.meaning: hotel service delivering food to guest rooms

румяный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic румяныи ('rosy, ruddy, blushing'), from Proto-Slavic *ruměnъ ('reddish, rosy'), formed from the Indo-European colour root *h₁rewdʰ- ('red', with loss of *d before *m: *rud-men- → *ruměn-; cognate with рдеть 'to glow red', руда 'ore', and English red / ruby).

history.meaning: rosy-cheeked; golden-brown (of baked pastry or bread)

русский.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic русьскыи ('pertaining to Rus''), formed from Русь ('Kievan Rus', the East Slavic people and land') + the adjectival suffix -ьск- (-ский). The ethnonym Русь itself is traced by Vasmer and most historical linguists via Finnic Ruotsi ('Swedes', literally 'rowers, men of the rowing crews') to Old Norse *rōþs- (related to Old Norse róa 'to row'), referring to the early Varangian river-traders and rulers along the waterways of Eastern Europe.

рухнуть.etymology: Semelfactive verb in -нуть formed from the root of рушить ('to pull down, demolish') and archaic рух ('commotion, movement, crash'), from Proto-Slavic *ruxъ / *ruxnǫti ('to move, crash down').

ручаться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed with -ся from ручать ('to guarantee, vouch'), inherited from Old East Slavic ручати, derived from рука ('hand', Proto-Slavic *rǫka), from the legal custom of clasping hands to pledge surety.

ручка.etymology: Formed in East Slavic with the diminutive suffix -ка from рука ('hand, arm', from Proto-Slavic *rǫka). First meaning 'a little hand', it was applied to anything grasped by the hand ('door handle, cup handle, knob'), and from the 19th century (via ручка с пером 'penholder') to a writing pen.

history.meaning: little hand; handle, knob; writing pen

ручник.etymology: Colloquial univerbation formed from ручной тормоз ('handbrake') using the noun suffix -ник, ultimately from рука ('hand', Proto-Slavic *rǫka).

ручной.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ручьныи ('of the hand, manual, tame'), from Proto-Slavic *rǫčьnъ, relational adjective of *rǫka (modern Russian рука, 'hand').

рушить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рушити ('to tear down, destroy, break up'), from Proto-Slavic *rušiti ('to break, stir up, demolish', causative/iterative related to *ruxъ and *rъvati).

рушиться.etymology: Reflexive form with -ся of рушить ('to pull down, demolish'), from Old East Slavic рушити ('to break, destroy'), from Proto-Slavic *rušiti ('to tear down, disturb'), cognate with Lithuanian raušti ('to dig up, tear').

рыба.etymology: An inherited Slavic word with close relatives across the Slavic languages. Its deeper origin is uncertain. Vasmer discusses a possible old taboo replacement and competing proposals; none should be presented to learners as a proven story.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: рыба

рыба.notes:
- Accusative plural equals the genitive (**рыб**) because the noun is animate.
- **Рыбы** is also the zodiac sign Pisces.

рыбак.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рыбакъ, formed with the agent suffix -ак from рыба ('fish', from Proto-Slavic *ryba).

рыбалка.etymology: Derived from dialectal/Southern and Ukrainian рибалка ('fisherman; gull; fishing'), formed with suffix -алка from рыба ('fish'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *ryba ('fish').

рыбий.etymology: Possessive/relational adjective inherited from Old East Slavic рыбии ('of a fish'), derived from рыба ('fish'), from Proto-Slavic *rybьjь (from *ryba 'fish').

рыбина.etymology: Augmentative and singulative noun formed from рыба ('fish', from Proto-Slavic *ryba) with the suffix -ина, denoting a single large fish.

рыбка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from рыба ('fish'), inherited from Old East Slavic рыба, from Proto-Slavic *ryba ('fish').

рыбный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рыбьныи, formed with suffix -ный from рыба ('fish'), from Proto-Slavic *rybьnъ ('abounding in fish, made of fish', from *ryba).

history.meaning: relating to fish, rich in fish

рыжий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рыжь ('reddish, rust-colored, ginger'), from Proto-Slavic *ryďь (< *rūdi̯os), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁roudh-yo- ('red, rust-colored'), from the root *h₁reudh- ('red', cognate with рдеть, руда, and English red).

рынок.etymology: Borrowed in Middle Russian via Polish rynek ('town market square, marketplace') from Middle High German rinc ('circle, ring, encircled town assembly or market place', modern German Ring, cognate with English ring).
рынок.notes: Drops the fleeting -о- in all oblique forms: рынок -> на рынке ('at the market').

рыться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed with -ся from рыть ('to dig, burrow'), inherited from Old East Slavic рыти, from Proto-Slavic *ryti ('to dig, root up'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rewH- ('to tear up, dig out').

рыцарский.etymology: Adjective in -ский formed from рыцарь ('knight'), borrowed via Polish rycerz (compare older East Slavic риторь / рыторь) from Middle High German ritter ('horseman, knight', related to reiten 'to ride').

рычаг.etymology: Borrowed via Polish ryczag / rydzag or Ukrainian ричаг from Middle High German *rîterzagel or more likely a Slavic formation in -аг; Vasmer favors borrowing via Polish from German Riegel / dialectal forms or Turkic rüčäg, though often folk-linked to рычать.

рычать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рычати ('to roar, bellow, growl'), from Proto-Slavic *ryčati (< *rykäti), an expressive/onomatopoeic verb built on the root *ryk- (seen in рык 'roar, growl').

рюкзак.etymology: Borrowed in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century from German Rucksack ('backpack'), originally an Alpine dialect compound of Rücken (Upper German Ruck, 'back, ridge') and Sack ('bag, sack'). The first element comes from Proto-Germanic *hrugjaz ('back, spine', cognate with English ridge), while Sack comes via Latin saccus and Greek σάκκος from Semitic *śaq ('cloth bag').

cognates.meaning: borrowed from the same German compound
cognates of the two German components

рюмка.etymology: Formed with the diminutive suffix -ка from older Russian рюма (attested in the 17th century), borrowed from German Römer (Low German römer, Dutch roemer), a traditional stemmed green-glass wine goblet (popularly connected with Latin rōmānum vitrum 'Roman glass' or Middle High German rüemen 'to boast, toast').

history.meaning: shot glass, small stemmed liqueur/vodka glass

рюмочка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -очка from рюмка ('stemmed shot glass, wineglass'), borrowed in the seventeenth century from Low German or Dutch roemer / German Römer ('green glass goblet').

ряд.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рядъ ('row, order, arrangement, pact, market stall line'), from Proto-Slavic *rędъ ('order, row, line'), continuing a Balto-Slavic and Indo-European root for arranging or fitting in order (compare Lithuanian rinda 'row, line' and English read /German Rat).
ряд.notes: Takes stressed **-у** in the locative after **в**: *в первом ряду* ('in the first row'), though *о ряде* in the prepositional.

рядовой.etymology: Relational adjective formed with -овой from ряд ('row, rank, line, order'), inherited from Old East Slavic рядъ, from Proto-Slavic *rędъ ('row, order, arrangement'); substantivized in military usage for a rank-and-file private soldier.

рядом.etymology: Grammaticalized instrumental singular of ряд ('row, line, series, order', from Old East Slavic рядъ, Proto-Slavic *rędъ): originally 'in the same row, side by side', hence the adverb 'nearby, next to (рядом с + instrumental)'.

history.meaning: in a row, side by side → nearby, next to

рёбрышко.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ышко from ребро ('rib'), inherited from Old East Slavic ребро, from Proto-Slavic *rebro ('rib'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rebh- ('to arch over, roof, enclose').

с.etymology: Merges two originally distinct Proto-Slavic prepositions that fell together in Old East Slavic съ: (1) *sъ(n) ('with, together with', taking the instrumental case; cognate with Sanskrit sám 'together' and Latin cum) and (2) *sъ ('down from, off, since', taking the genitive case; related to Old Prussian san-).

history.meaning: with ( + inst.); off, from, since ( + gen.)

с.notes: Governs the instrumental when meaning 'with' (с молоком) and the genitive when meaning 'from, off, since' (с работы, с утра); expands to со before consonant clusters (со мной, со стола).

сад.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic садъ and Proto-Slavic *sadъ ('planted orchard, garden, grove'), an o-grade noun built on the root of садить / сажать ('to plant, set in the ground', originally causative of сесть / сидеть 'to sit', from Proto-Indo-European *sed- 'to sit, set'). A сад is literally 'what has been set/planted in the ground' (especially fruit trees and shrubs).

cognates.meaning: to place, plant (from the same PIE causative *sodéyeti)

сад.notes: Takes the stressed locative -у after в: в саду ('in the garden').

садик.etymology: Diminutive of сад ('garden, orchard', inherited from Old East Slavic садъ, Proto-Slavic *sadъ 'planted place, garden', from the root of садить 'to plant, set'). In modern everyday Russian, садик is the universal colloquial shorthand for **детский сад** ('kindergarten, nursery school', itself a 19th-century calque of German Kindergarten, coined by Friedrich Fröbel in 1840).

садист.etymology: Borrowed from French sadiste ('one who derives pleasure from inflicting cruelty'), coined in late 19th-century psychiatry after the French writer Donatien Alphonse François, Marquis de Sade (1740–1814).

history.meaning: practitioner of sadism (after the Marquis de Sade)

садиться.etymology: Reflexive of садить ('to seat, plant', from Old East Slavic садити, Proto-Slavic *saditi, the o-grade causative of *sěsti 'to sit down', from PIE *sed- 'to sit'; cognate with English sit and set). Literally 'to seat oneself', serving as the imperfective partner of сесть ('to sit down').

садовый.etymology: Derived from сад ('garden, orchard', Proto-Slavic *sadъ) with the relational adjectival suffix -овый.

сажать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сажати ('to seat, plant', with East Slavic ж < *dj; compare Old Church Slavonic саждати), iterative of садить ('to seat, plant'), from Proto-Slavic *saditi (causative of *sěděti 'to sit').

сайт.etymology: Late 20th-century borrowing from English site (short for website), from Anglo-Norman / Middle French site ('place, position'), from Latin situs ('local position, site').

history.meaning: location on the World Wide Web

салага.etymology: Naval slang for an inexperienced recruit or rookie, transferred from the dialectal northern/southern Russian fish name салага ('small schooling fish, bleak or sprat', related to салака 'Baltic herring', borrowed from Finnic: Finnish salakka 'bleak').

салат.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French salade or German Salat from Northern Italian salata (standard Italian insalata, 'salted greens, salad'), from Vulgar Latin *(herba) salāta ('salted greens'), derived from Latin sāl ('salt').

сало.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сало ('animal fat, tallow, lard'), from Proto-Slavic *salo ('fat, grease'), formed with instrument/substance suffix *-dlo from *saditi ('to sit, settle', literally 'that which settles/deposits on meat').

салон.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French salon ('drawing room, reception hall, showroom'), borrowed from Italian salone ('large hall'), augmentative of sala ('hall', of Germanic *sal origin).

салфетка.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via German Salvet / Serviette (with dissimilation r...v > l...f) from Italian salvieta or French serviette ('table napkin, small towel'), derived from servir ('to serve at table'). Adapted into Russian with the feminine suffix -ка.

салют.etymology: Borrowed from French salut ('greeting, military salute, celebratory cannon/firework salvo') or German Salut, from Latin salūs, salūtis ('health, safety, greeting').

сам.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic самъ (f. сама, n. само, pl. сами, 'oneself, in person'), from Proto-Slavic *samъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *somHós ('same, one and the same'), directly cognate with English same, Ancient Greek ὁμός, and Sanskrit samá.

самаритянин.etymology: Derived with the ethnonymic suffix -янин from Old Church Slavonic Самария ('Samaria'), from Ancient Greek Σαμάρεια (Samáreia, ethnic noun Σαμαρείτης), from Hebrew שֹׁמְרוֹן (Šōmərōn); popularized by the biblical parable of the Good Samaritan.

самовлюблённый.etymology: Compound adjective formed from само- ('self-', from сам, Proto-Slavic *samъ) + влюблённый ('in love, enamored', passive participle of влюбить, from любить 'to love').

самовоспитываться.etymology: Compound reflexive verb formed from само- ('self-', Proto-Slavic *samъ) + воспитываться ('to be brought up, educated', from Old Church Slavonic въспитати 'to nourish, rear, bring up').

history.meaning: to discipline oneself, to build character

самодеятельность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with -ость from самодеятельный ('acting on one's own initiative; amateur'), a compound of само- ('self-') and деятельный ('active', from деяти 'to do, act', Proto-Slavic *dějati); in the Soviet era specialized for amateur artistic performances (художественная самодеятельность).

самолюбие.etymology: Compound noun attested via Church Slavonic tradition as самолюбие, calquing Ancient Greek φιλαυτία (philautía, 'self-love'), composed of само- ('self-', from сам) + любие (from любить 'to love', Proto-Slavic *ľubiti).

самолёт.etymology: Compound of само- ('self-', from сам) + лёт ('flight', from летать 'to fly', Proto-Slavic *lětati); originally used in Russian folklore (ковёр-самолёт 'flying carpet') and for river ferries/looms before being adopted by poet Vasily Kamensky (1910) and Soviet aviation for 'airplane'.

самостоятельно.etymology: Deadjectival adverb formed with -о from самостоятельный ('independent, self-standing'), a compound of само- ('self-') and стоятельный (from стоять 'to stand', Proto-Slavic *stojati), calquing German selbständig.

самострел.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic самострѣлъ ('crossbow, arbalest; spring-gun trap'), a compound of само- ('self-') + стрѣлъ (from стрѣляти / стрелять 'to shoot', Proto-Slavic *strěľati).

самоубийца.etymology: Compound agent noun formed from само- ('self-', from сам) + убийца ('killer, murderer', from убить 'to kill', Proto-Slavic *ubiti), modeled as a calque of New Latin suīcīda ('one who kills oneself').

history.meaning: person who commits or attempts suicide

самоуверенность.etymology: Abstract noun in -ость formed from самоуверенный ('self-confident, overconfident'), compound of само- ('self-', Proto-Slavic *samъ) + уверенный ('assured, confident', from вера 'faith, belief').

самочувствие.etymology: 19th-century compound calquing German Selbstgefühl / Befinden, formed from само- ('self-', Proto-Slavic *samъ) + чувствие / чувство ('feeling, sensation', from *čuti 'to feel').

самурай.etymology: Borrowed from Japanese 侍 (samurai, 'warrior retainer, samurai'), historically evolved from Old Japanese saburapi ('service, attendance on a noble'), nominalization of the verb saburapu ('to serve, wait upon').

самый.etymology: Formed as the long pronominal adjective of сам ('oneself, in person', Old East Slavic самъ, Proto-Slavic *samъ, from Proto-Indo-European *somHós 'same, one and the same', cognate with English same, Sanskrit samá, and Ancient Greek homós).

history.meaning: the very, right; the most (forming superlatives)

самый.notes: Used both to form the superlative of adjectives (самый лучший 'the very best') and with demonstratives or nouns to mean 'the very, right at' (в самом центре 'right in the very centre', тот же самый 'the exact same').

санаторий.etymology: Borrowed in the late nineteenth century via German Sanatorium from New Latin sānātōrium ('health resort, convalescent hospital'), derived from Late Latin sānātōrius ('healing, health-giving'), from Latin sānāre ('to heal, cure', from sānus 'healthy').

санитар.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French sanitaire ('sanitary, medical orderly'), from learned Latin sānitas ('health'), from sānus ('healthy, sound').

санитарный.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French sanitaire ('sanitary, relating to public health and hygiene') and adapted with the Russian adjectival suffix -ный, from Latin sānitās ('health, soundness'), derived from sānus ('healthy, sound').

санкт-петербург.etymology: Named by Tsar Peter the Great upon founding the city in May 1703 after his patron saint, the Apostle Saint Peter: modelled on Dutch Sankt-Pieterburch / German Sankt Petersburg ('Saint Peter's fortress/city', combining Latin sānctus 'holy, saint' + Greek Πέτρος 'Peter, rock' + Germanic Burg 'fortress, walled town').
санкт-петербург.notes: Colloquially shortened in everyday Russian to **Питер**.

сантехник.etymology: Twentieth-century Soviet syllabic abbreviation and derivative from санитарный техник ('sanitary technician'), combining санитарный ('sanitary', from Latin sānitas 'health') and техник ('technician', from German Techniker / Ancient Greek τεχνικός).

сантименты.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th centuries (reflecting older Russian transcription of French nasal en as ан) from French sentiments, plural of sentiment ('feeling, sensibility, tender emotion', from sentir 'to feel', Latin sentīre).

сантиметр.etymology: Borrowed from French centimètre ('one-hundredth of a metre'), compounded from Latin centum ('hundred') + French mètre ('metre'). Colloquially in Russian it also denotes a tailor's flexible measuring tape.

morphemes.meaning: one-hundredth (from Latin centum via French centi-)

санузел.etymology: Twentieth-century Soviet syllabic compound shortening санитарный узел ('sanitary unit/node'), combining санитарный ('sanitary', from Latin sānitas) and узел ('knot, hub, unit', from Proto-Slavic *vǫzьlъ).

сапог.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сапогъ (attested in the Primary Chronicle under 985), an early borrowing into East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic either from a Turkic or Proto-Bulgar source (cf. Chagatai säpük 'shoe') or from an archaic Slavic root of uncertain ultimate origin.

сапёр.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from French sapeur ('sapper, combat engineer who digs trenches'), derived from saper ('to dig a sap/trench, undermine'), from Middle French sappe ('spade, trench'), from Late Latin sappa ('hoe, mattock').

сауна.etymology: Borrowed from Finnish sauna ('Finnish bathhouse, sauna'), inherited from Proto-Finnic *sakna ('bathhouse, snow pit shelter').

сахар.etymology: Borrowed into Old East Slavic сахаръ directly from Byzantine Greek σάκχαρον (preserving Greek χ as Russian х, unlike Western European sugar/sucre via Arabic and Italian), ultimately from Sanskrit śárkarā ('grit, crystal sugar').

сахарный.etymology: Derived in Russian from сахар ('sugar') with the adjectival suffix -ный. Old East Slavic сахаръ was borrowed directly from Byzantine Greek sákhar (without the Arabic definite article al- that produced Spanish azúcar and French sucre), ultimately from Sanskrit śárkarā ('gravel, grit, candied sugar crystals').

сашкин.etymology: Colloquial possessive adjective formed with the suffix -ин from Сашка, an expressive hypocoristic of Саша, diminutive of the given name Александр (from Ancient Greek Ἀλέξανδρος, 'defender of men').

сбегать.etymology: Formed in Russian from the prefix с- + multidirectional бегать ('to run around'). When stressed on the root (**сбегать**, perfective), the prefix + multidirectional motion verb means 'to make a quick round trip running — to run somewhere and back'. (With stress on the ending, **сбегать**, it is the imperfective of сбежать 'to run down or run away'.)

history.meaning: to run somewhere and right back (quick errand)

сбегать.notes: In everyday speech, *Я быстро сбегаю в магазин* means 'I'll quickly pop/run over to the shop and back'.

сбежать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic събѣжати, formed from the prefix с- ('down from, away from') + бежать ('to run, flee', from Proto-Slavic *běžati).

сбережение.etymology: Verbal noun formed with the suffix -ение from сберечь ('to save, preserve, keep safe'), from с- + беречь (from Proto-Slavic *bergti 'to guard, care for').

сберечь.etymology: Perfective verb formed by adding the prefix с- to беречь ('to guard, keep safe, save'), inherited from Old East Slavic беречи, from Proto-Slavic *bergti ('to guard, take care of'), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰergʰ- ('to keep, shelter').

сбивание.etymology: Verbal noun formed with the suffix -ние from сбивать ('to knock down, whip, churn'), imperfective of сбить, composed of с- ('down from, together') + бить ('to beat, strike', Proto-Slavic *biti).

сбивать.etymology: Imperfective of сбить ('to knock down, knock off; to whip/churn'), formed with prefix с- ('down from; together') + бивать, iterative of бить ('to beat, strike', Proto-Slavic *biti).

сбить.etymology: Formed with prefix с- ('down off; together') from бить ('to strike, beat'), inherited from Old East Slavic събити, from Proto-Slavic *sъ-biti.

сближать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ать from сблизить ('to bring closer together'), composed of the prefix с- ('together') and близить (from близкий 'near, close', Proto-Slavic *blizъ).

сближение.etymology: Verbal noun formed with the suffix -ение from сблизить / сближать ('to bring closer together'), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *blizъ ('near').

сблизиться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed with -ся from сблизить ('to bring closer'), composed of the prefix с- ('together') + близить (from близкий 'close, near', Proto-Slavic *blizъ).

сбоку.etymology: Formed in East Slavic by fusing the preposition с ('from, on') with боку, the old genitive/locative singular of бок ('side, flank', Proto-Slavic *bokъ): 'on the side, from the side'.

history.meaning: on the side, to one side

сболтнуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective verb formed with the prefix с- and suffix -нуть from болтать ('to chatter, babble, stir'), an expressive Slavic verb of onomatopoeic/iterative origin (*bъltati, 'to splash, stir liquid, babble').

сбор.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съборъ ('gathering, assembly, collection'), formed from prefix с- ('together') + o-grade root бор- of брать ('to take, gather', Proto-Slavic *sъborъ).

сборище.etymology: Formed with the augmentative/pejorative collective suffix -ище from сбор ('gathering, assembly'), deverbal noun from собрать / сбирать ('to gather together', from с- + брать, Proto-Slavic *bьrati).

сборка.etymology: Action noun formed with the suffix -ка from собрать / собирать ('to gather, assemble'), from the prefix с- ('together') and the root of брать ('to take', Proto-Slavic *bьrati).

сбрасывать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ывать from сбросить ('to throw down, shed'), composed of the prefix с- ('down from, off') + бросить ('to throw', Proto-Slavic *brositi).

history.meaning: to throw down, shed; to reject a phone call

сбрить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- ('off, away') from брить ('to shave'), inherited from Old East Slavic брити, from Proto-Slavic *briti ('to cut with a sharp edge, shave'), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreyH- ('to cut, shear').

сбросить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- ('off, down from') from бросить ('to throw, cast'), from Proto-Slavic *brositi (originally 'to scrape off, strip, fling').

history.meaning: to drop, throw off; to lose (weight)

сбываться.etymology: Imperfective verb formed from сбыться ('to come true, be realized'), composed of the prefix с- + бывать (iterative of быть 'to be', Proto-Slavic *byti) + reflexive -ся.

history.meaning: to come to pass, be fulfilled

сбыться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic събытися ('to come to pass, happen, be fulfilled'), from Proto-Slavic *sъbyti sę, composed of *sъ- ('together, completely') + *byti ('to be, become') + reflexive *sę.

history.meaning: to come to pass, be realized

свадебный.etymology: Adjective formed with suffix -ный from свадьба ('wedding'), inherited from Old East Slavic сватьба (with voicing т > д before б), derived from сват ('matchmaker, kinsman by marriage', Proto-Slavic *svatьba).

свадьба.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сватьба ('matchmaking, betrothal, wedding'), with voicing assimilation of -тб- > -дьб-, from Proto-Slavic *svatьba, formed with the suffix *-ьba from *svatъ ('matchmaker, kinsman by marriage', Russian сват), itself related to *svojь ('one's own', Russian свой): a wedding was the ceremony making two families 'one's own kin'.

сваливать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ивать from свалить ('to dump, knock down; colloquially to leave, scram'), from с- + валить (Proto-Slavic *valiti 'to roll, topple').

history.meaning: to dump, pile; (slang) to get out, scram

свалить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- ('down, together') from валить ('to roll, fell, heap'), from Proto-Slavic *valiti (causative/iterative of *velti / *vьlti, from PIE *welH- 'to turn, roll').

history.meaning: to knock down, heap; (slang) to leave
to dump, pin blame on; (slang) to take off

свалиться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed with -ся from свалить ('to topple, knock down'), composed of с- ('down from') + валить (from Proto-Slavic *valiti 'to roll, tumble').

сварить.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing prefix с- + варить ('to boil, cook in liquid, brew', Old East Slavic варити, Proto-Slavic *variti, causative of *vьrěti 'to boil, bubble up', from *варъ 'boiling heat, boiling water').

history.meaning: to cook by boiling (soup, coffee, porridge)

свариться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive form in -ся of сварить ('to boil, cook'), formed with perfective prefix с- from варить ('to boil, cook'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *variti (causative of *vьrěti 'to boil, bubble').

history.meaning: to be cooked, be boiled, finish boiling

свежесть.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -есть (variant of -ость after a husher) from свежий ('fresh'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *svěžь ('fresh, cool, vigorous').

свежий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic свѣжии ('fresh, cool, vigorous'), from Proto-Slavic *svěžь, closely cognate with Lithuanian sviežias ('fresh'). Note that the standard Russian spelling has е (from old ѣ), whereas the Church Slavonic counterpart had я.

свекровь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic свекры (accusative свекръвь, which became the modern nominative), from Proto-Slavic *svekry ('husband's mother'), from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱruh₂ ('mother-in-law', cognate with Latin socrus, Sanskrit śvaśrū, German Schwiegermutter).

сверить.etymology: Formed in Russian from the prefix с- ('together, matching against one another') + верить / вера ('trust, faith, true standard', from Proto-Slavic *věra 'faith, truth'): literally 'to bring two texts, lists, or clocks together to verify that they match truly'.

history.meaning: to check against, compare for accuracy, collate

свериться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of сверить ('to check against a standard, collate, verify'), formed with prefix с- ('together, matching against') + верить / вера ('faith, trust, truth', from Proto-Slavic *věra): literally 'to verify by comparing two sources together'.

history.meaning: to collate, verify → to check against, consult (a map, watch, or notes)

сверкать.etymology: Iterative verb related to диалектальный сверкать / сверкнуть ('to flash, sparkle'), from Proto-Slavic *svьrkati (an expressive/sound-symbolic formation transferred from crackle/chirp of sparks to visual flashing, or blended with *svět- 'light').

свернуть.etymology: Prefixed perfective verb formed from с- ('together, up' or 'off, aside') + вернуть ('to turn, twist', from Proto-Slavic *vьrtěti / *vьrnǫti 'to turn', PIE *wert-). Because Russian с- merges Proto-Slavic *sъ- ('off, down from') and *sъn- ('together'), свернуть means both 'to turn off a road' and 'to roll up, fold up'.

history.meaning: to turn aside; to roll together
to turn (a corner); to roll up, fold; (idiom) свернуть горы 'to move mountains'

сверху.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase с верху ('from the top, on the top surface'), combining the preposition с ('from, off') with the genitive-locative singular (-у) of верх ('top, upper part', from Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ).

свести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съвести ('to lead together, bring down'), from Proto-Slavic *sъvesti, composed of *sъ- ('together, down from') + *vesti ('to lead', modern Russian вести).

history.meaning: to bring together; to cramp (of muscles)

свет.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic свѣтъ ('light; the visible world'), from Proto-Slavic *světъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *kʷéytos ('brightness, white light', from *kʷeyt- 'to shine, be bright, white'; cognate with Sanskrit śvetá 'white, bright' and English white).

светить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic свѣтити and Proto-Slavic *světiti ('to shine, give light'), a denominal verb built on свет ('light', Proto-Slavic *světъ, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeyt- 'to shine, be bright or white', cognate with English white and Sanskrit śvetá).
светить.notes: First-person singular has т -> ч mutation: я свечу, солнце светит.

светленький.etymology: Affectionate/attenuative adjective formed with the suffix -енький from светлый ('light, bright, fair-haired'), from Proto-Slavic *světьlъ (derived from *světъ 'light').

светлость.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from светлый ('bright, illustrious'); in the honorific sense 'Serene Highness / Grace' (Ваша Светлость), a calque of German Durchlaucht (itself calquing Latin Illustritas / Serenitas).

светлый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic свѣтлыи, from Proto-Slavic *světьlъ ('bright, shining, clear, light-coloured'), formed with the adjectival suffix *-ьlъ from *světъ ('light', Russian свет), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweyt- ('to shine, be bright or white'; cognate with English white).
светлый.notes: Russian distinguishes **светлый** ('light in colour, bright with light') from **лёгкий** ('light in weight or difficulty').

светофор.etymology: 20th-century hybrid compound formed from Russian свет ('light', Proto-Slavic *světъ) + connecting vowel -о- + Greek-derived -фор ('-bearer', from Ancient Greek φορός phorós 'carrying, bearing', as in семафор 'semaphore').

светский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ский from свет in its sense 'the world, secular society, high society' (where свет 'world' was calqued in Old Church Slavonic свѣтъ from Greek κόσμος; and 'high society' calqued French le grand monde).

свеча.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic свѣча ('candle, light', compare Old Church Slavonic свѣща), from Proto-Slavic *svěťa ('light, candle'), derived from *světъ ('light', Russian свет).

свечка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from свеча ('candle, taper'), from Old East Slavic свѣча (influenced by Church Slavonic свѣща), from Proto-Slavic *svěťa ('light, candle', < *svět-jā, from *světъ 'light').

свидание.etymology: Verbal noun in -ние formed on повидаться / свидаться ('to see one another, meet'), modeled on Polish widzenie (do widzenia) and French revoir (au revoir), combining the mutual prefix с- ('together') + видать ('to see', iterative of видеть) + -ние: 'a meeting face to face, appointment, or romantic date'.

history.meaning: seeing one another together → meeting, appointment, date

свидание.notes: Most familiar in **До свидания!** ('Goodbye!', literally 'Until [our next] meeting!').

свидетель.etymology: Altered under the folk-etymological influence of видеть ('to see') from Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic съвѣдѣтель ('one who knows with, witness', a calque on Greek συνειδώς / μάρτυς, built on съ- + вѣдѣти 'to know', Proto-Slavic *věděti).

свин.etymology: Masculine back-formation from свинья ('pig, swine'), inherited from Old East Slavic свиния, from Proto-Slavic *svinьja (originally a collective/adjective derivative of *svinъ 'swine', from PIE *suH-īnos, cognate with Latin suinus and English swine).

свинина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic свинина ('pork, swine flesh'), from Proto-Slavic *svinina, formed from *svinъ ('pertaining to pigs', modern свиной) with the meat-denoting suffix *-ina.

свинка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of свинья ('pig, swine'), inherited from Old East Slavic свиния, from Proto-Slavic *svinьja ('pig', derived from old adjective *svinъ 'pertaining to swine', PIE *suH-īnos).

history.meaning: little pig, piggy; guinea pig; mumps

свиной.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic свиныи ('pertaining to pigs'), from Proto-Slavic *svinъ, an ancient adjective from Proto-Indo-European *suH-īnós ('of swine', exact cognate with Latin suīnus, English swine, German Schwein).

свинья.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic свиния ('pig, sow'), from Proto-Slavic *svinьja, a collective/feminine noun derived from the adjective *svinъ ('porcine', from PIE *suH- 'pig, sow').

свистеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic свистѣти and Proto-Slavic *svistěti ('to whistle, hiss'), formed from the onomatopoeic Proto-Indo-European root *sweysd- ('to hiss, whistle'). The sibilant cluster *swis- directly imitates the sharp sound of air rushing through lips or reeds, paralleling English whistle and Latin sībilāre.

свитер.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century from English sweater ('heavy knitted woollen pullover', originally worn by athletes or rowers to produce sweat during training, from sweat + -er).

history.meaning: to perspire → heavy knitted athletic pullover

свобода.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic свобода (and reinforced by Old Church Slavonic свобода, alongside native dialectal слобода 'free settlement'), from Proto-Slavic *svoboda ('state of belonging to one's own clan as a free person, freedom'), built on the reflexive-possessive stem *svobъ / *svojь (Russian свой 'one's own', from PIE *s(w)e- 'self, own'; compare особа 'person').

history.stage: Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic

свободный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic свободьныи and Old Church Slavonic свободьнъ, formed from свобода ('freedom, liberty', Proto-Slavic *svoboda). Vasmer traces *svoboda to the reflexive-possessive root *svoj- / *svob- ('one's own', PIE *s(w)e-; compare свой 'one's own' and особа 'person'): originally 'belonging to one's own community of free kinsfolk, autonomous'.
свободный.notes: Used everyday when asking if a chair or table is taken: *Здесь свободно?* ('Is this seat free?').

сводить.etymology: Formed with prefix с- ('together' or 'down from'; as perfective, 'there and back') from водить ('to lead, conduct'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *sъ-voditi.

history.meaning: to bring together; (pf) to take someone somewhere

сводник.etymology: Agent noun formed with the suffix -ник from сводить ('to bring together, matchmake, procure'), composed of с- ('together') + водить ('to lead', Proto-Slavic *voditi).

сводный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from сводить / свести ('to bring together, combine'); in kinship terms (сводный брат/сестра 'step-sibling'), referring to children brought together from prior marriages.

сводчатый.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -чатый ('having the shape or feature of') from свод ('arch, architectural vault'), literally 'a bringing together' from сводить ('to bring together, join at the top', built on с- + водить 'to lead').

history.meaning: vault, arch (where masonry walls meet) → arched, vaulted

свозить.etymology: Perfective multidirectional verb (in the sense 'to take someone somewhere by vehicle and bring them back') formed with the prefix с- from возить ('to convey, transport', Proto-Slavic *voziti).

history.meaning: to take somewhere and back by vehicle

свой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic свои (f. своя, n. свое), from Proto-Slavic *svojь ('one's own'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *swóyos (built on the reflexive stem *swé- 'oneself'; cognate with Latin suus, Ancient Greek ἑός, and Sanskrit svá).
свой.notes: Refers back to the subject of the clause for any person ('my own, your own, his/her/our/their own').

свойство.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ство from свой ('one's own, proper to oneself', Proto-Slavic *svojь), modeled on Latin proprietas ('peculiar nature, property', from proprius 'one's own').

сволочь.etymology: Originally a collective noun meaning 'everything dragged/raked together into a heap: trash, weeds, riffraff, rabble', derived from сволочь / сволакивать ('to drag together'), from с- + волочь ('to drag', Proto-Slavic *velkti).

сворачивать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ивать from своротить / свернуть ('to turn aside, roll up, wind down'), composed of с- + воротить (from Proto-Slavic *vortiti 'to turn').

history.meaning: to turn; to roll up, wind down

своровать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- from воровать ('to steal, thieve'), derived from вор ('thief', in sixteenth–seventeenth century Muscovite Russian 'criminal, rebel, impostor').

связанный.etymology: Past passive participle of связать ('to tie together, bind, connect'), formed from с- ('together') + вязать ('to tie, bind, knit', from Proto-Slavic *vęzati).

связать.etymology: Formed with prefix с- ('together') from вязать ('to tie, bind, knit'), inherited from Old East Slavic съвязати, from Proto-Slavic *sъ-vęzati ('to bind together').

history.meaning: to tie up, bind; to knit

связаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of связать ('to tie together, connect'), formed from с- ('together') + вязать ('to tie, bind', Proto-Slavic *vęzati), meaning 'to get in touch with' or 'to get mixed up with'.

history.meaning: to get in touch, to contact; get involved with

связка.etymology: Noun formed with the suffix -ка from связать / связывать ('to tie together, bundle'), from с- + вязать (Proto-Slavic *vęzati 'to bind').

history.meaning: bunch, bundle; anatomical ligament or vocal cord

связывать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ывать from связать ('to tie together, bind, connect'), from Proto-Slavic *sъvęzati (*sъ- + *vęzati 'to bind').

связываться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed with -ся from связывать ('to connect, tie'), from с- + вязать (Proto-Slavic *vęzati); used both for getting in touch ('connecting with') and colloquially for getting entangled or messing with someone.

history.meaning: to contact; to get involved or mess with

связь.etymology: Deverbal feminine i-stem noun formed from связать ('to tie together, bind, connect'), built from the prefix с- ('together') and вязать ('to tie, bind, knit', Old East Slavic вязати, Proto-Slavic *vęzati).

святой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic святыи (reinforced by Old Church Slavonic свѩтъ), from Proto-Slavic *svętъ ('holy, sacred', originally 'strong, possessing spiritual power'; cognate with Lithuanian šventas, Avestan spənta-).

священный.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic свѧщенъ ('consecrated, sacred, holy', with the Characteristic South Slavic reflex -щ- < *-tj-), passive participle of свѧтити ('to sanctify, consecrate'), from Proto-Slavic *svętъ ('holy, sacred').

свёрток.etymology: Formed in Russian with the noun suffix -ок from свернуть / свёртывать ('to roll up, wrap up together'), combining с- ('together') + вертеть ('to turn, roll, wind', Proto-Slavic *vьrtěti): literally 'something rolled or wrapped up into a bundle'.

history.meaning: to roll/wrap up → wrapped parcel, bundle

свёрток.notes: Drops the fleeting vowel -о- in all oblique forms: *свёрток → свёртка, в свёртке*.

сгиб.etymology: Deverbal noun from сгибать ('to bend, fold'), built on prefix с- ('together') + the root гиб- ('bend, flex', related by ablaut to гнуть 'to bend', from Proto-Slavic *gъbnǫti / *gybati).

history.meaning: to fold, bend → crease, fold, bend
