сглазить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- and verbal suffix -ить from глаз ('eye'), referring to the folk belief of harming or jinxing someone by looking at them with an 'evil eye' (дурной глаз) or excessive praise.

history.meaning: to put the evil eye on, to jinx

сглупить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- (denoting a single completed act of behavior) from глупить ('to act foolishly'), derived from глупый ('foolish, stupid', Proto-Slavic *glupъ).

сгнить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the resultative prefix с- from гнить ('to rot, decay'), inherited from Old East Slavic гнити, from Proto-Slavic *gniti ('to rot, putrefy').

сговориться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed with the prefix с- ('together') and -ся from говорить ('to speak, talk', from Proto-Slavic *govoriti), literally 'to talk together until reaching a secret or mutual agreement'.

сгоревший.etymology: Formed as the past active participle of сгореть ('to burn down, burn out', from с- 'completely, down' + гореть 'to burn', Proto-Slavic *gorěti): 'burnt-out, blown (of a bulb or electrical fuse)'.

сгореть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съгорѣти ('to burn up, burn down'), formed from the perfective prefix с- + гореть ('to burn', from Proto-Slavic *gorěti).

сгрузить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- ('down from, off') from грузить ('to load'), derived from груз ('load, cargo, weight', related to Proto-Slavic *grǫziti 'to sink, submerge under weight').

сгущёнка.etymology: Colloquial univerbation formed with the suffix -ка from сгущённое молоко ('condensed milk'), where сгущённый is the past passive participle of сгустить ('to thicken, condense', built on с- 'together' + густой 'thick, dense', Proto-Slavic *gǫstъ).

сдавать.etymology: Imperfective of сдать ('to hand over, turn in, rent out, deal cards, pass an exam'), formed from the prefix с- ('off one's hands, over') + давать ('to give', Proto-Slavic *davati).

history.meaning: to hand in, rent out, return

сдаваться.etymology: Formed as the imperfective reflexive of сдаться ('to give oneself up, surrender, yield'), from с- + даваться (imperfective of даться, from дать 'to give', Proto-Slavic *dati) + -ся.
сдаваться.notes: Present tense drops the -ва- syllable and takes stressed endings: я не сдаюсь ('I don't give up'). Also used in квартира сдаётся ('flat for rent / to let').

сдать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съдати, formed with prefix с- ('off, over') from дать ('to give'), from Proto-Slavic *sъ-dati ('to hand over, deliver').

history.meaning: to return, to hand in; to pass (an exam); to deal (cards)

сдаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of сдать ('to hand over, yield, surrender'), formed from с- + дать ('to give', inherited from Proto-Slavic *dati).

сдача.etymology: Formed from сдать ('to hand over, give back') + the action/object suffix -ча (from Proto-Slavic *-jа after dental): originally 'the act of handing over or surrendering', and in everyday commerce 'the money handed back after payment, change'.

history.meaning: to hand over, return → handing over; money returned

сдача.notes: Useful cash-desk phrases: *без сдачи* ('exact change') and *Сдачи не надо* ('Keep the change').

сдвинуться.etymology: Reflexive intransitive form in -ся of сдвинуть ('to move from its place, shift'), formed from prefix с- ('from, off a spot; together') + двинуть ('to move', from Proto-Slavic *dvignǫti).

history.meaning: to budge, shift from one's place

сделанный.etymology: Past passive participle of сделать ('to do, make'), formed from the perfective prefix с- + делать ('to do, make', derived from дело 'deed, work', Old East Slavic дѣло, Proto-Slavic *dělo, from PIE *dʰeh₁- 'to do, place').

сделать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съдѣлати, from Proto-Slavic *sъdělati, the perfective counterpart of делать ('to do, make'), formed with the completive prefix с- (*sъ-) + делать (from дело 'deed, work', Proto-Slavic *dělo, PIE *dʰeh₁- 'to do, put').

history.meaning: to do, work → to complete, make

сделка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the suffix -ка from сделать(ся) (in the older commercial sense сделаться с кем-либо 'to come to terms, settle a transaction with someone'), built on с- ('together') + дело ('business, affair', Proto-Slavic *dělo).

сдержанный.etymology: Adjectival passive participle of сдержать ('to hold back, restrain, check'), composed of the prefix с- + держать ('to hold', from Proto-Slavic *dьržati).

сдержаться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed with -ся from сдержать ('to hold back, restrain'), from с- + держать (Proto-Slavic *dьržati).

сдерживать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ивать from сдержать ('to hold back, restrain'), composed of с- + держать (from Proto-Slavic *dьržati 'to hold').

сдуреть.etymology: Colloquial perfective verb formed with the prefix с- from дуреть ('to become foolish, lose one's wits'), derived from дура / дурак ('fool', from Proto-Slavic *durъ 'stupefied, wild, foolish').

history.meaning: to go crazy, lose one's mind

сеанс.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French séance ('sitting, session, performance'), derived from séant, present participle of Old French seoir ('to sit'), from Latin sedēre ('to sit').

себя.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic себе / себя, from Proto-Slavic *sebe (accusative/genitive of the reflexive pronoun), continuing the Proto-Indo-European reflexive stem *s(w)e- ('oneself'), cognate with Latin sē, German sich, and Sanskrit svá-.
себя.notes: **Себя** has no nominative form and refers back to the subject of the clause regardless of person, gender, or number (*я вижу себя*, *они видят себя*). The verbal suffix **-ся** is historically its reduced enclitic cousin.

север.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сѣверъ and Old Church Slavonic сѣверъ ('north, cold north wind'), from Proto-Slavic *sěverъ ('north, biting north wind'), cognate with Lithuanian šiaurė ('north') and šiaurus ('piercingly cold') and Latin caurus ('northwest wind').
север.notes: Takes на for location and motion: на севере ('in the north'), на север ('to the north').

северный.etymology: Derived with the adjectival suffix -ный from север ('north'), inherited from Old East Slavic сѣверъ and Proto-Slavic *sěverъ ('north, cold north wind'). The Slavic word descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *ḱeh₁wero- ('north, north wind'). It is directly cognate with Latin caurus ('northwest wind'), Lithuanian šiaurė ('north'), and English shower (originally 'a gust of cold wind or rain').

cognates.meaning: fall of rain (from PGmc *skūraz 'storm wind' < PIE *ḱeh₁wero-)

северо-запад.etymology: Compound compass noun joining север ('north', from Old East Slavic сѣверъ and Proto-Slavic *sěverъ 'north, cold north wind') + linking vowel -о- + запад ('west', literally 'setting/falling of the sun', from за- + падать).

севрюга.etymology: Attested in Russian since the sixteenth century (Домострой), borrowed from a Turkic language (compare Tatar сөйрәк / söyräk, Chuvash сӗврӗк, derived from Turkic *süvrü / *sivri 'sharp-pointed', referring to the stellate sturgeon's long, pointed snout).

сегодня.etymology: Сегодня grew from an older expression meaning of this day. Vasmer identifies it as an old genitive construction and records Old Russian сего дьне. The once-separate words became the ordinary adverb today; сего is an older form of the demonstrative сей, this.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: сегодня

сегодняшний.etymology: Derived within Russian from the adverb сегодня ('today') + temporal-adjectival suffix -шний (compare вчерашний, завтрашний). Сегодня itself univerbated Old East Slavic genitive сего дьне ('of this day', from demonstrative сь 'this' + дьнь 'day').
сегодняшний.notes: Because сего- was originally a genitive ending, the written г in сегодня and сегодняшний is pronounced [v] ([sʲɪˈvodʲnʲɪʂnʲɪj]), never [g].

седой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сѣдыи ('gray-haired, hoary'), from Proto-Slavic *sědъ (< *xoidos, with second palatalization before *ě), from the Proto-Indo-European color/shine root *ḱey- / *ḱHoyd- ('gray, pale, shining', cognate with сивый and сиять).

седьмой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic седьмыи ('seventh'), from Proto-Slavic *sedmъ (preserving the original *-d- of Proto-Indo-European *septmós 'seventh' that was simplified in the cardinal numeral семь < сежьмь < *sedmь).

сезон.etymology: Borrowed from French saison ('season of the year, proper time'), from Vulgar Latin *satiō, satiōnem, from Classical Latin satiō ('a sowing, planting time', from serere, satum 'to sow').

сезонный.etymology: Adjective formed with suffix -ный from сезон ('season'), borrowed from French saison ('season', from Latin satiō 'sowing time').

сей.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сь (feminine си, neuter се) and Proto-Slavic *sь ('this one right here'), from the Proto-Indo-European proximal demonstrative *ḱis ('this'), preserved in сейчас ('right this hour -> now'), сегодня ('of this day -> today'), and до сих пор ('until these times -> until now').

history.meaning: this (archaic, bookish, or emphatic in set phrases)

сей.notes: In modern speech сей survives mainly in fixed expressions: сию минуту ('this very minute / right away'), до сих пор ('up to now'), на сей раз ('this time').

сейф.etymology: Borrowed in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century from English safe ('strongbox, fireproof lockable cabinet'), substantivized from the adjective safe, from Old French sauf, from Latin salvus ('safe, unharmed').

сейчас.etymology: Univerbation of the Early Modern Russian phrase сей час ('this very hour, this instant'), combining the archaic proximal demonstrative сей ('this', from Proto-Slavic *sь, also preserved in сегодня) with час ('hour, moment, time').

секрет.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish sekret or French secret (and German Sekret) from Latin sēcrētum ('something set apart, hidden thing, mystery'), neuter past participle of sēcernere ('to separate, set apart': sē- 'apart' + cernere 'to sift, distinguish').

history.meaning: to set apart → hidden matter, secret

секрет.notes: In the set phrase *по секрету* ('in confidence, as a secret'), it takes the dative.

секретничать.etymology: Colloquial verb formed with the suffix -ничать from секретный / секрет ('secret', borrowed via French secret or Polish sekret from Latin sēcrētum 'something set apart, secret').

секретно.etymology: Deadjectival adverb and predicative formed with -о from секретный ('secret'), derived from секрет (borrowed via French secret / German Sekret from Latin sēcrētum).

секретный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from секрет ('secret'), borrowed in the Petrine era via French secret / German Sekret (or Polish sekret) from Latin sēcrētum ('something set apart, hidden thing, secret', from sēcernere 'to separate, set apart').

сексуальный.etymology: Derived with the adjectival suffix -ный from French sexuel or German sexuell, from Late Latin sexuālis ('pertaining to sex'), from Latin sexus ('sex, gender').

секта.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish sekta or German Sekte from Latin secta ('way of life, school of thought, religious faction'), from secāre ('to cut off') or sequī ('to follow').

секунда.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via German Sekunde or directly from Medieval Latin pars minūta secunda ('second small division [of an hour]', i.e. the division of the hour by sixty a second time, after pars minūta prīma 'minute'), from Latin secundus ('second, following').

history.meaning: second small division of an hour

секундочка.etymology: Affectionate double diminutive formed with the suffix -очка from секунда ('second'), borrowed via German Sekunde from Medieval Latin (pars minuta) secunda ('second diminished part [of an hour]', from Latin secundus 'second, following').

сельдерей.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Sellerie (or Dutch selderij) from French céleri, from Lombard Italian selleri, plural of sellero, from Late Latin selīnum, from Ancient Greek σέλινον (sélinon, 'parsley, celery').

сельдь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сельдь ('herring'), borrowed in the Viking Age from Old Norse sild ('herring', compare Swedish sill).

селёдка.etymology: Formed with the suffix -ка from сельдь ('herring', with East Slavic pleophonic/epenthetic development around the soft liquid in *селъдка > селёдка), ultimately from Old Norse sild ('herring').

семейка.etymology: Colloquial diminutive (often ironic) in -ка of семья ('family'), inherited from Old East Slavic сѣмия ('household, servants, family'), from Proto-Slavic *sěmьja ('household, members of a homestead').

семейный.etymology: Derived in Russian from семья ('family', stem семей- with vocalized fleeting е before -ный) + the adjectival suffix -ный.

семейство.etymology: Derived with collective/abstract suffix -ство from семья (stem семей-, 'household, family'), from Proto-Slavic *sěmьja.

семеро.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic семеръ / семеро and Proto-Slavic *sedmerъ ('group of seven'), formed with the collective numeral suffix *-erъ from *sedmь ('seven'). The base numeral descends from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥ ('seven'), where the cluster *-ptm- became *-dm- and then simplified to -м- in East Slavic. It is cognate with English seven, Latin septem, and Ancient Greek ἑπτά (heptá).

семнадцать.etymology: Contraction of Old East Slavic семь на десяте ('seven on ten'), formed from семь ('seven', Proto-Slavic *sedmь) + на ('on') + десяте (locative singular of десять 'ten', Proto-Slavic *desętь).

семь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic семь (simplified from earlier сежьмь; compare Old Church Slavonic седмь and Russian ordinal седьмой), from Proto-Slavic *sedmь, continuing Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥ ('seven'), cognate with English seven, Latin septem, and Ancient Greek ἑπτά.

семьсот.etymology: Compound numeral inherited from Old East Slavic семь сътъ ('seven hundreds'), combining семь ('seven', Proto-Slavic *sedmь) + сот (genitive plural of сто 'hundred', Proto-Slavic *sъto).

семья.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сѣмья ('household, members of a home including servants and family'), a collective derivative of Proto-Slavic *sěmь ('member of a household, person'), cognate with Lithuanian šeima ('family, household'), Gothic haims ('village, home'), and English home.

cognates.meaning: dwelling, household (from the same PIE root *ḱey- 'to lie, settle')

семья.notes: Etymologically distinct from семя ('seed', from *sěmę, root *sē- 'to sow'), even though the two words look very similar in modern Russian! Nominative plural shifts stress to the stem: семьи; genitive plural семей.

семьянин.etymology: Derived with the singulative/person suffix -янин (-ин) from семья ('family, household'), from Old East Slavic сѣмия ('household, domestic servants, family'), from Proto-Slavic *sěmьja (from PIE *ḱey- 'to lie, settle; home, beloved').

семя.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сѣмя ('seed, offspring'), from Proto-Slavic *sěmę ('seed'), a neuter *-men- stem from Proto-Indo-European *séh₁m̥n ('seed', from *seh₁- 'to sow', exact cognate with Latin sēmen and Old High German sāmo).

сентиментальный.etymology: Borrowed in the late 18th century via French sentimental from English sentimental (popularized across Europe by Laurence Sterne's 1768 novel *A Sentimental Journey*, translated by Nikolai Karamzin's generation), derived from sentiment ('feeling'), from Medieval Latin sentīmentum (Latin sentīre 'to feel').

сенча.etymology: Borrowed from Japanese 煎茶 (sencha, 'steamed and infused green tea'), a Sino-Japanese compound of 煎 (sen, 'to simmer, decoction, roast') and 茶 (cha, 'tea', from Middle Chinese dzya).

серверная.etymology: Substantivized feminine adjective (ellipsis of серверная комната 'server room') formed with -ная from сервер ('computer server'), borrowed from English server (from to serve, from Old French servir, from Latin servīre).

сервис.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English service ('customer assistance, maintenance, service system'), from Old French servise and Latin servitium ('service'), from servus ('servant, attendant'). Note the older 18th-century Russian doublet сервиз ('matched dinner or tea set'), borrowed earlier via French service.

сердечко.etymology: Diminutive in -ко of сердце ('heart'), inherited from Old East Slavic сьрдьце, from Proto-Slavic *sьrdьce ('heart', originally a diminutive of *sьrdь, from PIE *ḱḗr 'heart').

сердито.etymology: Formed as the short neuter and adverbial derivative in -о of сердитый ('angry, cross', built on сердце 'heart' / сердиться 'to be angry').

сердитый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сьрдитыи ('angry, wrathful, spirited'), formed with the adjective suffix -итый from сердце ('heart', which in Old East Slavic сьрдьце and older Russian also meant 'anger, wrath, temper', still preserved in the idiom в сердцах 'in a fit of anger', from Proto-Slavic *sьrdьce).

сердиться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сьрдитися and Proto-Slavic *sьrditi sę ('to be angry, take to heart, be wrathful'), derived from *sьrdьce (Russian сердце 'heart', because the heart was viewed as the seat of passion and anger).
сердиться.notes: First-person singular has д -> ж mutation: я сержусь; takes на + accusative (Не сердись на меня! 'Don't be angry with me!').

сердце.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сьрдьце ('heart'), from Proto-Slavic *sьrdьce, a diminutive extension of the ancient Proto-Indo-European root noun *ḱḗr / *ḱr̥d- ('heart'), directly cognate with English heart, German Herz, Latin cor (genitive cordis), Ancient Greek καρδία, and Lithuanian širdìs.
сердце.notes: The middle **д** is silent in nominative/accusative **сердце** (*сéрце*), but reappears clearly in the genitive plural **сердец**.

серебряный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic серебряныи ('made of silver'), formed with the material suffix -яный from серебро ('silver', showing East Slavic pleophony -ере- from Proto-Slavic *sьrebro, shared with Baltic — Lithuanian sidãbras — and Germanic — Gothic silubr, English silver — as an ancient Northern European metal wanderword).

середина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic середина ('middle, centre'), formed with the suffix -ина from середа ('middle', showing native East Slavic pleophony -ере- from Proto-Slavic *serda 'middle, heart', compare the Church Slavonic doublet среда 'Wednesday; environment').

сержант.etymology: Borrowed in the early eighteenth century via German Sergeant or directly from French sergent ('sergeant, officer's attendant'), from Old French serjant ('servant, foot soldier'), from Latin serviēns (present participle of servīre 'to serve').

сериал.etymology: Borrowed in the second half of the twentieth century from English serial ('story or broadcast published in installments'), from New Latin seriālis, from Latin seriēs ('row, chain, sequence').

серый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сѣръ / сѣрыи ('grey'), from Proto-Slavic *sěrъ (with East Slavic c- from the second palatalization of *xěrъ before *ě; compare West Slavic *šěrъ > Polish szary 'grey'), continuing a Proto-Indo-European colour root *ḱey-ro- ('dark grey, hoary'; cognate with English hoar / hoary and Old Norse hárr 'grey-haired').

серьга.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic серьга (attested in fourteenth-century wills), borrowed from a Turkic language (compare Kipchak/Chuvash *sürüg / *syrγa, Tatar сырга, Bashkir һырға 'earring, ring').

серьёзно.etymology: Adverb derived from the adjective серьёзный ('serious'), borrowed in the 18th century from French sérieux ('serious, grave'), from Medieval Latin sēriōsus and Classical Latin sērius ('earnest, grave, weighty').

серьёзный.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French sérieux ('serious, earnest, grave'), adapted with the Russian adjectival suffix -ный. French sérieux comes from Medieval Latin sēriōsus, from Classical Latin sērius ('grave, earnest, weighty').

серёжка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from серьга ('earring', with regular palatalized velar mutation г > ж and vowel insertion *серьжка > серёжка); also used botanically for tree catkins that hang like earrings.

сессия.etymology: Borrowed via Polish sesja or German Session from Latin sessiō ('a sitting, session of a court or assembly'), derived from sedēre (supine sessum, 'to sit').

сестра.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сестра, from Proto-Slavic *sestra ('sister', with regular Slavic insertion of -t- in *-sr-), from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr ('sister'; cognate with Latin soror, Sanskrit svásā, English sister).

сесть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сѣсти and Proto-Slavic *sěsti ('to sit down', originally formed with an nasal infix in the present tense *sędǫ 'I will sit down' from Proto-Indo-European *sed- 'to sit'), cognate with сидеть ('to be sitting'), сад ('garden'), and English sit.

history.meaning: to sit down; to board (transport); to set (of the sun); to run flat (of a battery)

сесть.notes: Future tense reflects the old nasal vowel *ę -> я: я сяду, ты сядешь, сядь! ('sit down!'); past tense сел, села.

сет.etymology: Borrowed in the twentieth century from English set (first in tennis 'a set of games', and later in restaurant and music contexts 'a curated set menu, sushi set, or DJ set'), from Middle English set, from Old English settan / Old French secte.

history.meaning: set (tasting menu, sushi set, tennis set)

сеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сѣть ('net, snare'), from Proto-Slavic *sětь ('net, snare'), from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂y- ('to bind, tie'; cognate with Lithuanianynas /ietas, Latin saeta, German Seil 'rope').

сжигать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the prefix с- and vowel-lengthened iterative stem -жигать (from *-žigati) corresponding to сжечь ('to burn down, incinerate'), from Proto-Slavic *žegti ('to burn', PIE *dʰegʷʰ-).

сжимать.etymology: Imperfective of сжать (сожму, 'to squeeze, compress, clench'), formed with prefix с- ('together') and iterative stem -жимать from жать (жму, 'to press, squeeze', Proto-Slavic *žęti, *žьmǫ).

сзади.etymology: Formed in East Slavic by fusing the preposition с ('from, at') with the old locative/genitive зади of зад ('back, rear part', Proto-Slavic *zadъ, built on за 'behind').

history.meaning: behind, at the back, on the back

си.etymology: In Italian/Spanish dialogue ('yes!'), borrowed from Italian sì / Spanish sí, from Latin sic ('thus, so [it is]'). As the seventh solfège note ('B'), formed by acronym from Latin Sancte Iohannes in the medieval hymn Ut queant laxis.

сигара.etymology: Borrowed in the early nineteenth century via French cigare from Spanish cigarro ('cigar'), commonly traced to Mayan sik'ar ('to smoke rolled tobacco leaves', from sik' 'tobacco').

сигарета.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French cigarette ('small paper-wrapped roll of tobacco'), diminutive of cigare ('cigar'), itself via Spanish cigarro (likely from Mayan sik'ar 'to smoke rolled tobacco leaves').

сигнал.etymology: Borrowed via German Signal or French signal from Medieval Latin signāle ('sign, signal'), substantivized neuter of Late Latin signālis ('serving as a sign'), from Latin signum ('mark, sign').

сигнализация.etymology: Borrowed via French signalisation or German Signalisierung / formed with -изация from сигнал ('signal'), ultimately from Medieval Latin signāle, from Latin signum ('mark, sign').

сиделка.etymology: Agent noun formed with the feminine/colloquial suffix -лка from сидеть ('to sit', from Proto-Slavic *sěděti), literally 'one who sits by a sickbed to watch over a patient'.

сиденье.etymology: Formed as a verbal/object noun in -енье from сидеть ('to sit', Proto-Slavic *sěděti): 'that on which one sits — a chair seat, bench, bicycle saddle, or car seat'.

сидеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сѣдѣти / сидѣти and Proto-Slavic *sěděti ('to sit, be in a sitting position'), a stative verb in *-ěti from Proto-Indo-European *sed- ('to sit'), cognate with Latin sedēre ('to sit'), Lithuanian sėdėti, and English sit.
сидеть.notes: First-person singular has д -> ж mutation: я сижу, ты сидишь. Indicates stationary position (сидеть на стуле, prepositional), whereas садиться / сесть indicates the action of sitting down (сесть на стул, accusative).

сидеться.etymology: Impersonal disposition reflexive verb formed with -ся from сидеть ('to sit'), inherited from Old East Slavic сѣдѣти, from Proto-Slavic *sěděti (from PIE *sed- 'to sit'); used chiefly with negation (не сидится 'cannot sit still').

history.meaning: (impersonal) to feel inclined to sit still

сила.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сила and Proto-Slavic *sila ('strength, power, force'), with exact Baltic cognates in Old Prussian seilin ('diligence, earnestness, spiritual power') and Lithuanian siela ('soul, spirit, inner strength').

силком.etymology: Adverbialized instrumental singular of a colloquial formation *силок (from сила 'strength, force', Proto-Slavic *sila), meaning 'by sheer force, forcibly'.

сильнее.etymology: Comparative degree formed with the suffix -ее from сильный ('strong, powerful') and сильно ('strongly'), derived from сила ('strength, force', from Proto-Slavic *sila).

сильнейший.etymology: Synthetic superlative adjective formed with the suffix -ейший from сильный ('strong'), derived from сила ('strength, force', from Proto-Slavic *sila).

сильно.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сильно, the short neuter and adverbial form of сильный ('strong', derived from сила 'strength'). In everyday Russian it also functions as an intensifier meaning 'very much, badly, heavily' (сильно устать 'to get very tired', сильно болеть 'to hurt badly').

сильный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сильныи and Proto-Slavic *silьnъ ('strong, powerful'), formed from сила ('strength, force') with the adjectival suffix -ный.
сильный.notes: Used in Russian for heavy weather: сильный дождь ('heavy rain'), сильный ветер ('strong/high wind').

сим-карта.etymology: Coined in the 1990s as a partial calque of English SIM card, combining the English telecommunications acronym SIM (Subscriber Identity Module) with Russian карта ('card', borrowed via German Karte and Polish karta from Latin charta).

симпатичный.etymology: Formed with the adjective suffix -ный from симпатия ('sympathy, liking, affinity') or adapted from French sympathique ('likeable, congenial, pleasant'), ultimately from Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sumpátheia, 'fellow-feeling').

симпатия.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via French sympathie or German Sympathie from Latin sympathīa, from Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sympátheia, 'fellow-feeling, affinity'), from σύν ('with') + πάθος ('feeling, emotion').

симулянт.etymology: Borrowed from German Simulant ('malingerer, one who feigns illness'), from Latin simulans, genitive simulantis, present participle of simulare ('to make like, imitate, feign', from similis 'like, similar').

синагога.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic синагога (and Latin synagōga) from Ancient Greek συναγωγή (synagōgḗ, 'assembly, place of congregation, synagogue', translating Hebrew בֵּית כְּנֶסֶת bēth knesset 'house of assembly'), derived from συνάγω (synágō, 'to bring together, gather', from σύν 'together' + ἄγω 'to lead').

синдром.etymology: Borrowed via French syndrome or German Syndrom from Medical Latin syndromē, from Ancient Greek συνδρομή (syndromḗ, 'concurrence of symptoms, running together'), from σύν ('together') + δρόμος ('course, running').

синий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic синии ('dark blue,bluish-dark'), from Proto-Slavic *siňь ('dark blue, livid, gleaming'). Russian famously divides English 'blue' into two distinct basic colours: синий (deep navy/cobalt blue) and голубой (sky blue).

синьора.etymology: Borrowed from Italian signora ('lady, madam, Mrs.'), feminine of signore ('lord, gentleman, Mr.'), from Latin senior ('older, elder', comparative of senex 'old', source of Spanish señora and French seigneur).

history.meaning: signora (Italian lady or polite form of address)

синяк.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -як from синий ('dark blue', inherited from Old East Slavic синии, from Proto-Slavic *siňь), referring to the bluish-purple discoloration of a contusion.

сиреневый.etymology: Relational and color adjective formed with the suffix -евый from сирень ('lilac shrub'), which was reshaped in Russian by folk-etymological association with синий ('blue') from earlier синель, borrowed via German Syringe from Botanical Latin syringa (from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ 'pipe, tube', referring to the hollow stems).

сироп.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from French sirop ('syrup'), from Medieval Latin sirupus, from Arabic شَرَاب (šarāb, 'drink, beverage, sweet potion'), from the verb šariba ('to drink').

сирота.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сирота ('orphan; poor dependent peasant'), from Proto-Slavic *sirota, formed with the suffix *-ota from the adjective *sirъ (Old East Slavic сирыи, archival Russian сирый 'orphaned, bereft, desolate').
сирота.notes: Common-gender noun in Russian (он круглый сирота / она круглая сирота 'an orphan who has lost both parents').

система.etymology: Borrowed via French système or German System / Polish система from Late Latin systema, from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma, 'organized whole, body composed of several parts'), from συνίστημι (sunístēmi, 'to set together, combine').

ситуация.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via Polish sytuacja or German Situation from French situation ('position, state of affairs'), derived from Medieval Latin situātiō ('location, placement'), from Latin situs ('site, position').

сиять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сияти and Proto-Slavic *sijati ('to shine, radiate light'). The verb traces back to the Proto-Indo-European root *skeh₂i- / *ḱeh₁y- ('to shine, glimmer, gleam'). Through Proto-Germanic *skīnaną, this same Indo-European root gave rise to English shine and shimmer.

сказать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съказати ('to declare, relate, tell'), formed from съ- (perfective prefix) + казати ('to show, point out, speak', from Proto-Slavic *kazati). Over time сказать became the suppletive perfective partner of говорить ('to speak, say').

history.meaning: to point out, tell in full

сказаться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed with -ся from сказать ('to say, tell', from с- + казать, Proto-Slavic *kazati 'to show, declare'); evolved from 'to declare oneself, make oneself known' to 'to have an effect, tell on'.

history.meaning: to affect, tell on, make itself felt

сказка.etymology: Formed with the suffix -ка from сказать / сказывать ('to tell, recount, narrate', from с- + казать, Proto-Slavic *kazati); in sixteenth–seventeenth century Muscovite Russian meant 'written testimony, deposition, census list' before specializing as 'folktale, fairy tale'.

сказочник.etymology: Agent noun formed with the suffix -ник from сказка ('fairy tale, folktale', with regular velar palatalization к > ч), denoting a teller or writer of fairy tales (and figuratively a spinner of tall tales).

скайп.etymology: Early 21st-century borrowing from the English proprietary name Skype, the voice/video telecommunications application launched in 2003 (coined by shortening 'Sky peer-to-peer' to Skyper, then Skype).

history.meaning: video and voice calling service (< Sky peer-to-peer)

скальпель.etymology: Borrowed via German Skalpell or French scalpel from Latin scalpellum ('small surgical knife, lancet'), diminutive of scalprum ('knife, chisel'), from scalpere ('to carve, scrape, cut').

скамейка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ейка from скамья ('bench'), borrowed early into Old East Slavic (attested as скамия / скамья) from Byzantine Greek σκαμνίον, from Late Latin scamellum / Latin scamnum ('step, stool, bench').

скамья.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic скамия ('bench, footstool'), borrowed via Byzantine Greek σκαμνίον (skamníon) from Late Latin scamellum / Classical Latin scamnum ('bench, stool, step').

скандал.etymology: Borrowed via French scandale or German Skandal from Late Latin scandalum ('cause of offense, stumbling block'), from Ancient Greek σκάνδαλον (skándalon, 'trigger of a trap, snare, stumbling block').

скандалить.etymology: Denominative verb in -ить formed from скандал ('scandal, noisy row'), borrowed via French scandale / German Skandal from Late Latin scandalum ('stumbling block, offense'), from Ancient Greek σκάνδαλον (skándalon, 'trap, snare, stumbling block').

history.meaning: snare, stumbling block, cause of offense

скатерть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съкатрьть. The leading scholarly explanation (Vasmer) traces it to Proto-Slavic *dъskatьrtь, a compound of доска 'board, table' + тереть 'to wipe, rub' — literally a 'table-wiper' cloth, though rival hypotheses exist.

скачок.etymology: Diminutive/single-action noun formed with the suffix -ок from скакать ('to jump, leap, gallop'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *skočiti / *skakati ('to leap, spring').

скважина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic скважина ('narrow cleft, chink, crevice, opening'), derived with the suffix -ина from скважня / щель (Proto-Slavic *skvažьna 'narrow opening, chink, pore'). Today it is most familiar in замочная скважина ('keyhole') and буровая скважина ('borehole, well').

сквер.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century directly from English square, specifically referring to a landscaped London-style garden square enclosed by railings or trees among city streets.

history.meaning: small public park or garden square

сквер.notes: In Russian площадь is a paved civic square, whereas сквер is a planted green garden square with benches and paths.

сквозняк.etymology: Noun formed with the suffix -няк from сквозной ('passing right through'), derived from the preposition/adverb сквозь ('through', Old East Slavic сквозѣ, from Proto-Slavic *skvozě).

history.meaning: draft (current of air through a room)

сквозь.etymology: Shortened from older Russian сквозе and Old East Slavic сквозѣ ('through'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *skvozě ('through a narrow opening or cleft'). Etymologists connect it to a Proto-Indo-European root *skʷeǵʰ- ('to pierce, slip through twigs or gaps'). It also gave rise to Russian сквозняк ('draft of wind blowing through a room').

скидка.etymology: Formed in Russian from скинуть / скидывать ('to throw off, knock off, reduce', combining с- 'off, down' + кидать 'to throw, toss') + the noun suffix -ка: literally 'an amount knocked off the price, a price reduction'.

history.meaning: to knock off part of a price

скидка.notes: Used with the preposition **со** in the instrumental: *со скидкой* ('at a discount').

скидываться.etymology: Imperfective of скинуться ('to chip in, pool money together'), formed from с- ('together, into one pile') + кидать ('to throw, toss', Proto-Slavic *kydati) + reciprocal -ся: literally 'to toss shares together into a common pot'.

history.meaning: to chip in, pool money together

скинуться.etymology: Colloquial reflexive verb formed with -ся from скинуть ('to throw together into one pile'), composed of the prefix с- ('together') + кинуть ('to throw, toss', Proto-Slavic *kynǫti), hence 'to pool money, chip in'.

склад.etymology: Deverbal noun from складывать / сложить ('to put together, stack, store', Old East Slavic съкласти / съкладъ), built from с- ('together') and класть ('to lay, put, stack', Proto-Slavic *klasti, stem *klad-). Denotes both a place where goods are stacked and stored ('warehouse, depot') and a mental or physical disposition ('turn of mind', склад ума).

складной.etymology: Derived in Russian from складывать / сложить ('to fold, put together', noun склад 'fold, arrangement') with the adjectival suffix -ной: 'designed to fold up, collapsible' (складной стул 'folding chair', складной нож 'pocketknife', складной метр 'folding rule').

складываться.etymology: Formed by adding the intransitive/middle postfix -ся to складывать ('to fold, put together', imperfective of сложить, from с- 'together' + класть 'to lay, put'): 'to fold up' or figuratively 'to take shape, work out'.

history.meaning: to fold up; to take shape

склеить.etymology: Formed with prefix с- ('together') from клеить ('to glue, paste'), derived from клей ('glue'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъlejь ('tree gum, glue').

history.meaning: to glue together, repair with glue

склон.etymology: Deverbal noun from склонить / склоняться ('to incline, slope downward'), built on prefix с- ('down') + клонить ('to bend, incline', from Proto-Slavic *kloniti).

сковорода.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сковорода ('frying pan', showing East Slavic pleophony -оро-; compare Old Church Slavonic сковрада and Polish skowroda), from Proto-Slavic *skovorda ('frying pan'). Vasmer connects the root with onomatopoeic words for sizzling and crackling over fire (compare скворчать / шкварчать 'to sizzle in fat' and шкварки 'cracklings').

сковородка.etymology: Diminutive in form (now the standard everyday word) formed with -ка from сковорода ('frying pan'), inherited from Old East Slavic сковорода, from Proto-Slavic *skovoroda ('frying pan, flat baking pan', showing East Slavic pleophony -оро- alongside Polish skowroda).

скользить.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic скользити (alongside Old East Slavic сльзъкыи 'slippery'), from Proto-Slavic *skъlziti / *slьzъkъ ('to slide, slip, glide on a smooth surface'), from an Indo-European s-mobile root *(s)h₃leyǵ- ('to slip, glide', cognate with English slide and slick and German schleichen).

скользкий.etymology: Formed with the adjective suffix -кий from the stem of скользить ('to slip, slide, glide'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *skьlzъkъ ('slippery'), from an Indo-European root with s-mobile meaning 'to slip, glide' (related to ползти 'to crawl, creep').

скользко.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicative formed with -о from скользкий ('slippery'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *skъlzъkъ, derived from *skьlznǫti / *skъlzati ('to slip, glide', from PIE *(s)kelg- 'slippery, smooth').

скользнуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective verb in -нуть from скользить ('to slip, slide, glide'), inherited from Old East Slavic скълзнути and Proto-Slavic *skъlznǫti ('to slip, glide over a smooth surface').

history.meaning: to slide → to slip, glide once

сколько.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic колико / сколько, from Proto-Slavic *koli / *koliko ('how much, how many', built on the interrogative stem *kʷo- 'who, what' + quantitative *-liko; compare Latin quantus and tālis), with initial с- generalized in Russian by analogy with столько ('so much, this much').

history.meaning: how much, how many (reshaped after столько)

сколько.notes: Governs the genitive singular with mass nouns (*сколько воды* 'how much water') and genitive plural with countable nouns (*сколько часов* 'how many hours').

скопить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- ('together') from копить ('to amass, accumulate, save up'), derived from копа ('heap, stack, shock of grain; sixty', from Proto-Slavic *kopa 'heap, pile').

скорая.etymology: Substantivized feminine adjective clipped from **скорая (медицинская) помощь** ('rapid medical aid, ambulance service'), from скорый ('fast, quick, speedy'), inherited from Old East Slavic скорыи and Proto-Slavic *skorъ ('fast, brisk').

скорее.etymology: Comparative degree formed with -ее from скорый ('quick, fast') and скоро ('quickly, soon'), from Proto-Slavic *skorъ ('fast, brisk'): means both 'more quickly, hurry up!' and 'rather, more likely' (*скорее всего* 'most likely').

скорейший.etymology: Synthetic superlative adjective formed with the suffix -ейший from скорый ('fast, quick, prompt'), inherited from Old East Slavic скорыи, from Proto-Slavic *skorъ ('fast, swift').

скорлупа.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic (with expressive prefix/s-mobile and metathesis from the root of кора 'bark, rind, crust' and лупить 'to peel, shell'), related to Proto-Slavic *skorupa ('crust, shell, shard', compare Czech skořepa, Polish skorupa).

скоро.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic скоро ('quickly, soon'), neuter short form and adverb of скорыи ('fast, brisk'), from Proto-Slavic *skorъ. In modern Russian, while быстро took over the primary sense 'fast in motion', скоро specialized mainly as 'soon, before long'.

скорость.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic скорость ('quickness, speed'), formed from скорый ('quick, fast', Proto-Slavic *skorъ) + the abstract feminine noun suffix -ость ('-ness'). Even after скорый yielded much of its everyday adjectival use to быстрый, скорость remained the standard Russian noun for physical and technical speed.

скорректировать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- from корректировать ('to correct, adjust'), borrowed from German korrigieren / Korrektur, from Latin corrigere (past participle corrēctus, 'to set straight, amend').

скорый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic скорыи ('quick, swift, prompt'), from Proto-Slavic *skorъ ('fast, brisk'), which Vasmer connects with Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- ('to leap, move briskly, cut'; compare Old High German skēri 'quick, sharp-witted').
скорый.notes: Preserved in key fixed expressions: **скорый поезд** ('express train'), **скорая помощь** ('ambulance / emergency medical service'), and **До скорого!** ('See you soon!').

скотина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic скотина ('head of cattle, livestock, beast'), formed with the singulative/collective suffix -ина from скотъ ('cattle, livestock; money', Proto-Slavic *skotъ).

скрипач.etymology: Agent noun formed with the suffix -ач from скрипка ('violin, fiddle'), derived from скрипеть ('to squeak, creak, scrape', from onomatopoeic Proto-Slavic *skripěti).

скрипеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic скрипѣти ('to creak, squeak, grate'), from Proto-Slavic *skripěti, an expressive sound-imitative root with Baltic and Germanic parallels (compare Lithuanian krykšti and English screech).

скрипка.etymology: A native Slavic formation from скрипеть 'to squeak, creak' + the instrument/noun suffix -ка. What began as an expressive word for a bowed folk fiddle became the standard literary word for the violin across East and West Slavic.

скрипнуть.etymology: Formed with the semelfactive suffix -нуть ('once') from скрипеть ('to creak, squeak, grate', Old East Slavic скрыпѣти, Proto-Slavic *skripěti / *skrypati), an expressive onomatopoeic Slavic root imitating the high-pitched friction of wood, hinges, or footsteps on snow.

скромничать.etymology: Colloquial verb formed with the behavioral suffix -ничать from скромный ('modest, unassuming').

history.meaning: to be modest, act coy or self-effacing

скромный.etymology: Borrowed in the seventeenth century via Polish skromny ('modest, frugal, restrained', compare Czech skrovný), from Proto-Slavic *skromьnъ ('cut within bounds, moderate', related to *kroma 'edge, border, slice' and *kromiti 'to trim, separate').

скрутить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- ('together') from крутить ('to twist, twirl, bind'), inherited from Old East Slavic крутити, from Proto-Slavic *krǫtiti ('to twist, turn').

history.meaning: to twist together, bind; to double someone over

скрывать.etymology: Imperfective of скрыть ('to hide, conceal, cover up'), formed from с- + крыть ('to cover', inherited from Old East Slavic крыти, from Proto-Slavic *kryti).

скрытый.etymology: Adjectival past passive participle of скрыть ('to hide, conceal'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *sъkryti (*sъ- + *kryti 'to cover').

скрыть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съкрыти ('to cover up, hide, conceal'), from Proto-Slavic *sъkryti, composed of the prefix *sъ- and *kryti ('to cover, roof', modern Russian крыть).

скрыться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed with -ся from скрыть ('to hide, cover up', from Proto-Slavic *sъkryti), meaning 'to hide oneself, disappear from view, escape'.

скудность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from скудный ('meager, scant, poor'), inherited from Old East Slavic скудьныи / Old Church Slavonic скѫдьнъ, from Proto-Slavic *skǫdъ ('scanty, insufficient').

скука.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic скука ('weariness, distress, boredom'), originally an expressive/sound-symbolic noun related to скучать and dialectal скучить / скука ('whining, pining, dreary ache', Proto-Slavic *skuka).

скупать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed from скупить ('to buy up in large quantities'), composed of the prefix с- ('together, up') + купать / купить ('to buy', from Proto-Slavic *kupiti, an early Germanic borrowing from Gothic kaupon).

скучать.etymology: Derived in Russian from скука ('boredom, dreary longing, pining'), originally an expressive East Slavic word (dial. скучать / докучать 'to pester, weary', linked by Vasmer to an onomatopoeic root *skuk- / *kuka 'pining, whining, huddling alone').

history.meaning: to miss (someone/something); to feel lonely or bored

скучать.notes: Takes по + dative when meaning 'to miss': скучать по дому ('to miss home / be homesick'), скучать по друзьям ('to miss one's friends').

скучно.etymology: Adverb and predicative short neuter of скучный ('boring, tedious, dreary'), derived from скука ('boredom, tedium, longing', related to докука and Proto-Slavic *kuka / *skǫka, originally onomatopoeic or expressive of moaning/fretting).

скучный.etymology: Formed in Russian from скука ('boredom, weariness, longing') + the adjectival suffix -ный (with к → ч before н). Vasmer connects East Slavic скука / докука with an expressive Slavic root *kuk- / *skuk- (originally 'groaning, pining, dreary fretting'; compare кукситься 'to mope').
скучный.notes: In standard Moscow pronunciation, the cluster *чн* in **скучный** and **скучно** is traditionally pronounced [шн] ([скушный], [скушна]).

rootFamily.gloss: to be bored; to miss someone

слабак.etymology: Colloquial noun formed with suffix -ак from слабый ('weak'), inherited from Old East Slavic слабыи, from Proto-Slavic *slabъ ('slack, loose, weak').

слабенький.etymology: Attenuative/affectionate diminutive adjective formed with the suffix -енький from слабый ('weak, feeble', inherited from Old East Slavic слабыи, from Proto-Slavic *slabъ).

слабительный.etymology: Adjective (often substantivized in the neuter слабительное 'laxative') formed with the suffix -тельный from слабить ('to loosen, purge the bowels'), derived from слабый ('weak, loose, slack', Proto-Slavic *slabъ).

слабо.etymology: Adverb and predicative (слабо 'weakly' / слабо 'too weak to dare, I bet you can't') formed from слабый ('weak'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *slabъ ('slack, weak').

history.meaning: weakly; (слабо) dare you, bet you can't

слабовидящий.etymology: Compound adjective/participle formed from слабо ('weakly, poorly', from Proto-Slavic *slabъ) + видящий ('seeing', present active participle of видеть 'to see', from Proto-Slavic *viděti).

слабость.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic слабость, formed with abstract suffix -ость from слабый ('weak'), from Proto-Slavic *slabostь (from *slabъ 'weak, slack').

слабый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic слабыи ('weak, slack, feeble'), from Proto-Slavic *slabъ ('slack, loose, weak'), from the Proto-Indo-European root *sleb- / *slob- ('to hang loosely, sag'), cognate with English sleep and German schlaff ('slack, limp').

слава.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic слава ('glory, fame, praise, rumour'), from Proto-Slavic *slava, a lengthened-grade noun built on the Proto-Indo-European root *ḱlew- ('to hear, be spoken of', the same root as слышать 'to hear' and слово 'word'; compare Ancient Greek κλέος 'fame, glory' and Sanskrit śrávas).

славиться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed with -ся from славить ('to praise, glorify, make famous'), inherited from Old East Slavic славити, from Proto-Slavic *slaviti, derived from *slava ('glory, fame, renown', from PIE *ḱlew- 'to hear').

славненько.etymology: Colloquial diminutive adverb formed with the suffix -енько from славный ('nice, lovely, glorious'), derived from слава ('glory, fame', Proto-Slavic *slava).

славный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic славьныи ('famous, glorious'), from Proto-Slavic *slavьnъ, derived from *slava ('fame, glory'); in colloquial Russian also weakened to 'nice, pleasant, fine'.

сладкий.etymology: Borrowed in its Church Slavonic form сладъкыи (replacing native East Slavic pleophonic солодкий, whose root survives in солод 'malt' and солодка 'licorice'), from Proto-Slavic *soldъkъ ('sweet, tasty, seasoned'), originally related to соль ('salt') and Lithuanian saldùs ('sweet', from an older sense 'well-seasoned, savoury' vs. insipid).

сладко.etymology: Adopted with the South Slavic / Church Slavonic liquid metathesis слад- (compare native East Slavic солод- in солод 'malt' and солодка 'liquorice') from Old Church Slavonic сладько ('sweetly'), the adverbial and short neuter form of сладкий ('sweet', Proto-Slavic *soldъkъ, cognate with Lithuanian saldus 'sweet' and ultimately related to соль 'salt' via the sense 'seasoned, tasty').
сладко.notes: Also used idiomatically in сладко спать ('to sleep sweetly / soundly').

сладость.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сладость ('sweetness', with non-pleophonic слад- < *sold-; compare native East Slavic солод 'malt'), formed from сладкий ('sweet', Proto-Slavic *soldъkъ).

слайсер.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century in professional restaurant and kitchen terminology from English slicer ('rotary food-slicing machine'), agent/instrument noun from slice (via Old French esclice 'splinter, slice', from Frankish *slītan 'to slit, split').

слева.etymology: Formed in East Slavic by fusing the preposition с ('from, on') with лева, the historical genitive singular short form of левый ('left', Proto-Slavic *lěvъ, cognate with Latin laevus): 'on the left, from the left'.

history.meaning: on the left, from the left

слева.notes: Distinguish static location **слева** ('on the left') from motion **налево** / **влево** ('to the left').

слегка.etymology: Adverb formed from the fusion of the preposition с ('from') with the genitive singular short form легка of лёгкий ('light, slight', from Proto-Slavic *lьgъkъ, PIE *h₁lengʷʰ-).

след.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic слѣдъ ('footprint, track, trail'), from Proto-Slavic *slědъ ('track, trace'), from Proto-Indo-European *sleydʰ- ('to slide, slip, leave a furrow', cognate with Lithuanian slysti 'to slide' and English slide).

следить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic слѣдити ('to track, follow footprints'), a denominative verb formed from слѣдъ / след ('footprint, track, trace', from Proto-Slavic *slědъ). From 'following someone's tracks', it broadened to 'to watch closely, keep an eye on, look after'.

history.meaning: to watch, follow, keep an eye on

следователь.etymology: Agent noun formed in nineteenth-century legal Russian with the suffix -тель from следовать ('to follow, investigate a trail'), derived from след ('track, trace', Proto-Slavic *slědъ), calquing French juge d'instruction / German Untersuchungsrichter.

следовать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic слѣдовати ('to follow in the tracks of'), formed from слѣдъ / след ('track, footprint, trail', Proto-Slavic *slědъ) + the verbal suffix -овать. From 'to follow a path or rule' it also developed the impersonal modal sense следует ('one ought to, it is proper to').

history.meaning: footprint, track → to follow the track

следом.etymology: Adverbialized instrumental singular of след ('footprint, track, trail', from Proto-Slavic *slědъ), literally 'by the track, in the footsteps of'.

следственный.etymology: Adjective formed with suffix -енный from следствие ('investigation, inquiry; consequence'), derived from следовать ('to follow a track, investigate'), built on след ('track, footprint, trace', Proto-Slavic *slědъ).

следствие.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic слѣдьствие ('following, consequence') and developed in Russian legal terminology from след ('track, clue') for 'official criminal investigation'.

следующий.etymology: Originally the present active participle of следовать ('to follow in the tracks of', derived from след 'footprint, track', Proto-Slavic *slědъ), fully lexicalized as the adjective meaning 'following, next'.

слеза.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сльза and Proto-Slavic *slьza ('tear, teardrop'). Nominative plural preserves ё: слёзы ('tears').
слеза.notes: Nominative plural shifts stress to the stem and vocalizes е -> ё: слёзы, genitive plural слёз.

слезть.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- ('down from, off') from лезть ('to climb, crawl'), inherited from Old East Slavic лѣзти, from Proto-Slavic *lězti ('to crawl, climb').

history.meaning: to climb down, get off; to peel off

слепо.etymology: Deadjectival adverb formed with -о from слепой ('blind'), inherited from Old East Slavic слѣпыи, from Proto-Slavic *slěpъ ('blind').

слепой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic слѣпъ, from Proto-Slavic *slěpъ ('blind'). Vasmer connects it with Baltic words such as Lithuanian slė̃pti ('to hide, conceal'), suggesting an original sense of 'hidden, darkened, veiled from sight'.

слететь.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- ('down from, off') from лететь ('to fly'), inherited from Old East Slavic летѣти, from Proto-Slavic *letěti ('to fly').

слететься.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed with the prefix с- ('together') and -ся from лететь ('to fly', Proto-Slavic *letěti), literally 'to fly together to one spot, flock together'.

слив.etymology: Deverbal noun formed by zero suffixation from слить / сливать ('to pour off, drain'), composed of the prefix с- ('off, down') + лить ('to pour', Proto-Slavic *liti).

history.meaning: to drain, pour off; (slang) to leak

слива.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic слива, from Proto-Slavic *sliva ('plum, plum tree'), named for the bluish-purple color of the fruit (from PIE *(s)līw- 'bluish, livid'; cognate with Latin līvidus 'bluish' and Old English slāh 'sloe').

сливать.etymology: Imperfective of слить ('to pour off, drain; to pour together, merge'), formed with prefix с- ('off, down; together') from ливать / лить ('to pour', Proto-Slavic *liti); in modern slang, 'to leak (info), dump, or throw a match'.

history.meaning: to drain, pour off; (slang) to dump, ditch, leak

сливки.etymology: Plural-only diminutive noun formed with the suffix -ки from сливать / слить ('to pour off, skim off the top of a liquid'), built from the prefix с- ('off, from the surface') and лить ('to pour', Proto-Slavic *liti). Literally, 'that which is skimmed or poured off the top of settled milk: cream'.

history.meaning: to pour/skim off the top → cream

сливочный.etymology: Derived in Russian from сливки ('dairy cream', plural diminutive of слив from сливать / слить 'to pour off, skim off the top': cream was traditionally skimmed or poured off the top of settled milk) with the adjectival suffix -ный (with к -> ч).

history.meaning: cream, made with cream (as in сливочное масло 'butter')

morphemes.meaning: noun suffix (-к- with fleeting о and к -> ч)

сливочный.notes: Standard in сливочное масло ('dairy butter', literally 'cream oil', distinguished from растительное масло 'vegetable oil').

слиток.etymology: Derived with the noun suffix -ок from слитый ('poured together, cast, fused'), past passive participle of слить (from с- + лить 'to pour, cast molten metal', Proto-Slavic *liti).

слить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сълити (Proto-Slavic *sъliti), formed from с- ('off from the top; or together') + лить ('to pour', Proto-Slavic *liti): 'to pour off, drain (water from boiled potatoes or pasta)' or 'to pour/merge together'.

history.meaning: to pour off; to pour together

слить.notes: Future tense inserts a fleeting о in the prefix before the zero-grade stem -ль-: я солью, ты сольёшь, они сольют; past tense слил, слила.

слиться.etymology: Reflexive form (-ся) of слить ('to pour together'), composed of the prefix с- ('together') and лить ('to pour, cast'). The base verb descends from Old East Slavic лити and Proto-Slavic *liti ('to pour, flow'), from the Proto-Indo-European root *leyH- ('to pour, flow'). Literally 'to pour into one another', it developed the figurative meaning 'to blend harmoniously into one'.

слишком.etymology: Formed in Russian by fusing the preposition с ('with') and the instrumental singular лишком of лишек ('excess, surplus, extra bit above the measure'), itself a diminutive of лихой / лишний ('excess, beyond measure', Proto-Slavic *lixъ 'left over, excessive, odd').

history.meaning: with an excess, with a bit over

слишком.notes: Written as two words (с лишком) when following a number to mean 'and a bit / and change' (три килограмма с лишком 'three kilos and a bit'), but as one word слишком before adjectives and adverbs to mean 'too' (слишком поздно 'too late').

словно.etymology: Grammaticalized in Russian as a comparative conjunction and particle from the neuter short-form adjective словно ('verbal, literal, in word only'), derived from слово ('word'), from Proto-Slavic *slovo.

слово.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic слово (old s-stem, genitive словесе; 'word, speech, discourse, lay'), from Proto-Slavic *slovo, continuing Proto-Indo-European *ḱléwos ('that which is heard, spoken word, renown', from *ḱlew- 'to hear'), directly cognate with Sanskrit śrávas and Ancient Greek κλέος.

слоган.etymology: Borrowed in the late twentieth century from English slogan, itself from Scottish Gaelic sluagh-ghairm ('battle cry of a clan or host'), compounded from sluagh ('army, host') + gairm ('cry, shout').

сложить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съложити (Proto-Slavic *sъložiti), formed from с- ('together') + ложить ('to lay, put', Proto-Slavic *ložiti): 'to put together, fold neatly (clothes or paper), stack up, or add numbers together'.

history.meaning: to fold; to stack, pack; to add up

сложиться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed with -ся from сложить ('to put together, fold, compose'), from Proto-Slavic *sъložiti (*sъ- + *ložiti 'to lay, place').

history.meaning: to take shape, work out, turn out

сложность.etymology: Formed in Russian from сложный ('complex, complicated, folded together', from сложить 'to put together, fold') + the abstract noun suffix -ость, modeled as a calque of Latin complexitas.

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

сложный.etymology: Derived from the root of сложить ('to put together, fold, compose'), built from с- ('together') + ложить / лечь ('to lay', with o-grade ablaut слог- / слож-). Literally meaning 'put together from multiple parts, composite, compound', it developed the modern sense 'complicated, complex, difficult'.

слой.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic слои (Proto-Slavic *slojь 'layer, stratum, streak in wood or stone'), an o-grade noun derived from the verbal root of стлать / слать ('to spread, lay flat', Proto-Slavic *stьlati) or *lьjati / лить ('to pour in a sheet').
слой.notes: Nominative plural has stressed ending -и: слои ('layers, coats').

сломанный.etymology: Originally the past passive participle of сломать ('to break', from с- + ломать 'to break', Proto-Slavic *lomati), used as an adjective meaning 'broken, out of order'.

сломать.etymology: Formed in Russian by adding the perfectivizing prefix с- to ломать ('to break', Proto-Slavic *lomati, iterative of *lomiti).

сломаться.etymology: Formed from сломать ('to break', combining perfective с- + ломать 'to break, fracture', Proto-Slavic *lomiti / *lamati) + the intransitive/middle suffix -ся: 'to break down, get broken, stop working'.

слон.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic слонъ, from Proto-Slavic *slonъ ('elephant'). Its deeper origin is disputed: Vasmer discusses both the medieval folk-etymological connection with слоняться / прислониться ('to lean against', reflecting the medieval bestiary belief that elephants had no knee joints and slept leaning against trees) and the hypothesis of an early borrowing from Turkic (compare Turkic arslan 'lion').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: слон

слон.notes: In Russian chess terminology, слон ('elephant') is the name of the bishop piece.

слоник.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ик from слон ('elephant'), inherited from Old East Slavic слонъ, from Proto-Slavic *slonъ ('elephant').

слопать.etymology: Colloquial perfective verb formed with the prefix с- from лопать ('to gobble, devour noisily'), an expressive/onomatopoeic verb imitating the sound of smacking lips or bursting.

слуга.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic слуга ('servant, retainer, attendant'), from Proto-Slavic *sluga (originally an abstract/collective feminine noun meaning 'service, retinue', which shifted to denote an individual male or female servant), cognate with Lithuanian slaugà ('service, care') and Old Irish slúag ('troop, host').

служба.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic служьба (and Old Church Slavonic слоужьба 'service, ministry, church service'), from Proto-Slavic *služьba, formed with the suffix *-ьba from *služiti ('to serve', Russian служить).

служебный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from служба ('service, duty, work', with mobile vowel е in *служьбьныи), inherited from Old East Slavic служьба, from Proto-Slavic *služьba (from *sluga 'servant').

служить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic служити (and Old Church Slavonic слоужити), from Proto-Slavic *služiti ('to serve'), a denominative verb formed from *sluga ('servant, attendant, retinue member', Russian слуга, with г > ж before -и-), cognate with Lithuanian slaugà ('service, care, nursing') and Old Irish slúag ('troop, host, retinue', whence English slogan).

history.meaning: to serve (in the military, civil service, church, or a role)

слух.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic слухъ and Proto-Slavic *sluxъ ('hearing, sense of hearing; rumour, report'), an o-grade noun built on the Indo-European root *ḱlew- ('to hear', cognate with слышать 'to hear', слушать 'to listen', слава 'fame, glory', and Ancient Greek kléos).

случай.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic сълучаи ('happening, chance occurrence, coincidence'), derived from сълучити сѧ (modern случиться 'to happen, come together by chance'), built on с- ('together') + лучить ('to hit a mark, meet, join', Proto-Slavic *lučiti).
случай.notes: Used in many everyday expressions: на всякий случай ('just in case'), в таком случае ('in that case').

случайно.etymology: Adverb of случайный ('accidental, chance'), formed from случай ('occurrence, chance event, occasion'), which was borrowed via Old Church Slavonic сълучаи from сълучитися / случиться ('to happen, come together by chance', related to лучить 'to hit a mark, bring together').
случайно.notes: Often used in polite questions: *Вы случайно не знаете...?* ('Do you happen to know...?').

случайность.etymology: Formed in Russian from случайный ('accidental, chance', derived from случай 'chance, incident') with the abstract-noun suffix -ость: 'a coincidence, chance occurrence, or accident'.

случайный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from случай ('occurrence, chance, case'), derived from случиться ('to happen, come to pass', built on с- + *lučiti 'to hit the mark, fall out by lot').

случаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive verb formed from случиться ('to happen, occur, come to pass'), derived from случай ('occurrence, chance', from Old Church Slavonic сълучаи, related to лучить 'to hit the mark, bring together').

случиться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сълучитися and Old Church Slavonic сълучити сѧ ('to come together, happen, occur'), formed from с- ('together') + лучить ('to hit a target, bring together, find', Proto-Slavic *lučiti, related to получить 'to receive, obtain') + -ся.

history.meaning: to meet, come to pass, happen

случиться.notes: Commonly heard in Что случилось? ('What happened? / What's wrong?').

слушание.etymology: Verbal noun formed from слушать ('to listen, hear') + the action-noun suffix -ние; from Proto-Slavic *slušati, related to *sluxъ ('hearing'). In legal usage, calqued on English/French court hearing.

слушать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic слушати, from Proto-Slavic *slušati ('to listen, pay heed'), an iterative/durative verb built on *sluxъ ('hearing, rumour'; Russian слух), from the Proto-Indo-European root *ḱlew- ('to hear'; cognate with Ancient Greek κλέος, Latin inclutus, and English listen).

cognates.meaning: to listen (from the same PIE root *ḱlew-)

слушаться.etymology: Reflexive form of слушать ('to listen', from Proto-Slavic *slušati, built on *sluxъ 'hearing' and *slyšati 'to hear', from PIE *ḱlew- 'to hear'). With the reflexive suffix -ся, слушаться developed the middle/reciprocal sense 'to heed, obey, listen to authority' (слушаться родителей).

слышать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic слышати ('to hear'), from Proto-Slavic *slyšati, an intensive/stative verb from the Proto-Indo-European root *ḱlew- ('to hear'; cognate with слух 'hearing', слава 'glory, fame', Ancient Greek κλύω 'to hear', Latin inclutus 'famous', and English loud / listen).

слышно.etymology: Impersonal predicate adverb ('it is audible, one can hear') formed from слышный ('audible'), derived from слышать ('to hear', Proto-Slavic *slyšati, from the PIE root *ḱlew- 'to hear').

history.meaning: audible → it can be heard, one can hear

слышно.notes: Takes a dative experiencer and an accusative object: *Мне вас хорошо слышно* ('I can hear you clearly').

слышный.etymology: Derived in Russian from слышать ('to hear', Old East Slavic слышати, Proto-Slavic *slyšati, a stative verb built on the root of слух 'hearing') with the adjectival suffix -ный: 'audible, able to be heard'.

rootFamily.gloss: it is audible / can be heard

слышный.notes: Most frequently used in the short forms слышен, слышна, слышно.

слюна.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic слюна ('saliva, spittle'), from Proto-Slavic *sľuna (< *slina / *sľuna, related to *slizь 'slime, mucus'), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ley- ('slimy, slippery').

слёзно.etymology: Deadjectival adverb formed with -о from слёзный ('tearful'), derived from слеза ('tear, teardrop', inherited from Old East Slavic слеза / сльза, from Proto-Slavic *slьza).

смазать.etymology: Formed from с- ('over a surface; or off') + мазать ('to smear, oil, grease, daub', Old East Slavic мазати, Proto-Slavic *mazati, related to масло 'butter, oil'): 'to oil, lubricate (hinges or a mechanism), or brush (pastry with butter or egg)'.
смазать.notes: Future tense shows з -> ж palatalization: я смажу, ты смажешь.

смазывать.etymology: Imperfective verb paired with смазать ('to grease, oil, brush with butter or glaze; to smudge'), formed from prefix с- + мазать ('to smear, anoint, coat', from Old East Slavic мазати and Proto-Slavic *mazati).

history.meaning: to coat, grease → to brush (pastry with glaze or butter), oil, lubricate

смарт-телевизор.etymology: Twenty-first-century compound formed from English smart (borrowed as смарт-) and Russian телевизор ('television set', from Greek τῆλε 'far' + Latin visor 'viewer').

смартфон.etymology: Borrowed in the early twenty-first century from English smartphone, compounded from smart ('intelligent, computerized') + phone (short for telephone, from Greek φωνή 'voice, sound').

смахнуть.etymology: Formed from с- ('off a surface') + махнуть ('to wave, sweep once', semelfactive of махать 'to wave', Proto-Slavic *maxati): 'to flick or brush off (dust, crumbs, or a teardrop) with a quick sweep of the hand or cloth'.

смежный.etymology: Adjective formed with the prefix с- ('together, sharing') and suffix -ный from межа ('boundary strip, border between fields'), from Old East Slavic межа, from Proto-Slavic *meďa (< *medjā, from PIE *médʰyos 'middle').

смекалка.etymology: Expressive Russian noun formed with the colloquial suffix -лка from смекать / смекнуть ('to figure out quickly, grasp, size up'). Vasmer connects смекать either with мекать / намекать ('to hint, surmise, think over') or by folk-etymological blending with сметка ('quick reckoning, estimate', from сметить 'to reckon, note').

смело.etymology: Adverb formed from смелый ('bold, brave, daring'), past verbal adjective in -лый of сметь ('to dare', inherited from Old East Slavic съмѣти, from Proto-Slavic *sъměti).

смелость.etymology: Derived from смелый ('bold, daring, brave') + the abstract noun suffix -ость; смелый is originally an l-participle adjective from сметь ('to dare'), from Proto-Slavic *sъměti.

смелый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic смѣлыи and Proto-Slavic *smělъ ('bold, daring, brave'), originally the past active participle in *-lъ of *směti (modern Russian сметь 'to dare, venture', cognate with Old High German gimuoan 'to strive').

смена.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from сменить ('to change, replace, relieve'), built from the prefix с- + менить ('to change, exchange', from мена 'exchange, barter', Proto-Slavic *měna, cognate with Lithuanian mainas 'exchange' and Latin mūnus). Denotes a replacement, a work or school shift, or the rising generation.

сменить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- from менить ('to change, exchange'), inherited from Old East Slavic мѣнити, from Proto-Slavic *měniti (derived from *měna 'change, exchange', PIE *mey- 'to change, exchange').

смертный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съмьртьныи ('mortal, fatal, deadly'), from Proto-Slavic *sъmьrtьnъ, relational adjective of *sъmьrtь (modern Russian смерть, 'death', from PIE *mer- 'to die').

смерть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съмьрть and Proto-Slavic *sъmьrtь ('death', literally 'a good/natural dying', formed with the prefix *sъ- 'good, own' + *mьrtь 'dying, death'), from Proto-Indo-European *mer- ('to die'), cognate with Latin mors (stem mort-), Sanskrit mṛti, and Lithuanian mirtis.

смета.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from сметать / смести ('to sweep together into one pile; to reckon up, estimate', from с- 'together' + метать 'to cast, throw' / мести 'to sweep', Proto-Slavic *sъmetati).

сметана.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sъmetana, derived from the passive participle of *sъmetati / сметать ('to sweep off, skim off the top'), referring to cream skimmed from the surface of settled milk.

сметь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic смѣти ('to dare, venture'), from Proto-Slavic *sъměti, historically a prefixed formation *sъ- + *měti ('to have mind/intent, know how').

смех.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic смѣхъ ('laughter'), from Proto-Slavic *směxъ (< *smoi-so-s), derived from the verb *smьjati sę (modern Russian смеяться, 'to laugh'), from Proto-Indo-European *smey- ('to smile, laugh').

смешать.etymology: Formed with the perfective/convergent prefix с- ('together') + мешать ('to mix, stir'), from Proto-Slavic *měšati ('to mix, knead'), iterative to *měsiti.

смешить.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *směšiti ('to make laugh'), a causative verb derived from *směxъ (Russian смех 'laughter'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *smey- ('to smile, laugh').

смешно.etymology: Formed as the short neuter and adverbial derivative in -о of смешной ('funny, laughable, ridiculous'), built on смех ('laughter', Proto-Slavic *směxъ, with х -> ш before -н-).

смешной.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic смѣшьныи, formed with suffix -ной from смех ('laughter'), from Proto-Slavic *směšьnъ (derived from *směxъ 'laughter', from *smějati sę 'to laugh').

смеяться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic смѣятися and Proto-Slavic *smьjati sę ('to laugh, smile'), from Proto-Indo-European *smey- ('to smile, laugh'), cognate with Sanskrit smáyate ('smiles'), Latvian smieties ('to laugh'), and English smile.
смеяться.notes: Takes над + instrumental when laughing at someone or something: смеяться над шуткой ('to laugh at a joke').

смирение.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic съмирѥниѥ ('humility, peaceableness, reconciliation'), verbal noun from съмирити ('to make peaceful, humble, subdue'), formed from съ- + миръ ('peace').

смириться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed with -ся from смирить ('to pacify, humble, subdue'), inherited from Old East Slavic съмирити / Old Church Slavonic съмирити, from Proto-Slavic *sъmiriti (from *mirъ 'peace').

history.meaning: to accept, come to terms with

смирно.etymology: Deadjectival adverb formed with -о from смирный ('peaceable, quiet, mild'), derived from Old East Slavic съмирьныи ('peaceful, humble', from с- + мир 'peace', Proto-Slavic *mirъ); used as the military drill command 'Attention!'.

смокинг.etymology: Borrowed in the late nineteenth century (via French smoking or German Smoking) from English smoking jacket ('short silk-lapelled evening jacket worn by gentlemen while smoking cigars'), from the gerund smoking (from Old English smocian).

смотреть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съмотрити ('to look closely, observe, consider'), from Proto-Slavic *sъmotriti, a prefixed derivative of *motriti ('to gaze, watch'; compare Lithuanian matýti 'to see'). Loss of the weak yer vowel in съ- created the initial cluster см-.

смотреться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed with -ся from смотреть ('to look, watch'), inherited from Old East Slavic смотрѣти / съмотрити, from Proto-Slavic *sъmotriti ('to look attentively, observe').

history.meaning: to look at oneself (in a mirror); to look, appear

смочь.etymology: Formed in Russian by adding the perfectivizing prefix с- to мочь ('to be able, can', Old East Slavic мочи, Proto-Slavic *mogti, cognate with English may and might).
смочь.notes: Provides the future tense for 'will be able to': я смогу, ты сможешь, они смогут; past tense смог, смогла ('managed to').

смс.etymology: Borrowed in the late 1990s from the English initialism SMS (Short Message Service), the telecommunications standard for mobile text messaging.

смущать.etymology: Adopted with the Church Slavonic consonant reflex -щ- (from Proto-Slavic *-tj-; compare native East Slavic мутить) from Old Church Slavonic съмущати ('to stir up, trouble, throw into confusion'), imperfective of съмутити / смутить, built on съ- + мутить ('to stir up sediment, make muddy or turbid', from Proto-Slavic *mǫtiti, related to мутный 'cloudy, troubled').

history.meaning: to stir up mud → to trouble, confuse

смывать.etymology: Imperfective of смыть ('to wash off, rinse away'), formed from the prefix с- ('off, away from a surface') + мыть ('to wash', Proto-Slavic *myti) + the imperfective suffix -вать.

rootFamily.gloss: to wash one's face and hands

смываться.etymology: Reflexive/passive form (-ся) of смывать ('to wash off, wash away'), formed with the prefix с- ('off, away from a surface') and the imperfective stem of мыть ('to wash'). The root descends from Proto-Slavic *myti ('to wash'), from the Proto-Indo-European root *mewH- ('wet, damp, to wash'). It is related to Russian мыло ('soap', originally 'washing agent' from *mydlo) and English mire.

смысл.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic смыслъ and Old Church Slavonic съмꙑслъ ('thought, intelligence, sense, meaning'), formed from the prefix с- / съ- ('together') and мысль ('thought', from Proto-Slavic *myslь).

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

смягчать.etymology: Formed as the imperfective counterpart of смягчить ('to soften, make gentler'), built from с- + мягкий ('soft', Proto-Slavic *mękъkъ, with гк -> гч): 'to soften (leather, wood, water, a tone, or a consonant)'.

смягчить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- from мягчить ('to make soft, soften'), derived from мягкий ('soft, tender', from Proto-Slavic *mękъkъ, PIE *menk- 'to knead, mash').

снаружи.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase с наружи ('from/on the outer surface'), built from с ('from, on') + наружа ('outer appearance, outside', itself formed from на ружу 'out into view, on the face/surface').

сначала.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase с начала ('from the beginning'), combining the preposition с ('from') + the genitive singular of начало ('beginning', from Proto-Slavic *načęlo, built on начать 'to begin').

history.meaning: at first, first; from the beginning

снег.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic снѣгъ, from Proto-Slavic *sněgъ ('snow'), from Proto-Indo-European *snóygʷʰos ('snow', o-grade of *sneygʷʰ- 'to snow'; cognate with Lithuanian sniegas, Gothic snaiws, English snow, Latin nix).

снежный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic снѣжьныи, formed with the adjective suffix -ный (with regular palatalization г → ж) from снег ('snow'), from Old East Slavic снѣгъ, Proto-Slavic *sněgъ, from Proto-Indo-European *snóygʷʰos ('snow'; cognate with English snow and German Schnee).

снизу.etymology: Formed in East Slavic by fusing the preposition с ('from') with низу, the old genitive/locative singular of низ ('bottom, lower part', Proto-Slavic *nizъ): 'from below, underneath, at the bottom'.

снимать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сънимати (Proto-Slavic *sъn-imati), the imperfective counterpart of снять ('to take off, remove'), formed from the prefix *sъn- ('down from, off') + *imati ('to take'). The original final -н of the prefix *sъn- fused with the root to create the productive Russian stem -нимать (extended by analogy to поднимать, понимать, принимать).

history.meaning: to take off (clothes); to remove; to rent (a flat); to photograph/film

сниматься.etymology: Reflexive imperfective verb formed with -ся from снимать ('to take off, remove; to photograph/film'), from Proto-Slavic *sъnьmati (*sъn- 'off, down from' + *jьmati 'to take').

history.meaning: to take off; to photograph or film
to come off; to be photographed or act in a film

снимок.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -ок from снимать / снять ('to take off, copy, photograph'), calquing French/German photographic usage ('to take an image off a subject').

сниться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed from снить ('to dream') + -ся, derived from сон (stem сн-, Old East Slavic сънъ 'sleep, dream'), from Proto-Slavic *sъnъ (< PIE *sup-no-s).

снова.etymology: Formed in East Slavic by fusing the preposition с ('from') with нова, the historical genitive singular short form of новый ('new', Proto-Slavic *novъ): literally 'from the new, afresh, anew'.

снос.etymology: Deverbal noun formed by zero suffixation from сносить / снести ('to carry down, tear down, demolish'), composed of с- ('down, away') + нести / носить ('to carry', Proto-Slavic *nesti / *nositi).

сносить.etymology: Imperfective of снести ('to carry down; to sweep away, demolish'), formed from с- ('down from, off') + носить ('to carry', inherited from Old East Slavic носити, Proto-Slavic *nositi): literally 'to take/carry down (a structure)', hence 'to demolish, pull down'.

history.meaning: to pull down, demolish; to carry down

снотворное.etymology: Substantivized neuter singular of the adjective снотворный ('sleep-inducing, soporific'), a compound calquing Latin somnifer / soporificus, formed from сон (stem сн-, 'sleep', Proto-Slavic *sъnъ) + connecting vowel -о- + -творный (from творить 'to make, produce').
